docs.title: B-01 · Pincode validator
docs.text:
Task: Create @Pincode, a Jakarta constraint for Indian pincodes (six digits, first digit 1–9), usable on fields and parameters.

Acceptance criteria - 560102 and 744101 are valid; 060102, 56010, 5601021, 56O102 are invalid. - null is valid (combine with @NotNull when required). - The error message is resolvable from a message bundle.

Hints

A @Constraint(validatedBy = …) annotation plus a ConstraintValidator<Pincode, String>; a precompiled Pattern. Ch 09.

Solution sketch 

@Documented
@Constraint(validatedBy = PincodeValidator.class)
@Target({FIELD, PARAMETER, RECORD_COMPONENT})
@Retention(RUNTIME)
public @interface Pincode {
    String message() default "{grocery.validation.pincode}";
    Class<?>[] groups() default {};
    Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}

public class PincodeValidator implements ConstraintValidator<Pincode, String> {
    private static final Pattern VALID = Pattern.compile("[1-9][0-9]{5}");
    @Override public boolean isValid(String value, ConstraintValidatorContext ctx) {
        return value == null || VALID.matcher(value).matches();
    }
}

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(strings = {"060102", "56010", "5601021", "56O102"})
void rejectsInvalid(String value) {
    assertThat(validator.validate(new Req(value))).hasSize(1);
}

docs.title: B-02 · Product API with problem details
docs.text:
Task: GET /api/v1/products/{sku} and GET /api/v1/products?category=&page=&size= backed by PostgreSQL, returning RFC 9457 problems for unknown SKUs and invalid parameters.

Acceptance criteria - Unknown SKU → 404 application/problem+json with code: PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND. - size > 100 → 400 with a field error. - Pages have a stable envelope (items, page, size, totalItems, hasNext). - @WebMvcTest for the controller; one Testcontainers test for the repository.

Hints

A @RestControllerAdvice mapping a ProductNotFoundException to ProblemDetail; @Validated on the controller with @Max(100) on size. Ch 08, 10, 15.

Solution sketch 
@RestControllerAdvice
class ErrorHandler {
    @ExceptionHandler(ProductNotFoundException.class)
    ProblemDetail notFound(ProductNotFoundException e) {
        var p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(NOT_FOUND, "Product %s not found".formatted(e.sku()));
        p.setType(URI.create("https://errors.grocery.in/product-not-found"));
        p.setProperty("code", "PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND");
        return p;
    }
}

docs.title: B-03 · Money value object
docs.text:
Task: An immutable Money in INR with addition, multiplication by quantity, comparison and JSON serialization as a decimal string.

Acceptance criteria - Money.rupees("0.10").plus(Money.rupees("0.20")) equals Money.rupees("0.30"). - Negative amounts are rejected at construction. - Scale normalized to 2 with HALF_UP. - Serialized as "578.00", not 578.0. - Money.rupees("1.0") equals Money.rupees("1.00").

Solution sketch

A record with a compact constructor normalizing scale and rejecting negatives; equality works because scale is normalized. Use @JsonValue on a toString() returning amount.toPlainString() and a @JsonCreator factory. Ch 11, 37.

docs.title: B-04 · Cart with ETags
docs.text:
Task: Cart endpoints returning a strong ETag; mutations require If-Match.

Acceptance criteria - GET /carts/{id} returns ETag: "3" (the version). - POST /carts/{id}/items without If-Match → 428; stale → 412; current → 200 with a new ETag. - Concurrent updates with the same ETag: exactly one succeeds. - Cart invariants (≤ 50 lines, 1–20 per line) tested without Spring.

Hints

JPA @Version as the ETag source; compare before mutating and let optimistic locking catch the race. Ch 08, 16, 37.

Solution sketch 

@PostMapping("/{id}/items")
ResponseEntity<CartView> add(@PathVariable UUID id,
                             @RequestHeader(value = HttpHeaders.IF_MATCH, required = false) String ifMatch,
                             @Valid @RequestBody AddItem req) {
    if (ifMatch == null) throw new PreconditionRequiredException();
    CartView view = delegate.addItem(id, parseVersion(ifMatch), req);   // throws StaleVersion → 412
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag("\"" + view.version() + "\"").body(view);
}
The concurrency test submits two updates with the same version on virtual threads and asserts one 200 and one 412.

docs.title: B-05 · Idempotent order creation
docs.text:
Task: POST /orders requires an Idempotency-Key; repeated requests return the original response without creating a second order.

Acceptance criteria - Same key + same body → same response, one order row. - Same key + different body → 422 IDEMPOTENCY_KEY_REUSED. - Concurrent duplicates → one order. - Keys expire after 24 h.

Hints

A table idempotency_record(key primary key, request_hash, response, created_at); insert first in the transaction so a concurrent duplicate hits the unique key. Ch 04.

docs.title: B-06 · Cached pricing with fail-open
docs.text:
Task: Cache priceFor(sku, pincode) in Redis with a 2-minute jittered TTL; Redis failures must not fail requests.

Acceptance criteria - Second call hits the cache (repository spy called once). - Different pincodes are different keys. - Stopping Redis: calls still succeed; grocery.cache.errors increments. - Evicting after a price change happens after commit.

Solution sketch

@Cacheable(cacheNames = "price", key = "#sku + '|' + #pincode"); a CachingConfigurer returning a CacheErrorHandler that logs and meters; eviction via @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT). Ch 21.

docs.title: B-07 · Resilient HTTP client
docs.text:
Task: An inventory client via an HTTP interface with 400 ms read timeout, one jittered retry for timeouts, a circuit breaker, and a fallback for shelf-stable items.

Acceptance criteria - WireMock delay of 2 s → call returns within 1 s with a DependencyException (perishable) or the fallback (shelf-stable). - 404 → Optional.empty(), not an exception. - After 20 failures the breaker is OPEN and calls return in < 50 ms. - No retry on 4xx.

Hints

Configure the request factory timeouts; @Retry wrapping @CircuitBreaker; ignore domain exceptions in the breaker. Ch 19, 26, 28.

docs.title: B-08 · Outbox and relay
docs.text:
Task: Implement the outbox table, a MANDATORY writer, and a polling relay using SKIP LOCKED.

Acceptance criteria - Writing outside a transaction throws. - A failure after both inserts leaves neither the order nor the outbox row. - Two relay instances never publish the same row concurrently. - A broker outage leaves rows pending; they publish on recovery. - grocery.outbox.pending gauge exposed.

Solution sketch 

select id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, headers
from outbox where sent_at is null
order by id limit 200
for update skip locked;
Publish each row, get() the send future with a timeout, mark sent; stop the batch on the first failure to preserve per-aggregate order. Ch 23, 36.

docs.title: B-09 · Idempotent Kafka consumer
docs.text:
Task: An inventory consumer for OrderPlaced that reserves stock exactly once per event, with DLT for malformed messages.

Acceptance criteria - The same event delivered twice → one reservation (Testcontainers Kafka). - Malformed JSON → DLT, partition continues. - Transient DB failure → retried with back-off. - Inbox rows older than 7 days are cleaned up.

Hints

Inbox insert in the same transaction as the reservation; ErrorHandlingDeserializer + DefaultErrorHandler with non-retryable classification. Ch 23.

docs.title: B-10 · Query-count-guarded order history
docs.text:
Task: GET /customers/{id}/orders returns 20 orders with lines and product names in at most 2 queries, with p95 < 300 ms at 150 req/s.

Acceptance criteria - Query-count test asserts ≤ 2 selects. - Composite index verified with EXPLAIN in a test on Testcontainers. - k6 open-model test with a p95 threshold.

Solution sketch

A DTO projection or @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"lines"}) with keyset pagination on (customer_id, placed_at desc); Hibernate statistics or a datasource proxy counting statements. Ch 13, 34.

docs.title: B-11 · Restartable batch job
docs.text:
Task: A catalog CSV import job with skips (≤ 100), a rejects file, and restart from the failure point.

Acceptance criteria - 10,000 rows with 25 malformed → COMPLETED, 25 in the rejects file with reasons. - Injected failure at row 6,000, then restart with the same parameters → exactly 10,000 rows, no duplicates. - More than 100 bad rows → FAILED with a clear exit status.

Hints

faultTolerant().skip(...).skipLimit(100), a SkipListener writing rejects, idempotent upsert writer, named reader. Ch 33.

docs.title: B-12 · Ownership authorization
docs.text:
Task: Customers can read only their own orders; ops staff can read any; sellers only orders containing their products.

Acceptance criteria - A parameterized access-matrix test covering anonymous (401), other customer (403 or 404), owner (200), ops (200), seller with and without items (200/403). - The check is enforced in one reusable AuthorizationManager or query scope.

Solution sketch

Owner-scoped queries for customers (findByRefAndCustomerId), an AuthorizationManager for sellers checking line ownership, hasRole('OPS') bypass, and the matrix test as the executable policy. Ch 17, 39.

docs.title: B-13 · Checkout saga
docs.text:
Task: Implement an orchestrated saga: reserve stock → authorize payment → confirm, with compensations and deadlines.

Acceptance criteria - Happy path → saga COMPLETED, order PAID. - Payment failure → stock released, order CANCELLED, saga COMPENSATED. - Duplicate failure event → exactly one release command. - PaymentAuthorized before StockReserved → ignored, counted. - Deadline passed → compensation; repeated compensation failure → STUCK + alert. - Late PaymentAuthorized after compensation → void issued.

Hints

Saga table with a version column; guarded transitions; commands via the outbox; a ShedLock-protected sweeper; a controllable Clock. Ch 36.

Solution sketch

See Chapter 36 §5.3 for the state machine and §6.5 for the test suite; the late-authorization case is an extra handler that, when the saga is terminal, emits VoidPaymentCommand instead of transitioning.

docs.title: B-14 · Tenant leak suite
docs.text:
Task: Add tenancy to two services and a reflective leak suite.

Acceptance criteria - Every repository find* method with no parameters returns only the current tenant's rows. - A native query is still filtered (RLS). - A pooled connection used for tenant A then B reports B's setting. - @Async and Kafka paths keep the tenant. - Missing tenant → exception, zero rows.

Hints

@TenantId, forced RLS with with check, TaskDecorator, Kafka header, and reflection over CrudRepository beans. Ch 38.

docs.title: B-15 · Platform starter
docs.text:
Task: Build grocery-platform-web-spring-boot-starter providing the correlation filter and problem-details handler.

Acceptance criteria - Both beans are present by default in a servlet app and absent in a non-web app. - Each backs off when the user defines their own. - Disabled by grocery.web.enabled=false. - Works without Micrometer Tracing on the classpath (FilteredClassLoader). - Invalid property fails with a message naming it. - IDE metadata generated.

Solution sketch

Chapter 41 §4.2–§5.5: @AutoConfiguration, compileOnly dependencies, imports file, @ConditionalOnMissingBean everywhere, ApplicationContextRunner tests.

docs.title: B-16 · Load test and fix
docs.text:
Task: Given a deliberately slow service (N+1, missing index, DEBUG string concatenation, remote call inside a transaction), find and fix the bottlenecks.

Acceptance criteria - An open-model k6 test with thresholds that fails before and passes after. - A wall-clock profile before and after, with the findings explained. - Each fix accompanied by a guard (query-count test, index check, ArchUnit rule for transactions).

Hints

Measure first; fix the widest frame; re-measure. None of the fixes is a JVM flag. Ch 34.

docs.title: B-17 · Upgrade a service
docs.text:
Task: Upgrade one capstone service from Boot 3.5 to 4.x using the Chapter 42 process.

Acceptance criteria - Deprecations at zero before the version change. - OpenRewrite patch attached and reviewed. - Properties migrator output resolved, then removed. - Golden-file, access-matrix and contract tests unchanged. - Cross-version Kafka and cache compatibility tests pass. - Performance within 10% of baseline. - A short retrospective: what broke, what the tests caught, what they missed.

docs.title: B-18 · Design review and ADR
docs.text:
Task: Review a colleague's RFC proposing to replace the polling outbox with Debezium CDC for all services.

Acceptance criteria - Written review with labelled comments (blocking/suggestion/question). - Identification of the replication-slot risk and required safeguards. - A recommendation with conditions (which services, triggers, prerequisites). - An ADR recording the decision with a revisit trigger.

What a strong answer includes

Supports CDC for high-volume services only; requires slot-lag and WAL alerts, max_slot_wal_keep_size, a runbook and a staging downtime test; keeps polling as the default; records the decision with a trigger (events/s or latency) and an owner. Ch 36, 43.

A Interview Bank · C Annotation Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Appendix C · Annotation Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
Want examples?

This page is the one-line lookup. The Annotations tab has every annotation with a grocery-platform example, its package, status and pitfalls — plus the full Outdated → Replacement list.

The annotations used throughout the handbook, grouped by area, with what each does, the pitfall that matters, and where it's explained. Proxy-based annotations are marked (proxy) — they need calls to go through the Spring proxy: public methods, no self-invocation (Chapter 04).

docs.title: C.1 Core container
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @Component / @Service / @Repository / @Controller Register a bean via scanning @Repository also translates persistence exceptions 02 @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) Declare @Bean methods Use false unless beans call each other's methods 02 @Bean Define a bean from a method static for BeanFactoryPostProcessors 02, 03 @Primary Default among multiple candidates Hides ambiguity — prefer explicit qualifiers for important choices 02 @Qualifier Select a specific bean Keep names stable 02 @Scope("prototype") New instance per lookup Injected into a singleton only once — use ObjectProvider 02 @Lazy Create on first use Moves failures from startup to runtime 02, 03 @Profile Activate by profile Prefer properties for feature flags 06 @Import Include configuration classes Library code shouldn't rely on the user's component scan 41 @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy Init / destroy callbacks Run on the target, not through proxies 03 @EventListener Handle application events Runs inside the publisher's transaction 03 @TransactionalEventListener Handle events at a transaction phase (default after commit) Needs REQUIRES_NEW if it writes to the DB 03, 16 @Order Ordering of beans, filters, chains Lower value = higher precedence 17 @DependsOn Force initialization order Usually a design smell 03

docs.title: C.2 Spring Boot
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @SpringBootApplication Configuration + auto-configuration + scanning Scans only its package and below 05 @ConfigurationProperties(prefix) Typed configuration Enable via @EnableConfigurationProperties or scanning 06 @EnableConfigurationProperties Register properties classes Use in auto-configuration 06, 41 @Validated (on properties) Validate at startup Fails fast with a property name 06 @DefaultValue Default for constructor-bound properties Keeps records immutable 06, 41 @DeprecatedConfigurationProperty Mark a property deprecated with replacement Keep the old one working for a major 41 @AutoConfiguration(before/after) Auto-configuration class Never plain @Configuration 41 @ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingClass Library presence Dependencies must be optional for this to be false 41 @ConditionalOnMissingBean Back off if the user defined one Put it on every starter bean 41 @ConditionalOnBean Require another bean Order-sensitive 41 @ConditionalOnProperty Feature toggle matchIfMissing for opt-out defaults 41 @ConditionalOnWebApplication Servlet vs reactive Batch apps share platform libraries 41 @ImportRuntimeHints Native-image hints Ship with the library 29, 41 @RegisterReflectionForBinding Reflection hints for DTOs For native images 29

docs.title: C.3 AOP and cross-cutting
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @Aspect + @Around / @Before Define advice Order aspects explicitly with @Order 04 @EnableAsync + @Async (proxy) Run on an executor Unbounded default queue; no transaction or security context 25 @EnableScheduling + @Scheduled Scheduled jobs Default pool of 1; set zone; one pod via ShedLock 25 @SchedulerLock (ShedLock) Cluster-wide single execution Not idempotency 25 @EnableCaching + @Cacheable (proxy) Cache results Explicit keys with every dimension 21 @CachePut / @CacheEvict (proxy) Update / evict Evict after commit 21 @Retryable (Spring Retry or Framework 7) (proxy) Retry Idempotent operations only; one retry layer 26 @ConcurrencyLimit (Framework 7) (proxy) Semaphore bulkhead Verify for your version 26 @CircuitBreaker / @Retry / @Bulkhead / @RateLimiter (Resilience4j) (proxy) Resilience Retry must wrap the breaker; ignore business exceptions 26 @Observed (proxy) Metrics + span Needs annotation support enabled 27 @Timed / @Counted (proxy) Metrics Low-cardinality tags only 27 @Idempotent (platform) (proxy) Idempotency keys Store key + result atomically 04 @Audited (platform) (proxy) Audit trail Record failures too; hashes, not values 39

docs.title: C.4 Web (MVC and WebFlux)
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @RestController Controller with serialized responses Return DTOs, not entities 08 @RequestMapping / @GetMapping / @PostMapping… Map requests Framework 7 adds a version attribute (verify) 08, 20 @PathVariable / @RequestParam Bind path / query Validate them (@Validated on the class) 08, 09 @RequestBody Bind the body byte[] for webhook signature verification 18 @RequestHeader Bind a header If-Match, Idempotency-Key 08, 04 @ResponseStatus Fixed status Prefer ResponseEntity for Location/ETag 08 @RestControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler Central error handling Doesn't see filter exceptions 10 @CrossOrigin CORS per controller Configure CORS through Security instead 17 @HttpExchange / @GetExchange… Declarative HTTP clients Build from Boot's RestClient.Builder 19 @ImportHttpServices (Boot 4) Register HTTP interface groups Verify for your version 19 @Operation / @Tag / @Schema (springdoc) OpenAPI documentation Reference the shared Problem schema 20

docs.title: C.5 Validation
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @Valid Cascade validation Needed on request bodies and nested objects 09 @Validated Enable method validation; groups On the class for parameter constraints 09 @NotNull / @NotBlank / @NotEmpty Presence @NotBlank for strings 09 @Size / @Min / @Max / @Positive Bounds Bound page sizes and batch sizes 09, 20 @Pattern / @Email Format Precompile in custom validators 09 @Constraint Custom constraint @Pincode, @IndianMobile, @Gstin 09

docs.title: C.6 JSON (Jackson)
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @JsonProperty Rename a field Renames are breaking changes 11 @JsonIgnore / @JsonIgnoreProperties Exclude Prefer separate DTOs 11 @JsonInclude(NON_NULL) Omit nulls Be consistent platform-wide 11 @JsonFormat Date/number format Prefer global ISO-8601 config 11 @JsonValue / @JsonCreator Value-object serialization For Money, ids 11, 37 @JsonTypeInfo / @JsonSubTypes Polymorphism Never default typing; allow-list subtypes 11 @JsonComponent (Boot 3) Register serializers Renamed in Boot 4 (verify) 11

docs.title: C.7 Data and transactions
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @Transactional (proxy) Transaction boundary Services only; no remote calls inside; checked exceptions don't roll back 16 @Transactional(readOnly = true) Read-only hint Enables optimizations; not a security control 16 propagation = REQUIRES_NEW Independent transaction Holds two connections 16 propagation = MANDATORY Must run inside a transaction Use for outbox writes 36 @Entity / @Table / @Id JPA mapping Keep entities out of the web layer 13 @Version Optimistic locking Source for ETags 13, 16 @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) Relationships Default EAGER on @ManyToOne — set LAZY 13 @EntityGraph Fetch plan per query N+1 fix 13 @Query Custom JPQL/SQL Native queries bypass Hibernate filters 13, 38 @Modifying Update/delete queries Clears nothing automatically — mind the persistence context 13 @TenantId (Hibernate 6+) Discriminator tenancy Doesn't cover native SQL — add RLS 38 @Convert / @Converter Attribute conversion Field encryption; encrypted columns aren't searchable 39 @Document / @Indexed (Mongo) Document mapping Create indexes via migrations 22

docs.title: C.8 Security
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @EnableWebSecurity / @EnableWebFluxSecurity Security configuration Define SecurityFilterChain beans 17, 31 @EnableMethodSecurity Method security Proxy rules apply 17 @PreAuthorize / @PostAuthorize (proxy) Method authorization Delegate complex rules to a bean 17 @AuthenticationPrincipal Inject the principal Jwt for resource servers 18 @WithMockUser / @WithUserDetails Test security Test anonymous, wrong role, wrong owner 17

docs.title: C.9 Messaging
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @KafkaListener Consume Kafka Idempotent handlers; concurrency ≤ partitions 23 @RetryableTopic + @DltHandler Non-blocking retries Loses ordering 23 @RabbitListener Consume RabbitMQ Don't requeue blindly 24 @JmsListener Consume JMS Idempotent by business key 24 @PulsarListener Consume Pulsar Choose the subscription type 24 @MessageMapping / @SendToUser STOMP over WebSocket Broker relay for multiple pods 32 @ApplicationModuleListener (Modulith) Reliable module events Monitor incomplete publications 37

docs.title: C.10 GraphQL, gRPC, batch, AI
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @QueryMapping / @MutationMapping GraphQL root fields Enforce ownership in resolvers 32 @SchemaMapping Field resolver N+1 across the network 32 @BatchMapping Batched field resolver Test call counts 32 @GrpcService gRPC service Starter-dependent import (verify) 32 @StepScope / @JobScope Late-bound batch beans Needed for job parameters in readers 33 @Tool / @ToolParam (Spring AI) Expose a tool to a model Identity from the session, never parameters 40

docs.title: C.11 Actuator and observability
docs.text: Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @Endpoint(id) + @ReadOperation Custom Actuator endpoint Secure it; management port 27, 41 @Selector Path segment in an endpoint e.g. /actuator/platform/{code} 41 @WriteOperation Mutating endpoint Audit it 41

docs.title: C.12 Testing
docs.text:
Annotation Purpose Pitfall Ch @SpringBootTest Full context Share contexts; avoid per-class variations 15 @WebMvcTest / @WebFluxTest Web slice Import your security config 15, 17 @DataJpaTest / @JdbcTest Data slice Use real PostgreSQL via Testcontainers 15 @JsonTest JSON slice Golden files 11 @RestClientTest Client slice MockRestServiceServer 19 @GraphQlTest GraphQL slice Assert batch counts 32 @MockitoBean / @MockitoSpyBean Replace/spy beans Replaces @MockBean (removed in Boot 4) 15 @ServiceConnection Wire Testcontainers Declare containers as shared beans 15, 28 @DynamicPropertySource Dynamic properties For services without connection details 15 @TestConfiguration Test-only beans Shared containers config 15, 28 @SpringBatchTest Batch utilities Test restart explicitly 33 @ApplicationModuleTest Modulith module test Bootstraps one module 37 @AnalyzeClasses + @ArchTest ArchUnit rules Freeze for legacy 28, 37 @Tag Test groups Separate nightly suites (ai-eval, e2e) 28, 40

B Coding Exercises · D Properties Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Appendix D · Properties Cheat Sheet
docs.text:
The configuration properties used across the handbook, grouped by area, with the production value the platform uses and the reason. Defaults are Boot's unless noted.

Verify names for your version

Property names occasionally change between Boot releases (the properties migrator reports them — Chapter 42). Values here are the platform's choices, not universal truths: derive yours from measurements (Chapter 34).

docs.title: D.1 Application and lifecycle
docs.text:
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service                       # used in logs, metrics, tracing
  main:
    banner-mode: off
    lazy-initialization: false                # keep failures at startup (Ch 03)
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s           # < pod grace period (Ch 03, 30)
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true                           # Java 21+; add bulkheads (Ch 25)
server:
  port: 8080
  shutdown: graceful                          # default since 3.4
  error:
    include-stacktrace: never                 # never leak internals (Ch 10, 39)
    include-message: never
  tomcat:
    max-http-form-post-size: 256KB
    connection-timeout: 5s
Property Platform value Why Ch spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase 25s Must fit inside terminationGracePeriodSeconds 03, 30 spring.threads.virtual.enabled true Blocking becomes cheap; downstream limits matter 25 server.shutdown graceful Drain in-flight requests 03 server.error.include-* never No stack traces or messages in responses 10

docs.title: D.2 Configuration
docs.text:
spring:
  config:
    import:
      - optional:file:/etc/grocery/application.yml          # ConfigMap (Ch 06, 30)

docs.title: D.6 Data

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db-rw:5432/orders
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20                     # from Little's law + DB budget (Ch 12)
      minimum-idle: 20
      connection-timeout: 2s                    # fail fast on exhaustion
      max-lifetime: 30m                         # below DB/LB idle limits
      leak-detection-threshold: 20s
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false                         # always (Ch 13)
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate                        # schema via Flyway only (Ch 14)
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
        default_batch_fetch_size: 50            # softens N+1
        query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch: true
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    baseline-on-migrate: false
  transaction:
    default-timeout: 10s                        # bound long transactions (Ch 16)
Property Platform value Why Ch hikari.maximum-pool-size 20 × pods × services must fit max_connections 12, 30 hikari.connection-timeout 2s Pool exhaustion becomes a fast, visible error 12 jpa.open-in-view false No lazy loading in the web layer 13 hibernate.ddl-auto validate Migrations own the schema 14 hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size 50 N+1 safety net, not a fix 13 spring.transaction.default-timeout 10s No unbounded transactions 16

docs.title: D.8 Kafka
docs.text:
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 10
        compression.type: lz4
    consumer:
      group-id: ${spring.application.name}
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false
      max-poll-records: 100
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer

        max.poll.interval.ms: 300000
    listener:
      ack-mode: batch
      concurrency: 3                            # ≤ partitions
      observation-enabled: true
    template:
      observation-enabled: true
    admin:
      auto-create: false                        # topics are infrastructure

docs.title: Appendix E · Spring Boot 3.5 vs 4.x Matrix
docs.text:
A consolidated view of the "Boot 3 vs 4" sections from every chapter, for planning an upgrade (Chapter 42) or answering "what changed?" quickly.

Verify before acting

Boot 4 and the Spring portfolio released alongside it (Framework 7, Security 7, Data, Batch, Cloud, AI) continued to evolve after much of this handbook was written. Items marked (verify) in the chapters are marked here too. Treat this matrix as a map of where to look, and confirm exact class names, packages, properties and defaults in the official migration guide and release notes for the versions you target.

docs.title: E.11 The upgrade order that works
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["On 3.5: fix deprecations,<br/>@MockBean → @MockitoBean,<br/>lambda Security DSL,<br/>RestTemplate → RestClient"] --> B[Platform starters + BOM on 4.x]
    B --> C[Pilot service:<br/>OpenRewrite + properties migrator]
    C --> D[Behaviour gates:<br/>golden files, access matrix,<br/>contracts, performance]
    D --> E["Waves; core services last;<br/>versioned cache namespaces;<br/>cross-version payload tests"]
    E --> F["Then adopt new features separately:<br/>API versioning, HTTP service groups,<br/>@Retryable, BeanRegistrar"]

The left-most box is where most of the work belongs: everything that can be done on 3.5 should be done on 3.5, so the version change itself is small, mechanical and easy to review.

D Properties Cheat Sheet · F Troubleshooting Playbook

docs.title: Appendix F · Troubleshooting Playbook
docs.text: Symptom → likely cause → first check → fix, consolidated from every chapter's troubleshooting table. Organized by what you observe, because that's how incidents start.

docs.title: F.0 First two minutes of any incident
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Something is wrong] --> B{Did anything change?<br/>deploy annotations, config, flags}
    B -- yes --> C[Roll back by digest / revert config<br/>Ch 29, 30]
    B -- no --> D[SLO dashboard: which journey, since when?]
    D --> E[Dependency panel: which client call is slow or failing?]
    E -- a dependency --> F[Breaker state, degradation counters,<br/>their dashboards — Ch 26]
    E -- none --> G[Saturation: pool pending, GC, CPU throttling,<br/>executor queues, consumer lag]
    G --> H[Trace a slow request → logs by traceId — Ch 27]
    H --> I[Profile one pod: wall-clock 60 s — Ch 34]

Restore first, understand second. Most regressions are changes; rollback is faster than diagnosis (Chapter 43).

docs.title: A · Interview Bank
docs.text: 341 questions with answers across five experience bands, plus system design and rapid-fire revision. It draws on the interview sections of all 44 chapters, adds cross-cutting questions that span several chapters, and is organized for two audiences: candidates preparing and interviewers running structured interviews (Chapter 43).

docs.title: How the bands work
docs.text:
Band Experience What the questions test B1 · 0–2 years Junior Vocabulary and mechanics: what things are and how to use them B2 · 2–5 years Mid-level Correct use under normal conditions; common pitfalls B3 · 5–8 years Senior How things work internally; failure modes; design within a service B4 · 8–12 years Staff / lead Cross-service design, operations, trade-offs, platform decisions B5 · 12–15+ years Principal / architect Strategy, organization, risk, and when not to use something System Design B3–B5 Grocery-domain design problems with model answers Rapid Fire All One-line answers for last-minute revision

Bands describe depth of reasoning, not years alone. A strong B2 candidate who explains why @Transactional fails on self-invocation, and what the proxy is doing, is showing B3 reasoning.

docs.title: For candidates
docs.text:
1. Read your band and the one above it. Interviews usually probe one level higher than the role to find the ceiling.
  2. Answer aloud before expanding the answer. The short answers here are deliberately short — a real answer adds an example from your own work.
  3. For every "how does X work?", be ready for "what happens when it fails?" — that follow-up separates bands more than any other.
  4. Build the capstone milestones (Chapter 44). A design question answered with "here's what I built and what broke" is far stronger than a textbook answer.

docs.title: For interviewers
docs.text:
Stage Suggested use Phone screen 4–6 questions from the candidate's band, across different chapters Technical depth Pick one domain, start one band below the role and follow the candidate upward System design One problem from the system-design page, scored with the rubric in Chapter 43 Rapid fire Warm-up or calibration only — never as a pass/fail filter

Follow the answer, not the script. The best signal comes from the second and third follow-up questions, which is why each answer here names the chapter where the deeper material lives.

docs.title: Answer format
docs.text:
Each question uses a collapsible block with a short answer — the core of what a good response contains — and a chapter reference for depth:

B2 · Example: why does @Transactional not work on a private method?

Short answer: Spring applies transactions through a proxy; calls to private methods (and self-invocations) don't pass through the proxy, so no transaction starts. See Chapters 04, 16.

Appendices · B1 · 0–2 years

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 Years
docs.text: Vocabulary and mechanics. A strong B1 candidate knows what each piece is, can use it correctly in a simple case, and knows where to look when it doesn't work.

docs.title: Java and build
docs.text:
B1 · What is a Spring Boot executable JAR?

Short answer: A JAR containing your classes, all dependencies under BOOT-INF/lib, and a launcher that sets up the classpath and calls your main method — runnable with java -jar. Ch 01, 29.

B1 · What does a BOM do in a Gradle or Maven build?

Short answer: It pins versions for a set of related dependencies so you declare them without versions and get a tested, compatible combination. Ch 01.

B1 · What is a Java record, and where is it useful in Spring applications?

Short answer: An immutable data carrier with generated constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Ideal for DTOs, configuration properties, events and value objects. Ch 01, 06, 37.

B1 · Why use BigDecimal for money?

Short answer: double cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so sums drift (₹0.1 + ₹0.2 ≠ ₹0.3). BigDecimal gives exact decimal arithmetic with explicit rounding. Ch 01, 11.

docs.title: Spring core
docs.text:
B1 · What is dependency injection?

Short answer: Objects receive their collaborators from the container instead of creating them, which makes code loosely coupled and testable. Ch 02.

B1 · Why prefer constructor injection?

Short answer: Dependencies are explicit and final, objects are never half-initialized, and tests can construct the class without Spring. Ch 02.

B1 · What is a bean?

Short answer: An object whose lifecycle is managed by the Spring container — created, wired, and destroyed by it. Ch 02.

B1 · What's the difference between @Component, @Service and @Repository?

Short answer: All register beans through scanning; @Service and @Repository communicate intent, and @Repository also enables persistence exception translation. Ch 02, 12.

B1 · What is the default bean scope?

Short answer: Singleton — one instance per application context. Singletons must therefore be stateless or thread-safe. Ch 02.

B1 · What does @PostConstruct do?

Short answer: Runs a method after dependencies are injected, for initialization that needs them. Ch 03.

B1 · What is AOP used for in Spring?

Short answer: Applying cross-cutting behaviour — transactions, security, caching, retries, logging — around method calls without changing the methods. Ch 04.

docs.title: Spring Boot fundamentals
docs.text:
B1 · What does @SpringBootApplication combine?

Short answer: @Configuration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan from the class's package downwards. Ch 05.

B1 · What is auto-configuration?

Short answer: Boot configures beans automatically based on what's on the classpath and in properties, and backs off when you define your own. Ch 05, 41.

B1 · What is a starter?

Short answer: A dependency that brings in a coherent set of libraries (and their auto-configuration) for a capability, such as spring-boot-starter-web. Ch 05, 41.

docs.title: Configuration and logging
docs.text:
B1 · How do profiles work?

Short answer: Named sets of configuration (application-prod.yml) activated with spring.profiles.active, letting the same artifact run differently per environment. Ch 06.

B1 · Why use @ConfigurationProperties instead of @Value?

Short answer: Typed, grouped, validated configuration with IDE metadata, rather than scattered string lookups. Ch 06.

B1 · Where should secrets like database passwords come from?

Short answer: A secret manager, mounted as files and read as a config tree — never committed to Git or baked into images. Ch 06, 39.

B1 · Why use parameterized log messages?

Short answer: log.debug("Order {}", ref) avoids building the string when the level is disabled; concatenation always pays the cost. Ch 07, 34.

B1 · Why should logs be structured (JSON) in production?

Short answer: Log platforms can index and search fields like traceId, tenantId and orderRef reliably, instead of parsing free text. Ch 07.

docs.title: Web layer
docs.text:
B1 · @Controller vs @RestController?

Short answer: @RestController adds @ResponseBody to every method, so return values are serialized (usually to JSON) rather than resolved as views. Ch 08.

B1 · Which status code should creating a resource return?

Short answer: 201 Created with a Location header pointing at the new resource. Ch 08.

B1 · @PathVariable vs @RequestParam?

Short answer: Path variables identify a resource (/orders/{ref}); request parameters filter, sort or paginate (?page=0&size=20). Ch 08.

B1 · How do you validate a request body?

Short answer: Add Jakarta constraints to the DTO (@NotBlank, @Size, @Min) and annotate the parameter with @Valid. Ch 09.

B1 · What is a problem-details response?

Short answer: A standard error body (RFC 9457) with type, title, status, detail and instance, which Spring supports via ProblemDetail. Ch 10.

B1 · Why shouldn't you return 200 with an error in the body?

Short answer: Clients, caches, monitoring and retries all key off status codes; hiding failures in a 200 breaks them. Ch 10, 20.

B1 · Why not expose JPA entities directly in API responses?

Short answer: It couples the API to the database schema, risks lazy-loading errors and leaks internal fields. Use DTOs. Ch 11, 13.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
B1 · What does a connection pool do?

Short answer: Reuses database connections instead of opening one per request, which is expensive. HikariCP is Boot's default. Ch 12.

B1 · What is SQL injection and how do you prevent it?

Short answer: User input interpreted as SQL. Prevent it with parameterized queries — never string concatenation. Ch 12, 39.

B1 · What is the N+1 problem?

Short answer: Loading a list with one query, then issuing one more query per item for a relationship — 1 + N queries instead of one or two. Ch 13.

B1 · Why use Flyway or Liquibase instead of ddl-auto=update?

Short answer: Versioned, reviewed, repeatable migrations applied the same way in every environment, instead of unpredictable schema changes generated at startup. Ch 14.

B1 · What does @Transactional do?

Short answer: Runs the method in a database transaction — commit on success, rollback on (unchecked) exceptions. Ch 16.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
B1 · Authentication vs authorization?

Short answer: Authentication establishes who you are; authorization decides what you may do. Ch 17.

B1 · 401 vs 403?

Short answer: 401: not authenticated (missing or invalid credentials). 403: authenticated but not allowed. Ch 17.

B1 · How should passwords be stored?

Short answer: Hashed with a slow, salted algorithm such as BCrypt or Argon2 via DelegatingPasswordEncoder — never plaintext or plain hashes. Ch 17.

B1 · What is a JWT, and is it encrypted?

Short answer: A signed token with a header, claims and signature. It is signed, not encrypted — anyone can read the claims, so no secrets or PII belong in it. Ch 18.

B1 · Why should the server compute order totals rather than trust the client?

Short answer: Anything sent by a client can be modified. Prices, discounts and totals must come from authoritative server-side data. Ch 39.

docs.title: HTTP clients, APIs, caching
docs.text:
B1 · Which HTTP client should new Spring code use?

Short answer: RestClient (or a declarative HTTP interface backed by it) for synchronous calls; WebClient for reactive. RestTemplate is in maintenance. Ch 19.

B1 · Why must every outbound HTTP call have a timeout?

Short answer: Without one, a slow dependency holds threads and connections indefinitely and can take your service down. Ch 19, 26.

B1 · What does @Cacheable do?

Short answer: Returns a cached result when the key is present; otherwise calls the method and stores the result. Requires @EnableCaching. Ch 21.

B1 · What's a backward-compatible API change?

Short answer: Adding an optional request field, a response field, or a new endpoint — existing clients keep working. Ch 20.

docs.title: Messaging and async
docs.text:
B1 · What is a Kafka topic, partition and consumer group?

Short answer: A topic is a named log split into ordered partitions; each partition is read by one consumer per group; each group gets every message. Ch 23.

B1 · What delivery guarantee does Kafka provide by default?

Short answer: At-least-once — messages may be redelivered, so consumers must be idempotent. Ch 23.

B1 · How is RabbitMQ different from Kafka?

Short answer: RabbitMQ is a queue with flexible routing — messages are removed once acknowledged. Kafka is a retained log — consumers track offsets and can replay. Ch 24.

B1 · What does @Async do?

Short answer: Runs the method on another thread from an executor, returning immediately. Requires @EnableAsync and a call through the proxy. Ch 25.

B1 · fixedDelay vs fixedRate in @Scheduled?

Short answer: fixedDelay waits after the previous run finishes (no overlap); fixedRate starts on a fixed schedule regardless of duration. Ch 25.

docs.title: Testing, packaging, operations
docs.text:
B1 · Unit test vs integration test?

Short answer: A unit test checks one class in isolation, fast and without infrastructure; an integration test checks components working together with real infrastructure. Ch 15, 28.

B1 · What is @WebMvcTest?

Short answer: A test slice loading only the web layer — controllers, advice, converters — with collaborators mocked. Ch 15.

B1 · Why use Testcontainers instead of H2?

Short answer: It runs the real database in Docker, so SQL, types and locking behave as in production. Ch 15, 28.

B1 · Why shouldn't containers run as root?

Short answer: It limits the damage of a compromise and is required by most cluster security policies. Ch 29.

B1 · Readiness vs liveness probes?

Short answer: Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether it's restarted. Liveness must not check dependencies. Ch 30.

docs.title: Observability and resilience
docs.text:
B1 · What does Spring Boot Actuator provide?

Short answer: Production endpoints: health (with probe groups), info, metrics/Prometheus, loggers, startup, env and more. Ch 27.

B1 · Why look at p99 latency rather than the average?

Short answer: Averages hide the slow tail that real users experience; p99 shows how bad it gets for 1 in 100 requests. Ch 27, 34.

B1 · What does a circuit breaker do?

Short answer: After repeated failures, it stops calling a dependency and fails fast (or falls back), then tries again later to see if it recovered. Ch 26.

B1 · When is it safe to retry a call?

Short answer: For idempotent operations failing transiently (timeouts, 5xx) — never blindly for non-idempotent writes such as payments. Ch 19, 26.

Interview Bank · B2 · 2–5 years

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 Years
docs.text: Correct use under normal conditions, and the common pitfalls. A strong B2 candidate owns features end to end and can explain why the obvious approach sometimes fails.

docs.title: Spring core and AOP
docs.text:
B2 · Why doesn't @Transactional (or @Cacheable, @Async) work on self-invocation?

Short answer: These are implemented by proxies. A call from one method to another in the same class goes through this, not the proxy, so the advice never runs. Move the method to another bean or restructure. Ch 04.

B2 · How do you resolve two beans of the same type?

Short answer: @Primary for a default, @Qualifier at the injection point, or inject a List/Map of all candidates. Ch 02.

B2 · What's the risk of injecting a prototype bean into a singleton?

Short answer: It's injected once, so the singleton always holds the same instance. Use ObjectProvider or method injection to get a new one each time. Ch 02.

B2 · Application events vs direct calls — when to use events?

Short answer: When the publisher shouldn't know its listeners (loose coupling within a service). Use @TransactionalEventListener when the reaction must happen only after commit. Ch 03.

B2 · What's the difference between @EventListener and @TransactionalEventListener?

Short answer: @EventListener runs immediately inside the publisher's transaction; @TransactionalEventListener runs at a transaction phase (default after commit), so it never reacts to rolled-back work. Ch 03, 16.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
B2 · Explain property source precedence.

Short answer: Command-line args and environment variables override profile-specific files, which override application.yml; imported config trees fit in according to import order. /actuator/env shows the effective result. Ch 06.

B2 · How do you validate configuration at startup?

Short answer: @ConfigurationProperties with @Validated and Jakarta constraints — invalid config fails the app with a message naming the property. Ch 06.

B2 · How do you change a log level at runtime?

Short answer: POST to /actuator/loggers/{name} (secured, on the management port). Ch 07, 27.

B2 · How do you get a correlation id into every log line?

Short answer: A filter sets it in the MDC per request (and clears it); the log pattern or JSON encoder includes it; tracing adds traceId/spanId automatically. Ch 07.

docs.title: Web, validation, errors, JSON
docs.text:
B2 · How do you centralize error handling?

Short answer: A @RestControllerAdvice mapping exceptions to ProblemDetail with stable error codes, plus handling for validation errors — one error contract for all endpoints. Ch 10.

B2 · How do you write a custom validation constraint?

Short answer: An annotation with @Constraint(validatedBy = …) and a ConstraintValidator implementation, e.g. @Pincode or @Gstin. Ch 09.

B2 · What are validation groups for?

Short answer: Applying different constraint sets in different contexts (create vs update) via @Validated(Create.class). Ch 09.

B2 · How do ETags prevent lost updates?

Short answer: The client sends If-Match with the version it read; the server rejects the write with 412 if the resource changed since. Ch 08, 16.

B2 · How do you make a POST idempotent?

Short answer: Require an Idempotency-Key; store the key with the result; on replay, return the stored result instead of re-executing. Ch 04.

B2 · How should money and dates be serialized in JSON?

Short answer: Money as decimal strings (or integer paise at gateways); dates as ISO-8601 with offsets. Verify with golden-file tests. Ch 11.

B2 · Why keep enums "open" in API contracts?

Short answer: So adding a value doesn't break older clients — they must tolerate unknown values rather than fail deserialization. Ch 11, 20.

docs.title: Data and transactions
docs.text:
B2 · How do you fix an N+1 query?

Short answer: Fetch joins, @EntityGraph, batch fetching, or a DTO projection — and add a query-count test so it doesn't return. Ch 13.

B2 · JpaRepository, JdbcClient or Spring Data JDBC — how do you choose?

Short answer: JPA for rich aggregates with change tracking; JDBC for simple, performance-critical or reporting queries; Spring Data JDBC for aggregate-oriented persistence without JPA's complexity. Ch 12, 13.

B2 · How should you paginate a large table?

Short answer: Offset pagination for small, shallow lists; keyset (cursor) pagination for deep or large lists, avoiding expensive offsets and counts. Ch 12, 20.

B2 · Why doesn't a checked exception roll back a transaction?

Short answer: By default only unchecked exceptions and errors trigger rollback; use rollbackFor for checked ones. Ch 16.

B2 · What does REQUIRES_NEW do, and when is it useful?

Short answer: Suspends the current transaction and starts a new one — useful for audit records that must persist even if the outer work rolls back. It holds two connections at once. Ch 16.

B2 · Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?

Short answer: Optimistic uses a version column and fails on conflict (good for low contention); pessimistic locks rows up front (SELECT … FOR UPDATE) for high-contention critical sections. Ch 16.

B2 · What's the expand/contract pattern?

Short answer: Make schema changes backward compatible in steps — add new structure, migrate and dual-write, switch reads, then remove the old — so old and new code both work during deploys. Ch 14.

docs.title: Security and tokens
docs.text:
B2 · How do you define multiple security configurations?

Short answer: Several SecurityFilterChain beans with securityMatcher and @Order; the first matching chain handles the request. Ch 17.

B2 · When is CSRF protection needed?

Short answer: When browsers send credentials automatically (cookies, Basic auth). Not for APIs authenticated by an Authorization header. Ch 17.

B2 · How do you enforce resource ownership?

Short answer: Scope queries by owner (returning 404), or use an AuthorizationManager/method security, and test with a second user. Ch 17.

B2 · Why validate the JWT audience claim?

Short answer: Otherwise a valid token issued for another API of the same issuer is accepted — a privilege escalation. Ch 18.

B2 · How does a service authenticate to another service?

Short answer: OAuth2 client credentials: a client id/secret obtains a scoped token that's cached and attached to outbound calls. Ch 18, 19.

B2 · How do you verify a webhook?

Short answer: HMAC over the raw body with the shared secret, constant-time comparison, deduplication by event id, then asynchronous processing. Ch 18.

docs.title: Clients, APIs and caching
docs.text:
B2 · What is an HTTP interface and why prefer it to Feign?

Short answer: An @HttpExchange Java interface backed by RestClient/WebClient — part of Spring Framework, sharing configuration and observability. Feign is in maintenance. Ch 19.

B2 · How do you translate downstream errors?

Short answer: A status handler at the client boundary mapping responses to domain or dependency exceptions — never forwarding raw downstream bodies. Ch 19, 10.

B2 · How do you deprecate an API version?

Short answer: Deprecation, Sunset and Link headers, usage telemetry per client, targeted outreach, brownouts, then 410 Gone. Ch 20.

B2 · How do you choose cache TTLs?

Short answer: From the business staleness budget, with jitter to avoid synchronized expiry, and shorter TTLs where invalidation could be missed. Ch 21.

B2 · What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?

Short answer: Many concurrent misses on an expired hot key hitting the source. Prevent with sync=true/locking, jittered TTLs, refresh-ahead or stale-while-revalidate. Ch 21.

B2 · Why must cache keys include every dimension?

Short answer: A key missing the customer, tenant or pincode serves one user's data to another — a correctness and security bug. Ch 21, 38.

docs.title: NoSQL, messaging, async
docs.text:
B2 · Which Redis structure for a leaderboard, a lock, a queue?

Short answer: Sorted set for leaderboards; SET NX PX with a token for locks; list or Streams for queues. Ch 22.

B2 · Filter vs query in a search request?

Short answer: Filters are boolean, cached and don't score (price, category, availability); queries compute relevance (text). Ch 22.

B2 · How do you handle a poison message in Kafka?

Short answer: ErrorHandlingDeserializer, classify non-retryable exceptions, and send them to a dead-letter topic instead of blocking the partition. Ch 23.

B2 · How do you make a Kafka consumer idempotent?

Short answer: An inbox table keyed by (consumer, eventId) written in the same transaction as the side effect, or conditional updates/upserts. Ch 23.

B2 · Blocking retries vs retry topics?

Short answer: Blocking retries preserve order but stall the partition; retry topics keep the partition moving but lose ordering — use them for commutative work. Ch 23.

B2 · Why is default-requeue-rejected: false important in RabbitMQ?

Short answer: Otherwise a failing message is requeued and redelivered in a tight loop — the classic poison-message incident. Ch 24.

B2 · What's wrong with the default task executor configuration?

Short answer: Its queue is effectively unbounded, so max-size is never reached and tasks accumulate until memory runs out. Bound the queue and set a rejection policy. Ch 25.

B2 · How do you stop a scheduled job running on every pod?

Short answer: ShedLock (a lock row), a Kubernetes CronJob, or leader election — and keep the job idempotent anyway. Ch 25.

docs.title: Resilience and observability
docs.text:
B2 · Why must the retry wrap the circuit breaker?

Short answer: So each attempt passes through the breaker and retries fail fast once it's open; reversed, retries keep hammering a dead dependency. Ch 26.

B2 · Why shouldn't business exceptions open a circuit breaker?

Short answer: They mean the dependency works; counting them (e.g. payment declines) opens the breaker on legitimate traffic. Ch 26.

B2 · What is a bulkhead?

Short answer: A cap on concurrent calls to one dependency, so it can't consume all threads or connections. Essential with virtual threads. Ch 25, 26.

B2 · Why must metric tags have low cardinality?

Short answer: Each distinct tag combination is a new time series; ids as tags explode storage and cost. High-cardinality data belongs in traces and logs. Ch 27.

B2 · How do metrics, traces and logs work together?

Short answer: Metrics detect and alert, traces show which hop is slow, logs explain the specific case — joined by traceId. Ch 27.

docs.title: Testing, packaging, Kubernetes
docs.text:
B2 · How do you keep a Spring test suite fast?

Short answer: Share contexts (consistent configuration), share containers, prefer slices and unit tests, avoid @DirtiesContext, run classes in parallel with unique data. Ch 15, 28.

B2 · How do you test an HTTP client's timeout?

Short answer: WireMock with a fixed delay (or Toxiproxy), asserting both the error mapping and that the call returned within budget. Ch 28.

B2 · Why layer a Docker image?

Short answer: Dependencies change rarely and your code often; separate layers mean a code change ships megabytes, not the whole JAR. Ch 29.

B2 · Why deploy by digest instead of tag?

Short answer: Tags are mutable; a digest identifies exact content, making promotion and rollback unambiguous. Ch 29.

B2 · Why is a preStop sleep recommended?

Short answer: Endpoint removal propagates asynchronously; a brief pause prevents traffic arriving after SIGTERM. Ch 30.

docs.title: Architecture and platform
docs.text:
B2 · Why shouldn't microservices share a database?

Short answer: It couples schemas and releases, defeating independent deployment. One writer per dataset; others get copies via events. Ch 35, 36.

B2 · What is the outbox pattern?

Short answer: Write the event into a table in the same transaction as the business change; a relay publishes it. Atomic, at-least-once, nothing lost. Ch 36.

B2 · What is an aggregate?

Short answer: A cluster of objects with one root that enforces invariants and is the transaction boundary; other aggregates are referenced by id. Ch 37.

B2 · Why must tools in an AI assistant derive identity from the session?

Short answer: Tool arguments come from model output influenced by user input; a user id parameter lets a manipulated model access other users' data. Ch 40.

B2 · Why is @ConditionalOnMissingBean important in a starter?

Short answer: It lets applications override the starter's bean; without it they must exclude the whole auto-configuration. Ch 41.

B2 · How do you prepare for a major Spring Boot upgrade?

Short answer: Fix deprecations on the current version, upgrade to its latest minor, then use OpenRewrite and the properties migrator — and verify behaviour with golden files and contract tests. Ch 42.

docs.title: Core, Boot and configuration
docs.text:
B2 · How do you run code once the application is ready to serve?

Short answer: An ApplicationRunner/CommandLineRunner (runs before readiness flips, good for warm-up) or an ApplicationReadyEvent listener (after readiness). Choose by whether traffic should wait for it. Ch 03.

B2 · What is ObjectProvider for?

Short answer: Lazy or optional injection — get a bean if available, a new prototype each call, or iterate candidates — without failing startup when it's absent. Ch 02, 41.

B2 · How do you exclude an auto-configuration?

Short answer: spring.autoconfigure.exclude or @SpringBootApplication(exclude = …). If you need it often, the starter is missing a property toggle or @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Ch 05, 41.

B2 · How do profile groups help?

Short answer: They compose several profiles under one name (prod → prod-db, prod-kafka), keeping activation simple and configuration modular. Ch 06.

B2 · How do you keep secrets out of /actuator/env output?

Short answer: Boot sanitizes keys that look like secrets; restrict the endpoint's exposure, keep it on the management port, and use show-values: never or when-authorized. Ch 06, 27.

B2 · Why mount a ConfigMap as a file rather than dozens of env vars?

Short answer: A YAML file supports maps and lists, avoids env-var name mangling, is reviewable as one unit, and triggers a rollout via a config hash. Ch 06, 30.

docs.title: Web, validation, JSON
docs.text:
B2 · How do you validate path and query parameters?

Short answer: Put constraints on the parameters and annotate the controller class with @Validated; violations produce ConstraintViolationException, which the advice maps to 400. Ch 09.

B2 · How do you return field-level validation errors in a stable format?

Short answer: Map MethodArgumentNotValidException in the advice to a problem body with an errors array of {field, code, message}, using message codes rather than raw text. Ch 09, 10.

B2 · How do you version error codes without breaking clients?

Short answer: Treat codes as a public contract: add new ones freely, never repurpose or rename existing ones, and publish a generated catalog. Ch 10, 20.

B2 · How do you customize the ObjectMapper without losing Boot's defaults?

Short answer: Use spring.jackson.* properties or a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer (or its Jackson 3 equivalent) rather than defining a new ObjectMapper bean from scratch. Ch 11.

B2 · What's the danger of @JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = false) on consumers?

Short answer: Any new field from the producer breaks deserialization; tolerant readers ignore unknown fields so producers can evolve additively. Ch 11, 23.

B2 · How do you return 201 with a Location header?

Short answer: ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(view), building the URI with ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest().path("/{ref}"). Ch 08.

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
B2 · When would you use JdbcClient over JPA in the same service?

Short answer: For reporting queries, bulk updates, hot read paths or anything where you want exact SQL and no persistence-context overhead. Ch 12.

B2 · What is @Modifying and its pitfall?

Short answer: Marks an update/delete JPQL query. It bypasses the persistence context, so loaded entities become stale unless you clear or refresh them. Ch 13.

B2 · Why set @ManyToOne(fetch = LAZY) explicitly?

Short answer: @ManyToOne defaults to eager loading, which silently adds joins or queries everywhere the entity is loaded. Ch 13.

B2 · How do batch inserts work in Hibernate?

Short answer: Set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size with ordered inserts/updates; avoid IDENTITY generation, which disables insert batching — use sequences. Ch 13.

B2 · How should a Flyway migration be written for a large table?

Short answer: Additive and backward compatible, with concurrent index creation and batched backfills, rehearsed on production-sized data. Ch 14.

B2 · What does @Transactional(readOnly = true) buy you?

Short answer: Hibernate skips dirty checking and flushes, and drivers or routing can use replicas. It isn't a security control. Ch 16.

B2 · How do you route reads to a replica?

Short answer: A routing DataSource keyed on transaction read-only status, accepting replica lag — never for reads that must see a just-committed write. Ch 12.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
B2 · How do you test a secured endpoint with a JWT?

Short answer: spring-security-test's jwt() post-processor (or mockJwt() for WebFlux) with claims and authorities, plus at least one integration test with a really signed token. Ch 18.

B2 · How do you map token claims to roles?

Short answer: A JwtAuthenticationConverter combining scope authorities with an allow-listed mapping from a roles claim to ROLE_*. Ch 18.

B2 · How do you rate-limit OTP login?

Short answer: Separate limits on OTP requests and verification attempts, per mobile and per IP, in a shared store like Redis, with lockout and alerting. Ch 17, 22.

B2 · Why store refresh tokens hashed?

Short answer: A database leak must not yield usable credentials; store a hash with family and device metadata, and rotate on use. Ch 18.

B2 · How should CORS be configured with Spring Security?

Short answer: Through http.cors(...) with a CorsConfigurationSource, listing exact origins, so preflight requests are handled before authentication. Ch 17.

docs.title: Clients, caching, NoSQL
docs.text:
B2 · How do you propagate trace context to downstream calls?

Short answer: Build clients from Boot's injected builders; Micrometer Tracing adds traceparent automatically. Add your correlation id with an interceptor. Ch 19, 27.

B2 · Why disable automatic retries in the Apache HTTP client?

Short answer: Retries are a policy decision (idempotency, budgets, one layer) made explicitly above the client, not silently inside it. Ch 19, 26.

B2 · Caffeine or Redis for a cache?

Short answer: Caffeine for tiny, hot, staleness-tolerant data per pod; Redis when consistency across pods or survival across restarts matters. Ch 21.

B2 · Should you cache null results?

Short answer: Often, briefly, to stop repeated misses for non-existent keys — with explicit eviction when the entity appears. Ch 21.

B2 · How do you warm a cache without slowing readiness too much?

Short answer: Warm only the top-N keys in a runner before readiness; fill the rest lazily or asynchronously. Ch 21, 29.

B2 · Why use StringRedisTemplate instead of a raw RedisTemplate?

Short answer: Readable string keys and values, no JDK serialization, and no class-instantiation risks from payloads. Ch 22.

docs.title: Messaging and async
docs.text:
B2 · How do you choose a Kafka message key?

Short answer: The aggregate id whose events must stay ordered (order reference, SKU), which also co-locates them on one partition. Ch 23.

B2 · What does auto.offset.reset control?

Short answer: Where a consumer group with no committed offset starts: earliest to process history, latest for live-only feeds. Ch 23.

B2 · Why disable topic auto-creation in production?

Short answer: Auto-created topics get default partitions, replication and retention nobody reviewed; topics are infrastructure. Ch 23.

B2 · What is a batch listener good for?

Short answer: Throughput when handling items together is cheaper — bulk indexing, bulk inserts — with idempotent processing and careful error handling. Ch 23.

B2 · How do you propagate MDC and security context to @Async tasks?

Short answer: A TaskDecorator (context propagation) and DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor on the executor; transactions never propagate and shouldn't. Ch 07, 17, 25.

B2 · Why prefer a sweeper over per-order timers?

Short answer: A periodic query with SKIP LOCKED is idempotent, self-healing after downtime and needs no per-entity state. Ch 25.

docs.title: Resilience, observability, testing, operations
docs.text:
B2 · What's a good fallback, and what's a bad one?

Short answer: Good: last-known values with a staleness bound, simpler computations, queue-for-later. Bad: invented prices or payment results, or catching everything and returning empty results. Ch 26.

B2 · How do you expose a custom business metric?

Short answer: A Micrometer counter, timer or summary with low-cardinality tags (channel, payment method), registered once and tested. Ch 27.

B2 · How do you write a health indicator that shouldn't affect readiness?

Short answer: Implement HealthIndicator, return a custom status like DEGRADED with details, and leave it out of the readiness group. Ch 27.

B2 · Why assert async behaviour with Awaitility rather than sleeps?

Short answer: Sleeps are either too short (flaky) or too long (slow); Awaitility polls until the condition holds or a timeout expires. Ch 15.

B2 · How do you share containers across test classes?

Short answer: Declare them as beans in a shared @TestConfiguration with @ServiceConnection, and keep context configuration consistent so the context cache reuses them. Ch 15, 28.

B2 · What's startupProbe for?

Short answer: Giving slow-starting pods time to boot without making the liveness probe lenient forever. Ch 30.

B2 · Why is maxUnavailable: 0 common for request-serving services?

Short answer: Rolling updates never reduce serving capacity below the current replica count. Ch 30.

B2 · Why must maxReplicas consider the database?

Short answer: Every pod brings a connection pool; pods × pool × services must fit max_connections. Ch 12, 30.

B1 · 0–2 years · B3 · 5–8 years

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 Years
docs.text: How things work internally, how they fail, and how to design within a service. A strong B3 candidate owns a service, explains mechanisms rather than recipes, and answers "what happens when it breaks?" without prompting.

docs.title: Container, lifecycle and proxies
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through the lifecycle of a Spring bean.

Short answer: Definition registered → BeanFactoryPostProcessors modify definitions → instantiation → property/constructor injection → Aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessor before-init → @PostConstruct / afterPropertiesSet → after-init (where proxies are created) → ready → on shutdown @PreDestroy / destroy. Ch 03.

B3 · Where exactly are AOP proxies created, and why does that matter?

Short answer: In postProcessAfterInitialization by an auto-proxy creator. Consequences: @PostConstruct runs on the target (no advice), self-calls bypass the proxy, and final classes or methods can't be proxied with CGLIB. Ch 03, 04.

B3 · JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB?

Short answer: JDK proxies implement interfaces; CGLIB subclasses the class. Boot defaults to CGLIB (proxy target class), which needs non-final classes and methods. Ch 04.

B3 · How does SmartLifecycle help with graceful shutdown?

Short answer: Components start and stop in phases; consumers and schedulers can stop before the web server and pools, so in-flight work drains in a controlled order. Ch 03, 30.

docs.title: Auto-configuration and configuration
docs.text:
B3 · How does Boot decide which auto-configurations apply?

Short answer: It reads the AutoConfiguration.imports files, filters by exclusions and fast class conditions, orders by before/after, and registers classes whose conditions pass — after user configuration, which is why @ConditionalOnMissingBean works. Ch 05, 41.

B3 · How do you debug a missing bean?

Short answer: /actuator/conditions or --debug — the condition evaluation report states exactly which condition didn't match and why. Ch 41.

B3 · What are the pitfalls of @ConditionalOnBean?

Short answer: It's evaluated against the registry as it's being built, so a bean defined later isn't seen. Use explicit ordering, or ObjectProvider for optional collaborators. Ch 41.

docs.title: Web and JSON internals
docs.text:
B3 · Trace a request through Spring MVC.

Short answer: Filters (security, correlation) → DispatcherServlet → handler mapping → interceptors → argument resolvers and validation → controller → return-value handling and message conversion → exception resolvers (advice) on failure. Ch 08, 10.

B3 · Why don't exceptions thrown in filters reach @ControllerAdvice?

Short answer: Filters run before the DispatcherServlet; handle errors in the filter, or delegate to a HandlerExceptionResolver, to keep one error format. Ch 10, 17.

B3 · How do you prevent polymorphic deserialization vulnerabilities?

Short answer: Avoid default typing; use explicit subtypes with allow-lists; restrict trusted packages for Kafka/Redis serializers; prefer typed serializers per cache. Ch 11, 21, 23.

docs.title: Data and transactions
docs.text:
B3 · Explain the JPA persistence context and dirty checking.

Short answer: Managed entities are tracked for the transaction; at flush, Hibernate compares state to snapshots and issues updates. Large contexts cost memory and flush time; clear or use projections for bulk reads. Ch 13.

B3 · Why is open-in-view dangerous?

Short answer: It keeps the session open during view rendering, enabling lazy loading outside the service layer — hidden queries, N+1 and connections held for the whole request. Ch 13.

B3 · Describe transaction propagation modes that matter in practice.

Short answer: REQUIRED joins or creates; REQUIRES_NEW suspends and creates (two connections); MANDATORY requires an existing one (used for outbox writes); NOT_SUPPORTED suspends. Ch 16, 36.

B3 · What happens when an inner REQUIRED method throws and the outer catches it?

Short answer: The shared transaction is marked rollback-only; the outer commit then throws UnexpectedRollbackException. Ch 16.

B3 · Why must remote calls stay outside transactions?

Short answer: A slow call holds a database connection and locks for its whole duration, exhausting the pool; and a rollback can't undo the remote side effect. Ch 16.

B3 · How do you size a HikariCP pool?

Short answer: From concurrency (Little's law) and database capacity, usually small; watch pending. Multiply by pods and services to check against max_connections. Ch 12, 34.

B3 · How do you run a migration on a 40-million-row table without downtime?

Short answer: Expand/contract, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, batched backfills, avoiding long ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks, and rehearsal on production-sized data with time and lock budgets. Ch 14, 28.

docs.title: Security internals
docs.text:
B3 · Describe the security filter chain flow.

Short answer: Context loading, headers, CORS, CSRF, authentication filters, anonymous, ExceptionTranslationFilter, then AuthorizationFilter; denials become 401 via the entry point or 403 via the access-denied handler. Ch 17.

B3 · Walk through JWT validation.

Short answer: Extract bearer token → decoder parses header → key by kid from cached JWKS → signature → validators (timestamps with skew, issuer, audience, custom) → converter to authorities. Ch 18.

B3 · How does key rotation avoid downtime?

Short answer: Publish old and new keys in the JWKS; sign with the new kid; decoders refresh on unknown kid; remove the old key only after the longest token lifetime. Ch 18.

B3 · How do you implement immediate revocation with JWTs?

Short answer: Short access-token lifetime plus a jti deny list checked by a validator, and refresh-token family revocation with reuse detection. Ch 18.

docs.title: Clients, caching, search
docs.text:
B3 · Connect, read and connection-request timeouts — what does each protect against?

Short answer: Connect: establishing TCP/TLS. Read: waiting for data. Connection-request: waiting for a pooled connection — pool exhaustion is invisible without it. Ch 19.

B3 · How does timeout budgeting work across a call chain?

Short answer: Each hop gets a share of the caller's remaining deadline, including retries; downstream timeouts must be shorter than upstream ones. Ch 19, 34.

B3 · When should cache eviction happen relative to the transaction?

Short answer: After commit — otherwise another thread repopulates the cache from pre-commit state. Ch 21.

B3 · How do you invalidate local caches across pods?

Short answer: Broadcast events (Kafka or Redis pub/sub) consumed by every pod, or versioned key prefixes; keep a short TTL as a safety net. Ch 21.

B3 · How do you reindex search without downtime?

Short answer: New index with the new mapping, bulk load from the source of truth plus catch-up, validate counts and golden queries, then an atomic alias swap. Ch 22.

B3 · What are the limits of a Redis distributed lock?

Short answer: It's an efficiency lock: GC pauses and failover can allow two holders. Use database constraints, conditional updates or fencing tokens for correctness. Ch 22.

docs.title: Messaging internals
docs.text:
B3 · Explain consumer-group rebalancing and how to make deploys smooth.

Short answer: Membership changes reassign partitions; cooperative sticky assignment moves only what's needed, static membership lets a restarting pod reclaim its partitions, and idempotent processing makes any replay harmless. Ch 23.

B3 · What do Kafka transactions guarantee — and not?

Short answer: Atomic produce and offset commits within Kafka for read-process-write flows. They do not include your database; that requires the outbox. Ch 23, 36.

B3 · What happens if processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms?

Short answer: The consumer is evicted, a rebalance occurs and uncommitted records are redelivered. Reduce batch size, speed up processing or pause explicitly. Ch 23.

B3 · How do you retry a RabbitMQ message after 30 seconds without blocking?

Short answer: Publish to a TTL queue without consumers whose dead-letter exchange routes back to the work exchange, with an attempt counter; park after N attempts. Ch 24.

docs.title: Concurrency, resilience, observability
docs.text:
B3 · What actually changes when you enable virtual threads?

Short answer: Request handling and executors create a virtual thread per task; blocking is cheap, so thread count stops limiting throughput and downstream resources become the bottleneck — bulkheads become essential. Ch 25.

B3 · What is pinning?

Short answer: A virtual thread that can't unmount blocks its carrier — historically synchronized around blocking I/O (fixed in JDK 24), still native frames. Detect with JFR or jdk.tracePinnedThreads. Ch 25.

B3 · Explain retry amplification.

Short answer: Retries at several layers multiply load (3×3×3 = 27 requests per user action) when a dependency is already struggling. Use one retry layer, jitter, budgets and circuit breakers. Ch 26.

B3 · Should an open circuit breaker make the pod unready?

Short answer: No — every pod would drop out, and the degraded path the breaker enables would never serve traffic. Surface it in health details and alerts. Ch 26, 30.

B3 · What does the Observation API give you over plain metrics?

Short answer: One instrumentation point producing metrics and spans, with low-cardinality keys for tags and high-cardinality keys for span attributes. Ch 27.

B3 · Head vs tail sampling?

Short answer: Head sampling decides at the start and may drop the trace you need; tail sampling decides in the collector after seeing the whole trace, keeping errors and slow requests. Ch 27.

docs.title: Testing, packaging, Kubernetes, reactive
docs.text:
B3 · How does consumer-driven contract testing prevent breakage?

Short answer: Consumers publish pacts of their real expectations; providers verify them in CI; can-i-deploy blocks a release that would break a consumer in production. Ch 28.

B3 · How does CDS improve startup?

Short answer: A training run archives parsed class data that later starts map directly; it must match the JDK and classpath, so regenerate on every upgrade. Ch 29.

B3 · Walk through what happens when a pod is deleted.

Short answer: Marked terminating and removed from endpoints (asynchronously) → preStop → SIGTERM → readiness refuses → requests drain → lifecycle phases stop → pools close → exit, or SIGKILL after the grace period. Ch 30.

B3 · Explain assembly time vs subscription time in Reactor.

Short answer: Building the chain creates a blueprint; nothing runs until subscription, when demand flows upstream and signals downstream. Hence "nothing happened" bugs and confusing stack traces. Ch 31.

B3 · How do you choose a backpressure strategy?

Short answer: By data semantics: drop or keep-latest for live values, bounded buffer for bursts, limitRate for paged data — never unbounded buffering on infinite streams. Ch 31.

docs.title: Protocols, batch, performance
docs.text:
B3 · How do you fix N+1 in GraphQL?

Short answer: @BatchMapping/DataLoader to fetch all keys at a level in one call, plus a test asserting the downstream call count. Ch 32.

B3 · Why are gRPC deadlines better than per-hop timeouts?

Short answer: A deadline is absolute and propagated, so the whole chain gives up together and no work continues after the caller has. Ch 32.

B3 · What makes a batch job restartable?

Short answer: Stable identifying parameters, deterministic reader ordering, idempotent writes, and readers persisting position in the execution context — proven by a fail-then-restart test with exact counts. Ch 33.

B3 · Explain Little's law and how you use it.

Short answer: Concurrency = throughput × latency. It sizes pools and bulkheads and explains why rising latency exhausts resources. Ch 34.

B3 · What is coordinated omission?

Short answer: Closed-model load tests stop sending requests while the system is slow, hiding queueing. Use an open (arrival-rate) model. Ch 34.

B3 · How do you find a memory leak?

Short answer: Watch heap after full GC over time; if the floor rises, take a heap dump and follow the dominator tree to GC roots — often an unbounded cache or uncleared ThreadLocal. Ch 34.

docs.title: Distributed data and architecture
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through an orchestrated saga's failure handling.

Short answer: Persisted state with guarded transitions; step failures arrive as events and move to compensating; compensations run only for completed steps and are idempotent; a sweeper enforces deadlines; repeated failure goes to STUCK with an alert. Ch 36.

B3 · What are the operational risks of CDC with Debezium?

Short answer: A stalled replication slot retains WAL and can fill the disk; connector lag delays events; schema changes can break connectors. Alert on slot lag and set max_slot_wal_keep_size. Ch 36.

B3 · How do you decide aggregate boundaries?

Short answer: By invariants that must hold at the same instant; if seconds of eventual consistency are acceptable, use separate aggregates connected by events. Ch 37.

B3 · How does the Modulith event publication registry work?

Short answer: Publications are persisted in the business transaction and completed when listeners succeed; incomplete ones can be republished — an in-process outbox, making later extraction mechanical. Ch 37.

B3 · How do you prove tenant isolation?

Short answer: A reflective leak suite over every repository with two seeded tenants, plus tests for native queries (RLS), pooled-connection state, async and messaging paths — in every build. Ch 38.

B3 · How would you implement a data-erasure request across many services?
