Short answer: Catalog-driven orchestration so nothing is missed; per-service erase and export; anonymize where retention is legally required and record the basis; verify no data remains; audit the whole request. Ch 39.

B3 · How do you evaluate an AI feature in CI?

Short answer: A golden set with property assertions, plus refusal, prompt-injection (in retrieved content) and authorization tests that also check the audit trail — run nightly and gating prompt or model changes. Ch 40.

B3 · How do you test auto-configuration honestly?

Short answer: ApplicationContextRunner with back-off tests for each bean and FilteredClassLoader to simulate missing optional libraries. Ch 41.

B3 · How do you test cross-version message compatibility during an upgrade?

Short answer: Deserialize real payloads captured from the old version with the new stack, and payloads from the new stack with an old-configured mapper — both directions, per topic. Ch 42.

docs.title: Leadership (B3 entry level)
docs.text:
B3 · How do you lead a SEV-1 incident?

Short answer: Assign roles (commander, comms, operations), restore first by rollback or degradation, keep a timeline, update on a cadence, then run a blameless review with owned actions. Ch 43.

B3 · What makes a good post-incident action?

Short answer: Specific, owned, dated, and changing a system — a test, alert or library default — rather than asking people to be more careful. Ch 43.

docs.title: Container and configuration internals
docs.text:
B3 · What's the difference between a BeanFactoryPostProcessor and a BeanPostProcessor?

Short answer: The former modifies bean definitions before instantiation (placeholders, scopes); the latter modifies or wraps bean instances around initialization (proxies, injection). Ch 03.

B3 · Why must BeanFactoryPostProcessor @Bean methods be static?

Short answer: They run before regular beans exist; a non-static method forces early instantiation of the enclosing configuration and can break processing. Ch 03.

B3 · How are circular dependencies handled, and why are they a smell?

Short answer: Constructor cycles fail at startup (and Boot disallows field-injection cycles by default); cycles usually indicate a missing abstraction or misplaced responsibility. Ch 02.

B3 · What does proxyBeanMethods = false change?

Short answer: No CGLIB subclass for the configuration, so calling one @Bean method from another creates a new instance instead of returning the singleton — faster startup, but inject dependencies as parameters. Ch 02.

B3 · How does relaxed binding work?

Short answer: Properties bind from kebab, camel, underscore and environment-variable forms to the same @ConfigurationProperties field. Ch 06.

B3 · How does an EnvironmentPostProcessor differ from @PropertySource?

Short answer: It runs very early, before the context, and can add or reorder property sources with explicit precedence; @PropertySource is processed later and has limited precedence control. Ch 06, 41.

docs.title: Web and error handling internals
docs.text:
B3 · How do argument resolvers work, and when would you write one?

Short answer: HandlerMethodArgumentResolvers build controller parameters from the request; write one for cross-cutting context such as the current customer or tenant. Ch 08.

B3 · How does content negotiation pick a converter?

Short answer: From the Accept header and produces attributes against registered HttpMessageConverters; mismatches yield 406. Ch 08.

B3 · How do you keep one error format for filter and controller exceptions?

Short answer: Filters catch and delegate to the HandlerExceptionResolver, and security uses custom entry points and access-denied handlers writing problem bodies. Ch 10, 17.

B3 · How does method validation work internally?

Short answer: A MethodValidationPostProcessor adds an AOP interceptor for @Validated beans; proxy rules therefore apply. Ch 09.

docs.title: Data internals
docs.text:
B3 · When does Hibernate flush?

Short answer: Before commit, before queries that may be affected (auto flush), and on explicit flush(). Unexpected flushes cause surprising SQL timing and constraint errors. Ch 13.

B3 · Why does pagination with a collection fetch join misbehave?

Short answer: Hibernate can't paginate rows of a join in SQL, so it paginates in memory; enable the fail-fast setting and use two queries (ids, then fetch). Ch 13.

B3 · How do isolation levels affect the platform?

Short answer: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed; lost updates are prevented by optimistic locking or conditional updates rather than raising isolation globally. Ch 16.

B3 · How do you detect long-running transactions in production?

Short answer: pg_stat_activity for idle-in-transaction sessions, Hikari active-connection durations, and a transaction timeout. Ch 12, 16.

B3 · What does SKIP LOCKED enable?

Short answer: Multiple workers claiming different rows from the same queue table without blocking — the basis of relays, sweepers and job tables. Ch 12, 25, 36.

B3 · How do you keep migrations backward compatible during rolling deploys?

Short answer: Old code must work against the new schema: add before use, dual-write, switch reads, remove last — never drop or rename in the same release. Ch 14.

docs.title: Security internals
docs.text:
B3 · How does method security evaluate @PreAuthorize?

Short answer: An authorization interceptor evaluates the expression (or a bean method) against the current authentication before invoking the method; denials throw AccessDeniedException. Ch 17.

B3 · What is refresh-token reuse detection?

Short answer: Rotated refresh tokens are single-use; if a used token reappears, the whole family is revoked because one copy was stolen. Ch 18.

B3 · Why must webhook verification use raw bytes?

Short answer: Parsing and re-serializing changes the bytes (whitespace, ordering, number formats), so the HMAC no longer matches — or worse, matches different content. Ch 18.

B3 · How does a security context get lost, and how do you find out?

Short answer: Thread hops without propagation (async, executors, reactive schedulers); symptoms are anonymousUser in audits or unexpected 401/403 inside background work. Ch 17, 25.

docs.title: Clients, caching, search
docs.text:
B3 · How does @Cacheable(sync = true) work and what are its limits?

Short answer: It uses the cache's get(key, loader) so one thread computes per key per JVM; it can't be combined with unless and doesn't coordinate across pods. Ch 21.

B3 · How do typed Redis serializers reduce risk?

Short answer: No type information in payloads, so a poisoned entry can't instantiate arbitrary classes, and DTO changes fail predictably. Ch 21.

B3 · How do you implement stale-while-revalidate?

Short answer: Store a value with a freshness timestamp and a longer hard TTL; serve stale values immediately and refresh asynchronously. Ch 21.

B3 · Why put synonyms in the search analyzer only?

Short answer: Search-time synonyms can change without reindexing; index-time synonyms are faster but require a reindex for every change. Ch 22.

B3 · How do Lua scripts provide atomicity in Redis?

Short answer: The server executes the script without interleaving other commands; pass keys via KEYS for cluster slot routing. Ch 22.

docs.title: Messaging
docs.text:
B3 · How does ErrorHandlingDeserializer prevent poison-pill loops?

Short answer: It catches deserialization failures and hands the container a failed record with headers, so the error handler can route it to the DLT instead of failing the poll forever. Ch 23.

B3 · How do you replay dead letters safely?

Short answer: Seek by time, filter, republish to the original topic with audit, and only after consumers are idempotent and the root cause is fixed. Ch 23.

B3 · What does static membership change during rolling deploys?

Short answer: A consumer with a stable group.instance.id can restart within the session timeout without triggering a rebalance, keeping its partitions. Ch 23.

B3 · Why are publisher confirms asynchronous, and how do you use them with an outbox?

Short answer: The broker acknowledges later; mark outbox rows sent only in the confirm callback, correlated by id. Ch 24.

B3 · How does Pulsar's Key_Shared differ from Kafka partitions?

Short answer: It preserves per-key ordering while distributing keys across consumers dynamically, without a fixed partition count. Ch 24.

docs.title: Concurrency, resilience, observability
docs.text:
B3 · How does ThreadPoolTaskExecutor decide when to create threads?

Short answer: Up to core size, then queue; only when the queue is full does it grow to max size; beyond that the rejection policy runs. Ch 25.

B3 · Why never pool virtual threads?

Short answer: Pools amortize expensive creation; virtual threads are cheap. Pooling reintroduces a limit in the wrong place — use semaphores for concurrency limits. Ch 25.

B3 · What is a retry budget?

Short answer: A cap on retries as a fraction of successful traffic (e.g. 10%), so retries stop when a dependency is struggling. Ch 26.

B3 · How do you choose circuit-breaker thresholds?

Short answer: From measured latency and error distributions: slow-call threshold above normal p99, time-based windows, minimum calls suited to traffic, business errors ignored. Ch 26.

B3 · How do multi-window burn-rate alerts work?

Short answer: Page only when both a short and a long window exceed a burn-rate threshold, catching real outages quickly while ignoring brief blips. Ch 27.

B3 · How do you guard metric cardinality automatically?

Short answer: MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags on risky meters, URI templates asserted in tests, and allow-lists for tag values. Ch 27.

docs.title: Testing, packaging, Kubernetes
docs.text:
B3 · Why does a Spring test suite create many contexts, and how do you fix it?

Short answer: Each distinct configuration (mock beans, properties, profiles) is a new cache key; standardize with composed test annotations and shared configuration. Ch 15.

B3 · How do you test @ConditionalOnClass branches?

Short answer: ApplicationContextRunner with FilteredClassLoader to hide the class. Ch 41.

B3 · How do you size JVM memory for a container?

Short answer: Set a memory limit and MaxRAMPercentage around 70–75%, then measure RSS: metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers live outside the heap. Ch 29.

B3 · How does a config change reach running pods safely?

Short answer: Via a rollout triggered by a config-hash annotation, not runtime reloading, so every pod runs the same reviewed configuration. Ch 06, 30.

B3 · Why must NetworkPolicies allow DNS?

Short answer: Service discovery resolves through kube-dns; blocking UDP 53 breaks every outbound call. Ch 30.

docs.title: Architecture, tenancy, platform
docs.text:
B3 · How do domain events differ from integration events?

Short answer: Domain events describe changes inside a context, often in-process; integration events are published contracts for other services, versioned and evolved carefully. Ch 23, 37.

B3 · Why can't Hibernate @TenantId alone guarantee isolation?

Short answer: Native queries, JDBC access and bulk operations bypass it; database RLS provides the second layer. Ch 38.

B3 · How does an idempotent receiver work in Spring Integration?

Short answer: A MetadataStore records processed message keys and discards repeats — the integration-flow equivalent of an inbox. Ch 33.

B3 · How do you make AI tool output safe to use?

Short answer: Structured output validated against domain constraints, session-scoped tools, and human review for anything consequential. Ch 40.

B2 · 2–5 years · B4 · 8–12 years

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 Years
docs.text: Cross-service design, operations, trade-offs and platform decisions. A strong B4 candidate reasons across several teams' systems, states trade-offs unprompted, and knows how a design behaves in production at 9 p.m. during a sale.

docs.title: Architecture and boundaries
docs.text:
B4 · How do you decide service boundaries?

Short answer: From business capabilities and bounded contexts found in the domain language, aligned with team ownership and different change and scaling profiles — validated by asking whether the service can deploy alone, owns its data and avoids synchronous chatter with neighbours. Ch 35, 37.

B4 · Modular monolith or microservices for a new platform?

Short answer: Modular monolith with verified boundaries unless there is a concrete need for independent deployment, scaling or ownership. It keeps local transactions and cheap refactoring while the domain is being learned, and makes later extraction a refactor. Ch 37.

B4 · How do you assess whether a platform is a distributed monolith?

Short answer: Check for ordered deployments, shared schemas, synchronous depth per user action, lockstep shared-library upgrades, unversioned contracts and local development needing many services. Fix the shared database first. Ch 35.

B4 · When do you replicate data between services instead of calling?

Short answer: For display and read-heavy access where seconds of staleness are acceptable; call the owner synchronously when the value must be authoritative for a decision (prices at checkout, stock at reservation). Ch 35, 36.

B4 · How do you extract a service from a monolith safely?

Short answer: Modularize in place; stand up the service read-only; route reads through the gateway with shadow comparison; move table ownership and writes; have the monolith call or consume events; delete old code and revoke grants — each step reversible. Ch 35, 37.

B4 · How do you classify subdomains and what follows?

Short answer: Core (invest: rich models, hexagonal, strongest engineers), supporting (pragmatic), generic (buy or keep simple). It directs effort to where differentiation lives. Ch 37.

docs.title: Data consistency
docs.text:
B4 · Design consistency for checkout across five services.

Short answer: Outbox per service; inbox idempotency per consumer; an orchestrated saga with persisted state, deadlines and compensations; immediate 201 with PLACED and asynchronous progression; read models for history; two-directional reconciliation hourly; dashboards for open and stuck sagas. Ch 36.

B4 · When do you fix the boundary instead of building a saga?

Short answer: When two services must change together to protect one invariant — merging the data into one service gives a local transaction and removes a class of failures. Sagas are for steps that genuinely belong to different capabilities. Ch 36, 37.

B4 · Polling outbox or CDC — how do you decide platform-wide?

Short answer: Polling as the default for simplicity; CDC for high-volume or latency-sensitive services when the team can operate Kafka Connect and replication slots safely. Record it in an ADR with a revisit trigger. Ch 36, 43.

B4 · What does a mature reconciliation strategy look like?

Short answer: Pairs reconciled on a cadence matched to financial risk, in both directions, windows excluding in-flight work, drift metrics with alerts, tickets instead of silent auto-repair for money, and drift causes reviewed as defects. Ch 33, 36.

docs.title: APIs and integration
docs.text:
B4 · How do you govern APIs across many services?

Short answer: A written standard, lint rules and spec diffing in CI, a platform library implementing errors, pagination and headers, contract tests with a deploy gate, SDK generation, and per-client version telemetry. Ch 20, 28, 41.

B4 · You must change a field used by a million installed apps. How?

Short answer: Never mutate meaning in place: add the new field, dual-populate, version the representation, migrate clients with telemetry-driven outreach, retire the old field after a sunset window; gateways can adapt the long tail. Ch 20.

B4 · How do you choose between REST, GraphQL, gRPC and messaging?

Short answer: REST for public and most internal APIs; a GraphQL BFF where clients aggregate many resources with varying needs; gRPC for high-volume internal hot paths with deadlines; events wherever the caller doesn't need the result now. Record each choice. Ch 32, 35.

B4 · Design a mobile BFF.

Short answer: One service owning no data or business rules, aggregating concurrently with timeouts, breakers and partial-failure handling, batch loaders everywhere, persisted queries and limits, shared error codes, separate scaling, and contract tests with app teams. Ch 32.

B4 · How do you migrate 40 Feign clients?

Short answer: Interface by interface to HTTP interfaces behind ports, mapping decoders to status handlers and retryers to explicit policy, running both behind a flag with contract tests, then deleting Feign. Ch 19, 42.

docs.title: Messaging at platform scale
docs.text:
B4 · Design the event architecture for the order lifecycle.

Short answer: Versioned topics keyed by order reference; outbox publishing; per-service consumer groups with inbox idempotency; classified error handling with DLTs and replay tooling; governed topic configs; schema evolution rules with contract tests; lag, DLT and outbox dashboards. Ch 23, 36.

B4 · How do you choose partition counts?

Short answer: From peak throughput over per-consumer throughput, plus headroom for parallelism and per-key ordering limits; growth reshuffles keys, so start generous but bounded by broker overhead. Ch 23.

B4 · Kafka, RabbitMQ or a database queue?

Short answer: Kafka for fan-out, replay and ordered throughput; RabbitMQ for routed work queues with priorities, delays and per-message acks; a PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED queue for single-consumer, modest-volume work that must be transactional with your data. Ch 23, 24.

B4 · How do you migrate an incompatible event schema?

Short answer: New versioned topic; producers dual-publish; consumers migrate one by one; retire the old topic when its consumer groups are gone — measured from the broker. Ch 23.

docs.title: Security and tenancy
docs.text:
B4 · Design the token architecture for customers, staff, services and partners.

Short answer: OTP + PKCE with rotating refresh tokens for customers; OIDC SSO with passkeys and MFA for staff; client credentials for services; signed webhooks for partners; audience-scoped short-lived tokens; centralized claim mapping; documented rotation and revocation. Ch 18.

B4 · Gateway or service — where is authentication enforced?

Short answer: Both: the gateway validates tokens and applies quotas; services re-validate and enforce authorization and ownership. Never trust injected identity headers. Ch 17, 35.

B4 · Design multi-tenancy for 500 tenants with a long tail.

Short answer: Shared schema with @TenantId and forced RLS; tenant from the token; platform-provided propagation; tenant-aware cache keys by default; per-tier quotas; a leak suite in CI; dedicated databases or cells for the largest; catalog-driven export and deletion. Ch 38.

B4 · What are the costs of database-per-tenant at scale?

Short answer: Connection multiplication, N migrations with partial failures and version skew, N backup and monitoring targets, slower incident response and higher spend — justified for a handful of tenants, not hundreds. Ch 38.

B4 · Design the security architecture for a consumer platform.

Short answer: Layered trust boundaries; consumer and staff identity separated; mTLS and NetworkPolicy internally; least-privilege DB users with RLS and field encryption; append-only audit; signed images with admission control; CI security gates; DSR workflows; rehearsed incident response. Ch 39.

B4 · How do you reduce PCI scope?

Short answer: Never let card data reach your servers — gateway-hosted or SDK card entry, tokens for repeat payments, signed webhooks and segmentation. Ch 39.

docs.title: Resilience, performance, operations
docs.text:
B4 · Define a resilience policy for a platform.

Short answer: A per-dependency table of timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead and degradation mode, implemented in a platform library, visible in metrics, chaos-tested, reviewed when SLAs change and referenced in runbooks. Ch 26.

B4 · Application resilience or service mesh?

Short answer: Mesh for transport: mTLS, connection timeouts, outlier ejection, traffic shifting. Application for semantics: idempotency-aware retries, fallbacks, error translation. Retries in exactly one layer. Ch 26, 30.

B4 · How do you prepare a platform for 5× traffic?

Short answer: Forecast per service, breakpoint tests per pod, a written capacity model for pods, connections, partitions and cache; open-model full-journey load tests at 1.5× with profiling; soak and spike tests; game days; pre-scaling; deploy freeze. Ch 34, 44.

B4 · A team wants to double the connection pool to fix latency. Response?

Short answer: Check pool pending and query durations first; pool waits usually mean slow queries or long transactions. Fix those, then size against database capacity — a bigger pool moves contention into the database. Ch 12, 34.

B4 · Design observability for 26 services.

Short answer: Platform library with common tags, cardinality guards, SLO histograms and health conventions; OTLP to a collector doing tail sampling and redaction; templated dashboards with deploy annotations; SLOs per critical journey with burn-rate alerts and runbooks; contract tests for metric names. Ch 27.

B4 · How do you decide what to alert on?

Short answer: Symptoms users feel (SLO burn, business-metric drops) and conditions about to become user-visible (lag, backlog, saturation). Everything else is a dashboard. Every alert has an owner and a runbook. Ch 27.

B4 · Standardize Kubernetes configuration for 26 services.

Short answer: A Helm library chart encoding probes, shutdown timing, security context, resources, PDB, spread, network policy and scrape annotations; per-service overrides; GitOps delivery; conformance checks; game days. Ch 30.

B4 · How do you run a Diwali sale operationally?

Short answer: Scheduled pre-scaling, verified connection and partition budgets, capacity raised in advance, deploy freeze, rehearsed rollback, staffed incident roles, degradation switches ready, SLO burn dashboards watched. Ch 30, 43, 44.

docs.title: Delivery and testing
docs.text:
B4 · Design the image pipeline for many services.

Short answer: Layered images, SBOM, scan with a fixable-high/critical gate, sign with provenance, push by commit, deploy to staging by digest, contract and smoke gates, promote the same digest, weekly base rebuilds or rebases, and fleet dashboards. Ch 29.

B4 · Design the test strategy for 26 services.

Short answer: Fast unit and slice tests; integration on real infrastructure with shared containers; contract tests with a broker gate; event golden files; shared ArchUnit rules; nightly mutation, performance, chaos and flake detection; a few owned end-to-end journeys reused as synthetic monitors. Ch 15, 28.

B4 · CI takes 40 minutes and people bypass it. What do you do?

Short answer: Measure, split fast and slow jobs, fix context and container sharing, parallelize, cache, move mutation and performance to nightly, delete redundant end-to-end tests, and defend a budget. Ch 28.

docs.title: Platform engineering and upgrades
docs.text:
B4 · What becomes a platform library?

Short answer: Cross-cutting concerns most services need, stable enough to standardize, with no business logic and a team to own it; extract on the third copy. Ch 41.

B4 · How do you govern platform libraries?

Short answer: Named owners, semantic versioning with N-1 support, changelogs and compatibility matrices, release checklists including back-off and native tests, and fleet version telemetry. Ch 41.

B4 · How do you run a Boot major upgrade across 26 services?

Short answer: Readiness phase (deprecations, blockers), platform libraries first, a pilot, waves from low-risk to core, canary with SLO analysis outside freeze windows, a readiness scorecard and dashboard, then cleanup. Ch 42.

B4 · How do you fund upgrade work against feature pressure?

Short answer: Make it continuous: a fixed quarterly allocation, automated dependency updates, and a dashboard translating support-window and CVE risk into business terms. Ch 42, 43.

docs.title: AI and leadership
docs.text:
B4 · Design a support assistant for a consumer platform.

Short answer: Authenticated, tenant-scoped RAG with thresholds; read-only, session-scoped, audited tools; delimited context; handoff on empty retrieval; token quotas; breaker with human fallback; CI evaluation; cost and quality metrics; a feature flag; legal review of data flows. Ch 40.

B4 · How do you decide whether an AI feature should ship?

Short answer: Worst output and its control, a working non-AI fallback, budgets for cost and latency, measurable quality with regression detection, and a lawful data flow. Any unclear answer means not ready. Ch 40.

B4 · How do you set technical direction for several teams?

Short answer: A short strategy with honest diagnosis tied to business outcomes, a few explicit bets and non-goals, individual pre-alignment, paved roads that make it easy to follow, and visible progress metrics. Ch 43.

B4 · How do you govern architecture without becoming a bottleneck?

Short answer: Most decisions stay in teams; RFCs with deadlines only for cross-cutting or irreversible changes; standards enforced by libraries and CI; recorded, time-boxed exceptions. Ch 43.

B4 · How do you use delivery metrics without them being gamed?

Short answer: Measure systems, not people; discuss trends rather than targets; pair each metric with its counter-metric; use them to decide where to help. Ch 43.

B3 · 5–8 years · B5 · 12–15+ years

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ Years
docs.text: Strategy, organization, risk, and knowing when not to use something. A strong B5 candidate reasons about the organization as a system: how technical choices shape teams, cost and risk over years, and how to move a large estate without breaking it.

docs.title: Strategy and architecture
docs.text:
B5 · When would you advise against microservices?

Short answer: Small teams, unclear domains, modest scale, or no operational capability for CI/CD, observability and on-call. A well-modularized monolith delivers most benefits at far lower cost and keeps the option to split later. Ch 35, 37.

B5 · How does organizational design shape service architecture?

Short answer: Conway's law: systems mirror communication structures. Long-lived teams owning capabilities produce clean boundaries; services split across teams, or teams owning many unrelated services, produce coupling regardless of technology. Ch 35, 43.

B5 · What does DDD actually buy an organization?

Short answer: A shared language between business and engineering, and boundaries aligned with how the business changes — so changes stay local. The strategic work matters more than the tactical patterns. Ch 37.

B5 · When is DDD the wrong investment?

Short answer: Simple CRUD systems, short-lived projects, generic subdomains, or no access to domain experts. Tactical patterns without strategic understanding produce ceremony without benefit. Ch 37.

B5 · How do you decide whether a new datastore or broker is justified?

Short answer: Demonstrate that the workload doesn't fit what you run, accept the operational cost (backups, upgrades, on-call, security review), confirm data can be rebuilt, and default to extending what exists. Ch 22, 24.

B5 · What's your position on forwarding user tokens between services?

Short answer: Avoid it — it spreads user credentials and makes every service a confused deputy. Use service identity plus explicit user context, and token exchange only where true delegation is required. Ch 18.

docs.title: Consistency, data and risk
docs.text:
B5 · What's the real cost of eventual consistency?

Short answer: It spreads beyond engineering: product designs pending states, support explains delays, finance accepts reconciliation windows, operations monitors drift. The organizational agreement on acceptable inconsistency is the hard part. Ch 36.

B5 · How do you keep distributed-data complexity from compounding?

Short answer: Boundaries that keep invariants local; a small set of standardized patterns in platform libraries; no ad-hoc variants; reconciliation for every cross-service invariant; saga count reviewed as an architectural health metric. Ch 36, 41.

B5 · What's the biggest risk in financial batch processing?

Short answer: Silent wrongness — jobs that succeed with bad numbers. Mitigate with reconciliation steps, business-total monitoring, dual controls on payout artifacts, immutable audit and rehearsed restarts. Ch 33.

B5 · Is batch processing obsolete in an event-driven architecture?

Short answer: No. Settlements, reconciliation, regulatory reporting and bulk corrections need point-in-time consistency, restartability and auditable artifacts. Events keep things current; batch proves they're correct. Ch 33.

docs.title: Reliability and operations
docs.text:
B5 · How does resilience relate to SLOs and error budgets?

Short answer: Resilience turns dependency failures into degraded successes, protecting availability; degradation must be measured separately so the organization distinguishes healthy, degraded and down, and budget burn directs investment to the weakest dependency. Ch 26, 27.

B5 · How does observability change engineering culture?

Short answer: It replaces opinion with evidence: SLOs align product and engineering, error budgets fund reliability work, reviews start from data, and instrumentation becomes part of "done". Ch 27.

B5 · When is Kubernetes the wrong choice?

Short answer: Small estates a managed PaaS covers, teams without capacity for cluster operations, or workloads better served by serverless. It pays off with many services, varied scaling and a platform team. Ch 30.

B5 · How do packaging choices affect reliability?

Short answer: Startup time bounds how fast you scale during incidents; image size bounds rollback speed; digest promotion determines trust in what's running; base-image hygiene sets exposure windows. They are reliability decisions disguised as build configuration. Ch 29.

B5 · How do you build performance into engineering culture?

Short answer: Budgets in design, load tests and profiles as normal deliverables, regression gates in CI, owned capacity models, incident reviews producing performance actions, and visible cost of decisions. Ch 34.

B5 · When is 'good enough' performance the right answer?

Short answer: When budgets are met with adequate headroom at forecast peak; beyond that, effort returns less than features or reliability work. Ch 34.

docs.title: Security, compliance, AI
docs.text:
B5 · How do you prioritize security investment?

Short answer: By risk across trust boundaries, informed by threat models and incident history. The highest returns are usually supply chain, staff access and authorization correctness — not exotic attacks. Ch 39.

B5 · What does a healthy security culture look like?

Short answer: Engineers threat model as part of design, secure defaults are the easy path, findings are defects with owners, incidents produce blameless reviews, and raising concerns is rewarded. Ch 39, 43.

B5 · How does multi-tenancy affect business economics?

Short answer: Isolation is a pricing tier: shared schema keeps small tenants nearly free; dedicated databases and cells carry real cost and must be sold accordingly, or engineering absorbs costs the contract never covered. Ch 38.

B5 · What's the hardest part of multi-tenancy?

Short answer: Sustained discipline — every feature, query, cache, job and integration can leak. Platform defaults, database-level enforcement and automated leak tests make correctness independent of memory. Ch 38.

B5 · Where should AI not be used?

Short answer: Decisions needing determinism, explainability or legal defensibility — pricing, refunds, fraud, credit, anything binding — plus latency-critical paths and problems where rules or conventional models do better. The strategy includes an explicit "not here" list. Ch 40.

B5 · What's the biggest organizational risk with AI features?

Short answer: Shipping demos without engineering discipline — no evaluation, cost controls, tool authorization or fallback — treating a non-deterministic remote dependency as a library call. Ch 40.

docs.title: Platform, upgrades, protocols
docs.text:
B5 · What's the cost of a platform abstraction?

Short answer: Support burden, release cadence, upgrade dependency and a learning curve. Worth it when it removes real duplication and enforces correctness; harmful when it thinly wraps a library or removes decisions teams should make. Ch 41.

B5 · How do you avoid a platform team becoming a bottleneck?

Short answer: Small, overridable libraries; no lockstep upgrades; N-1 support; contributions from service teams; deleting what's unused. A platform that says "wait for our release" too often gets routed around. Ch 41.

B5 · What does a healthy upgrade culture look like?

Short answer: Upgrades are boring — small, frequent, automated, measured and owned — with tests trusted enough that teams upgrade without fear. Ch 42.

B5 · When would you let a system stay on an old version?

Short answer: When retirement is near, exposure is isolated and upgrade cost exceeds residual risk — recorded, time-bound and revisited. Indefinite exceptions are how estates fall three majors behind. Ch 42.

B5 · What are the hidden costs of GraphQL?

Short answer: Runtime cost control, a new caching model, schema governance across teams, observability and rate limiting that don't come free, and the risk of a BFF accumulating business logic. Ch 32.

B5 · How do you avoid protocol sprawl?

Short answer: REST by default, a documented reason and owner for anything else, platform support for the sanctioned few, and periodic review of whether each non-REST interface still earns its complexity. Ch 32.

B5 · Does reactive still matter after virtual threads?

Short answer: Yes, for a narrower set: streaming with backpressure, connection-dense workloads and cancellation-heavy composition. For request/response services, MVC on virtual threads is the simpler default. Ch 25, 31.

docs.title: Leadership and organization
docs.text:
B5 · What distinguishes a principal engineer's impact?

Short answer: Multiplying others — direction many teams follow willingly, leverage through platforms, standards and people, expensive mistakes prevented, and an organization better able to change safely, measured over years. Ch 43.

B5 · How do you handle a strong disagreement with another senior leader?

Short answer: Understand their goals and constraints, find shared outcomes, bring data, experiment on reversible parts, escalate only with a clearly framed decision, and commit fully once made. Ch 43.

B5 · How do you know an engineering organization is healthy?

Short answer: Delivery metrics improving, incidents rarer and shorter, upgrades routine, standards adopted willingly, engineers growing and staying, cost per unit of value stable or falling, and people raising concerns early. Ch 43.

B5 · How do you keep architecture from eroding over years?

Short answer: Mechanical enforcement (ArchUnit, Modulith verification, contract gates, starters), generated documentation, ADRs with revisit triggers, clear ownership, and periodic context-map reviews against how the business actually changes. Ch 37, 41, 43.

B5 · How do you prevent broker, database and framework sprawl across teams?

Short answer: A decision guide, platform support for the sanctioned options, review for anything new with an operating owner and upgrade story, and a default of "use what we run" unless the workload demonstrably doesn't fit. Ch 24, 35, 43.

B5 · What makes a technical strategy effective?

Short answer: An honest diagnosis, a direction tied to business outcomes, a few explicit bets and non-goals, paved roads that make it easy to follow, and progress people can see. Ch 43.

docs.title: Scenario prompts for B5 interviews
docs.text:
B5 scenario · Every release needs four services deployed in order

Expect: diagnosis of the coupling (shared schema, shared domain library, unversioned APIs, synchronous chains); a strategy that splits schemas with grants, replaces the shared model with platform starters and per-client DTOs, introduces additive versioning with consumer-driven contracts, moves non-critical work to events; progress measured with DORA and scorecards; leadership through RFCs, pilots and paved roads. Ch 20, 28, 35, 41, 43.

B5 scenario · The same class of outage happened three times this year

Expect: a theme review across incidents rather than three local fixes; identification of the systemic factor (for example synchronous calls without timeouts); platform changes (default timeouts in the client starter, CI checks, review checklist); verification by game day; and a note on why the previous reviews didn't find it. Ch 26, 41, 43.

B5 scenario · The board wants 'an AI strategy' in 90 days

Expect: identification of use cases where AI explains, drafts or routes with measurable value; an explicit list of where it won't be used; engineering prerequisites (evaluation, tool authorization, cost controls, fallbacks, data-flow review); a pilot with success metrics; and governance rather than a platform bet. Ch 40, 43.

B5 scenario · Cloud spend grew 60% while orders grew 20%

Expect: normalize to cost per order; find the top drivers by service; separate growth from waste (idle requests, cardinality, log volume, unbounded AI usage, over-provisioned dedicated tenants); fix with right-sizing, startup improvements enabling faster scale-down, caching and query fixes; institutionalize a monthly cost review. Ch 27, 29, 30, 34, 38, 43.

B4 · 8–12 years · System Design

System Design · B Coding Exercises

docs.title: System Design
docs.text: Grocery-domain design problems with model answers. Each follows the same structure an interviewer expects: clarify → estimate → design → deep dive → failure modes → trade-offs. Model answers are outlines of what a strong candidate covers, with chapter references for depth — not scripts to recite.

docs.title: How to approach a design question
docs.text:
Step Time (45 min) What good looks like Clarify requirements 5 min Users, scale, consistency needs, SLOs, what's out of scope Estimate 3 min Requests/s, data volume, peak multiplier — rough is fine High-level design 10 min Services, data ownership, sync vs async, one diagram Deep dive 15 min The hardest part, in detail: consistency, a hot path, a failure mode Failure and operations 7 min What breaks, how it degrades, how you'd know Trade-offs and evolution 5 min What you'd change at 10× or with more time

Interviewers score reasoning, not diagrams. "We'd use Kafka" earns nothing; "events here because notification must not block checkout, keyed by order ref for ordering, with an outbox so the publish can't be lost" earns a lot.

docs.title: SD-1 · Checkout for an online grocery platform
docs.text:
Prompt: Design checkout: cart to confirmed order, including stock reservation and payment. Peak 3,000 orders/min during a sale.

Model answer outline

Clarify: Consistency for money and stock is strict; notifications and loyalty can lag. Checkout p99 < 2 s, availability 99.5%. Payments via an external gateway with webhooks.

Estimate: 50 orders/s peak; ~4 API calls per order ≈ 200 req/s at checkout; each order ~5 lines → 250 reservations/s.

Design: 

flowchart LR
    App --> GW[Gateway] --> O[order-service]
    O -->|price, before TX| P[pricing]
    O -->|TX: order + saga + outbox| DB[(orders DB)]
    DB -->|relay| K[(Kafka)]
    K --> I[inventory] --> K
    K --> PAY[payment] --> RZ[Gateway]
    RZ -->|signed webhook| PAY
    K --> N[notification]
- Order created in one transaction with saga state and an outbox row; respond 201 PLACED immediately. - Orchestrated saga: reserve stock → authorize payment → confirm. Deadlines, guarded transitions, compensations (release stock, void payment). - Idempotency key on the POST; inbox idempotency in every consumer. - Authoritative pricing fetched before the transaction, with timeout, breaker and cached-price degradation.

Deep dive — the saga: persisted state with version for optimistic locking; out-of-order events counted and ignored; a timeout sweeper; STUCK after repeated compensation failure with a page.

Failure modes: payment gateway down → 503 + Retry-After, sagas compensate at deadline; broker down → outbox accumulates, nothing lost; pricing slow → cached price flagged "may vary"; late payment after compensation → auto-void.

Operations: SLO burn-rate alerts; open/stuck saga gauges; hourly reconciliation orders ↔ payments ↔ reservations.

Trade-offs: 201 PLACED rather than synchronous PAID trades immediate certainty for availability and latency; polling outbox before CDC; orchestration over choreography for visibility.

Chapters: 04, 16, 19, 23, 26, 36, 44.

docs.title: SD-2 · Product search with typo tolerance and facets
docs.text:
Prompt: 2 million SKUs, Indian vocabulary ("aata", "dahi"), filters by brand, price and pincode availability, facets, p95 < 400 ms.

Model answer outline

Design: PostgreSQL as source of truth; outbox events → indexer → OpenSearch behind an alias. Indexer loads projections from the source rather than trusting event payloads.

Mapping: text fields with search-time synonyms (atta/aata/flour), fuzziness AUTO; keyword for brand/category; scaled_float for price; availability as a list of serviceable pincodes; popularity for boosting.

Query: multi-match with field boosts; filters (not queries) for structured constraints; aggregations for facets; search_after with a unique tiebreaker for pagination.

Deep dive — reindexing: new index with new mapping, bulk load, catch-up from Kafka offsets, golden-query validation, atomic alias swap, old index kept for rollback.

Failure modes: cluster down → breaker + category browse from PostgreSQL; index lag alert; zero-result-rate alert as a quality signal.

Trade-offs: eventual consistency (sellers see their own changes from the owner, not search); search-time synonyms trade query cost for no-reindex updates.

Chapters: 22, 23, 26, 36.

docs.title: SD-3 · Live delivery tracking
docs.text:
Prompt: 8,000 riders ping location every 5 s; up to 40,000 customers watch their order's rider live.

Model answer outline

Estimate: 1,600 pings/s inbound; 40,000 long-lived outbound connections.

Design: rider pings → ingest service (WebFlux) → Redis geo + pub/sub, sampled history to PostgreSQL via R2DBC; customers connect via SSE to a WebFlux stream service subscribed per rider.

Deep dive — backpressure: live positions use onBackpressureDrop plus sample(2s) — stale positions are worthless and buffering per slow client is a memory leak; heartbeats every 20 s; idle timeout; doFinally cleanup; open-connection gauge as the capacity metric.

Security: token validated at connect; ownership check that the order belongs to the customer; no rider PII beyond first name and position.

Failure modes: rollout disconnects clients → SSE auto-reconnect; Redis blip → stream pauses, resumes; slow mobile networks → drops, not buffers.

Trade-offs: SSE over WebSocket (push-only, automatic reconnect); WebFlux here specifically, MVC elsewhere.

Chapters: 22, 31, 32.

docs.title: SD-4 · Rider dispatch
docs.text:
Prompt: Assign each packed order to exactly one nearby rider; express orders first; retry if nobody accepts within 30 s; never assign two riders.

Model answer outline

Design: RabbitMQ topic exchange with quorum queues per priority class; competing consumers; publisher confirms from an outbox; prefetch low for fair distribution.

Deep dive — exactly one rider: rider claimed with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED; assignment row with a unique constraint on order; release the rider if the insert loses the race. Redelivery is harmless because the operation is idempotent.

Retry: TTL queue + dead-letter back to the work exchange with an attempt header; park after N attempts and alert a human dispatch desk.

Rider channel: WebSocket + STOMP with a broker relay so user destinations reach the right pod; heartbeats; authenticated CONNECT.

Failure modes: rider pool exhausted → delayed retry; poison task → parked immediately; broker node loss → quorum queues.

Trade-offs: RabbitMQ (per-message routing, priority, delay) over Kafka (replayable log) for this flow specifically.

Chapters: 12, 24, 32.

docs.title: SD-5 · Multi-tenant white-label marketplace
docs.text:
Prompt: Offer the platform to regional chains: 400 small tenants and 3 large ones, strict isolation, per-tenant branding.

Model answer outline

Model: shared schema with tenant_id for the long tail; database per tenant for the three large ones; the same code via a routing connection provider.

Enforcement: tenant from the token (validated against subdomain); @TenantId; forced RLS with transaction-local settings; tenant-aware cache keys by default; propagation through async, Kafka headers, outbound HTTP; scheduled jobs loop over tenants explicitly.

Deep dive — proof: reflective leak suite over every repository plus native queries, pooled-connection reset, async and messaging tests, in every build.

Noisy neighbours: per-tenant rate limits and quotas; statement timeouts; large tenants in their own cells.

Lifecycle: onboarding as a saga; export and deletion driven by the service catalog with evidence reports.

Trade-offs: shared schema is cheap but relies on enforcement layers; dedicated databases isolate but multiply migrations and connections.

Chapters: 35, 36, 38, 39.

docs.title: SD-6 · Weekly seller settlement
docs.text:
Prompt: 14,000 sellers, 2.8 million order lines per week, commission and TDS, bank payout file; must be restartable and correct.

Model answer outline

Design: Spring Batch job run as a Kubernetes CronJob (Forbid, no automatic retry): validate → partitioned calculation by seller → aggregate → payout file → reconcile → publish via outbox.

Deep dive — correctness: identifying parameters include the period; paging readers with unique sort keys; idempotent writes keyed by (order_line_id, run_date); a reconciliation step that fails the job before producing a wrong file.

Parallelism: partitions by seller groups balanced by volume, sized against database connections.

Operations: metrics on durations and totals; alerts on failure, missed runs, and deviation from last week's totals; runbook for restart.

Security: bank details field-encrypted; payout changes held 24 h after a bank-account change.

Chapters: 33, 36, 39.

docs.title: SD-7 · Support assistant with order lookup
docs.text:
Prompt: An AI assistant answers "where is my order?" and policy questions, deflecting tickets without inventing answers.

Model answer outline

Design: tenant-scoped RAG over policies (pgvector) with a similarity threshold; tools for order status and recent orders; human handoff queue.

Deep dive — safety: tools derive identity from the session, re-check ownership, are read-only and audited; retrieved content delimited in the user message; empty retrieval → handoff; refund or complaint language → escalation; output caps and per-tenant token quotas.

Resilience: provider behind a breaker and bulkhead; fallback is a human.

Quality: CI evaluation suite with golden, refusal, injection and authorization tests; metrics for deflection, escalation, cost per conversation.

Compliance: minimize data sent to the provider; processing agreement; residency review.

Chapters: 17, 26, 38, 39, 40.

docs.title: SD-8 · Platform upgrade programme
docs.text:
Prompt: Move 26 services from Boot 3.5 to Boot 4 within two quarters without incidents during Diwali.

Model answer outline

Plan: fix deprecations on 3.5; upgrade platform starters and BOM first with a compatibility matrix; pilot on a low-risk service; waves from supporting to core; core services outside the freeze window with canary on SLOs.

Deep dive — behaviour safety: golden-file JSON tests, access matrix, contract tests, performance baselines, cross-version Kafka and cache compatibility (versioned cache namespaces).

Tracking: readiness scorecard per service; fleet version dashboard; regressions attributed to the upgrade.

Separation: adopt new Boot 4 features (API versioning, HTTP service groups) only after the upgrade is green.

Chapters: 29, 30, 41, 42.

docs.title: SD-9 · Observability for the platform
docs.text:
Prompt: On-call engineers must answer "what's broken and since when?" in two minutes.

Model answer outline

Signals: metrics with common tags and cardinality guards; traces via OTLP with tail sampling keeping errors and slow requests; JSON logs with traceId and tenantId.

SLOs: per critical journey with multi-window burn-rate alerts; every alert links a runbook and dashboard.

Dashboards: SLO → traffic (RED) → dependencies (with breaker state and degradation counters) → resources (USE) → async (lag, DLT, outbox) → business metrics, with deploy annotations.

Business metrics: orders/min vs last week — catching failures that look technically healthy.

Governance: contract tests for metric names; quarterly cardinality and cost review.

Chapters: 07, 27.

docs.title: SD-10 · Resilience for a slow dependency
docs.text:
Prompt: The pricing service's p99 jumps from 80 ms to 4 s every few days. Checkout must stay up.

Model answer outline

Immediate: timeout inside the checkout budget (600 ms), one retry with jitter for idempotent reads, bulkhead, breaker ignoring business exceptions and counting slow calls.

Degradation: last-known price from Redis (≤ 15 min) flagged "may vary"; fail honestly if none exists; never invent prices.

Load protection: priority load shedding — search before checkout.

Verification: Toxiproxy latency chaos test asserting bounded checkout latency and breaker transitions.

Root cause: profile pricing under load; likely query or pool contention; performance regression gate afterwards.

Chapters: 19, 21, 26, 28, 34.

docs.title: Scoring rubric (B4)
docs.text:
Dimension 1 3 5 Requirements Jumps to tech Clarifies scale, consistency, SLOs Identifies the business trade-off first Data and consistency One DB Ownership per service Consistency model justified per flow Failure Ignored Timeouts, retries, idempotency Degradation per dependency, reconciliation Operations None Metrics and alerts SLOs, runbooks, rollout and rollback Trade-offs States a choice Compares options Knows when they'd change their mind Communication Monologue Structured Checks understanding and adapts

See Chapter 43 for calibrating interviewers.

B5 · 12–15+ years · Rapid Fire

docs.title: 1. JDKs via SDKMAN
docs.text:
We use Java 21 for Spring Boot 3.5 examples and Java 25 for Spring Boot 4.x examples.

Install SDKMAN and JDKs
curl -s "https://get.sdkman.io" | bash
source "$HOME/.sdkman/bin/sdkman-init.sh"

sdk list java | grep -E "21\.|25\."   # pick current Temurin builds
sdk install java 21.0.x-tem           # replace x with the latest patch shown
sdk install java 25.0.x-tem
sdk default java 25.0.x-tem

java -version

Per-project JDK

Add a .sdkmanrc file (java=25.0.x-tem) to the repo root and run sdk env. Gradle toolchains (Chapter 01) make the build itself independent of your shell JDK.

docs.title: Part 1 · Foundations
docs.text:
Chapters 01–15 · 0–5 years. The core container, Spring Boot, configuration, logging, the web layer, data access and testing — everything a service needs to be correct.

Primary bands: B1–B3. Every chapter follows the same nine-part structure — introduction, core concepts, internals, Levels 1–4 of hands-on code, Boot 3 vs 4, production playbook, and interview questions — so you can read any chapter at the depth your band needs.

Chapter 01 · Java & Build Prerequisites for Spring 02 · Spring Framework Core — IoC & Dependency Injection 03 · Bean Lifecycle, Events & Extension Points 04 · AOP — Aspect-Oriented Programming 05 · Spring Boot Fundamentals 06 · Externalized Configuration 07 · Logging 08 · Building REST APIs with Spring MVC 09 · Validation 10 · Error Handling & Problem Details 11 · JSON & Serialization 12 · Data Access Fundamentals — JDBC 13 · Spring Data JPA & Hibernate 14 · Database Migrations 15 · Testing Fundamentals

See Reading Paths for suggested routes through the handbook by experience level and goal.

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Spring Boot is not a separate language — it is a set of libraries running on the JVM and assembled by a build tool. Most "Spring problems" in real teams are actually Java-version problems or build problems in disguise:

  • ClassNotFoundException: javax.servlet.Filter after an upgrade — a dependency still on Java EE, not Jakarta EE.
  • NoSuchMethodError at startup — two versions of the same library on the classpath because someone overrode a version the Spring Boot BOM already manages.
  • Parameter name information not available — code compiled without the -parameters flag, which Spring Framework 6.1+ requires for name-based binding.
  • A build that works on one laptop and fails in CI — different JDKs, no toolchain, no locked dependencies.

In the grocery marketplace we run 26 services in one Gradle monorepo. If every service declared its own versions, plugins and compiler flags, upgrading from Boot 3.5 to 4.x would mean editing 26 build files by hand. This chapter sets up the foundation that makes the rest of the handbook — and that upgrade — boring.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — Java features, Gradle basics, first app B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — BOM, version catalog, multi-module B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 6 — dependency resolution internals, convention plugins B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — reproducibility, upgrade strategy, supply chain B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 7, 8, 9 — platform standards and governance

docs.title: 2.1 Java features Spring relies on
docs.text:
Spring Boot 3.x and 4.x both have a Java 17 baseline. Everything in Java 17 is fair game in framework code, and newer features are used when available.

Feature Java Why it matters in Spring code Records 16 DTOs, @ConfigurationProperties, projections, events — immutable and concise Sealed classes/interfaces 17 Closed domain hierarchies (PaymentResult), exhaustive switch Pattern matching for instanceof 16 Cleaner exception handlers and converters Text blocks 15 Native SQL in @Query, JSON in tests, prompts in Spring AI Switch expressions 14 Mapping enums/status codes Pattern matching for switch + record patterns 21 Exhaustive handling of sealed results Virtual threads 21 spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true — cheap blocking I/O SequencedCollection 21 getFirst()/getLast() on lists and ordered sets Stream gatherers 24 Custom intermediate stream operations Scoped values 25 (final) Immutable per-request context, alternative to ThreadLocal Flexible constructor bodies 25 Validate arguments before super(...) Module import declarations, compact source files 25 Scripts and small tools, rarely in services Structured concurrency Preview in 25 Fan-out calls (price + stock + delivery ETA) with one lifetime

Why records are everywhere in this handbook

A record gives you a canonical constructor, equals, hashCode and toString with no boilerplate, and it cannot be mutated. Spring binds @ConfigurationProperties to records through their constructor, Jackson serializes them out of the box, and Spring Data can project query results into them.

docs.title: 2.2 Build tools: Gradle and Maven
docs.text:
A build tool does four jobs: resolve dependencies, compile, test, and package. Spring Boot adds a plugin to each tool that repackages your application into an executable JAR and applies Spring's dependency management.

Gradle 9 (Kotlin DSL) Maven 3.9+ Build file build.gradle.kts (code) pom.xml (declarative XML) Speed Incremental builds, build cache, configuration cache Slower on large repos Multi-module settings.gradle.kts + convention plugins Parent POM + modules Spring Boot plugin org.springframework.boot spring-boot-maven-plugin Version management Version catalog + BOM platform spring-boot-starter-parent or imported BOM

This handbook uses Gradle 9 Kotlin DSL as primary with Maven in tabs.

docs.title: 2.3 BOM and dependency management
docs.text:
A Bill of Materials (BOM) is a POM that lists tested, compatible versions for hundreds of libraries without adding them to your build. spring-boot-dependencies is Spring Boot's BOM. When you import it, you write:

build.gradle.kts
implementation("com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind") // no version

and the BOM fills in the version Spring Boot was tested with.

Rule #1 of Spring builds

Never hard-code a version for a library the Spring Boot BOM already manages, unless you have a documented reason (CVE fix before the next Boot patch). Override through the BOM's property instead, so the whole family moves together.

docs.title: 2.4 Version catalogs
docs.text: A version catalog (gradle/libs.versions.toml) is a single file that names every dependency and plugin used in the repo. Build files then refer to libs.spring.boot.starter.web instead of string coordinates. It gives you one place to upgrade, IDE auto-completion, and type safety.

docs.title: 2.5 Multi-module monorepo
docs.text:
One Git repository, many Gradle projects:

  • libs/* — shared libraries (plain JARs, no Spring Boot plugin).
  • services/* — deployable Spring Boot applications (executable JARs).
  • build-logic — convention plugins: reusable build scripts that encode "how every Java module is built" and "how every Spring service is built".

docs.title: 2.6 Spring Initializr
docs.text: start.spring.io (also built into IntelliJ and VS Code) generates a starter project: build file, wrapper, main class, test and application.properties. Good for learning; in a monorepo you will create services from your own template instead.

docs.title: 2.7 The wrapper
docs.text: gradlew / mvnw scripts plus a small JAR pin the exact build-tool version in the repo. Everyone — developers and CI — runs the same version. Always commit the wrapper and always use it.

docs.title: 2.8 Reproducible builds
docs.text: A build is reproducible when the same source produces byte-identical output on any machine. Ingredients: pinned JDK (toolchain), pinned build tool (wrapper), pinned dependencies (BOM + locking), and archives without timestamps or filesystem ordering.

docs.title: 3.1 From source to executable JAR
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[settings.gradle.kts<br/>which projects exist] --> B[Configuration phase<br/>evaluate build scripts,<br/>apply plugins]
    B --> C[Dependency resolution<br/>BOM constraints +<br/>conflict resolution]
    C --> D[compileJava<br/>javac with -parameters]
    D --> E[processResources]
    E --> F[test<br/>JUnit Platform]
    F --> G[bootJar<br/>repackage into<br/>executable JAR]
    G --> H[catalog-service.jar]

Gradle runs in three phases: initialization (read settings.gradle.kts, decide which projects exist), configuration (run every build script, build the task graph), and execution (run only the tasks needed, skipping up-to-date ones).

docs.title: 3.2 How the Spring Boot plugin reacts to other plugins
docs.text:
The org.springframework.boot Gradle plugin does little on its own; it reacts when other plugins are applied:

When you apply Spring Boot plugin adds java bootJar task, bootRun task, configures jar with -plain classifier, adds -parameters to JavaCompile io.spring.dependency-management Imports the spring-boot-dependencies BOM automatically application bootStartScripts, bootDistZip org.graalvm.buildtools.native AOT processing tasks and nativeCompile

Two ways to apply the BOM in Gradle

  1. io.spring.dependency-management plugin — Maven-like behaviour, supports overriding via properties (extra["jackson.version"]).
  2. Gradle native platform — implementation(platform(SpringBootPlugin.BOM_COORDINATES)). Faster and more "Gradle-native", but you override versions with constraints or by resolving a different BOM.

This handbook uses the native platform in convention plugins, which works well with version catalogs.

docs.title: 3.3 Dependency conflict resolution
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[catalog-service] --> B[spring-boot-starter-web]
    A --> C[razorpay-java 1.x]
    B --> D[jackson-databind<br/>BOM version]
    C --> E[jackson-databind<br/>older version]
    D & E --> F{Gradle resolution}
    F -->|highest version wins,<br/>BOM constraint participates| G[jackson-databind<br/>BOM version]
    H{Maven resolution} -->|nearest definition wins,<br/>dependencyManagement overrides| G
  • Gradle picks the highest requested version among all paths; platforms add constraints that participate in that decision. enforcedPlatform forces BOM versions even downward.
  • Maven picks the nearest declaration in the tree, but <dependencyManagement> (which the BOM populates) overrides transitive versions.

Diagnose with:

Terminal
./gradlew :services:catalog-service:dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-databind --configuration runtimeClasspath
mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=com.fasterxml.jackson.core

docs.title: 3.4 Inside the executable JAR
docs.text:
catalog-service.jar (layout)
META-INF/MANIFEST.MF          Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher
                              Start-Class: in.grocery.catalog.CatalogApplication
org/springframework/boot/loader/...   the launcher classes
BOOT-INF/classes/             your compiled code and resources
BOOT-INF/lib/                 every dependency JAR, unpacked is NOT required
BOOT-INF/classpath.idx        classpath order
BOOT-INF/layers.idx           layers for Docker images (Chapter 29)

java -jar starts JarLauncher, which builds a class loader able to read nested JARs from BOOT-INF/lib, then invokes your Start-Class main method.

Loader package changed in Boot 3.2

Since Spring Boot 3.2 the launcher lives in org.springframework.boot.loader.launch. If you have custom Dockerfiles that reference org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher, update them.

docs.title: 3.5 Why -parameters matters
docs.text:
Spring binds constructor and method arguments by name: @PathVariable Long id, @RequestParam String pincode, constructor-bound @ConfigurationProperties, @Cacheable(key = "#sku"). The name must be present in bytecode.

Spring Framework 6.1 removed LocalVariableTableParameterNameDiscoverer (which read debug info). Parameter names now come only from the -parameters compiler flag. The Spring Boot Gradle plugin and spring-boot-starter-parent add it automatically — but if you configure javac yourself in a library module (no Boot plugin), you must add it.

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Multi-module monorepo with a version catalog
5.2 Level 3 — Modern Java in the domain
docs.text:
The pricing module needs to express "a payment either succeeded, failed or is pending" with no other possibilities, and GST depends on whether seller and buyer are in the same state.

in/grocery/common/payment/PaymentResult.java
package in.grocery.common.payment;

import in.grocery.common.money.Money;
import java.time.Instant;

public sealed interface PaymentResult
        permits PaymentResult.Captured, PaymentResult.Failed, PaymentResult.Pending {

    record Captured(String razorpayPaymentId, Money amount, Instant capturedAt) implements PaymentResult {}

    record Failed(String code, String reason, boolean retryable) implements PaymentResult {}

    record Pending(String razorpayOrderId, Instant expiresAt) implements PaymentResult {}
}
in/grocery/common/payment/PaymentMessages.java
package in.grocery.common.payment;

public final class PaymentMessages {

    private PaymentMessages() {}

    public static String describe(PaymentResult result) {
        return switch (result) {                                            // (1)!
            case PaymentResult.Captured(var id, var amount, var at) ->
                    "Paid ₹%s (ref %s)".formatted(amount.amount(), id);
            case PaymentResult.Failed(var code, var reason, var retryable) when retryable ->
                    "Payment failed (%s). Please try again.".formatted(reason);
            case PaymentResult.Failed f ->
                    "Payment declined: " + f.reason();
            case PaymentResult.Pending p ->
                    "Waiting for payment until " + p.expiresAt();
        };                                                                  // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Record deconstruction patterns and a guarded case (when) — Java 21.
  2. No default branch: the compiler proves the switch is exhaustive because the interface is sealed. Add a fourth result type and this stops compiling — exactly what you want.
in/grocery/common/tax/GstCalculator.java
package in.grocery.common.tax;

import in.grocery.common.money.Money;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

public final class GstCalculator {

    public sealed interface GstBreakup permits IntraState, InterState {}
    public record IntraState(Money cgst, Money sgst) implements GstBreakup {}
    public record InterState(Money igst) implements GstBreakup {}

    public GstBreakup calculate(Money taxable, BigDecimal ratePercent,
                                String sellerStateCode, String buyerStateCode) {
        if (sellerStateCode.equals(buyerStateCode)) {
            BigDecimal half = ratePercent.divide(BigDecimal.TWO);
            return new IntraState(taxable.percent(half), taxable.percent(half));
        }
        return new InterState(taxable.percent(ratePercent));
    }
}
in/grocery/common/tax/GstCalculatorTest.java
package in.grocery.common.tax;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import in.grocery.common.money.Money;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class GstCalculatorTest {

    private final GstCalculator calculator = new GstCalculator();

    @Test
    void sameStateSplitsIntoCgstAndSgst() {
        var result = calculator.calculate(Money.ofRupees("1000"), new BigDecimal("5"), "29", "29");
        assertThat(result).isEqualTo(new GstCalculator.IntraState(
                Money.ofRupees("25.00"), Money.ofRupees("25.00")));
    }

    @Test
    void differentStateIsIgst() {
        var result = calculator.calculate(Money.ofRupees("1000"), new BigDecimal("18"), "29", "27");
        assertThat(result).isEqualTo(new GstCalculator.InterState(Money.ofRupees("180.00")));
    }
}

Virtual threads and SequencedCollection — fetching price, stock and delivery ETA for a product page:

in/grocery/catalog/product/ProductPageAssembler.java
package in.grocery.catalog.product;

import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;

public class ProductPageAssembler {

    public record ProductPage(String sku, String price, int stock, String eta) {}

    interface PriceClient { String priceFor(String sku, String pincode); }
    interface StockClient { int stockFor(String sku, String pincode); }
    interface EtaClient { String etaFor(String pincode); }

    private final PriceClient prices;
    private final StockClient stock;
    private final EtaClient eta;

    public ProductPageAssembler(PriceClient prices, StockClient stock, EtaClient eta) {
        this.prices = prices;
        this.stock = stock;
        this.eta = eta;
    }

    public ProductPage assemble(String sku, String pincode) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException {
        try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {   // (1)!
            Future<String> price = executor.submit(() -> prices.priceFor(sku, pincode));
            Future<Integer> qty = executor.submit(() -> stock.stockFor(sku, pincode));
            Future<String> when = executor.submit(() -> eta.etaFor(pincode));
            return new ProductPage(sku, price.get(), qty.get(), when.get());
        }                                                                     // (2)!
    }

    public static String cheapestFirstLabel(List<String> sortedLabels) {
        return sortedLabels.getFirst();                                       // (3)!
    }
}
  1. One cheap virtual thread per blocking call. Three calls run in parallel.
  2. ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19: close() waits for tasks.
  3. SequencedCollection.getFirst() (Java 21) instead of get(0).

Preview: structured concurrency

Java 25 has StructuredTaskScope as a preview API. It cancels sibling tasks if one fails, which the code above does not. Chapter 25 covers it; don't use preview APIs in production services without --enable-preview governance.
