docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist (build level)
docs.text:
• Upgrade to the latest 3.5.x first and fix every deprecation warning (-Werror helps).
  • Upgrade Gradle wrapper to 9.x: ./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.x.
  • Move JDK toolchain to 21 or 25 (17 still works).
  • Bump the Boot version in the version catalog — one line for all 26 services.
  • Replace starters with Boot 4 names (or use classic starters temporarily).
  • Add spring-boot-properties-migrator as runtimeOnly for one release to report renamed properties.
  • Run OpenRewrite's Spring Boot 4 migration recipe (check the current recipe name in the OpenRewrite catalog).
  • Regenerate lock files and SBOMs; review the diff.
  • Update custom Dockerfiles referencing launcher classes.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. One version source. Boot version lives in libs.versions.toml; nothing else declares Spring-managed versions.
  2. Toolchains, not JAVA_HOME. The build declares its JDK.
  3. Convention plugins over subprojects {}. Cross-project configuration in the root script breaks configuration cache and hides logic.
  4. Lock and scan. Dependency locking + SBOM + SCA scanner in CI.
  5. Warnings are errors. Deprecations are future upgrade breakages.
  6. api vs implementation discipline in libraries: expose only what consumers must compile against.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Overriding a BOM-managed version inline

build.gradle.kts
implementation("com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind:2.13.0") // drifts from other Jackson modules

✅ Override the whole family through the BOM (when truly needed)

Kotlin
// with io.spring.dependency-management
extra["jackson-bom.version"] = "2.19.x"
// or with native platforms: import the newer jackson-bom platform AFTER the Spring Boot BOM

❌ Root-level subprojects {} configuration

build.gradle.kts
subprojects {
    apply(plugin = "java")
    dependencies { "implementation"("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web") } // libraries get web too!
}

✅ Explicit convention plugins — plugins { id("grocery.spring-service") } only in services.

❌ Fat shared "common" library pulling Spring Web, JPA and Kafka into every service.

✅ Small, focused libraries (grocery-common holds only domain value types) — heavy integrations become starters (Chapter 41).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix NoSuchMethodError / NoClassDefFoundError at startup Mixed library versions dependencyInsight; remove inline versions; align via BOM ClassNotFoundException: javax.* Dependency not migrated to Jakarta EE Upgrade library or find Jakarta variant Parameter name information not available Missing -parameters Add compiler flag (automatic with Boot plugin) Unsupported class file major version 69 Tool (old Gradle/ASM) doesn't understand Java 25 bytecode Upgrade Gradle/plugins; use toolchain CI resolves different versions than local No locking, dynamic versions Dependency locking, no + versions Duplicate/plain JAR in Docker image Both jar and bootJar produced Disable jar task in services Slow builds No build cache / configuration cache org.gradle.caching=true, --configuration-cache

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Wrapper committed and checksum-verified (distributionSha256Sum)
  • Toolchain declared; CI and local use same JDK vendor/version
  • Single BOM import; no inline versions for managed libraries
  • Dependency locking enabled
  • SBOM generated and exposed
  • -parameters present in all modules
  • build-info generated for /actuator/info
  • Architecture tests in every service

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is the difference between Spring Framework and Spring Boot?

Short answer: Spring Framework provides the core features — dependency injection, MVC, transactions, data access. Spring Boot sits on top and removes setup work: starters, auto-configuration, embedded server, executable JARs and production features like Actuator.

Deep answer: Boot doesn't replace any Spring feature; it configures them for you based on what's on the classpath and in your properties, and it lets you override any default by defining your own bean.

Follow-ups: What is a starter? What does @SpringBootApplication contain?

Red flags: "Spring Boot is a different framework from Spring."

B1 · What is a Spring Boot starter?

Short answer: A dependency descriptor that pulls in a coherent set of libraries for one capability, e.g. spring-boot-starter-webmvc brings Spring MVC, Jackson and embedded Tomcat.

Deep answer: A starter usually contains no code — just a POM listing dependencies. Auto-configuration classes in Boot's modules then detect those libraries and configure beans.

Follow-ups: How would you create your own starter? (Chapter 41)

Red flags: Thinking starters contain the configuration code themselves.

B1 · Why do we not write versions for Spring dependencies in the build file?

Short answer: The Spring Boot BOM (spring-boot-dependencies) manages them. Importing it gives tested, compatible versions.

Follow-ups: How do you override one? What is a BOM?

Red flags: "Gradle picks the latest version automatically."

B1 · What is the Gradle/Maven wrapper and why commit it?

Short answer: Scripts (gradlew, mvnw) that download and run a pinned build-tool version so every developer and CI uses the same one.

Red flags: Installing Gradle globally and running gradle build in CI.

B1 · What Java version does Spring Boot 3 / 4 require?

Short answer: Both require Java 17 as the minimum. Boot 4 supports newer versions including Java 25.

Follow-ups: Name Java 17+ features you use in Spring code.

B1 · Why use a record for a DTO?

Short answer: Immutable, concise, auto-generated equals/hashCode/toString, and Jackson and Spring binding support them.

Follow-ups: Can a JPA entity be a record? (No — entities need a no-arg constructor and mutable state for proxies.)

B1 · What happens when you run java -jar app.jar on a Spring Boot JAR?

Short answer: The manifest's Main-Class is Spring Boot's JarLauncher, which sets up a class loader for nested JARs in BOOT-INF/lib and then calls your application's main method (the Start-Class).

Red flags: "The JVM directly runs my main class."

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Explain implementation vs api vs compileOnly vs runtimeOnly in Gradle.

Short answer: implementation — needed to compile and run, not exposed to consumers. api — exposed transitively to consumers' compile classpath (only in java-library). compileOnly — compile time only (annotations, provided APIs). runtimeOnly — only at runtime (JDBC drivers, properties-migrator).

Deep answer: Using implementation by default reduces recompilation and prevents consumers from depending on your internals.

Follow-ups: Where would you put jspecify? A JDBC driver?

B2 · How does Gradle resolve version conflicts vs Maven?

Short answer: Gradle chooses the highest version across the graph (constraints and platforms participate). Maven chooses the nearest declaration but dependencyManagement overrides transitive versions.

Follow-ups: How do you diagnose? (dependencyInsight, mvn dependency:tree) What is enforcedPlatform?

Red flags: Not knowing the difference and just adding exclusions until it works.

B2 · What is a version catalog and why use it?

Short answer: A TOML file declaring all dependency and plugin coordinates with aliases. Single upgrade point, type-safe accessors, shared across modules and build-logic.

B2 · Your app fails with Parameter name information not available. Why?

Short answer: Code compiled without -parameters. Spring 6.1+ no longer reads debug info for parameter names.

Deep answer: Happens typically in a library module built without the Boot plugin, or custom javac config. Fix: add the flag or use explicit names (@PathVariable("id")).

B2 · How would you structure a monorepo with shared code and many services?

Short answer: libs/ for small focused libraries, services/ for deployables, build-logic/ convention plugins, central version catalog, repositories declared once in settings.

Follow-ups: What goes into a shared library and what must not?

Red flags: A giant common module with every dependency.

B2 · Sealed interfaces — how do they help in a Spring codebase?

Short answer: They model closed result hierarchies (payment results, validation outcomes). Combined with pattern-matching switch, the compiler enforces that every case is handled.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · The Spring Boot Gradle plugin 'reacts' to other plugins. What does that mean?

Short answer: It registers callbacks via plugins.withType(...). Applying java adds bootJar/bootRun and -parameters; applying io.spring.dependency-management imports the BOM; applying GraalVM's plugin adds AOT tasks.

Follow-ups: Why does jar produce a -plain JAR?

B3 · io.spring.dependency-management plugin vs platform(...) — which do you choose?

Short answer: The plugin gives Maven-style semantics and easy property overrides but adds its own resolution logic. Native platforms are faster, align with Gradle's model and version catalogs. For large monorepos I prefer native platforms in convention plugins.

Follow-ups: How do you override a single library with native platforms? (Constraint, or import a newer family BOM after Boot's.)

B3 · How do you make a Spring Boot build reproducible?

Short answer: Toolchain + wrapper with checksum + BOM + dependency locking + reproducible archive settings + build-info without timestamps.

Follow-ups: How do you verify it? (Build twice, compare checksums.)

B3 · Explain the executable JAR's structure and why it matters for Docker.

Short answer: Classes in BOOT-INF/classes, libs in BOOT-INF/lib, launcher at root, layers.idx groups files by change frequency. Layered extraction lets Docker cache dependency layers so only your code layer changes per build.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How would you roll out a Spring Boot major upgrade across 26 services?

Short answer: Centralize versions (catalog + conventions) first. Upgrade to latest 3.5.x, eliminate deprecations with -Werror. Then switch the catalog to 4.x on a branch, apply OpenRewrite, fix shared libraries first, then services in dependency order behind CI. Release services incrementally; they communicate over HTTP/Kafka so mixed versions are fine.

Deep answer: Key risks: shared libraries compiled against Jackson 2 used by Boot 4 services; custom auto-configurations; Security DSL changes. Use a compatibility matrix and canary deployments with SLO monitoring.

Follow-ups: How do you handle a shared library used by both 3.5 and 4.x services during transition?

Red flags: Big-bang upgrade with no incremental release plan.

B4 · A transitive dependency has a critical CVE and Boot's next patch is two weeks away. What do you do?

Short answer: Override that library family's version through the BOM mechanism (property or a newer family BOM), add a comment with the CVE and a removal ticket, run full tests, ship. Remove the override when Boot's patch arrives.

Follow-ups: How do you find every service affected? (SBOMs / /actuator/sbom, SCA dashboards.)

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What build standards would you set for an engineering org of 100+ Java engineers?

Short answer: Golden-path templates, convention plugins published internally, central version governance, mandatory SBOM + SCA + license checks, reproducible builds, architecture tests, build performance SLOs (remote build cache), and a documented override process via ADRs.

Follow-ups: How do you balance team autonomy with standardization?

B5 · Monorepo vs polyrepo for a 26-service platform — defend your choice.

Short answer: Monorepo for a single product team structure: atomic cross-service changes, one version catalog, easy refactoring, consistent tooling. Costs: build performance at scale (needs build cache, affected-module CI), access control, and blast radius. Polyrepo when teams/products are independent and release cadence varies widely.

Red flags: Dogmatic answer without costs.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · After adding the Razorpay SDK, order-service fails at startup with NoSuchMethodError in Jackson.

Run ./gradlew :services:order-service:dependencyInsight --dependency jackson. The SDK likely brings an old jackson-databind or a different Jackson module version. With Gradle, highest wins — so if the SDK requests a newer module than Boot's BOM, modules can become misaligned. Fix by aligning the Jackson family through its BOM, excluding the SDK's transitive Jackson, and adding a test that starts the context.

Scenario · Builds pass locally but CI produces a JAR with a different Netty version.

Dynamic version or unlocked transitive resolution plus a newly published artifact. Enable dependency locking, commit lockfiles, fail CI on lock drift, and forbid +/latest.release versions.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Pincode value type

Create a record Pincode in grocery-common that accepts exactly six digits, first digit 1–9, and exposes region() returning the first digit as the postal region. Include tests.

Solution Pincode.java
package in.grocery.common.address;

import java.util.Objects;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;

public record Pincode(String value) {

    private static final Pattern FORMAT = Pattern.compile("[1-9][0-9]{5}");

    public Pincode {
        Objects.requireNonNull(value, "pincode");
        value = value.strip();
        if (!FORMAT.matcher(value).matches()) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Invalid pincode: " + value);
        }
    }

    public int region() {
        return value.charAt(0) - '0';
    }
}
PincodeTest.java
package in.grocery.common.address;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatIllegalArgumentException;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.ParameterizedTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.params.provider.ValueSource;

class PincodeTest {

    @Test
    void acceptsValidPincode() {
        assertThat(new Pincode(" 560001 ").region()).isEqualTo(5);
    }

    @ParameterizedTest
    @ValueSource(strings = {"056001", "56001", "5600011", "56000A", ""})
    void rejectsInvalid(String raw) {
        assertThatIllegalArgumentException().isThrownBy(() -> new Pincode(raw));
    }
}

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Spring Boot 3 and 4 both need Java 17+; this handbook uses 21 for 3.5 and 25 for 4.x.
  • The Spring Boot BOM is the single source of truth for versions — never fight it with inline versions.
  • Version catalog + convention plugins make a 26-service upgrade a one-line change.
  • -parameters is mandatory since Framework 6.1; the Boot plugin adds it, plain libraries must add it themselves.
  • Toolchains, wrapper, locking and reproducible archives make builds identical everywhere.
  • Boot 4 introduces modular starters and Jackson 3 — plan build changes before code changes.
  • Records and sealed types are the foundation of clean domain code in every later chapter.

00 Handbook Overview · 02 IoC & Dependency Injection

docs.title: 02 · Spring Framework Core — IoC & Dependency Injection
1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Every other chapter in this handbook — web, data, security, messaging, AI — is just beans managed by a container. If you understand how the container finds, creates, wires and scopes beans, you can reason about almost any Spring behaviour: why @Transactional sometimes does nothing, why a test loads the wrong implementation, why startup fails with "expected single matching bean but found 2".

In the grocery marketplace, the cart service needs a PricingService, which needs a GstCalculator, a PromotionEngine and a PriceRepository. Without a container, the main method would construct all of that by hand, in the right order, and every test would repeat it. Swapping Razorpay for a mock gateway in local development would mean editing code. Inversion of Control moves that responsibility into Spring: you describe what you need, the container decides how and when to build it.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — beans, injection, stereotypes B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — qualifiers, scopes, ObjectProvider, conditional wiring B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5 — bean definitions, full vs lite @Configuration, circular references B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 3, 6, 7 — programmatic registration, null-safety, startup design B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 7, 8, 9 — container design trade-offs, governance

docs.title: 2.1 Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection
docs.text:
Inversion of Control (IoC) — objects don't create their collaborators; something outside gives them collaborators. Dependency Injection (DI) is the technique: dependencies are passed in (usually via the constructor).

Analogy: a restaurant kitchen. The chef (your class) doesn't grow vegetables or buy knives. The kitchen manager (container) makes sure the right ingredients and tools are at the station before service starts.

Benefits: loose coupling, testability (pass a fake in tests), configurability (choose implementation by profile/property), and centralized lifecycle management.

docs.title: 2.2 Bean
docs.text: A bean is an object whose lifecycle is managed by the Spring container. Not every object is a bean: entities, DTOs, value objects like Money are created with new or by frameworks — they are data, not services.

docs.title: 2.3 BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext
docs.text:
BeanFactory ApplicationContext Role Core DI container BeanFactory + enterprise features Instantiation Lazy by default Eagerly pre-instantiates singletons at refresh Events No ApplicationEventPublisher i18n No MessageSource Resources Basic ResourceLoader/ResourcePatternResolver Environment/profiles No Environment Post-processors Must register manually Detected and applied automatically

In practice you always use an ApplicationContext. Spring Boot creates AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext for servlet apps (the exact class names vary slightly between Boot 3 and 4).

docs.title: 2.4 Bean definitions
docs.text: Before any object exists, Spring builds a BeanDefinition — metadata: class, scope, lazy flag, constructor arguments, init/destroy methods, primary flag, dependencies. Definitions come from component scanning, @Bean methods, @Import, auto-configuration, or programmatic registration.

docs.title: 2.5 Ways to declare beans
docs.text:
Mechanism Use when @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller/@RestController Your own classes @Bean method in @Configuration Third-party classes, or construction needs logic @Import Pull in configuration explicitly (libraries, starters) Auto-configuration Boot's conditional defaults BeanRegistrar (Framework 7) / BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor Programmatic, dynamic registration

Stereotypes: @Service and @Controller are semantic @Components. @Repository additionally enables persistence exception translation (via PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor) — vendor exceptions become DataAccessExceptions.

docs.title: 2.6 @Configuration full mode vs lite mode
docs.text:
• Full mode: @Configuration classes (with proxyBeanMethods = true, the default) are CGLIB-subclassed. Calling one @Bean method from another returns the same singleton from the container.
  • Lite mode: @Bean methods in a @Component class, or @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false). Inter-bean method calls are plain Java calls and create new instances.

Spring Boot's own auto-configurations use proxyBeanMethods = false for faster startup and smaller footprint, and inject dependencies as method parameters instead.

docs.title: 2.7 Injection styles
docs.text:
Style Verdict Constructor ✅ Default. Immutable (final), mandatory deps explicit, easy to test, fails fast Setter Optional dependencies or reconfigurable beans only Field (@Autowired on field) ❌ Hidden dependencies, no final, needs reflection in tests

Since Spring 4.3, a class with a single constructor doesn't need @Autowired.

docs.title: 2.8 Resolving ambiguity
docs.text:
When more than one bean matches a type:

Tool Meaning @Qualifier("name") Pick by qualifier/bean name at the injection point Custom qualifier annotation Type-safe qualifier (@Gateway(RAZORPAY)) @Primary Default choice when not otherwise specified @Fallback (6.2+) Use only if no other candidate exists — the inverse of @Primary Parameter name matching bean name Last-resort match (requires -parameters) Inject List<T> / Map<String,T> Take all candidates

docs.title: 2.9 ObjectProvider<T>
docs.text: A lazy, optional handle to beans: getIfAvailable(), getIfUnique(), stream(), orderedStream(), getObject(args). Use it for optional dependencies, prototype lookup from singletons, and breaking eager initialization chains.

docs.title: 2.10 Scopes
docs.text:
Scope Instances Typical use singleton (default) One per container Stateless services prototype New per request to container Stateful helpers, builders request One per HTTP request Request-scoped context session One per HTTP session Rare in stateless APIs application One per ServletContext Rare websocket One per WebSocket session STOMP apps Custom (thread, tenant) You define Multi-tenancy (Chapter 38)

Injecting a shorter-lived bean into a singleton requires a scoped proxy (proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS) or ObjectProvider.

docs.title: 2.11 Lazy initialization
docs.text: @Lazy (per bean or injection point) or spring.main.lazy-initialization=true (global). Faster startup, but configuration errors surface on first request instead of at startup.

docs.title: 2.12 Circular dependencies
docs.text: A → B → A. Spring Boot forbids them by default since 2.6 (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false). Constructor-injection cycles can never be resolved without proxies. A cycle is a design smell: usually a missing third component or a misplaced responsibility.

docs.title: 2.13 @DependsOn
docs.text: Forces initialization order when there is no direct reference (e.g. a Flyway migration must run before a cache warmer). Prefer real dependencies or lifecycle phases (Chapter 03).

docs.title: 2.14 Programmatic registration — BeanRegistrar (Framework 7)
docs.text: Framework 7 adds a first-class API for registering beans programmatically with a functional style, designed to be AOT- and native-friendly. Useful when the number or type of beans depends on configuration (e.g. one client bean per configured payment gateway).

docs.title: 2.15 Null-safety with JSpecify
docs.text: Framework 7 / Boot 4 adopt JSpecify annotations: @NullMarked on a package means "everything is non-null unless marked @Nullable". Tools like NullAway and IDEs then flag null misuse at compile time. Framework 6.x uses Spring's own org.springframework.lang.Nullable.

docs.title: 3.1 Container refresh — where beans come from
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as SpringApplication
    participant Ctx as ApplicationContext
    participant Reg as BeanDefinitionRegistry
    participant BFPP as BeanFactoryPostProcessors
    participant BF as DefaultListableBeanFactory

    App->>Ctx: refresh()
    Ctx->>BFPP: invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors
    Note over BFPP: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses<br/>@Configuration, @ComponentScan, @Import,<br/>@Bean, auto-configuration imports
    BFPP->>Reg: register BeanDefinitions
    Ctx->>BF: registerBeanPostProcessors
    Note over BF: AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor,<br/>CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor,<br/>AOP auto-proxy creator...
    Ctx->>BF: preInstantiateSingletons()
    loop each non-lazy singleton
        BF->>BF: getBean(name) → createBean
    end
    Ctx->>App: ContextRefreshedEvent

Key class: ConfigurationClassPostProcessor — a BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor that turns annotations into bean definitions. Nothing is instantiated while definitions are being collected.

docs.title: 3.2 Creating one bean
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[getBean pricingService] --> B{singleton in cache?<br/>DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry}
    B -- yes --> Z[return]
    B -- no --> C[resolve BeanDefinition<br/>merge parent definitions]
    C --> D[createBeanInstance<br/>choose constructor or factory method]
    D --> E[resolve constructor args<br/>DependencyDescriptor → resolveDependency]
    E --> F[populateBean<br/>field/setter injection]
    F --> G[initializeBean<br/>Aware → BPP before → init → BPP after]
    G --> H[BPP after may wrap in AOP proxy]
    H --> I[register in singleton cache]
    I --> Z

Main methods live in AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory: createBean → doCreateBean → createBeanInstance → populateBean → initializeBean. Dependency resolution is DefaultListableBeanFactory.resolveDependency, which:

  1. Finds candidates by type (findAutowireCandidates).
  2. Filters by qualifiers (QualifierAnnotationAutowireCandidateResolver).
  3. If still multiple: prefers @Primary, then non-@Fallback, then highest @Priority, then name match with the parameter/field name.
  4. Throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException if still ambiguous, or NoSuchBeanDefinitionException if none and required.

docs.title: 3.3 Singleton caches and circular references
docs.text:
DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry keeps three maps:

Cache Holds singletonObjects Fully initialized beans earlySingletonObjects Early references already handed out singletonFactories Factories that can produce an early reference (possibly proxied)

For setter/field cycles, Spring can expose an early reference to A while B is being created. For constructor cycles this is impossible — A's constructor can't run until B exists. Boot disables early-reference cycles entirely by default, so both fail fast with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException.

docs.title: 3.4 Full-mode @Configuration proxy
3.5 Scoped proxies
docs.text: A request-scoped RequestContext injected into a singleton CartDelegate is actually a proxy created at startup. Every method call on the proxy looks up the real instance for the current request from RequestContextHolder. Outside a request, calls throw ScopeNotActiveException (older versions: IllegalStateException).

docs.title: 4. Hands-On Code — Level 1 (Beginner)
docs.text: Goal: see DI working with constructor injection, and understand what happens without Spring.

docs.title: 4.1 Without a container
4.2 With Spring
4.3 Unit test — no Spring needed
5.1 Level 2 — Multiple implementations: payment gateways
docs.text:
The payment service supports Razorpay in production and a fake gateway locally, and can refund through a secondary gateway.

in/grocery/payment/gateway/PaymentGateway.java
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import java.math.BigDecimal;

public interface PaymentGateway {
    String code();
    String createOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amountInRupees);
}
in/grocery/payment/gateway/RazorpayGateway.java
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Primary                                                   // (1)!
public class RazorpayGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String code() { return "RAZORPAY"; }
    public String createOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return "order_rzp_" + orderId;                     // real HTTP call in Chapter 19
    }
}
  1. Default choice when a single PaymentGateway is requested.
in/grocery/payment/gateway/CashfreeGateway.java
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Qualifier("secondary")
public class CashfreeGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String code() { return "CASHFREE"; }
    public String createOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return "cf_" + orderId;
    }
}
in/grocery/payment/gateway/NoOpGateway.java
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Fallback;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Fallback                                                   // (1)!
public class NoOpGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String code() { return "NOOP"; }
    public String createOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) { return "noop_" + orderId; }
}
  1. Spring Framework 6.2+: chosen only if no other non-fallback candidate remains.
in/grocery/payment/service/PaymentService.java
package in.grocery.payment.service;

import in.grocery.payment.gateway.PaymentGateway;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.function.Function;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final PaymentGateway primary;
    private final PaymentGateway secondary;
    private final Map<String, PaymentGateway> byCode;

    public PaymentService(PaymentGateway primary,                          // (1)!
                          @Qualifier("secondary") PaymentGateway secondary, // (2)!
                          List<PaymentGateway> all) {                      // (3)!
        this.primary = primary;
        this.secondary = secondary;
        this.byCode = all.stream().collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableMap(PaymentGateway::code, Function.identity()));
    }

    public String startPayment(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return primary.createOrder(orderId, amount);
    }

    public String startWith(String gatewayCode, String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        PaymentGateway gateway = byCode.get(gatewayCode);
        if (gateway == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unsupported gateway " + gatewayCode);
        return gateway.createOrder(orderId, amount);
    }

    public String failover(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        return secondary.createOrder(orderId, amount);
    }
}
  1. @Primary resolves this to Razorpay.
  2. Qualifier picks Cashfree.
  3. All three implementations, ordered by @Order/Ordered if present.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — Full vs lite @Configuration
5.3 Level 3 — Scopes: request context and prototype builders
5.4 Level 3 — Optional dependencies and conditional wiring
5.5 Level 3 — Diagnosing a circular dependency
docs.text:
OrderService.java
@Service class OrderService { OrderService(InventoryService inv) {} }
@Service class InventoryService { InventoryService(OrderService orders) {} }  // ❌ cycle
Startup failure
The dependencies of some of the beans in the application context form a cycle:
┌─────┐
|  orderService defined in file [.../OrderService.class]
↑     ↓
|  inventoryService defined in file [.../InventoryService.class]
└─────┘
Action: Relying upon circular references is discouraged and they are prohibited by default.

✅ Fix by design: inventory shouldn't call back into orders. It publishes an event (StockReserved) or the shared logic moves to a third component (ReservationPolicy) that both depend on.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Before
        O1[OrderService] <--> I1[InventoryService]
    end
    subgraph After
        O2[OrderService] --> R[ReservationPolicy]
        I2[InventoryService] --> R
        I2 -. StockReserved event .-> O2
    end

docs.title: 6.1 Type-safe qualifier + configuration-driven gateway registry
docs.text:
Qualifier strings are typo-prone. A custom annotation makes them compile-checked.

in/grocery/payment/gateway/Gateway.java
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import java.lang.annotation.Documented;
import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Qualifier;

@Qualifier                                                 // (1)!
@Documented
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD, ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.FIELD})
public @interface Gateway {
    Provider value();

    enum Provider { RAZORPAY, CASHFREE }
}
  1. Meta-annotated with @Qualifier, so Spring treats it (and its attribute) as a qualifier.
in/grocery/payment/config/PaymentProperties.java
package in.grocery.payment.config;

import in.grocery.payment.gateway.Gateway.Provider;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull;
import java.time.Duration;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("grocery.payment")
public record PaymentProperties(
        @NotNull Provider primary,
        Provider secondary,
        @NotNull Duration timeout) {}
application.yml
grocery:
  payment:
    primary: RAZORPAY
    secondary: CASHFREE
    timeout: 3s
in/grocery/payment/gateway/GatewayRegistry.java
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import in.grocery.payment.config.PaymentProperties;
import in.grocery.payment.gateway.Gateway.Provider;
import java.util.EnumMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.jspecify.annotations.Nullable;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.AnnotationUtils;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.aop.support.AopUtils;

@Component
public class GatewayRegistry {

    private final Map<Provider, PaymentGateway> gateways = new EnumMap<>(Provider.class);
    private final Provider primary;
    private final @Nullable Provider secondary;               // (1)!

    public GatewayRegistry(List<PaymentGateway> all, PaymentProperties props) {
        for (PaymentGateway g : all) {
            Gateway ann = AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation(AopUtils.getTargetClass(g), Gateway.class); // (2)!
            if (ann != null && gateways.putIfAbsent(ann.value(), g) != null) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Duplicate gateway for " + ann.value());
            }
        }
        if (!gateways.containsKey(props.primary())) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Primary gateway " + props.primary() + " is not registered"); // (3)!
        }
        this.primary = props.primary();
        this.secondary = props.secondary();
    }

    public PaymentGateway primary() {
        return gateways.get(primary);
    }

    public Optional<PaymentGateway> secondary() {
        return Optional.ofNullable(secondary).map(gateways::get);
    }
}
  1. JSpecify: explicit about what can be null. With @NullMarked on the package, everything else is non-null.
  2. AopUtils.getTargetClass — beans may be AOP proxies (metrics, retries); annotations live on the target class.
  3. Fail at startup, not on the first payment at 2 a.m.
in/grocery/payment/package-info.java
@NullMarked
package in.grocery.payment;

import org.jspecify.annotations.NullMarked;

@NullMarked scope

@NullMarked on a package applies to that package only, not sub-packages. Add a package-info.java to each package, or place it on a module declaration.

in/grocery/payment/gateway/RazorpayGateway.java (production shape)
package in.grocery.payment.gateway;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Gateway(Gateway.Provider.RAZORPAY)
public class RazorpayGateway implements PaymentGateway {
    public String code() { return "RAZORPAY"; }
    public String createOrder(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) { return "order_rzp_" + orderId; }
}

Injection points can also use the qualifier directly:

Type-safe qualifier + configuration-driven gateway registry (snippet)
public RefundService(@Gateway(Gateway.Provider.CASHFREE) PaymentGateway refunds) { ... }

docs.title: 6.2 Programmatic registration with BeanRegistrar (Spring Framework 7)
docs.text:
Sellers can be onboarded with per-seller webhook signing keys. One WebhookVerifier bean per configured seller group:

Spring Boot 4.x (Framework 7)Spring Boot 3.5 (Framework 6.2) in/grocery/seller/config/WebhookVerifierRegistrar.java
package in.grocery.seller.config;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanRegistrar;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.BeanRegistry;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.Binder;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.Bindable;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;

public class WebhookVerifierRegistrar implements BeanRegistrar {

    public record WebhookVerifier(String group, String secretRef) {}

    @Override
    public void register(BeanRegistry registry, Environment env) {
        List<String> groups = Binder.get(env)
                .bind("grocery.seller.webhook-groups", Bindable.listOf(String.class))
                .orElse(List.of());

        for (String group : groups) {
            registry.registerBean("webhookVerifier-" + group, WebhookVerifier.class,
                    spec -> spec.supplier(ctx -> new WebhookVerifier(group, "vault:seller/" + group)));
        }
    }
}
in/grocery/seller/config/SellerConfig.java
package in.grocery.seller.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Import;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@Import(WebhookVerifierRegistrar.class)
class SellerConfig {}
in/grocery/seller/config/WebhookVerifierRegistrar.java
package in.grocery.seller.config;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.beans.BeansException;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.support.BeanDefinitionRegistry;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.support.BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.support.RootBeanDefinition;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.Bindable;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.Binder;
import org.springframework.context.EnvironmentAware;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;

public class WebhookVerifierRegistrar implements BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor, EnvironmentAware {

    public record WebhookVerifier(String group, String secretRef) {}

    private Environment env;

    @Override
    public void setEnvironment(Environment environment) { this.env = environment; }

    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanDefinitionRegistry(BeanDefinitionRegistry registry) throws BeansException {
        List<String> groups = Binder.get(env)
                .bind("grocery.seller.webhook-groups", Bindable.listOf(String.class))
                .orElse(List.of());
        for (String group : groups) {
            var def = new RootBeanDefinition(WebhookVerifier.class,
                    () -> new WebhookVerifier(group, "vault:seller/" + group));
            registry.registerBeanDefinition("webhookVerifier-" + group, def);
        }
    }
}

Register it with a static @Bean method so it's created before regular beans:

Programmatic registration with BeanRegistrar (Spring Framework 7) (snippet)
@Bean
static WebhookVerifierRegistrar webhookVerifierRegistrar() { return new WebhookVerifierRegistrar(); }

Verify

BeanRegistrar is new in Spring Framework 7. Confirm the exact BeanRegistry / spec method names (supplier, prototype, lazyInit, description) against the Framework 7 reference — Core Technologies › Programmatic Bean Registration.

docs.title: 6.3 Production test: context wiring is correct
6.4 Startup-time guardrails
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace org.springframework.lang.Nullable/NonNull with JSpecify equivalents; add @NullMarked package by package.
  • Replace @MockBean/@SpyBean with @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean (do it on 3.5 first).
  • Review custom BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessors — consider BeanRegistrar for AOT friendliness.
  • Remove any allow-circular-references: true by fixing cycles before upgrading.
  • Remove allow-bean-definition-overriding: true; use @ConditionalOnMissingBean or @Primary.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Constructor injection, final fields, no @Autowired on single constructors.
  2. Program to interfaces at integration boundaries (gateways, clients, repositories); concrete classes are fine for internal services.
  3. Keep beans stateless. Singletons are shared across all request threads.
  4. Fail at startup: validate configuration and wiring in constructors or @PostConstruct.
  5. proxyBeanMethods = false for your @Configuration classes; inject via parameters.
  6. Type-safe qualifiers over strings.
  7. No cycles — treat BeanCurrentlyInCreationException as a design review trigger.
  8. Too many constructor parameters (> 5–6) means the class does too much. Split it.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Field injection

CartService.java
@Service
public class CartService {
    @Autowired private PricingService pricing;   // hidden, mutable, reflection-only in tests
}

✅ Constructor injection

CartService.java
@Service
public class CartService {
    private final PricingService pricing;
    public CartService(PricingService pricing) { this.pricing = pricing; }
}

❌ Mutable state in a singleton

CheckoutService.java
@Service
public class CheckoutService {
    private Cart currentCart;                    // shared across ALL users — data leak
}

✅ Pass state as method arguments or use a request/prototype scope deliberately.

❌ Service locator

Anti-patterns (snippet)
PricingService p = applicationContext.getBean(PricingService.class); // hides dependencies

✅ Inject it, or ObjectProvider<PricingService> if it's truly optional/lazy.

❌ Calling a @Bean method in lite mode

✅ Declare the dependency as a @Bean method parameter.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix NoSuchBeanDefinitionException Class not scanned (outside base package), missing starter, condition not met Move package, @Import, check --debug condition report NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException Multiple candidates @Primary, @Qualifier, @Fallback, or inject List BeanCurrentlyInCreationException / cycle report Circular dependency Redesign; events; extract component Prototype bean behaves like singleton Injected directly into singleton ObjectProvider or scoped proxy ScopeNotActiveException Request-scoped bean used outside request (async, scheduler) Pass data explicitly; don't use request scope in async code Annotation not found on bean Bean is a proxy AopUtils.getTargetClass, AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation Slow startup Heavy constructors, eager remote calls Move I/O to ApplicationRunner/SmartLifecycle; use /actuator/startup

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• No field injection (enforce with ArchUnit)
  • Circular references and bean overriding disabled
  • Configuration validated at startup
  • Qualifiers are type-safe
  • @NullMarked on packages (Boot 4)
  • Startup time measured and budgeted
  • Wiring tests with ApplicationContextRunner for conditional beans

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is Inversion of Control?

Short answer: Objects don't create their dependencies; an external container provides them. Control over object creation and wiring is inverted from the class to Spring.

Follow-ups: What's the difference between IoC and DI?

Red flags: Confusing IoC with "Spring calls my methods" only.

B1 · What are the types of dependency injection? Which is preferred?

Short answer: Constructor, setter and field. Constructor injection is preferred — immutable, explicit, testable, fails fast.

Red flags: "Field injection because it's shorter."

B1 · Difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller?

Short answer: All register beans via scanning. @Service/@Controller are semantic. @Repository adds persistence exception translation. @Controller is also detected by Spring MVC as a handler.

B1 · What is the default bean scope?

Short answer: Singleton — one instance per application context.

Follow-ups: Is a Spring singleton the same as the GoF Singleton pattern? (No — one per container, not per JVM/class loader.)

B1 · Do you need @Autowired on a constructor?

Short answer: Not if the class has exactly one constructor (since Spring 4.3). With multiple constructors, mark the one to use.

B1 · What is @Bean and when do you use it instead of @Component?

Short answer: A method-level annotation in a configuration class that returns an object to register as a bean. Use it for third-party classes you can't annotate, or when construction needs logic.

B1 · What happens if two beans implement the same interface and you inject the interface?

Short answer: Startup fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException unless you use @Primary, @Qualifier, @Fallback, a matching parameter name, or inject a List.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Explain @Primary vs @Qualifier vs @Fallback.

Short answer: @Qualifier selects explicitly at the injection point and wins over everything. @Primary marks the default candidate. @Fallback (6.2) marks a candidate used only if no other remains.

Follow-ups: Two @Primary beans of the same type? (Ambiguity error.)

B2 · How do you inject a prototype bean into a singleton correctly?

Short answer: Inject ObjectProvider<T> (or Provider<T>) and call getObject() each time, use a scoped proxy, or a @Lookup method. Direct injection gives one instance forever.

B2 · What is ObjectProvider and when do you use it?

Short answer: A lazy/optional handle for beans: getIfAvailable, ifAvailable, getIfUnique, stream. Used for optional dependencies, prototypes, and lazy lookup without ApplicationContext.

B2 · Full vs lite @Configuration — what's the difference?

Short answer: Full mode (proxyBeanMethods = true) CGLIB-proxies the class so calling a @Bean method returns the container singleton. Lite mode doesn't proxy; calls create new objects. Lite mode is faster and native-friendly; inject dependencies via method parameters.

Red flags: Not knowing inter-bean calls can create duplicate instances.

B2 · How do you inject a request-scoped bean into a singleton?

Short answer: Use proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS (or INTERFACES). The singleton holds a proxy that resolves the current request's instance on each call.

Follow-ups: What happens in an @Async method? (Scope not active.)

B2 · Why does Spring Boot forbid circular dependencies by default?

Short answer: They indicate poor design, make initialization order fragile, and with constructor injection can't be resolved. Boot 2.6+ sets allow-circular-references=false.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through how Spring creates a singleton bean.

Short answer: getBean → check singleton cache → merge definition → createBean → resolveBeforeInstantiation (BPPs can short-circuit) → createBeanInstance (constructor resolution) → populateBean → initializeBean (Aware, BPP before, init methods, BPP after — proxies created here) → register singleton.

Follow-ups: Where does @Autowired field injection happen? (AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor.postProcessProperties during populateBean.)

B3 · How does Spring resolve which bean to inject when multiple match?

Short answer: DefaultListableBeanFactory.resolveDependency → candidates by type → qualifier filtering → primary → non-fallback → @Priority → name match → else exception.

B3 · Explain the three-level singleton cache.

Short answer: singletonObjects (complete), earlySingletonObjects (early references handed out), singletonFactories (produce early refs, possibly wrapped by SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor.getEarlyBeanReference so the early ref is already the proxy). Enables setter/field cycles; not constructor cycles.

B3 · What is a BeanDefinition and who creates it?

Short answer: Metadata describing how to create a bean. Created by ConfigurationClassPostProcessor (scan, @Bean, @Import), by auto-configuration processing, or programmatically. Definitions can be modified by BeanFactoryPostProcessors before any bean exists.

B3 · Why might an annotation lookup on an injected bean return null?

Short answer: The bean is a proxy (CGLIB subclass or JDK proxy). Use AopUtils.getTargetClass and AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation/MergedAnnotations.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · When would you register beans programmatically, and how in Framework 6 vs 7?

Short answer: When bean count/type depends on configuration (tenants, gateways, per-region clients). Framework 6: BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor (static @Bean) or GenericApplicationContext.registerBean. Framework 7: BeanRegistrar imported via @Import, designed for AOT/native.

Follow-ups: Why must a BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor @Bean method be static?

B4 · How do you keep a 26-service platform's startup time under control?

Short answer: Measure with BufferingApplicationStartup + /actuator/startup, avoid I/O in constructors, lite-mode configs, trim auto-configurations and starters, CDS/AOT cache (Chapter 29), lazy init only where safe, and budget startup in CI.

B4 · What's your view on JSpecify null-safety adoption in a large codebase?

Short answer: Adopt package by package with @NullMarked, enforce with NullAway in CI as warnings then errors, start at API boundaries (DTOs, service interfaces). It turns runtime NPEs into compile-time errors and aligns with Framework 7's own annotations.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · Is DI still worth it with records, functional style and virtual threads? Defend.

Short answer: Yes for lifecycle, configuration and cross-cutting concerns (transactions, security, observability via proxies) that the container applies uniformly. But keep the domain core framework-free: pure Java values and functions, with Spring at the edges. DI is plumbing, not architecture.

Follow-ups: How would you test the domain without Spring?

B5 · What container rules would you enforce org-wide and how?

Short answer: Constructor injection only, no cycles, no overriding, no ApplicationContext lookups in business code, type-safe qualifiers, @NullMarked. Enforced with ArchUnit rules in a shared test library, Boot properties in the golden-path template, and review checklists — documented in an ADR.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Local profile sends real SMS to customers

A developer runs with spring.profiles.active=local but also has grocery.sms.enabled=true inherited from a shared application.yml. Both msg91Sender and consoleSender are created. ObjectProvider.ifAvailable throws NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException when more than one candidate exists — so either startup-time wiring picked the wrong one elsewhere, or someone "fixed" the error by marking msg91Sender @Primary, and real SMS went out.

Fix: make the conditions mutually exclusive — msg91Sender gets @Profile("!local") in addition to the property condition; set grocery.sms.enabled=false in application-local.yml. Add an ApplicationContextRunner test per profile asserting exactly which SmsSender exists.

Scenario · After adding metrics AOP, the gateway registry fails with 'Primary gateway not registered'

The registry reads @Gateway via g.getClass(), which is now a CGLIB proxy class. Use AopUtils.getTargetClass(g) with AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation, or put the provider on the interface method (code()) instead of relying on annotations.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Pincode-based delivery partner selection

Delivery uses different DeliveryPartner beans per region: OwnFleetPartner for metro pincodes (region digits 1–6 in this exercise) and ThirdPartyPartner elsewhere. Write a DeliveryRouter that receives all partners via constructor injection and selects by Pincode.region() (from Chapter 01's exercise), failing at startup if any region 1–9 is uncovered.

Solution DeliveryPartner.java
package in.grocery.delivery;

import java.util.Set;

public interface DeliveryPartner {
    Set<Integer> regions();
    String book(String orderId);
}
DeliveryRouter.java
package in.grocery.delivery;

import in.grocery.common.address.Pincode;
import java.util.HashMap;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.IntStream;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class DeliveryRouter {

    private final Map<Integer, DeliveryPartner> byRegion = new HashMap<>();

    public DeliveryRouter(List<DeliveryPartner> partners) {
        for (DeliveryPartner p : partners) {
            for (int region : p.regions()) {
                DeliveryPartner existing = byRegion.putIfAbsent(region, p);
                if (existing != null) {
                    throw new IllegalStateException("Region " + region + " covered twice");
                }
            }
        }
        List<Integer> missing = IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 9).boxed()
                .filter(r -> !byRegion.containsKey(r)).toList();
        if (!missing.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Uncovered regions: " + missing);
        }
    }

    public String book(String orderId, Pincode pincode) {
        return byRegion.get(pincode.region()).book(orderId);
    }
}
DeliveryRouterTest.java
package in.grocery.delivery;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatIllegalStateException;

import in.grocery.common.address.Pincode;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Set;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class DeliveryRouterTest {

    record Partner(String name, Set<Integer> regions) implements DeliveryPartner {
        public String book(String orderId) { return name + ":" + orderId; }
    }

    @Test
    void routesByRegion() {
        var router = new DeliveryRouter(List.of(
                new Partner("fleet", Set.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)),
                new Partner("3pl", Set.of(7, 8, 9))));
        assertThat(router.book("O1", new Pincode("560001"))).isEqualTo("fleet:O1");
        assertThat(router.book("O2", new Pincode("781001"))).isEqualTo("3pl:O2");
    }

    @Test
    void failsWhenRegionMissing() {
        assertThatIllegalStateException()
                .isThrownBy(() -> new DeliveryRouter(List.of(new Partner("fleet", Set.of(1, 2)))))
                .withMessageContaining("Uncovered regions");
    }
}

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• IoC moves object creation and wiring into the container; DI is how dependencies arrive — use constructors.
  • Spring first builds bean definitions, then instantiates singletons at refresh; ConfigurationClassPostProcessor and AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory are the core.
  • Resolve ambiguity with qualifiers → @Primary → @Fallback, or inject all candidates.
  • Lite-mode @Configuration with parameter injection is the modern default.
  • Shorter-lived scopes in singletons need ObjectProvider or scoped proxies.
  • Circular dependencies are design bugs, prohibited by default.
  • Framework 7 adds BeanRegistrar and JSpecify null-safety.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Framework Reference — Core Technologies › The IoC Container (bean overview, dependencies, scopes, Java-based configuration, programmatic registration)
  • Spring Boot Reference — Spring Beans and Dependency Injection, Testing › ApplicationContextRunner
  • JSpecify documentation — User Guide

01 Java & Build Prerequisites · 03 Bean Lifecycle, Events & Extension Points

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 02 showed how beans are wired. This chapter shows when things happen — and how to plug your own code into those moments.

Production incidents in Spring services often come down to timing:

  • A cache warmer runs in a constructor, calls the pricing service before the DataSource is ready, and the pod crash-loops.
  • A Kafka consumer keeps polling during shutdown, processes half an order, and the pod is killed mid-transaction.
  • An "order placed" SMS is sent from an event listener, but the database transaction then rolls back. The customer gets an SMS for an order that doesn't exist.
  • Kubernetes sends traffic to a pod that is "started" but whose catalog cache is still empty, so the first 2,000 requests hit the database at once.

Each of these has a precise fix in Spring's lifecycle model: SmartLifecycle phases, @TransactionalEventListener, readiness states, and the right extension point.

In the grocery marketplace, events are also how services stay decoupled inside a service: OrderService publishes OrderPlaced, and notification, loyalty, analytics and inventory reservation react without OrderService knowing they exist. That same idea scales up to Kafka in Chapter 23 and Spring Modulith in Chapter 37.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy, @EventListener, profiles B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — transactional events, async listeners, conditions, SpEL B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — post-processors, SmartLifecycle, graceful shutdown B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — readiness, EnvironmentPostProcessor, platform extension design B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — event-driven design inside and across services

docs.title: 2.1 The bean lifecycle in one sentence per phase
docs.text:
1. Instantiate — constructor runs (constructor injection happens here).
  2. Populate — field and setter injection.
  3. Aware callbacks — the bean is told its name, class loader, bean factory, application context.
  4. Before-init post-processing — BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization; @PostConstruct runs here.
  5. Init callbacks — InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet(), then a custom init method.
  6. After-init post-processing — postProcessAfterInitialization; AOP proxies are created here.
  7. Ready — bean is in the singleton cache and used.
  8. Destroy — on context close: @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy(), custom destroy method.

docs.title: 2.2 Initialization callbacks
docs.text:
Mechanism Coupling to Spring Recommendation @PostConstruct (jakarta.annotation) None (Jakarta standard) ✅ Default choice InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet() Spring interface Framework/library code @Bean(initMethod = "start") None in the class Third-party classes

Order when several exist: @PostConstruct → afterPropertiesSet() → initMethod.

Initialization is not the place for heavy work

@PostConstruct runs while the context is still being built. Other beans may not be ready, AOP proxies around this bean don't exist yet (so @Transactional on the same bean won't apply), and failures abort startup. Use it for validation and cheap setup only. Warm-up and I/O belong in ApplicationRunner or SmartLifecycle.

docs.title: 2.3 Destruction callbacks
docs.text:
Mechanism Notes @PreDestroy Default choice DisposableBean.destroy() Spring interface @Bean(destroyMethod = "...") Default is inferred: a public close() or shutdown() method is called automatically

Order: @PreDestroy → destroy() → destroyMethod. Prototype beans are never destroyed by the container — whoever gets them owns cleanup.

docs.title: 2.4 Aware interfaces
docs.text: BeanNameAware, BeanClassLoaderAware, BeanFactoryAware, EnvironmentAware, ResourceLoaderAware, ApplicationEventPublisherAware, MessageSourceAware, ApplicationContextAware. They exist mainly for framework code. In application code, inject what you need (Environment, ApplicationEventPublisher) through the constructor instead.

docs.title: 2.5 Container extension points
docs.text: Extension point Operates on Runs Typical use BeanDefinitionRegistryPostProcessor Registry of definitions First Add/remove bean definitions BeanFactoryPostProcessor Bean definitions Before any bean instantiated Modify definitions (placeholders, scopes, validation rules) BeanPostProcessor Bean instances Around each bean's init Wrap in proxies, inject, validate InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor Before/after instantiation Per bean Short-circuit creation, custom injection SmartInitializingSingleton One bean After all singletons created Cross-bean validation, registry building SmartLifecycle Components with start/stop After refresh / on close, by phase Consumers, schedulers, servers ApplicationContextInitializer The context, before refresh Very early Add property sources, set profiles EnvironmentPostProcessor (Boot) Environment Before context creation Load config from custom sources

docs.title: 2.6 Lifecycle and SmartLifecycle
docs.text:
Lifecycle gives start(), stop(), isRunning(). SmartLifecycle adds:

  • isAutoStartup() — start automatically after refresh.
  • getPhase() — lower phases start first and stop last. Default phase is Integer.MAX_VALUE (starts last, stops first).
  • stop(Runnable callback) — asynchronous stop; call the callback when done. The container waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s) per phase.

The embedded web server itself is a SmartLifecycle — that's how Boot orders "stop accepting HTTP" before "close DataSource".

docs.title: 2.7 Application events
docs.text:
• Publishing: inject ApplicationEventPublisher and call publishEvent(Object). Any object works (it's wrapped in a PayloadApplicationEvent); records are ideal.
  • Listening: annotate a method with @EventListener. The parameter type selects the event. Supports generics, condition (SpEL), @Order, @Async.
  • Synchronous by default: listeners run on the publisher's thread, inside the publisher's transaction, and an exception propagates back to the publisher.
  • Returning a value from a listener publishes it as a new event (chaining).

docs.title: 2.8 Transactional events
docs.text:
@TransactionalEventListener defers the listener until a transaction phase:

Phase Runs Use AFTER_COMMIT (default) After successful commit Notifications, outbound messages, cache eviction AFTER_ROLLBACK After rollback Compensation, alerting AFTER_COMPLETION After commit or rollback Cleanup BEFORE_COMMIT Just before commit, still in transaction Last validations, flushing aggregates

If no transaction is active, the event is dropped unless fallbackExecution = true.

The AFTER_COMMIT trap

In AFTER_COMMIT, the transaction is committed but its resources are still bound to the thread. Database writes in the listener will not be committed unless the listener starts a new transaction (@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW)). Since Spring Framework 6.1, putting @Transactional on a @TransactionalEventListener with any propagation other than REQUIRES_NEW or NOT_SUPPORTED fails at startup — exactly to prevent this bug.

docs.title: 2.9 Spring Boot application events
docs.text:
Boot publishes events across the whole startup, not just the context refresh:

Event When Can use beans? ApplicationStartingEvent Start of run() No ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent Environment ready, no context No ApplicationContextInitializedEvent Context created, initializers run No ApplicationPreparedEvent Definitions loaded, before refresh No ContextRefreshedEvent Refresh completed Yes WebServerInitializedEvent Server started, port known Yes ApplicationStartedEvent Context refreshed, before runners Yes AvailabilityChangeEvent (Liveness CORRECT) Right after started Yes Runners execute ApplicationRunner, CommandLineRunner Yes ApplicationReadyEvent After runners Yes AvailabilityChangeEvent (Readiness ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC) Right after ready Yes ApplicationFailedEvent Startup failed Maybe

Events before the context exists can't be received by @EventListener beans — register those listeners with SpringApplication.addListeners(...) or in META-INF/spring.factories.

docs.title: 2.10 Availability: liveness and readiness
docs.text:
• Liveness — "is the process healthy or should it be restarted?" (CORRECT / BROKEN)
  • Readiness — "should it receive traffic?" (ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC / REFUSING_TRAFFIC)

Boot exposes them as /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness. Readiness becomes ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC only after runners finish — so warm-up in an ApplicationRunner naturally delays traffic. Your code can change state with AvailabilityChangeEvent.publish(...).

docs.title: 2.11 SpEL — Spring Expression Language
docs.text:
Syntax Meaning Example ${...} Property placeholder (resolved from Environment) @Value("${grocery.cart.max-items:50}") #{...} SpEL expression (evaluated) @Value("#{${grocery.cart.max-items} * 2}")

SpEL appears in @Value, @EventListener(condition), @Cacheable(key), @PreAuthorize, @ConditionalOnExpression, Spring Integration and more. It can call methods, reference beans (@beanName), use #root, method arguments (#order, #p0), safe navigation (?.), Elvis (?:), collection selection (.?[...]) and projection (.![...]).

Never evaluate user input as SpEL

StandardEvaluationContext can call arbitrary methods and types — evaluating a user-supplied string is remote code execution. For expressions from untrusted sources use SimpleEvaluationContext (read-only data binding) or, better, don't use SpEL.

docs.title: 2.12 Environment, property sources and profiles
docs.text:
Environment = active profiles + an ordered list of PropertySources (command-line args, env vars, application.yml files, config server...). The first source containing a key wins. Chapter 06 covers the full order.

Profiles switch bean sets and configuration:

  • @Profile("local"), @Profile("!prod"), expressions like @Profile("prod & india").
  • Activate with spring.profiles.active, group with spring.profiles.group.*.
  • Profile-specific files: application-local.yml.

docs.title: 2.13 Conditions
docs.text: @Conditional(MyCondition.class) registers a bean only if MyCondition.matches(...) returns true. Spring Boot adds a family built on SpringBootCondition: @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnBean, @ConditionalOnWebApplication, @ConditionalOnExpression, @ConditionalOnResource, @ConditionalOnCloudPlatform, @ConditionalOnThreading (virtual threads), and more. Profiles themselves are implemented as a condition (ProfileCondition).

docs.title: 3.1 Full lifecycle of a singleton
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant BF as AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory
    participant Bean as OrderService
    participant BPP as BeanPostProcessors
    participant Ctx as AbstractApplicationContext

    BF->>Bean: constructor (dependencies resolved)
    BF->>Bean: populateBean — @Autowired fields/setters
    BF->>Bean: invokeAwareMethods — BeanNameAware, BeanFactoryAware
    BF->>BPP: postProcessBeforeInitialization
    Note over BPP: ApplicationContextAwareProcessor → *Aware<br/>CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor → @PostConstruct
    BF->>Bean: afterPropertiesSet(), then initMethod
    BF->>BPP: postProcessAfterInitialization
    Note over BPP: AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator<br/>may return a PROXY instead of the bean
    Ctx->>Bean: SmartInitializingSingleton.afterSingletonsInstantiated()
    Ctx->>Ctx: finishRefresh → LifecycleProcessor.onRefresh() → SmartLifecycle.start() by phase
    Ctx->>Ctx: publish ContextRefreshedEvent
    Note over Ctx: ... application runs ...
    Ctx->>Ctx: close() → ContextClosedEvent
    Ctx->>Ctx: LifecycleProcessor.onClose() → SmartLifecycle.stop() reverse phase
    Ctx->>Bean: @PreDestroy → destroy() → destroyMethod

Key classes:

  • AbstractAutowireCapableBeanFactory.initializeBean() — Aware, BPP before, init methods, BPP after.
  • InitDestroyAnnotationBeanPostProcessor (superclass of CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor) — finds @PostConstruct / @PreDestroy.
  • DisposableBeanAdapter — unifies all destroy styles, including inferred close().
  • DefaultLifecycleProcessor — starts and stops Lifecycle beans grouped by phase.
  • AbstractApplicationContext.refresh() — the master sequence: prepareRefresh, obtainFreshBeanFactory, invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors, registerBeanPostProcessors, initMessageSource, initApplicationEventMulticaster, onRefresh (web server created here), registerListeners, finishBeanFactoryInitialization, finishRefresh.

docs.title: 3.2 Why post-processors themselves are special
docs.text:
BeanFactoryPostProcessors and BeanPostProcessors are instantiated very early, before regular beans. Consequences:

  • Declare their @Bean methods static so the enclosing @Configuration class doesn't have to be instantiated early.
  • Beans they depend on are created early too and miss post-processing (no AOP, no @Transactional). Spring logs Bean 'x' ... is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors. Treat that INFO log as a warning.

docs.title: 3.3 Event publishing path
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[OrderService.placeOrder] -->|publishEvent OrderPlaced| C[AbstractApplicationContext]
    C --> M[SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster]
    M -->|resolve listeners by type,<br/>cache by event+source type| L1["ApplicationListenerMethodAdapter<br/>@EventListener"]
    M --> L2["TransactionalApplicationListenerMethodAdapter<br/>@TransactionalEventListener"]
    L1 -->|condition SpEL true?| X1[invoke method<br/>same thread]
    L2 -->|transaction active?| S[register TransactionSynchronization]
    S -->|afterCommit| X2[invoke method]
    X1 -->|"@Async"| E[TaskExecutor thread]
  • EventListenerMethodProcessor (a SmartInitializingSingleton) scans beans for @EventListener methods after all singletons exist and registers an ApplicationListenerMethodAdapter for each.
  • SimpleApplicationEventMulticaster invokes listeners synchronously unless it has a TaskExecutor (don't set one globally — use @Async per listener).
  • @TransactionalEventListener adapters register a TransactionSynchronization with TransactionSynchronizationManager; the transaction manager calls it at the right phase.

docs.title: 3.4 Graceful shutdown sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K8s as Kubernetes
    participant JVM
    participant Ctx as ApplicationContext
    participant Web as WebServerGracefulShutdownLifecycle
    participant Con as OrderSlaWatcher (SmartLifecycle)
    participant DS as HikariDataSource

    K8s->>JVM: SIGTERM
    JVM->>Ctx: shutdown hook → close()
    Ctx->>Ctx: readiness → REFUSING_TRAFFIC, ContextClosedEvent
    Ctx->>Web: stop (highest phase first)
    Note over Web: stop accepting new requests,<br/>wait for in-flight ones
    Ctx->>Con: stop(callback)
    Note over Con: finish current batch, then callback.run()
    Ctx->>DS: destroy → close() (inferred)
    JVM-->>K8s: exit 0

Since Spring Boot 3.4, server.shutdown=graceful is the default. Each phase waits up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase.

docs.title: 3.5 Condition evaluation
docs.text:
ConditionEvaluator.shouldSkip() is called by ConfigurationClassParser and ConfigurationClassBeanDefinitionReader for each @Configuration class, @Bean method and scanned component. Conditions run in two phases — PARSE_CONFIGURATION and REGISTER_BEAN — which is why @ConditionalOnBean only sees beans already registered. It is reliable in auto-configuration (ordered) but fragile in your own configuration classes.

Run the app with --debug (or debug=true) to print the condition evaluation report, or look at /actuator/conditions.

4.2 Your first event
4.3 Test that the event is published
4.4 Profiles in two minutes
5.1 Level 2 — Transactional, ordered, conditional and async listeners
5.2 Level 2 — Listener that writes to the database after commit
5.3 Level 2 — Custom condition: feature flags
5.4 Level 3 — BeanFactoryPostProcessor enforcing platform rules
docs.text:
Platform rule: grocery services are stateless — no session-scoped beans, and no @Lazy beans in production (lazy beans hide startup failures).

in/grocery/common/platform/StatelessPlatformRules.java
package in.grocery.common.platform;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.Arrays;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.beans.BeansException;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.BeanDefinition;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.BeanFactoryPostProcessor;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.ConfigurableListableBeanFactory;
import org.springframework.context.EnvironmentAware;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;
import org.springframework.core.env.Profiles;

public class StatelessPlatformRules implements BeanFactoryPostProcessor, EnvironmentAware {

    private Environment environment;

    @Override
    public void setEnvironment(Environment environment) {       // (1)!
        this.environment = environment;
    }

    @Override
    public void postProcessBeanFactory(ConfigurableListableBeanFactory factory) throws BeansException {
        boolean prod = environment.acceptsProfiles(Profiles.of("prod"));
        List<String> violations = new ArrayList<>();

        Arrays.stream(factory.getBeanDefinitionNames()).forEach(name -> {
            BeanDefinition def = factory.getBeanDefinition(name);
            String className = def.getBeanClassName();
            if (className == null || !className.startsWith("in.grocery.")) return;   // (2)!

            if ("session".equals(def.getScope())) {
                violations.add(name + " is session-scoped");
            }
            if (prod && def.isLazyInit()) {
                violations.add(name + " is lazy in prod");
            }
        });

        if (!violations.isEmpty()) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Platform rule violations: " + violations);
        }
    }
}
  1. EnvironmentAware instead of injection: BFPPs run before normal injection is possible.
  2. Only our code; don't police framework beans.
in/grocery/common/platform/PlatformRulesConfig.java
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class PlatformRulesConfig {
    @Bean
    static StatelessPlatformRules statelessPlatformRules() {   // (1)!
        return new StatelessPlatformRules();
    }
}
  1. static — BFPPs must be created before the configuration class instance.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — BeanPostProcessor timing outbound clients
docs.text:
Every bean annotated @ExternalClient (Razorpay, SMS, maps API) gets latency logging. This is a hand-made proxy — Chapter 04 shows how AOP does it declaratively.

in/grocery/common/client/ExternalClient.java
package in.grocery.common.client;

import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.TYPE)
public @interface ExternalClient {
    String value();   // logical name, e.g. "razorpay"
}
in/grocery/common/client/ExternalClientTimingPostProcessor.java
package in.grocery.common.client;

import org.aopalliance.intercept.MethodInterceptor;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.aop.framework.ProxyFactory;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.config.BeanPostProcessor;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.AnnotationUtils;

public class ExternalClientTimingPostProcessor implements BeanPostProcessor {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("external-clients");

    @Override
    public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String beanName) {        // (1)!
        ExternalClient ann = AnnotationUtils.findAnnotation(bean.getClass(), ExternalClient.class);
        if (ann == null) {
            return bean;
        }
        ProxyFactory factory = new ProxyFactory(bean);
        factory.setProxyTargetClass(true);                                               // (2)!
        factory.addAdvice((MethodInterceptor) invocation -> {
            long start = System.nanoTime();
            try {
                return invocation.proceed();
            } finally {
                long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
                log.info("{}.{} took {} ms", ann.value(), invocation.getMethod().getName(), ms);
            }
        });
        return factory.getProxy();                                                       // (3)!
    }
}
  1. After init — the bean is fully configured.
  2. CGLIB subclass so callers injecting the concrete class still work.
  3. Returning a different object replaces the bean in the container.

Register with a static @Bean, same as above. Test it:

ExternalClientTimingPostProcessorTest.java
package in.grocery.common.client;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.aop.support.AopUtils;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.runner.ApplicationContextRunner;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

class ExternalClientTimingPostProcessorTest {

    @ExternalClient("maps")
    static class MapsClient {
        public int distanceKm(String from, String to) { return 7; }
    }

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    static class Cfg {
        @Bean static ExternalClientTimingPostProcessor bpp() { return new ExternalClientTimingPostProcessor(); }
        @Bean MapsClient mapsClient() { return new MapsClient(); }
    }

    @Test
    void wrapsAnnotatedBeansInProxy() {
        new ApplicationContextRunner().withUserConfiguration(Cfg.class).run(ctx -> {
            MapsClient client = ctx.getBean(MapsClient.class);
            assertThat(AopUtils.isAopProxy(client)).isTrue();
            assertThat(client.distanceKm("560001", "560034")).isEqualTo(7);
        });
    }
}
