docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace any remaining javax.annotation.PostConstruct with jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct (Boot 2 → 3).
  • Find @TransactionalEventListener + @Transactional combinations; switch to REQUIRES_NEW.
  • Check custom EnvironmentPostProcessors, ApplicationContextInitializers and spring.factories keys against the 4.x migration guide.
  • Make @Bean methods for BFPPs/BPPs static.
  • Verify spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase < Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
  • Replace @ConditionalOnProperty(havingValue = "true") for booleans with @ConditionalOnBooleanProperty (optional clean-up).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Constructors for wiring, @PostConstruct for validation, runners/lifecycle for work.
  2. Side effects after commit: @TransactionalEventListener for notifications; outbox for anything that must not be lost.
  3. Async listeners use a bounded, named executor with metrics — never the default unbounded one.
  4. Events are records, named in past tense (OrderPlaced, PaymentCaptured), carrying IDs and the minimum data listeners need.
  5. static @Bean methods for post-processors; keep their dependencies minimal.
  6. Graceful shutdown tuned end-to-end: preStop hook delay + phase timeout + termination grace period (Chapter 30).
  7. Readiness reflects "can I serve?", liveness reflects "am I broken?".
  8. Conditions extend SpringBootCondition so they show up in reports.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ I/O in @PostConstruct

Anti-patterns (snippet)
@PostConstruct
void init() {
    prices = pricingClient.fetchAll();   // remote call during context build; slow, fragile, no proxies yet
}

✅ ApplicationRunner (blocks readiness, not context creation) — see 6.2.

❌ Sending notifications in a plain @EventListener inside a transaction

Anti-patterns (snippet)
@EventListener
void sms(OrderPlaced e) { smsClient.send(...); }   // sent even if the transaction rolls back

✅ @TransactionalEventListener (+ @Async if slow).

❌ Writing to DB in AFTER_COMMIT without a new transaction — silently not committed (and rejected at startup on 6.1+ if annotated REQUIRED).

❌ Business logic in BeanPostProcessors — they run for every bean and are invisible to readers. Keep them for cross-cutting infrastructure.

❌ Ignoring the stop callback — shutdown hangs for the full timeout, Kubernetes sends SIGKILL, in-flight work is lost.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix @Transactional ignored in @PostConstruct Proxy not created yet / self-call Move work to a runner or another bean @EventListener not called Listener bean not scanned, event type mismatch, condition false, event published before listener registration Check scan, types, --debug; for early Boot events register via spring.factories Transactional listener never fires No active transaction fallbackExecution = true or publish inside @Transactional Listener writes lost after commit No REQUIRES_NEW Add it; consider outbox "is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors" Bean created early by a BPP/BFPP dependency static @Bean, lazy lookup, reduce BPP dependencies Shutdown takes exactly 30s Stop callback not invoked / blocking task Always call callback; interruptible loops Pod receives traffic before cache warm Warm-up in ApplicationReadyEvent listener run async, or readiness probe not enabled Warm up in ApplicationRunner; enable probes All pods restart during DB outage Liveness tied to DB health Remove external checks from liveness group

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• No remote calls in constructors or @PostConstruct
  • Notifications use @TransactionalEventListener
  • Durable side effects use outbox / Modulith registry
  • Async listener executor bounded and instrumented
  • BFPP/BPP @Bean methods are static
  • Graceful shutdown verified in a staging kill test
  • Liveness and readiness groups configured deliberately
  • Custom conditions visible in /actuator/conditions

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Describe the Spring bean lifecycle.

Short answer: Instantiate → inject dependencies → Aware callbacks → BeanPostProcessor before-init (@PostConstruct) → afterPropertiesSet/init method → BeanPostProcessor after-init (proxies) → in use → on close @PreDestroy → destroy() → destroy method.

Follow-ups: Where are AOP proxies created? What happens to prototype beans on shutdown?

Red flags: Putting @PostConstruct before dependency injection.

B1 · What is @PostConstruct used for?

Short answer: To run code once after the bean is constructed and its dependencies injected — validation, cheap initialization.

Red flags: "To call external APIs and load data at startup."

B1 · Which package do @PostConstruct and @PreDestroy come from in Boot 3/4?

Short answer: jakarta.annotation (Jakarta Annotations). They were javax.annotation in Boot 2.

B1 · How do you publish and listen to an event in Spring?

Short answer: Inject ApplicationEventPublisher, call publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(...)). Listen with a method annotated @EventListener taking OrderPlaced.

Follow-ups: Is the listener synchronous? (Yes by default.)

B1 · What is a Spring profile?

Short answer: A named set of beans and configuration activated by spring.profiles.active. Used for environment differences like local vs prod.

B1 · Difference between ${...} and #{...}?

Short answer: ${} is a property placeholder resolved from the Environment; #{} is a SpEL expression that is evaluated.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Why use @TransactionalEventListener instead of @EventListener for sending an SMS?

Short answer: @EventListener runs immediately inside the transaction; if it later rolls back, the SMS was sent for an order that doesn't exist. @TransactionalEventListener (default AFTER_COMMIT) runs only after a successful commit.

Follow-ups: What if there's no transaction? (Dropped unless fallbackExecution = true.)

B2 · A listener in AFTER_COMMIT saves an entity but nothing is persisted. Why?

Short answer: The original transaction is already committed; the listener participates in it and nothing commits again. Use @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW). Framework 6.1+ fails fast if you use the default propagation.

B2 · Are Spring events synchronous or asynchronous? How do you make them async?

Short answer: Synchronous, same thread and transaction. Add @Async on the listener (with @EnableAsync and a configured executor). Avoid setting an executor on the multicaster globally.

Follow-ups: What happens to exceptions in async listeners? (Go to AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, not the publisher.)

B2 · How do you order multiple listeners for the same event?

Short answer: @Order on the listener methods (lower first). Only meaningful for synchronous listeners.

B2 · How would you write a custom condition?

Short answer: Implement Condition (or extend SpringBootCondition for reporting), wrap it in an annotation meta-annotated with @Conditional, read the Environment via ConditionContext.

B2 · What's the order of Spring Boot startup events?

Short answer: Starting → EnvironmentPrepared → ContextInitialized → Prepared → ContextRefreshed → (WebServerInitialized) → Started → liveness CORRECT → runners → Ready → readiness ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC. ApplicationFailedEvent on failure.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Difference between BeanFactoryPostProcessor and BeanPostProcessor?

Short answer: BFPP modifies bean definitions before any bean exists (e.g. placeholder resolution). BPP modifies or wraps bean instances around initialization (e.g. AOP proxies, @Autowired).

Follow-ups: Why declare them with static @Bean methods?

B3 · Why should BeanPostProcessor @Bean methods be static?

Short answer: Post-processors are created before regular beans. A non-static method forces early instantiation of the whole @Configuration class and its dependencies, which then miss post-processing (no proxies). Spring logs "not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors".

B3 · How does SmartLifecycle phase ordering work?

Short answer: Lower phase starts first and stops last. Default is Integer.MAX_VALUE. stop(Runnable) is async; the container waits up to timeout-per-shutdown-phase for callbacks per phase.

Follow-ups: Where does the web server's graceful shutdown sit? How do you make a consumer stop after HTTP but before DB?

B3 · How does graceful shutdown work in Spring Boot?

Short answer: SIGTERM → shutdown hook → context close → readiness REFUSING → lifecycle stop by phase: web server stops accepting and drains in-flight requests, then other lifecycle beans, then destroy callbacks (pools closed). Controlled by server.shutdown=graceful and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase.

B3 · Where would you put cache warm-up and why?

Short answer: In an ApplicationRunner: context is fully built (proxies, transactions work) and readiness isn't ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC until runners complete, so probes hold traffic back. Not in @PostConstruct (context incomplete) and not async in ApplicationReadyEvent (traffic arrives before warm-up ends).

B3 · How does @EventListener get registered internally?

Short answer: EventListenerMethodProcessor (a SmartInitializingSingleton + BFPP) scans beans after all singletons are created and registers ApplicationListenerMethodAdapters (or transactional variants via TransactionalEventListenerFactory) with the multicaster.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · In-process events vs Kafka vs outbox — when to use which?

Short answer: In-process events decouple components inside a service but aren't durable. Kafka decouples services but publishing isn't atomic with the DB commit (dual write). The transactional outbox (or Modulith's publication registry) writes the event in the same transaction and relays it later — use it whenever losing the side effect is unacceptable.

Follow-ups: How do you make the relay idempotent? (Chapter 36)

B4 · How do you design liveness and readiness for a service depending on DB, Redis and Razorpay?

Short answer: Liveness: internal only (no dependency checks). Readiness: include DB and Redis if the service can't serve without them; exclude Razorpay (degrade instead, circuit breaker). Custom readiness changes for staleness conditions. Avoid synchronized restarts.

B4 · How would you load secrets from a vault before the context starts?

Short answer: Config data import (spring.config.import=vault:// with Spring Cloud Vault, or configtree: for mounted files). For custom sources, an EnvironmentPostProcessor registered in spring.factories. Never fetch secrets in beans — auto-configured DataSources need them before beans exist.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you prevent event-driven code inside a service from becoming untraceable?

Short answer: Event catalog with owners, past-tense record events in a dedicated package, ArchUnit rules on who may publish/listen, observability (Micrometer observations around listeners), Spring Modulith documentation and event publication registry, and a rule that cross-module events are the only coupling.

B5 · What startup and shutdown standards would you mandate for a 26-service platform?

Short answer: Budgets (startup < X s measured via /actuator/startup), no I/O in constructors, warm-up in runners, probes enabled and reviewed, graceful shutdown timeouts aligned with K8s, kill tests in staging, consumers as SmartLifecycle with explicit phases, all encoded in the golden-path template and ADRs.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · During deployments, some customers get 'order failed' though the order exists

The order-service pod receives SIGTERM, the web server drains, but the Kafka-based payment-confirmation consumer (default phase) is stopped at the same time the DataSource closes; in-flight confirmation processing fails midway. Fix: consumer as SmartLifecycle with a phase lower than the web server's shutdown phase but stopping before pools close, idempotent processing, commit offsets only after DB commit, and timeout-per-shutdown-phase aligned with the grace period.

Scenario · After adding a custom BeanPostProcessor, @Transactional stopped working on PriceRepositoryImpl

The BPP's @Bean method wasn't static and the BPP injected PriceRepositoryImpl to build a lookup. That forced early creation before the auto-proxy creator was registered, so the repository never got a transactional proxy. Make the method static and resolve dependencies lazily via ObjectProvider.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Stock-low alert

Inventory publishes StockChanged(sku, pincodeHub, available) inside a transaction. Write listeners so that (1) after commit, if available < 10, an async StockLow alert is logged; (2) the alert fires at most once per SKU+hub per hour. Include a test.

Solution StockAlertListener.java
package in.grocery.inventory.alert;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentMap;
import org.springframework.context.ApplicationEventPublisher;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.event.TransactionalEventListener;

@Component
public class StockAlertListener {

    public record StockChanged(String sku, String hub, int available) {}
    public record StockLow(String sku, String hub, int available) {}

    private static final Duration COOLDOWN = Duration.ofHours(1);

    private final ApplicationEventPublisher publisher;
    private final Clock clock;
    private final ConcurrentMap<String, Instant> lastAlert = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    public StockAlertListener(ApplicationEventPublisher publisher, Clock clock) {
        this.publisher = publisher;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @TransactionalEventListener(condition = "#e.available() < 10")
    public void onStockChanged(StockChanged e) {
        String key = e.sku() + "@" + e.hub();
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        boolean[] fire = {false};
        lastAlert.compute(key, (k, prev) -> {
            if (prev == null || prev.plus(COOLDOWN).isBefore(now)) {
                fire[0] = true;
                return now;
            }
            return prev;
        });
        if (fire[0]) {
            publisher.publishEvent(new StockLow(e.sku(), e.hub(), e.available()));
        }
    }
}
StockAlertListenerTest.java
package in.grocery.inventory.alert;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import in.grocery.inventory.alert.StockAlertListener.StockChanged;
import in.grocery.inventory.alert.StockAlertListener.StockLow;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class StockAlertListenerTest {

    @Test
    void alertsOncePerCooldown() {
        List<Object> published = new ArrayList<>();
        var clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-09-22T05:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
        var listener = new StockAlertListener(published::add, clock);

        listener.onStockChanged(new StockChanged("MILK-1L", "BLR-HSR", 4));
        listener.onStockChanged(new StockChanged("MILK-1L", "BLR-HSR", 3));

        assertThat(published).containsExactly(new StockLow("MILK-1L", "BLR-HSR", 4));
    }
}

The SpEL condition is applied by the container; the unit test calls the method directly, so it only exercises the cooldown logic. Add an integration test with TransactionTemplate + @RecordApplicationEvents to cover the condition and commit phase. For multiple pods, move the cooldown map to Redis (SET key NX EX 3600, Chapter 22).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Lifecycle order: construct → inject → Aware → @PostConstruct → init → proxy → use → @PreDestroy → destroy.
  • Proxies are created after initialization — @PostConstruct can't rely on @Transactional of its own bean.
  • BFPPs change definitions; BPPs change instances. Declare both with static @Bean methods.
  • SmartLifecycle phases control start/stop order; always invoke the stop callback.
  • @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) for side effects; REQUIRES_NEW for DB writes; outbox for durability.
  • Warm up in ApplicationRunner — readiness waits for runners.
  • Liveness ≠ readiness; never tie liveness to dependencies.
  • Never evaluate untrusted SpEL; use SimpleEvaluationContext for stored rules.

  • Spring Boot Reference — SpringApplication › Application Events and Listeners, Application Availability, Graceful Shutdown, Creating Your Own Auto-configuration › Condition Annotations

02 IoC & Dependency Injection · 04 AOP

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Some requirements cut across every layer: log how long each service call takes, write an audit record whenever an order is cancelled, reject duplicate "place order" requests, start a transaction, check permissions, retry a flaky call. Written by hand, that code gets copy-pasted into hundreds of methods, drowns the business logic, and is forgotten in the one method where it mattered.

Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) lets you write such a concern once and declare where it applies. You already use it every day, often without noticing:

You write Spring applies via AOP @Transactional TransactionInterceptor @Cacheable CacheInterceptor @Async AsyncExecutionInterceptor @PreAuthorize AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor @Validated on a class MethodValidationInterceptor @Retryable (Framework 7) Retry interceptor from core resilience @Observed, @Timed Micrometer ObservedAspect, TimedAspect

So understanding AOP is not optional: it explains the most common "Spring bug" of all — "my @Transactional doesn't work" — and it gives you a clean tool for your own platform concerns.

In the grocery marketplace we'll build three aspects: service timing, an audit trail for sensitive operations (order cancellation, refunds, price overrides), and an idempotency guard so a customer double-tapping "Pay ₹1,249" on a slow 4G connection doesn't create two orders.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — vocabulary, a first aspect B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — pointcuts, custom annotations, ordering, self-invocation B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5 — proxy creation internals, JDK vs CGLIB, interceptor chain B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — production aspects, ordering with transactions, performance B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — when AOP is the wrong tool, governance

docs.title: 2.1 Vocabulary
docs.text: Term Meaning Grocery example Cross-cutting concern Behaviour needed in many places, unrelated to the business rule Auditing Aspect Module that encapsulates a concern AuditAspect Join point A point in execution where advice can run. In Spring AOP: method execution only OrderService.cancel(...) running Pointcut Predicate selecting join points "methods annotated @Audited" Advice Code that runs at selected join points "write audit row after return" Advisor Pointcut + advice (Spring's internal pairing) — Target The original object OrderService instance Proxy Object wrapping the target that applies advice CGLIB subclass of OrderService Weaving Linking aspects with targets Spring: at runtime via proxies Introduction Adding interfaces/methods to existing types @DeclareParents (rare)

docs.title: 2.2 Spring AOP vs AspectJ
docs.text:
Spring AOP AspectJ (full) Weaving Runtime, proxy-based Compile-time, post-compile, or load-time Join points Public (and protected/package with CGLIB) method execution on Spring beans Method call/execution, field access, constructors, static init, any object Self-invocation ❌ Not advised ✅ Advised Private/final methods ❌ ✅ Setup Nothing extra ajc compiler or -javaagent Syntax Uses AspectJ annotations and pointcut language Same + native .aj syntax

Spring AOP uses AspectJ's annotations and expression parser but not its weaver. For 95% of enterprise needs, Spring AOP is enough.

docs.title: 2.3 Proxies: JDK dynamic vs CGLIB
docs.text:
JDK dynamic proxy CGLIB proxy Mechanism Implements the target's interfaces Generates a subclass of the target Requires At least one interface Non-final class, non-final methods Injectable as Interface type only Interface or concrete class Spring Boot default — ✅ (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true)

Consequences of subclass proxies:

  • final classes can't be proxied — including records, which are implicitly final. Don't put @Transactional or @Cacheable on a record bean.
  • final, private and static methods are never advised.
  • Kotlin classes are final by default — the kotlin-spring (all-open) compiler plugin opens Spring-annotated classes.
  • Spring uses Objenesis to create the proxy instance without calling your constructor a second time.

docs.title: 2.4 Advice types
docs.text:
Annotation Runs Can change flow? @Before Before the method Only by throwing @AfterReturning(returning = "r") After normal return Can read the result @AfterThrowing(throwing = "ex") After an exception Can't swallow it (can rethrow a different one) @After Always (like finally) No @Around Wraps the call; you call proceed() ✅ Full control: skip, retry, change args/result

Rule of thumb: use the least powerful advice that works. @Around is easy to get wrong (forgetting proceed(), swallowing exceptions, returning the wrong type).

docs.title: 2.5 Pointcut designators supported by Spring AOP
docs.text:
Designator Matches Example execution(...) Method signature execution(* in.grocery..service.*Service.*(..)) within(...) Types/packages within(in.grocery.order..*) this(T) Proxy is instance of T this(in.grocery.common.Auditable) target(T) Target is instance of T target(in.grocery.payment.gateway.PaymentGateway) args(...) Runtime argument types, also binds args(orderId, ..) @annotation(A) Method has annotation @annotation(in.grocery.common.audit.Audited) @within(A) Declaring type has annotation @within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service) @target(A) Runtime target class has annotation @target(in.grocery.common.client.ExternalClient) @args(A) Runtime args carry annotation rarely used bean(name) Spring-specific: bean name pattern bean(*Gateway)

execution syntax: execution(modifiers? returnType declaringType? name(params) throws?)

  • * — any one element; .. in a package — any sub-packages; (..) — any parameters; (*) — exactly one; (String, ..) — first is String.
  • Combine with &&, ||, !. Reuse via named @Pointcut methods.

Prefer annotations over package patterns

@annotation(Audited) is explicit — readers see @Audited on the method. execution(* in.grocery..*.*(..)) is invisible magic that silently starts matching new classes. Use package pointcuts only for truly universal concerns (timing, tracing).

docs.title: 2.6 Ordering
docs.text:
• Across aspects: @Order (or Ordered) on the aspect class. Lower value = higher precedence = outermost — runs first on the way in, last on the way out.
  • Within one aspect: by advice type — @Around, @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing precedence; @After effectively runs after @AfterReturning/@AfterThrowing of the same aspect. Split concerns into separate aspects if order matters.
  • Spring's own interceptors (@Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async) default to Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE. Their order is configurable on the @Enable... annotations (e.g. @EnableTransactionManagement(order = ...)).

docs.title: 2.7 The self-invocation problem
2.8 Real-world uses — and misuses
docs.text:
✅ Good fits: observability (timing, tracing), auditing, idempotency, security checks, retries, tenant/context propagation, feature-flag gates, method-level validation.

❌ Poor fits: business rules ("apply GST"), conditional logic that readers need to see, anything whose order relative to other aspects is fragile and unobvious.

docs.title: 3.1 Proxy creation
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Bean OrderService initialized] --> B[postProcessAfterInitialization<br/>AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator]
    B --> C["find candidate Advisors<br/>- @Aspect beans → BeanFactoryAspectJAdvisorsBuilder<br/>- Advisor beans e.g. BeanFactoryTransactionAttributeSourceAdvisor"]
    C --> D{any Advisor's pointcut<br/>matches a method of this class?<br/>AopUtils.canApply}
    D -- no --> E[return original bean]
    D -- yes --> F[ProxyFactory<br/>sort advisors by order]
    F --> G{proxyTargetClass<br/>or no interfaces?}
    G -- yes --> H[ObjenesisCglibAopProxy<br/>subclass]
    G -- no --> I[JdkDynamicAopProxy<br/>interface proxy]
    H & I --> J[proxy registered as the bean]

Key classes:

  • AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator — a SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor registered by @EnableAspectJAutoProxy (auto-configured by Boot's AopAutoConfiguration).
  • ReflectiveAspectJAdvisorFactory — turns each advice method of an @Aspect into an InstantiationModelAwarePointcutAdvisor.
  • AspectJExpressionPointcut — parses and matches pointcut expressions (class filter + method matcher; runtime matching only for args/this/target binding).
  • ProxyFactory / DefaultAopProxyFactory — decides JDK vs CGLIB.
  • The same auto-proxy creator also handles Advisor beans from @EnableTransactionManagement, @EnableCaching, method security, etc. — one proxy per bean holding all advisors.

docs.title: 3.2 Invocation: the interceptor chain
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Caller as OrderController
    participant Proxy as CGLIB proxy (OrderService)
    participant Chain as ReflectiveMethodInvocation
    participant Idem as IdempotencyAspect @Order(10)
    participant Audit as AuditAspect @Order(20)
    participant Tx as TransactionInterceptor (LOWEST)
    participant Target as OrderService target

    Caller->>Proxy: placeOrder(cmd)
    Proxy->>Chain: getInterceptorsAndDynamicInterceptionAdvice(method)
    Chain->>Idem: invoke → proceed()
    Idem->>Audit: proceed()
    Audit->>Tx: proceed()
    Tx->>Tx: begin transaction
    Tx->>Target: placeOrder(cmd)
    Target-->>Tx: result
    Tx->>Tx: commit
    Tx-->>Audit: result
    Audit-->>Idem: result (audit written)
    Idem-->>Caller: result (stored for replay)
  • The advisor chain for each method is computed once and cached (AdvisedSupport.getInterceptorsAndDynamicInterceptionAdvice).
  • Each proceed() moves to the next interceptor; the last one invokes the target via reflection (JDK) or a generated fast-path (CGLIB).
  • For methods matched by no advisor, the CGLIB proxy dispatches directly to the target — the overhead is a single extra call.

docs.title: 3.3 Why self-invocation bypasses advice
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    C[Caller] -->|calls| P[Proxy]
    P -->|advice chain| T[Target.placeOrder]
    T -->|this.reserveStock| T2[Target.reserveStock]
    P -. never involved .-> T2

The proxy only sees calls that go through it. Fixes, in order of preference:

  1. Move the method to another bean (usually the right design anyway).
  2. Inject the proxy of yourself lazily (@Lazy self-reference or ObjectProvider<OrderService>) — works, but smells.
  3. AopContext.currentProxy() with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true) — couples code to Spring AOP.
  4. Programmatic API (TransactionTemplate) instead of the annotation.
  5. AspectJ weaving — advises self-calls, at the cost of build/runtime complexity.

docs.title: 3.4 Proxy creation for @Configuration classes is different
docs.text: @Configuration full-mode CGLIB enhancement (Chapter 02) is not AOP — it's done by ConfigurationClassEnhancer for @Bean method interception. Don't confuse the two.

in/grocery/common/audit/AuditAspect.java
package in.grocery.common.audit;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.function.Supplier;
import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.aspectj.lang.reflect.CodeSignature;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Aspect
@Component
@Order(20)
public class AuditAspect {

    private final AuditSink sink;
    private final Supplier<String> currentActor;   // from security context in Chapter 17
    private final Clock clock;

    public AuditAspect(AuditSink sink, Supplier<String> currentActor, Clock clock) {
        this.sink = sink;
        this.currentActor = currentActor;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Around("@annotation(audited)")                                             // (1)!
    public Object audit(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Audited audited) throws Throwable {
        Instant start = clock.instant();
        String entityId = resolveEntityId(pjp, audited.entityIdArg());
        try {
            Object result = pjp.proceed();
            sink.write(record(audited, entityId, AuditRecord.Outcome.SUCCESS, null, start));
            return result;
        } catch (Throwable ex) {
            sink.write(record(audited, entityId, AuditRecord.Outcome.FAILURE, ex.getClass().getSimpleName(), start));
            throw ex;                                                           // (2)!
        }
    }

    private AuditRecord record(Audited a, String entityId, AuditRecord.Outcome outcome, String error, Instant start) {
        Instant end = clock.instant();
        return new AuditRecord(a.action(), entityId, currentActor.get(), outcome, error,
                end.toEpochMilli() - start.toEpochMilli(), end);
    }

    private static String resolveEntityId(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, String argName) {
        if (argName.isEmpty()) return "n/a";
        String[] names = ((CodeSignature) pjp.getSignature()).getParameterNames();  // (3)!
        Object[] args = pjp.getArgs();
        for (int i = 0; i < names.length; i++) {
            if (names[i].equals(argName)) return String.valueOf(args[i]);
        }
        throw new IllegalStateException("@Audited entityIdArg '" + argName + "' not found on " + pjp.getSignature());
    }
}
  1. Annotation binding: the parameter name audited in the expression binds the actual annotation instance into the advice parameter.
  2. Record the failure, then rethrow the same exception — never swallow.
  3. Parameter names require -parameters (Chapter 01).

Understanding ProxyFactory demystifies everything the container does, and it's the fastest way to unit-test an aspect.

in/grocery/common/audit/AuditAspectTest.java
package in.grocery.common.audit;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatIllegalStateException;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.time.ZoneOffset;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.aop.aspectj.annotation.AspectJProxyFactory;

class AuditAspectTest {

    static class RefundService {
        @Audited(action = "REFUND", entityIdArg = "paymentId")
        public String refund(String paymentId, int amountPaise) {
            if (amountPaise <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("bad amount");
            return "rfnd_" + paymentId;
        }
    }

    private final List<AuditRecord> written = new ArrayList<>();
    private final AuditAspect aspect = new AuditAspect(
            written::add, () -> "ops@grocery.in",
            Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2026-09-22T06:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC));

    private RefundService proxied() {
        AspectJProxyFactory factory = new AspectJProxyFactory(new RefundService());   // (1)!
        factory.addAspect(aspect);
        return factory.getProxy();
    }

    @Test
    void writesSuccessRecord() {
        assertThat(proxied().refund("pay_123", 5000)).isEqualTo("rfnd_pay_123");
        assertThat(written).singleElement().satisfies(r -> {
            assertThat(r.action()).isEqualTo("REFUND");
            assertThat(r.entityId()).isEqualTo("pay_123");
            assertThat(r.outcome()).isEqualTo(AuditRecord.Outcome.SUCCESS);
        });
    }

    @Test
    void writesFailureRecordAndRethrows() {
        assertThatIllegalStateException().isThrownBy(() -> proxied().refund("pay_9", 0));
        assertThat(written).singleElement()
                .extracting(AuditRecord::outcome).isEqualTo(AuditRecord.Outcome.FAILURE);
    }
}
  1. No Spring context at all — millisecond-fast tests of pointcuts and advice.

docs.text:
Question: should the audit record be written inside the business transaction (atomic with the change) or outside (records failures caused by commit, e.g. constraint violations at flush)?

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Audit @Order(20) outside tx (LOWEST)"
        A1[Audit] --> T1[Tx begin] --> M1[method] --> C1[commit] --> A1b[Audit writes result incl. commit failure]
    end
    subgraph "Tx order 10, Audit order 20 → audit inside tx"
        T2[Tx begin] --> A2[Audit] --> M2[method] --> A2b[Audit writes in same tx] --> C2[commit]
    end
in/grocery/common/tx/TransactionOrderConfig.java
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@EnableTransactionManagement(order = 10)          // (1)!
class TransactionOrderConfig {}
  1. Transaction interceptor now wraps outside AuditAspect (order 20), so the audit insert joins the business transaction and rolls back with it. Choose deliberately — and document it in an ADR, because it's invisible in code.

Verify

Boot auto-configures transaction management. Declaring @EnableTransactionManagement yourself is allowed and takes precedence, but confirm with /actuator/conditions that you haven't disabled other defaults (e.g. proxy-target-class). Set proxyTargetClass = true if your code injects concrete classes.

docs.title: Idempotency guard for order placement
docs.text:
Problem: mobile clients retry POST /orders on timeouts. Without protection, a slow Razorpay response on a festival day produces duplicate orders and double charges.

Design:

  • Client sends Idempotency-Key header (UUID) — Controller copies it into the command.
  • @Idempotent(key = "...") on the Delegate method, evaluated with SpEL.
  • Store states: absent → IN_PROGRESS → COMPLETED(result), TTL 24h.
  • Concurrent duplicate while in progress → 409 Conflict. Duplicate after completion → replay the stored result.
  • Failure → release the key so the client can retry.
  • The aspect wraps outside the transaction so a result is stored only after commit.
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Absent
    Absent --> InProgress: reserve(key) OK
    InProgress --> Completed: method returned (after commit)
    InProgress --> Absent: method threw → release
    Completed --> Completed: duplicate → replay stored result
    InProgress --> InProgress: concurrent duplicate → 409
    Completed --> [*]: TTL expired
in/grocery/common/idempotency/Idempotent.java
package in.grocery.common.idempotency;

import java.lang.annotation.Documented;
import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

@Documented
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface Idempotent {
    /** SpEL evaluated against method arguments, e.g. "#command.idempotencyKey()". */
    String key();
    /** Logical operation, part of the stored key. */
    String scope();
    /** ISO-8601 duration. */
    String ttl() default "PT24H";
}
in/grocery/common/idempotency/IdempotencyStore.java
package in.grocery.common.idempotency;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;

public interface IdempotencyStore {

    sealed interface Entry permits InProgress, Completed {}
    record InProgress() implements Entry {}
    record Completed(Object result) implements Entry {}

    /** Atomically create IN_PROGRESS if absent. Returns the existing entry otherwise. */
    Optional<Entry> reserve(String key, Duration ttl);

    void complete(String key, Object result, Duration ttl);

    void release(String key);
}
in/grocery/common/idempotency/InMemoryIdempotencyStore.java
package in.grocery.common.idempotency;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentMap;

/** Single-instance store for tests and local profile. Production uses Redis SET NX PX (Chapter 22). */
public class InMemoryIdempotencyStore implements IdempotencyStore {

    private record Slot(Entry entry, Instant expiresAt) {}

    private final ConcurrentMap<String, Slot> slots = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Clock clock;

    public InMemoryIdempotencyStore(Clock clock) {
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<Entry> reserve(String key, Duration ttl) {
        Instant now = clock.instant();
        Slot[] existing = new Slot[1];
        slots.compute(key, (k, slot) -> {
            if (slot != null && slot.expiresAt().isAfter(now)) {
                existing[0] = slot;
                return slot;
            }
            return new Slot(new InProgress(), now.plus(ttl));
        });
        return Optional.ofNullable(existing[0]).map(Slot::entry);
    }

    @Override
    public void complete(String key, Object result, Duration ttl) {
        slots.put(key, new Slot(new Completed(result), clock.instant().plus(ttl)));
    }

    @Override
    public void release(String key) {
        slots.remove(key);
    }
}

in/grocery/common/idempotency/IdempotencyAspect.java
package in.grocery.common.idempotency;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Counter;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.lang.reflect.Method;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap;
import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.aspectj.lang.reflect.MethodSignature;
import org.springframework.context.expression.MethodBasedEvaluationContext;
import org.springframework.core.DefaultParameterNameDiscoverer;
import org.springframework.core.Ordered;
import org.springframework.core.ParameterNameDiscoverer;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.expression.Expression;
import org.springframework.expression.spel.standard.SpelExpressionParser;
import org.springframework.util.StringUtils;

@Aspect
@Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 10)                                          // (1)!
public class IdempotencyAspect {

    private final IdempotencyStore store;
    private final SpelExpressionParser parser = new SpelExpressionParser();
    private final ParameterNameDiscoverer names = new DefaultParameterNameDiscoverer();
    private final Map<String, Expression> expressions = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); // (2)!
    private final Counter replays;
    private final Counter conflicts;

    public IdempotencyAspect(IdempotencyStore store, MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.store = store;
        this.replays = meters.counter("grocery.idempotency", "result", "replay");
        this.conflicts = meters.counter("grocery.idempotency", "result", "conflict");
    }

    @Around("@annotation(idempotent)")
    public Object guard(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Idempotent idempotent) throws Throwable {
        Method method = ((MethodSignature) pjp.getSignature()).getMethod();
        String clientKey = evaluateKey(idempotent.key(), method, pjp.getArgs());
        if (!StringUtils.hasText(clientKey)) {
            throw new IllegalArgumentException("Idempotency-Key is required");
        }
        String key = idempotent.scope() + ":" + clientKey;
        Duration ttl = Duration.parse(idempotent.ttl());

        Optional<IdempotencyStore.Entry> existing = store.reserve(key, ttl);
        if (existing.isPresent()) {
            return switch (existing.get()) {                                    // (3)!
                case IdempotencyStore.Completed(Object result) -> {
                    replays.increment();
                    yield result;
                }
                case IdempotencyStore.InProgress p -> {
                    conflicts.increment();
                    throw new IdempotencyConflictException(clientKey);
                }
            };
        }

        try {
            Object result = pjp.proceed();                                      // (4)!
            store.complete(key, result, ttl);
            return result;
        } catch (Throwable ex) {
            store.release(key);                                                 // (5)!
            throw ex;
        }
    }

    private String evaluateKey(String spel, Method method, Object[] args) {
        Expression expression = expressions.computeIfAbsent(spel, parser::parseExpression);
        var context = new MethodBasedEvaluationContext(null, method, args, names);  // (6)!
        Object value = expression.getValue(context);
        return value == null ? null : value.toString();
    }
}
  1. Outermost: wraps validation, auditing and the transaction, so complete(...) only runs after a successful commit.
  2. Parse each expression once.
  3. Pattern matching over the sealed Entry type — exhaustive, no default.
  4. The whole business operation, including commit.
  5. On failure the key is freed so the client's retry can proceed. (For payments, a failed-but-charged state needs reconciliation — Chapter 36.)
  6. Expressions come from annotations in our code, never from requests, so the standard evaluation context is acceptable here.
in/grocery/common/idempotency/IdempotencyConfig.java
package in.grocery.common.idempotency;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.time.Clock;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnMissingBean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class IdempotencyConfig {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(IdempotencyStore.class)
    IdempotencyStore inMemoryIdempotencyStore(Clock clock) {
        return new InMemoryIdempotencyStore(clock);
    }

    @Bean
    IdempotencyAspect idempotencyAspect(IdempotencyStore store, MeterRegistry meters) {
        return new IdempotencyAspect(store, meters);
    }
}

Using it in the four-layer order service:

in/grocery/order/web/OrderController.java
package in.grocery.order.web;

import in.grocery.order.delegate.OrderDelegate;
import in.grocery.order.delegate.PlaceOrderCommand;
import in.grocery.order.delegate.OrderView;
import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestHeader;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderController {

    private final OrderDelegate delegate;

    OrderController(OrderDelegate delegate) {
        this.delegate = delegate;
    }

    record PlaceOrderRequest(@jakarta.validation.constraints.NotBlank String cartId) {}

    @PostMapping
    ResponseEntity<OrderView> place(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") String idempotencyKey,
                                    @Valid @RequestBody PlaceOrderRequest request) {
        OrderView view = delegate.place(new PlaceOrderCommand(idempotencyKey, request.cartId()));
        return ResponseEntity.status(201).body(view);
    }
}
in/grocery/order/delegate/OrderDelegate.java
package in.grocery.order.delegate;

import in.grocery.common.idempotency.Idempotent;
import in.grocery.order.service.OrderPlacementService;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class OrderDelegate {

    private final OrderPlacementService service;

    public OrderDelegate(OrderPlacementService service) {
        this.service = service;
    }

    @Idempotent(key = "#command.idempotencyKey()", scope = "order-place")
    public OrderView place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
        return OrderView.from(service.place(command.cartId()));  // service method is @Transactional
    }
}

Why the Delegate, not the Service?

The Delegate is the orchestration boundary: it owns the "one request = one operation" contract. The Service stays pure business logic with its transaction. With the aspect outermost, the stored result is the DTO the client received — replaying it is exactly correct.

Production test, including concurrency:

in/grocery/common/idempotency/IdempotencyAspectTest.java
package in.grocery.common.idempotency;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.simple.SimpleMeterRegistry;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.aop.aspectj.annotation.AspectJProxyFactory;

class IdempotencyAspectTest {

    record Cmd(String idempotencyKey, String cartId) {}

    static class Placement {
        final AtomicInteger calls = new AtomicInteger();
        volatile CountDownLatch gate = new CountDownLatch(0);

        @Idempotent(key = "#cmd.idempotencyKey()", scope = "order-place")
        public String place(Cmd cmd) throws InterruptedException {
            calls.incrementAndGet();
            gate.await();
            return "ORD-" + cmd.cartId();
        }
    }

    private final SimpleMeterRegistry meters = new SimpleMeterRegistry();
    private final Placement target = new Placement();
    private final Placement proxy = proxy(target);

    private Placement proxy(Placement t) {
        var factory = new AspectJProxyFactory(t);
        factory.setProxyTargetClass(true);
        factory.addAspect(new IdempotencyAspect(new InMemoryIdempotencyStore(Clock.systemUTC()), meters));
        return factory.getProxy();
    }

    @Test
    void replaysCompletedResult() throws Exception {
        assertThat(proxy.place(new Cmd("k-1", "C1"))).isEqualTo("ORD-C1");
        assertThat(proxy.place(new Cmd("k-1", "C1"))).isEqualTo("ORD-C1");
        assertThat(target.calls).hasValue(1);
        assertThat(meters.counter("grocery.idempotency", "result", "replay").count()).isEqualTo(1.0);
    }

    @Test
    void concurrentDuplicateGetsConflict() throws Exception {
        target.gate = new CountDownLatch(1);
        try (var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
            Future<String> first = pool.submit(() -> proxy.place(new Cmd("k-2", "C2")));
            while (target.calls.get() == 0) Thread.onSpinWait();               // first is inside the method

            assertThatThrownBy(() -> proxy.place(new Cmd("k-2", "C2")))
                    .isInstanceOf(IdempotencyConflictException.class);

            target.gate.countDown();
            assertThat(first.get()).isEqualTo("ORD-C2");
        }
        assertThat(target.calls).hasValue(1);
    }

    static class FailingPlacement extends Placement {
        @Override
        @Idempotent(key = "#cmd.idempotencyKey()", scope = "order-place")
        public String place(Cmd cmd) {
            calls.incrementAndGet();
            throw new IllegalStateException("out of stock");
        }
    }

    @Test
    void failureReleasesKey() {
        var failing = new FailingPlacement();
        Placement p = proxy(failing);
        List<Throwable> errors = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
            try { p.place(new Cmd("k-3", "C3")); } catch (Throwable t) { errors.add(t); }
        }
        assertThat(errors).hasSize(2).allMatch(IllegalStateException.class::isInstance); // retry allowed, not 409
        assertThat(failing.calls).hasValue(2);
    }
}

Replay must be the same request

A client reusing a key with a different body is a bug or an attack. Production stores a hash of the request (e.g. SHA-256 of the canonical command) with the key and returns 422 Unprocessable Content on mismatch. Add a fingerprint SpEL attribute to @Idempotent as an exercise.

docs.title: Micrometer annotations — AOP you don't have to write
docs.text:
application.yml
management:
  observations:
    annotations:
      enabled: true      # Boot 3.2+: auto-configures ObservedAspect, TimedAspect, CountedAspect
Micrometer annotations — AOP you don't have to write (snippet)
@Observed(name = "grocery.pricing.quote", contextualName = "quote-cart")
public CartQuote quote(String cartId) { ... }   // metrics + trace span, Chapter 27

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Rename AOP starter for Boot 4.
  • Search for aspects on final classes/records (they were silently not proxied, or fail) — fix design.
  • Decide whether to keep Spring Retry or move to core @Retryable; don't mix both on one method.
  • Re-run aspect tests with AspectJProxyFactory; pointcut syntax is unchanged.
  • Verify ordering of custom aspects vs transaction/caching interceptors still matches your ADR.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Annotation-driven pointcuts for business-visible concerns (@Audited, @Idempotent).

  2. Explicit @Order on every custom aspect, with a documented ordering table for the platform:

    Order Aspect Why HIGHEST + 10 Idempotency Outermost; stores post-commit result HIGHEST + 20 Security (method) Reject before any work 20 Audit Record outcome including commit failures LOWEST Transaction, cache Framework defaults

  3. Never swallow exceptions in @Around/@AfterThrowing.

  4. Keep advice cheap — it runs on every matched call. No blocking I/O in timing aspects.
  5. Test aspects in isolation with AspectJProxyFactory, plus one integration test proving wiring.
  6. Prefer existing aspects — Micrometer @Observed, method security, core @Retryable — over custom ones.
  7. Document each custom aspect: what it matches, order, failure behaviour.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Broad pointcut with side effects

Anti-patterns (snippet)
@Before("execution(* in.grocery..*.*(..))")      // matches everything: config, filters, repositories...
public void log(JoinPoint jp) { log.info("args={}", jp.getArgs()); } // leaks PII (mobile numbers, addresses)

✅ Narrow, annotation-based pointcuts; log IDs, not payloads.

❌ Forgetting to return proceed()'s result

Anti-patterns (snippet)
@Around("@annotation(Timed)")
public void time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable { pjp.proceed(); }  // caller always gets null

✅ public Object time(...) { return pjp.proceed(); }

❌ Business logic in aspects — "apply 10% discount on Diwali" inside an aspect makes pricing untraceable.

❌ @Transactional on private methods or self-calls — silently ignored.

❌ Aspect depending on beans that it advises — can create early-initialization problems and cycles.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Advice never runs Aspect not a bean; pointcut doesn't match; self-invocation; method private/final; class is a record Add @Component; test pointcut with AspectJProxyFactory; move method to another bean BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException JDK proxy but injecting concrete class Keep CGLIB default or inject interface Cannot subclass final class CGLIB on final class Remove final, or don't advise it Wrong order (audit rolled back / missing) Aspect order vs transaction interceptor Set explicit orders; document error Type referred to is not an annotation type Pointcut refers to annotation by simple name without binding / wrong FQN Use FQN or bind as parameter 0 formal unbound in pointcut Advice parameter not bound in expression Match names in args()/@annotation(); add argNames High CPU in profiler under AspectJExpressionPointcut Runtime-matching pointcuts (args, this) on hot paths Prefer static execution/@annotation Replayed response differs from original Result mutated after storing Store immutable DTOs (records)

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every custom aspect has explicit order and a test
  • No aspect logs request bodies or PII
  • Pointcuts are annotation-based or narrowly scoped
  • Aspect ordering documented in an ADR
  • Idempotency on all non-idempotent public POST endpoints that create money-moving entities
  • Self-invocation checked in code review (ArchUnit or IDE inspections)

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is AOP and why use it?

Short answer: A way to modularize cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security) in aspects applied to many methods declaratively, instead of repeating that code in each method.

Follow-ups: Name Spring features built on AOP.

B1 · Define aspect, advice, pointcut and join point.

Short answer: Aspect — module of a concern. Advice — the code that runs. Pointcut — expression choosing where. Join point — a point in execution (in Spring, a method execution).

B1 · What advice types exist?

Short answer: @Before, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @After (finally), @Around (wraps and controls the call).

B1 · Why doesn't my aspect run even though it has @Aspect?

Short answer: @Aspect doesn't register a bean. Add @Component or a @Bean method, and ensure the AspectJ starter is on the classpath.

B1 · Which Spring annotations are implemented using AOP?

Short answer: @Transactional, @Cacheable/@CacheEvict, @Async, @PreAuthorize, @Validated (method validation), @Retryable, Micrometer @Observed/@Timed.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Explain the self-invocation problem and how to fix it.

Short answer: Spring AOP is proxy-based; a call from one method to another in the same object uses this, not the proxy, so advice (e.g. @Transactional) is skipped. Fix by moving the method to another bean, using a programmatic API (TransactionTemplate), self-injecting the proxy, AopContext.currentProxy(), or AspectJ weaving.

Red flags: "Make the method public" (necessary but not sufficient).

B2 · JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB proxy?

Short answer: JDK proxies implement interfaces; CGLIB subclasses the class. Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB. CGLIB can't proxy final classes/methods; JDK proxies can only be injected as the interface type.

B2 · Can you apply @Transactional to a private method?

Short answer: No effect with Spring AOP — private methods aren't overridable or visible to the proxy. (Framework 6 CGLIB proxies can advise protected and package-private methods, but not private.)

B2 · How do you control the order of multiple aspects?

Short answer: @Order or Ordered on the aspect class; lower value is higher precedence (outermost). Within one aspect, order by advice type — split into separate aspects if order matters.

B2 · How do you get the annotation instance inside advice?

Short answer: Bind it: @Around("@annotation(audited)") public Object x(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Audited audited).

B2 · Why are records a problem for AOP-based annotations?

Short answer: Records are implicitly final; CGLIB can't subclass them. Use records for data, classes for services.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does Spring create AOP proxies internally?

Short answer: AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator (a BPP) in postProcessAfterInitialization collects advisors (from @Aspect beans and Advisor beans), checks if any pointcut matches the bean's class/methods, then builds a proxy via ProxyFactory — ObjenesisCglibAopProxy or JdkDynamicAopProxy. The proxy replaces the bean in the container.

B3 · How is a method call executed through a proxy with several advisors?

Short answer: The proxy gets the cached interceptor chain for that method and creates a ReflectiveMethodInvocation (or CglibMethodInvocation); each interceptor calls proceed() to pass control to the next; the last invokes the target.

B3 · Difference between this() and target() pointcut designators?

Short answer: this matches the proxy's type; target matches the target object's type. With JDK proxies, this(ConcreteClass) doesn't match because the proxy only implements interfaces.

B3 · What's the performance cost of Spring AOP?

Short answer: Proxy creation at startup (pointcut matching per bean) and a small per-call overhead for advised methods (interceptor chain). Negligible compared to I/O. Watch runtime-matching pointcuts (args with binding) on hot paths and heavy work inside advice.

B3 · Is @Configuration CGLIB enhancement the same as AOP?

Short answer: No. ConfigurationClassEnhancer subclasses @Configuration classes to intercept @Bean method calls and return container singletons. It's unrelated to advisors and @Aspect.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Should an audit aspect run inside or outside the transaction? Defend.

Short answer: Inside (transaction outermost) → audit is atomic with the change, but a rollback erases evidence of the attempt. Outside (audit outermost) → captures commit failures and attempts, but audit write is a separate transaction (needs its own, and can fail independently). Regulatory audit of attempts favours outside with a separate REQUIRES_NEW or async sink; audit of changes favours inside or CDC. Make it explicit via orders and an ADR.

B4 · How would you implement API idempotency in Spring?

Short answer: Idempotency-Key header, atomic reserve in Redis (SET NX PX) with IN_PROGRESS/COMPLETED states, aspect outermost so the result is stored post-commit, replay stored response, 409 for concurrent duplicates, request fingerprint to detect key reuse with a different body, TTL 24h, and metrics. For payments add reconciliation with the gateway.

B4 · When would you choose AspectJ weaving over Spring AOP?

Short answer: When you need advice on self-calls, non-Spring objects (entities), field access, constructors, or very hot paths where proxies hurt. Cost: build plugin or -javaagent, harder debugging, team familiarity. Rare in typical services.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · AOP makes behaviour invisible. How do you govern it in a large codebase?

Short answer: Only platform-owned aspects in shared libraries, annotation-based opt-in, a documented ordering table, ArchUnit rules forbidding package-wide pointcuts outside the platform module, observability of aspect behaviour (metrics), and review checklists for self-invocation. Business logic stays out of aspects.

B5 · Is AOP still relevant with virtual threads, records and functional style?

Short answer: Yes — the container still applies transactions, security, observability and resilience uniformly through proxies. But functional composition (decorators, TransactionTemplate, higher-order functions) is often clearer for local concerns. Use AOP where uniformity across hundreds of methods matters; use explicit composition where readability matters.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Customers charged twice during Big Billion-style sale

Timeline: POST /orders takes 12s during a Razorpay slowdown; the app retries after 10s; the load balancer also retries on 504. Two orders are created and both captured. Fix: idempotency aspect on the order delegate with Redis store, client-generated keys persisted across app retries, gateway-side idempotency (Razorpay order receipt IDs), LB retry disabled for non-idempotent methods, and a nightly reconciliation job to auto-refund duplicates.

Scenario · @Cacheable on PriceService.priceFor returns stale prices only for bulk quotes

quoteCart() in the same class loops and calls this.priceFor(sku) — self-invocation bypasses the cache proxy, so bulk quotes hit the DB (not stale!) while single lookups hit the cache (stale after a price change without eviction). Two problems: self-invocation (move lookup to PriceLookup bean) and missing @CacheEvict on price updates.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · @SlowCallAlert(thresholdMs = 500)

Write an aspect that logs a WARN with method name and duration when an annotated method exceeds its threshold, and increments a Micrometer counter grocery.slow.calls{method=...}. Test it with AspectJProxyFactory and a fake slow method.

Solution SlowCallAlert.java
package in.grocery.common.aop;

import java.lang.annotation.ElementType;
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import java.lang.annotation.Target;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Target(ElementType.METHOD)
public @interface SlowCallAlert {
    long thresholdMs();
}
SlowCallAlertAspect.java
package in.grocery.common.aop;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;

@Aspect
public class SlowCallAlertAspect {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(SlowCallAlertAspect.class);
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    public SlowCallAlertAspect(MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.meters = meters;
    }

    @Around("@annotation(alert)")
    public Object watch(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, SlowCallAlert alert) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();
        } finally {
            long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
            if (ms > alert.thresholdMs()) {
                String method = pjp.getSignature().toShortString();
                log.warn("Slow call {} took {} ms (threshold {} ms)", method, ms, alert.thresholdMs());
                meters.counter("grocery.slow.calls", "method", method).increment();
            }
        }
    }
}
SlowCallAlertAspectTest.java
package in.grocery.common.aop;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.simple.SimpleMeterRegistry;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.aop.aspectj.annotation.AspectJProxyFactory;

class SlowCallAlertAspectTest {

    static class SearchService {
        @SlowCallAlert(thresholdMs = 50)
        public void search(long sleepMs) throws InterruptedException { Thread.sleep(sleepMs); }
    }

    @Test
    void countsOnlySlowCalls() throws Exception {
        var meters = new SimpleMeterRegistry();
        var factory = new AspectJProxyFactory(new SearchService());
        factory.addAspect(new SlowCallAlertAspect(meters));
        SearchService proxy = factory.getProxy();

        proxy.search(0);
        proxy.search(80);

        assertThat(meters.get("grocery.slow.calls").counter().count()).isEqualTo(1.0);
    }
}

In production prefer a Micrometer Timer with SLO buckets and alert in Prometheus; this aspect is for teams without that yet, or for targeted diagnostics.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Spring AOP = runtime proxies applying advisors (pointcut + advice) to method executions of beans.
  • Boot defaults to CGLIB: no final classes/methods, no records, no private methods.
  • Self-invocation bypasses every proxy-based annotation — split beans or use programmatic APIs.
  • AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator builds one proxy per bean combining your aspects with @Transactional, @Cacheable, security, etc.
  • Order is explicit and important — especially relative to transactions.
  • Prefer annotation-based pointcuts, cheap advice, and never swallow exceptions.
  • Idempotency, auditing and observability are excellent aspect use cases; business rules are not.
  • Test aspects fast with AspectJProxyFactory.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Framework Reference — Core › Aspect Oriented Programming with Spring (AOP concepts, @AspectJ support, proxying mechanisms, Spring AOP APIs)
  • Spring Framework Reference — Core › Resilience Features (Framework 7)
  • Spring Boot Reference — Observability › Annotations ; AOP auto-configuration properties
  • AspectJ Programming Guide — Pointcuts

03 Bean Lifecycle, Events & Extension Points · 05 Spring Boot Fundamentals

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapters 02–04 were Spring Framework. This chapter is about what Spring Boot adds on top: starters, auto-configuration, the SpringApplication bootstrap, embedded servers and the developer experience around them.

Boot's promise is "opinionated defaults that get out of your way". Add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa and a PostgreSQL driver, set a URL, and you get a pooled DataSource, an EntityManagerFactory, a transaction manager, repositories, health checks and metrics — no configuration class written.

That magic becomes a liability when you don't understand it:

  • "Why is there a second ObjectMapper and my date format is ignored?" — you defined one and Boot's backed off, but a library created another.
  • "Why did the service start on port 8080 with an H2 database in production?" — H2 was on the runtime classpath through a test utility module.
  • "Why did the Boot 4 upgrade break our shared library?" — it relied on an auto-configuration class in a package that moved during modularization.

For the grocery platform we'll also build a small platform auto-configuration so every one of the 26 services gets the same clock, request-context handling and failure diagnostics simply by adding one dependency. (Chapter 41 turns it into a full starter.)

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — starters, @SpringBootApplication, runners, DevTools B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — overriding defaults, excluding auto-configs, condition report, embedded server tuning B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — SpringApplication.run internals, auto-configuration ordering, failure analyzers B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7 — platform auto-configuration, Boot 4 modularization strategy B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 7, 8, 9 — opinionated platforms, when to fight or embrace Boot defaults

docs.title: 2.1 What Spring Boot adds
docs.text: Capability What it gives you Starters Curated dependency sets per capability Auto-configuration Conditional default beans based on classpath, properties and existing beans SpringApplication Opinionated bootstrap: environment, profiles, banner, context type, runners, events Externalized configuration Layered properties from files, env, args, secrets (Chapter 06) Embedded servers Tomcat or Jetty inside your JAR Executable JARs java -jar deployment (Chapter 01, 29) Production features Actuator: health, metrics, info (Chapter 27) Developer tools DevTools restart, Docker Compose and Testcontainers integration Testing support Slices, ApplicationContextRunner, service connections (Chapters 15, 28)

docs.title: 2.2 @SpringBootApplication
2.3 Starters
docs.text:
A starter is a POM with dependencies and (usually) no code.

Starter (Boot 3.5 name) Brings spring-boot-starter Core, logging (Logback), YAML (SnakeYAML) spring-boot-starter-web Spring MVC, Jackson, embedded Tomcat spring-boot-starter-webflux WebFlux, Reactor Netty spring-boot-starter-data-jpa Hibernate, Spring Data JPA, HikariCP spring-boot-starter-jdbc JdbcClient/JdbcTemplate, HikariCP spring-boot-starter-validation Hibernate Validator spring-boot-starter-security Spring Security spring-boot-starter-actuator Actuator, Micrometer spring-boot-starter-test JUnit Jupiter, AssertJ, Mockito, Spring Test, JSONassert, Awaitility, ...

Swap technologies by excluding and adding starters (e.g. Tomcat → Jetty).

docs.title: 2.4 Auto-configuration
docs.text:
An auto-configuration is a @Configuration class annotated with @AutoConfiguration and listed in:

Example
META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports

Each one is guarded by conditions (Chapter 03) — typically:

JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration.java
@AutoConfiguration(after = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class)
@ConditionalOnClass(JdbcTemplate.class)            // library present?
@ConditionalOnSingleCandidate(DataSource.class)    // exactly one DataSource?
public class JdbcTemplateAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(JdbcOperations.class) // did the user define one? then back off
    JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate(DataSource ds, JdbcProperties props) { ... }
}

The golden rule: your beans win. Auto-configurations are processed after user configuration, and @ConditionalOnMissingBean makes them back off.

docs.title: 2.5 Customizing defaults — the ladder
docs.text:
From least to most invasive:

  1. Properties — spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null
  2. Customizer beans — Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer / JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer, WebServerFactoryCustomizer, RestClientCustomizer, HikariConfig via properties
  3. Replace a bean — define your own ObjectMapper; Boot backs off (you lose Boot's customizations)
  4. Exclude an auto-configuration — spring.autoconfigure.exclude=... or @SpringBootApplication(exclude = ...)
  5. Write your own auto-configuration

Always start at the top of the ladder.

docs.title: 2.6 SpringApplication
docs.text:
Beyond SpringApplication.run(App.class, args) you can configure:

Setting Code / property Web application type setWebApplicationType(WebApplicationType.NONE) / spring.main.web-application-type=none Banner banner.txt, spring.main.banner-mode=off Lazy initialization spring.main.lazy-initialization=true Additional profiles setAdditionalProfiles("india") Default properties setDefaultProperties(...) (lowest precedence) Startup metrics setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(n)) Listeners/initializers addListeners, addInitializers Fluent builder / hierarchies SpringApplicationBuilder

Web application type deduction: SERVLET if Spring MVC and a servlet API are present; REACTIVE if WebFlux is present and MVC isn't; otherwise NONE.

docs.title: 2.7 Runners
docs.text: ApplicationRunner (parsed ApplicationArguments) and CommandLineRunner (raw String[]) run once, after the context is started and before ApplicationReadyEvent. Order them with @Order. An exception in a runner fails startup. Uses: warm-up, one-off maintenance, CLI tools built with Boot.

docs.title: 2.8 Failure analyzers
docs.text: When startup fails, Boot tries registered FailureAnalyzers to turn a stack trace into a human message with Description and Action — e.g. "Port 8080 was already in use" or "Failed to configure a DataSource: 'url' attribute is not specified". You can add your own.

docs.title: 2.9 Embedded servers
docs.text:
Server Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Notes Tomcat ✅ default ✅ default Most common Jetty ✅ ✅ (Jetty 12) Lower memory, good HTTP/2 Undertow ✅ ❌ removed Not compatible with Servlet 6.1 Reactor Netty WebFlux default WebFlux default Non-servlet

Key properties: server.port, server.shutdown, server.tomcat.threads.max, server.tomcat.max-connections, server.tomcat.accept-count, server.max-http-request-header-size, server.http2.enabled, server.compression.enabled, server.ssl.* / SSL bundles.

Virtual threads: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true (Java 21+) makes Tomcat/Jetty handle requests on virtual threads and switches several executors (@Async, scheduling, Kafka listener containers) to virtual threads.

docs.title: 2.10 DevTools
docs.text:
spring-boot-devtools (as developmentOnly) provides:

  • Automatic restart when classes change — two class loaders: a base loader for third-party JARs (unchanged) and a restart loader for your code (thrown away on restart), so restarts are fast.
  • Development property defaults — caching off for templates, extra web logging.
  • Global settings in ~/.config/spring-boot/.

DevTools disables itself when running from a fully packaged JAR (java -jar), and is excluded from the executable archive by default. Never ship it.

docs.title: 2.11 Boot 4 modularization
docs.text:
In Boot 3.x, nearly all auto-configurations live in one large spring-boot-autoconfigure JAR, and spring-boot-starter-test pulls every test utility. Boot 4 splits this into focused modules per technology (web MVC, JDBC, JPA, Kafka, …), each with its own auto-configuration, properties and test support, with starters to match. Benefits: smaller classpaths, faster startup and condition evaluation, clearer ownership, fewer "surprise" auto-configurations. For migration, Boot 4 ships classic starters that reproduce the old all-in-one arrangement.

Verify

Module, package and starter names in Boot 4 are defined in the Spring Boot 4.0 Migration Guide. Code that imports auto-configuration classes directly (tests, @ImportAutoConfiguration, exclude = ...) is where most breakage appears.

docs.title: 3.1 SpringApplication.run(...)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant M as main()
    participant SA as SpringApplication
    participant L as SpringApplicationRunListeners
    participant Env as ConfigurableEnvironment
    participant Ctx as ApplicationContext

    M->>SA: new SpringApplication(sources)
    Note over SA: deduce WebApplicationType<br/>load ApplicationContextInitializers & ApplicationListeners<br/>from META-INF/spring.factories<br/>deduce main class
    M->>SA: run(args)
    SA->>SA: createBootstrapContext()
    SA->>L: starting → ApplicationStartingEvent
    SA->>Env: prepareEnvironment()
    Note over Env: property sources, profiles,<br/>EnvironmentPostProcessors (config data: application.yml, imports)
    SA->>L: environmentPrepared
    SA->>SA: printBanner()
    SA->>Ctx: createApplicationContext() via ApplicationContextFactory
    SA->>Ctx: prepareContext() — initializers, load primary sources as bean definitions
    SA->>L: contextPrepared / contextLoaded
    SA->>Ctx: refresh() (Chapter 03) — auto-config, beans, web server
    SA->>L: started → ApplicationStartedEvent
    SA->>SA: callRunners()
    SA->>L: ready → ApplicationReadyEvent

SpringApplication itself uses Spring's SpringFactoriesLoader to find ApplicationContextInitializer, ApplicationListener, EnvironmentPostProcessor, FailureAnalyzer and SpringApplicationRunListener implementations in META-INF/spring.factories — which is how libraries hook in before any bean exists.

docs.title: 3.2 How auto-configurations are selected
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["@EnableAutoConfiguration"] --> B[AutoConfigurationImportSelector<br/>a DeferredImportSelector]
    B --> C[read all AutoConfiguration.imports files<br/>from every JAR via ImportCandidates]
    C --> D[remove exclusions<br/>exclude, excludeName, spring.autoconfigure.exclude]
    D --> E[AutoConfigurationImportFilter<br/>fast pre-filter using<br/>spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties<br/>OnClass / OnBean / OnWebApplication]
    E --> F["sort by @AutoConfiguration before/after,<br/>@AutoConfigureOrder"]
    F --> G[process as configuration classes<br/>AFTER all user configuration]
    G --> H["full condition evaluation<br/>per class and per @Bean"]
    H --> I[ConditionEvaluationReport<br/>--debug, /actuator/conditions]

Details that matter:

  • Deferred: DeferredImportSelector guarantees auto-configurations are processed after your @Configuration classes, which is why @ConditionalOnMissingBean sees your beans.
  • Pre-filtering: the annotation processor spring-boot-autoconfigure-processor writes META-INF/spring-autoconfigure-metadata.properties so classes whose @ConditionalOnClass fails are skipped without loading them — a big startup win with hundreds of candidates.
  • Ordering: only affects auto-configurations relative to each other. Never use @AutoConfigureAfter on a normal @Configuration — it has no effect.
  • Don't component-scan auto-configurations. AutoConfigurationExcludeFilter in @SpringBootApplication prevents it, but a custom @ComponentScan elsewhere can accidentally pick them up and bypass ordering.

docs.title: 3.3 Embedded server startup
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[refresh → onRefresh] --> B[ServletWebServerApplicationContext.createWebServer]
    B --> C[ServletWebServerFactory bean<br/>TomcatServletWebServerFactory]
    C --> D[WebServerFactoryCustomizers applied<br/>ports, threads, compression, SSL]
    D --> E[Tomcat created, NOT yet accepting]
    E --> F[beans instantiated<br/>DispatcherServlet registered]
    F --> G[finishRefresh → WebServerStartStopLifecycle.start]
    G --> H[connector started, port bound<br/>WebServerInitializedEvent]

The server is created early (so servlet-context-aware beans can use it) but starts accepting connections only after all singletons exist, via a SmartLifecycle. That's why the app never receives a request while half-initialized.

docs.title: 3.4 Failure analysis
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Exception during run] --> B[SpringApplication.handleRunFailure]
    B --> C[ApplicationFailedEvent]
    B --> D[FailureAnalyzers from spring.factories]
    D --> E{analyzer returns<br/>FailureAnalysis?}
    E -- yes --> F[LoggingFailureAnalysisReporter<br/>APPLICATION FAILED TO START<br/>Description / Action]
    E -- no --> G[stack trace]

AbstractFailureAnalyzer<T> walks the cause chain and matches the first exception of type T.

docs.title: 4.1 A service with zero configuration classes
4.2 See what Boot configured
docs.text:
Terminal
./gradlew bootRun --args='--debug'
Condition evaluation report (excerpt)
============================
CONDITIONS EVALUATION REPORT
============================

Positive matches:
-----------------
   DataSourceAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnClass found required classes 'javax.sql.DataSource', ... (OnClassCondition)

   JdbcClientAutoConfiguration matched:
      - @ConditionalOnSingleCandidate (types: org.springframework.jdbc.core.namedparam.NamedParameterJdbcTemplate; SearchStrategy: all) found a single bean ...

Negative matches:
-----------------
