04 AOP · 06 Externalized Configuration

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
The same JAR must run on a developer's laptop, in CI, in staging and in three production regions — with different database URLs, Razorpay keys, delivery radius limits and feature switches. Externalized configuration is how Spring Boot lets one artifact adapt to each environment without rebuilding.

It's also where a surprising number of outages start:

  • A ConfigMap key SPRING_DATASOURCE_URl (lowercase l) is silently ignored; the service falls back to a default and connects to the wrong database.
  • A property is typed 3000 meaning milliseconds in one service and seconds in another.
  • A secret ends up in application-prod.yml, committed to Git, and exposed via /actuator/env.
  • An operator raises grocery.cart.max-items to 5000 to fix a complaint and brings down the pricing service with oversized requests — nothing validated the value.

This chapter teaches exactly where properties come from, in what order, how they bind to typed Java objects, and how to validate and secure them. For the grocery platform we'll design a configuration architecture: defaults in the JAR, environment specifics from Kubernetes ConfigMaps, secrets from mounted files or Vault — all bound to validated records that fail fast at startup.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — application.yml, @Value, profiles B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — @ConfigurationProperties records, validation, relaxed binding, env vars B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5 — property source order, config data imports, config trees, Binder API B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7 — configuration architecture, secrets, runtime refresh trade-offs B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — governance, config as a product, change safety

docs.title: 2.1 Property sources and precedence
docs.text:
Boot assembles the Environment from many property sources. When the same key exists in several, the higher source wins. From lowest to highest:

# Source 1 Default properties (SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties) 2 @PropertySource annotations on @Configuration classes 3 Config data — application.properties/.yml files and spring.config.imports 4 Random values (random.*) 5 OS environment variables 6 Java system properties (-Dkey=value) 7 JNDI attributes 8 ServletContext init parameters 9 ServletConfig init parameters 10 SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON (env var or system property with inline JSON) 11 Command-line arguments (--key=value) 12 properties attribute of tests (@SpringBootTest(properties = ...)) 13 @DynamicPropertySource in tests 14 @TestPropertySource 15 DevTools global settings (~/.config/spring-boot) when DevTools active

Mental model

The closer to the running process, the stronger. Files in the JAR are weakest; env vars override them; command-line args override env vars; tests override everything.

@PropertySource is weak and late

It's added only when the configuration class is parsed — too late for properties that auto-configuration or logging needs early (spring.main.*, logging.*). Prefer spring.config.import.

docs.title: 2.2 Config data files and their order
docs.text:
Boot looks for application.properties / application.yml in these locations (later overrides earlier):

  1. classpath:/
  2. classpath:/config/
  3. file:./ (current directory)
  4. file:./config/
  5. file:./config/*/ (immediate sub-directories)

Within the config data layer:

  1. application.yml inside the JAR
  2. application-{profile}.yml inside the JAR
  3. application.yml outside the JAR
  4. application-{profile}.yml outside the JAR

If .properties and .yml exist in the same location, .properties wins. Pick one format per project. This handbook uses YAML.

Override locations with spring.config.location (replaces defaults) or spring.config.additional-location (adds). Both must be set before config data loads — as env vars, system properties or command-line args.

docs.title: 2.3 Profiles
docs.text:
• Activate: spring.profiles.active=prod (env: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod).
  • Profile-specific files: application-prod.yml.
  • Documents inside one YAML file separated by ---, activated with spring.config.activate.on-profile.
  • Profile groups: spring.profiles.group.prod=prod-db,prod-kafka,india.
  • Include: spring.profiles.include adds profiles (only in non-profile-specific documents).
  • Default profile: default, used when none is active.
  • Expressions in @Profile and on-profile: prod & !mumbai, staging | perf.

What profile-specific documents can't do

spring.profiles.active, spring.profiles.include and spring.profiles.group can't be set inside profile-specific files or on-profile documents — Boot fails at startup. Activation must come from outside the thing being activated.

docs.title: 2.4 Other activation conditions
docs.text: spring.config.activate.on-cloud-platform=kubernetes activates a document only on a detected platform (Kubernetes, Cloud Foundry, Heroku, Azure App Service, ...).

docs.title: 2.5 spring.config.import
docs.text:
Pull more config data in, relative to the declaring file:

application.yml
spring:
  config:
    import:
      - optional:file:./local-overrides.yml       # optional: don't fail if missing
      - classpath:grocery-defaults.yml
      - configtree:/var/run/secrets/grocery/       # one file per property
      - optional:configserver:                     # Spring Cloud Config
      - optional:vault://                          # Spring Cloud Vault

Imported files take precedence over the file that imports them. Import order matters: later imports win.

docs.title: 2.6 Config trees
docs.text:
Kubernetes mounts Secrets/ConfigMaps as one file per key. A config tree maps that to properties:

Example
/var/run/secrets/grocery/
├── razorpay/
│   ├── key-id          → razorpay.key-id
│   └── key-secret      → razorpay.key-secret
└── db.password         → db.password

configtree:/var/run/secrets/grocery/ — directory names become dot-separated prefixes. Values are read lazily and can be bound to String, byte[], etc.

docs.title: 2.7 @Value
docs.text:
@Value (snippet)
@Value("${grocery.cart.max-items:50}") int maxItems;
  • ${key:default} — placeholder with default.
  • Works anywhere, including SpEL (#{...}).
  • Limited: one value at a time, no validation, no metadata, weak relaxed binding (use canonical kebab-case names), string-typed errors at runtime.

Use @Value for one-offs; use @ConfigurationProperties for anything that is a group of settings.

docs.title: 2.8 @ConfigurationProperties
docs.text:
Binds a whole prefix to a typed object. Preferred style in Boot 3/4: immutable records.

CartProperties.java
@ConfigurationProperties("grocery.cart")
public record CartProperties(
        @DefaultValue("50") int maxItems,
        @DefaultValue("30m") Duration reservationTtl) {}

Register with @EnableConfigurationProperties(CartProperties.class) or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan on the application class.

Features:

  • Constructor binding for records/immutable classes (automatic when there is a single constructor).
  • Nested objects, lists, maps, enums.
  • Units: Duration (10s, 500ms, 2h, ISO PT10S), Period (7d), DataSize (10MB), with @DurationUnit / @DataSizeUnit for bare numbers.
  • Validation with @Validated + Jakarta constraints — fails startup on invalid values.
  • Metadata for IDE auto-completion via spring-boot-configuration-processor.
  • Third-party binding: @ConfigurationProperties on a @Bean method binds onto an object you create.

docs.title: 2.9 Relaxed binding
docs.text:
@ConfigurationProperties matches names flexibly:

Source Form for grocery.cart.maxItems Properties/YAML (recommended) grocery.cart.max-items (kebab case) Also accepted grocery.cart.maxItems, grocery.cart.max_items Environment variable GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS List index in env var GROCERY_SELLERS_0_NAME → grocery.sellers[0].name

Environment variable rules: replace . with _, remove -, uppercase. Dashes are dropped, not turned into underscores — max-items → MAXITEMS.

Map keys with special characters need brackets: grocery.gst-rates.[5.0]=... keeps 5.0 as the key instead of treating . as nesting.

docs.title: 2.10 Random values
docs.text: ${random.uuid}, ${random.int}, ${random.int(1000,2000)}, ${random.long}, ${random.value} — useful for instance IDs or test ports. Not a secrets generator.

docs.title: 2.11 Secrets and encryption
docs.text:
Boot itself has no built-in property encryption. Options:

Approach Notes Kubernetes Secrets as env vars Simple; visible in kubectl describe to some roles; in process env Kubernetes Secrets as files + configtree: Better; not in env; supports rotation with restart Spring Cloud Vault (vault://) Dynamic secrets (DB credentials with leases), central audit Cloud secret managers (AWS/Azure/GCP) Via Spring Cloud AWS/Azure/GCP config data imports External Secrets Operator / CSI driver Syncs vault → K8s Secret files Encrypted values ({cipher} in Spring Cloud Config) Decrypted by config server or client Jasypt (third-party) Encrypted values in files; the key becomes the new secret

Never commit secrets to Git, even in "prod-only" files.

docs.title: 2.12 Spring Cloud Config
docs.text: A central server (backed by Git, Vault, JDBC, …) serving configuration per application/profile/label. Clients import it with spring.config.import=configserver:http://config:8888. Useful when many services share configuration and you want versioned, audited changes outside Kubernetes. With Kubernetes-native tooling (GitOps + ConfigMaps), many teams no longer need it.

docs.title: 2.13 Configuration metadata
docs.text: spring-boot-configuration-processor (annotation processor) generates META-INF/spring-configuration-metadata.json from @ConfigurationProperties classes: names, types, defaults, Javadoc descriptions, deprecations. IDEs use it for completion and validation. additional-spring-configuration-metadata.json adds hints (allowed values) and deprecations manually.

docs.title: 3.1 Building the Environment
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant SA as SpringApplication
    participant Env as StandardEnvironment
    participant EPPL as EnvironmentPostProcessorApplicationListener
    participant CDE as ConfigDataEnvironment
    participant Loc as ConfigDataLocationResolvers
    participant Ldr as ConfigDataLoaders

    SA->>Env: create (system props, env vars sources)
    SA->>Env: add command-line args, default props
    SA->>EPPL: ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent
    EPPL->>EPPL: run EnvironmentPostProcessors in order
    EPPL->>CDE: ConfigDataEnvironmentPostProcessor
    CDE->>Loc: resolve locations (classpath:/, file:./config/, imports)
    Loc->>Ldr: StandardConfigDataLoader (yml/properties),<br/>ConfigTreeConfigDataLoader, configserver, vault...
    Ldr-->>CDE: ConfigData (property sources)
    Note over CDE: 1. load initial files (no profile)<br/>2. process imports recursively<br/>3. determine active profiles<br/>4. load profile-specific files and on-profile docs<br/>5. process their imports
    CDE->>Env: add config data property sources in precedence order

Key classes: ConfigDataEnvironment, ConfigDataLocationResolver, ConfigDataLoader, StandardConfigDataLocationResolver, ConfigTreeConfigDataLoader. Spring Cloud Config and Vault plug in by providing their own resolver/loader pairs (registered in spring.factories).

docs.title: 3.2 Binding a @ConfigurationProperties record
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["@ConfigurationProperties class registered<br/>EnableConfigurationProperties / Scan"] --> B[ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor<br/>or bean creation for constructor-bound types]
    B --> C[ConfigurationPropertiesBinder]
    C --> D[Binder over ConfigurationPropertySources<br/>adapts every PropertySource to canonical names]
    D --> E[ValueObjectBinder: constructor binding<br/>JavaBeanBinder: setter binding]
    E --> F[ApplicationConversionService<br/>String → Duration, DataSize, enum, ZoneId...]
    F --> G{"@Validated?"}
    G -- yes --> H[ValidationBindHandler<br/>Jakarta Bean Validation]
    H -->|violations| X[BindValidationException<br/>→ failure analyzer message]
    G -- no --> I[bean ready]
    H -->|valid| I
  • ConfigurationPropertySource wraps each PropertySource and maps names to a canonical form (grocery.cart.max-items). Relaxed binding happens here — env var sources get a special mapper (SystemEnvironmentPropertyMapper).
  • Binder is also a public API: Binder.get(env).bind("grocery.cart", CartProperties.class) — handy in EnvironmentPostProcessors and conditions (Chapter 03).
  • Binding failures produce clear failure-analyzer output listing property, value, origin and reason.

docs.title: 3.3 Origins — where did this value come from?
docs.text:
Every property value tracks its origin (OriginTrackedValue): file name and line, env var name, command-line arg. /actuator/env/{name} and binding error messages show it:

Example
Property: grocery.cart.max-items
Value: "5000"
Origin: "GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS" from property source "systemEnvironment"
Reason: must be less than or equal to 200

This is the single most useful debugging feature for configuration.

docs.title: 4.1 Your first application.yml
docs.text:
src/main/resources/application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: cart-service

server:
  port: 8082

grocery:
  cart:
    max-items: 50
    free-delivery-threshold: 499
    welcome-message: "Welcome to ${spring.application.name}!"   # (1)!
  1. Placeholders can reference other properties.

docs.title: 4.2 Reading values with @Value
4.3 Profiles
docs.text:
src/main/resources/application-local.yml
grocery:
  cart:
    max-items: 500           # generous limit for manual testing
logging:
  level:
    in.grocery: debug
Terminal
./gradlew bootRun --args='--spring.profiles.active=local'
curl localhost:8082/cart/info
# {"maxItems":500,"freeDeliveryAbove":499,"message":"Welcome to cart-service!"}

docs.title: 4.4 Overriding from outside
docs.text:
Terminal
# environment variable (relaxed binding: dots→underscores, dashes removed, uppercase)
GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS=75 java -jar cart-service.jar

# system property
java -Dgrocery.cart.max-items=80 -jar cart-service.jar

# command-line argument (strongest of the three)
java -jar cart-service.jar --grocery.cart.max-items=90

@Value and env vars

@Value("${grocery.cart.max-items}") still finds GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS because Boot's env-var property source supports this mapping for canonical kebab-case names. It does not work for camelCase keys like ${grocery.cart.maxItems} — another reason to use kebab case everywhere.

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Typed, validated configuration with a record
5.2 Level 2 — Testing configuration binding
5.3 Level 2 — Multi-document YAML and profile groups
docs.text:
application.yml — order-service
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: [prod-db, prod-kafka, india]          # (1)!
      staging: [staging-db, prod-kafka, india]

grocery:
  order:
    auto-cancel-unpaid-after: 15m

---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: india                           # (2)!
grocery:
  order:
    currency: INR
    timezone: Asia/Kolkata

---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: "prod-db"
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 30

---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: "local | test"                   # (3)!
grocery:
  order:
    auto-cancel-unpaid-after: 2m
  1. SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod activates four profiles.
  2. Documents are processed in order; later documents override earlier ones.
  3. Profile expressions work in on-profile.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Environment variables in Kubernetes
docs.text:
k8s/order-service-configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service
data:
  SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: "prod"
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: "jdbc:postgresql://orders-db.prod:5432/orders"
  GROCERY_ORDER_AUTOCANCELUNPAIDAFTER: "20m"              # (1)!
  GROCERY_CART_CITYOVERRIDES_BLR: "399"                    # (2)!
  GROCERY_DELIVERY_HUBS_0_CODE: "BLR-HSR"                  # (3)!
  GROCERY_DELIVERY_HUBS_0_RADIUSKM: "6"
  GROCERY_DELIVERY_HUBS_1_CODE: "BLR-WHF"
  GROCERY_DELIVERY_HUBS_1_RADIUSKM: "8"
  1. auto-cancel-unpaid-after → dashes removed → AUTOCANCELUNPAIDAFTER.
  2. Map key via env var. Keys are lower-cased by the env mapping in some cases — map keys with case sensitivity are unreliable through env vars; prefer YAML via config file mounts for maps.
  3. List element via _0_.

Env vars vs mounted config file

For more than a handful of properties, mount a ConfigMap as a file and import it: spring.config.import=optional:file:/etc/grocery/application.yml. YAML is reviewable, supports maps and lists naturally, and avoids env-var name mangling. Keep env vars for the few settings needed before config data loads (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT).

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Secrets with config trees
5.6 Level 3 — Binding third-party objects and using the Binder API
5.7 Level 3 — Map keys with special characters
docs.text:
application.yml
grocery:
  tax:
    gst-rates:
      "[0.0]": [fresh-vegetables, fresh-fruits, milk]      # (1)!
      "[5.0]": [tea, edible-oil, packaged-atta]
      "[12.0]": [butter, ghee, dry-fruits]
      "[18.0]": [biscuits, soap, toothpaste]
TaxProperties.java
@ConfigurationProperties("grocery.tax")
public record TaxProperties(Map<String, List<String>> gstRates) {}
  1. Brackets (quoted in YAML) keep 5.0 as a single key. Without them, 5.0 would be interpreted as nested key 5 → 0.

GST rates are illustrative

Actual GST slabs and item classifications change by government notification. In production, rates come from a managed tax master (database with effective dates), not static configuration.

docs.title: 6.1 Configuration architecture for the grocery platform
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph JAR[Inside the JAR — reviewed in PRs]
        A[application.yml<br/>safe defaults for every property]
        B[application-local.yml<br/>laptop overrides]
    end
    subgraph Platform[Platform library]
        P[grocery-defaults.yml<br/>org-wide defaults via import]
    end
    subgraph K8s[Kubernetes — GitOps repo per environment]
        C[ConfigMap file → /etc/grocery/application.yml<br/>env-specific, non-secret]
        D[Secret files → /var/run/secrets/grocery/<br/>configtree]
        E[Env vars: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE,<br/>SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT]
    end
    V[Vault / cloud secret manager] -->|External Secrets Operator| D
    P --> A
    A --> C
    C --> D
    E -. bootstraps .-> C
    style D fill:#fde2e2

Rules:

Layer Contains Never contains application.yml in JAR Every property with a safe default Secrets, environment URLs Platform defaults Org-wide timeouts, JSON, observability Service-specific settings ConfigMap file Environment URLs, limits, feature switches Secrets Secret files Credentials, signing keys Anything else Env vars Bootstrap only (profile, import) Bulk configuration services/payment-service/src/main/resources/application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: payment-service
  config:
    import:
      - classpath:grocery-defaults.yml                      # from grocery-platform library
      - optional:file:/etc/grocery/application.yml          # ConfigMap mount
      - optional:configtree:/var/run/secrets/grocery/       # Secret mount

grocery:
  payment:
    razorpay:
      enabled: true
      timeout: 3s
libs/grocery-platform/src/main/resources/grocery-defaults.yml
server:
  shutdown: graceful
  max-http-request-header-size: 16KB
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
  jackson:
    default-property-inclusion: non_null
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
  endpoint:
    env:
      show-values: never                                    # (1)!
    configprops:
      show-values: never
  1. Since Boot 3, /actuator/env and /actuator/configprops mask all values by default; when-authorized shows them to users with the configured role. Keep production at never or when-authorized with a tight role.

docs.title: 6.2 Cross-field validation
docs.text:
Some rules involve several properties. Domain rule for the order service: a soft stock reservation must outlive the unpaid-order auto-cancel window — otherwise an order could lose its stock and still be paid a minute later.

in/grocery/order/config/OrderProperties.java
package in.grocery.order.config;

import jakarta.validation.constraints.AssertTrue;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotNull;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.time.ZoneId;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.bind.DefaultValue;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("grocery.order")
public record OrderProperties(
        @DefaultValue("15m") @NotNull Duration autoCancelUnpaidAfter,
        @DefaultValue("20m") @NotNull Duration stockReservationTtl,
        @DefaultValue("Asia/Kolkata") ZoneId timezone,
        @DefaultValue("INR") String currency) {

    @AssertTrue(message = "stock-reservation-ttl must be longer than auto-cancel-unpaid-after")  // (1)!
    public boolean isReservationLongerThanAutoCancel() {
        return stockReservationTtl.compareTo(autoCancelUnpaidAfter) > 0;
    }
}
  1. A boolean is... method is validated like a property — simple cross-field validation with standard Jakarta constraints. An operator who lowers the reservation TTL below the cancel window gets a startup failure instead of oversold stock.

Validation forces the domain conversation

Writing the constraint makes the team state the rule explicitly ("reservation must outlive auto-cancel"). Many configuration incidents are really undocumented domain rules.

docs.title: 6.3 Custom sanitizing for Actuator
docs.text:
When show-values: when-authorized is used for on-call engineers, still mask anything that looks like a secret:

in/grocery/platform/actuator/GrocerySanitizingConfig.java
package in.grocery.platform.actuator;

import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.endpoint.SanitizableData;
import org.springframework.boot.actuate.endpoint.SanitizingFunction;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class GrocerySanitizingConfig {

    private static final Pattern SENSITIVE =
            Pattern.compile(".*(secret|password|token|key|credential|otp|aadhaar|pan).*", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE);

    @Bean
    SanitizingFunction groceryKeysSanitizer() {
        return data -> SENSITIVE.matcher(data.getKey()).matches()
                ? data.withValue(SanitizableData.SANITIZED_VALUE)
                : data;
    }

    @Bean
    SanitizingFunction secretFileSanitizer() {
        return data -> data.getPropertySource() != null
                && data.getPropertySource().getName().contains("configtree")      // (1)!
                ? data.withValue(SanitizableData.SANITIZED_VALUE)
                : data;
    }
}
  1. Anything from mounted secrets is masked regardless of its name.

docs.title: 6.4 Startup configuration report (non-secret)
docs.text:
On-call engineers often need "what config is this pod running?" without Actuator access. Log a curated, safe summary once:

in/grocery/order/startup/EffectiveConfigLogger.java
package in.grocery.order.startup;

import in.grocery.order.config.OrderProperties;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.boot.context.event.ApplicationReadyEvent;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.core.env.Environment;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
class EffectiveConfigLogger {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("effective-config");

    private final OrderProperties order;
    private final Environment env;

    EffectiveConfigLogger(OrderProperties order, Environment env) {
        this.order = order;
        this.env = env;
    }

    @EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)
    void logSummary() {
        log.info("profiles={} autoCancel={} reservationTtl={} tz={} dbHost={}",
                String.join(",", env.getActiveProfiles()),
                order.autoCancelUnpaidAfter(),
                order.stockReservationTtl(),
                order.timezone(),
                hostOnly(env.getProperty("spring.datasource.url", "n/a")));          // (1)!
    }

    private static String hostOnly(String jdbcUrl) {
        return jdbcUrl.replaceAll("^jdbc:\\w+://([^/:]+).*$", "$1");
    }
}
  1. Host only — URLs can embed credentials (?password=).

docs.title: 6.5 Runtime configuration changes — what's safe
docs.text:
Mechanism Changes Risk Restart with new config (rolling deploy) Everything Safest; auditable via GitOps Spring Cloud @RefreshScope + /actuator/refresh Beans in refresh scope re-created; @ConfigurationProperties rebound Partial state; different pods at different values; hard to reason about Spring Cloud Kubernetes config reload Triggers refresh/restart on ConfigMap change Same as above, automated Feature-flag service Per-request decisions Designed for runtime change; the right tool for toggles Database-backed settings with cache Business parameters (promotions, tax master) Needs versioning and audit

Platform recommendation

Configuration changes = deployments. Use a rolling restart for config, a feature-flag service for toggles, and database-backed masters (with effective dates) for business parameters like GST rates and delivery charges. Avoid @RefreshScope on anything touching connection pools, security or thread pools.

docs.title: 6.6 Integration test: full config layering
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Properties migrator
docs.text:
Kotlin
runtimeOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-properties-migrator")   // one release only

At startup it reports renamed/removed properties with their origin and temporarily maps old names to new ones. Remove it once the report is clean.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Add spring-boot-properties-migrator, run each service in staging, fix all reported keys, remove the migrator.
  • Search ConfigMaps/Helm values (not just src/main/resources) for renamed properties — env-var forms included.
  • Replace @ConstructorBinding on single-constructor types (no longer needed since 3.0).
  • Switch nullable annotations to JSpecify on properties classes.
  • Recheck spring.autoconfigure.exclude and any property keyed by class name.
  • Verify Actuator show-values settings after upgrade.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Every property has a safe default in application.yml — environments override only what differs.
  2. @ConfigurationProperties records + @Validated for anything beyond a one-off value. Fail fast.
  3. Kebab-case everywhere in files; document env-var forms in the service README.
  4. Units in the value (30s, 64KB), never unit-less numbers.
  5. Secrets only from secret stores (config tree / Vault); override toString() on properties records holding secrets; trim values.
  6. Config changes = deployments via GitOps; feature flags for runtime toggles.
  7. Metadata processor in every module with properties.
  8. Know where a value came from — use origins in /actuator/env/{name} (secured).

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Scattered @Value for a group of settings

Anti-patterns (snippet)
@Value("${grocery.delivery.radius-km}") int radius;
@Value("${grocery.delivery.slot-minutes}") int slot;
@Value("${grocery.delivery.max-orders-per-slot}") int maxOrders;   // no validation, no defaults doc, repeated in 4 classes

✅ One DeliveryProperties record injected where needed.

❌ Unit-less durations

Configuration
grocery.payment.timeout: 3000     # ms? s? Depends on who wrote the code

✅ grocery.payment.timeout: 3s bound to Duration.

❌ Secrets in YAML "just for prod", or show-values: always in production.

❌ Profiles per environment containing everything (application-prod.yml with 300 lines duplicated from staging) — drift guaranteed. Profiles should hold small deltas; environments differ through external config.

❌ Using profiles as feature flags (@Profile("express-delivery")) — mixes deployment environment with product behaviour. Use properties + conditions (Chapter 03) or a flag service.

❌ Mutable @ConfigurationProperties beans modified at runtime by application code.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Env var ignored Wrong mapping (dash turned into _, typo, lowercase) GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS; check /actuator/env Value from wrong file Precedence misunderstanding; .properties beats .yml in same location Check origin in /actuator/env/{key} spring.profiles.active in profile file fails startup Not allowed in profile-specific docs Set from env/args; use groups @PropertySource values not seen by auto-config Loaded too late spring.config.import Map key split into nested keys Dots in key Bracket notation "[5.0]" Webhook signature mismatch Trailing newline in mounted secret Strip values Failed to bind properties ... No converter found Unsupported type or wrong format Use supported types; register @ConfigurationPropertiesBinding converter Record property always null Name mismatch (camelCase vs kebab), missing registration @ConfigurationPropertiesScan; check metadata Secret visible in logs Record toString() Override toString()

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• All settings grouped into validated @ConfigurationProperties records
  • Safe defaults in the JAR; environment deltas only in ConfigMaps
  • Secrets via config tree / Vault; none in Git; toString() masked; values trimmed
  • Actuator env/configprops values never or when-authorized
  • Custom SanitizingFunction for domain-sensitive keys
  • Properties migrator run before each major upgrade
  • Configuration metadata generated; README lists env-var forms
  • Config changes flow through GitOps with review

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · application.properties vs application.yml?

Short answer: Same content, different syntax. YAML is hierarchical and supports multiple documents with ---. If both exist in the same location, .properties wins. Pick one.

B1 · How do you read a property in code?

Short answer: @Value("${key:default}") for single values, or a @ConfigurationProperties class/record for a group. Prefer the latter.

B1 · What is a Spring profile and how do you activate one?

Short answer: A named configuration set. Activate via spring.profiles.active (property, env var SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, or --spring.profiles.active=). Files application-{profile}.yml load for active profiles.

B1 · How would you override a property without changing the JAR?

Short answer: Env var, system property (-D), command-line arg (--key=value), or an external application.yml in ./config/ or via spring.config.import.

B1 · What's the env var name for grocery.cart.max-items?

Short answer: GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS — dots to underscores, dashes removed, uppercase.

Red flags: GROCERY_CART_MAX_ITEMS (would map to grocery.cart.max.items).

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Why prefer @ConfigurationProperties over @Value?

Short answer: Type safety, grouping, validation, relaxed binding, IDE metadata, immutability with records, easier testing, and one place to document settings.

B2 · How do you validate configuration at startup?

Short answer: @Validated on the properties class plus Jakarta constraints (@Min, @NotBlank, @Valid for nested), with spring-boot-starter-validation. Cross-field rules via @AssertTrue methods or compact-constructor checks.

B2 · How are Duration and DataSize properties written?

Short answer: With units: 30s, 500ms, 2h, 7d (Period) or ISO-8601 (PT30S); sizes 10MB, 64KB. Bare numbers default to ms/bytes unless @DurationUnit/@DataSizeUnit is set.

B2 · What are profile groups?

Short answer: spring.profiles.group.prod=prod-db,prod-kafka — activating prod activates the members. Lets you compose small focused profiles.

B2 · How do you bind a list or map from environment variables?

Short answer: Lists with index segments: GROCERY_HUBS_0_CODE. Maps with key segments, but case and special characters are unreliable — prefer mounted YAML for maps.

B2 · How do you test a @ConfigurationProperties record?

Short answer: ApplicationContextRunner with withPropertyValues(...), asserting bound values and hasFailed() for invalid input — no full app context needed.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Explain property source precedence in Spring Boot.

Short answer: Lowest: defaults, @PropertySource, config data files (JAR then external, generic then profile-specific), random; then env vars, system properties, JNDI/servlet params, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, command-line args; tests add properties, @DynamicPropertySource, @TestPropertySource on top.

B3 · How does spring.config.import work and what is a config tree?

Short answer: Imports additional config data (files, config trees, config server, Vault) resolved by ConfigDataLocationResolver/ConfigDataLoader pairs; imported sources override the importing file. A config tree maps a directory of files (one per key, e.g. Kubernetes Secret mounts) to properties.

B3 · Why is @PropertySource discouraged in Boot apps?

Short answer: It's added when configuration classes are parsed — after logging and some auto-configuration decisions — and has low precedence. spring.config.import loads during environment preparation.

B3 · What is the Binder API and when do you use it?

Short answer: Programmatic binding over ConfigurationPropertySources — Binder.get(env).bind(prefix, Bindable.of(T)). Used in EnvironmentPostProcessors, conditions, BeanRegistrars — anywhere before or outside bean creation.

B3 · How does relaxed binding work for environment variables internally?

Short answer: ConfigurationPropertySources adapt the system environment source with SystemEnvironmentPropertyMapper, which maps GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS to candidate canonical names (grocery.cart.maxitems) and matches against the canonical form of the target (grocery.cart.max-items → dashes ignored for comparison).

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the configuration and secrets architecture for 26 services on Kubernetes.

Short answer: Safe defaults in JARs; platform-wide defaults via an imported file from a shared library; per-environment non-secret config as ConfigMap files in a GitOps repo; secrets from Vault/cloud manager synced as files and imported as config trees; env vars only for bootstrap; validated records; Actuator sanitization; config changes deploy via rolling restart; feature flags for runtime toggles; business parameters in databases with audit.

B4 · Would you use @RefreshScope? When not?

Short answer: Rarely. It recreates beans lazily on refresh, so pods drift and partial state appears. Never for data sources, security, thread pools or clients with connection pools. Prefer restarts; use feature flags or DB-backed settings for runtime changes.

B4 · How do you rotate a database password with zero downtime?

Short answer: Dual credentials (old and new valid simultaneously), update secret, rolling restart so new pods use the new password, then revoke the old. With Vault dynamic secrets, leases rotate automatically and Hikari pools must be recreated (max-lifetime shorter than lease). Test in staging.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · Configuration caused 40% of last year's incidents. What do you change?

Short answer: Treat config as code: typed validated records, schema/metadata, GitOps review with owners, policy checks in CI (e.g. conftest/OPA on Helm values), staged rollouts of config like code, drift detection, config diff in deployment notes, startup summaries, and clear separation of config vs flags vs business data. Measure change failure rate for config changes separately.

B5 · Spring Cloud Config vs Kubernetes-native config — which would you pick?

Short answer: With Kubernetes and GitOps already in place, native ConfigMaps/Secrets + External Secrets usually win: fewer moving parts, same review workflow as manifests. Spring Cloud Config fits multi-runtime estates (VMs + K8s), central encryption needs, or teams without GitOps. Either way, avoid runtime refresh as the default change mechanism.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · After a ConfigMap change, some pods use the new delivery radius and some the old

The team used Spring Cloud Kubernetes reload with @RefreshScope on DeliveryRadiusService. Refresh events reached pods at different times, and one pod's refresh failed validation and kept old values silently. Fix: remove runtime reload for this setting, roll a restart through the Deployment (config hash annotation triggers rollout), and move per-hub radius to the delivery master data with an admin UI and audit.

Scenario · Razorpay webhooks fail signature verification only in production

The webhook secret was created with kubectl create secret generic --from-file, storing a trailing newline, and mounted as a config tree. Locally the env var had no newline. Fix: strip in the properties compact constructor, add a test (see 6.6), and document secret creation with --from-literal or printf.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Delivery hubs configuration

Bind this YAML to validated records. Rules: at least one hub; codes unique and matching [A-Z]{3}-[A-Z]{3}; radius 1–15 km; pincode-prefixes non-empty 3-digit strings. Provide a method hubFor(String pincode) returning the first hub whose prefix matches. Test valid and invalid cases.

application.yml
grocery:
  delivery:
    hubs:
      - code: BLR-HSR
        radius-km: 6
        pincode-prefixes: ["560"]
      - code: MUM-AND
        radius-km: 5
        pincode-prefixes: ["400"]
Solution DeliveryProperties.java
package in.grocery.delivery.config;

import jakarta.validation.Valid;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.AssertTrue;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Max;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Min;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.NotEmpty;
import jakarta.validation.constraints.Pattern;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated;

@Validated
@ConfigurationProperties("grocery.delivery")
public record DeliveryProperties(@NotEmpty List<@Valid Hub> hubs) {

    public record Hub(
            @Pattern(regexp = "[A-Z]{3}-[A-Z]{3}") String code,
            @Min(1) @Max(15) int radiusKm,
            @NotEmpty List<@Pattern(regexp = "\\d{3}") String> pincodePrefixes) {}

    public DeliveryProperties {
        hubs = hubs == null ? List.of() : List.copyOf(hubs);
    }

    @AssertTrue(message = "hub codes must be unique")
    public boolean isHubCodesUnique() {
        return hubs.stream().map(Hub::code).distinct().count() == hubs.size();
    }

    public Optional<Hub> hubFor(String pincode) {
        return hubs.stream()
                .filter(h -> h.pincodePrefixes().stream().anyMatch(pincode::startsWith))
                .findFirst();
    }
}
DeliveryPropertiesTest.java
package in.grocery.delivery.config;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfigurations;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.validation.ValidationAutoConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.EnableConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.runner.ApplicationContextRunner;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

class DeliveryPropertiesTest {

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @EnableConfigurationProperties(DeliveryProperties.class)
    static class Cfg {}

    private final ApplicationContextRunner runner = new ApplicationContextRunner()
            .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(ValidationAutoConfiguration.class))
            .withUserConfiguration(Cfg.class);

    @Test
    void bindsAndRoutes() {
        runner.withPropertyValues(
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].code=BLR-HSR",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].radius-km=6",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].pincode-prefixes[0]=560",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[1].code=MUM-AND",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[1].radius-km=5",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[1].pincode-prefixes[0]=400")
              .run(ctx -> {
                  var p = ctx.getBean(DeliveryProperties.class);
                  assertThat(p.hubFor("560034")).get().extracting(DeliveryProperties.Hub::code).isEqualTo("BLR-HSR");
                  assertThat(p.hubFor("110001")).isEmpty();
              });
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsDuplicateCodes() {
        runner.withPropertyValues(
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].code=BLR-HSR", "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].radius-km=6",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].pincode-prefixes[0]=560",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[1].code=BLR-HSR", "grocery.delivery.hubs[1].radius-km=4",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[1].pincode-prefixes[0]=560")
              .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).hasFailed());
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsRadiusOutOfRange() {
        runner.withPropertyValues(
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].code=BLR-HSR", "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].radius-km=40",
                "grocery.delivery.hubs[0].pincode-prefixes[0]=560")
              .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).hasFailed());
    }
}

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The Environment is an ordered stack of property sources; closer to the process wins.
  • Config data loads from standard locations, then imports, then profile-specific files — know the order and use origins to debug.
  • @ConfigurationProperties records + @Validated give typed, immutable, fail-fast configuration; @Value is for one-offs.
  • Relaxed binding maps GROCERY_CART_MAXITEMS to grocery.cart.max-items; use kebab case in files.
  • Secrets come from config trees or Vault — mask toString(), trim values, sanitize Actuator.
  • Config changes are deployments; runtime toggles belong in a flag service.
  • Before Boot 4, run the properties migrator.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Boot Reference — Core Features › Externalized Configuration (all subsections, especially Config Data, Type-safe Configuration Properties, Relaxed Binding, Configuration Trees)
  • Spring Boot Reference — Configuration Metadata
  • Spring Boot Reference — Actuator › Sanitize Sensitive Values
  • Spring Cloud Config and Spring Cloud Vault reference documentation

05 Spring Boot Fundamentals · 07 Logging

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
At 9:40 p.m. on a Diwali sale night, customers in Pune report "payment done but order not placed". You have 26 services, 180 pods and one question: what happened to order ORD-7f3a91c2? The answer is only as good as your logs.

Good logging is not "more log.info". It is:

  • Structured — JSON with consistent fields, so Loki/Elasticsearch/CloudWatch can filter by orderId instead of grepping text.
  • Correlated — every line carries traceId/requestId, so one search shows the order's path through gateway → order → payment → inventory.
  • Leveled correctly — ERROR pages someone; DEBUG is off in production but can be switched on for one package without a restart.
  • Safe — no mobile numbers, OTPs, card data or Aadhaar numbers in logs (India's DPDP Act makes this a legal issue, not just a hygiene one).
  • Cheap — asynchronous where needed, never blocking request threads on disk I/O, and not so voluminous that the log bill exceeds the compute bill.

Spring Boot gives you a solid default (SLF4J + Logback, sensible patterns), built-in structured logging since 3.4, runtime level changes via Actuator, and automatic trace correlation with Micrometer Tracing. This chapter turns those into a platform standard.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — SLF4J, levels, parameterized messages B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — log groups, files, logback-spring.xml, MDC B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — logging system bootstrap, structured logging, async appenders, context propagation B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — platform logging standard, PII masking, cost control B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — logs vs metrics vs traces, compliance, observability strategy

docs.title: 2.1 The logging stack
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Your code<br/>org.slf4j.Logger] --> B[SLF4J API 2.x]
    L1[Libraries using<br/>JCL / JUL / Log4j API] --> BR[Bridges<br/>jcl-over-slf4j built into spring-jcl,<br/>jul-to-slf4j, log4j-to-slf4j]
    BR --> B
    B --> C[Logback<br/>default backend]
    C --> D[Appenders<br/>Console · File · Async]
    D --> E[stdout → container runtime → log collector]
  • SLF4J is the API you code against. Never import Logback or Log4j classes in business code.
  • Logback is Boot's default implementation (spring-boot-starter-logging, included by every starter).
  • Log4j2 is the alternative (spring-boot-starter-log4j2, excluding spring-boot-starter-logging).
  • Bridges route other logging APIs (JUL, JCL, Log4j API) into SLF4J so everything ends up in one place.

docs.title: 2.2 Levels
docs.text:
Level Use for Production default ERROR A request/operation failed and needs attention; typically alerts On WARN Unexpected but handled (retry succeeded, fallback used, validation of external data failed) On INFO Business milestones and lifecycle (order placed, service started) — sparingly On DEBUG Diagnostic detail for developers Off; enable per package on demand TRACE Very fine-grained (framework internals, payloads in dev) Off

Rule: one ERROR per failure, logged where it is handled, not at every layer it passes through.

docs.title: 2.3 Parameterized messages and the fluent API
docs.text:
Parameterized messages and the fluent API (snippet)
log.info("Order {} placed for ₹{}", orderId, total);       // ✅ formatting only if INFO enabled
log.info("Order " + orderId + " placed");                  // ❌ string built even when disabled
log.error("Payment failed for order {}", orderId, ex);     // ✅ exception as last arg → stack trace

SLF4J 2's fluent API adds structured key-value pairs:

Parameterized messages and the fluent API (snippet)
log.atInfo()
   .setMessage("Order placed")
   .addKeyValue("orderId", orderId)
   .addKeyValue("amount", total)
   .log();

With structured logging, key-value pairs become JSON fields — searchable without parsing the message.

docs.title: 2.4 Configuring through properties
docs.text:
Property Example Meaning logging.level.<logger> logging.level.in.grocery.payment: debug Level per package/class logging.level.root warn Default for everything logging.group.<name> logging.group.checkout: in.grocery.cart, in.grocery.order Named set of loggers logging.level.<group> logging.level.checkout: debug Level for the whole group logging.pattern.console %d %-5level [%thread] %logger - %msg%n Text pattern logging.file.name /var/log/grocery/order.log Enable file output logging.logback.rollingpolicy.* max-file-size: 50MB, max-history: 7 Rolling for files logging.structured.format.console ecs JSON to console (Boot 3.4+) logging.threshold.console info Minimum level for an appender

Built-in groups: web (Spring MVC, codecs, HTTP logging) and sql (JDBC, jOOQ, Hibernate SQL).

docs.title: 2.5 Custom configuration files
docs.text:
File Loaded by Spring extensions (<springProfile>, <springProperty>) logback-spring.xml Spring Boot, after the Environment is ready ✅ logback.xml Logback itself, very early ❌ log4j2-spring.xml Spring Boot ✅ (Spring lookups)

Always use the -spring variants.

docs.title: 2.6 Structured logging (Boot 3.4+)
docs.text:
Built-in JSON formats:

Format For ecs Elastic Common Schema — Elasticsearch/OpenSearch/Kibana gelf Graylog Extended Log Format logstash Logstash JSON Fully-qualified class name Your own StructuredLogFormatter application.yml
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs
    ecs:
      service:
        name: order-service
        version: 1.4.2
        environment: prod

MDC entries and SLF4J key-value pairs are included in the JSON output.

docs.title: 2.7 MDC — Mapped Diagnostic Context
docs.text:
A per-thread map (MDC.put("orderId", id)) whose entries appear on every log line from that thread. Used for request IDs, customer IDs (hashed), tenant/seller IDs.

MDC is thread-local

It doesn't follow your work to another thread (@Async, CompletableFuture, virtual-thread executors, Reactor). Use context propagation (Micrometer's context-propagation library, ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator) or tracing, which handles this for you. And always remove entries in finally — pooled threads carry stale MDC into the next request.

docs.title: 2.8 Trace correlation
docs.text: With Micrometer Tracing on the classpath (Chapter 27), Boot puts traceId and spanId into the MDC and the default console pattern includes them via logging.pattern.correlation. With structured logging, ECS output includes them automatically.

docs.title: 2.9 Runtime level changes
docs.text:
Actuator's loggers endpoint:

Terminal
curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/in.grocery.payment
curl -X POST localhost:8080/actuator/loggers/in.grocery.payment \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'

Changes are per pod and lost on restart — which is usually what you want for diagnostics.

docs.title: 2.10 Logs, metrics, traces — know the difference
docs.text:
Signal Answers Cost profile Logs What exactly happened in this case? Grows with traffic × verbosity Metrics How much/how often/how fast, overall? Grows with cardinality, not traffic Traces Where did time go across services for this request? Sampled

Don't use logs for things metrics answer ("count of orders per minute") — it's expensive and slow.

docs.title: 3.1 Logging system bootstrap
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant SA as SpringApplication
    participant LAL as LoggingApplicationListener
    participant LS as LoggingSystem (LogbackLoggingSystem)
    participant Env as Environment

    SA->>LAL: ApplicationStartingEvent
    LAL->>LS: LoggingSystem.get(classLoader)<br/>detect Logback / Log4j2 / JUL
    LAL->>LS: beforeInitialize() — quiet default, install JUL bridge
    SA->>Env: prepare environment (config data)
    SA->>LAL: ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent
    LAL->>LS: initialize(context, configLocation, logFile)
    Note over LS: logging.config? → load it<br/>else logback-spring.xml / logback.xml?<br/>else Boot defaults (defaults.xml, console-appender.xml)
    LAL->>LS: apply logging.level.*, logging.group.*
    LAL->>LAL: register LoggingSystem bean, shutdown hook

Key points:

  • Logging initializes after the Environment is prepared, so logging.* properties from all sources (including config imports and profiles) apply.
  • It initializes before the ApplicationContext — which is why logging can't be configured with beans, and why @PropertySource can't affect logging.
  • logback.xml (non-spring) is picked up by Logback itself when the first logger is created — before Boot's properties exist.
  • LoggingSystemProperties copies Boot properties (e.g. logging.pattern.console) into system properties like CONSOLE_LOG_PATTERN that Boot's Logback defaults reference.

docs.title: 3.2 A log call, end to end
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["log.info(msg, args)"] --> B{TurboFilters<br/>e.g. duplicate suppression}
    B --> C{Effective level ≥ INFO?}
    C -- no --> Z[return — near-zero cost]
    C -- yes --> D[Create ILoggingEvent<br/>captures MDC copy, KV pairs, thread, timestamp]
    D --> E[Appenders attached to logger + ancestors<br/>additivity]
    E --> F[AsyncAppender → queue]
    F --> G[Worker thread → Encoder<br/>pattern or StructuredLogEncoder]
    E --> H[ConsoleAppender → Encoder → stdout]
  • Level check first: disabled levels cost one comparison. Argument evaluation still happens — avoid expensive calls in log arguments (log.debug("{}", toJson(order))), or guard with isDebugEnabled() / use suppliers via the fluent API.
  • Additivity: an event goes to the logger's appenders and all ancestors' appenders unless additivity="false" — the cause of duplicated log lines.
  • Structured logging plugs in as Boot's StructuredLogEncoder, which delegates to the chosen StructuredLogFormatter.

docs.title: 3.3 Context propagation across threads
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant R as Request thread (MDC: requestId, traceId)
    participant D as ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator
    participant W as Async worker thread

    R->>D: submit(task)
    D->>D: ContextSnapshot.captureAll() — MDC, tracing, security (via ThreadLocalAccessors)
    D->>W: wrapped task
    W->>W: snapshot.setThreadLocals() — restore MDC
    W->>W: run task → logs carry requestId, traceId
    W->>W: restore previous values (clean up)

Boot auto-configures ThreadPoolTaskExecutor/SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor builders to apply a single TaskDecorator bean if one exists; define ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator as that bean.

docs.title: 4.1 Logging in a service
4.2 Levels and groups in application.yml
docs.text:
application.yml
logging:
  level:
    root: info
    in.grocery: info
    org.hibernate.SQL: warn
  group:
    checkout: in.grocery.cart, in.grocery.order, in.grocery.payment

---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: local
logging:
  level:
    checkout: debug            # whole group at once
    sql: debug                 # built-in group: shows SQL statements

docs.title: 4.3 Default console output
docs.text:
Output
2026-09-22T11:05:14.231+05:30  INFO 48213 --- [order-service] [nio-8083-exec-1] [3f1c9a2e7b0d4c11-8a7e2f19c4d05b33] i.g.order.service.OrderService : Order ORD-1a2b3c placed, total ₹578.00

Timestamp, level, PID, application name, thread, trace correlation (when tracing is present), abbreviated logger, message.

docs.title: 4.4 Change a level at runtime
docs.text:
application.yml
management:
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,loggers
Terminal
curl -X POST localhost:8083/actuator/loggers/in.grocery.order \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'
# ... reproduce the issue ...
curl -X POST localhost:8083/actuator/loggers/in.grocery.order \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":null}'   # reset

Secure the loggers endpoint

Anyone who can POST to /actuator/loggers can turn on TRACE for everything and flood your disks or leak payloads. Expose it only on the management port behind authentication (Chapter 27).

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Structured JSON logs with built-in ECS
docs.text:
application.yml
spring:
  application:
    name: order-service
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs
    ecs:
      service:
        name: ${spring.application.name}
        version: "@project.version@"      # or from build-info
        environment: ${GROCERY_ENV:local}
Structured JSON logs with built-in ECS (snippet)
log.atInfo()
   .setMessage("Order placed")
   .addKeyValue("orderId", orderId)
   .addKeyValue("amountPaise", total.movePointRight(2).longValueExact())
   .addKeyValue("pincode", pincode)
   .log();
Output (formatted for reading)
{
  "@timestamp": "2026-09-22T05:35:14.231Z",
  "log.level": "INFO",
  "process.pid": 48213,
  "process.thread.name": "tomcat-handler-12",
  "service.name": "order-service",
  "service.version": "1.4.2",
  "service.environment": "prod",
  "log.logger": "in.grocery.order.service.OrderService",
  "message": "Order placed",
  "traceId": "3f1c9a2e7b0d4c11",
  "spanId": "8a7e2f19c4d05b33",
  "orderId": "ORD-1a2b3c",
  "amountPaise": 57800,
  "pincode": "411001",
  "ecs.version": "8.11"
}

Keep local pretty, prod JSON

JSON is unreadable in a terminal. Enable structured logging only outside the local profile (5.3).

Verify — JSON field names

Exact field names (e.g. how MDC and key-value pairs are nested, traceId vs trace.id) depend on the Boot version and format. Check the output of your version before writing dashboards and alerts against it.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — MDC for business context
5.3 Level 2 — logback-spring.xml with profiles
docs.text:
When you need more than properties offer — per-profile appenders, async wrapping, a separate audit file:

src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml
<configuration>
    <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/defaults.xml"/>      <!-- (1) -->
    <springProperty name="APP" source="spring.application.name" defaultValue="grocery"/>

    <springProfile name="local | test">
        <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/console-appender.xml"/>
        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>

    <springProfile name="!(local | test)">
        <appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
            <encoder class="org.springframework.boot.logging.logback.StructuredLogEncoder">   <!-- (2) -->
                <format>ecs</format>
                <charset>UTF-8</charset>
            </encoder>
        </appender>

        <appender name="ASYNC_JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">
            <queueSize>8192</queueSize>
            <discardingThreshold>20</discardingThreshold>                             <!-- (3) -->
            <neverBlock>true</neverBlock>                                              <!-- (4) -->
            <includeCallerData>false</includeCallerData>
            <appender-ref ref="JSON"/>
        </appender>

        <root level="INFO">
            <appender-ref ref="ASYNC_JSON"/>
        </root>
    </springProfile>
</configuration>
  1. Reuse Boot's defaults (conversion rules, color converters, default patterns).
  2. Boot's structured encoder, same formats as the properties.
  3. When the queue is 80% full, drop TRACE/DEBUG/INFO events (keep WARN/ERROR).
  4. Under extreme pressure, drop events rather than block request threads. Trade-off: you may lose logs during a spike — metrics must carry what you can't afford to lose.

Properties vs XML

Once logback-spring.xml exists, some logging.* properties (patterns, structured format) only apply if your XML references Boot's includes/properties. Levels (logging.level.*) always apply. Choose one primary mechanism and document it.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Context propagation to async code
5.5 Level 3 — Logging exceptions correctly
5.6 Level 3 — HTTP request logging, safely
docs.text:
Framework's CommonsRequestLoggingFilter logs request URI/query/headers/payload at DEBUG. Use it only in lower environments, never with payloads in production:

HTTP request logging, safely (snippet)
@Bean
@Profile("local | test")
CommonsRequestLoggingFilter requestLogging() {
    var f = new CommonsRequestLoggingFilter();
    f.setIncludeQueryString(true);
    f.setIncludePayload(true);
    f.setMaxPayloadLength(2_000);
    f.setHeaderPredicate(h -> !h.equalsIgnoreCase("authorization") && !h.equalsIgnoreCase("cookie"));
    return f;
}
Configuration
logging.level.org.springframework.web.filter.CommonsRequestLoggingFilter: debug

Production access logs come from the gateway/ingress and from HTTP server metrics, not from application payload logging.

docs.title: Platform logging standard: JSON formatter with PII masking
docs.text:
Requirements for all grocery services:

  1. JSON on stdout outside local, with a fixed schema: ts, level, service, env, logger, thread, msg, traceId, spanId, requestId plus key-value pairs.
  2. PII masking of Indian mobile numbers, emails, UPI IDs, PAN, Aadhaar-like 12-digit numbers — in the message and in values.
  3. Stack traces as one field, truncated to a maximum length.
  4. No ERROR without a stack trace or error code (lint in review).

6.2 Custom structured formatter
6.3 Formatter test

7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace hand-rolled Logstash encoders (logstash-logback-encoder) with built-in structured logging where it meets requirements — one fewer dependency.
  • Rename logback.xml → logback-spring.xml.
  • Verify JSON field names after upgrading; update dashboards/alerts.
  • Check custom formatters compile against Boot 4 (Jackson 3 if used).
  • Confirm ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator wiring and MDC accessors still apply.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. SLF4J API only in application code; parameterized messages or the fluent API.
  2. JSON to stdout in all deployed environments; human format locally.
  3. Correlate via tracing IDs; add a small set of business keys via MDC (orderId, sellerId).
  4. Log once, where handled; ERROR means action needed.
  5. No PII, no secrets — log identifiers; masking as a safety net.
  6. Async appenders with bounded queues in high-throughput services.
  7. Levels adjustable at runtime via a secured Actuator endpoint.
  8. Metrics for counting, traces for latency, logs for detail.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ System.out.println / e.printStackTrace() — bypass levels, formatting and shipping.

❌ log.error("Error: " + e) — string concatenation, no stack trace, e.toString() only.

✅ log.error("Payment capture failed for order {}", orderId, e)

❌ Logging entire request/response bodies in production — PII, cost, latency.

❌ log.debug("Cart: {}", objectMapper.writeValueAsString(cart)) — serialization runs even when DEBUG is off.

✅ if (log.isDebugEnabled()) { ... } or the fluent API with a supplier: log.atDebug().addArgument(() -> toJson(cart)).log("Cart: {}").

❌ MDC.put without removal in pooled threads.

❌ Duplicate log lines from additivity in custom XML.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix SLF4J: Class path contains multiple SLF4J providers Both Logback and Log4j2 (or slf4j-simple) present Exclude one; ./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency slf4j <springProfile> ignored File named logback.xml Rename to logback-spring.xml Log level property has no effect Wrong logger name; level set in XML overrides Check /actuator/loggers; remove XML level Duplicate lines Appender on both logger and root with additivity additivity="false" Missing traceId in async logs No context propagation ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator Wrong/stale orderId on unrelated requests MDC not cleaned Remove in finally/afterCompletion Latency spikes with heavy logging Synchronous appender on slow stdout/disk Async appender, lower volume Logs lost during spike neverBlock dropping Accept, or increase queue; rely on metrics Log bill doubled DEBUG left on / per-item logging Level governance, retention tiers, sampling

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Structured JSON with documented schema; dashboards built on it
  • traceId/spanId present on every line, including async work
  • PII review in code review checklist; masker enabled
  • /actuator/loggers secured on the management port
  • Async appender configured for high-throughput services
  • One ERROR per failure; alerting rules based on ERROR rate and error codes
  • Retention and cost limits agreed with platform/security

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Why use SLF4J instead of Logback or Log4j directly?

Short answer: SLF4J is an API facade; the backend (Logback, Log4j2) can change without code changes, and all libraries' logs end up in one place.

B1 · What are the log levels and when do you use each?

Short answer: ERROR (failure needing attention), WARN (unexpected but handled), INFO (important milestones), DEBUG (diagnostics), TRACE (very detailed).

B1 · Why use {} placeholders instead of string concatenation?

Short answer: The message is only formatted if the level is enabled, saving CPU and allocations; it's also cleaner.

B1 · How do you change the log level for one package?

Short answer: logging.level.in.grocery.payment=debug in configuration, or at runtime via /actuator/loggers.

B1 · How do you log an exception with its stack trace?

Short answer: Pass it as the last argument: log.error("Failed for {}", id, ex).

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · logback.xml vs logback-spring.xml?

Short answer: logback.xml is loaded by Logback directly and early; logback-spring.xml is loaded by Spring Boot after the Environment is prepared, enabling <springProfile> and <springProperty>. Use the -spring variant.

B2 · What is MDC and what's the main pitfall?

Short answer: A thread-local map whose entries appear in every log line from that thread. Pitfalls: not propagated to other threads, and leaking into later requests if not removed.

B2 · What are log groups?

Short answer: Named sets of loggers (logging.group.checkout=...) whose level you set together. Boot provides web and sql.

B2 · How do you get JSON logs in Spring Boot 3.4+?

Short answer: logging.structured.format.console=ecs (or gelf, logstash, or a custom formatter class name).

B2 · Why shouldn't you log and rethrow at every layer?

Short answer: Duplicate stack traces and alerts for one failure, noisy and expensive logs. Wrap with context and log once where the exception is handled.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · When and how does Spring Boot initialize logging?

Short answer: LoggingApplicationListener detects the LoggingSystem on ApplicationStartingEvent, then initializes it on ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEvent using logging.* properties and config files — before the ApplicationContext exists.

B3 · How do you propagate MDC and trace context to @Async methods?

Short answer: Register a ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator bean (Boot applies it to its executors) with Micrometer context-propagation; register thread-local accessors for MDC keys. Tracing context is handled by Micrometer Tracing.

B3 · What does an AsyncAppender trade off?

Short answer: Lower latency on request threads versus possible loss of events (queue full with neverBlock, or on crash) and loss of caller data. Tune queue size and discarding threshold.

B3 · Why does log.debug("{}", expensive()) still cost CPU when DEBUG is off?

Short answer: Arguments are evaluated before the call. Guard with isDebugEnabled() or pass a supplier via the fluent API.

B3 · How does trace correlation appear in logs?

Short answer: Micrometer Tracing puts traceId/spanId into MDC; Boot's default pattern includes them via logging.pattern.correlation, and structured formats include them as fields.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design a logging standard for 26 services.

Short answer: Platform library with JSON formatter and schema, trace correlation, curated MDC keys, PII masking, async appenders, level governance, secured runtime changes, retention tiers, error-code conventions, dashboards and alerts built on fields, and code-review checklist for PII.

B4 · How do you comply with data-protection rules (e.g. DPDP Act) in logs?

Short answer: Don't log personal data; log pseudonymous IDs. Mask as a safety net. Restrict access to logs, set retention limits, support deletion requests through ID-based data (not free text in logs), and audit logging practices.

B4 · Logs are 30% of cloud cost. What do you do?

Short answer: Measure volume per service/logger, remove per-item and DEBUG logs, replace counting logs with metrics, sample repetitive warnings, shorter retention for low levels, drop noisy framework logs at the collector, and set budgets per team.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you decide between logs, metrics and traces for a new requirement?

Short answer: Aggregate questions (rates, latencies, saturation) → metrics; cross-service latency and causality → traces; case-specific forensic detail → logs; regulatory evidence → audit trail (separate, durable, not logs). Define SLOs on metrics, debug with traces, confirm with logs.

B5 · Should audit events go to application logs?

Short answer: No. Audit needs durability, integrity and retention guarantees logs don't give (async drops, sampling, retention policies). Use a dedicated audit store/topic (Chapter 04's AuditSink), possibly also logging a reference.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Customer phone numbers found in production logs during a security review

Source: log.info("OTP sent to {}", mobile) in identity-service and exception messages including request bodies. Actions: hotfix to log customerId instead; enable platform masker; purge affected log indices per policy; add a CI rule (grep/ArchUnit/custom Checkstyle) flagging logs with parameters named mobile|phone|email; add PII to review checklist; notify DPO per incident process.

Scenario · Traces show payment calls but logs from the async notification step lack traceId

@Async executor lacked a context-propagating decorator because the team defined its own ThreadPoolTaskExecutor bean without applying the TaskDecorator. Fix: build executors via Boot's ThreadPoolTaskExecutorBuilder (which applies the decorator) or set it explicitly; add the propagation test from 5.4.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Log a Razorpay webhook safely

Write a method logWebhook(String eventType, String paymentId, String payloadJson) that logs at INFO with key-value pairs event, paymentId, and the payload only at DEBUG, masked, truncated to 1,000 chars, without serializing or masking when DEBUG is off. Test that the payload isn't processed when DEBUG is disabled.

Solution WebhookLogger.java
package in.grocery.payment.webhook;

import in.grocery.platform.logging.PiiMasker;
import java.util.function.UnaryOperator;
import org.slf4j.Logger;

public class WebhookLogger {

    private final Logger log;
    private final UnaryOperator<String> masker;

    public WebhookLogger(Logger log) {
        this(log, PiiMasker::mask);
    }

    WebhookLogger(Logger log, UnaryOperator<String> masker) {
        this.log = log;
        this.masker = masker;
    }

    public void logWebhook(String eventType, String paymentId, String payloadJson) {
        log.atInfo().setMessage("Razorpay webhook received")
           .addKeyValue("event", eventType)
           .addKeyValue("paymentId", paymentId)
           .log();
        if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
            String masked = masker.apply(payloadJson);
            log.debug("Webhook payload: {}", masked.length() > 1000 ? masked.substring(0, 1000) + "…" : masked);
        }
    }
}
WebhookLoggerTest.java
package in.grocery.payment.webhook;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import ch.qos.logback.classic.Level;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.Logger;
import ch.qos.logback.classic.LoggerContext;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class WebhookLoggerTest {

    @Test
    void doesNotMaskPayloadWhenDebugDisabled() {
        Logger logger = new LoggerContext().getLogger("webhook");
        logger.setLevel(Level.INFO);
        AtomicInteger maskCalls = new AtomicInteger();

        new WebhookLogger(logger, s -> { maskCalls.incrementAndGet(); return s; })
                .logWebhook("payment.captured", "pay_1", "{\"contact\":\"9876543210\"}");

        assertThat(maskCalls).hasValue(0);
    }

    @Test
    void masksPayloadWhenDebugEnabled() {
        Logger logger = new LoggerContext().getLogger("webhook");
        logger.setLevel(Level.DEBUG);
        AtomicInteger maskCalls = new AtomicInteger();

        new WebhookLogger(logger, s -> { maskCalls.incrementAndGet(); return s; })
                .logWebhook("payment.captured", "pay_1", "{}");

        assertThat(maskCalls).hasValue(1);
    }
}

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• SLF4J API + Logback by default; bridges funnel all libraries into one pipeline.
  • Boot initializes logging after the Environment, before the context — configure with logging.* and logback-spring.xml.
  • Structured logging (ECS/GELF/Logstash/custom) is built in since Boot 3.4 — use JSON everywhere except local.
  • Correlation comes from tracing + MDC; propagate context to async work.
  • Log once where handled; ERROR means action.
  • No PII — mask as a safety net, not the plan.
  • Protect latency with async appenders; control cost with levels, sampling and metrics.
