docs.title: Migration strategy for the monorepo
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[1. Annotation-only DTOs<br/>compile unchanged] --> B[2. Platform JSON module<br/>dual implementation or<br/>port to Jackson 3]
    B --> C[3. Custom serializers,<br/>mixins, customizers ported]
    C --> D[4. Replace ObjectMapper injection<br/>with JsonMapper, remove try/catch]
    D --> E[5. Contract tests: API JSON,<br/>Kafka events, Redis values<br/>byte-compare before/after]

Persisted JSON is a contract too

Kafka events and Redis/DB JSON written by Boot 3.5 services will be read by Boot 4 services (and vice versa during rollout). Changed defaults (date formats, property ordering, null handling, enum handling) can break consumers. Record sample payloads from production and run them through both mappers in tests before upgrading.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Inventory custom serializers, deserializers, modules, ObjectMapper beans and new ObjectMapper() calls.
  • Remove explicit jackson-datatype-jsr310/jdk8/parameter-names dependencies for Boot 4.
  • Port customizers and mixin/component annotations.
  • Replace JsonProcessingException catches.
  • Golden-file tests for API responses and event payloads under both versions.
  • Check Redis serializers and Kafka JsonSerializer/JsonDeserializer configurations (Chapters 21, 23).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. One Boot-managed mapper, customized via properties/customizers; extra mappers derived from it.
  2. Records for DTOs; per-DTO naming via @JsonNaming.
  3. Money as decimal strings (or paise integers at gateway boundaries); never floats.
  4. Instant/OffsetDateTime/LocalDate; no LocalDateTime in APIs.
  5. Tolerant readers: ignore unknown properties, default unknown enums.
  6. Separate DTOs over @JsonView for different audiences.
  7. Safe polymorphism: logical names, closed subtype lists, default implementation.
  8. Stream large payloads; set read constraints for public endpoints.
  9. Mask PII in log/audit serialization.
  10. Golden-file tests for public JSON contracts and events.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ new ObjectMapper() in a service — misses Boot configuration, modules, and wastes CPU (mappers are expensive to create; caches per instance).

❌ double price in DTOs — 0.1 + 0.2 problems and lost scale.

❌ LocalDateTime deliveryTime — the app guesses the zone.

❌ activateDefaultTyping for convenience in caches or APIs.

❌ Returning entities with bidirectional relationships → infinite recursion (@JsonManagedReference band-aids); use DTOs.

❌ Global SNAKE_CASE strategy because one partner uses it.

❌ Strict unknown-property failure (fail-on-unknown-properties: true) on consumers — every producer addition becomes an outage.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix InvalidDefinitionException: Java 8 date/time type not supported Hand-made mapper without JSR-310 module (Jackson 2) Use Boot's mapper Dates as arrays [2026,9,22] WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS enabled in custom mapper Use Boot's defaults Cannot construct instance ... no Creators Record/class without parameter names; missing -parameters Compile with -parameters; @JsonCreator UnrecognizedPropertyException Strict mapper Tolerate unknown properties InvalidFormatException for enum Unknown enum value Default value strategy Offset lost after round trip ADJUST_DATES_TO_CONTEXT_TIME_ZONE Compare instants or disable feature Infinite recursion / StackOverflowError Bidirectional entity graph DTOs costPrice visible to customers Missing @JsonView on endpoint / shared DTO Separate DTOs Webhook signature mismatch Verified re-serialized JSON instead of raw bytes Verify raw body first Slow responses with large lists Building full list in memory Stream

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• No new ObjectMapper() outside tests (ArchUnit rule)
  • Money and time types follow platform rules
  • Enum forward compatibility enabled and documented to clients
  • Read constraints configured for public endpoints
  • No default typing anywhere processing external input
  • Log/audit mapper masks @Sensitive
  • Golden-file JSON tests for APIs and events
  • Jackson 3 migration plan with cross-version payload tests

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Which library does Spring Boot use for JSON by default?

Short answer: Jackson — Jackson 2 in Boot 3.x, Jackson 3 in Boot 4.x — via the web starters.

B1 · How do you rename a JSON field?

Short answer: @JsonProperty("mrp") on the field or record component.

B1 · How do you exclude null fields?

Short answer: @JsonInclude(NON_NULL) on the class/field, or globally spring.jackson.default-property-inclusion=non_null.

B1 · How are Java records serialized?

Short answer: Components become JSON properties; deserialization uses the canonical constructor.

B1 · Why not use double for prices?

Short answer: Binary floating point can't represent decimals exactly; rounding errors in totals. Use BigDecimal (and send as string or minor units).

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you customize Boot's ObjectMapper without replacing it?

Short answer: spring.jackson.* properties, or a builder customizer bean, Module beans, @JsonComponent/@JsonMixin (renamed in Boot 4).

B2 · How should dates be represented in APIs?

Short answer: ISO-8601 strings; Instant for timestamps (UTC), OffsetDateTime for zone-relevant times, LocalDate for dates; avoid LocalDateTime.

B2 · How do you make a value object serialize as a single string?

Short answer: @JsonValue on the accessor and @JsonCreator on a factory/constructor — or a mixin if you can't annotate the class.

B2 · How do you handle unknown enum values from newer producers?

Short answer: @JsonEnumDefaultValue with READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_USING_DEFAULT_VALUE, or read as null; handle the unknown case explicitly.

B2 · How do you test JSON serialization in isolation?

Short answer: @JsonTest with JacksonTester, which loads Boot's Jackson configuration only.

B2 · How do you call an API that uses snake_case while your API uses camelCase?

Short answer: @JsonNaming(SnakeCaseStrategy.class) on that client's DTOs, not a global naming strategy.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Why must the ObjectMapper be shared and not reconfigured at runtime?

Short answer: It caches serializers/deserializers per type; creation is expensive; reconfiguring after use gives inconsistent behaviour and isn't thread-safe. Jackson 3 enforces immutability.

B3 · How does Jackson handle polymorphic types safely?

Short answer: @JsonTypeInfo(use = NAME) with an explicit @JsonSubTypes list (closed set), optional defaultImpl for unknown types. Avoid Id.CLASS and default typing for untrusted data.

B3 · What are StreamReadConstraints and why tune them?

Short answer: Limits on nesting depth, number length, string length (and document size) enforced by the parser to prevent resource-exhaustion attacks. Defaults are generous; public APIs can use far tighter limits.

B3 · @JsonView vs separate DTOs?

Short answer: Views reuse one class for multiple projections but are easy to misuse (endpoint without view exposes everything). Separate DTOs are explicit and safer; views fit when projections are many and nearly identical.

B3 · How do you stream a large JSON array in Spring MVC?

Short answer: StreamingResponseBody with a JsonGenerator writing elements from a streamed source (JDBC stream), or NDJSON. Avoid building a full list.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · What breaks when migrating from Jackson 2 to Jackson 3?

Short answer: Coordinates and packages of core/databind (annotations unchanged), immutable mappers and builder-based config, unchecked exceptions, renamed serializer SPI and generator methods, built-in date/time and changed defaults, Boot customizer and annotation renames, Spring converter classes. Persisted/evented JSON contracts need cross-version tests.

B4 · How would you mask PII in logs while keeping API responses unchanged?

Short answer: Annotation (@Sensitive) + serializer modifier registered only on a separate, derived "log mapper"; the primary mapper remains unmasked. Plus a text-level masker in the log formatter as a safety net (Chapter 07).

B4 · Design the JSON conventions for the platform's public API.

Short answer: camelCase, ISO dates with explicit offsets, money as decimal strings with currency implied or explicit, open enums, nulls omitted, unknown fields ignored, stable ordering, RFC 9457 errors, documented in OpenAPI with examples and linted in CI.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you evolve JSON contracts consumed by mobile apps, other services and data pipelines?

Short answer: Additive changes only by default; tolerant readers everywhere; schema registry or OpenAPI/AsyncAPI with compatibility checks in CI; consumer-driven contract tests; explicit versioning and dual publishing for breaking changes; deprecation telemetry.

B5 · JSON vs Protobuf/Avro for internal service-to-service and events?

Short answer: JSON: human-readable, universal, no codegen, larger and slower. Protobuf/Avro: compact, schema-enforced, evolution rules, faster — better for high-volume Kafka topics and gRPC. Many platforms use JSON at the edge and Avro/Protobuf internally with a schema registry.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · After Boot 4 upgrade of order-service, analytics jobs fail to parse order events

Jackson 3 changed a default (e.g. property ordering or date/number representation) and the analytics parser was order-/format-sensitive. Fix: pin explicit formats (@JsonFormat, @JsonPropertyOrder) for event DTOs, golden-file tests across versions, schema validation for events, and make consumers tolerant.

Scenario · Customers see ₹289 instead of ₹289.00 and totals off by a paisa

API returned BigDecimal as JSON numbers; JavaScript dropped trailing zeros and summed with floats. Fix: money as strings (Money with @JsonValue), totals computed server-side, client uses a decimal library for display only.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Paise type for gateway DTOs

Create record Paise(long value) that serializes as a JSON number, deserializes from number only (reject strings and decimals), and converts to/from Money. Test round trips and rejection of "57800" and 578.5.

Solution Paise.java
package in.grocery.common.money;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonCreator;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation.JsonValue;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

public record Paise(long value) {

    public Paise {
        if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative paise");
    }

    @JsonCreator(mode = JsonCreator.Mode.DELEGATING)
    public static Paise of(long value) {
        return new Paise(value);
    }

    @JsonValue
    public long value() {
        return value;
    }

    public static Paise from(Money money) {
        return new Paise(money.amount().movePointRight(2).longValueExact());
    }

    public Money toMoney() {
        return new Money(BigDecimal.valueOf(value).movePointLeft(2));
    }
}
PaiseJsonTest.java
package in.grocery.common.money;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.DeserializationFeature;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.cfg.CoercionAction;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.cfg.CoercionInputShape;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.type.LogicalType;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class PaiseJsonTest {

    private final ObjectMapper mapper = strict();

    private static ObjectMapper strict() {
        ObjectMapper m = new ObjectMapper()
                .disable(DeserializationFeature.ACCEPT_FLOAT_AS_INT);                 // reject 578.5
        m.coercionConfigFor(LogicalType.Integer)
         .setCoercion(CoercionInputShape.String, CoercionAction.Fail);                // reject "57800"
        return m;
    }

    @Test
    void roundTrip() throws Exception {
        assertThat(mapper.writeValueAsString(new Paise(57800))).isEqualTo("57800");
        assertThat(mapper.readValue("57800", Paise.class)).isEqualTo(new Paise(57800));
        assertThat(Paise.from(Money.parse("578.00")).toMoney()).isEqualTo(Money.parse("578.00"));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsStringsAndDecimals() {
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> mapper.readValue("\"57800\"", Paise.class)).isNotNull();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> mapper.readValue("578.5", Paise.class)).isNotNull();
    }
}

In production, apply these coercion settings in the gateway client's mapper (derived from Boot's), not globally. (The test builds a plain mapper only to keep the exercise self-contained.)

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Boot configures one shared Jackson mapper — customize it, don't replace it.
  • Boot 4 = Jackson 3: new packages for core/databind, same annotations, immutable mappers, unchecked exceptions, renamed SPI.
  • Records + per-DTO naming; money as strings/paise; explicit time types.
  • Tolerant readers: unknown properties ignored, unknown enums defaulted.
  • Safe polymorphism with logical names; never default typing on untrusted input.
  • Separate DTOs over @JsonView; stream large payloads; tighten read constraints.
  • Mask PII with a dedicated log mapper; golden-file tests protect contracts across upgrades.

10 Error Handling & Problem Details · 12 Data Access — JDBC

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Every grocery order, cart, price and stock count ends up in a relational database — PostgreSQL in our platform. Before reaching for JPA (Chapter 13), you need to understand the layer everything sits on: JDBC, connection pools and Spring's data-access abstractions. It matters because:

  • Most database incidents are pool incidents. "Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms" during a flash sale is a HikariCP message, not a PostgreSQL one — caused by pool sizing, slow queries holding connections, leaks, or virtual threads flooding a pool of 10.
  • JDBC is often the right tool. Stock reservations with UPDATE ... WHERE available >= ?, bulk price updates from a seller feed, reporting queries with window functions, streaming 200,000 rows for an export — plain SQL with JdbcClient is clearer and faster than an ORM for these.
  • Spring's exception translation turns vendor error codes into a meaningful hierarchy (DuplicateKeyException, CannotAcquireLockException, transient vs non-transient) so retry and error-mapping logic doesn't depend on PostgreSQL's SQLState strings.
  • Read replicas and multiple databases appear quickly at scale — catalog reads from a replica, reports from an analytics database.

This chapter builds the JDBC foundation of the platform: DataSource and HikariCP tuning, JdbcClient (Framework 6.1+) and JdbcTemplate, mapping to records, generated keys, batch updates, streaming, stored procedures, Spring Data JDBC, exception translation, integration tests with Testcontainers, the cart repository from Chapter 08 as a real SQL implementation with optimistic concurrency, and read/write routing to a replica.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — DataSource, JdbcClient queries and updates B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — named parameters, batching, generated keys, exception translation, Testcontainers B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — pool internals, connection binding, streaming, locking SQL patterns B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — pool sizing across pods, read replicas, multiple DataSources B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — database strategy, ORM vs SQL decisions

docs.title: 2.1 The stack
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["Repository (your code)"] --> B["JdbcClient / JdbcTemplate / NamedParameterJdbcTemplate"]
    B --> C["DataSourceUtils<br/>transaction-bound connection or new one"]
    C --> D["DataSource = HikariCP pool"]
    D --> E["JDBC driver (PostgreSQL)"]
    E --> F[(PostgreSQL)]
    B -.-> X["SQLExceptionTranslator<br/>→ DataAccessException hierarchy"]

docs.title: 2.2 DataSource and connection pool
docs.text:
A DataSource hands out connections. Creating a physical connection (TCP + TLS + auth) takes milliseconds to tens of milliseconds, so production code always uses a pool. Boot's default pool is HikariCP, auto-configured from spring.datasource.* when a JDBC driver and spring-boot-starter-jdbc (or data-jpa) are present.

Property Default Meaning spring.datasource.url / username / password — Connection details spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size 10 Max connections (idle + in use) spring.datasource.hikari.minimum-idle = max Keep pool full (recommended: leave equal) spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout 30s Wait for a free connection before failing spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime 30m Retire connections before DB/proxy/firewall kills them spring.datasource.hikari.idle-timeout 10m Only relevant if minimum-idle < max spring.datasource.hikari.keepalive-time (version-dependent) Ping idle connections to keep NAT/proxies from dropping them spring.datasource.hikari.leak-detection-threshold 0 (off) Log a stack trace if a connection is held longer than this spring.datasource.hikari.pool-name auto Appears in metrics and logs

docs.title: 2.3 Spring's JDBC APIs
docs.text:
API Since Style Use JdbcClient Framework 6.1 / Boot 3.2 Fluent, named or positional params, maps to records Default for new code JdbcTemplate Forever Positional ? params, callbacks Batch operations, legacy code NamedParameterJdbcTemplate — :name params Batch with named params SimpleJdbcInsert / SimpleJdbcCall — Metadata-driven insert / stored procedure call Procedures, quick inserts Spring Data JDBC — Repositories over aggregates, no lazy loading Simple aggregate persistence

All of them participate in Spring-managed transactions and translate exceptions.

docs.title: 2.4 Mapping rows
docs.text: Approach Example Record/class by column names .query(ProductRow.class) — sku → sku, selling_price → sellingPrice (underscore mapping) RowMapper<T> lambda (rs, n) -> new Product(rs.getString("sku"), ...) — explicit, fast, type-safe Single value .query(Integer.class).single() Map per row .query().listOfRows() — for dynamic reports ResultSetExtractor Whole result set, e.g. building aggregates from joins

docs.title: 2.5 Exception translation
docs.text:
JDBC throws checked SQLExceptions with vendor codes. Spring translates them into the unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy:

Exception Typical cause Retry? DuplicateKeyException Unique constraint violated No — business conflict DataIntegrityViolationException FK/NOT NULL/check violated No EmptyResultDataAccessException single() found nothing No IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException single() found many No — bug CannotAcquireLockException / PessimisticLockingFailureException Lock timeout, deadlock Yes (with backoff) QueryTimeoutException Statement timeout Maybe TransientDataAccessResourceException Connection dropped Yes CannotGetJdbcConnectionException Pool exhausted / DB down Maybe — careful, can amplify BadSqlGrammarException SQL error No — bug

Base types TransientDataAccessException vs NonTransientDataAccessException let resilience logic decide retries generically (Chapter 26).

docs.title: 2.6 Transactions — just enough for this chapter
docs.text: With Spring-managed transactions (@Transactional, Chapter 16), all JDBC calls in one transaction on the same thread share one connection, bound to the thread by DataSourceTransactionManager (or JpaTransactionManager). Outside a transaction, each JDBC call borrows a connection and returns it immediately (auto-commit).

docs.title: 2.7 Schema initialization
docs.text:
• Flyway/Liquibase (Chapter 14) — the production way.
  • schema.sql / data.sql with spring.sql.init.mode=always — only for demos and tests. Default embedded runs them only for embedded databases.

docs.title: 2.8 Spring Data JDBC
docs.text: Repository interfaces (CrudRepository, ListCrudRepository) over aggregates mapped to tables, with no lazy loading, no dirty checking, no session: save() writes the whole aggregate; loading reads it fully. Simpler and more predictable than JPA; less powerful for complex object graphs. A good middle ground for small bounded contexts.

docs.title: 3.1 HikariCP borrowing and returning
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Request thread
    participant H as HikariPool
    participant B as ConcurrentBag
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    T->>H: getConnection()
    H->>B: borrow(timeout)
    alt thread-local list has an idle connection
        B-->>H: reuse (fast path)
    else shared list has idle connection
        B-->>H: CAS state NOT_IN_USE → IN_USE
    else none idle and pool < max
        H->>DB: add connection asynchronously
        B-->>H: wait on handoff queue (up to connectionTimeout)
    else pool at max
        B-->>H: wait... or SQLTransientConnectionException after connectionTimeout
    end
    H-->>T: ProxyConnection
    T->>DB: queries
    T->>H: close() → returns to bag (resets autocommit, isolation, readOnly if changed)
  • ProxyConnection.close() returns the connection; it doesn't close the socket.
  • Hikari tracks state changes (autocommit, isolation, read-only, schema) and resets them on return.
  • max-lifetime retires each connection (with jitter) and replaces it in the background.

docs.title: 3.2 JdbcClient → connection → translation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["jdbc.sql(...).param(...).query(Row.class).list()"] --> B[JdbcTemplate.query]
    B --> C["DataSourceUtils.getConnection(ds)<br/>tx-bound via TransactionSynchronizationManager, or new"]
    C --> D[PreparedStatement<br/>bind params via StatementCreatorUtils]
    D --> E[execute → ResultSet]
    E --> F[RowMapper per row<br/>DataClassRowMapper for records]
    F --> G[release: close statement,<br/>DataSourceUtils.releaseConnection]
    D -.->|SQLException| H[SQLErrorCodeSQLExceptionTranslator<br/>/ SQLStateSQLExceptionTranslator]
    H --> I[DataAccessException subtype]
  • DataClassRowMapper maps columns to record constructor parameters, converting snake_case to camelCase.
  • Connection release outside a transaction returns the connection immediately after the statement — a loop of 100 queries borrows and returns 100 times (cheap with Hikari, but still a reason to use a transaction or batch for multi-statement work).
  • Translation uses sql-error-codes.xml per database product (detected from connection metadata) and falls back to SQLState classes.

docs.title: 3.3 Streaming results
docs.text: queryForStream() / .stream() keeps the ResultSet open while you consume. For PostgreSQL, the driver only streams (uses a cursor) when auto-commit is off (inside a transaction) and fetch size > 0; otherwise it loads everything into memory. The stream must be closed (try-with-resources) or the connection leaks.

docs.title: 4.2 A repository with JdbcClient
4.3 First integration test with Testcontainers
5.1 Level 2 — Generated keys, IN clauses, explicit row mappers
5.2 Level 2 — Batch updates
docs.text:
Seller price feeds update thousands of SKUs:

in/grocery/catalog/repository/PriceBatchRepository.java
package in.grocery.catalog.repository;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.namedparam.NamedParameterJdbcTemplate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.namedparam.SqlParameterSource;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.namedparam.SqlParameterSourceUtils;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Repository
public class PriceBatchRepository {

    public record PriceUpdate(String sku, BigDecimal sellingPrice) {}

    private final NamedParameterJdbcTemplate jdbc;

    public PriceBatchRepository(NamedParameterJdbcTemplate jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    @Transactional                                                                          // (1)!
    public int[] apply(List<PriceUpdate> updates) {
        SqlParameterSource[] batch = SqlParameterSourceUtils.createBatch(updates);           // from record accessors
        return jdbc.batchUpdate("""
                update product set selling_price = :sellingPrice, updated_at = now()
                where sku = :sku and :sellingPrice <= mrp
                """, batch);                                                                // (2)!
    }
}
  1. One transaction, one connection, all-or-nothing.
  2. Returns affected rows per statement: 0 means SKU unknown or price above MRP — the caller reports those rows back to the seller.
application.yml — make batches real batches
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/catalog?reWriteBatchedInserts=true     # (1)!
  1. PostgreSQL driver rewrites batched INSERTs into multi-row inserts — often 5–10× faster. (Updates are still sent as a pipelined batch.)

For very large loads (100k+ rows), split into chunks of 500–1,000 per batch and consider PostgreSQL COPY via the driver's CopyManager.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Stock reservation with a conditional update
docs.text:
The classic JDBC win: an atomic check-and-decrement without locks held in application code.

in/grocery/inventory/repository/StockRepository.java
package in.grocery.inventory.repository;

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;

@Repository
public class StockRepository {

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    public StockRepository(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    /** @return true if reserved; false if insufficient stock. */
    public boolean reserve(String hub, String sku, int qty) {
        int rows = jdbc.sql("""
                        update stock set available = available - :qty, reserved = reserved + :qty
                        where hub_code = :hub and sku = :sku and available >= :qty
                        """)                                                                   // (1)!
                .param("qty", qty).param("hub", hub).param("sku", sku)
                .update();
        return rows == 1;
    }
}
  1. The WHERE available >= :qty makes the check and update one atomic statement — no read-modify-write race between two customers buying the last packet of milk. Chapter 16 covers when you need explicit locking instead.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Streaming a large export
5.5 Level 3 — Stored procedures and functions
docs.text:
The finance team owns a PostgreSQL function computing a seller's settlement:

in/grocery/seller/repository/SettlementRepository.java
package in.grocery.seller.repository;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.LocalDate;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;

@Repository
public class SettlementRepository {

    public record Settlement(BigDecimal gross, BigDecimal commission, BigDecimal tcs, BigDecimal net) {}

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    public SettlementRepository(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    public Settlement compute(String sellerId, LocalDate periodStart, LocalDate periodEnd) {
        return jdbc.sql("select * from finance.compute_settlement(:seller, :from, :to)")   // (1)!
                .param("seller", sellerId).param("from", periodStart).param("to", periodEnd)
                .query(Settlement.class)
                .single();
    }
}
  1. PostgreSQL functions returning a row/table are called with plain SELECT — simplest and works with JdbcClient. For procedures with OUT parameters (or other databases), use SimpleJdbcCall.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Exception translation in practice
5.7 Level 3 — Spring Data JDBC for a small aggregate
docs.text:
The delivery-partner bounded context is simple: a partner with vehicle documents.

in/grocery/delivery/partner/DeliveryPartner.java
package in.grocery.delivery.partner;

import java.time.LocalDate;
import java.util.Set;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.Id;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.Version;
import org.springframework.data.relational.core.mapping.MappedCollection;
import org.springframework.data.relational.core.mapping.Table;

@Table("delivery_partner")
public record DeliveryPartner(
        @Id Long id,
        String name,
        String mobile,
        String hubCode,
        @Version Integer version,                                           // (1)!
        @MappedCollection(idColumn = "partner_id") Set<VehicleDocument> documents) {   // (2)!

    @Table("vehicle_document")
    public record VehicleDocument(String type, String number, LocalDate validTill) {}
}
  1. Optimistic locking built in: concurrent saves → OptimisticLockingFailureException.
  2. Documents are part of the aggregate: saved and loaded with the partner (delete-and-reinsert on save).
DeliveryPartnerRepository.java
public interface DeliveryPartnerRepository extends ListCrudRepository<DeliveryPartner, Long> {

    List<DeliveryPartner> findByHubCode(String hubCode);                         // derived query

    @Query("select * from delivery_partner where mobile = :mobile")
    Optional<DeliveryPartner> findByMobile(String mobile);
}

Add spring-boot-starter-data-jdbc. Chapter 13 compares JDBC, Spring Data JDBC and JPA in depth.

docs.title: 6.1 The cart repository in SQL, with optimistic concurrency
docs.text:
Chapter 08's in-memory CartRepository becomes PostgreSQL. The cart lines are stored as JSONB — the cart is always read and written as a whole, is short-lived, and never queried by line.

V3__cart.sql
create table cart (
    id           uuid primary key,
    customer_id  varchar(20) not null,
    quantities   jsonb not null default '{}'::jsonb,   -- {"MILK-1L": 2, "ATTA-5KG": 1}
    version      bigint not null,
    updated_at   timestamptz not null default now()
);
create index cart_customer_idx on cart (customer_id);
in/grocery/cart/repository/JdbcCartRepository.java
package in.grocery.cart.repository;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.core.type.TypeReference;
import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;       // JsonMapper / tools.jackson on Boot 4
import in.grocery.cart.service.Cart;
import in.grocery.cart.service.CartNotFoundException;
import in.grocery.cart.service.CartVersionConflict;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;

@Repository
@Primary                                                                                     // replaces the in-memory one
class JdbcCartRepository implements CartRepository {

    private static final TypeReference<Map<String, Integer>> QUANTITIES = new TypeReference<>() {};

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper json;

    JdbcCartRepository(JdbcClient jdbc, ObjectMapper json) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.json = json;
    }

    @Override
    public Cart insert(Cart cart) {
        jdbc.sql("insert into cart (id, customer_id, quantities, version) values (:id, :customer, cast(:q as jsonb), :v)")
            .param("id", UUID.fromString(cart.id()))
            .param("customer", cart.customerId())
            .param("q", write(cart.quantities()))
            .param("v", cart.version())
            .update();
        return cart;
    }

    @Override
    public Optional<Cart> find(String id) {
        return jdbc.sql("select id, customer_id, quantities::text as q, version from cart where id = :id")
                .param("id", UUID.fromString(id))
                .query((rs, n) -> new Cart(rs.getString("id"), rs.getString("customer_id"),
                        read(rs.getString("q")), rs.getLong("version")))
                .optional();
    }

    @Override
    public Cart update(Cart updated, long expectedVersion) {
        int rows = jdbc.sql("""
                        update cart set quantities = cast(:q as jsonb), version = :newVersion, updated_at = now()
                        where id = :id and version = :expected
                        """)                                                                // (1)!
                .param("q", write(updated.quantities()))
                .param("newVersion", updated.version())
                .param("id", UUID.fromString(updated.id()))
                .param("expected", expectedVersion)
                .update();
        if (rows == 1) return updated;
        boolean exists = jdbc.sql("select count(*) from cart where id = :id")
                .param("id", UUID.fromString(updated.id())).query(Integer.class).single() > 0;
        if (!exists) throw new CartNotFoundException(updated.id());
        throw new CartVersionConflict(updated.id(), expectedVersion);                          // (2)!
    }

    private String write(Map<String, Integer> quantities) {
        try {
            return json.writeValueAsString(quantities);
        } catch (com.fasterxml.jackson.core.JsonProcessingException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException(e);
        }
    }

    private Map<String, Integer> read(String q) {
        try {
            return json.readValue(q, QUANTITIES);
        } catch (com.fasterxml.jackson.core.JsonProcessingException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Corrupt cart JSON", e);
        }
    }
}
  1. Compare-and-set on version: a single statement, no locks held between read and write — the database-level half of Chapter 08's ETag/If-Match flow.
  2. Distinguish "gone" (404) from "changed" (412) with a cheap follow-up query only on the failure path.

docs.title: 6.2 Pool sizing for virtual threads and many pods
docs.text:
With spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, 2,000 concurrent requests may all try to borrow a connection. The pool becomes the concurrency limiter:

flowchart LR
    subgraph "order-service × 6 pods"
        P1[pod 1<br/>pool 20]
        P2[pod 2<br/>pool 20]
        P3[...]
        P6[pod 6<br/>pool 20]
    end
    P1 & P2 & P3 & P6 --> PGB[PgBouncer<br/>optional, transaction pooling]
    PGB --> PG[(PostgreSQL<br/>max_connections 300<br/>~16 vCPU)]

Rules of thumb:

Rule Why Σ (pool size × pods × services) + admin headroom ≤ DB max_connections Otherwise scale-out causes connection refusals Start near 2 × DB cores total across all clients, then measure Past that, more connections = more contention, not throughput Keep minimum-idle = maximum-pool-size Fixed-size pool, no churn connection-timeout 2–5s for request paths Fail fast (503) instead of piling up waiting requests max-lifetime a few minutes below DB/proxy idle kill Avoid "connection reset" on dead sockets Statement timeout in the DB (options=-c statement_timeout=5s) A runaway query can't hold a connection forever HPA max replicas bounded by the connection budget Autoscaling can DoS your own database application-prod.yml — order-service
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db:5432/orders?reWriteBatchedInserts=true&options=-c%20statement_timeout=5000
    hikari:
      pool-name: orders-rw
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      minimum-idle: 20
      connection-timeout: 3s
      max-lifetime: 25m
      keepalive-time: 2m
      leak-detection-threshold: 20s          # log holders > 20s (tune; off in hot paths if noisy)

Metrics to watch (Micrometer, Chapter 27): hikaricp.connections.active, .pending, .acquire (timer), .usage (time held), .timeout (counter). Pending > 0 sustained or acquire p99 rising = the pool is the bottleneck.

docs.title: 6.3 Read replica routing
docs.text:
Catalog browsing and order history are read-heavy and tolerate a little replication lag. Send read-only transactions to the replica.

Spring Framework 6.2+ (Boot 3.4+ / 4.x)Spring Framework 6.0/6.1 — AbstractRoutingDataSource in/grocery/platform/db/ReadReplicaDataSourceConfig.java
package in.grocery.platform.db;

import com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource;
import javax.sql.DataSource;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceProperties;
import org.springframework.boot.context.properties.ConfigurationProperties;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Primary;
import org.springframework.jdbc.datasource.LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class ReadReplicaDataSourceConfig {

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("grocery.datasource.primary")
    DataSourceProperties primaryProperties() { return new DataSourceProperties(); }

    @Bean
    @ConfigurationProperties("grocery.datasource.replica")
    DataSourceProperties replicaProperties() { return new DataSourceProperties(); }

    @Bean(defaultCandidate = false)                                                   // (1)!
    @ConfigurationProperties("grocery.datasource.primary.hikari")
    HikariDataSource primaryPool(DataSourceProperties primaryProperties) {
        return primaryProperties.initializeDataSourceBuilder().type(HikariDataSource.class).build();
    }

    @Bean(defaultCandidate = false)
    @ConfigurationProperties("grocery.datasource.replica.hikari")
    HikariDataSource replicaPool(DataSourceProperties replicaProperties) {
        HikariDataSource ds = replicaProperties.initializeDataSourceBuilder().type(HikariDataSource.class).build();
        ds.setReadOnly(true);                                                          // (2)!
        return ds;
    }

    @Bean
    @Primary
    DataSource dataSource(HikariDataSource primaryPool, HikariDataSource replicaPool) {
        LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy proxy = new LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy(primaryPool);  // (3)!
        proxy.setReadOnlyDataSource(replicaPool);                                              // (4)!
        return proxy;
    }
}
  1. Framework 6.2's defaultCandidate = false: the pools exist as beans (metrics, health) but aren't candidates for plain DataSource injection — only the routing proxy is.
  2. Belt and braces: the replica pool refuses writes.
  3. The lazy proxy defers fetching a physical connection until the first statement — by then the transaction's read-only flag is known.
  4. Framework 6.2+: read-only transactions (@Transactional(readOnly = true)) use the replica pool automatically.
ReadWriteRoutingDataSource.java
class ReadWriteRoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override
    protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly() ? "replica" : "primary";
    }
}
// wrap in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the key is evaluated after the transaction starts
application-prod.yml — catalog-service
grocery:
  datasource:
    primary:
      url: jdbc:postgresql://catalog-db-rw:5432/catalog
      username: ${CATALOG_DB_USER}
      password: ${CATALOG_DB_PASSWORD}
      hikari:
        pool-name: catalog-rw
        maximum-pool-size: 10
    replica:
      url: jdbc:postgresql://catalog-db-ro:5432/catalog
      username: ${CATALOG_DB_USER}
      password: ${CATALOG_DB_PASSWORD}
      hikari:
        pool-name: catalog-ro
        maximum-pool-size: 30
Usage
@Transactional(readOnly = true)                  // → replica
public PageResponse<ProductSummary> browse(...) { ... }

@Transactional                                   // → primary
public void updatePrice(...) { ... }

Read-your-writes

After a customer places an order, "My Orders" served from a lagging replica may not show it. For flows that must see their own writes, read from the primary (a non-readOnly transaction or explicit primary routing for N seconds after a write), or pass the new data in the response. Monitor replica lag and fail over reads to the primary when lag exceeds a threshold.

Verify

Confirm LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy#setReadOnlyDataSource and @Bean(defaultCandidate = false) against your Framework version (both 6.2+). Declaring your own DataSource bean makes Boot's DataSourceAutoConfiguration back off — Flyway, health and metrics then use your @Primary proxy; make sure Flyway runs against the primary (use spring.flyway.url/credentials or a FlywayDataSource-qualified bean).

docs.title: 6.4 Test: routing really happens
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace legacy JdbcTemplate query-callback code with JdbcClient where touched.
  • Custom DataSource beans: move to defaultCandidate = false pattern where multiple pools exist.
  • Update test slice imports and starters for Boot 4.
  • Recheck Hikari property names and defaults after upgrades (keepalive, validation).
  • JSpecify: handle @Nullable returns (queryForObject etc.) explicitly.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. JdbcClient + records for new SQL code; explicit RowMappers on hot paths.
  2. Always bind parameters; whitelist identifiers.
  3. Atomic SQL (UPDATE ... WHERE condition) instead of read-modify-write in Java.
  4. Batch bulk writes; chunk very large loads; reWriteBatchedInserts.
  5. Stream large reads inside read-only transactions with a fetch size; close streams.
  6. Pool sizing is a platform budget across pods and services; fail fast on acquisition.
  7. Statement timeouts in the database; leak-detection-threshold in lower environments.
  8. Catch specific DataAccessExceptions only where they carry domain meaning.
  9. Test against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection.
  10. Read replicas only for lag-tolerant reads; design read-your-writes explicitly.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ String concatenation in SQL — injection.

❌ N queries in a loop (for (sku : skus) findBySku(sku)) — use IN/any(:array) or a join.

❌ Remote calls while holding a connection (inside a transaction) — Razorpay latency becomes pool exhaustion.

Anti-patterns (snippet)
@Transactional
public void placeOrder(...) {
    orders.insert(...);
    razorpay.createOrder(...);     // ❌ 2–10s with a DB connection held
    orders.markPaymentPending(...);
}

✅ Commit, then call out; or outbox (Chapter 36).

❌ Huge pools ("set 200 to be safe") — more connections, more DB contention, lower throughput.

❌ Unclosed Streams from queryForStream — leaked connections.

❌ select * in production queries — breaks record mapping on schema additions and fetches unneeded columns (fine only in tests/demos).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Connection is not available, request timed out after 30000ms Pool exhausted: slow queries, long transactions, leaks, too small pool Check hikaricp.connections.usage, leak detection, remote calls in tx; tune Apparent connection leak detected Connection held beyond threshold Stack trace shows borrower; close streams; shorten tx FATAL: sorry, too many clients already Σ pools > max_connections Budget pools; PgBouncer; limit replicas Stream loads all rows / OOM Auto-commit on or fetch size 0 Read-only transaction + fetch size This connection has been closed / Connection reset max-lifetime > infra idle timeout Lower max-lifetime, keepalive DataClassRowMapper fails to map Column name/type mismatch Alias columns (as selling_price) or explicit mapper BadSqlGrammarException on in () Empty collection Guard empty input Duplicate rows inserted on retry No idempotency Unique constraints + handle DuplicateKeyException Replica returns stale data Replication lag Read-your-writes strategy

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Pool size per service documented against DB max_connections
  • connection-timeout short on request paths; statement timeout set
  • Hikari metrics on dashboards; alerts on pending/timeouts
  • No remote calls inside transactions (review + ArchUnit where possible)
  • All SQL parameterized; identifier whitelists
  • Repository integration tests on PostgreSQL via Testcontainers
  • Streams closed; exports use fetch size
  • Replica usage reviewed for read-your-writes

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is a DataSource and why use a connection pool?

Short answer: A factory for database connections. Pools (HikariCP in Boot) reuse connections because creating them is expensive.

B1 · JdbcClient vs JdbcTemplate?

Short answer: Both are Spring JDBC helpers. JdbcClient (6.1+) is a fluent API with named/positional params and easy record mapping; JdbcTemplate is the older callback-style API, still used for batches.

B1 · How do you prevent SQL injection?

Short answer: Bind parameters (:name / ?); never concatenate input. Whitelist identifiers that can't be bound.

B1 · What does Spring's exception translation do?

Short answer: Converts checked SQLExceptions with vendor codes into unchecked DataAccessException subclasses like DuplicateKeyException.

B1 · How does Boot know which database to connect to?

Short answer: From spring.datasource.url/username/password and the JDBC driver on the classpath; it auto-configures HikariCP.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you get a generated primary key after insert?

Short answer: KeyHolder with JdbcClient.update(keyHolder, "id") (or JdbcTemplate with PreparedStatementCreator/SimpleJdbcInsert).

B2 · How do you perform batch updates efficiently?

Short answer: NamedParameterJdbcTemplate.batchUpdate / JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate in a transaction, chunked; enable driver batch rewriting (reWriteBatchedInserts for PostgreSQL).

B2 · How do you avoid a race when decrementing stock?

Short answer: Single conditional update UPDATE ... SET available = available - ? WHERE available >= ? and check affected rows; or explicit locking when more logic is needed.

B2 · How do you test repositories against a real database?

Short answer: @JdbcTest (or @DataJpaTest) with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE), Testcontainers PostgreSQL and @ServiceConnection; migrations via Flyway.

B2 · What happens to connections outside a transaction?

Short answer: Each JDBC operation borrows a connection in auto-commit mode and returns it immediately.

B2 · Spring Data JDBC vs JPA?

Short answer: Spring Data JDBC maps aggregates with no lazy loading, dirty checking or session — simpler and explicit. JPA offers a persistence context, lazy loading, rich mappings — more powerful, more pitfalls.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does Spring bind a JDBC connection to a transaction?

Short answer: The transaction manager obtains a connection, disables auto-commit and binds a ConnectionHolder to the thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager; DataSourceUtils.getConnection returns it to all JDBC calls in that transaction.

B3 · How do you stream millions of rows from PostgreSQL without OOM?

Short answer: Inside a transaction (auto-commit off), set fetch size, use queryForStream/JdbcClient.stream(), consume incrementally, and close the stream. Stream to the client via StreamingResponseBody.

B3 · How do you size a HikariCP pool?

Short answer: Start small (~2× DB cores total across clients), keep pool fixed-size, ensure Σ pools ≤ DB max connections, measure acquire time/pending/usage, and fix slow queries before growing pools.

B3 · What changes for connection pools with virtual threads?

Short answer: Request concurrency is no longer limited by threads; the pool becomes the limiter. Keep pool sizes bounded, use short acquisition timeouts, and add bulkheads/rate limiting so thousands of virtual threads don't queue on the pool.

B3 · Transient vs non-transient DataAccessException?

Short answer: Transient (lock failures, timeouts, dropped connections) may succeed on retry; non-transient (constraint violations, bad SQL) won't. Retry policies key off this hierarchy.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design read-replica usage for the catalog service.

Short answer: Primary and replica pools, routing by transaction read-only flag via LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy (6.2 read-only DataSource or routing DataSource), migrations/writes on primary only, lag monitoring, read-your-writes handling, replica pool sized for read traffic, fallback to primary on lag.

B4 · An incident: pool exhaustion every evening at 8 pm. How do you investigate?

Short answer: Dashboards for active/pending/usage; correlate with traffic and slow query logs (pg_stat_statements); enable leak detection; look for remote calls inside transactions, long reports on the request path, lock waits; fix causes, then consider pool size, PgBouncer, or moving reports to replica/batch.

B4 · When do you choose plain SQL over JPA?

Short answer: Bulk operations, reporting, atomic conditional updates, database-specific features (JSONB, window functions, CTEs), streaming, and simple aggregates where ORM overhead and pitfalls outweigh benefits. Many services mix: JPA for aggregates, JdbcClient for queries.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How would you govern database connections across 26 services and one shared PostgreSQL cluster?

Short answer: Connection budgets per service tied to HPA limits, PgBouncer where appropriate, database-per-service direction, statement timeouts, dashboards and alerts, capacity reviews before sales events, and a golden-path DataSource configuration in the platform library.

B5 · Database per service vs shared database for the grocery platform?

Short answer: Database (or at least schema with owned access) per service for autonomy and independent scaling; shared read models via events/CDC rather than cross-service joins. A shared cluster with separate databases/users is a pragmatic middle ground with connection budgets.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · During a sale, checkout fails with 'Connection is not available' while DB CPU is only 30%

placeOrder held a transaction across the Razorpay order-creation call; Razorpay latency rose to 4s, so each checkout held a connection 4s; pool of 20 × 6 pods saturated. Fix: move the gateway call outside the transaction (create order in PENDING, commit, call Razorpay, update), add timeouts and circuit breaker, alert on hikaricp.connections.pending.

Scenario · A nightly seller report crashes order-service with OutOfMemoryError

Report used query(...).list() for 3M rows. Fix: stream with fetch size in a read-only transaction to a file/StreamingResponseBody, move to a batch job (Chapter 33) against the replica, and paginate by keyset.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Idempotent coupon redemption

Table coupon_redemption(coupon_code, customer_id, order_ref, redeemed_at) with unique (coupon_code, customer_id) and a coupon(code, max_redemptions, redeemed_count) table. Implement redeem(code, customerId, orderRef) that: increments redeemed_count only if below max (atomically), records the redemption, is idempotent for the same orderRef, and returns REDEEMED, ALREADY_REDEEMED, or EXHAUSTED. Test with Testcontainers.

Solution V9__coupons.sql
create table coupon (code varchar(20) primary key, max_redemptions int not null, redeemed_count int not null default 0);
create table coupon_redemption (
    coupon_code varchar(20) not null references coupon(code),
    customer_id varchar(20) not null,
    order_ref   varchar(20) not null,
    redeemed_at timestamptz not null default now(),
    primary key (coupon_code, customer_id)
);
CouponRepository.java
package in.grocery.promotion.repository;

import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Repository;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Repository
public class CouponRepository {

    public enum Result { REDEEMED, ALREADY_REDEEMED, EXHAUSTED }

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    public CouponRepository(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    @Transactional
    public Result redeem(String code, String customerId, String orderRef) {
        var existing = jdbc.sql("select order_ref from coupon_redemption where coupon_code = :c and customer_id = :u")
                .param("c", code).param("u", customerId).query(String.class).optional();
        if (existing.isPresent()) {
            return existing.get().equals(orderRef) ? Result.REDEEMED : Result.ALREADY_REDEEMED;   // idempotent retry
        }
        int claimed = jdbc.sql("""
                update coupon set redeemed_count = redeemed_count + 1
                where code = :c and redeemed_count < max_redemptions
                """).param("c", code).update();
        if (claimed == 0) return Result.EXHAUSTED;
        jdbc.sql("insert into coupon_redemption (coupon_code, customer_id, order_ref) values (:c, :u, :o)")
            .param("c", code).param("u", customerId).param("o", orderRef).update();   // PK guards concurrent duplicates
        return Result.REDEEMED;
    }
}
CouponRepositoryTest.java
@JdbcTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@AutoConfigureFlyway
@Testcontainers
@Import(CouponRepository.class)
class CouponRepositoryTest {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine");

    @Autowired CouponRepository coupons;
    @Autowired JdbcClient jdbc;

    @BeforeEach
    void seed() {
        jdbc.sql("insert into coupon (code, max_redemptions) values ('DIWALI50', 1)").update();
    }

    @Test
    void redeemIdempotentAndExhausted() {
        assertThat(coupons.redeem("DIWALI50", "C-1", "ORD-1")).isEqualTo(CouponRepository.Result.REDEEMED);
        assertThat(coupons.redeem("DIWALI50", "C-1", "ORD-1")).isEqualTo(CouponRepository.Result.REDEEMED);
        assertThat(coupons.redeem("DIWALI50", "C-1", "ORD-2")).isEqualTo(CouponRepository.Result.ALREADY_REDEEMED);
        assertThat(coupons.redeem("DIWALI50", "C-2", "ORD-3")).isEqualTo(CouponRepository.Result.EXHAUSTED);
    }
}

Under concurrency, two requests from the same customer may both pass the first select; the primary key makes the second insert fail and its transaction rolls back (including its count increment). Map that DuplicateKeyException to ALREADY_REDEEMED at the service level, or retry once.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• HikariCP + JdbcClient + records is the modern Spring JDBC stack.
  • The pool is a shared, finite budget — size it across pods, fail fast, watch acquire/pending/usage metrics.
  • Bind every parameter; whitelist identifiers.
  • Atomic conditional SQL beats read-modify-write; CAS on version gives optimistic concurrency.
  • Batch writes, stream reads (read-only transaction + fetch size + close).
  • Exception translation gives meaningful, retry-aware exceptions.
  • Never hold connections across remote calls.
  • Read replicas via LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy (6.2+), with a read-your-writes plan.
  • Test against real PostgreSQL with Testcontainers and @ServiceConnection.

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
JPA with Hibernate is the most widely used — and most widely misused — part of the Spring ecosystem. It lets you work with an object model (Order with OrderLines and a DeliveryAddress) while Hibernate generates SQL, tracks changes, manages identity and caches entities. Spring Data JPA adds repositories so a findByCustomerIdAndStatus method needs no implementation.

The productivity is real. So are the failure modes, and every one of them has shown up in production grocery systems:

  • N+1 queries: the "My Orders" screen loads 20 orders, then 20 queries for lines, then 200 queries for products — 221 queries and 1.8 seconds.
  • LazyInitializationException in a controller — "fixed" by turning on Open Session in View, which then holds database connections during JSON serialization and remote calls.
  • Lost updates: two warehouse staff update the same stock record; the last save silently wins.
  • Accidental mass updates: dirty checking flushes a changed entity nobody meant to save.
  • Pagination in memory: JOIN FETCH + Pageable loads 400,000 rows to return 20.
  • Slow inserts: IDENTITY ids disable JDBC batching, so importing 50,000 products issues 50,000 round trips.

This chapter explains how JPA really works — persistence context, entity states, flushing, proxies — and builds the order-service persistence layer properly: mapping, ids, embeddables, relationships, repositories and queries, projections, specifications, keyset scrolling, auditing, soft delete, N+1 prevention with tests that count statements, optimistic and pessimistic locking, caching, and the Hibernate 6.6 → 7 changes in Boot 4.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — entities, repositories, derived queries B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — relationships, fetch strategies, projections, pagination, auditing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — persistence context, flush, proxies, N+1, locking, batching B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — aggregate design, performance, Hibernate 7 migration B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — when (not) to use JPA, data architecture

docs.title: 2.1 The layers
docs.text: Layer What it is Jakarta Persistence (JPA) Specification: annotations, EntityManager, JPQL, Criteria API Hibernate ORM Implementation (Boot's default provider) with many extensions Spring ORM LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean, JpaTransactionManager, exception translation, shared EntityManager proxy Spring Data JPA Repository interfaces, derived queries, @Query, specifications, paging, auditing Spring Boot Auto-configures all of the above from spring.jpa.* and spring.datasource.*

docs.title: 2.2 Entity and its states
docs.text:
An entity is a class annotated @Entity with an @Id, mapped to a table. Requirements: non-final class, non-final persistent methods (for proxies), a no-arg constructor (protected is fine). Records can't be entities (final, immutable) — but can be embeddables and projections.

stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Transient: new Order()
    Transient --> Managed: persist()
    Managed --> Removed: remove()
    Managed --> Detached: transaction/persistence context ends,<br/>detach(), clear()
    Detached --> Managed: merge() (returns a managed copy)
    Removed --> [*]: flush/commit → DELETE
    Managed --> Managed: field changes → UPDATE at flush (dirty checking)
    [*] --> Managed: find()/query results

docs.title: 2.3 Persistence context
docs.text:
The persistence context (Hibernate Session) is a first-level cache and unit of work bound to a transaction:

  • Identity guarantee: within one context, find(Order, 42) returns the same Java object every time.
  • Dirty checking: at flush, Hibernate compares managed entities with their loaded snapshot and issues UPDATEs — no save() call needed for managed entities.
  • Write-behind: SQL is queued and sent at flush — before commit, before queries that might be affected (FlushMode.AUTO), or on explicit flush().

docs.title: 2.4 Identifiers
docs.text:
Strategy SQL Batching inserts Notes IDENTITY Auto-increment / identity column ❌ Hibernate must insert immediately to learn the id Simple; slow bulk inserts SEQUENCE (pooled optimizer) nextval once per allocationSize ids ✅ Recommended for PostgreSQL UUID Generated in Java ✅ Random UUIDv4 fragments B-tree indexes; prefer time-ordered UUIDs Assigned (natural key) App sets id ✅ Spring Data needs help to know "new vs existing" (Persistable, @Version)

Keep surrogate ids internal and expose a separate business reference (order_ref = "ORD-7F3A91C2") in APIs — no enumeration attacks, no leaking volumes.

docs.title: 2.5 Value types: embeddables and converters
docs.text:
• @Embeddable — a value object stored in the owner's table (DeliveryAddress → address_line1, address_pincode...). Records are supported as embeddables in recent Hibernate/JPA versions.
  • AttributeConverter<X, Y> — map a single attribute type to a column (Money ↔ numeric, Pincode ↔ varchar).
  • Enums — always @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING); ORDINAL breaks when someone reorders constants.

docs.title: 2.6 Relationships
docs.text:
Mapping Default fetch Guidance @ManyToOne EAGER Always set fetch = LAZY @OneToOne EAGER Set LAZY; prefer @MapsId shared primary key @OneToMany LAZY Use for aggregate children only; mappedBy + @ManyToOne on child @ManyToMany LAZY Avoid; model the join as an entity (ProductTag) when it has attributes @ElementCollection LAZY Small collections of values (tags)

Owning side = the side with the foreign key (@ManyToOne / @JoinColumn). Only the owning side's changes are persisted; keep both sides in sync with helper methods (order.addLine(line)).

Cascade and orphan removal: within an aggregate (Order → OrderLine), cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true. Never cascade across aggregates (order → customer, line → product).

docs.title: 2.7 Fetching strategies and N+1
docs.text:
N+1: 1 query for the parents + N queries for each parent's lazy association. Fixes:

Fix How Trade-off JOIN FETCH in JPQL select o from Order o join fetch o.lines where ... Row duplication; can't safely paginate collection fetches @EntityGraph On repository method Same as join fetch, declarative Batch fetching hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 / @BatchSize N+1 → 1 + N/50 queries; works with pagination DTO projection Select exactly the columns needed No entities, no lazy loading at all Two-step Page ids first, then fetch entities with graph where id in :ids Correct pagination with collections

docs.title: 2.8 Spring Data repositories
docs.text:
classDiagram
    Repository <|-- CrudRepository
    CrudRepository <|-- ListCrudRepository
    Repository <|-- PagingAndSortingRepository
    PagingAndSortingRepository <|-- ListPagingAndSortingRepository
    ListCrudRepository <|-- JpaRepository
    ListPagingAndSortingRepository <|-- JpaRepository
    JpaRepository : flush()
    JpaRepository : saveAllAndFlush()
    JpaRepository : deleteAllInBatch()
    JpaRepository : getReferenceById()
    class JpaSpecificationExecutor
    class QueryByExampleExecutor

Query options, from simplest to most flexible:

  1. Derived queries — findByCustomerIdAndStatusOrderByPlacedAtDesc(...).
  2. @Query JPQL — explicit, validated at startup.
  3. @Query(nativeQuery = true) — database-specific SQL.
  4. Specifications / Criteria / Querydsl — dynamic filters.
  5. Custom repository fragment — any code (JdbcClient, EntityManager).

docs.title: 2.9 Projections
docs.text: Kind Example Notes Interface-based (closed) interface OrderSummary { String getOrderRef(); BigDecimal getTotal(); } Only selected columns queried Class/record-based (DTO) record OrderSummary(String orderRef, BigDecimal total) Constructor expression; explicit Dynamic <T> List<T> findByCustomerId(String id, Class<T> type) Caller chooses projection Open interface (@Value("#{...}")) SpEL Loads full entity — avoid

docs.title: 2.10 Pagination and scrolling
docs.text:
API Returns Cost Page<T> Content + total count Two queries (data + count) Slice<T> Content + hasNext One query (fetches size+1) Window<T> + ScrollPosition (keyset) Content + position to continue Index-friendly; no offset scanning Limit parameter Top-N —

Deep offsets (OFFSET 100000) scan and discard rows — use keyset scrolling for infinite lists like order history.

docs.title: 2.11 Locking
docs.text: Type Mechanism Use Optimistic @Version column; UPDATE ... WHERE version = ? Default for user edits; conflicts are rare Pessimistic @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) → SELECT ... FOR UPDATE Hot rows with guaranteed contention (slot capacity) SKIP LOCKED Native query Work queues (pick next unassigned delivery)

docs.title: 2.12 Auditing and soft delete
docs.text:
• Spring Data auditing: @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy, @LastModifiedBy with @EnableJpaAuditing and AuditorAware.
  • Hibernate Envers: full revision history tables.
  • Soft delete: Hibernate @SoftDelete (6.4+) or @SQLDelete + @SQLRestriction.

docs.title: 2.13 Open Session in View (OSIV)
docs.text: Boot enables spring.jpa.open-in-view=true by default (and logs a warning). It keeps the persistence context — and a database connection — open for the entire web request, including view rendering and JSON serialization, so lazy loading "works" in controllers. Disable it in API services: it hides N+1 queries and holds connections during slow work.

docs.title: 3.1 Bootstrapping
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[HibernateJpaAutoConfiguration] --> B["LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean<br/>scans @Entity under main package<br/>or @EntityScan"]
    B --> C[Hibernate builds metamodel<br/>SessionFactory: SQL, persisters, caches]
    A --> D[JpaTransactionManager]
    A --> E[Shared EntityManager proxy<br/>injectable via constructor]
    F["JpaRepositoriesAutoConfiguration<br/>@EnableJpaRepositories"] --> G[JpaRepositoryFactoryBean per interface]
    G --> H["Query lookup at startup:<br/>derived → PartTree → JPQL<br/>@Query → validated"]
    G --> I[Proxy implementing your interface<br/>SimpleJpaRepository + query methods + fragments]

Derived and @Query JPQL queries are parsed and validated at startup — a typo fails the boot, not the first request.

docs.title: 3.2 A request through a repository
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as OrderService (@Transactional)
    participant R as OrderRepository proxy
    participant EM as EntityManager (transaction-scoped)
    participant PC as Persistence context
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    S->>R: findByOrderRef("ORD-1")
    R->>EM: createQuery(JPQL)
    EM->>PC: flush if AUTO and pending changes affect query
    EM->>DB: SELECT ...
    DB-->>EM: rows
    EM->>PC: hydrate entity, store snapshot, register as managed
    EM-->>S: Order (lines = uninitialized PersistentBag proxy)
    S->>S: order.markPacked() (field change)
    S->>S: order.getLines().size()
    PC->>DB: SELECT lines WHERE order_id = ? (lazy init)
    Note over S: method returns → commit
    S->>PC: flush: dirty check → UPDATE customer_order SET status=?, version=? WHERE id=? AND version=?
    PC->>DB: UPDATE
    DB-->>S: COMMIT

Key classes: SessionImpl, StatefulPersistenceContext, DefaultFlushEventListener, ActionQueue (ordered inserts/updates/deletes), EntityPersister, PersistentBag/PersistentSet (lazy collections), ByteBuddy proxies for lazy @ManyToOne.

docs.title: 3.3 save() — persist or merge?
docs.text:
SimpleJpaRepository.save(entity) calls entityInformation.isNew(entity):

  • New (id null, or @Version null, or Persistable.isNew() true) → em.persist(entity) and returns the same instance.
  • Otherwise → em.merge(entity) → SELECT to load the current state, copy fields, return a different managed instance.

Consequences: assigned-id entities without @Version always merge (extra SELECT, and save() returns a different object — use the returned one). For managed entities inside a transaction, calling save() is unnecessary.

docs.title: 3.4 Flush ordering and batching
docs.text: At flush, ActionQueue executes: inserts → updates → collection removals → collection updates → deletes. With hibernate.jdbc.batch_size and order_inserts/order_updates, statements of the same type are grouped into JDBC batches. IDENTITY ids force immediate inserts, defeating this.

docs.title: 3.5 Lazy proxies and equals/hashCode
docs.text:
A lazy @ManyToOne returns a generated subclass proxy. Implications:

  • getClass() on a proxy isn't the entity class → use Hibernate.getClass(obj) or instanceof in equals.
  • Accessing any non-id property initializes it (a query) — outside a session → LazyInitializationException.
  • Entity equals/hashCode: base on the id with care (id is null before persist). A common robust pattern: equals by id when non-null; hashCode = constant per class.

docs.text:
services/order-service/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(libs.spring.boot.starter.data.jpa)
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    implementation("org.flywaydb:flyway-core")

application.yml
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false                          # (1)!
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate                         # (2)!
    properties:

        jdbc:

        order_inserts: true

  1. Disable OSIV (see 2.13).
  2. Flyway owns the schema (Chapter 14); Hibernate only validates that mappings match. Never update in production.
  3. Turn Hibernate's "pagination in memory" warning into an error.
