5.6 Level 3 — Dynamic search with Specifications
docs.text:
Admin order search with optional filters (status, pincode, date range, min total):

in/grocery/order/repository/OrderSpecs.java
package in.grocery.order.repository;

import in.grocery.common.money.Money;
import in.grocery.order.domain.Order;
import in.grocery.order.domain.OrderStatus;
import java.time.Instant;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.domain.Specification;

public final class OrderSpecs {

    private OrderSpecs() {}

    public static Specification<Order> hasStatus(OrderStatus status) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> status == null ? null : cb.equal(root.get("status"), status);    // (1)!
    }

    public static Specification<Order> inPincode(String pincode) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> pincode == null ? null : cb.equal(root.get("address").get("pincode"), pincode);
    }

    public static Specification<Order> placedBetween(Instant from, Instant to) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> {
            if (from == null && to == null) return null;
            if (from == null) return cb.lessThan(root.get("placedAt"), to);
            if (to == null) return cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(root.get("placedAt"), from);
            return cb.and(cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(root.get("placedAt"), from), cb.lessThan(root.get("placedAt"), to));
        };
    }

    public static Specification<Order> subtotalAtLeast(BigDecimal min) {
        return (root, query, cb) -> min == null ? null
                : cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(root.get("subtotal").as(BigDecimal.class), min);
    }
}
  1. Returning null means "no restriction" — composable optional filters.
Dynamic search with Specifications (snippet)
Page<Order> result = orders.findAll(
        Specification.allOf(hasStatus(status), inPincode(pincode), placedBetween(from, to), subtotalAtLeast(min)),
        PageRequest.of(page, size, Sort.by(Sort.Direction.DESC, "placedAt")));

Type-safe attribute names

String attribute names ("placedAt") break silently on rename. Generate the JPA static metamodel (hibernate-jpamodelgen annotation processor → Order_.placedAt) or use Querydsl. Spring Data JPA 4 also evolves the Specification API (e.g. PredicateSpecification) — verify for Boot 4.

docs.title: 5.7 Level 3 — Pessimistic locking for slot capacity
docs.text:
Delivery slots have fixed capacity; during a sale thousands of customers race for the 7–9 a.m. slot. Optimistic locking would produce a storm of retries; a short row lock is the right tool.

in/grocery/delivery/domain/DeliverySlot.java (excerpt)
@Entity
@Table(name = "delivery_slot")
public class DeliverySlot {
    @Id private String slotId;
    private int capacity;
    private int booked;
    @Version private Long version;

    public boolean tryBook() {
        if (booked >= capacity) return false;
        booked++;
        return true;
    }
}
in/grocery/delivery/repository/SlotRepository.java
public interface SlotRepository extends JpaRepository<DeliverySlot, String> {

    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)                                                       // (1)!
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "2000"))          // (2)!
    @Query("select s from DeliverySlot s where s.slotId = :id")
    Optional<DeliverySlot> lockById(@Param("id") String id);
}
  1. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (Hibernate may render FOR NO KEY UPDATE on PostgreSQL) — concurrent bookers queue on the row.
  2. Wait at most 2 s; then PessimisticLockingFailureException/CannotAcquireLockException → 503 "slot busy, retry". Keep the locked transaction short: lock, check, increment, commit — no remote calls.
SlotBookingService.java
@Transactional
public boolean book(String slotId) {
    DeliverySlot slot = slots.lockById(slotId).orElseThrow(() -> new SlotNotFoundException(slotId));
    return slot.tryBook();                                                                        // dirty checking → UPDATE on commit
}

Even simpler

For a pure counter, Chapter 12's atomic SQL (update ... set booked = booked + 1 where booked < capacity) needs no lock at all. Use pessimistic locking when the decision needs more logic than a single WHERE clause can express.

docs.title: 5.8 Level 3 — SKIP LOCKED work queue
docs.text:
Assigning packed orders to delivery partners from several pods:

SKIP LOCKED work queue (snippet)
@Query(value = """
        select * from customer_order
        where status = 'PACKED' and assigned_partner is null
        order by placed_at
        limit :batch
        for update skip locked
        """, nativeQuery = true)
List<Order> claimNextBatch(@Param("batch") int batch);

Each pod locks different rows; no two pods assign the same order, and nobody waits.

docs.title: 6.1 The order placement service end to end
6.2 Hibernate settings for production
docs.text:
application-prod.yml — order-service
spring:
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc:
          batch_size: 50
          time_zone: UTC                                  # (1)!
        order_inserts: true
        order_updates: true
        default_batch_fetch_size: 50
        query:
          fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch: true
          in_clause_parameter_padding: true               # (2)!
          plan_cache_max_size: 2048
        connection:
          provider_disables_autocommit: true              # (3)!
        session:
          events:
            log:
              LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS: 200              # (4)!
  datasource:
    hikari:
      auto-commit: false
  1. Store Instants consistently in UTC regardless of the JVM zone.
  2. Pads IN (?, ?, ?) lists to powers of two → fewer distinct SQL strings → better plan-cache hit rate.
  3. With Hikari auto-commit: false, Hibernate can skip toggling auto-commit on every transaction start — lets it delay acquiring the connection until the first statement.
  4. Hibernate's slow-query log — a cheap early warning (property name valid for Hibernate 6.x; verify for 7).

docs.title: 6.3 Second-level cache for reference data
docs.text:
Categories and GST rate masters change rarely and are read constantly.

Category.java
@Entity
@org.hibernate.annotations.Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE, region = "category")
public class Category { ... }
application.yml
spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        cache:
          use_second_level_cache: true
          region.factory_class: jcache
        javax.cache.provider: com.github.benmanes.caffeine.jcache.spi.CaffeineCachingProvider   # verify key name

Local L2 caches across pods

A Caffeine-backed L2 cache is per pod: pod A updates a category; pod B keeps serving the old one until expiry. Use L2 only for data that tolerates staleness with a short TTL, or a distributed provider — or cache at the service layer with explicit invalidation (Chapter 21). For most services, no L2 cache is the safest default.

docs.title: 6.4 Custom repository fragment with JdbcClient
docs.text:
Heavy reporting queries don't belong in JPQL:

in/grocery/order/repository/OrderStatsRepository.java
public interface OrderStatsRepository {
    record HourlyGmv(java.time.Instant hour, java.math.BigDecimal gmv, long orders) {}
    List<HourlyGmv> hourlyGmv(java.time.Instant from, java.time.Instant to);
}
in/grocery/order/repository/OrderStatsRepositoryImpl.java
class OrderStatsRepositoryImpl implements OrderStatsRepository {                               // (1)!

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    OrderStatsRepositoryImpl(JdbcClient jdbc) { this.jdbc = jdbc; }

    @Override
    public List<HourlyGmv> hourlyGmv(Instant from, Instant to) {
        return jdbc.sql("""
                select date_trunc('hour', placed_at) as hour, sum(subtotal + delivery_fee) as gmv, count(*) as orders
                from customer_order
                where placed_at >= :from and placed_at < :to and status <> 'CANCELLED' and not deleted
                group by 1 order by 1
                """)
                .param("from", from).param("to", to)
                .query(HourlyGmv.class).list();
    }
}
OrderRepository.java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Order>, OrderStatsRepository { ... }
  1. The Impl suffix lets Spring Data combine it into the repository proxy. Both JPA and JdbcClient share the same transaction and connection when called within @Transactional.

Mixing JPA and JDBC in one transaction

JdbcClient doesn't see un-flushed JPA changes. If you modify entities and then query with JDBC in the same transaction, call entityManager.flush() first (JPQL/HQL queries auto-flush; native/JDBC may not).

docs.title: 6.5 Aggregate integration test with optimistic locking
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• On Boot 3.5, fix every Hibernate deprecation warning (-Werror from Chapter 01 helps).
  • Replace @Where/@WhereJoinTable with @SQLRestriction; legacy Criteria with JPA Criteria/HQL.
  • Re-run all repository integration tests and query-count tests — SQL generation can change between major versions.
  • Check custom types (UserType), naming strategies, and dialect settings (Hibernate auto-detects dialect; remove explicit legacy dialect classes).
  • Review Specification usages against Spring Data JPA 4 API changes.
  • Verify ddl-auto=validate passes against production-like schema.
  • Update test slice dependencies/imports.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Aggregates, not object graphs: entities within an aggregate are mapped; across aggregates, store ids.
  2. LAZY everywhere; load what you need per use case (graph, join fetch, projection, batch size).
  3. DTO projections for reads, entities for writes.
  4. SEQUENCE ids with pooled allocation + JDBC batching.
  5. @Version on every mutable aggregate root.
  6. OSIV off; ddl-auto=validate; Flyway owns schema.
  7. Keyset scrolling for long lists; never paginate collection fetch joins.
  8. Query-count tests for list/detail endpoints.
  9. Short transactions; no remote calls inside; bulk updates with explicit flush/clear.
  10. Mix in JdbcClient for reporting and bulk SQL.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ FetchType.EAGER "to avoid LazyInitializationException" — loads huge graphs on every query, can't be turned off per query.

❌ Bidirectional everything — Product.orderLines loads every order line ever when touched.

❌ Returning entities from controllers — lazy loading during serialization (OSIV) or LazyInitializationException; API coupled to schema.

❌ CascadeType.ALL on @ManyToOne — deleting a line deletes the product.

❌ Lombok @Data on entities — equals/hashCode/toString over lazy associations → N+1, stack overflows.

❌ findAll() then filter in Java.

❌ save() in a loop of 50,000 with IDENTITY ids — 50,000 round trips.

❌ ddl-auto: update in production — no review, no rollback, drifts silently.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix LazyInitializationException Accessing lazy association after transaction Fetch within the use case (graph/projection) inside the transaction Hundreds of queries per request N+1 Join fetch/graph/batch size/projection; query-count tests HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch Paginating a fetch join Two-step fetch; now an error via fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException Concurrent update Map to 409/412; retry where safe Slow bulk inserts IDENTITY ids, no batching Sequences, batch_size, order_inserts, chunk + flush/clear Memory grows in batch job Persistence context holds all entities flush() + clear() every N items, or JDBC Schema validation fails on startup Mapping ≠ schema Fix migration or mapping Updates to fields not persisted Entity detached; modified outside transaction Load and modify within @Transactional Unexpected UPDATEs Dirty checking on mutable fields / converters returning new instances each time Immutable value types with correct equals; read-only transactions MultipleBagFetchException Fetch-joining two List collections Use Set, separate queries, or batch fetching

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• OSIV disabled; ddl-auto=validate
  • All @ManyToOne/@OneToOne lazy
  • @Version on aggregate roots; conflicts mapped to 409/412
  • Sequence ids with allocation size matching DB sequences
  • JDBC batching enabled
  • Query-count tests on list/detail paths
  • Slow-query logging (Hibernate + database)
  • No entities in API responses
  • L2 cache used only deliberately

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA?

Short answer: JPA is the specification; Hibernate implements it; Spring Data JPA adds repository abstractions on top.

B1 · What is a derived query?

Short answer: A repository method whose name (findBySlug, countByStatus) Spring Data parses into a query.

B1 · Why does JPA need a no-arg constructor?

Short answer: Hibernate instantiates entities (and proxies) reflectively before populating fields.

B1 · @Enumerated(ORDINAL) vs STRING?

Short answer: ORDINAL stores position — breaks when constants are reordered or inserted. Use STRING.

B1 · What does @Transactional give a repository call?

Short answer: A persistence context and database transaction spanning the method; changes to managed entities are flushed and committed at the end.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · What is the N+1 problem and how do you fix it?

Short answer: One query for parents plus one per parent for a lazy association. Fix with join fetch/@EntityGraph, batch fetching, or DTO projections; verify with query-count tests.

B2 · FetchType.LAZY vs EAGER — defaults and recommendation?

Short answer: @ManyToOne/@OneToOne default EAGER; collections LAZY. Make everything LAZY and fetch per use case.

B2 · What is Open Session in View and why disable it?

Short answer: Keeps the persistence context (and a connection) open for the whole web request so lazy loading works in views/serialization. It hides N+1s and holds connections during slow work; disable it for APIs.

B2 · Page vs Slice vs Window?

Short answer: Page includes a total count (extra query); Slice only knows whether there's a next page; Window supports keyset scrolling with positions — efficient for deep lists.

B2 · Interface projections vs DTO projections?

Short answer: Both select only needed columns (closed projections). DTO/record projections are explicit and type-safe; open interface projections with SpEL load full entities.

B2 · How do you implement optimistic locking?

Short answer: @Version field; Hibernate adds WHERE version = ? and increments it; conflicts throw OptimisticLockException (Spring: ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException).

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Explain the persistence context and dirty checking.

Short answer: A transaction-scoped identity map of managed entities with loaded-state snapshots. At flush, Hibernate compares current and snapshot state and issues UPDATEs for changes — no explicit save needed.

B3 · When does Hibernate flush?

Short answer: Before commit, before queries whose results might be affected (FlushMode.AUTO for JPQL/HQL), and on explicit flush(). Native/JDBC queries may not trigger it.

B3 · How does Spring Data's save() decide between persist and merge?

Short answer: isNew() — id null, version null, or Persistable.isNew(). New → persist; otherwise merge (SELECT + copy, returns a different instance).

B3 · Why do IDENTITY ids hurt batch inserts?

Short answer: Hibernate must execute each INSERT immediately to obtain the generated id, so it can't batch. Sequences with pooled optimizers allocate ids in memory.

B3 · Why can't you paginate a collection fetch join?

Short answer: Rows are duplicated per child; SQL LIMIT would cut parents' collections. Hibernate falls back to in-memory pagination. Use two-step fetch or batch fetching.

B3 · Pessimistic vs optimistic locking — when to use which?

Short answer: Optimistic for low-contention user edits (cheap, detects conflicts). Pessimistic for known hot rows where retries would storm (slot capacity), with lock timeouts and short transactions. SKIP LOCKED for queues.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you design aggregates with JPA?

Short answer: Aggregate root with @Version, children via mappedBy with cascade/orphanRemoval, value objects as embeddables/converters, invariants in methods, references to other aggregates by id, repositories only for roots, small aggregates for contention.

B4 · A list endpoint went from 50 ms to 2 s after a feature. How do you diagnose?

Short answer: Hibernate statistics/datasource-proxy query counts, slow query log, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, check new lazy associations touched in mapping code (N+1), missing indexes, eager fetches introduced; add a query-count regression test.

B4 · What changes in Hibernate 7 matter for a Boot 4 migration?

Short answer: Removal of long-deprecated APIs (save/update/saveOrUpdate, @Where, legacy Criteria), Jakarta Persistence 3.2, Jakarta Data support, possible SQL generation differences; fix deprecations on 6.6 first and rerun query-count and integration tests.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · When would you not use JPA?

Short answer: Read-heavy reporting, bulk/ETL workloads, heavy use of database-specific SQL, event-sourced models, simple aggregates better served by Spring Data JDBC, or teams without the expertise to manage ORM pitfalls. Mixed approaches are normal.

B5 · How do you prevent ORM performance regressions across 26 services?

Short answer: Platform defaults (OSIV off, batching, validate), query-count tests in CI, slow-query dashboards, code review checklists (EAGER, cascades, entities in APIs), architecture tests, and performance tests before sale events.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · 'My Orders' times out for customers with 800 orders

Endpoint used Page with OFFSET and fetch-joined lines; Hibernate paginated in memory and the count query scanned all rows. Fix: keyset scrolling with composite index (customer_id, placed_at desc, id desc), DTO projection for list cards, lines loaded only on the detail view.

Scenario · Warehouse stock counts drift after concurrent updates

Two staff edit the same Stock entity; no @Version, last write wins. Fix: @Version, 409 with current state to the UI, atomic SQL for increments/decrements, and audit trail with Envers.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Seller product with tags and prices

Model SellerProduct (aggregate root, @Version) with @ElementCollection tags and @OneToMany PriceHistory entries (append-only). Write a repository method that loads products of a seller with tags without N+1 for a page of 20, and a test asserting ≤ 3 statements.

Solution SellerProduct.java (excerpt)
@Entity
@Table(name = "seller_product")
public class SellerProduct {
    @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "sp_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "sp_seq", sequenceName = "seller_product_seq", allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;
    private String sellerId;
    private String sku;
    @Version private Long version;

    @ElementCollection
    @CollectionTable(name = "seller_product_tag", joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "product_id"))
    @Column(name = "tag")
    @BatchSize(size = 50)
    private Set<String> tags = new HashSet<>();

    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "product", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
    @OrderBy("effectiveFrom desc")
    private List<PriceHistory> prices = new ArrayList<>();

    protected SellerProduct() {}
    // factory, addTag, changePrice(...) appends PriceHistory
    public Set<String> getTags() { return Collections.unmodifiableSet(tags); }
}
SellerProductRepository.java
public interface SellerProductRepository extends JpaRepository<SellerProduct, Long> {
    Page<SellerProduct> findBySellerId(String sellerId, Pageable pageable);   // tags via @BatchSize
}
SellerProductQueryCountTest.java (core assertion)
@Test
void pageWithTagsIsBounded() {
    Page<SellerProduct> page = products.findBySellerId("S-1", PageRequest.of(0, 20));
    page.forEach(p -> p.getTags().size());                         // initialize tags
    assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(3);   // page + count + 1 batched tag query
}

@BatchSize(size = 50) loads tags for up to 50 products in one IN query, keeping pagination correct (no fetch join on the page query). Price history is loaded only on the product detail use case.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• JPA = persistence context + dirty checking + write-behind; know entity states and flush timing.
  • Aggregates with lazy associations, value objects, @Version, and ids across boundaries.
  • N+1 is the default outcome of naive code — prevent with graphs, batch fetching, projections and query-count tests.
  • Sequences + batching for write performance; keyset scrolling for deep lists.
  • Optimistic locking by default, pessimistic/SKIP LOCKED for hot rows and queues.
  • OSIV off, ddl-auto=validate, Flyway owns the schema.
  • Boot 4 brings Hibernate 7 / Jakarta Persistence 3.2 / Spring Data JPA 4 — clear deprecations on 3.5 first.

docs.text:

  • Spring Boot Reference — Data › SQL › JPA and Spring Data JPA; Testing › Data JPA Tests
  • Hibernate ORM User Guide (6.6 and 7.x) — Fetching, Batching, Locking, Caching, Soft delete
  • Hibernate ORM 7 migration guide; Jakarta Persistence 3.2 specification

12 Data Access — JDBC · 14 Database Migrations

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Code is easy to roll back: redeploy the previous image. Databases are not. Once a migration drops a column, adds a NOT NULL constraint or rewrites a 40-million-row table, there is no "undo" button — and while it runs, it may be holding locks that stop checkout.

Schema changes in the grocery platform happen weekly: new GST columns on invoices, delivery slot tables, seller onboarding fields, indexes for new search filters. They must be:

  • Versioned and reviewable — the schema is code, in Git, next to the entity that uses it.
  • Repeatable across environments — laptop, CI, staging and production reach the exact same schema.
  • Safe under traffic — no long locks, no downtime, compatible with both the old and new application version during a rolling deploy.
  • Recoverable — a failed migration leaves a known state and a clear roll-forward path.

Spring Boot integrates Flyway and Liquibase: add the dependency and migrations run on startup. That's the easy part. This chapter covers the hard part too: zero-downtime schema evolution (expand/contract), lock-safe PostgreSQL migrations, large backfills, running migrations as a Kubernetes Job versus at startup, CI checks, and a complete multi-release example that renames a column in customer_order without dropping a single request.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — Flyway basics, naming, running migrations B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — repeatable migrations, Java migrations, Liquibase, testing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — locking, transactions, CONCURRENTLY, backfills B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — expand/contract across releases, migration jobs, rollback strategy B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — schema governance, change management at scale

docs.title: 2.1 Migration tools
docs.text:
Flyway Liquibase Change format Plain SQL (and Java) XML/YAML/JSON/SQL changelogs with changesets Mental model Ordered, immutable scripts Changesets with ids, authors, preconditions, contexts Database abstraction You write the SQL Can generate SQL per database Rollback Undo scripts (paid edition) Rollback blocks per changeset (community) Learning curve Very low Moderate Boot integration spring.flyway.* spring.liquibase.*

This handbook uses Flyway with SQL migrations — PostgreSQL is the only database and SQL is what reviewers understand. Liquibase is shown for comparison.

docs.title: 2.2 Flyway essentials
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Versioned migration V<version>__<description>.sql — runs once, in version order Repeatable migration R__<description>.sql — reruns whenever its checksum changes (views, functions) Schema history table flyway_schema_history: version, description, checksum, success, installed_on Checksum Detects edits to applied migrations → validation fails Baseline Adopt Flyway on an existing database: mark version N as applied Callbacks SQL/Java hooks: beforeMigrate, afterMigrate, ... Java migrations Classes extending BaseJavaMigration for logic SQL can't express Placeholders ${schema} substituted at runtime Out-of-order Allow applying a lower version after higher ones (hotfix branches) clean Drops everything — disabled by default since Flyway 10; keep it that way

Never edit an applied migration

Once V14__add_gst.sql ran anywhere shared, it's history. Fix mistakes with V15__fix_gst.sql. Editing breaks checksums in every environment where it already ran.

docs.title: 2.3 How Boot runs migrations
docs.text:
With flyway-core (plus flyway-database-postgresql for Flyway 10+) on the classpath, FlywayAutoConfiguration:

  1. Builds a Flyway instance from spring.flyway.* using the application DataSource (or a dedicated one).
  2. Runs migrate() during context startup before JPA's EntityManagerFactory initializes (so ddl-auto=validate sees the new schema).
  3. Lets you replace the strategy with a FlywayMigrationStrategy bean (e.g. validate only).

Key properties:

Property Default Notes spring.flyway.enabled true Disable when migrations run as a separate Job spring.flyway.locations classpath:db/migration Multiple locations allowed, e.g. vendor-specific spring.flyway.baseline-on-migrate false For adopting existing databases spring.flyway.validate-on-migrate true Checksum validation spring.flyway.out-of-order false Keep false in production unless you know why spring.flyway.clean-disabled true Never enable in shared environments spring.flyway.url/user/password app DataSource Separate privileged migration user spring.flyway.placeholders.* — Script placeholders

docs.title: 2.4 Zero-downtime schema changes: expand and contract
docs.text:
During a rolling deploy, old and new application versions run simultaneously against the same schema. Every schema change must be compatible with both.

flowchart LR
    A["Release N<br/>app v1 + schema S1"] --> B["EXPAND<br/>add new structures<br/>(nullable column, new table, index)<br/>app v1 still works"]
    B --> C["Release N+1<br/>app v2 writes new + old (dual write)<br/>reads new with fallback"]
    C --> D["MIGRATE DATA<br/>backfill in batches"]
    D --> E["Release N+2<br/>app v3 reads/writes new only"]
    E --> F["CONTRACT<br/>drop old structures<br/>after v2 is fully gone"]

Classification of changes:

Change Safe in one step? How Add nullable column ✅ Direct Add column with non-volatile default (PG 11+) ✅ Metadata-only, no rewrite (volatile defaults like gen_random_uuid() rewrite the table) Add NOT NULL column without default ❌ Add nullable → backfill → add constraint NOT VALID → VALIDATE Add index ⚠️ CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (non-transactional) Add foreign key ⚠️ ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT Rename column/table ❌ Expand/contract: new column, dual write, backfill, switch, drop Drop column ⚠️ Only after no deployed version reads it (and JPA mapping removed) Change column type ❌ New column + backfill, or careful USING on small tables Large UPDATE/DELETE ❌ Batches outside the schema migration

docs.title: 2.5 PostgreSQL locking in one table
docs.text:
Operation Lock taken Blocks ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (brief) Everything — including reads — while waiting/holding CREATE INDEX SHARE Writes for the whole build CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE Other DDL; not reads/writes ADD CONSTRAINT ... NOT VALID Brief ACCESS EXCLUSIVE / weaker for FK Minimal VALIDATE CONSTRAINT SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE Not reads/writes

The lock queue problem

Even a "fast" ALTER TABLE needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. If a long-running report holds a lock on customer_order, the ALTER waits — and every new query on that table queues behind the ALTER. Checkout stops. Always set lock_timeout (e.g. 5s) in migrations so they fail fast and retry, instead of freezing production.

docs.title: 2.6 Where migrations run
docs.text:
Option Pros Cons On application startup (Boot default) Simple; schema and code in lockstep Slow migrations delay readiness; every pod attempts (Flyway serializes with a DB lock); needs DDL privileges in app user Kubernetes Job / Helm pre-upgrade hook Separate privileged user; clear logs; app starts fast More deployment plumbing Init container Runs before app container per pod Runs per pod; same lock contention CI/CD pipeline step Central control Pipeline needs DB network access

Platform rule: startup migrations for small, fast changes; a migration Job for anything long-running or requiring elevated privileges, and backfills as batch jobs.

docs.title: 2.7 Rollback strategy
docs.text:
Database rollbacks are rarely safe (data written after the change would be lost). Prefer:

  • Roll forward: fix with a new migration.
  • Backward-compatible schema: the previous app version keeps working on the new schema, so rolling back the app never requires rolling back the database.
  • Backups/PITR for disasters, not for routine rollbacks.

docs.title: 3.1 Flyway migrate
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant Boot as FlywayAutoConfiguration
    participant FW as Flyway
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    Boot->>FW: migrate() (via FlywayMigrationInitializer bean)
    FW->>DB: ensure flyway_schema_history exists
    FW->>DB: acquire lock (PostgreSQL advisory lock)
    FW->>FW: scan locations → resolved migrations (SQL + Java), compute checksums
    FW->>DB: read applied migrations
    FW->>FW: validate: checksums, missing, failed, ordering
    loop each pending migration
        FW->>DB: BEGIN (unless non-transactional)
        FW->>DB: execute statements
        FW->>DB: INSERT into flyway_schema_history (success=true)
        FW->>DB: COMMIT
    end
    FW->>DB: release lock
    Boot->>Boot: continue: EntityManagerFactory (ddl-auto=validate)
  • Concurrency: multiple pods starting together block on the lock; the first applies migrations, the rest find nothing pending.
  • PostgreSQL DDL is transactional — a failed migration rolls back completely (except non-transactional statements like CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY).
  • Ordering with JPA: Boot makes the EntityManagerFactory depend on the Flyway initializer bean, so validation sees the migrated schema.

docs.title: 3.2 Liquibase update
docs.text: Liquibase reads a changelog (db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml), acquires DATABASECHANGELOGLOCK, compares changesets (id + author + file path) against DATABASECHANGELOG, checks preconditions and contexts/labels, and executes pending changesets in order, recording MD5 checksums.

dependencies {
    implementation("org.flywaydb:flyway-core")

docs.title: 4.4 Test that migrations apply cleanly
5.1 Level 2 — Configuration per environment
docs.text:
application.yml
spring:
  flyway:
    locations: classpath:db/migration
    validate-migration-naming: true             # (1)!
    clean-disabled: true
    placeholders:
      app_user: order_app
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: local
spring:
  flyway:
    locations: classpath:db/migration,classpath:db/testdata     # (2)!
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod
spring:
  flyway:
    enabled: false                               # (3)!
  1. Fail if a file in the location doesn't follow the naming pattern (e.g. V3_add.sql with one underscore would otherwise be silently ignored).
  2. Seed data only locally — never mix test data into production locations.
  3. Production runs migrations in a dedicated Job (Level 4).

Placeholders in scripts:

V20__grant_app_user.sql
grant select, insert, update, delete on all tables in schema public to ${app_user};

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — Java migration for logic SQL can't express
docs.text:
Normalizing legacy pincodes stored as "560 001"/"560-001":

src/main/java/db/migration/V21__normalize_pincodes.java
package db.migration;                                                             // (1)!

import java.sql.PreparedStatement;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.Statement;
import org.flywaydb.core.api.migration.BaseJavaMigration;
import org.flywaydb.core.api.migration.Context;

public class V21__normalize_pincodes extends BaseJavaMigration {

    @Override
    public void migrate(Context context) throws Exception {
        var conn = context.getConnection();
        try (Statement select = conn.createStatement();
             ResultSet rs = select.executeQuery(
                     "select id, addr_pincode from customer_address where addr_pincode !~ '^[1-9][0-9]{5}$'");
             PreparedStatement update = conn.prepareStatement(
                     "update customer_address set addr_pincode = ? where id = ?")) {
            int batch = 0;
            while (rs.next()) {
                String normalized = rs.getString(2).replaceAll("[^0-9]", "");
                if (normalized.matches("[1-9][0-9]{5}")) {
                    update.setString(1, normalized);
                    update.setLong(2, rs.getLong(1));
                    update.addBatch();
                    if (++batch % 500 == 0) update.executeBatch();
                }
            }
            update.executeBatch();
        }
    }
}
  1. Flyway scans db/migration on the classpath for Java classes too. With Boot, Java migrations can also be Spring beans implementing JavaMigration — Boot passes them to Flyway, so they can use injected services (use sparingly: migrations should not depend on application code that will change).

Java migrations are frozen history too

Don't call application classes (entities, services) from migrations — when that code changes next year, replaying V21 on a fresh database breaks. Keep migrations self-contained.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — The same change in Liquibase
docs.text:
src/main/resources/db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml
databaseChangeLog:
  - include:
      file: db/changelog/2026/09/0001-add-hsn-code.yaml
db/changelog/2026/09/0001-add-hsn-code.yaml
databaseChangeLog:
  - changeSet:
      id: 0001-add-hsn-code
      author: catalog-team
      preConditions:
        - onFail: MARK_RAN
        - not:
            columnExists:
              tableName: product
              columnName: hsn_code
      changes:
        - addColumn:
            tableName: product
            columns:
              - column:
                  name: hsn_code
                  type: varchar(8)
      rollback:
        - dropColumn:
            tableName: product
            columnName: hsn_code
application.yml
spring:
  liquibase:
    change-log: classpath:db/changelog/db.changelog-master.yaml
    contexts: prod

Pick one tool per service.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Lock-safe migrations on PostgreSQL
docs.text:
Every production migration starts with timeouts:

V30__add_invoice_gst_columns.sql
set lock_timeout = '5s';                  -- (1)
set statement_timeout = '60s';

alter table invoice add column cgst_amount numeric(12,2);
alter table invoice add column sgst_amount numeric(12,2);
alter table invoice add column igst_amount numeric(12,2);
alter table invoice add column place_of_supply varchar(2);
  1. If the table is busy, fail after 5 s instead of queueing all traffic behind the ALTER. The deployment retries later. SET (without LOCAL) lasts for the session; Flyway uses one connection per migration run.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Indexes without blocking writes
5.6 Level 3 — NOT NULL and foreign keys without long locks
5.7 Level 3 — Backfills are not migrations
docs.text:
Filling place_of_supply for 40 million historical orders inside a Flyway migration would run for an hour in one transaction, bloating the table and blocking deploys. Instead:

  • The migration adds the nullable column (instant).
  • A batch job (Spring Batch, Chapter 33, or a simple scheduled task) backfills in chunks with pauses.
  • A later migration adds the constraint once the job reports zero remaining rows.
in/grocery/order/backfill/PlaceOfSupplyBackfill.java
package in.grocery.order.backfill;

import java.time.Duration;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class PlaceOfSupplyBackfill {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PlaceOfSupplyBackfill.class);
    private final JdbcClient jdbc;

    public PlaceOfSupplyBackfill(JdbcClient jdbc) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
    }

    /** Runs until done; each chunk is its own short transaction (auto-commit). */
    public long run(int chunkSize, Duration pause) throws InterruptedException {
        long total = 0;
        while (true) {
            int updated = jdbc.sql("""
                    with batch as (
                        select id from customer_order
                        where place_of_supply is null
                        order by id
                        limit :chunk
                        for update skip locked
                    )
                    update customer_order o
                    set place_of_supply = s.gst_state_code
                    from batch, pincode_state s
                    where o.id = batch.id and s.pincode_prefix = left(o.addr_pincode, 3)
                    """)                                                                   // (1)!
                    .param("chunk", chunkSize)
                    .update();
            total += updated;
            if (updated == 0) break;
            log.info("Backfilled {} rows (total {})", updated, total);
            Thread.sleep(pause);                                                           // (2)!
        }
        return total;
    }
}
  1. Chunked by primary key, SKIP LOCKED so it never waits on rows the application is updating. Rows whose pincode prefix isn't in the mapping stay null — the job must report them for manual fixing, or the loop exits when updated == 0 with leftovers.
  2. Throttle to protect replication lag and I/O.

docs.title: 6.1 Zero-downtime rename: total → subtotal + delivery_fee
docs.text:
Business change: the order table has a single total column; finance wants subtotal and delivery_fee separately (GST applies differently). The old app reads total. Here's the full sequence across three releases, never breaking a running version.

gantt
    title Expand / contract across releases
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    axisFormat  %d %b
    section Schema
    V40 expand — add subtotal, delivery_fee (nullable)       :s1, 2026-10-01, 1d
    V41 constraints NOT VALID + VALIDATE                      :s2, 2026-10-08, 1d
    V42 contract — drop total                                  :s3, 2026-10-22, 1d
    section Application
    v1.40 dual-write total + new columns, read total           :a1, 2026-10-01, 7d
    Backfill job                                               :b1, 2026-10-02, 5d
    v1.41 read new columns, still write total                  :a2, 2026-10-08, 14d
    v1.42 stop writing total                                   :a3, 2026-10-15, 7d

Release 1 — expand + dual write

V40__order_split_total_expand.sql
set lock_timeout = '5s';
alter table customer_order add column subtotal numeric(12,2);
alter table customer_order add column delivery_fee numeric(8,2);
Order entity in v1.40 (excerpt)
@Column(name = "total", nullable = false)
private BigDecimal total;                 // still the source of truth for reads

@Column(name = "subtotal")
private BigDecimal subtotal;              // new, written alongside
@Column(name = "delivery_fee")
private BigDecimal deliveryFee;

void recalculate() {
    this.subtotal = linesTotal();
    this.deliveryFee = fee;
    this.total = subtotal.add(deliveryFee);   // dual write keeps old readers correct
}

Backfill job (as in 5.7) fills subtotal/delivery_fee for old rows from total and the fee rules.

Release 2 — enforce and switch reads

V41__order_split_total_constraints.sql
set lock_timeout = '5s';
alter table customer_order add constraint customer_order_subtotal_nn check (subtotal is not null) not valid;
alter table customer_order add constraint customer_order_delivery_fee_nn check (delivery_fee is not null) not valid;
alter table customer_order validate constraint customer_order_subtotal_nn;
alter table customer_order validate constraint customer_order_delivery_fee_nn;

App v1.41 reads subtotal + delivery_fee, still writes total (so v1.40 pods during the rollout and any rollback to v1.40 keep working).

Release 3 — stop writing, then contract

App v1.42 removes the total field from the entity (ddl-auto=validate doesn't complain about extra columns). Only after every v1.41 pod is gone and a rollback to v1.41 is no longer planned:

V42__order_split_total_contract.sql
set lock_timeout = '5s';
alter table customer_order alter column subtotal set not null;
alter table customer_order alter column delivery_fee set not null;
alter table customer_order drop constraint customer_order_subtotal_nn;
alter table customer_order drop constraint customer_order_delivery_fee_nn;
alter table customer_order drop column total;

Views and triggers as bridges

For renames used by many consumers (reporting tools, other services' read models), a compatibility view or a temporary trigger that keeps the old column in sync can replace application-level dual writes. Remove the bridge in the contract step.

docs.title: 6.2 Migration Job in Kubernetes
docs.text:
The app image contains the migrations; a Job runs the same image in "migrate-only" mode with a privileged database user. The app itself runs with spring.flyway.enabled=false and a least-privilege user.

in/grocery/order/migrate/MigrateOnlyRunner.java
package in.grocery.order.migrate;

import org.flywaydb.core.Flyway;
import org.springframework.boot.ApplicationArguments;
import org.springframework.boot.ApplicationRunner;
import org.springframework.boot.ExitCodeGenerator;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Profile;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
@Profile("migrate")
class MigrateOnlyRunner implements ApplicationRunner, ExitCodeGenerator {

    private final Flyway flyway;                                                         // (1)!
    private int exit = 0;

    MigrateOnlyRunner(Flyway flyway) {
        this.flyway = flyway;
    }

    @Override
    public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
        var result = flyway.migrate();
        exit = result.success ? 0 : 1;
    }

    @Override
    public int getExitCode() {
        return exit;
    }
}
  1. In the migrate profile, Flyway is enabled and configured with migration credentials; spring.main.web-application-type=none; JPA validation can stay on to prove the schema matches.
application-migrate.yml
spring:
  main:
    web-application-type: none
  flyway:
    enabled: true
    user: ${ORDERS_MIGRATION_USER}
    password: ${ORDERS_MIGRATION_PASSWORD}
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate

Run migrate() once

With spring.flyway.enabled=true, Boot's FlywayMigrationInitializer already migrates during startup. Either rely on that (and make the runner just exit 0), or register a FlywayMigrationStrategy bean that does nothing so the runner is the only caller. Don't migrate twice.

helm/order-service/templates/migrate-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: order-service-migrate-{{ .Release.Revision }}
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade,pre-install
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 900
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          args: ["--spring.profiles.active=prod,migrate"]
          envFrom:
            - secretRef:
                name: order-service-migration-credentials

The Helm upgrade only proceeds to roll out new pods if the migration Job succeeds.

docs.title: 6.3 CI pipeline checks
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[PR opened] --> B[Lint migrations<br/>naming, forbidden patterns,<br/>e.g. Squawk for PostgreSQL]
    B --> C[Apply all migrations<br/>to empty PostgreSQL<br/>Testcontainers]
    C --> D["@DataJpaTest with ddl-auto=validate<br/>entities ↔ schema"]
    D --> E[Apply to anonymized<br/>prod-size snapshot<br/>measure duration and locks]
    E --> F[Previous app version's<br/>integration tests against<br/>NEW schema]
    F --> G[Merge]

The last step is the key one for zero downtime: N-1 app on N schema must pass.

A simple forbidden-pattern check that runs in the build:

MigrationLintTest.java
package in.grocery.order;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.regex.Pattern;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class MigrationLintTest {

    private static final Path DIR = Path.of("src/main/resources/db/migration");
    private static final List<Pattern> FORBIDDEN = List.of(
            Pattern.compile("(?i)create\\s+(unique\\s+)?index\\s+(?!concurrently)"),          // (1)!
            Pattern.compile("(?i)alter\\s+table\\s+\\S+\\s+rename\\s+column"),
            Pattern.compile("(?i)add\\s+column\\s+\\S+\\s+[^,;]*not\\s+null(?![^;]*default)"),
            Pattern.compile("(?i)\\bdrop\\s+table\\b(?!\\s+if\\s+exists\\s+tmp_)"));

    @Test
    void newMigrationsFollowSafetyRules() throws IOException {
        try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(DIR)) {
            files.filter(f -> f.getFileName().toString().matches("V(\\d+)__.*\\.sql"))
                 .filter(f -> version(f) >= 30)                                                // (2)!
                 .forEach(f -> {
                     String sql = read(f);
                     assertThat(sql).as("%s must set lock_timeout", f.getFileName()).containsIgnoringCase("lock_timeout");
                     FORBIDDEN.forEach(p -> assertThat(p.matcher(sql).find())
                             .as("%s matches forbidden pattern %s", f.getFileName(), p).isFalse());
                 });
        }
    }

    private static int version(Path f) {
        return Integer.parseInt(f.getFileName().toString().replaceAll("^V(\\d+)__.*", "$1"));
    }

    private static String read(Path f) {
        try { return Files.readString(f); } catch (IOException e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
    }
}
  1. Non-concurrent index creation on existing tables blocks writes (new tables in the same migration are an exception — add an allow-list comment if needed).
  2. Rules apply from the version they were introduced — history is not rewritten.

Use a real linter too

Tools like Squawk (PostgreSQL migration linter) understand SQL rather than regex and catch many more lock hazards. Regex rules are a cheap first line.

docs.title: 6.4 Schema drift detection
docs.text:
Someone ran a manual CREATE INDEX in production during an incident. Now environments differ.

  • Nightly job runs flyway validate and a schema diff (e.g. pg_dump --schema-only of staging vs production, or Liquibase diff) and alerts on differences.
  • Incident procedure: every manual change is followed within a day by a migration that makes it official (create index if not exists ...).

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Add flyway-database-postgresql if coming from Flyway 9.
  • Check Flyway/Liquibase property renames with the properties migrator.
  • Update test annotations and custom Flyway beans for Boot 4 packages.
  • Re-run the full migration set on an empty database and a snapshot after upgrading Flyway.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Schema changes are migrations in Git, reviewed like code; never ddl-auto=update.
  2. Never edit applied migrations; roll forward.
  3. Every migration is backward compatible with the currently deployed app version (expand/contract).
  4. lock_timeout in every production migration; CONCURRENTLY for indexes; NOT VALID + VALIDATE for constraints.
  5. Backfills are jobs, chunked and throttled, not migrations.
  6. Migrations run with a privileged user, the app with least privilege; long migrations in a Job.
  7. CI applies migrations to empty DB, validates JPA mappings, and runs N-1 app tests against the new schema.
  8. Monitor migration duration, locks (pg_locks, pg_stat_activity) and replication lag during deploys.
  9. Small, frequent migrations beat big-bang schema releases.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN in one release — old pods crash mid-rollout.

❌ CREATE INDEX on a hot 40M-row table without CONCURRENTLY — writes blocked for minutes.

❌ UPDATE customer_order SET ... over all rows in a migration — hour-long transaction, bloat, replication lag.

❌ Editing V14 because "it hasn't reached prod yet" — it has reached staging and three laptops.

❌ Test data in production migration locations.

❌ flyway clean enabled anywhere shared.

❌ Dropping a column the previous app version still maps with JPA — rollback becomes impossible.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Validate failed: Migration checksum mismatch Applied migration edited Revert the edit; new migration; repair only with full understanding Detected failed migration to version X Previous run failed (non-transactional) Fix manually, flyway repair, re-run Unsupported Database: PostgreSQL Missing Flyway database module Add flyway-database-postgresql Pods stuck at startup Waiting for Flyway lock / long migration Move to Job; check pg_locks Traffic freezes during deploy ALTER waiting on lock with queue behind it lock_timeout; deploy off-peak; kill blocker Migration ignored Wrong naming (V3_x.sql), wrong location validate-migration-naming; check locations Schema-validation: missing column at startup Entity ahead of migration Ensure migration included and ordered INVALID index after failed concurrent build Interrupted CONCURRENTLY DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY and retry

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Flyway (or Liquibase) in every service with a database
  • Migration user separate from app user
  • Lint + empty-DB apply + JPA validate + N-1 compatibility in CI
  • lock_timeout convention enforced
  • Backfill job pattern documented
  • Migration Job for production with Helm hook
  • Drift detection scheduled
  • Deploy runbook covers failed-migration recovery

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Why use a migration tool instead of ddl-auto=update?

Short answer: Versioned, reviewable, repeatable, ordered changes with history; update is unreviewed, can't drop/rename safely, and diverges between environments.

B1 · What is a versioned vs repeatable migration in Flyway?

Short answer: Versioned (V1__x.sql) runs once in order; repeatable (R__x.sql) reruns whenever its content changes — used for views and functions.

B1 · Where does Flyway record what it applied?

Short answer: The flyway_schema_history table with version, checksum, success flag and timestamps.

B1 · What happens if you edit an applied migration?

Short answer: Checksum validation fails on the next run. Add a new migration instead.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How does Boot order Flyway and JPA?

Short answer: Flyway migrates during startup before the EntityManagerFactory initializes, so ddl-auto=validate sees the migrated schema.

B2 · When would you write a Java migration?

Short answer: When logic is awkward in SQL (data transformation with rules, calling a library). Keep it self-contained — no application classes.

B2 · Flyway vs Liquibase?

Short answer: Flyway: plain SQL, minimal model, easy. Liquibase: changesets with preconditions, contexts, database-agnostic changes, rollback blocks. Choose one per service.

B2 · How do you test migrations?

Short answer: Apply all to an empty PostgreSQL in Testcontainers, validate JPA mappings with ddl-auto=validate, lint scripts, and apply to a production-size snapshot for timing.

B2 · Why does Flyway 10+ need an extra dependency for PostgreSQL?

Short answer: Database support was modularized; flyway-database-postgresql provides it.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How do you add an index to a large, busy PostgreSQL table?

Short answer: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in a non-transactional migration, with lock_timeout, handling INVALID indexes on failure.

B3 · How do you add a NOT NULL column to a large table without downtime?

Short answer: Add nullable (or with constant default on PG 11+), backfill in batches, add CHECK ... NOT VALID, VALIDATE, then SET NOT NULL (cheap with validated check on PG 12+), drop the check.

B3 · What is the lock queue problem?

Short answer: DDL needing ACCESS EXCLUSIVE waits behind existing locks, and all later queries queue behind it — a short DDL causes a long outage. Use lock_timeout and retry.

B3 · What happens when several pods start and run Flyway at once?

Short answer: Flyway takes a database lock; one pod migrates, others wait then find nothing to do. Long migrations delay all pods' readiness — use a Job for long ones.

B3 · How do you backfill a new column on 40 million rows?

Short answer: In a separate, resumable job — batches of a few thousand rows keyed by primary key, committed individually, throttled, and idempotent — never inside the Flyway migration, which would hold one long transaction and lock. Verify with a rehearsal on production-sized data.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Walk through renaming a column with zero downtime.

Short answer: Expand (add new column), dual write in app, backfill, switch reads to new column (still writing old), stop writing old, contract (drop old) once no deployed/rollback version uses it. Constraints via NOT VALID/VALIDATE. Possibly views/triggers as bridges.

B4 · Migrations at startup or in a Job?

Short answer: Startup for small fast changes (simple, lockstep). Job/pre-upgrade hook for long migrations, privileged credentials, clearer failure handling and faster pod startup. Backfills as separate batch jobs.

B4 · How do you roll back a bad release that included a migration?

Short answer: Design so you don't need to: backward-compatible migrations mean rolling back the app is enough. Fix forward with a new migration. Restore from PITR only for data-destroying accidents.

B4 · How do migrations work when old and new pods run at the same time?

Short answer: Every migration must be compatible with the code version still running: expand first (add nullable columns, new tables), deploy code that handles both shapes, contract only in a later release. Destructive changes in the same release as the code that stops using the column break the rollout and the rollback.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you govern schema changes across 26 services and several teams?

Short answer: Database-per-service ownership, migration conventions (lint, lock timeouts, expand/contract), CI gates including N-1 compatibility, DBA review for high-risk patterns, migration Jobs with observability, drift detection, deploy windows for large-table changes, and a shared runbook.

B5 · Events and read models depend on table structure via CDC. What changes?

Short answer: Schema changes become contract changes for downstream consumers (Debezium topics). Use outbox tables with explicit event schemas instead of raw table CDC where possible, version event schemas, and include consumers in the expand/contract plan.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A 'small' migration took checkout down for 4 minutes

ALTER TABLE customer_order ADD COLUMN public_id uuid NOT NULL DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() — a volatile default forces PostgreSQL to rewrite all 40M rows under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (constant and even now()-style stable defaults are evaluated once and stored as metadata; volatile ones are evaluated per row). Fix: add the column nullable without default, set the default for new rows (ALTER COLUMN SET DEFAULT gen_random_uuid() — metadata only), backfill existing rows in batches, then NOT VALID/VALIDATE/SET NOT NULL. Add a lint rule for volatile defaults in ADD COLUMN.

Scenario · Rollback after a failed release fails with 'column total does not exist'

Release dropped total in the same deploy that stopped using it; rolling back the app to the previous version (which still mapped total) failed JPA validation. Fix: separate contract migration into a later release; restore column from backup data if needed; add N-1 compatibility test in CI.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Split customer.full_name into first_name and last_name

Write the migrations (expand, constraints, contract) and a chunked backfill job for a 5M-row customer table. The app is deployed with rolling updates. Include lock timeouts and describe what each app release does.

Solution V50__customer_names_expand.sql
set lock_timeout = '5s';
alter table customer add column first_name varchar(80);
alter table customer add column last_name  varchar(80);

App r50: writes full_name and first_name/last_name (split on first space); reads full_name.

CustomerNameBackfill.java (core loop)
int updated;
do {
    updated = jdbc.sql("""
            with batch as (
                select id from customer where first_name is null
                order by id limit :chunk for update skip locked
            )
            update customer c set
                first_name = split_part(c.full_name, ' ', 1),
                last_name  = nullif(substr(c.full_name, length(split_part(c.full_name, ' ', 1)) + 2), '')
            from batch where c.id = batch.id
            """).param("chunk", 2_000).update();
    Thread.sleep(200);
} while (updated > 0);
V51__customer_names_constraint.sql
set lock_timeout = '5s';
alter table customer add constraint customer_first_name_nn check (first_name is not null) not valid;
alter table customer validate constraint customer_first_name_nn;

App r51: reads first_name/last_name, still writes full_name (rollback-safe). App r52: stops writing full_name; entity no longer maps it.

V53__customer_names_contract.sql (after r51 is fully retired)
set lock_timeout = '5s';
alter table customer alter column first_name set not null;
alter table customer drop constraint customer_first_name_nn;
alter table customer drop column full_name;

last_name stays nullable — many people legitimately have a single name. Validation rules are a domain decision, not a migration convenience.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The schema is code: versioned, immutable migrations, reviewed and tested.
  • Boot runs Flyway before JPA; ddl-auto=validate proves mappings match.
  • Every change must work with the old and new app — expand, migrate, contract across releases.
  • On PostgreSQL: lock_timeout, CONCURRENTLY, NOT VALID + VALIDATE, no volatile defaults on ADD COLUMN, no big updates in migrations.
  • Backfills are throttled batch jobs.
  • Long migrations run as Jobs with privileged users; apps run least-privilege.
  • Roll forward, don't roll back schemas; keep the previous app version compatible.

  • Liquibase documentation — Changelogs, Preconditions, Rollback
