13 Spring Data JPA & Hibernate · 15 Testing Fundamentals

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Twenty-six services, a mobile app that can't be force-upgraded, and a Diwali sale where a bad deploy costs crores — the only thing that makes weekly releases safe is a test suite the team trusts. "Trusts" means three things: it catches real regressions, it doesn't cry wolf (no flaky tests), and it runs fast enough that nobody skips it.

Spring Boot gives you a lot: a test starter with JUnit Jupiter, AssertJ, Mockito and Spring Test; slice tests that boot only the layer under test; context caching so 300 tests share a handful of application contexts; MockMvc/MockMvcTester for controllers; bean overriding with @MockitoBean; and Testcontainers integration for real databases.

Used badly, the same tools produce a suite where every test is @SpringBootTest, 40 different contexts start, @MockitoBean is sprinkled everywhere, and CI takes 35 minutes to tell you a date assertion broke because midnight passed.

This chapter builds the platform's testing foundation: what to test where, unit tests without Spring, each slice with a real example, context caching economics, deterministic time and data builders, @MockitoBean/@TestBean, parameterized tests, async assertions, and composed annotations that make the right test style the easy one. Chapter 28 covers integration, contract and architecture testing; Chapter 34 covers performance testing.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — JUnit, AssertJ, Mockito, first slice tests B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — slices, @MockitoBean, @SpringBootTest modes, data builders B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — context caching, test configuration, determinism, parallelism B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — suite architecture, CI speed, flakiness budgets B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — testing strategy and quality gates across teams

docs.title: 2.1 The shape of the suite
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    E["End-to-end / user journeys<br/>a handful · minutes · Chapter 28"] --- I
    I["Integration: service + real DB/broker<br/>tens · seconds each"] --- S
    S["Slice tests: web, JPA, JSON, client<br/>hundreds · ~100 ms each"] --- U
    U["Unit tests: domain, mappers, policies<br/>thousands · sub-ms, no Spring"]

Rules of thumb for a grocery service:

Layer What it proves Typical count Unit Business rules, calculations, state machines, value objects 60–70% Slice Wiring of one layer: HTTP contract, SQL mapping, JSON shape 20–30% Integration The service works against real PostgreSQL/Kafka/Redis 5–10% End-to-end Critical journeys across services A few per platform

docs.title: 2.2 The toolbox in spring-boot-starter-test
docs.text: Library Use JUnit Jupiter Test engine: @Test, @Nested, @ParameterizedTest, lifecycle AssertJ Fluent assertions (assertThat(...)) Mockito Mocks and stubs for collaborators Spring Test ApplicationContext for tests, MockMvc, TestRestTemplate, caching JSONassert / JsonPath JSON assertions Awaitility Waiting for asynchronous conditions XMLUnit XML comparison

docs.title: 2.3 Unit tests: no Spring at all
docs.text:
If a class's dependencies can be passed in a constructor (they can — Chapter 02), it's testable with new. No context, no annotations, microseconds per test. Most business logic belongs here.

Mock collaborators you own (repositories, gateways) — not value objects, not List, not the JDK.

docs.title: 2.4 @SpringBootTest
docs.text:
Loads the full application context. webEnvironment decides how much:

Value Meaning MOCK (default) Mock servlet environment; use MockMvc/MockMvcTester RANDOM_PORT Real embedded server on a random port; TestRestTemplate/RestTestClient, @LocalServerPort DEFINED_PORT Real server on the configured port (avoid — port clashes) NONE No web server

docs.title: 2.5 Slice tests
docs.text:
Each slice auto-configures only the beans of one layer and excludes regular @Components:

Slice Loads Typical assertions @WebMvcTest Controllers, advices, filters, converters, MockMvc Status codes, JSON, validation, security rules @DataJpaTest Entities, repositories, TestEntityManager, transactional Mappings, queries, constraints @JdbcTest / @DataJdbcTest DataSource, JdbcClient / Spring Data JDBC SQL, translation @JsonTest Jackson configuration, JacksonTester Serialization contracts @RestClientTest RestClient/RestTemplate builders + MockRestServiceServer Outbound HTTP, error mapping @DataRedisTest, @DataMongoTest, @GraphQlTest, @JooqTest, @WebFluxTest Their technology —

Slices are fast because the context is small — and they force you to notice when a controller needs "just one service" injected.

docs.title: 2.6 Replacing beans in tests
docs.text: Tool Since Behaviour @MockitoBean Framework 6.2 Replaces (or adds) a bean with a Mockito mock @MockitoSpyBean 6.2 Wraps the real bean in a spy @TestBean 6.2 Replaces a bean with the value from a static factory method — no Mockito @MockBean / @SpyBean Boot ≤3.x Deprecated in 3.4, removed in Boot 4 @TestConfiguration — Extra/overriding beans for a test (not picked up by component scanning) @Import — Pull in specific configuration classes

docs.title: 2.7 Context caching — the biggest lever on suite speed
docs.text:
Spring caches contexts by a key built from: configuration classes, active profiles, property sources, @MockitoBean definitions, web environment, context customizers, resource overrides. Same key → the same context is reused across test classes.

Every distinct key starts another context (seconds each, plus memory). Two rules:

  1. Standardize test setups (composed annotations) so keys repeat.
  2. Avoid @DirtiesContext unless a test genuinely corrupts state — it evicts the context and forces a restart.

docs.title: 2.8 Transactional tests
docs.text:
@DataJpaTest (and @Transactional on a test class) wraps each test in a transaction that is rolled back. Benefits: isolation, no cleanup. Pitfalls:

  • Commit-time behaviour (constraint checks at commit, @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT)) never happens — use TestTransaction, @Commit, or a TransactionTemplate in a non-transactional test.
  • Code under test that requires a new transaction (REQUIRES_NEW) sees the test's uncommitted data differently than production would.

docs.title: 2.9 Determinism
docs.text:
Flaky tests destroy trust faster than missing tests. The usual causes and fixes:

Cause Fix Instant.now() / LocalDate.now() Inject a Clock; use Clock.fixed in tests Random data/ids Seeded generator or fixed values Thread.sleep for async Awaitility with a condition Shared mutable state between tests Fresh fixtures; no static caches Test order dependence Each test sets up its own data Time zones / locales Set explicitly (Asia/Kolkata, en-IN) Real network calls Mock servers, Testcontainers

docs.title: 2.10 Test data builders
docs.text: Object mothers/builders keep tests readable and resilient: anOrder().withLine("MILK-1L", 2).placed() instead of ten constructor arguments repeated 40 times.

docs.title: 3.1 The Spring TestContext framework
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant J as JUnit Jupiter
    participant E as SpringExtension
    participant TCM as TestContextManager
    participant Cache as ContextCache
    participant Boot as SpringBootContextLoader

    J->>E: beforeAll(testClass)
    E->>TCM: prepareTestInstance
    TCM->>TCM: build MergedContextConfiguration<br/>(classes, profiles, properties, customizers)
    TCM->>Cache: get(key)
    alt hit
        Cache-->>TCM: cached ApplicationContext
    else miss
        TCM->>Boot: loadContext(config)
        Boot->>Boot: SpringApplication with test settings,<br/>auto-config filtered by slice annotation
        Boot-->>Cache: store (default max 32 contexts, LRU)
    end
    TCM->>TCM: inject @Autowired fields, apply @MockitoBean overrides
    J->>E: beforeEach → TestExecutionListeners<br/>(transaction, mock reset, SQL scripts, events)
    J->>J: run @Test
    J->>E: afterEach → rollback, reset mocks

TestExecutionListeners do the per-test work: TransactionalTestExecutionListener (rollback), MockitoResetTestExecutionListener, SqlScriptsTestExecutionListener (@Sql), ApplicationEventsTestExecutionListener (@RecordApplicationEvents), DirtiesContextTestExecutionListener.

docs.title: 3.2 How a slice narrows the context
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["@WebMvcTest(CartController.class)"] --> B["Adds @AutoConfigure... annotations<br/>for the web layer only"]
    B --> C["TypeExcludeFilter:<br/>include @Controller, @ControllerAdvice, WebMvcConfigurer,<br/>Filter, HandlerInterceptor, Converter"]
    C --> D["Exclude @Component, @Service, @Repository"]
    D --> E[spring.autoconfigure.exclude of unrelated auto-configs<br/>via spring-boot-test-autoconfigure.properties]
    E --> F[Small context: DispatcherServlet, converters,<br/>your controller, MockMvc]

Because services and repositories are excluded, every collaborator the controller needs must be supplied — normally with @MockitoBean.

docs.title: 3.3 MockMvc vs a real server
docs.text: MockMvc calls the DispatcherServlet directly with mock request/response objects: no socket, no servlet container, no real filters unless registered. It's fast and exercises mappings, converters, validation, advices and (when configured) Spring Security's filter chain. A real server (RANDOM_PORT) additionally exercises the container, connectors, servlet filters as deployed, and serialization over the wire.

docs.title: 4.1 A unit test of business logic
4.2 A unit test with Mockito
4.3 A web slice test
5.1 Level 2 — Test data builders and a fixed clock
5.2 Level 2 — @SpringBootTest with a real server
5.3 Level 2 — Testing an outbound HTTP client
5.4 Level 3 — Context caching economics
5.5 Level 3 — Composed annotations for the platform
5.6 Level 3 — One database container for the whole suite
docs.text:
Starting a PostgreSQL container per test class is slow. Share one:

src/test/java/in/grocery/platform/test/ContainersConfig.java
package in.grocery.platform.test;

import org.springframework.boot.test.context.TestConfiguration;
import org.springframework.boot.testcontainers.service.connection.ServiceConnection;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer;
import org.testcontainers.utility.DockerImageName;

@TestConfiguration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class ContainersConfig {

    @Bean
    @ServiceConnection                                                                   // (1)!
    PostgreSQLContainer<?> postgres() {
        return new PostgreSQLContainer<>(DockerImageName.parse("postgres:17-alpine"))
                .withReuse(true);                                                        // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Boot starts the container as a bean and points spring.datasource.* at it. Because it's part of the cached context, all tests importing this configuration share one container and one context.
  2. With testcontainers.reuse.enable=true in ~/.testcontainers.properties, the container survives between local runs — seconds instead of minutes. (Not used in CI.)
src/test/java/in/grocery/order/TestOrderApplication.java
package in.grocery.order;

import in.grocery.platform.test.ContainersConfig;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;

/** Run the app locally with real infrastructure: ./gradlew bootTestRun */
public class TestOrderApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.from(OrderApplication::main).with(ContainersConfig.class).run(args);   // (1)!
    }
}
  1. Boot 3.1+: start the application from tests with Testcontainers-provided infrastructure — no local PostgreSQL install.

docs.title: 5.7 Level 3 — Asynchronous assertions
6.1 The platform test strategy
6.2 Deterministic, parallel-safe data
docs.text:
Parallel tests against one database need isolation without @DirtiesContext:

src/test/java/in/grocery/platform/test/UniqueIds.java
package in.grocery.platform.test;

import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;

/** Unique but readable ids so parallel tests never collide on unique constraints. */
public final class UniqueIds {

    private static final AtomicLong SEQ = new AtomicLong();

    private UniqueIds() {}

    public static String orderRef() {
        return "ORD-T%05d".formatted(SEQ.incrementAndGet());
    }

    public static String customerId() {
        return "C-T%05d".formatted(SEQ.incrementAndGet());
    }
}

Each test creates its own customer and orders; nothing is deleted between tests; assertions are scoped by the generated ids. This is faster and far more parallel-friendly than truncating tables.

docs.title: 6.3 A full-stack test of the checkout path
6.4 CI configuration and quality gates
6.5 Flaky test policy
docs.text: Rule Detail Quarantine, don't ignore Tag @Tag("flaky"), exclude from the gate, create a ticket with an owner and a due date Never rerun blindly Retry plugins hide real races; if used, report retries as failures in the dashboard Budget More than 1% flaky → stop feature work and fix the suite Root causes Time, ordering, shared state, async waits, ports, container startup, clock skew, locale Detection Nightly job runs the suite N times and reports non-deterministic outcomes

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace @MockBean/@SpyBean with @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean before upgrading (works on 3.4+).
  • Update slice annotation imports and test starter dependencies for Boot 4.
  • Check JUnit 6 changes (removed deprecations, extension APIs) if your build pulls it.
  • Migrate MockMvc assertions to MockMvcTester/RestTestClient where convenient (optional but consistent).
  • Re-measure suite duration and context counts after upgrading.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Push logic down to plain classes and test it without Spring.
  2. One slice per layer, @SpringBootTest only for real integration.
  3. Composed annotations to standardize contexts and keep the cache hot.
  4. Fixed Clock, unique ids, builders — determinism by construction.
  5. Awaitility, never sleep.
  6. Testcontainers as beans with @ServiceConnection, shared across the suite.
  7. Assert the contract (status, code, JSON shape), not internal messages.
  8. Separate fast and slow suites; run classes in parallel.
  9. Coverage gates on business packages, mutation testing for critical logic (Chapter 28).
  10. Treat flakiness as a build-breaking defect.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ @SpringBootTest for everything — 40-second suites that test Spring, not your code.

❌ Mocking what you don't own (JdbcClient, RestClient, EntityManager) — tests pass, production fails; use slices/Testcontainers instead.

❌ Asserting log messages or exception text as the contract.

❌ @DirtiesContext to fix state leaks — fix the leak.

❌ Thread.sleep(2000) for async behaviour.

❌ Shared mutable fixtures (static List of orders) across tests.

❌ Testing getters/setters for coverage while the checkout flow has no test.

❌ @Transactional on integration tests that must observe commits — after-commit listeners and constraints never fire.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Suite takes minutes; many "Starting ... Application" lines Too many distinct contexts Composed annotations, shared properties, fewer @MockitoBean variants No qualifying bean of type ... in a slice Collaborator excluded by the slice @MockitoBean or @Import the needed configuration Test passes alone, fails in suite Shared state / ordering Unique data per test, no statics, reset mocks LazyInitializationException in a test but not in prod @DataJpaTest transaction boundaries differ Fetch within the query or assert inside a transaction After-commit listener never runs Test is transactional (rolled back) Non-transactional integration test Mockito strict stubbing failure Unused stub Remove it (it documents nothing) Mockito ... self-attaching ... dynamic agent warning on JDK 21+ Inline mock maker attaching dynamically Configure -javaagent for mockito-core in the test task Testcontainers slow on every class Container per class Container as a bean in a shared @TestConfiguration, reuse locally Random failures at midnight / month end now() in code Inject Clock

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Business rules covered by fast unit tests
  • Each controller has a web slice test incl. error statuses
  • Each repository has a slice test on real PostgreSQL
  • JSON contracts covered by @JsonTest golden files
  • Outbound clients tested with MockRestServiceServer
  • Critical journeys covered by integration tests with containers
  • Context cache statistics reviewed; < ~5 contexts per service
  • Fast suite under ~2 minutes; integration suite under ~10
  • Flaky tests tracked with owners

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What comes with spring-boot-starter-test?

Short answer: JUnit Jupiter, Spring Test, AssertJ, Mockito, JSONassert, JsonPath, Awaitility, XMLUnit.

B1 · What's the difference between a unit test and a @SpringBootTest?

Short answer: A unit test instantiates the class directly with fakes/mocks and runs in microseconds; @SpringBootTest starts the whole application context.

B1 · What is @WebMvcTest for?

Short answer: Testing controllers with a slim context: mappings, validation, JSON, error handling, with MockMvc and mocked collaborators.

B1 · How do you test that a method throws?

Short answer: assertThatThrownBy(() -> ...).isInstanceOf(X.class) (AssertJ) or assertThrows (JUnit).

B1 · What replaced @MockBean?

Short answer: @MockitoBean (and @MockitoSpyBean), from Spring Framework 6.2; @MockBean is removed in Boot 4.

B1 · Why use a parameterized test?

Short answer: One test method covering many input/expected pairs — less duplication, clearer boundaries.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · When do you use @SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)?

Short answer: When you need the real servlet container and an HTTP client (filters, connectors, end-to-end serialization). Otherwise MOCK with MockMvc is faster.

B2 · How do you test a repository?

Short answer: @DataJpaTest/@JdbcTest with @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) against a Testcontainers PostgreSQL, with Flyway migrations applied.

B2 · What does @DataJpaTest do about transactions?

Short answer: Each test runs in a transaction rolled back afterwards — fast and isolated, but commit-time behaviour isn't exercised.

B2 · How do you test outgoing HTTP calls?

Short answer: @RestClientTest with MockRestServiceServer (request expectations and canned responses), or WireMock for full-stack behaviour (Chapter 28).

B2 · How do you avoid flaky time-based tests?

Short answer: Inject a Clock and use Clock.fixed in tests; never call Instant.now() directly in business code.

B2 · What's @TestConfiguration and how does it differ from @Configuration?

Short answer: It's not picked up by component scanning; it applies only where imported or nested in the test class — so it can't leak into other tests.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does Spring's test context cache work and what breaks it?

Short answer: Contexts are cached by a key from configuration classes, profiles, properties, bean overrides, web environment and customizers. Ad-hoc properties, different @MockitoBean sets, extra profiles and @DirtiesContext create or evict contexts and slow the suite.

B3 · How does a slice annotation restrict the context?

Short answer: It applies @AutoConfigure... annotations for that technology, filters component scanning with a TypeExcludeFilter (only web/JPA/... component types) and excludes unrelated auto-configurations.

B3 · MockMvc vs a real server — what's not covered by MockMvc?

Short answer: The servlet container, connectors/HTTP parsing, filters registered outside the MVC context, real network serialization and timeouts.

B3 · How do you run tests in parallel safely with Spring?

Short answer: Enable JUnit parallel execution for classes, keep contexts shared and thread-safe, avoid static mutable state, generate unique data per test rather than truncating tables, and watch container/database connection limits.

B3 · When is mocking the wrong tool?

Short answer: For framework/infrastructure types (repositories' SQL behaviour, HTTP clients' serialization) — mocks encode assumptions that production violates. Use slices with real infrastructure instead.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the test strategy for a service with 200 endpoints.

Short answer: Unit tests for domain logic; one web slice test per controller covering contract and error paths; persistence slices on real PostgreSQL; client slices for integrations; a handful of integration tests for critical journeys; contract tests with consumers; architecture tests; separate fast/slow suites; standardized composed annotations; quality gates on business packages.

B4 · The suite takes 25 minutes. How do you cut it?

Short answer: Measure per-class time and context counts; convert @SpringBootTest to slices; unify contexts; share containers; parallelize classes; split fast/slow tasks and run them concurrently in CI; cache Gradle and Docker layers; remove redundant end-to-end tests.

B4 · How do you handle flaky tests organizationally?

Short answer: Detect (nightly repeated runs), quarantine with ownership and deadlines, never blind-retry in the gate, treat the flake rate as a tracked metric, and budget time to fix root causes.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What does 'good coverage' mean to you?

Short answer: Coverage is a diagnostic, not a goal. Gate on business-critical packages, require tests for every bug fix, use mutation testing where correctness matters most, and measure escaped defects and change failure rate instead of chasing a percentage.

B5 · How do you keep tests from becoming a maintenance burden?

Short answer: Test behaviour through stable contracts (HTTP, events), not internals; builders and shared fixtures; avoid over-mocking; delete redundant tests; refactor tests like production code; keep them fast so they're run.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A regression reached production: order totals excluded delivery fee for express slots

Unit tests covered DeliveryFeePolicy but the delegate that assembled CartView summed only line totals; no test asserted the API response total. Fix: add a web slice test asserting the JSON total, add the case to the checkout integration test, and add a rule that every bug fix ships with a failing-then-passing test at the level the bug escaped.

Scenario · CI is green but the same suite fails locally for one developer

Their machine is on Asia/Kolkata while CI runs UTC, and a test asserted a formatted date. Fix: pin timezone and locale in the test task (systemProperty("user.timezone", "Asia/Kolkata")), inject Clock, and assert on Instants rather than formatted strings.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Test the cart item limit end to end

CartProperties.maxItems is 50. Write (1) a unit test proving CartService rejects the 51st distinct SKU, and (2) a web slice test proving the API returns 422 with code = CART_ITEM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, using the platform error handler. Keep both fast and independent of the database.

Solution CartServiceLimitTest.java
package in.grocery.cart.service;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThatThrownBy;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.anyLong;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;

import in.grocery.cart.config.CartProperties;
import in.grocery.cart.repository.CartRepository;
import in.grocery.cart.repository.CatalogLookup;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.LinkedHashMap;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;
import org.mockito.Mock;
import org.mockito.junit.jupiter.MockitoExtension;

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class CartServiceLimitTest {

    @Mock CartRepository repository;
    @Mock CatalogLookup catalog;

    private static CartProperties props() {
        return new CartProperties(50, 20, java.time.Duration.ofMinutes(30),
                new CartProperties.FreeDelivery(new BigDecimal("499"), true),
                org.springframework.util.unit.DataSize.ofKilobytes(64),
                java.util.List.of("tobacco"), Map.of());
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsFiftyFirstDistinctSku() {
        Map<String, Integer> fifty = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < 50; i++) fifty.put("SKU-" + i, 1);
        given(repository.find("c1")).willReturn(Optional.of(new Cart("c1", "C-1", fifty, 5)));

        var service = new CartService(repository, catalog, props());

        assertThatThrownBy(() -> service.addItem("c1", "SKU-NEW", 1))
                .isInstanceOf(CartItemLimitExceededException.class);
    }
}
CartItemControllerLimitTest.java
package in.grocery.cart.web;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.any;
import static org.mockito.ArgumentMatchers.eq;
import static org.mockito.BDDMockito.given;

import in.grocery.cart.delegate.CartDelegate;
import in.grocery.cart.service.CartItemLimitExceededException;
import in.grocery.platform.test.GroceryWebTest;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.MockitoBean;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.assertj.MockMvcTester;

@GroceryWebTest(controllers = CartItemController.class)
class CartItemControllerLimitTest {

    @Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;
    @MockitoBean CartDelegate delegate;

    @Test
    void limitExceededIs422WithCode() {
        given(delegate.addItem(eq("c1"), any())).willThrow(new CartItemLimitExceededException(50));

        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/api/carts/c1/items")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("{\"sku\":\"SKU-NEW\",\"quantity\":1}"))
                .hasStatus(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY)
                .bodyJson()
                .satisfies(json -> {
                    assertThat(json).extractingPath("$.code").isEqualTo("CART_ITEM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED");
                    assertThat(json).extractingPath("$.maxItems").isEqualTo(50);
                });
    }
}

The unit test owns the rule; the slice test owns the contract. Neither needs a database, and both run in milliseconds.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Most tests are plain JUnit on classes built with constructor injection; Spring appears only where wiring is the thing under test.
  • Slices (@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest) give layer-level confidence at ~100 ms each.
  • Context caching decides suite speed — standardize setups with composed annotations, avoid @DirtiesContext.
  • @MockitoBean/@MockitoSpyBean/@TestBean replace @MockBean.
  • Determinism comes from fixed clocks, unique ids, builders and Awaitility.
  • Testcontainers as beans with @ServiceConnection share one database across the suite.
  • Assert contracts (status, error code, JSON shape), not internals.
  • Flaky tests are defects — quarantine with owners, fix root causes.

docs.text:
Chapters 16–34 · 3–8 years. Transactions, security, clients, APIs, caching, messaging, concurrency, resilience, observability, testing at scale, packaging, Kubernetes, reactive, protocols, batch and performance — everything a service needs to survive production.

Primary bands: B2–B4. Every chapter follows the same nine-part structure — introduction, core concepts, internals, Levels 1–4 of hands-on code, Boot 3 vs 4, production playbook, and interview questions — so you can read any chapter at the depth your band needs.

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
@Transactional is one annotation and a hundred production incidents. In the grocery platform, transactions decide whether:

  • an order row exists without its lines because an exception was swallowed by a checked-exception rule;
  • stock is decremented twice because a REQUIRES_NEW call was a self-invocation and never started a new transaction;
  • checkout holds a database connection for eight seconds while Razorpay is slow, exhausting the pool (Chapter 12);
  • an "order placed" SMS goes out for an order that rolled back (Chapter 03);
  • two customers both book the last delivery slot under READ COMMITTED;
  • a Kafka event is published but the database commit fails — the dual-write problem.

Transactions are where correctness, concurrency and performance meet. This chapter goes deep: what Spring actually does around your method, all seven propagation modes with what they mean in SQL, isolation levels and the anomalies they do and don't prevent (including write skew, which surprises people on PostgreSQL), rollback rules, read-only optimizations, the self-invocation trap, programmatic transactions, synchronization callbacks, retrying serialization failures, transaction boundaries in the four-layer architecture, and why we use the outbox instead of XA for Kafka.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — @Transactional basics, rollback rules B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — propagation, isolation, read-only, self-invocation B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — interceptor internals, synchronization, retries, boundaries B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — architecture, outbox vs XA, observability of transactions B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — consistency strategy across services

docs.title: 2.1 ACID, briefly
docs.text: Property Meaning in our world Atomicity Order + lines + outbox row all commit, or none do Consistency Constraints (stock ≥ 0, price ≤ MRP) hold before and after Isolation Concurrent checkouts don't see each other's half-done work Durability Committed orders survive a pod crash

docs.title: 2.2 Spring's abstraction
docs.text:
Type Role PlatformTransactionManager Strategy interface: getTransaction, commit, rollback DataSourceTransactionManager JDBC: binds a Connection to the thread JpaTransactionManager JPA: binds an EntityManager (and exposes its JDBC connection) JtaTransactionManager Global/XA transactions (rare, avoid) TransactionTemplate Programmatic transactions TransactionSynchronizationManager Thread-bound resources + synchronization callbacks @Transactional Declarative demarcation via AOP (Chapter 04)

Boot auto-configures one transaction manager: JpaTransactionManager when JPA is present (it manages JDBC too, so JdbcClient joins the same transaction), otherwise DataSourceTransactionManager.

docs.title: 2.3 @Transactional attributes
docs.text: Attribute Default Notes propagation REQUIRED How to behave if a transaction already exists isolation DEFAULT (database default; READ_COMMITTED on PostgreSQL) Concurrency semantics readOnly false Hints: Hibernate skips dirty checking; connection marked read-only; enables replica routing (Chapter 12) timeout / timeoutString none Seconds; enforced via statement timeouts where supported rollbackFor / noRollbackFor — Override the default rule transactionManager the only one Qualifier when several exist label — Custom labels readable by the transaction manager

docs.title: 2.4 Propagation — all seven
docs.text:
Propagation No transaction exists A transaction exists REQUIRED (default) Start a new one Join it REQUIRES_NEW Start a new one Suspend the outer, start an independent one, resume after SUPPORTS Run without a transaction Join it NOT_SUPPORTED Run without one Suspend it, run without MANDATORY Throw IllegalTransactionStateException Join it NEVER Run without one Throw NESTED Start a new one Savepoint inside the existing one (JDBC transaction manager only) 
flowchart TB
    subgraph REQUIRED
        A1[outer BEGIN] --> A2[inner joins] --> A3[single COMMIT]
    end
    subgraph REQUIRES_NEW
        B1[outer BEGIN] --> B2[outer SUSPENDED<br/>new connection] --> B3[inner BEGIN/COMMIT] --> B4[outer resumes] --> B5[outer COMMIT]
    end
    subgraph NESTED
        C1[outer BEGIN] --> C2[SAVEPOINT] --> C3[inner work] --> C4{failure?}
        C4 -- yes --> C5[ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT<br/>outer continues]
        C4 -- no --> C6[RELEASE SAVEPOINT]
    end

REQUIRES_NEW uses a second connection

The outer transaction still holds its connection while the inner one runs. Each nesting level doubles connection usage — a pool of 20 with nested REQUIRES_NEW under load can deadlock itself: all connections held by outer transactions waiting for a connection for the inner one.

Rollback-only propagation

If an inner REQUIRED method throws and the outer catches the exception and continues, the transaction was already marked rollback-only; at commit Spring throws UnexpectedRollbackException. "Handling" an exception from a joined transaction doesn't undo the rollback marking — use REQUIRES_NEW (or NESTED) if the inner work must be able to fail independently.

docs.title: 2.5 Isolation levels and anomalies
docs.text:
Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom Write skew READ_UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible possible READ_COMMITTED (PostgreSQL default) no possible possible possible REPEATABLE_READ (PostgreSQL: snapshot isolation) no no no (in PostgreSQL) possible SERIALIZABLE (PostgreSQL: SSI) no no no no — conflicting transactions fail with a serialization error

Vocabulary with grocery examples:

  • Lost update — two staff read stock 10, both set 9; one update vanishes. Prevented by @Version (Chapter 13) or atomic SQL (Chapter 12), not by READ_COMMITTED.
  • Write skew — two transactions each check "slot has capacity" (both see 9/10), then each insert a booking → 11 bookings. REPEATABLE_READ on PostgreSQL does not prevent this; SERIALIZABLE, a lock, or a constraint does.

PostgreSQL specifics

PostgreSQL uses MVCC: readers never block writers. REPEATABLE_READ and SERIALIZABLE transactions can fail at commit (or mid-statement) with SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure) or 40P01 (deadlock) — these are retryable and must be retried by the application.

docs.title: 2.6 Rollback rules
docs.text:
By default Spring rolls back on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException, Error) and commits on checked exceptions. This surprises everyone once:

Rollback rules (snippet)
@Transactional
public void importRow(...) throws IOException {     // checked
    repository.save(entity);
    if (bad) throw new IOException("bad row");        // ← COMMITS the save
}

Fix with @Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class) — or, better, use unchecked domain exceptions (Chapter 10) throughout.

docs.title: 2.7 readOnly = true
docs.text:
• Hibernate sets FlushMode.MANUAL: no dirty checking, no accidental updates, less memory.
  • The JDBC connection is marked read-only (PostgreSQL then rejects writes with an error).
  • Enables read-replica routing (Chapter 12).
  • Makes intent explicit to readers.

Use it on every query-only service method.

docs.title: 2.8 Where transactions belong
docs.text:
In the four-layer pattern:

Layer Transaction Controller ❌ never Delegate ❌ usually not (it orchestrates; idempotency lives here) Service ✅ the transaction boundary — one business operation Repository ❌ (participates in the caller's transaction)

Boot's Spring Data repositories are transactional per method by default (SimpleJpaRepository is @Transactional(readOnly = true) with write methods overridden) — enough for a single call, never enough for a business operation.

docs.title: 2.9 What must not happen inside a transaction
docs.text:
• Remote calls (payment gateway, other services) — latency is multiplied by connection hold time.
  • Long computations, file/report generation.
  • Thread.sleep, waiting on locks/queues.
  • Sending Kafka/SMS/email directly — use after-commit hooks or the outbox.

docs.title: 2.10 The dual-write problem and the outbox
docs.text:
Writing to the database and publishing to Kafka can't be atomic without XA:

flowchart LR
    subgraph "Dual write (broken)"
        A1[INSERT order] --> A2[COMMIT] --> A3[publish to Kafka] --> A4{publish fails?}
        A4 -- yes --> A5[order exists, no event<br/>inventory never reserved]
    end
    subgraph "Outbox (correct)"
        B1[INSERT order] --> B2[INSERT outbox row] --> B3[COMMIT one transaction]
        B3 --> B4[relay reads outbox<br/>publishes to Kafka<br/>marks sent / retries]
    end

Chapter 36 builds the full outbox and relay; this chapter shows the transactional half.

docs.title: 2.11 XA / JTA — why not
docs.text: Global (two-phase commit) transactions across PostgreSQL and Kafka/JMS look attractive and cost: extra latency, an additional transaction coordinator to operate, in-doubt transactions holding locks after crashes, poor support in cloud-managed services, and Boot 3 dropped its embedded Atomikos integration. Prefer local transaction + outbox + idempotent consumers.

docs.title: 3.1 The transaction interceptor
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant P as Proxy (CGLIB)
    participant TI as TransactionInterceptor
    participant TAS as AnnotationTransactionAttributeSource
    participant TM as JpaTransactionManager
    participant TSM as TransactionSynchronizationManager
    participant T as Target service

    C->>P: place(command)
    P->>TI: invoke
    TI->>TAS: getTransactionAttribute(method, targetClass)
    Note over TAS: reads @Transactional (method first,<br/>then class), caches per method
    TI->>TM: getTransaction(attribute)
    TM->>TSM: existing transaction bound?
    alt none
        TM->>TM: open EntityManager / Connection,<br/>setAutoCommit(false), apply isolation/readOnly/timeout
        TM->>TSM: bind resource + mark synchronization active
    else exists
        TM->>TM: apply propagation (join / suspend / savepoint)
    end
    TI->>T: proceed()
    alt success
        TI->>TM: commit → flush (JPA) → beforeCommit → COMMIT → afterCommit → afterCompletion
    else exception
        TI->>TI: rollbackOn(ex)? (unchecked, or rollbackFor)
        TI->>TM: rollback (or setRollbackOnly if joined) → afterCompletion
    end
    TM->>TSM: unbind resources, resume suspended transaction if any

Key classes: TransactionInterceptor/TransactionAspectSupport, AbstractPlatformTransactionManager (the propagation state machine), TransactionSynchronizationManager (thread-bound ConnectionHolder/EntityManagerHolder + synchronizations), DataSourceUtils/EntityManagerFactoryUtils (resource lookup used by JdbcClient and repositories).

docs.title: 3.2 Why self-invocation breaks it (again)
docs.text: The proxy is only involved on calls from outside the bean (Chapter 04). this.reserve(...) runs the target method directly — no interceptor, no transaction attribute, no new transaction. Symptoms are silent: REQUIRES_NEW is ignored, readOnly isn't applied, a method that "must" be transactional runs with auto-commit.

docs.title: 3.3 When SQL actually runs
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["@Transactional method starts"] --> B{"Hibernate: lazy connection acquisition<br/>(auto-commit disabled in pool)"}
    B --> C[first query/flush → BEGIN on a real connection]
    C --> D[work: entity changes queued]
    D --> E[flush at commit / before affected queries]
    E --> F[COMMIT]
    F --> G["afterCommit synchronizations<br/>e.g. @TransactionalEventListener"]

With spring.datasource.hikari.auto-commit=false and hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true (Chapter 13), Hibernate defers borrowing a connection until the first statement — a read-only method that ends up not querying costs nothing.

docs.title: 3.4 Synchronizations
docs.text: TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(...) adds callbacks: beforeCommit, beforeCompletion, afterCommit, afterCompletion(status). Spring uses them for @TransactionalEventListener, JPA flush/close, and connection release. Your code can use them for cache invalidation and "publish after commit" — though the event listener is usually cleaner.

docs.title: 4.1 One business operation, one transaction
4.2 The checked-exception surprise
4.3 Proving rollback in a test
5.1 Level 2 — Propagation in practice: audit that must survive rollback
docs.text:
Failed payment attempts must be recorded even when the business transaction rolls back.

in/grocery/payment/service/PaymentAttemptRecorder.java
package in.grocery.payment.service;

import in.grocery.payment.repository.PaymentAttemptRepository;
import java.time.Clock;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Propagation;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class PaymentAttemptRecorder {

    private final PaymentAttemptRepository attempts;
    private final Clock clock;

    public PaymentAttemptRecorder(PaymentAttemptRepository attempts, Clock clock) {
        this.attempts = attempts;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)                     // (1)!
    public void record(String orderRef, String gateway, String outcome, String reason) {
        attempts.insert(orderRef, gateway, outcome, reason, clock.instant());
    }
}
  1. Independent transaction: commits (or fails) on its own. It must be a separate bean — a REQUIRES_NEW method called from within the same class does nothing (self-invocation).
in/grocery/payment/service/PaymentService.java (excerpt)
@Transactional
public void capture(String orderRef, PaymentResult result) {
    switch (result) {
        case PaymentResult.Captured c -> { /* update order, ledger */ }
        case PaymentResult.Failed f -> {
            recorder.record(orderRef, "RAZORPAY", "FAILED", f.reason());        // survives the rollback below
            throw new PaymentDeclinedException(f.reason());
        }
        case PaymentResult.Pending p -> { /* ... */ }
    }
}

Keep REQUIRES_NEW rare and short

Each one holds a second connection. This recorder does a single insert and returns. Never wrap a long operation or another remote call in REQUIRES_NEW.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — UnexpectedRollbackException in the wild
5.3 Level 2 — Read-only and replica routing
5.4 Level 3 — Serialization failures and retry
docs.text:
Slot booking with SERIALIZABLE is correct but can fail; correctness comes from retrying.

in/grocery/delivery/service/SlotBookingService.java
package in.grocery.delivery.service;

import in.grocery.delivery.repository.SlotRepository;
import org.springframework.dao.ConcurrencyFailureException;
import org.springframework.retry.annotation.Backoff;
import org.springframework.retry.annotation.Retryable;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Isolation;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class SlotBookingService {

    private final SlotRepository slots;

    public SlotBookingService(SlotRepository slots) {
        this.slots = slots;
    }

    @Retryable(retryFor = ConcurrencyFailureException.class, maxAttempts = 4,
               backoff = @Backoff(delay = 25, multiplier = 2.0, random = true))          // (1)!
    @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE, timeout = 3)                      // (2)!
    public boolean book(String slotId) {
        int booked = slots.countBookings(slotId);
        int capacity = slots.capacity(slotId);
        if (booked >= capacity) return false;
        slots.insertBooking(slotId);
        return true;
    }
}
  1. Retry must wrap the transaction — the outer proxy retries a whole new transaction. Order matters: @Retryable's advisor must run outside @Transactional's (configure orders explicitly, Chapter 04). Jitter (random = true) avoids retry storms.
  2. SERIALIZABLE makes the read-then-insert safe against write skew; PostgreSQL detects conflicts and raises 40001, which Spring translates to a ConcurrencyFailureException subtype.

Cheaper alternatives first

A check-and-increment SQL statement (Chapter 12) or a unique constraint on (slot_id, booking_seq) solves this without SERIALIZABLE. Use serializable isolation when the invariant spans multiple rows or tables and can't be expressed as one statement or constraint.

Spring Boot 3.5 — Spring RetrySpring Boot 4.x — Framework 7 core resilience RetryConfig.java
@EnableRetry
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class RetryConfig {}
ResilienceConfig.java
@EnableResilientMethods
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class ResilienceConfig {}

// org.springframework.resilience.annotation.Retryable — verify attribute names (Chapter 26)

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Programmatic transactions
docs.text:
Useful when boundaries are dynamic, inside non-Spring code, or to avoid self-invocation.

in/grocery/inventory/service/StockSyncService.java
package in.grocery.inventory.service;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.support.TransactionTemplate;

@Service
public class StockSyncService {

    private final TransactionTemplate tx;                                     // (1)!
    private final StockRepository stock;

    public StockSyncService(TransactionTemplate tx, StockRepository stock) {
        this.tx = tx;
        this.stock = stock;
    }

    /** Sync a hub's stock in chunks: one transaction per chunk, progress preserved on failure. */
    public int sync(String hub, List<StockUpdate> updates, int chunkSize) {
        int applied = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < updates.size(); i += chunkSize) {
            List<StockUpdate> chunk = updates.subList(i, Math.min(updates.size(), i + chunkSize));
            applied += tx.execute(status -> {                                  // (2)!
                int n = stock.applyAll(hub, chunk);
                if (n != chunk.size()) {
                    status.setRollbackOnly();                                  // (3)!
                    return 0;
                }
                return n;
            });
        }
        return applied;
    }
}
  1. Boot auto-configures a TransactionTemplate bean (Boot 3.x+); otherwise build one from the transaction manager.
  2. Explicit, visible boundaries — no proxies, no self-invocation trap.
  3. Programmatic rollback without throwing.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — After-commit work
5.7 Level 3 — Testing transactional behaviour
6.1 Checkout: correct boundaries around a slow gateway
docs.text:
Requirements: create the order atomically with its outbox event; never hold a database connection during the Razorpay call; be idempotent; keep after-commit work out of the transaction.

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    participant D as OrderDelegate (@Idempotent)
    participant S1 as OrderPlacementService
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant RZ as Razorpay
    participant S2 as PaymentInitiationService
    participant K as Outbox relay → Kafka

    D->>S1: placeOrder(command)          
    activate S1
    Note over S1,DB: TX1 (short): insert order + lines + outbox(OrderPlaced)
    S1->>DB: COMMIT
    deactivate S1
    D->>RZ: createOrder(amount)  ← no transaction, no DB connection held
    RZ-->>D: order_rzp_xxx (or timeout)
    D->>S2: attachGatewayOrder(orderRef, gatewayRef)
    activate S2
    Note over S2,DB: TX2 (short): update order, insert outbox(PaymentInitiated)
    S2->>DB: COMMIT
    deactivate S2
    K-->>K: relay publishes outbox rows
in/grocery/order/service/OrderPlacementService.java
package in.grocery.order.service;

import in.grocery.order.domain.DeliveryAddress;
import in.grocery.order.domain.Order;
import in.grocery.order.outbox.OutboxWriter;
import in.grocery.order.repository.OrderRepository;
import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class OrderPlacementService {

    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final OutboxWriter outbox;
    private final Clock clock;

    public OrderPlacementService(OrderRepository orders, OutboxWriter outbox, Clock clock) {
        this.orders = orders;
        this.outbox = outbox;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Transactional(timeout = 5)                                                            // (1)!
    public Order place(String orderRef, String customerId, DeliveryAddress address,
                       in.grocery.common.money.Money fee, List<LineRequest> lines) {
        Order order = Order.place(orderRef, customerId, address, fee, clock.instant());
        lines.forEach(l -> order.addLine(l.sku(), l.name(), l.quantity(), l.unitPrice()));
        Order saved = orders.save(order);
        outbox.append("order", saved.getOrderRef(), "OrderPlaced",                         // (2)!
                new OrderPlacedPayload(saved.getOrderRef(), customerId, saved.total().asString()));
        return saved;
    }

    public record LineRequest(String sku, String name, int quantity, in.grocery.common.money.Money unitPrice) {}
}
  1. A hard ceiling: if this transaction can't finish in 5 s, something is wrong; fail instead of holding a connection.
  2. The event is written in the same transaction — atomic with the order. No Kafka client here.
in/grocery/order/outbox/OutboxWriter.java
package in.grocery.order.outbox;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;        // JsonMapper on Boot 4
import java.time.Clock;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.jdbc.core.simple.JdbcClient;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Propagation;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class OutboxWriter {

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper json;
    private final Clock clock;

    public OutboxWriter(JdbcClient jdbc, ObjectMapper json, Clock clock) {
        this.jdbc = jdbc;
        this.json = json;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)                                    // (1)!
    public void append(String aggregateType, String aggregateId, String eventType, Object payload) {
        try {
            jdbc.sql("""
                    insert into outbox (id, aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, created_at)
                    values (:id, :type, :aggId, :event, cast(:payload as jsonb), :now)
                    """)
                .param("id", UUID.randomUUID())
                .param("type", aggregateType)
                .param("aggId", aggregateId)
                .param("event", eventType)
                .param("payload", json.writeValueAsString(payload))
                .param("now", clock.instant())
                .update();
        } catch (com.fasterxml.jackson.core.JsonProcessingException e) {
            throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot serialize outbox payload", e);
        }
    }
}
  1. MANDATORY is the whole point: writing an outbox row outside a transaction would be a silent correctness bug, so the container refuses it (IllegalTransactionStateException). Note that JdbcClient shares the JPA transaction's connection (JpaTransactionManager), so the insert and the entity flush commit together.
in/grocery/order/delegate/OrderDelegate.java
@Component
public class OrderDelegate {

    private final OrderPlacementService placement;
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    private final PaymentInitiationService paymentInitiation;

    @Idempotent(key = "#command.idempotencyKey()", scope = "order-place")                  // Chapter 04
    public OrderView place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
        Order order = placement.place(command.orderRef(), command.customerId(),            // TX1
                command.address(), command.fee(), command.lines());

        String gatewayRef;
        try {
            gatewayRef = gateway.createOrder(order.getOrderRef(), order.total().amount()); // (1)!
        } catch (DependencyException e) {
            paymentInitiation.markGatewayUnavailable(order.getOrderRef());                 // TX2'
            throw e;
        }
        paymentInitiation.attachGatewayOrder(order.getOrderRef(), gatewayRef);             // TX2
        return OrderView.from(order, gatewayRef);
    }
}
  1. Outside any transaction — no connection is held while Razorpay is slow. The delegate is the orchestration layer precisely so services can keep their transactions small.

docs.title: 6.2 Transaction observability
docs.text:
You can't tune what you can't see. Two cheap tools:

in/grocery/platform/tx/TransactionMetrics.java
package in.grocery.platform.tx;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Timer;
import org.aspectj.lang.ProceedingJoinPoint;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Around;
import org.aspectj.lang.annotation.Aspect;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.core.Ordered;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;

/** Times every @Transactional method and warns about long-running transactions. */
@Aspect
@Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE - 1)                                                       // (1)!
public class TransactionMetrics {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(TransactionMetrics.class);
    private static final long WARN_MS = 1_000;

    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    public TransactionMetrics(MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.meters = meters;
    }

    @Around("@annotation(org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional)")
    public Object measure(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        String name = pjp.getSignature().getDeclaringType().getSimpleName() + "." + pjp.getSignature().getName();
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        String outcome = "success";
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();
        } catch (Throwable t) {
            outcome = "failure";
            throw t;
        } finally {
            long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000;
            Timer.builder("grocery.transaction")
                 .tag("method", name).tag("outcome", outcome)
                 .publishPercentileHistogram()
                 .register(meters)
                 .record(java.time.Duration.ofMillis(ms));
            if (ms > WARN_MS) {
                log.warn("Long transaction {} took {} ms", name, ms);                       // (2)!
            }
        }
    }
}
  1. Just inside the transaction interceptor (LOWEST_PRECEDENCE) so the measurement covers the transaction, not only the method body. Verify ordering against your configuration (Chapter 04).
  2. Alert on this: long transactions precede pool exhaustion.

Database-side checks during incidents:

SQL
-- longest running transactions right now
select pid, now() - xact_start as duration, state, left(query, 120) as query
from pg_stat_activity
where xact_start is not null and state <> 'idle'
order by duration desc limit 10;

-- idle in transaction: the classic "connection held during a remote call"
select count(*) from pg_stat_activity where state = 'idle in transaction';

docs.title: 6.3 Platform rules encoded as tests
6.4 Decision guide
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Need to change data] --> B{Single row, single statement expressible?}
    B -- yes --> C["Atomic SQL: UPDATE ... WHERE condition<br/>(Chapter 12) — no locks, no retries"]
    B -- no --> D{Invariant spans rows/tables?}
    D -- no --> E["@Transactional + @Version<br/>optimistic locking (Chapter 13)"]
    D -- yes --> F{Contention high?}
    F -- no --> G["SERIALIZABLE + retry on 40001"]
    F -- yes --> H["Pessimistic lock on a designated row<br/>(SELECT FOR UPDATE), short transaction"]
    C & E & G & H --> I{Side effects outside the DB?}
    I -- yes --> J["Outbox row in the same transaction<br/>+ relay (Chapter 36)"]
    I -- no --> K[Done]

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm aspect ordering (retry outside transaction) still holds after switching retry implementations.
  • Re-check custom TransactionManagerCustomizers and imports for moved packages.
  • Review @Transactional on non-public methods flagged by newer tooling.
  • Re-run transactional integration tests (propagation, rollback rules) after upgrade.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. One business operation = one transaction, opened in the service layer.
  2. Short transactions: no remote calls, no file I/O, no sleeps; set timeout.
  3. readOnly = true on every query method.
  4. Unchecked domain exceptions so default rollback rules do the right thing.
  5. REQUIRES_NEW sparingly, always in another bean, always short.
  6. Atomic SQL or optimistic locking before reaching for isolation levels or pessimistic locks.
  7. Retry 40001/deadlocks with jittered backoff, retry outside the transaction.
  8. Outbox for cross-system side effects; after-commit listeners for in-process ones.
  9. Measure: transaction duration histogram, idle in transaction, pool pending.
  10. Encode the rules (ArchUnit + review checklist).

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ @Transactional on the controller or delegate — transaction spans HTTP serialization and orchestration.

❌ Remote call inside a transaction (the single most common cause of pool exhaustion).

❌ @Transactional on a private method or via self-invocation — silently no transaction.

❌ Catching exceptions from a joined REQUIRED call and continuing → UnexpectedRollbackException.

❌ Batch import as one giant transaction.

❌ Raising isolation to SERIALIZABLE globally "to be safe" — serialization failures everywhere without retries.

❌ Manual connection.commit() or entityManager.getTransaction() inside a Spring-managed transaction.

❌ Publishing to Kafka inside the transaction (dual write) — use the outbox.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only Inner REQUIRED failed, outer swallowed it REQUIRES_NEW/NESTED, or don't swallow Changes not persisted No transaction (self-invocation, non-public method, missing annotation) or checked exception committed then rolled back elsewhere Check proxying; rollbackFor TransactionRequiredException Write outside a transaction (e.g. MANDATORY writer or JPA flush) Add @Transactional at the right boundary CannotAcquireLockException / deadlock Lock ordering, long transactions Consistent ordering, shorter transactions, retry could not serialize access due to concurrent update (40001) Serializable/repeatable-read conflict Retry with backoff Pool exhaustion, idle in transaction high Remote calls or slow work inside transactions Move calls out; timeouts TransactionTimedOutException timeout exceeded Investigate slow SQL; raise only with evidence Read-only method fails with "cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction" Write path marked readOnly Correct the annotation After-commit listener never runs No transaction active / test rolled back Ensure a real transaction commits Two REQUIRES_NEW levels hang under load Pool starvation (connections held by outer transactions) Remove nesting; increase pool only as a stopgap

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Transaction boundaries only in services; verified by ArchUnit
  • No remote calls inside transactions
  • readOnly on all queries; replica routing where applicable
  • Timeouts set on write transactions
  • Retry policy for serialization/deadlock errors
  • Outbox used for all cross-system effects
  • Transaction duration metrics + idle in transaction alerts
  • Propagation choices documented (especially every REQUIRES_NEW)

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What does @Transactional do?

Short answer: Spring wraps the method in a transaction: begin before, commit after, roll back on unchecked exceptions — implemented with an AOP proxy and a PlatformTransactionManager.

B1 · Which exceptions cause a rollback by default?

Short answer: RuntimeException and Error. Checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor says otherwise.

B1 · Where should @Transactional go: controller, service or repository?

Short answer: The service — one business operation per transaction.

B1 · What does readOnly = true do?

Short answer: Signals a query-only transaction: Hibernate skips dirty checking, the connection is marked read-only, and it can be routed to a replica.

B1 · What is the default isolation level?

Short answer: DEFAULT — whatever the database uses; PostgreSQL's default is READ COMMITTED.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Explain REQUIRED vs REQUIRES_NEW.

Short answer: REQUIRED joins an existing transaction (one commit). REQUIRES_NEW suspends it and runs in an independent transaction on a second connection, committing separately.

B2 · Why doesn't @Transactional work on a method called from the same class?

Short answer: Self-invocation bypasses the proxy, so the interceptor never runs. Move the method to another bean or use TransactionTemplate.

B2 · What causes UnexpectedRollbackException?

Short answer: A joined inner transaction failed and marked the transaction rollback-only; the outer code caught the exception and tried to commit.

B2 · What's NESTED propagation?

Short answer: A savepoint inside the current transaction (JDBC transaction manager): inner failure rolls back to the savepoint, the outer can continue. Not supported by JpaTransactionManager in the general case.

B2 · Why must remote calls stay out of transactions?

Short answer: They hold a database connection (and locks) for the duration; a slow dependency then exhausts the pool and takes down unrelated endpoints.

B2 · How do you make sure an SMS is sent only if the order commits?

Short answer: @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) (Chapter 03), or an outbox row written in the same transaction for durability.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through what TransactionInterceptor does.

Short answer: Reads the @Transactional attribute (cached), asks the transaction manager for a transaction per propagation, binds resources to the thread via TransactionSynchronizationManager, proceeds, then commits or rolls back based on rollbackOn, running synchronizations and restoring any suspended transaction.

B3 · Which anomalies does PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ prevent, and which not?

Short answer: It's snapshot isolation: no dirty or non-repeatable reads, and no phantoms — but write skew is still possible. SERIALIZABLE (SSI) prevents it by aborting conflicting transactions with 40001.

B3 · How do you handle serialization failures?

Short answer: Retry the whole transaction with jittered exponential backoff and a small attempt limit, ensuring the retry advice wraps the transactional proxy (fresh transaction per attempt) and the operation is idempotent.

B3 · How does JdbcClient share a transaction with JPA?

Short answer: JpaTransactionManager binds the EntityManager and exposes its JDBC Connection as the bound resource for that DataSource, so DataSourceUtils hands the same connection to JdbcClient. Flush JPA changes first if the SQL must see them.

B3 · Why can nested REQUIRES_NEW deadlock the connection pool?

Short answer: Each level holds a connection while waiting for another; with enough concurrency all connections are held by outer transactions and none can be acquired for inner ones — a self-inflicted deadlock the database can't detect.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you design checkout with a slow payment gateway?

Short answer: Short TX1 writing order + outbox, commit; call the gateway outside any transaction with timeouts and circuit breaker; short TX2 to record the gateway reference/outcome; idempotency key at the delegate; relay publishes events; reconciliation job for in-doubt payments.

B4 · Outbox vs XA for database + Kafka atomicity?

Short answer: XA adds a coordinator, latency, in-doubt transactions and poor cloud support. Outbox keeps a single local transaction, publishes asynchronously with at-least-once delivery, and requires idempotent consumers — the standard choice.

B4 · How do you find transactions that hold connections too long?

Short answer: Transaction duration histogram per method, Hikari usage/pending metrics, PostgreSQL pg_stat_activity (idle in transaction, xact_start), slow query logs, plus alerts and a long-transaction warning log.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you reason about consistency across 26 services?

Short answer: Strong consistency inside an aggregate/service via local ACID transactions; across services, eventual consistency with sagas, outbox, idempotent consumers and compensations; make the business-visible consequences explicit (e.g. "stock is reserved within seconds"), and design UX for it.

B5 · What standards would you set for transactions platform-wide?

Short answer: Boundary in services only; timeouts mandatory; no remote calls; readOnly for queries; outbox for side effects; documented propagation exceptions; metrics and alerts; ArchUnit enforcement; incident runbook for lock/serialization storms.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Nightly price import leaves the database half-updated

Import ran as one transaction over 5,000 rows; a constraint violation on row 4,800 rolled everything back, but the job reported partial success from an in-memory counter. Fix: per-row (or per-chunk) transactions via TransactionTemplate, report results from committed work, make the job resumable, and stop swallowing exceptions inside a shared transaction.

Scenario · Sale evening: p99 latency spikes and idle in transaction climbs

A new coupon feature called the promotion service inside the order transaction. Each checkout held a connection for the promotion call's latency (up to 3 s). Fix: fetch coupon data before the transaction (or after commit), set transaction timeouts, add the long-transaction alert, and add the ArchUnit rule against remote calls in services.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Wallet debit with correct transactional semantics

wallet(customer_id, balance_paise, version) and wallet_txn(id, customer_id, order_ref, amount_paise, type). Implement debit(customerId, orderRef, amountPaise) that: is atomic, rejects insufficient balance with a domain exception, is idempotent per order_ref (unique constraint), and records an audit row even when the debit fails — then write tests proving each property.

Solution WalletService.java
package in.grocery.wallet.service;

import in.grocery.platform.error.DomainException;
import in.grocery.platform.error.ErrorCode;
import org.springframework.dao.DuplicateKeyException;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class WalletService {

    public static final class InsufficientBalanceException extends DomainException {
        public InsufficientBalanceException(long available) {
            super(ErrorCode.PAYMENT_DECLINED, "insufficient wallet balance", "wallet balance too low");
        }
    }

    private final WalletRepository wallets;
    private final WalletAuditRecorder audit;          // separate bean, REQUIRES_NEW

    public WalletService(WalletRepository wallets, WalletAuditRecorder audit) {
        this.wallets = wallets;
        this.audit = audit;
    }

    @Transactional(timeout = 3)
    public void debit(String customerId, String orderRef, long amountPaise) {
        try {
            int rows = wallets.debitIfSufficient(customerId, amountPaise);      // atomic conditional UPDATE
            if (rows == 0) {
                audit.record(customerId, orderRef, amountPaise, "INSUFFICIENT");
                throw new InsufficientBalanceException(wallets.balance(customerId));
            }
            wallets.insertTxn(customerId, orderRef, amountPaise, "DEBIT");       // unique(order_ref)
            audit.record(customerId, orderRef, amountPaise, "DEBITED");
        } catch (DuplicateKeyException retryOfSameOrder) {
            throw new AlreadyDebitedException(orderRef);                          // idempotent: caller treats as success
        }
    }
}
WalletAuditRecorder.java
@Service
public class WalletAuditRecorder {
    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final Clock clock;

    WalletAuditRecorder(JdbcClient jdbc, Clock clock) { this.jdbc = jdbc; this.clock = clock; }

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW, timeout = 2)
    public void record(String customerId, String orderRef, long amount, String outcome) {
        jdbc.sql("insert into wallet_audit (customer_id, order_ref, amount_paise, outcome, at) " +
                 "values (:c, :o, :a, :r, :t)")
            .param("c", customerId).param("o", orderRef).param("a", amount)
            .param("r", outcome).param("t", clock.instant())
            .update();
    }
}
WalletServiceTest.java (key assertions)
@Test
void insufficientBalanceRollsBackButAudits() {
    seedWallet("C-1", 1000);
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> wallets.debit("C-1", UniqueIds.orderRef(), 5000))
            .isInstanceOf(WalletService.InsufficientBalanceException.class);
    assertThat(balanceOf("C-1")).isEqualTo(1000);                       // rolled back
    assertThat(auditRows("C-1")).extracting("outcome").contains("INSUFFICIENT");   // committed separately
}

@Test
void duplicateOrderRefIsIdempotent() {
    seedWallet("C-2", 10_000);
    String ref = UniqueIds.orderRef();
    wallets.debit("C-2", ref, 5_000);
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> wallets.debit("C-2", ref, 5_000)).isInstanceOf(AlreadyDebitedException.class);
    assertThat(balanceOf("C-2")).isEqualTo(5_000);                      // debited exactly once
}

Note the ordering: the conditional UPDATE prevents lost updates without locking, the unique constraint on order_ref gives idempotency, and the audit uses REQUIRES_NEW so it survives the rollback. On the duplicate call the debit transaction rolls back completely, while its audit row stays — which is exactly what an audit trail should do.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Spring transactions are AOP + a transaction manager + thread-bound resources; the proxy rules from Chapter 04 all apply.
  • Propagation decides join/suspend/savepoint; REQUIRES_NEW costs an extra connection; swallowing exceptions from joined transactions causes UnexpectedRollbackException.
  • Isolation prevents some anomalies, not all — lost updates and write skew need @Version, atomic SQL, locks or SERIALIZABLE + retry.
  • Default rollback is on unchecked exceptions — use unchecked domain exceptions.
  • Short transactions, readOnly queries, timeouts, no remote calls.
  • Outbox, not XA, for database + Kafka atomicity; after-commit listeners for in-process effects.
  • Observe transactions (duration histogram, idle in transaction) before they become pool incidents.
