15 Testing Fundamentals · 17 Spring Security Fundamentals

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Everything in the grocery platform is behind a security decision: a customer may see their cart, a seller may edit their catalog, an operations user may cancel any order, a delivery partner may update only assigned deliveries, and Razorpay may call exactly one webhook endpoint with a signature.

Getting this wrong is the most expensive class of bug. Real incidents this chapter's patterns prevent:

  • IDOR — GET /api/carts/{id} returns someone else's cart because the controller checked authentication but not ownership.
  • Missing method-level checks — an internal admin endpoint reachable from the public gateway because one route wasn't matched.
  • CSRF on a cookie-session admin portal — a malicious page triggers "cancel all orders" as a logged-in operator.
  • Password handling — plaintext or MD5 in a legacy table, no upgrade path.
  • Security context loss — @Async code runs as anonymous, silently skipping checks or failing.

Spring Security is a filter chain with an authentication model and an authorization model. Once those three ideas are clear, the DSL stops being magic.

This chapter covers the fundamentals with the grocery platform's actual needs: the filter chain and where your code plugs in, SecurityFilterChain beans with the lambda DSL, authentication providers (including OTP for Indian mobile numbers), password encoding and upgrades, request- and method-level authorization, ownership checks with a custom AuthorizationManager, CSRF for the admin portal versus stateless APIs, CORS with Security in play, sessions, and testing. Chapter 18 covers JWT, OAuth2, the authorization server, passkeys and webhook signatures.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — filter chain, basic rules, password encoding B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — multiple chains, method security, CSRF/CORS, testing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — internals, custom authentication, ownership authorization B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — platform security config, migration to Security 7 B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — authorization architecture and governance

docs.title: 2.1 The three questions
docs.text: Question Spring Security concept Who are you? Authentication — Authentication, AuthenticationManager, providers What are you allowed to do? Authorization — AuthorizationManager, request matchers, method security How do I protect the transport and session? Filters: CSRF, CORS, headers, session management

docs.title: 2.2 The filter chain
docs.text:
Spring Security is a servlet Filter (springSecurityFilterChain, registered via DelegatingFilterProxy) that delegates to FilterChainProxy, which picks the first matching SecurityFilterChain and runs its filters in order.

flowchart TB
    R[Request] --> DFP[DelegatingFilterProxy]
    DFP --> FCP[FilterChainProxy]
    FCP --> M{which SecurityFilterChain matches?}
    M --> C1["/api/seller-integrations/** → API-key chain"]
    M --> C2["/api/** → stateless chain"]
    M --> C3["/admin/** → session chain"]
    C2 --> F1[SecurityContextHolderFilter]
    F1 --> F2[HeaderWriterFilter]
    F2 --> F3[CorsFilter]
    F3 --> F4[CsrfFilter]
    F4 --> F5[Authentication filters<br/>e.g. BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter]
    F5 --> F6[AnonymousAuthenticationFilter]
    F6 --> F7[ExceptionTranslationFilter]
    F7 --> F8[AuthorizationFilter]
    F8 --> APP[DispatcherServlet → your controller]

Two filters deserve special attention:

  • ExceptionTranslationFilter catches AuthenticationException → entry point (401) and AccessDeniedException → 403 (or entry point if anonymous). This is why security errors don't reach @ControllerAdvice by default (Chapter 10).
  • AuthorizationFilter (Security 6+, replacing FilterSecurityInterceptor) applies the request-level rules.

docs.title: 2.3 SecurityFilterChain beans
docs.text:
Boot auto-configures a default chain (everything authenticated, HTTP Basic + form login, generated password) only if you define none. In production you define one or more:

SecurityFilterChain beans (snippet)
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")                 // which requests this chain handles
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth...)     // rules
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())               // stateless API
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(STATELESS))
        .build();
}

Order matters — annotate chains with @Order when their matchers could overlap; the first match wins and no later chain is consulted.

docs.title: 2.4 Authentication model
docs.text: Type Role Authentication The token: principal, credentials, authorities, isAuthenticated() SecurityContext / SecurityContextHolder Thread-bound holder of the current Authentication AuthenticationManager → ProviderManager Delegates to a list of AuthenticationProviders AuthenticationProvider Knows how to authenticate one kind of token (DaoAuthenticationProvider, JwtAuthenticationProvider, your OTP provider) UserDetailsService Loads a user by username for DaoAuthenticationProvider PasswordEncoder Hashes and verifies passwords SecurityContextRepository Where the context is persisted between requests (session, or none for stateless)

docs.title: 2.5 Password storage
docs.text:
PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() produces a DelegatingPasswordEncoder that stores an algorithm prefix: {bcrypt}$2a$10$.... It can verify old formats while writing new ones — the migration path for legacy hashes. With UserDetailsPasswordService, Spring Security upgrades a user's hash automatically on successful login.

Never store plaintext, MD5, SHA-1, or unsalted hashes. BCrypt (cost 10–12), Argon2id or PBKDF2 are the sane choices.

docs.title: 2.6 Authorization: request level
docs.text:
Authorization: request level (snippet)
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
    .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/public/**").permitAll()
    .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("OPS")
    .requestMatchers("/api/sellers/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_seller")
    .anyRequest().authenticated())
  • hasRole("OPS") checks the authority ROLE_OPS (the prefix is added for you).
  • Rules are evaluated in order; the first matching rule decides. Put specific rules before general ones, and always end with anyRequest().
  • access(AuthorizationManager) plugs in custom logic.

docs.title: 2.7 Authorization: method level
docs.text:
@EnableMethodSecurity enables @PreAuthorize, @PostAuthorize, @PreFilter, @PostFilter (AOP — Chapter 04 rules apply: public methods, no self-invocation).

Authorization: method level (snippet)
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('OPS')")
public void forceCancel(String orderRef) { ... }

Use method security for service-level rules (especially ones reachable from more than one entry point), and request matchers for coarse routing. Avoid writing complex SpEL — put the logic in an AuthorizationManager or a bean method (@PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.canCancel(#orderRef, authentication)")).

docs.title: 2.8 Ownership (the IDOR problem)
docs.text:
"Authenticated" is not "authorized for this resource". Three places to enforce ownership:

Where How Notes Query findByIdAndCustomerId(...) returns empty → 404 Simplest, fastest, no leakage Method security @PostAuthorize("returnObject.customerId == authentication.name") Loads the object first Custom AuthorizationManager Reusable rule at request or method level Best for cross-cutting rules

The platform default: scope the query by owner and return 404, plus a method-security backstop on sensitive operations.

docs.title: 2.9 CSRF
docs.text:
CSRF protection matters when the browser automatically attaches credentials: cookies (sessions) or HTTP Basic. It is unnecessary for APIs authenticated with an Authorization header on every request.

Surface CSRF Admin portal (session cookie) Enabled, cookie-based token readable by the SPA /api/** with bearer tokens Disabled (no ambient credentials) Webhooks Disabled; authenticated by signature (Chapter 18)

docs.title: 2.10 CORS with Security
docs.text: When Spring Security is present, configure CORS through Security (http.cors(...) with a CorsConfigurationSource bean) so preflight OPTIONS requests are handled before authentication.

docs.title: 2.11 Sessions
docs.text: Policy Use STATELESS APIs with per-request credentials — no HttpSession, no JSESSIONID IF_REQUIRED (default) Form-login portals Session fixation protection On by default (changeSessionId) Concurrency control Limit sessions per user (admin portal) Spring Session + Redis Shared sessions across pods

docs.title: 2.12 Security context and threads
docs.text: SecurityContextHolder is thread-local. Work handed to another thread (@Async, executors, virtual-thread tasks) loses it unless you propagate: DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor/...Runnable, or Micrometer context propagation (Chapter 07). Symptoms: "anonymous" in audit logs, or AccessDeniedException inside async code.

docs.title: 3.1 Authentication flow (username/password)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Browser
    participant F as UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter
    participant AM as ProviderManager
    participant P as DaoAuthenticationProvider
    participant UDS as UserDetailsService
    participant PE as PasswordEncoder
    participant SCR as SecurityContextRepository

    C->>F: POST /login (username, password)
    F->>AM: authenticate(UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken)
    AM->>P: supports(token)? → authenticate
    P->>UDS: loadUserByUsername
    UDS-->>P: UserDetails (hash, authorities, flags)
    P->>PE: matches(raw, encoded)
    alt matches
        P-->>AM: authenticated token (credentials erased)
        AM-->>F: Authentication
        F->>SCR: save SecurityContext (session)
        F->>C: redirect / 200
    else no match
        P-->>AM: BadCredentialsException
        AM-->>F: AuthenticationException → failure handler (401)
    end

ProviderManager tries providers in order and rethrows the last exception if none succeed; it erases credentials from the resulting token by default.

docs.title: 3.2 Authorization flow
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[AuthorizationFilter] --> B[RequestMatcherDelegatingAuthorizationManager]
    B --> C{first matching rule}
    C --> D[AuthorityAuthorizationManager / custom manager]
    D --> E{granted?}
    E -- yes --> F[continue filter chain]
    E -- no --> G[AccessDeniedException]
    G --> H[ExceptionTranslationFilter]
    H --> I{anonymous?}
    I -- yes --> J[AuthenticationEntryPoint → 401]
    I -- no --> K[AccessDeniedHandler → 403]

Method security works the same way one level down: AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor consults an AuthorizationManager<MethodInvocation> built from @PreAuthorize.

docs.title: 3.3 Where security errors become responses
docs.text: ExceptionTranslationFilter runs before the DispatcherServlet, so @ControllerAdvice never sees AccessDeniedException thrown by the filter chain. To emit the platform's ProblemDetail (Chapter 10), configure an AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler — Level 4 does this. (Method-security denials do happen inside the dispatch and can be handled by an advice.)

docs.text:
The order-service serves customers (bearer tokens), operations staff (session portal) and sellers (API keys).

in/grocery/order/config/SecurityChains.java
package in.grocery.order.config;

import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.Ordered;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.http.SessionCreationPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.security.web.csrf.CookieCsrfTokenRepository;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class SecurityChains {

    @Bean
    @Order(1)                                                                            // (1)!
    SecurityFilterChain webhooks(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
                .securityMatcher("/webhooks/**")
                .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().permitAll())                  // (2)!
                .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
                .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    @Order(2)
    SecurityFilterChain sellerIntegrations(HttpSecurity http, ApiKeyAuthFilter apiKeys) throws Exception {
        return http
                .securityMatcher("/api/seller-integrations/**")
                .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().hasAuthority("SCOPE_seller-integration"))
                .addFilterBefore(apiKeys, org.springframework.security.web.authentication
                        .UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)                      // (3)!
                .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
                .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    @Order(3)
    SecurityFilterChain customerApi(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
                .securityMatcher("/api/**")
                .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                        .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll()
                        .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("OPS")
                        .anyRequest().authenticated())
                .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))              // Chapter 18
                .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
                .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    @Order(Ordered.LOWEST_PRECEDENCE)
    SecurityFilterChain adminPortal(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
                .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                        .requestMatchers("/login", "/css/**", "/js/**").permitAll()
                        .anyRequest().hasRole("OPS"))
                .formLogin(form -> form.loginPage("/login").permitAll())
                .logout(logout -> logout.logoutSuccessUrl("/login?logout"))
                .csrf(csrf -> csrf.csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse()))   // (4)!
                .sessionManagement(s -> s
                        .sessionFixation(f -> f.changeSessionId())
                        .maximumSessions(2))
                .build();
    }
}
  1. Explicit ordering — the most specific matcher first. Without @Order, overlapping chains cause startup errors or surprising matches.
  2. Webhook endpoints authenticate by signature inside the handler (Chapter 18), not by the filter chain; the chain still applies headers and disables sessions.
  3. A custom filter placed before the username/password filter position.
  4. Session-based portal keeps CSRF on, with a cookie the SPA can read.

5.3 Level 2 — OTP authentication for customers
docs.text:
Indian consumer apps log in with a mobile number and a one-time password. Model it as a custom AuthenticationProvider.

in/grocery/identity/security/OtpAuthenticationToken.java
package in.grocery.identity.security;

import java.util.Collection;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AbstractAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.core.GrantedAuthority;

public class OtpAuthenticationToken extends AbstractAuthenticationToken {

    private final String mobile;
    private final String otp;
    private final String customerId;

    private OtpAuthenticationToken(String mobile, String otp, String customerId,
                                   Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> authorities) {
        super(authorities);
        this.mobile = mobile;
        this.otp = otp;
        this.customerId = customerId;
        setAuthenticated(customerId != null);
    }

    public static OtpAuthenticationToken unauthenticated(String mobile, String otp) {
        return new OtpAuthenticationToken(mobile, otp, null, java.util.List.of());
    }

    public static OtpAuthenticationToken authenticated(String mobile, String customerId,
                                                       Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> authorities) {
        return new OtpAuthenticationToken(mobile, null, customerId, authorities);
    }

    @Override public Object getCredentials() { return otp; }
    @Override public Object getPrincipal() { return customerId != null ? customerId : mobile; }
    public String mobile() { return mobile; }
}
in/grocery/identity/security/OtpAuthenticationProvider.java
package in.grocery.identity.security;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AuthenticationProvider;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.BadCredentialsException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.LockedException;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.AuthenticationException;
import org.springframework.security.core.authority.SimpleGrantedAuthority;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class OtpAuthenticationProvider implements AuthenticationProvider {

    public interface OtpStore {
        /** Consumes the OTP: true only on first correct use within TTL. Counts failures per mobile. */
        boolean consume(String mobile, String otp);
        boolean isLockedOut(String mobile);
    }

    public interface CustomerDirectory {
        String findOrCreateCustomerId(String mobile);
    }

    private final OtpStore otps;
    private final CustomerDirectory customers;

    public OtpAuthenticationProvider(OtpStore otps, CustomerDirectory customers) {
        this.otps = otps;
        this.customers = customers;
    }

    @Override
    public Authentication authenticate(Authentication authentication) throws AuthenticationException {
        OtpAuthenticationToken token = (OtpAuthenticationToken) authentication;
        if (otps.isLockedOut(token.mobile())) {
            throw new LockedException("Too many attempts");                                  // (1)!
        }
        if (!otps.consume(token.mobile(), String.valueOf(token.getCredentials()))) {
            throw new BadCredentialsException("Invalid OTP");                                // (2)!
        }
        String customerId = customers.findOrCreateCustomerId(token.mobile());
        return OtpAuthenticationToken.authenticated(token.mobile(), customerId,
                List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_CUSTOMER")));
    }

    @Override
    public boolean supports(Class<?> authentication) {
        return OtpAuthenticationToken.class.isAssignableFrom(authentication);
    }
}
  1. Rate limiting belongs here: 5 attempts per mobile per 15 minutes, and a separate limit on OTP requests (Chapter 26) — otherwise the login endpoint is an SMS-cost DoS.
  2. Single-use consumption prevents replay; OTPs are stored hashed with a short TTL in Redis.

The login controller calls authenticationManager.authenticate(OtpAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(mobile, otp)) and, on success, issues a JWT (Chapter 18).

docs.text:
Goals: identical behaviour across 26 services, platform error format for 401/403, security events audited, and rules that are tested.

in/grocery/platform/security/GrocerySecurityDefaults.java
package in.grocery.platform.security;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.time.Clock;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.condition.ConditionalOnMissingBean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.security.web.AuthenticationEntryPoint;
import org.springframework.security.web.access.AccessDeniedHandler;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
public class GrocerySecurityDefaults {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    AuthenticationEntryPoint groceryEntryPoint(Clock clock) {                                   // (1)!
        return (request, response, ex) -> writeProblem(request, response, 401,
                "UNAUTHENTICATED", "Authentication is required", clock);
    }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    AccessDeniedHandler groceryAccessDeniedHandler(Clock clock) {
        return (request, response, ex) -> writeProblem(request, response, 403,
                "FORBIDDEN", "You are not allowed to perform this action", clock);
    }

    private static void writeProblem(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response,
                                     int status, String code, String detail, Clock clock) throws IOException {
        response.setStatus(status);
        response.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);                       // (2)!
        response.getWriter().write("""
                {"type":"https://errors.grocery.in/%s","title":"%s","status":%d,"detail":"%s",
                 "instance":"%s","code":"%s","retryable":false,"timestamp":"%s","errors":[]}
                """.formatted(code.toLowerCase().replace('_', '-'), code.replace('_', ' '), status,
                detail, request.getRequestURI(), code, clock.instant()));
    }
}
  1. Without these, Spring Security returns an empty 401/403 (or an HTML login page) and clients see a different error shape than everywhere else (Chapter 10).
  2. Hand-written JSON keeps this free of the mapper and safe to run inside the filter chain. Alternatively, delegate to the HandlerExceptionResolver as in Chapter 10's filter recipe.
in/grocery/platform/security/SecurityAuditListener.java
package in.grocery.platform.security;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.context.event.EventListener;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.event.AbstractAuthenticationFailureEvent;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.event.AuthenticationSuccessEvent;
import org.springframework.security.authorization.event.AuthorizationDeniedEvent;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class SecurityAuditListener {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("security-audit");

    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    public SecurityAuditListener(MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.meters = meters;
    }

    @EventListener
    public void onSuccess(AuthenticationSuccessEvent event) {
        meters.counter("grocery.auth", "outcome", "success").increment();
    }

    @EventListener
    public void onFailure(AbstractAuthenticationFailureEvent event) {                            // (1)!
        String type = event.getException().getClass().getSimpleName();
        meters.counter("grocery.auth", "outcome", "failure", "reason", type).increment();
        log.warn("Authentication failure ({}) for principal hash {}", type,
                Integer.toHexString(String.valueOf(event.getAuthentication().getName()).hashCode()));   // (2)!
    }

    @EventListener
    public void onDenied(AuthorizationDeniedEvent<?> event) {
        meters.counter("grocery.authz", "outcome", "denied").increment();
    }
}
  1. Spring Security publishes application events for authentication outcomes; AuthorizationDeniedEvent requires the authorization event publisher to be configured (SpringAuthorizationEventPublisher bean) — verify for your version.
  2. Never log the mobile number or username in clear text (Chapter 07); a stable hash is enough to spot brute force.

docs.title: 6.2 Rate limiting the login endpoint
6.3 Securing Actuator
docs.text:
application-prod.yml
management:
  server:
    port: 9090                                     # (1)!
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,loggers,startup
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized
      probes:
        enabled: true
in/grocery/platform/security/ActuatorSecurityConfig.java
@Bean
@Order(0)
SecurityFilterChain actuator(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
            .securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())                                    // (2)!
            .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                    .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to(HealthEndpoint.class, InfoEndpoint.class)).permitAll()
                    .anyRequest().hasRole("PLATFORM"))
            .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
            .build();
}
  1. A separate management port keeps Actuator off the public ingress entirely — the strongest control.
  2. EndpointRequest matchers adapt automatically to the configured base path. Probes stay open for Kubernetes; everything else (including loggers, which can flood logs) requires a platform role.

Verify

EndpointRequest lives in Boot's Actuator autoconfigure package and moves in Boot 4's modularization; check the import.

docs.title: 6.4 Security tests that encode the rules
6.5 Checklist-driven review
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[New endpoint] --> B{Which chain matches?}
    B --> C{Authenticated required?}
    C --> D{Ownership enforced<br/>query-scoped or AuthorizationManager?}
    D --> E{Method-security backstop<br/>on the service?}
    E --> F{Input validated<br/>Chapter 09?}
    F --> G{Errors use platform format?}
    G --> H{Security test added?}

Every PR adding an endpoint answers these seven questions. Most IDOR bugs die at step D.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 / Security 6.5 Boot 4.x / Security 7 Configuration style Lambda DSL recommended; non-lambda deprecated Lambda DSL only — deprecated methods removed WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter Removed (since 5.7/6.0) Removed Request matchers requestMatchers(...); AntPathRequestMatcher deprecated PathPatternRequestMatcher — Ant matcher removed (verify) Authorization authorizeHttpRequests + AuthorizationManager Same Method security @EnableMethodSecurity Same Authorization events Opt-in publisher Same (verify bean/config name) CSRF SPA recipe 6.x deferred tokens + XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler Changed again — verify against 7.x docs Passkeys / one-time tokens 6.4+ Available (Chapter 18) Servlet API 6.0 6.1 Spring Boot 3.5 / Security 6.5Spring Boot 4.x / Security 7 Spring Boot 3.5 / Security 6.5 (snippet)

        .requestMatchers(new AntPathRequestMatcher("/api/admin/**")).hasRole("OPS")
        .anyRequest().authenticated());
Spring Boot 4.x / Security 7 (snippet)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Remove any non-lambda DSL usage while still on 6.x (deprecation warnings guide you).
  • Replace explicit AntPathRequestMatcher/MvcRequestMatcher constructions with string matchers or PathPatternRequestMatcher.
  • Re-test every security rule after the upgrade — matcher semantics (trailing slashes, servlet path) are the classic silent break.
  • Re-verify the CSRF configuration for SPAs against 7.x documentation.
  • Check imports of Actuator EndpointRequest and Boot security auto-configuration classes.
  • Review custom filters for Servlet 6.1 behaviour and for context clearing.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Explicit SecurityFilterChain beans, ordered, each ending with anyRequest().
  2. Deny by default; open only what must be public, per method and path.
  3. Enforce ownership with owner-scoped queries (404) plus method-security backstops.
  4. Stateless APIs: no sessions, CSRF off, credentials per request; sessions and CSRF for the cookie-based portal.
  5. Delegating password encoder, BCrypt 10–12, automatic upgrades; never custom crypto.
  6. Rate-limit authentication (OTP request, OTP verify, login) per identity and per IP.
  7. Platform error format for 401/403 via entry point and denied handler.
  8. Audit and meter authentication/authorization outcomes; alert on spikes.
  9. Actuator on a separate port, probes public, everything else restricted.
  10. Security tests per endpoint: anonymous, wrong role, wrong owner, right owner.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ permitAll() on a broad prefix ("we'll secure it in the gateway") — services must not trust the network.

❌ Missing anyRequest() — unmatched requests pass through unauthenticated.

❌ Ownership checks in the controller body only (easy to forget in the next endpoint).

❌ Complex SpEL in @PreAuthorize querying repositories inline — untestable and slow.

❌ Disabling CSRF on a cookie-session portal "because the SPA breaks".

❌ Logging usernames, mobile numbers, tokens or API keys.

❌ SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...) without creating a fresh context (and without clearing it afterwards in stateless filters).

❌ Storing API keys or OTPs in plaintext.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Everything returns 401 after adding the starter Default chain active Define your own SecurityFilterChain 403 on every POST from the SPA CSRF enabled without a token Correct CSRF setup, or stateless + bearer tokens 401 instead of 403 Anonymous request to a protected route Expected; check the client sends credentials Rules ignored Another chain matched first Order chains; check securityMatcher CORS preflight fails with 401 CORS not configured through Security http.cors(...) + CorsConfigurationSource @PreAuthorize ignored Self-invocation, non-public method, missing @EnableMethodSecurity Fix proxying Audit shows anonymousUser in async code Context not propagated DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor 403 body is empty HTML No AccessDeniedHandler Platform handlers (6.1) Users can read others' data Missing ownership check Owner-scoped query + AuthorizationManager Login works locally, fails behind ingress X-Forwarded-* not honoured; secure cookie flags server.forward-headers-strategy, cookie settings

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• One chain per surface, ordered, anyRequest() present
  • Ownership enforced and tested for every resource endpoint
  • Passwords/API keys/OTPs hashed; rotation supported
  • Login and OTP endpoints rate-limited
  • 401/403 use the platform problem format
  • Security events audited and metered
  • Actuator restricted; management port separate
  • Security headers (HSTS, CSP, nosniff, frame-ancestors) set
  • Security tests for anonymous/wrong-role/wrong-owner paths

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · How does Spring Security plug into a servlet application?

Short answer: A DelegatingFilterProxy registers springSecurityFilterChain, which is a FilterChainProxy that selects the first matching SecurityFilterChain and runs its filters before the DispatcherServlet.

B1 · Authentication vs authorization?

Short answer: Authentication establishes who the caller is; authorization decides what they may do.

B1 · What does hasRole('OPS') check?

Short answer: The authority ROLE_OPS — the prefix is added automatically. hasAuthority checks the exact string.

B1 · How should passwords be stored?

Short answer: Hashed with a slow, salted algorithm (BCrypt/Argon2) via DelegatingPasswordEncoder, which prefixes the algorithm and can verify legacy formats.

B1 · Why do I get 401 for one endpoint and 403 for another?

Short answer: 401 when no (or invalid) credentials were supplied; 403 when the caller is authenticated but lacks permission.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you define multiple security configurations?

Short answer: Several SecurityFilterChain beans, each with a securityMatcher and @Order; the first matching chain handles the request entirely.

B2 · When is CSRF protection needed?

Short answer: When credentials are attached automatically by the browser (cookies/Basic). Not needed for APIs using an Authorization header per request.

B2 · How do you write a custom authentication mechanism (e.g. OTP)?

Short answer: A custom Authentication token, an AuthenticationProvider that validates it (with rate limiting and single-use semantics), optionally a filter to extract credentials, registered in the AuthenticationManager.

B2 · @PreAuthorize vs request matchers?

Short answer: Matchers protect URLs coarsely at the filter level; method security protects service methods wherever they're called from. Use both — defence in depth.

B2 · How do you test security rules?

Short answer: @WebMvcTest with the security configuration imported, spring-security-test (@WithMockUser, csrf() post-processor), asserting 401/403/200 for anonymous, wrong role, wrong owner and correct user.

B2 · Why must API keys be hashed in the database?

Short answer: They're credentials; a database leak would otherwise hand over every seller's access. Store a hash/HMAC, compare in constant time, support rotation.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Describe the request flow through the security filter chain.

Short answer: Context loaded (SecurityContextHolderFilter) → headers → CORS → CSRF → authentication filters populate the context → anonymous → ExceptionTranslationFilter (catches later exceptions) → AuthorizationFilter evaluates rules → application. Denials surface as 401 via the entry point or 403 via the denied handler.

B3 · Why don't AccessDeniedExceptions from the filter chain hit @ControllerAdvice?

Short answer: They're thrown and handled in the filter chain, before the DispatcherServlet. Configure AuthenticationEntryPoint/AccessDeniedHandler, or delegate to the HandlerExceptionResolver. Method-security denials do reach advices.

B3 · How do you implement resource ownership checks cleanly?

Short answer: Scope queries by owner (returning 404), and/or implement AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext> using URI variables, reusable in the DSL and via @PreAuthorize("@bean.method(...)").

B3 · What happens to the security context in @Async methods?

Short answer: Nothing propagates by default (thread-local). Use DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor/Runnable, context propagation, or MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCAL.

B3 · How does DelegatingPasswordEncoder enable migration?

Short answer: The stored hash carries an {id} prefix, so old algorithms can still be verified while new passwords use the current one; with UserDetailsPasswordService, hashes are upgraded on successful login.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design authorization for customers, sellers, ops and delivery partners.

Short answer: Separate chains per surface; roles for coarse capabilities and scopes for token-based clients; ownership rules as reusable AuthorizationManagers; method security on sensitive service operations; audit and metrics for denials; tests per rule; documented role/permission catalog reviewed with the business.

B4 · Gateway or service — where do you enforce authentication?

Short answer: Both. The gateway does coarse checks (valid token, rate limits, WAF), services re-validate tokens and enforce fine-grained authorization: never trust the network or an upstream header.

B4 · What are the pitfalls upgrading to Spring Security 7?

Short answer: Removal of deprecated non-lambda DSL and Ant matchers (matcher semantics differ subtly), CSRF/SPA configuration changes, and moved Boot packages. Every rule needs a test; run the full security test suite before and after.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you keep authorization rules understandable as the platform grows?

Short answer: A single source of truth for roles/permissions, rules expressed as named managers rather than scattered SpEL, tests as executable specification, PR checklist for new endpoints, periodic access reviews, and telemetry on denials to find both bugs and abuse.

B5 · Roles, scopes or policy engine (OPA/Cedar)?

Short answer: Roles/scopes suffice for most services; a policy engine helps with complex, frequently changing, cross-service rules (tenant hierarchies, delegated admin) at the cost of another moving part and a new failure mode. Start simple, externalize only where variability justifies it.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A customer sees another customer's order after a refactor

The new GET /api/orders/{orderRef} handler used findByOrderRef instead of the owner-scoped query and no chain rule covered the new path (an earlier permitAll prefix matched). Fixes: owner-scoped query, access(orderAccess) on /api/orders/{orderRef}/**, method-security backstop, a security test per role/owner combination, and a PR checklist item.

Scenario · OTP SMS costs spike overnight

An attacker looped OTP requests for random numbers; there was a limit on verification attempts but none on OTP requests. Fixes: per-mobile and per-IP limits on requests, CAPTCHA/device attestation after N attempts, alerting on OTP volume, and a cost dashboard.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Seller catalog isolation

GET/PUT /api/sellers/{sellerId}/products/** must be accessible only to that seller (token authority SCOPE_seller with claim seller_id) or to ROLE_OPS. Implement an AuthorizationManager, wire it in the chain, and write tests for: anonymous → 401, other seller → 403, own seller → 200, ops → 200.

Solution SellerAccess.java
package in.grocery.seller.security;

import java.util.function.Supplier;
import org.springframework.security.authorization.AuthorizationDecision;
import org.springframework.security.authorization.AuthorizationManager;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.resource.authentication.JwtAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.web.access.intercept.RequestAuthorizationContext;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component("sellerAccess")
public class SellerAccess implements AuthorizationManager<RequestAuthorizationContext> {

    @Override
    public AuthorizationDecision check(Supplier<Authentication> authentication, RequestAuthorizationContext ctx) {
        Authentication auth = authentication.get();
        if (auth == null || !auth.isAuthenticated()) return new AuthorizationDecision(false);
        boolean ops = auth.getAuthorities().stream().anyMatch(a -> a.getAuthority().equals("ROLE_OPS"));
        if (ops) return new AuthorizationDecision(true);

        String pathSeller = ctx.getVariables().get("sellerId");
        String tokenSeller = auth instanceof JwtAuthenticationToken jwtAuth
                ? ((Jwt) jwtAuth.getToken()).getClaimAsString("seller_id")
                : null;
        boolean isSeller = auth.getAuthorities().stream().anyMatch(a -> a.getAuthority().equals("SCOPE_seller"));
        return new AuthorizationDecision(isSeller && pathSeller != null && pathSeller.equals(tokenSeller));
    }
}
SecurityChains.java (rule)
.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
    .requestMatchers("/api/sellers/{sellerId}/**").access(sellerAccess)
    .anyRequest().authenticated())
SellerAccessTest.java
@WebMvcTest(SellerProductController.class)
@Import({SecurityChains.class, SellerAccess.class})
class SellerAccessTest {

    @Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;
    @MockitoBean SellerProductDelegate delegate;

    private static RequestPostProcessor seller(String sellerId) {
        return SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt()
                .jwt(j -> j.claim("seller_id", sellerId))
                .authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_seller"));
    }

    @Test
    void anonymousIs401() {
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/sellers/S-1/products")).hasStatus(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
    }

    @Test
    void otherSellerIs403() {
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/sellers/S-1/products").with(seller("S-2")))
                .hasStatus(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);
    }

    @Test
    void ownSellerIsAllowed() {
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/sellers/S-1/products").with(seller("S-1"))).hasStatusOk();
    }

    @Test
    @WithMockUser(roles = "OPS")
    void opsIsAllowed() {
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/sellers/S-1/products")).hasStatusOk();
    }
}

The same manager can back @PreAuthorize("@sellerAccess.check(...)")-style checks on service methods; keep one rule, used twice.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Spring Security is a filter chain in front of the DispatcherServlet; know which chain matches and what each filter does.
  • Define your own SecurityFilterChains, ordered, deny-by-default, always ending with anyRequest().
  • Authentication = token + provider + (optionally) UserDetailsService; authorization = AuthorizationManager at request and method level.
  • Ownership is the bug that matters — scope queries by owner and back it with method security.
  • CSRF for cookie sessions, stateless for APIs; configure CORS through Security.
  • Hash everything credential-shaped; rate-limit authentication endpoints.
  • 401/403 must use the platform error format; audit and meter security events.
  • Security 7 removes the old DSL and Ant matchers — retest every rule when upgrading.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Security Reference — Architecture, Authentication, Authorization (AuthorizationManager, method security), Protection Against Exploits (CSRF, headers), Testing
  • Spring Boot Reference — Security (auto-configuration, Actuator security)
  • OWASP — Application Security Verification Standard, API Security Top 10 (Chapter 39 goes deeper)

16 Transactions Deep Dive · 18 Tokens, OAuth2 & Modern Auth

docs.title: 18 · Spring Security — Tokens, OAuth2 & Modern Auth
1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 17 built the filter chains and authorization rules. This chapter answers the question they depend on: where does the Authentication come from in a distributed platform?

The grocery platform has five different answers, and each is a different protocol:

Caller Mechanism Customer app (Flutter/Angular) Short-lived JWT access token + rotating refresh token, issued after OTP login Operations staff OAuth2 / OIDC login against the corporate identity provider, session in the admin portal Service → service (order → pricing) OAuth2 client credentials token, attached automatically to outbound calls Seller integrations API keys today, client credentials tomorrow Razorpay No token at all — an HMAC signature over the raw webhook body

Get any of these wrong and the consequences are severe: tokens that can't be revoked when a phone is stolen, an admin portal that accepts tokens issued for the customer app, a webhook endpoint anyone can call to mark orders as paid, or a refresh-token design that lets a stolen token live for 90 days.

This chapter covers the resource-server side (validating JWTs properly, including audience, issuer, clock skew and key rotation), issuing tokens with Spring Authorization Server, refresh-token rotation with reuse detection, revocation, OAuth2 login for staff, client credentials for service-to-service calls, multi-issuer setups, passkeys and one-time tokens, and webhook signature verification done right.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — what a JWT is, resource server basics B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — claims→authorities, OAuth2 login, client credentials B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — validation internals, rotation, revocation, webhooks B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — token architecture, multi-issuer, migration B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — identity strategy, build vs buy

docs.title: 2.1 OAuth2 and OIDC in one table
docs.text: Term Meaning here Resource server Our APIs — validate tokens, enforce scopes Authorization server Issues tokens (our own Spring Authorization Server, or Okta/Auth0/Keycloak) Client The app requesting tokens (mobile app, admin portal, order-service calling pricing) Resource owner The customer Access token Short-lived credential sent on every API call Refresh token Long-lived credential used only to get new access tokens ID token (OIDC) Proof of authentication for login flows — never used as an API credential Scope What the token is allowed to do (orders:read) Grant How a token is obtained: authorization code + PKCE (users), client credentials (services)

docs.title: 2.2 JWT anatomy
docs.text:
header.payload.signature, base64url-encoded, signed (RS256/ES256 asymmetric, HS256 symmetric).

Claim Purpose Platform value iss Issuer https://id.grocery.in sub Subject C-1043221 (customer id) aud Audience grocery-api exp / iat / nbf Expiry / issued / not-before 15 minutes jti Token id Used for revocation lists scope Space-separated scopes orders:read orders:write cart custom App claims seller_id, roles, device_id, amr

A JWT is signed, not secret

Anyone holding the token can read the payload. Never put PII (mobile number, address), card data or secrets in claims. Keep claims small — they travel on every request.

docs.title: 2.3 JWT vs opaque tokens
docs.text:
JWT Opaque (reference) token Validation Local signature check (fast, offline) Introspection call to the authorization server Revocation Hard — needs a denylist or very short expiry Immediate Size Larger (claims) Small Coupling Consumers need the JWKS Consumers need the introspection endpoint

Platform choice: short-lived JWTs (15 min) for APIs + refresh tokens + a jti denylist for immediate revocation of stolen sessions.

docs.title: 2.4 Resource server configuration
docs.text:
application.yml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://id.grocery.in        # discovers the JWKS URI
          audiences: grocery-api                   # verify the audience (Boot 3.4+; verify)

Boot builds a JwtDecoder (Nimbus) that downloads and caches the JWK set, verifies the signature by kid, and runs validators (exp, nbf, iss, and any you add).

docs.title: 2.5 From claims to authorities
docs.text:
By default Spring maps the scope/scp claim to authorities prefixed SCOPE_. Application roles usually live in a custom claim, so a JwtAuthenticationConverter maps both:

Example
scope: "orders:read orders:write"  → SCOPE_orders:read, SCOPE_orders:write
roles: ["OPS"]                     → ROLE_OPS
sub:   "C-1043221"                 → principal name

docs.title: 2.6 Scopes vs roles vs attributes
docs.text:
Model Question it answers Use Scope What is this client/token allowed to request? Per-token capability (orders:write) Role What is this user in the organization? Coarse organizational permission (ROLE_OPS) Attribute (ABAC) Does this specific resource belong to them? Ownership (seller_id, customer_id) — Chapter 17

Real endpoints usually need all three: a token with orders:write, a user who isn't blocked, and an order that belongs to them.

docs.title: 2.7 Refresh tokens
docs.text:
• Short access tokens (10–15 min) limit the damage of a leak.
  • Rotation: every refresh returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one.
  • Reuse detection: if an already-used refresh token appears again, the whole token family is revoked (someone cloned it).
  • Store only a hash of the refresh token, with device metadata for "log out other devices".

docs.title: 2.8 Revocation
docs.text: Need Mechanism Logout on one device Delete that refresh token family Stolen phone / account compromise Revoke all families + add active jtis to a denylist until their exp Employee offboarding Identity provider deactivation + short tokens Compromised signing key Rotate JWKS keys, remove the old kid

docs.title: 2.9 OAuth2 login for staff
docs.text: oauth2Login() performs the authorization-code flow with the corporate IdP, creating a session in the admin portal. Group/role claims from the IdP map to ROLE_* authorities.

docs.title: 2.10 Service-to-service: client credentials
docs.text:
order-service holds a client id/secret, requests a token with scope pricing:read, caches it until expiry, and attaches it to outbound calls. Spring Security's OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager does the acquisition and refresh; an interceptor attaches the header (Chapter 19).

Don't relay the customer's token blindly

Forwarding a customer access token to internal services makes every service a confused deputy — any service could use it anywhere. Use client credentials for service identity plus explicit context (customer id) in the request, or token exchange if delegation is genuinely required.

docs.title: 2.11 Webhook authentication
docs.text:
Webhooks are unauthenticated HTTP with a signature:

  1. Read the raw body bytes (never a re-serialized object).
  2. Compute HMAC-SHA256(secret, rawBody).
  3. Compare in constant time with the provider's header.
  4. Deduplicate by event id (idempotency).
  5. Respond 2xx quickly; process asynchronously.

docs.title: 2.12 Passkeys and one-time tokens
docs.text: Spring Security 6.4+ supports WebAuthn/passkeys (http.webAuthn(...)) and one-time token login (magic links). Passkeys remove passwords for the admin portal; one-time tokens are a good fallback and a clean "reset" path.

docs.title: 3.1 Bearer token validation
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Mobile app
    participant BF as BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter
    participant AM as ProviderManager → JwtAuthenticationProvider
    participant D as NimbusJwtDecoder
    participant JWKS as JWK set cache
    participant V as OAuth2TokenValidators
    participant C as JwtAuthenticationConverter

    App->>BF: Authorization: Bearer eyJ...
    BF->>AM: BearerTokenAuthenticationToken
    AM->>D: decode(token)
    D->>D: parse header → kid, alg
    D->>JWKS: public key for kid (cached, refetch on unknown kid)
    D->>D: verify signature
    D->>V: exp/nbf (with clock skew), iss, aud, custom
    alt invalid
        V-->>BF: JwtValidationException → 401 with WWW-Authenticate
    end
    D-->>AM: Jwt (claims)
    AM->>C: convert claims → authorities, principal
    AM-->>BF: JwtAuthenticationToken
    BF->>BF: set SecurityContext, continue chain
  • The JWK set is cached; an unknown kid triggers a refresh, which makes key rotation transparent as long as the old key stays published for the lifetime of old tokens.
  • Validation failures produce 401 with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" header — Chapter 17's entry point turns it into the platform problem format.

docs.title: 3.2 Authorization code + PKCE (customer app)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Customer app
    participant AS as Authorization server
    participant API as grocery API

    U->>U: generate code_verifier, code_challenge
    U->>AS: /oauth2/authorize?client_id&code_challenge&scope
    AS->>U: login (OTP) → consent → redirect with code
    U->>AS: /oauth2/token (code + code_verifier)
    AS-->>U: access_token (15m) + refresh_token (rotating)
    U->>API: Bearer access_token
    Note over U,AS: on 401: POST /oauth2/token grant_type=refresh_token

PKCE is mandatory for public clients (mobile/SPA) — there's no client secret that can be kept secret on a phone.

docs.title: 3.3 Client credentials
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[order-service] -->|client_id + secret, scope=pricing:read| B[Authorization server]
    B -->|access_token 5–15 min| A
    A -->|Authorization: Bearer ...| C[pricing-service]
    A -.->|cached until expiry<br/>OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager| A

docs.title: 4.1 A resource server in ten lines
4.2 Reading the token in a controller
4.3 Testing with a mock JWT
5.1 Level 2 — Strict validation: audience, issuer, clock skew, authorities
5.2 Level 2 — Customer context from the token
docs.text:
Chapter 08 read X-Customer-Id from a header (a placeholder). Now it comes from the verified token:

in/grocery/platform/web/CurrentCustomerArgumentResolver.java (token version)
@Override
public Object resolveArgument(MethodParameter parameter, ModelAndViewContainer mav,
                              NativeWebRequest request, WebDataBinderFactory binderFactory) {
    Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
    if (!(auth instanceof JwtAuthenticationToken jwtAuth)) {
        throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Customer token required");
    }
    Jwt jwt = jwtAuth.getToken();
    String pincode = request.getHeader("X-Pincode");                                                 // (1)!
    return new CustomerContext(jwt.getSubject(), pincode, jwt.getClaimAsString("channel"));
}
  1. The customer id is now unforgeable; the pincode remains a request hint (it's not a security claim — serviceability is validated server-side anyway).

Never trust identity headers from the network

X-Customer-Id was fine as a development placeholder behind a trusted gateway. In production, either the gateway strips and re-adds such headers with mTLS between it and the services, or (better) services validate tokens themselves — which is what we do here.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — OAuth2 login for the admin portal
5.4 Level 3 — Issuing tokens: OTP login with Spring Authorization Server
docs.text:
The identity-service is our authorization server. Customers authenticate with OTP (Chapter 17) and receive tokens with platform claims.

identity-service/build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server")
in/grocery/identity/config/AuthorizationServerConfig.java (excerpt)
@Bean
RegisteredClientRepository registeredClients(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    RegisteredClient mobileApp = RegisteredClient.withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
            .clientId("grocery-mobile")
            .clientAuthenticationMethod(ClientAuthenticationMethod.NONE)                      // (1)!
            .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.AUTHORIZATION_CODE)
            .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.REFRESH_TOKEN)
            .redirectUri("in.grocery.app://oauth2/callback")
            .scope("cart").scope("orders:read").scope("orders:write")
            .clientSettings(ClientSettings.builder().requireProofKey(true).build())            // (2)!
            .tokenSettings(TokenSettings.builder()
                    .accessTokenTimeToLive(Duration.ofMinutes(15))
                    .refreshTokenTimeToLive(Duration.ofDays(60))
                    .reuseRefreshTokens(false)                                                 // (3)!
                    .build())
            .build();

    RegisteredClient orderService = RegisteredClient.withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
            .clientId("order-service")
            .clientSecret(encoder.encode(System.getenv("ORDER_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET")))
            .clientAuthenticationMethod(ClientAuthenticationMethod.CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC)
            .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.CLIENT_CREDENTIALS)                  // (4)!
            .scope("pricing:read").scope("inventory:write")
            .tokenSettings(TokenSettings.builder().accessTokenTimeToLive(Duration.ofMinutes(10)).build())
            .build();

    return new InMemoryRegisteredClientRepository(mobileApp, orderService);                     // (5)!
}

@Bean
OAuth2TokenCustomizer<JwtEncodingContext> tokenCustomizer(CustomerDirectory customers) {
    return context -> {
        if (OAuth2TokenType.ACCESS_TOKEN.equals(context.getTokenType())) {
            context.getClaims().claim("aud", List.of("grocery-api"));                           // (6)!
            Authentication principal = context.getPrincipal();
            if (principal instanceof OtpAuthenticationToken otp) {
                context.getClaims().claim("channel", "mobile");
                context.getClaims().claim("roles", List.of("CUSTOMER"));
            }
        }
    };
}
  1. Public client — no secret on a phone.
  2. PKCE required.
  3. Rotating refresh tokens.
  4. Machine client for service-to-service.
  5. In production use a JDBC-backed repository so clients are configuration, not code.
  6. Audience so resource servers can verify the token is for them.

Key management: the JWKSource must be backed by persisted keys (not generated per start, or every restart invalidates all tokens), support two active keys during rotation, and publish both at /oauth2/jwks.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Refresh-token rotation with reuse detection
docs.text:
Spring Authorization Server rotates refresh tokens when reuseRefreshTokens(false) is set. Reuse detection — revoking a whole family when an old token reappears — is application logic worth adding for mobile apps:

in/grocery/identity/token/RefreshTokenFamilyService.java
package in.grocery.identity.token;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class RefreshTokenFamilyService {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("security-audit");

    public record Family(String familyId, String customerId, String deviceId, boolean revoked) {}

    private final RefreshTokenRepository tokens;
    private final TokenDenyList denyList;
    private final Clock clock;

    public RefreshTokenFamilyService(RefreshTokenRepository tokens, TokenDenyList denyList, Clock clock) {
        this.tokens = tokens;
        this.denyList = denyList;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    /** Called when a refresh token is presented. */
    public void onRefreshPresented(String tokenHash) {
        Optional<RefreshTokenRow> row = tokens.findByHash(tokenHash);
        if (row.isEmpty()) {
            throw new InvalidRefreshTokenException();
        }
        RefreshTokenRow token = row.get();
        if (token.usedAt() != null) {                                                          // (1)!
            log.warn("Refresh token reuse detected for family {} — revoking family", token.familyId());
            revokeFamily(token.familyId(), "reuse-detected");
            throw new InvalidRefreshTokenException();
        }
        tokens.markUsed(tokenHash, clock.instant());
    }

    public void revokeFamily(String familyId, String reason) {
        tokens.revokeFamily(familyId, clock.instant(), reason);
        tokens.activeAccessTokenIds(familyId)                                                   // (2)!
              .forEach(jti -> denyList.add(jti, Duration.ofMinutes(20)));
    }
}
  1. A used-but-not-rotated token means someone replayed a stolen copy — kill the whole family; the legitimate user simply logs in again.
  2. Outstanding access tokens can't be un-signed; deny them by jti until they expire.
in/grocery/platform/security/DenyListJwtValidator.java
package in.grocery.platform.security;

import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.OAuth2Error;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.OAuth2TokenValidator;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.OAuth2TokenValidatorResult;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;

/** Rejects access tokens whose jti has been revoked. Backed by Redis with TTL = token lifetime. */
public class DenyListJwtValidator implements OAuth2TokenValidator<Jwt> {

    private final TokenDenyList denyList;

    public DenyListJwtValidator(TokenDenyList denyList) {
        this.denyList = denyList;
    }

    @Override
    public OAuth2TokenValidatorResult validate(Jwt jwt) {
        String jti = jwt.getId();
        if (jti != null && denyList.contains(jti)) {                                            // (1)!
            return OAuth2TokenValidatorResult.failure(new OAuth2Error("invalid_token", "Token revoked", null));
        }
        return OAuth2TokenValidatorResult.success();
    }
}
  1. One Redis lookup per request. Keep the deny list small (only revoked tokens, TTL = remaining lifetime) and fail open or closed deliberately: if Redis is down, the platform choice is to fail open for reads and closed for writes — document it.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Multi-issuer (tenant or migration)
docs.text:
During a migration from a legacy identity provider, both issuers are valid for a while:

Multi-issuer (tenant or migration) (snippet)
@Bean
AuthenticationManagerResolver<HttpServletRequest> issuerResolver(JwtDecoder legacy, JwtDecoder current) {
    Map<String, AuthenticationManager> managers = Map.of(
            "https://legacy-id.grocery.in", new ProviderManager(new JwtAuthenticationProvider(legacy)),
            "https://id.grocery.in", new ProviderManager(new JwtAuthenticationProvider(current)));
    return new JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver(managers::get);                            // (1)!
}

// in the chain:
.oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.authenticationManagerResolver(issuerResolver))
  1. Routes by the iss claim. Only listed issuers are accepted — never resolve issuers dynamically from the token.

docs.title: 5.7 Level 3 — Passkeys and one-time tokens for staff
docs.text:
AdminAuthConfig.java (Security 6.4+)
http.webAuthn(webAuthn -> webAuthn
        .rpName("Grocery Admin")
        .rpId("admin.grocery.in")                                                                // (1)!
        .allowedOrigins("https://admin.grocery.in"))
    .oneTimeTokenLogin(ott -> ott
        .tokenGenerationSuccessHandler(emailOneTimeTokenHandler));                               // (2)!
  1. Passkeys are bound to the domain — phishing-resistant, which passwords and OTP SMS are not.
  2. Magic link sent by email as a fallback/recovery path. Tokens must be single-use, short-lived and rate-limited.

Verify

WebAuthn and one-time token APIs are recent (Security 6.4) and evolving in 7. Check the reference for required repositories (PublicKeyCredentialUserEntityRepository, UserCredentialRepository — implement persistent versions; the defaults are in-memory).

docs.title: 6.1 Razorpay webhook: signature, replay protection, fast ack
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant RZ as Razorpay
    participant W as WebhookController
    participant V as SignatureVerifier
    participant D as Dedupe store (Redis)
    participant Q as Processing (async/outbox)

    RZ->>W: POST /webhooks/razorpay (raw body + X-Razorpay-Signature)
    W->>V: verify(rawBody, signature)
    alt invalid
        V-->>RZ: 401 (logged, metered)
    end
    W->>D: setIfAbsent(event id, TTL 7d)
    alt duplicate
        W-->>RZ: 200 (already processed)
    end
    W->>Q: enqueue event (insert row / publish)
    W-->>RZ: 200 within ~100 ms
in/grocery/payment/webhook/RazorpaySignatureVerifier.java
package in.grocery.payment.webhook;

import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import javax.crypto.Mac;
import javax.crypto.spec.SecretKeySpec;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class RazorpaySignatureVerifier {

    private final byte[] secret;

    public RazorpaySignatureVerifier(in.grocery.payment.config.RazorpayProperties props) {
        this.secret = props.webhookSecret().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8);                    // (1)!
    }

    public boolean isValid(byte[] rawBody, String signatureHeader) {
        if (signatureHeader == null || rawBody == null) return false;
        try {
            Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
            mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256"));
            byte[] expected = mac.doFinal(rawBody);
            byte[] provided = hexToBytes(signatureHeader.trim());
            return provided != null && MessageDigest.isEqual(expected, provided);                 // (2)!
        } catch (Exception e) {
            return false;                                                                         // (3)!
        }
    }

    private static byte[] hexToBytes(String hex) {
        int len = hex.length();
        if (len % 2 != 0) return null;
        byte[] out = new byte[len / 2];
        for (int i = 0; i < len; i += 2) {
            int hi = Character.digit(hex.charAt(i), 16);
            int lo = Character.digit(hex.charAt(i + 1), 16);
            if (hi < 0 || lo < 0) return null;
            out[i / 2] = (byte) ((hi << 4) + lo);
        }
        return out;
    }
}
  1. The secret comes from a mounted file, trimmed (Chapter 06's trailing-newline trap) — a stray \n breaks every signature.
  2. Constant-time comparison: String.equals leaks timing information about how many bytes matched.
  3. Never distinguish "bad hex" from "bad signature" in the response — one 401 for all failures.
in/grocery/payment/webhook/RazorpayWebhookController.java
package in.grocery.payment.webhook;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;        // JsonMapper on Boot 4
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.time.Duration;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.http.ResponseEntity;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestHeader;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
class RazorpayWebhookController {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger("security-audit");

    private final RazorpaySignatureVerifier verifier;
    private final WebhookDedupeStore dedupe;
    private final WebhookIngestService ingest;
    private final ObjectMapper json;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    RazorpayWebhookController(RazorpaySignatureVerifier verifier, WebhookDedupeStore dedupe,
                              WebhookIngestService ingest, ObjectMapper json, MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.verifier = verifier;
        this.dedupe = dedupe;
        this.ingest = ingest;
        this.json = json;
        this.meters = meters;
    }

    @PostMapping(path = "/webhooks/razorpay", consumes = "application/json")
    ResponseEntity<Void> receive(@RequestBody byte[] rawBody,                                    // (1)!
                                 @RequestHeader(value = "X-Razorpay-Signature", required = false) String signature,
                                 @RequestHeader(value = "X-Razorpay-Event-Id", required = false) String eventId) {
        if (!verifier.isValid(rawBody, signature)) {
            meters.counter("grocery.webhook", "provider", "razorpay", "outcome", "invalid-signature").increment();
            log.warn("Rejected Razorpay webhook with invalid signature (event {})", eventId);
            return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED).build();
        }
        String id = eventId != null ? eventId : sha256Hex(rawBody);                              // (2)!
        if (!dedupe.firstTime(id, Duration.ofDays(7))) {
            meters.counter("grocery.webhook", "provider", "razorpay", "outcome", "duplicate").increment();
            return ResponseEntity.ok().build();                                                   // (3)!
        }
        ingest.accept(id, new String(rawBody, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));                            // (4)!
        meters.counter("grocery.webhook", "provider", "razorpay", "outcome", "accepted").increment();
        return ResponseEntity.ok().build();
    }
}
  1. Raw bytes — parsing to an object and re-serializing changes the bytes and breaks the HMAC. (@RequestBody byte[] works because Spring has a byte-array message converter.)
  2. Fall back to a body hash if the provider doesn't send an event id.
  3. Duplicates are normal: providers retry until they see a 2xx.
  4. Persist quickly (an inbox row), then process asynchronously — webhook endpoints must answer in milliseconds, not after a payment reconciliation.
RazorpayWebhookControllerTest.java
@WebMvcTest(RazorpayWebhookController.class)
@Import({SecurityChains.class, RazorpaySignatureVerifier.class})
class RazorpayWebhookControllerTest {

    private static final String SECRET = "whsec_test";

    @Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;
    @MockitoBean WebhookDedupeStore dedupe;
    @MockitoBean WebhookIngestService ingest;

    private static String sign(String body) throws Exception {
        Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
        mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(SECRET.getBytes(UTF_8), "HmacSHA256"));
        return HexFormat.of().formatHex(mac.doFinal(body.getBytes(UTF_8)));
    }

    @Test
    void validSignatureIsAccepted() throws Exception {
        given(dedupe.firstTime(any(), any())).willReturn(true);
        String body = "{\"event\":\"payment.captured\"}";

        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/webhooks/razorpay")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .header("X-Razorpay-Signature", sign(body))
                .header("X-Razorpay-Event-Id", "evt_1")
                .content(body))
                .hasStatusOk();
        then(ingest).should().accept(eq("evt_1"), any());
    }

    @Test
    void tamperedBodyIsRejected() throws Exception {
        String body = "{\"event\":\"payment.captured\"}";
        String signature = sign(body);

        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/webhooks/razorpay")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .header("X-Razorpay-Signature", signature)
                .content("{\"event\":\"payment.captured\",\"amount\":1}"))
                .hasStatus(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
        then(ingest).shouldHaveNoInteractions();
    }

    @Test
    void duplicateEventIsAcknowledgedWithoutProcessing() throws Exception {
        given(dedupe.firstTime(any(), any())).willReturn(false);
        String body = "{\"event\":\"payment.captured\"}";

        assertThat(mvc.post().uri("/webhooks/razorpay")
                .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .header("X-Razorpay-Signature", sign(body))
                .header("X-Razorpay-Event-Id", "evt_2")
                .content(body))
                .hasStatusOk();
        then(ingest).shouldHaveNoInteractions();
    }
}

docs.title: 6.2 Token architecture summary
docs.text: Token Lifetime Audience Claims Revocation Customer access 15 min grocery-api sub, scope, roles, channel, jti Deny list by jti Customer refresh 60 days, rotating authorization server opaque Family revocation, reuse detection Staff session 8 h idle admin portal — Session invalidation, IdP deactivation Service (client credentials) 10 min grocery-api sub=client id, scope Short lifetime; client secret rotation Webhook — — — Secret rotation (two active secrets during rollover)

docs.title: 6.3 Operational concerns
docs.text: Concern Practice Key rotation Two keys in JWKS; sign with the new one, keep the old until max token age passes; automate Secret rotation Support two valid webhook secrets/client secrets during rollover Clock skew NTP everywhere; 30 s validator leeway JWKS availability Cache with a long TTL; a JWKS outage must not fail all requests instantly (consider stale-while-error) Observability Metrics for auth failures by reason, token age at use, refresh rates, deny-list size Incident playbook "Compromised customer": revoke families + deny jti; "compromised client": rotate secret, revoke tokens; "compromised signing key": rotate JWKS, force re-login

docs.title: 6.4 Migration path for the platform
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Today: X-Customer-Id header<br/>(trusted gateway)"] --> B[Issue JWTs from identity-service<br/>gateway validates]
    B --> C[Services validate tokens themselves<br/>header ignored]
    C --> D[Seller API keys → client credentials]
    D --> E[Staff passwords → OIDC SSO + passkeys]

Each step is independently deployable and testable; the header is removed only after every service validates tokens.
