docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Pin and test the authorization server upgrade separately from resource servers (they can differ in version).
  • Verify audience/issuer validation still applies after upgrade (a silently dropped validator is invisible until an incident).
  • Re-run token tests with real signed tokens (not only mocked Jwts) in integration tests.
  • Check WebAuthn/one-time token APIs against the new reference.
  • Confirm JWKS caching behaviour and key rotation with a staged rotation drill.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Short access tokens, rotating refresh tokens, reuse detection; store hashes only.
  2. Validate issuer, audience, expiry (with small skew) and signature — all four, always.
  3. Map claims to authorities in one place; allow-list role mappings.
  4. Client credentials for service identity, not forwarded user tokens.
  5. Webhooks: raw-body HMAC, constant-time compare, dedupe, fast 2xx, async processing.
  6. Rotate keys and secrets on a schedule, with two valid values during rollover.
  7. Revocation plan (jti deny list + family revocation) and an incident runbook.
  8. No PII in claims; keep tokens small.
  9. Passkeys/SSO for staff; MFA for privileged roles.
  10. Test with real signed tokens in at least one integration test per service.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Long-lived access tokens ("30 days, simpler") — no practical revocation.

❌ Skipping audience validation — any token from the issuer works everywhere.

❌ alg: none or accepting the algorithm from the token header (use a decoder that pins algorithms; Nimbus does).

❌ Storing JWTs in localStorage for web clients (XSS) — prefer memory + refresh via secure cookie, or a BFF.

❌ Forwarding the customer's token to internal services.

❌ Verifying webhook signatures over re-serialized JSON.

❌ equals() for signature comparison.

❌ Generating signing keys at startup (all tokens die on restart; multiple pods sign with different keys).

❌ Putting the mobile number or address in claims.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix 401 with invalid_token and no detail Signature/issuer/audience/expiry failure Log the validation error server-side (not to the client); check clock, kid, audience Works locally, 401 in production Different issuer/JWKS, clock skew, secret mismatch Compare iss/aud, check NTP, verify secret mounts All tokens invalid after a restart Signing keys generated in memory Persist keys; JWKS with stable kid Random 401s after key rotation Old kid removed too early Keep old keys for max token lifetime Refresh loop / users logged out constantly Rotation without storing new token; reuse detection false positives (parallel refreshes) Serialize refresh per device; tolerate a short grace window Webhook always 401 Trailing newline in secret, re-serialized body, wrong encoding Trim secret, use raw bytes, hex vs base64 Duplicate order updates from webhooks No dedupe Event-id dedupe + idempotent processing Service-to-service 403 Missing scope on the client registration Add scope; verify authority prefix (SCOPE_)

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Issuer, audience, expiry, signature validated in every service
  • Access tokens ≤ 15 min; refresh tokens rotating with reuse detection
  • Deny list + family revocation implemented and exercised in a drill
  • JWKS keys persisted, rotation automated and rehearsed
  • Webhook secrets rotated; signature verification tested against tampering
  • No PII in claims (reviewed)
  • Auth metrics and alerts (failure spikes, deny-list growth)
  • Integration test using a real signed token per service

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is a JWT and is it encrypted?

Short answer: A signed, base64url-encoded token with header, claims and signature. It's signed, not encrypted — anyone can read the claims, so no secrets or PII belong there.

B1 · How do you turn a Spring Boot app into a resource server?

Short answer: Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server, set spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri, and enable oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(...)) in the filter chain.

B1 · Access token vs refresh token?

Short answer: The access token is short-lived and sent on every API call; the refresh token is long-lived, sent only to the authorization server to get new access tokens.

B1 · What is a scope?

Short answer: A capability granted to a token (orders:read). Spring maps the scope claim to SCOPE_* authorities.

B1 · Where does the token go in a request?

Short answer: The Authorization: Bearer <token> header.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you map custom claims to roles?

Short answer: A JwtAuthenticationConverter with a custom JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter that reads roles and prefixes ROLE_, combined with the default scope converter.

B2 · Why validate the audience claim?

Short answer: Otherwise a token issued for a different API of the same issuer is accepted — a privilege escalation across services.

B2 · JWT vs opaque tokens?

Short answer: JWTs validate locally (fast, no call) but are hard to revoke; opaque tokens require introspection but can be revoked instantly. Mitigate JWT revocation with short lifetimes and a jti deny list.

B2 · How does a service authenticate to another service?

Short answer: OAuth2 client credentials: the service holds a client id/secret, gets a token with the needed scope, caches it, and attaches it to outbound calls (OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager + interceptor).

B2 · How do you test a secured endpoint without a real token?

Short answer: spring-security-test's jwt() request post-processor (or @WithMockUser), plus at least one integration test with a genuinely signed token.

B2 · How should refresh tokens be stored server-side?

Short answer: Hashed, with family/device metadata, expiry and used-at timestamps — never in clear text.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through JWT validation in Spring Security.

Short answer: BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter extracts the token → JwtAuthenticationProvider → NimbusJwtDecoder parses the header, fetches the key by kid from the cached JWK set, verifies the signature, then runs validators (timestamp with skew, issuer, audience, custom) → converter builds authorities → context set.

B3 · How does key rotation work without downtime?

Short answer: Publish both old and new keys in the JWKS; sign new tokens with the new kid; decoders refresh the JWK set when they see an unknown kid; remove the old key only after the longest possible token lifetime.

B3 · How do you implement immediate revocation with JWTs?

Short answer: A jti deny list checked by a custom OAuth2TokenValidator, entries expiring with the token; plus refresh-token family revocation so no new access tokens are issued. Keep access-token lifetime short so the list stays small.

B3 · How do you verify a webhook signature correctly?

Short answer: HMAC over the raw request bytes with the shared secret, constant-time comparison, then dedupe by event id and process asynchronously. Never parse-then-re-serialize before verifying.

B3 · What is refresh-token reuse detection and why does it matter?

Short answer: Rotated refresh tokens are single-use; if an old one is presented again, either the user's copy or the attacker's was replayed — revoke the whole family. It limits the value of a stolen refresh token.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the token architecture for customers, staff, services and partners.

Short answer: Per-audience access tokens with scopes; OTP + PKCE authorization code for the mobile app with rotating refresh tokens; OIDC SSO (+ passkeys) with sessions for staff; client credentials for services; signed webhooks for partners; centralized claim mapping; documented lifetimes, rotation and revocation procedures.

B4 · Own authorization server or SaaS (Okta/Auth0/Keycloak)?

Short answer: SaaS buys compliance, MFA, threat detection and operations at a per-user cost and vendor lock-in; Spring Authorization Server gives full control over OTP/India-specific flows and data residency at the cost of running critical security infrastructure yourself. Many platforms use SaaS for staff and their own server for consumer flows.

B4 · How do you migrate 26 services from gateway-injected identity headers to token validation?

Short answer: Issue tokens first and have the gateway validate them while still setting headers; roll services over to token-based resolution one at a time behind a flag; monitor for services still reading the header; finally strip the header at the gateway and remove the code path.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What's your position on forwarding user tokens between services?

Short answer: Avoid it: it spreads user credentials widely and makes every service a confused deputy. Use service identity plus explicit user context; where true delegation is required (acting on behalf of a user in a third-party system), use token exchange with narrowly scoped, short-lived tokens.

B5 · How do you handle a suspected key or secret compromise at 2 a.m.?

Short answer: Rehearsed runbook: rotate the key/secret (both values valid during rollover), invalidate affected token families, populate the deny list, force re-authentication for impacted users, verify via metrics that old kid/secret traffic drops to zero, then post-mortem with detection improvements.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Orders marked paid without payment

The webhook endpoint parsed JSON first and verified the HMAC over the re-serialized body, so verification "worked" in tests but any body producing the same parsed object passed — and a misconfiguration made the check optional when the header was absent. Fixes: verify raw bytes, require the header, reject on any failure, add tamper tests (6.1), rotate the secret, reconcile affected orders against Razorpay.

Scenario · After a JWKS rotation, 30% of requests fail with 401

The old key was removed immediately while 15-minute tokens were still valid, and one service's decoder cached the JWK set for an hour without refreshing on unknown kid. Fixes: keep old keys for at least max token lifetime, ensure decoders refresh on unknown kid (Nimbus does, with rate limits), rehearse rotation in staging, alert on invalid_token spikes.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Scope + ownership for seller order access

Sellers call GET /api/sellers/{sellerId}/orders. Require: token audience grocery-api, scope orders:read, and seller_id claim matching the path. Implement the validator/converter configuration and a test using a signed token (not a mock) via a test JWK.

Solution TestTokens.java (integration-test helper)
public final class TestTokens {

    private static final RSAKey KEY = generate();                      // com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.RSAKey

    public static String jwks() { return new JWKSet(KEY.toPublicJWK()).toString(); }

    public static String sellerToken(String sellerId) throws JOSEException {
        JWTClaimsSet claims = new JWTClaimsSet.Builder()
                .issuer("https://id.test")
                .subject(sellerId)
                .audience("grocery-api")
                .claim("scope", "orders:read")
                .claim("seller_id", sellerId)
                .jwtID(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
                .issueTime(Date.from(Instant.now()))
                .expirationTime(Date.from(Instant.now().plusSeconds(300)))
                .build();
        SignedJWT jwt = new SignedJWT(new JWSHeader.Builder(JWSAlgorithm.RS256).keyID(KEY.getKeyID()).build(), claims);
        jwt.sign(new RSASSASigner(KEY));
        return jwt.serialize();
    }
}
SellerOrderAccessTest.java
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
@Import(ContainersConfig.class)
class SellerOrderAccessTest {

    static MockWebServer jwksServer;                                    // serves TestTokens.jwks()

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.jwk-set-uri",
                () -> jwksServer.url("/jwks").toString());
        r.add("grocery.token.issuer", () -> "https://id.test");
        r.add("grocery.token.audience", () -> "grocery-api");
    }

    @Autowired TestRestTemplate rest;

    @Test
    void ownSellerIsAllowed() throws Exception {
        var headers = new HttpHeaders();
        headers.setBearerAuth(TestTokens.sellerToken("S-1"));
        var response = rest.exchange("/api/sellers/S-1/orders", HttpMethod.GET, new HttpEntity<>(headers), String.class);
        assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.OK);
    }

    @Test
    void otherSellerIsForbidden() throws Exception {
        var headers = new HttpHeaders();
        headers.setBearerAuth(TestTokens.sellerToken("S-2"));
        var response = rest.exchange("/api/sellers/S-1/orders", HttpMethod.GET, new HttpEntity<>(headers), String.class);
        assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);
    }

    @Test
    void wrongAudienceIsUnauthorized() throws Exception { /* token with aud=analytics-api → 401 */ }
}

The chain reuses SellerAccess from Chapter 17 (.requestMatchers("/api/sellers/{sellerId}/**").access(sellerAccess)) with .hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders:read") composed via AuthorizationManagers.allOf(...). A signed-token test catches misconfigurations (missing audience validator, wrong claim name) that mocked Jwts never will.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Validate signature + issuer + audience + expiry on every token; audience is the one teams forget.
  • Short access tokens + rotating refresh tokens + reuse detection, with a jti deny list for immediate revocation.
  • Map claims to authorities once, in a platform converter; allow-list role mappings.
  • Client credentials for service identity; don't forward user tokens.
  • OIDC SSO and passkeys for staff; OTP + PKCE for consumers.
  • Webhooks: raw-body HMAC, constant-time compare, dedupe, fast 2xx, async processing.
  • Persist signing keys, rotate with overlap, rehearse it.
  • Test with real signed tokens at least once per service.

17 Spring Security Fundamentals · 19 HTTP Clients

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Every grocery service is also an HTTP client: order-service calls pricing and inventory, payment-service calls Razorpay, delivery-service calls a maps provider, notification-service calls an SMS gateway. Outbound calls are where most production latency and most cascading failures come from.

The failure pattern is always the same:

  1. A dependency slows from 80 ms to 4 s.
  2. Our calls have no timeout (or a 60 s default).
  3. Threads and database connections pile up waiting (Chapter 12, 16).
  4. Our service becomes unavailable — for endpoints that don't even use that dependency.

The fix is boring and mechanical: every outbound call has a connect timeout, a read timeout, a bounded connection pool, explicit error translation, and retries only where they're safe. Add observability (Chapter 27) and a circuit breaker (Chapter 26) and a slow dependency becomes a degraded feature instead of an outage.

Spring now offers three clients — RestClient (synchronous, modern), WebClient (reactive) and RestTemplate (maintenance) — plus HTTP interfaces, a declarative style that replaces Feign. Boot 4 adds HTTP service client groups that configure and register those interfaces for you.

This chapter builds the platform's outbound stack: a configured RestClient per dependency, declarative interfaces, timeouts and pools, error translation to the Chapter 10 exceptions, token propagation for service-to-service calls, a production Razorpay client with idempotency, and tests.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — RestClient basics, timeouts B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — HTTP interfaces, error handling, headers, testing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — request factories, pools, keep-alive, propagation B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — client platform design, timeout budgets, migration B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — inter-service communication strategy

docs.title: 2.1 Which client?
docs.text:
Client Style Status Use RestClient (Framework 6.1) Synchronous, fluent ✅ Default choice Everything blocking, including with virtual threads HTTP interfaces (@HttpExchange) Declarative, backed by RestClient/WebClient ✅ Preferred for typed clients Service-to-service APIs WebClient Reactive, non-blocking ✅ WebFlux services, streaming, high fan-out RestTemplate Synchronous, template 🟡 Maintenance Legacy code only Spring Cloud OpenFeign Declarative 🟡 Maintenance Migrate to HTTP interfaces

With virtual threads (Chapter 25), blocking RestClient calls scale well — the reactive stack is no longer required just for concurrency.

docs.title: 2.2 Request factories
docs.text:
RestClient/RestTemplate delegate the actual HTTP to a ClientHttpRequestFactory:

Factory Notes HttpComponentsClientHttpRequestFactory (Apache HttpClient 5) Best control: pooling, keep-alive, per-route limits, response timeout JdkClientHttpRequestFactory (JDK HttpClient) No extra dependency; HTTP/2; per-request timeout JettyClientHttpRequestFactory Jetty stack ReactorClientHttpRequestFactory Reactor Netty (blocking bridge) SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory HttpURLConnection; avoid

Boot picks one based on the classpath and lets you configure timeouts centrally with spring.http.client.* (Boot 3.4+).

docs.title: 2.3 Timeouts — the three that matter
docs.text:
Timeout Meaning Typical Connect TCP + TLS handshake 1–2 s Read / response Waiting for (the start of) the response Tight, per dependency Total / request Whole call including retries Budgeted

Timeout budget: if the incoming request must answer in 2 s, and there are two sequential downstream calls, each can have at most ~800 ms including retries. A downstream timeout larger than the caller's own timeout is always a bug.

docs.title: 2.4 Connection pools
docs.text:
HTTPS handshakes are expensive; pools reuse connections. Key settings (Apache HttpClient 5):

Setting Meaning maxTotal Connections across all routes maxPerRoute Connections per host — the one that actually limits a single dependency validateAfterInactivity Re-validate idle connections before use (stale sockets) timeToLive / keep-alive Retire connections before load balancers drop them connection-request timeout How long to wait for a pooled connection (fail fast!)

docs.title: 2.5 Error handling
docs.text:
RestClient throws by default for 4xx/5xx: HttpClientErrorException/HttpServerErrorException (subclasses of RestClientResponseException). Translate at the client boundary into platform exceptions (Chapter 10):

Downstream Platform exception 400/422 with known error code Domain exception (e.g. PaymentDeclinedException) 401/403 DependencyException (config problem — alert) 404 Often a domain "not found", sometimes an empty Optional 429 DependencyException with retry-after 5xx / timeout / connect failure DependencyException.unavailable/timeout

Never let a downstream error body reach our clients unchanged.

docs.title: 2.6 Retries — only where safe
docs.text:
Call Retry? GET (idempotent) ✅ on timeout/5xx/connect errors PUT/DELETE (idempotent by definition) ✅ with care POST creating something ❌ unless the API supports an idempotency key 4xx ❌ (except 429 with backoff)

Always use jittered exponential backoff, a small attempt count (2–3), and a total budget. Retries plus a circuit breaker prevent retry storms (Chapter 26).

docs.title: 2.7 Headers you should propagate
docs.text: Header Why traceparent (W3C) Distributed tracing — added automatically by Micrometer Tracing X-Request-Id Log correlation (Chapter 07) Authorization Service credentials (client credentials token, Chapter 18) Idempotency-Key For non-idempotent POSTs you must be able to retry Accept-Language Localized downstream errors

docs.title: 2.8 HTTP interfaces
3.1 A RestClient call
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Service
    participant RC as RestClient
    participant I as Interceptors / observation
    participant F as ClientHttpRequestFactory
    participant P as Connection pool
    participant D as Dependency

    S->>RC: get().uri("/prices/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(PriceResponse.class)
    RC->>I: apply interceptors (auth, headers, tracing)
    I->>F: createRequest(uri, method)
    F->>P: lease connection (connection-request timeout)
    P->>D: TCP/TLS if new, else reuse
    F->>D: request (connect + read timeouts apply)
    D-->>F: response
    RC->>RC: status handlers (onStatus / defaultStatusHandler)
    RC->>RC: message converter → PriceResponse
    RC-->>S: object (or translated exception)
    F->>P: release connection back to the pool
  • Observation wraps the call (http.client.requests timer with uri, method, status, outcome tags) when the client is built from Boot's auto-configured builder.
  • Interceptors see the request before the factory — the right place for auth and correlation headers.

docs.title: 3.2 How Boot configures the builder
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[HttpClientAutoConfiguration<br/>+ RestClientAutoConfiguration] --> B[ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder<br/>detects Apache / Jetty / JDK]
    B --> C[ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings<br/>spring.http.client.connect-timeout, read-timeout, redirects]
    A --> D[RestClient.Builder prototype bean]
    D --> E[RestClientCustomizer beans<br/>ordered]
    D --> F[Message converters from Jackson config]
    D --> G[ObservationRegistry for metrics/tracing]
    E --> H[Your per-dependency RestClient beans]

Inject RestClient.Builder (a prototype bean) and call build() per dependency — never RestClient.create(), which skips all of the above.

docs.title: 3.3 Timeouts and where they fire
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[lease connection] -->|connection-request timeout| B[connect]
    B -->|connect timeout| C[TLS handshake]
    C --> D[send request]
    D -->|read/response timeout| E[first byte of response]
    E -->|socket timeout per read| F[body streaming]

A dependency that accepts the connection and then stalls is caught by the read timeout, not the connect timeout. Both are required.

6.1 The Razorpay client

Requirements: basic auth from mounted secrets, tight timeouts, no retries on capture, idempotency on order creation, error translation to domain/dependency exceptions (Chapter 10), no secret ever logged, and metrics per operation.

in/grocery/payment/client/razorpay/RazorpayApi.java
package in.grocery.payment.client.razorpay;

import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestBody;
import org.springframework.web.service.annotation.GetExchange;
import org.springframework.web.service.annotation.HttpExchange;
import org.springframework.web.service.annotation.PostExchange;

@HttpExchange
public interface RazorpayApi {

    record OrderRequest(long amount, String currency, String receipt, Map<String, String> notes) {}
    record OrderResponse(String id, long amount, String currency, String status, String receipt) {}
    record PaymentResponse(String id, String orderId, long amount, String status, String method,
                           String errorCode, String errorReason) {}
    record RefundRequest(long amount, Map<String, String> notes) {}
    record RefundResponse(String id, String paymentId, long amount, String status) {}

    @PostExchange("/v1/orders")
    OrderResponse createOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest request);

    @GetExchange("/v1/payments/{paymentId}")
    PaymentResponse payment(@PathVariable String paymentId);

    @PostExchange("/v1/payments/{paymentId}/refund")
    RefundResponse refund(@PathVariable String paymentId, @RequestBody RefundRequest request);
}
in/grocery/payment/client/razorpay/RazorpayClientConfig.java
package in.grocery.payment.client.razorpay;

import in.grocery.payment.config.RazorpayProperties;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.util.Base64;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpHeaders;
import org.springframework.http.client.ClientHttpRequestFactory;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;
import org.springframework.web.client.support.RestClientAdapter;
import org.springframework.web.service.invoker.HttpServiceProxyFactory;

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class RazorpayClientConfig {

    @Bean
    RestClient razorpayRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, RazorpayProperties props,
                                  ClientHttpRequestFactory pooledRequestFactory,
                                  RazorpayErrorHandler errorHandler) {
        String basic = Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString(
                (props.keyId() + ":" + props.keySecret()).getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));   // (1)!
        return builder
                .baseUrl(props.baseUrl().toString())
                .requestFactory(pooledRequestFactory)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION, "Basic " + basic)
                .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.USER_AGENT, "grocery-payment-service")
                .defaultStatusHandler(errorHandler)                                            // (2)!
                .build();
    }

    @Bean
    RazorpayApi razorpayApi(RestClient razorpayRestClient) {
        return HttpServiceProxyFactory
                .builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(razorpayRestClient))
                .build()
                .createClient(RazorpayApi.class);
    }
}
  1. Credentials from the config tree (Chapter 06), never logged; RazorpayProperties.toString() masks them.
  2. Central error translation (next).
in/grocery/payment/client/razorpay/RazorpayErrorHandler.java
package in.grocery.payment.client.razorpay;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;        // JsonMapper on Boot 4
import in.grocery.payment.client.RazorpayErrorTranslator;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import org.slf4j.Logger;
import org.slf4j.LoggerFactory;
import org.springframework.http.client.ClientHttpResponse;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.ResponseErrorHandler;

@Component
class RazorpayErrorHandler implements ResponseErrorHandler {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(RazorpayErrorHandler.class);

    private final ObjectMapper json;

    RazorpayErrorHandler(ObjectMapper json) {
        this.json = json;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean hasError(ClientHttpResponse response) throws IOException {
        return response.getStatusCode().isError();
    }

    @Override
    public void handleError(ClientHttpResponse response) throws IOException {
        int status = response.getStatusCode().value();
        String body = new String(response.getBody().readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8);
        String errorCode = null;
        String reason = null;
        try {
            var node = json.readTree(body).path("error");
            errorCode = node.path("code").asText(null);
            reason = node.path("reason").asText(null);
        } catch (Exception ignored) {
            // non-JSON error body (gateway HTML page) — treat as unavailable
        }
        log.warn("Razorpay error status={} code={} reason={}", status, errorCode, reason);      // (1)!
        throw RazorpayErrorTranslator.translate(status, errorCode, reason);                     // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Log the classification, not the body (it can contain customer contact details).
  2. Reuses Chapter 10's translator: known declines → PaymentDeclinedException (422), everything else → DependencyException (503/504).
in/grocery/payment/service/RazorpayGatewayAdapter.java
package in.grocery.payment.service;

import in.grocery.payment.client.razorpay.RazorpayApi;
import in.grocery.platform.error.DependencyException;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Timer;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.client.ResourceAccessException;

@Component
public class RazorpayGatewayAdapter implements in.grocery.payment.gateway.PaymentGateway {

    private final RazorpayApi api;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    public RazorpayGatewayAdapter(RazorpayApi api, MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.api = api;
        this.meters = meters;
    }

    @Override
    public String code() {
        return "RAZORPAY";
    }

    @Override
    public String createOrder(String orderRef, BigDecimal amountInRupees) {
        Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(meters);
        String outcome = "success";
        try {
            var response = api.createOrder(new RazorpayApi.OrderRequest(
                    amountInRupees.movePointRight(2).longValueExact(),                          // paise
                    "INR",
                    orderRef,                                                                    // (1)!
                    Map.of("order_ref", orderRef)));
            return response.id();
        } catch (ResourceAccessException networkOrTimeout) {                                    // (2)!
            outcome = "timeout";
            throw DependencyException.timeout("razorpay", networkOrTimeout);
        } catch (RuntimeException e) {
            outcome = "failure";
            throw e;
        } finally {
            sample.stop(Timer.builder("grocery.gateway.call")
                    .tag("gateway", "RAZORPAY").tag("operation", "createOrder").tag("outcome", outcome)
                    .publishPercentileHistogram()
                    .register(meters));
        }
    }
}
  1. receipt is our order reference — Razorpay treats it as a natural key, so a retried creation returns the same order instead of a duplicate. That's what makes a retry safe here; the platform's own idempotency aspect (Chapter 04) covers the rest of the flow.
  2. Connect failures, read timeouts and DNS problems surface as ResourceAccessException — translate them distinctly so dashboards can separate "gateway slow" from "gateway rejected".

docs.title: 6.2 Timeout budget for checkout
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Mobile app<br/>timeout 8 s"] --> B["Gateway<br/>timeout 6 s"]
    B --> C["order-service<br/>budget 5 s"]
    C --> D["pricing 600 ms<br/>×2 attempts"]
    C --> E["inventory 500 ms"]
    C --> F["razorpay 3 s<br/>no retry"]
    C --> G["DB transactions<br/>≤ 500 ms"]

Rules encoded in the platform:

Rule Value Sum of downstream worst cases + DB < caller budget checked in review Client timeout < caller's remaining budget always Retries counted in the worst case always Payment calls never retried automatically; reconciled asynchronously Timeout properties per dependency, in configuration, not hard-coded

docs.title: 6.3 Platform client library
6.4 Testing the production client
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace RestTemplate with RestClient (same request factories, same interceptors).
  • Convert hand-written clients to HTTP interfaces; adopt Boot 4 groups once on 4.x.
  • Move timeouts from code into spring.http.client.* / per-group properties.
  • Migrate OpenFeign clients: @FeignClient → @HttpExchange interface + RestClient (error decoders → status handlers, Feign retryer → explicit retry).
  • Re-verify timeout and pool settings after factory API changes; add an integration test with a delayed stub.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. One configured client bean per dependency, built from Boot's builder — never RestClient.create().
  2. Connect + read + connection-request timeouts on every client, tuned per dependency and inside the caller's budget.
  3. Bounded pool with maxPerRoute, idle validation and TTL; fail fast when exhausted.
  4. Translate errors at the boundary into platform exceptions; never forward downstream bodies.
  5. Retry only idempotent operations, at one layer, with jitter and a circuit breaker.
  6. Propagate trace, correlation and service credentials via interceptors.
  7. Idempotency keys (or natural keys) for non-idempotent POSTs you might retry.
  8. Metrics per dependency and operation (http.client.requests + your own), alert on error rate and p99.
  9. Declarative HTTP interfaces for typed clients; keep DTOs separate from your domain.
  10. Test error paths and timeouts, not only the happy path.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ No timeouts (defaults are effectively infinite for some factories).

❌ RestClient.create() / new RestTemplate() — no observability, no converters, no customizers.

❌ Building a client inside the method that calls it — new pool, new TLS handshake per call.

❌ Retrying POST /payments/capture — double charges.

❌ Retrying at gateway and service and client.

❌ Passing downstream error bodies to customers (leaks internals, couples clients).

❌ Calling downstream services inside a database transaction (Chapter 16).

❌ Logging request/response bodies of payment or identity calls.

❌ Unbounded parallel fan-out (1,000 SKUs → 1,000 concurrent calls) without a bulkhead.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Latency spikes with no downstream errors Pool exhaustion (queuing for a connection) Raise maxPerRoute deliberately, shorten timeouts, add bulkhead ResourceAccessException: Read timed out Downstream slow Check budget; circuit breaker; is the timeout right? Connection reset by peer after idle periods Stale pooled connections validateAfterInactivity, TTL below LB idle timeout Retries multiply load during incidents Retries at several layers Single retry layer + circuit breaker Duplicate orders/refunds Retrying non-idempotent POST Idempotency key or natural key; disable retries 401 from an internal service Token not attached/expired OAuth2 interceptor; check registration id and scopes Missing traces across services Client not built from Boot's builder Use the injected builder IllegalStateException: Cannot use a builder after build() Reusing a mutated builder clone() per client Works in tests, fails in cluster DNS/keep-alive/proxy differences Test with WireMock + delays; check service mesh timeouts

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every outbound dependency has a named client bean with timeouts and pool settings
  • Timeout budget documented per endpoint and reviewed
  • Error translation covers 4xx/5xx/timeout/connect
  • Retry policy explicit (and absent for payments)
  • Idempotency keys where retries are possible
  • Trace/correlation/auth headers propagated
  • Metrics and alerts per dependency; pool metrics exposed
  • Timeout and error-path tests exist

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Which HTTP client should new Spring code use?

Short answer: RestClient for synchronous calls (or an HTTP interface backed by it); WebClient for reactive/streaming. RestTemplate is in maintenance.

B1 · Why inject RestClient.Builder instead of creating a client directly?

Short answer: Boot's builder carries message converters, timeouts, customizers and observability; RestClient.create() has none of that.

B1 · Which timeouts must you set?

Short answer: Connect and read (plus connection-request when pooling). Without them a slow dependency blocks threads indefinitely.

B1 · How do you pass path and query parameters safely?

Short answer: URI templates with variables (uri("/prices/{sku}?pincode={p}", sku, p)) — Spring encodes them.

B1 · What happens on a 404 by default with RestClient?

Short answer: retrieve() throws HttpClientErrorException.NotFound unless you register a status handler.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · What is an HTTP interface and why prefer it to Feign?

Short answer: A Java interface annotated with @HttpExchange whose proxy is backed by RestClient/WebClient — part of Spring Framework, same configuration and observability as other clients. Spring Cloud OpenFeign is in maintenance.

B2 · How do you map downstream errors to your own?

Short answer: defaultStatusHandler/onStatus on the client (or a ResponseErrorHandler) translating status and error codes into domain or dependency exceptions — never forwarding the raw body.

B2 · Which calls are safe to retry?

Short answer: Idempotent ones (GET, PUT, DELETE) on timeouts/5xx/connect errors, with jittered backoff; non-idempotent POSTs only with an idempotency key or natural key.

B2 · How do you attach a service token to outbound calls?

Short answer: Spring Security's OAuth2 client (OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager) with the RestClient interceptor for client-credentials tokens; it caches and refreshes automatically.

B2 · How do you test an HTTP client?

Short answer: @RestClientTest + MockRestServiceServer for request/response expectations and error mapping; WireMock for delays, faults and full-stack behaviour.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · What's the difference between connect, read and connection-request timeouts?

Short answer: Connect covers establishing TCP/TLS; read covers waiting for response data; connection-request covers waiting for a pooled connection. Pool exhaustion shows up as the third and is invisible if it's unset.

B3 · How do you size an HTTP connection pool?

Short answer: maxPerRoute ≈ expected concurrent calls to that host (throughput × latency, Little's law), bounded by the dependency's capacity; keep total sane across dependencies; watch lease wait time and adjust.

B3 · Why do idle pooled connections cause 'connection reset'?

Short answer: Load balancers/NATs drop idle connections silently; a later request on that socket fails. Fix with idle validation, TTL shorter than the infrastructure's idle timeout and eviction.

B3 · How does observability work for outbound calls?

Short answer: Clients built from Boot's builder create Micrometer observations — http.client.requests timer with method/uri/status/outcome tags — and tracing propagates traceparent headers automatically.

B3 · How do timeout budgets work across a call chain?

Short answer: Each hop gets a share of the caller's remaining deadline, including retries; downstream timeouts must be strictly smaller than upstream ones, otherwise the caller gives up first and the work is wasted.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the outbound client platform for 26 services.

Short answer: A shared library providing configured clients (timeouts, pools, interceptors, error translation, metrics), HTTP interfaces per dependency, per-dependency properties, documented timeout budgets, retry/circuit-breaker policy, and contract tests with consumers.

B4 · When is a service mesh the better place for retries and timeouts?

Short answer: A mesh gives uniform, language-agnostic policy and mTLS, but doesn't know semantics (is this POST idempotent?) and duplicates in-app policy if both are enabled. Common split: mesh for connection-level concerns and mTLS; app for semantic retries, idempotency and error translation — never both retrying.

B4 · How do you migrate 40 Feign clients?

Short answer: Interface-by-interface to @HttpExchange with RestClient, mapping decoders to status handlers, Feign retryer to explicit policy, and Ribbon/LoadBalancer to service DNS or spring-cloud-loadbalancer; keep both temporarily behind a flag with contract tests comparing behaviour.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · Synchronous HTTP, messaging or gRPC between services?

Short answer: Synchronous HTTP for request/response with a user waiting; messaging for work that can be asynchronous (and to decouple availability); gRPC for high-volume internal RPC with schemas. Prefer async wherever the user doesn't need the result now — it removes latency coupling entirely.

B5 · How do you prevent a slow dependency from becoming an outage?

Short answer: Timeout budgets, bounded pools and bulkheads, circuit breakers with fallbacks, degradation paths (cached prices, default delivery fee), retries at one layer, load shedding at the gateway, and chaos/latency tests to prove it works.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Pricing slows to 3 s; checkout goes down completely

order-service had no read timeout, so request threads and their database connections waited; the pool emptied and unrelated endpoints failed. Fixes: 600 ms read timeout with 2 attempts, connection-request timeout 200 ms, circuit breaker with a cached-price fallback, move the pricing call out of the transaction, and alert on http.client.requests p99 per dependency.

Scenario · Customers charged twice during a network blip

The payment adapter retried createOrder and the capture call on ResourceAccessException. Order creation was safe (Razorpay dedupes by receipt), capture was not. Fixes: disable retries on capture, reconcile with the gateway asynchronously, add idempotency keys end to end, and add a test asserting no retry on non-idempotent operations.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Inventory client with a fallback

Build an InventoryApi HTTP interface (GET /api/stock/{sku}?hub=...), a RestClient with 400 ms read timeout and pooled factory, error translation (404 → Optional.empty(), 5xx/timeout → DependencyException), one retry for timeouts, and a service method that falls back to "assume available" for non-perishable categories when the dependency is down. Test all four paths.

Solution InventoryApi.java
@HttpExchange("/api/stock")
public interface InventoryApi {
    record StockResponse(String sku, String hub, int available) {}

    @GetExchange("/{sku}")
    StockResponse stock(@PathVariable String sku, @RequestParam String hub);
}
InventoryClientConfig.java
@Bean
RestClient inventoryRestClient(RestClient.Builder builder, ClientHttpRequestFactory pooledRequestFactory,
                               InventoryProperties props) {
    return builder
            .baseUrl(props.baseUrl())
            .requestFactory(pooledRequestFactory)
            .defaultStatusHandler(HttpStatusCode::isError, (req, res) -> {
                if (res.getStatusCode().value() == 404) throw new StockNotFoundException(req.getURI().getPath());
                throw DependencyException.unavailable("inventory-service", null);
            })
            .build();
}

@Bean
InventoryApi inventoryApi(RestClient inventoryRestClient) {
    return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(inventoryRestClient))
            .build().createClient(InventoryApi.class);
}
InventoryLookupService.java
@Service
public class InventoryLookupService {

    private final InventoryApi inventory;
    private final RetryTemplate retry;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    public Optional<Integer> available(String sku, String hub) {
        try {
            return retry.execute(ctx -> Optional.of(inventory.stock(sku, hub).available()));   // retries timeouts
        } catch (StockNotFoundException e) {
            return Optional.empty();
        }
    }

    /** Degrade gracefully: non-perishables are assumed available if inventory is down. */
    public boolean isPurchasable(String sku, String hub, boolean perishable) {
        try {
            return available(sku, hub).orElse(0) > 0;
        } catch (DependencyException e) {
            meters.counter("grocery.inventory.fallback", "perishable", String.valueOf(perishable)).increment();
            if (perishable) throw e;                                                            // never guess for fresh items
            return true;                                                                        // reconciled at reservation
        }
    }
}
InventoryLookupServiceTest.java (paths)
@Test void returnsQuantity() { /* 200 → Optional.of(12) */ }
@Test void missingSkuIsEmpty() { /* 404 → Optional.empty() */ }
@Test void serverErrorPropagatesForPerishables() { /* 500 → DependencyException */ }
@Test void nonPerishableFallsBackToPurchasable() { /* 500 → true, counter incremented */ }

The fallback is a business decision (risk of overselling shelf-stable goods vs blocking checkout) — document it, meter it, and reconcile at reservation time.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• RestClient + HTTP interfaces are the modern stack; RestTemplate and Feign are legacy.
  • Build clients from Boot's builder so they get converters, customizers and observability.
  • Timeouts and bounded pools on every dependency, fitting a documented timeout budget.
  • Translate errors at the boundary; never forward downstream bodies.
  • Retry only idempotent calls, at one layer, with jitter — pair with a circuit breaker.
  • Propagate trace, correlation and service tokens; use idempotency keys for risky POSTs.
  • Boot 4 adds HTTP service client groups — declarative registration plus per-group properties.
  • Test error paths and timeouts, not just the happy path.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Framework Reference — Web › REST Clients (RestClient, WebClient, HTTP interfaces, RestTemplate)
  • Spring Boot Reference — Web › Calling REST Services; HTTP Clients (spring.http.client.*, request factories, service groups)
  • Spring Security Reference — OAuth2 Client › RestClient integration
  • Apache HttpClient 5 documentation — connection management and timeouts

18 Tokens, OAuth2 & Modern Auth · 20 API Design & Versioning

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
The grocery platform's APIs are consumed by an Angular web app, a Flutter mobile app installed on millions of phones, 26 internal services, seller integrations and partner marketplaces. Two facts follow:

  1. You cannot force clients to upgrade. A Flutter build from eight months ago is still calling POST /api/orders during the Diwali sale.
  2. Every design decision becomes permanent. A field named total that sometimes includes delivery fee will be encoded in four client codebases within a week.

Good API design is therefore mostly about evolution: making additive changes easy, breaking changes visible and rare, and giving clients the signals (versions, deprecation headers, error codes) they need to adapt on their own schedule.

This chapter pulls together the conventions used throughout the handbook — resources and status codes (Chapter 08), validation errors and problem details (Chapters 09, 10), idempotency (Chapter 04), ETags and conditional requests (Chapter 08), pagination (Chapter 13) — into a platform API standard, then covers versioning (including Spring Framework 7's built-in support), deprecation with Deprecation/Sunset headers, OpenAPI documentation, a generated error catalog, rate-limit signalling, and CI checks that catch breaking changes before they ship.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — resource naming, status codes, OpenAPI basics B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — pagination, filtering, bulk endpoints, documentation B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — versioning mechanics, compatibility rules B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — platform standards, deprecation programme, CI gates B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — API governance and product thinking

docs.title: 2.1 Resource design
docs.text: Rule Example Plural nouns for collections /api/orders, /api/products Identify resources by a business reference, not a database id /api/orders/ORD-7F3A91C2 Nest only for true containment (one level) /api/carts/{cartId}/items/{sku} Verbs only for genuine actions that aren't CRUD POST /api/orders/{ref}/cancellations Query parameters for filtering/sorting/pagination ?category=dairy&sort=price,asc&size=20 kebab-case in paths, camelCase in JSON /api/delivery-slots → {"slotId": ...} No response envelope return the resource; metadata in headers or a page wrapper

docs.title: 2.2 The platform's non-negotiables
docs.text: Concern Standard Chapter Errors RFC 9457 problem details + code, traceId 10 Validation errors errors[] with field, code, message 09, 10 Creation 201 + Location 08 Concurrency strong ETag + If-Match (428/412) 08 Idempotency Idempotency-Key on money-moving POSTs 04 Pagination page/size or opaque cursor, capped 08, 13 Money decimal strings; paise integers at gateways 11 Time ISO-8601, Instant/OffsetDateTime 11 Enums open — clients tolerate unknown values 11 Auth Bearer tokens, scopes + ownership 17, 18 Rate limits RateLimit-* / Retry-After headers 26

docs.title: 2.3 Compatible vs breaking changes
docs.text:
Change Compatible? Add an optional request field ✅ Add a response field ✅ (clients must ignore unknown fields) Add a new endpoint / enum value ✅ (enums: only if clients tolerate unknowns) Relax a validation rule ✅ Make an optional request field required ❌ Remove or rename a field ❌ Change a field's type or format (289.00 → 28900) ❌ Change status codes or error code meanings ❌ Tighten validation ❌ (in practice) Change pagination defaults ⚠️ often breaking in effect

Tolerant reader on both sides makes most evolution free: ignore unknown fields (Boot's default), never assume field order, treat enums as open.

docs.title: 2.4 Versioning strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Example Pros Cons URI path /api/v1/orders Visible, cacheable, trivially routable Version leaks into every URL; duplicated routes Header X-API-Version: 2 Clean URLs, per-request Invisible in logs/browsers unless logged Media type Accept: application/vnd.grocery.v2+json HTTP-native content negotiation Awkward for clients and tooling Query param ?v=2 Easy to test Pollutes caching, easy to forget No versioning, additive only — Simplest Only works while you never need a breaking change

Platform choice: major version in the path for the public API (visible, easy to route and monitor) and Framework 7's built-in versioning for fine-grained minor versions within a major — with additive evolution as the default so versions stay rare.

docs.title: 2.5 Framework 7 API versioning
docs.text:
Spring Framework 7 (Boot 4) adds first-class versioning to Spring MVC and WebFlux:

Framework 7 API versioning (snippet)
configurer.useRequestHeader("X-API-Version");   // or usePathSegment(n) / useQueryParam("v") / useMediaTypeParameter(...)

Handler methods then declare a version:

Framework 7 API versioning (snippet)
@GetMapping(path = "/{cartId}", version = "1")     // exactly version 1
@GetMapping(path = "/{cartId}", version = "1.2+")  // 1.2 and later (baseline)

Requests with an unsupported version are rejected before reaching a handler. Clients built with RestClient/WebClient can set a default API version too.

Verify

This API is new. Confirm configuration method names, the version attribute syntax ("1.2+"), default/required version settings, the exception types for unsupported versions, and any spring.mvc.apiversion.* properties in the Framework 7 / Boot 4 reference before standardizing on them.

docs.title: 2.6 Deprecation signalling
docs.text:
Header Meaning Spec Deprecation: @1789552800 or true The resource/version is deprecated (with a timestamp) RFC 9745 Sunset: Sat, 01 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT When it stops working RFC 8594 Link: <https://docs.grocery.in/api/migrations/v2>; rel="deprecation" Migration guide RFC 8288 Warning (legacy) Free-text notice obsolete — prefer the above

Headers alone don't retire an API; a deprecation programme (telemetry per client/version, direct outreach, deadlines) does.

docs.title: 2.7 Documentation: code-first vs contract-first
docs.text:
Code-first (springdoc) Contract-first (OpenAPI file) Source of truth Java code openapi.yaml in Git Drift risk Low (generated) Needs generation/verification Design review After code Before code Client SDKs Generated from the generated spec Generated from the spec

Platform approach: code-first with springdoc, but the generated spec is committed and diffed in CI, which gives contract-first's review benefits without maintaining two artefacts.

docs.title: 2.8 Pagination, filtering, sorting — the contract
docs.text:
Example
GET /api/products?category=dairy&minPrice=20&maxPrice=100&sort=price,asc&page=0&size=20
GET /api/orders?cursor=eyJwbGFjZWRBdCI6...&size=20
Rule Detail Cap size max-page-size: 100, documented Whitelist sort fields reject others with 400 Deep lists use cursors opaque, forward-only Page response shape is stable items, page, size, totalItems, totalPages, hasNext (Chapter 08) Filters are AND-combined, optional absent = no restriction

docs.title: 2.9 Bulk endpoints
docs.text:
For "price 200 SKUs" or "update 500 stock rows", a per-item loop over HTTP is wasteful. Design bulk endpoints with per-item results:

JSON
POST /api/prices/bulk        →  200 OK
{
  "results": [
    {"sku": "MILK-1L", "status": "OK", "price": "66.00"},
    {"sku": "NOPE-1",  "status": "NOT_FOUND", "code": "PRODUCT_NOT_FOUND"}
  ]
}

Bound the batch size (e.g. 500), keep the overall status 200 when the request itself was valid, and give each item its own status and error code.

docs.title: 2.10 Rate limiting signals
docs.text:
When throttling (Chapter 26), tell the client what happened:

Example
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
RateLimit-Limit: 100
RateLimit-Remaining: 0
RateLimit-Reset: 42
Retry-After: 42

Plus a problem body with code: RATE_LIMITED so the app can back off instead of hammering.

docs.title: 3.1 Version resolution in Framework 7
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Request] --> B[ApiVersionStrategy resolves the version<br/>header / path segment / query / media type]
    B --> C{version present?}
    C -- no --> D{default version configured?}
    D -- no & required --> E[400 — missing API version]
    D -- yes --> F[use default]
    C -- yes --> G{supported version?}
    G -- no --> H[400 / 404 — unsupported version]
    G -- yes --> I[RequestMappingHandlerMapping<br/>matches version condition]
    I --> J{fixed 'v' or baseline 'v+'}
    J --> K[most specific matching handler wins]

The version becomes another request condition alongside path, method, params, headers, consumes and produces — so two handlers can share a path and differ only by version.

docs.title: 3.2 How springdoc builds the OpenAPI document
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[springdoc starter] --> B[Scan RequestMappingHandlerMapping]
    B --> C["Read @Operation, @Schema, @Parameter,<br/>Jakarta validation constraints, Jackson annotations"]
    C --> D[Build OpenAPI model]
    D --> E["/v3/api-docs (JSON) & /v3/api-docs.yaml"]
    D --> F["Swagger UI at /swagger-ui.html"]
    G["OpenApiCustomizer / OperationCustomizer beans"] --> D

Validation annotations become schema constraints (minimum, maxLength, pattern), and @JsonProperty/@JsonNaming shape property names — which is why Chapters 09 and 11 are prerequisites for good documentation.

docs.title: 4.1 Add OpenAPI
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui:2.8.x")   // verify version for Boot 4
application.yml
springdoc:
  api-docs:
    path: /v3/api-docs
  swagger-ui:
    path: /swagger-ui.html
    operations-sorter: method
---
spring.config.activate.on-profile: prod
springdoc:
  swagger-ui:
    enabled: false          # (1)!
  1. Serve the spec to internal tooling, but don't expose an interactive UI publicly (it's also an information-disclosure surface). Some teams publish the UI on the management port or an internal portal instead.

docs.title: 4.2 Documenting an endpoint
4.3 The generated spec
docs.text:
Terminal
curl -s localhost:8082/v3/api-docs.yaml | head -40
Configuration
openapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: cart-service
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /api/v1/carts/{cartId}/items:
    post:
      tags: [Cart]
      summary: Add an item to the cart
      requestBody:
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              $ref: '#/components/schemas/AddItemRequest'
components:
  schemas:
    AddItemRequest:
      type: object
      properties:
        sku:
          type: string
          pattern: "[A-Z0-9-]{3,40}"      # from @Pattern (Chapter 09)
        quantity:
          type: integer
          minimum: 1
          maximum: 20
      required: [sku, quantity]

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Shared OpenAPI components
5.2 Level 2 — Documenting idempotency and concurrency headers
5.3 Level 2 — Bulk pricing endpoint
5.4 Level 3 — Introducing version 2 of an endpoint
docs.text:
The cart response changes total (which included delivery) into subtotal + deliveryFee + total — a breaking change for clients that summed lines themselves.

Boot 3.5 — path versioning with a shared serviceBoot 4 — built-in versioning CartV1Controller.java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/carts")
class CartV1Controller {

    private final CartDelegate delegate;

    @GetMapping("/{cartId}")
    ResponseEntity<CartViewV1> get(@PathVariable String cartId, @CurrentCustomer CustomerContext customer) {
        CartView view = delegate.getCartFor(customer.customerId(), cartId);
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .eTag("\"" + view.version() + "\"")
                .header("Deprecation", "@1793491200")                                  // (1)!
                .header("Sunset", "Sun, 01 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT")
                .header("Link", "<https://docs.grocery.in/api/migrations/cart-v2>; rel=\"deprecation\"")
                .body(CartViewV1.from(view));                                           // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Machine-readable deprecation (RFC 9745) and sunset (RFC 8594) dates.
  2. V1 DTO built from the same domain view — one implementation, two representations.
ApiVersionConfig.java
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class ApiVersionConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
    @Override
    public void configureApiVersioning(ApiVersionConfigurer configurer) {
        configurer.useRequestHeader("X-API-Version")
                  .addSupportedVersions("1", "2")
                  .setDefaultVersion("1");                                              // (1)!
    }
}
CartController.java
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/carts")
class CartController {

    @GetMapping(path = "/{cartId}", version = "1")
    ResponseEntity<CartViewV1> getV1(...) { ... }

    @GetMapping(path = "/{cartId}", version = "2")
    ResponseEntity<CartViewV2> getV2(...) { ... }
}
  1. Old clients that send no version keep getting v1. Verify these APIs against the Framework 7 reference.

Version usage telemetry — you can't retire what you can't measure:

in/grocery/platform/web/ApiVersionMetricsInterceptor.java
@Override
public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler) {
    String version = req.getRequestURI().startsWith("/api/v1/") ? "1"
            : req.getHeader("X-API-Version") != null ? req.getHeader("X-API-Version") : "unknown";
    meters.counter("grocery.api.requests",
            "version", version,
            "client", clientId(req),                                                        // (1)!
            "endpoint", pattern(req)).increment();
    return true;
}
  1. From the token's client id (Chapter 18) or a User-Agent allow-list — this is what lets you email the three teams still on v1 instead of guessing.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Generating the error catalog
docs.text:
Chapter 10 defined ErrorCode with title/detail message keys. Generate the public catalog from it so documentation can't drift:

src/test/java/in/grocery/platform/error/ErrorCatalogGeneratorTest.java
package in.grocery.platform.error;

import static org.assertj.core.api.Assertions.assertThat;

import java.io.IOException;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Locale;
import java.util.ResourceBundle;
import java.util.stream.Collectors;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;

class ErrorCatalogGeneratorTest {

    @Test
    void generatesMarkdownCatalogAndFailsOnMissingMessages() throws IOException {
        ResourceBundle bundle = ResourceBundle.getBundle("grocery-errors", Locale.ENGLISH);

        var missing = java.util.Arrays.stream(ErrorCode.values())
                .filter(c -> !bundle.containsKey(c.titleKey()) || !bundle.containsKey(c.detailKey()))
                .map(Enum::name)
                .toList();
        assertThat(missing).as("error codes without messages").isEmpty();                    // (1)!

        String markdown = java.util.Arrays.stream(ErrorCode.values())
                .map(c -> "| `%s` | %d | %s | %s | %s |".formatted(
                        c.name(), c.status().value(), bundle.getString(c.titleKey()),
                        bundle.getString(c.detailKey()), c.retryable() ? "yes" : "no"))
                .collect(Collectors.joining("\n"));

        Path out = Path.of("build/generated-docs/error-catalog.md");                         // (2)!
        Files.createDirectories(out.getParent());
        Files.writeString(out, """
                # Grocery API error catalog

                | Code | HTTP | Title | Detail template | Retryable |
                |---|---|---|---|---|
                """ + markdown + "\n");
    }
}
  1. A test, not a script: adding an error code without messages fails the build.
  2. Published with the docs site and linked from every type URI.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Client SDK generation
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts (spec + SDK)
tasks.register<Exec>("generateOpenApiSpec") {                                                // (1)!
    dependsOn("bootTestRun")   // or use springdoc's Gradle plugin to start the app and dump the spec
    commandLine("sh", "-c", "curl -s http://localhost:8082/v3/api-docs.yaml -o src/main/resources/openapi/cart-service.yaml")
}

tasks.register<Exec>("generateTypeScriptClient") {
    dependsOn("generateOpenApiSpec")
    commandLine("npx", "@openapitools/openapi-generator-cli", "generate",
            "-i", "src/main/resources/openapi/cart-service.yaml",
            "-g", "typescript-angular",
            "-o", "build/clients/angular")                                                   // (2)!
}
  1. The spec is committed so its diff is visible in code review (5.7).
  2. Generated clients keep the web and mobile teams in sync with the contract automatically; regenerate on every release.

docs.title: 6.1 The platform API standard (the actual document)
docs.text:
docs/api-standard.md (excerpt)
## 1. URLs
- `/api/v{major}/<plural-resource>`; kebab-case; business references as ids.
## 2. Methods & statuses
- POST create → 201 + Location; PATCH partial; DELETE → 204; see the status table.
## 3. Payloads
- camelCase JSON; money as decimal strings; ISO-8601 times with offsets; enums are open.
## 4. Errors
- RFC 9457 + `code`, `traceId`, `retryable`, `errors[]`; codes from the shared catalog.
## 5. Concurrency & idempotency
- Mutable resources expose strong ETags; mutations require If-Match (428/412).
- Money-moving POSTs require Idempotency-Key.
## 6. Pagination
- `page`/`size` (max 100) or opaque `cursor`; stable page envelope.
## 7. Versioning
- Additive by default. Breaking changes → new major version, with Deprecation + Sunset headers
  and a minimum 6-month overlap.
## 8. Documentation
- OpenAPI generated, committed, linted; examples for every operation; errors referenced by code.
## 9. Rate limits
- RateLimit-* headers; 429 with `code: RATE_LIMITED` and Retry-After.

docs.title: 6.2 CI gates: lint and breaking-change detection
docs.text:
.github/workflows/api.yml (excerpt)
      - name: Generate spec
        run: ./gradlew generateOpenApiSpec

      - name: Fail if the committed spec is stale
        run: git diff --exit-code src/main/resources/openapi/            # (1)!

      - name: Lint with Spectral
        run: npx @stoplight/spectral-cli lint src/main/resources/openapi/*.yaml --ruleset .spectral.yaml

      - name: Detect breaking changes vs main
        run: |
          git show origin/main:src/main/resources/openapi/cart-service.yaml > /tmp/base.yaml
          npx @redocly/cli diff /tmp/base.yaml src/main/resources/openapi/cart-service.yaml --fail-on breaking   # (2)!
  1. The spec in Git must match the code — no silent drift.
  2. Breaking changes fail the build unless the PR carries a breaking-change-approved label and a version bump. Tools: Redocly, openapi-diff, or oasdiff.
.spectral.yaml (platform rules)
extends: ["spectral:oas"]
rules:
  grocery-problem-errors:
    description: Error responses must use application/problem+json
    given: $.paths[*][*].responses[?(@property >= '400')].content
    then:
      field: application/problem+json
      function: truthy
  grocery-no-snake-case:
    given: $.components.schemas[*].properties[*]~
    then:
      function: pattern
      functionOptions: { match: "^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9]*$" }
  grocery-operation-tags: { given: $.paths[*][*], then: { field: tags, function: truthy } }
  grocery-examples-required: { given: $.paths[*][*].responses[?(@property == '200')], then: { field: content, function: truthy } }

docs.title: 6.3 Deprecation programme
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Announce: docs + changelog + email<br/>Deprecation & Sunset headers live] --> B[Monitor usage per client & version]
    B --> C[Nudge: 90/60/30 days<br/>targeted outreach to top callers]
    C --> D[Brownout: short outages of v1<br/>on announced days]
    D --> E[Sunset: v1 returns 410 Gone<br/>with migration link]
in/grocery/platform/web/SunsetFilter.java
/** After the sunset date, retired versions answer 410 with a problem body pointing at the migration guide. */
@Override
protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
        throws ServletException, IOException {
    if (req.getRequestURI().startsWith("/api/v1/") && clock.instant().isAfter(props.v1SunsetAt())) {
        res.setStatus(HttpStatus.GONE.value());                                              // (1)!
        res.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
        res.setHeader("Link", "<https://docs.grocery.in/api/migrations/v2>; rel=\"deprecation\"");
        res.getWriter().write(problemJson("API_VERSION_RETIRED", 410,
                "API v1 was retired on " + props.v1SunsetAt() + ". Migrate to v2.", req.getRequestURI()));
        return;
    }
    chain.doFilter(req, res);
}
  1. 410 Gone is honest and actionable; a silent 404 sends client teams debugging the wrong thing.

Dashboards to run the programme: requests per version per client, unique clients per version, error rates after brownouts, and days-to-sunset countdown.

docs.title: 6.4 Documentation quality rules
docs.text:
Rule Why Every operation has a summary, tags, and at least one response example Generated SDKs and UIs are useless without them Every 4xx/5xx references the shared Problem schema and lists possible codes Clients switch on codes, not text Request examples use realistic Indian data (560102, ORD-…, ₹289.00) Catches format misunderstandings early Security requirements documented per operation (scopes) Integrators know what to request Deprecated operations marked deprecated: true with a migration link Shows up in SDKs and UIs Listing possible error codes per operation
@ApiResponse(responseCode = "422", description = """
        Business rule violated. Possible codes:
        `CART_ITEM_LIMIT_EXCEEDED`, `PINCODE_NOT_SERVICEABLE`, `OUT_OF_STOCK`.
        See the [error catalog](https://errors.grocery.in/).""",
        content = @Content(mediaType = "application/problem+json",
                schema = @Schema(ref = "#/components/schemas/Problem")))

docs.title: 6.5 Contract tests as the real guarantee
docs.text:
OpenAPI describes; tests enforce. The platform runs consumer-driven contract tests (Chapter 28) plus a lightweight spec-conformance check:

OpenApiConformanceTest.java (sketch)
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
class OpenApiConformanceTest {

    @Test
    void responsesMatchTheSpec() {
        // 1. fetch /v3/api-docs
        // 2. for each documented example request, call the endpoint
        // 3. validate the response against the declared schema
        //    (e.g. with an OpenAPI request/response validator library)
    }
}

The point is not 100% coverage but catching the classic drift: a field renamed in code, documented under the old name, and shipped to clients.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Decide whether to keep path versioning (simplest for gateways/caches) or adopt header versioning; don't mix within one API.
  • If adopting Framework 7 versioning: configure a default version so existing clients keep working, and verify behaviour for missing/unsupported versions.
  • Regenerate and diff the OpenAPI spec after the upgrade — Jackson 3 and package moves can change schemas subtly.
  • Update generated SDKs and notify client teams.
  • Re-check springdoc compatibility before upgrading Boot.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Additive evolution by default; versions are a last resort.
  2. One platform standard, applied by every service and enforced by lint rules.
  3. Errors by code, documented in a generated catalog.
  4. Idempotency and ETags on the operations that need them, documented as headers.
  5. Cap and whitelist page sizes, sort fields, bulk batch sizes.
  6. Spec generated, committed, linted, diffed in CI; breaking changes need explicit approval.
  7. Deprecation with headers, telemetry and outreach — plus brownouts before sunset.
  8. Generate client SDKs for web and mobile from the spec.
  9. Contract tests with consumers (Chapter 28) — documentation is not a guarantee.
  10. Measure API usage per client and version continuously.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ 200 OK with {"status": "error"} — breaks every HTTP-aware tool.

❌ Response envelopes ({"data": …, "meta": …}) on every endpoint — noise for little benefit.

❌ Exposing database ids and column names as the API contract.

❌ Version in every URL bumped for additive changes — churn without value.

❌ Deprecating without telemetry — you'll never dare to sunset.

❌ Documenting by hand in a wiki — it's wrong within a sprint.

❌ Breaking enums: adding values without telling clients to tolerate unknowns.

❌ Unbounded bulk endpoints or page sizes.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Mobile app crashes after a deploy New enum value or removed field Tolerant readers; treat as breaking; hotfix + contract tests Clients ignore Retry-After Not documented / not sent Send RateLimit-* + Retry-After, document in SDK Swagger UI shows no examples Missing @Schema(example=...)/response examples Lint rule requiring examples Spec drifts from code Manual spec, or generated but not committed Generate in CI and fail on diff Two clients disagree on total semantics Ambiguous field naming Rename via versioned change; document units and inclusions Version usage unknown No telemetry Per-version, per-client counters Breaking change shipped unnoticed No diff gate oasdiff/Redocly --fail-on breaking

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• API standard documented and linked from every repo
  • OpenAPI generated, committed, linted, diffed in CI
  • Shared Problem schema and generated error catalog published
  • Idempotency/ETag/pagination conventions applied and documented
  • Version telemetry per client
  • Deprecation headers + sunset plan for anything deprecated
  • SDKs regenerated each release
  • Contract tests with the top consumers

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What makes an API RESTful in practice?

Short answer: Resources identified by URLs, standard HTTP methods with their semantics, correct status codes, representations in JSON, statelessness, and use of HTTP features (caching, conditional requests) instead of reinventing them.

B1 · Where do you put filtering and pagination parameters?

Short answer: Query parameters (?category=dairy&page=0&size=20), with capped sizes and whitelisted sort fields.

B1 · What is OpenAPI and how do you get it in Spring Boot?

Short answer: A machine-readable API description. Add springdoc-openapi; it generates the spec from controllers, DTOs and annotations, and serves Swagger UI.

B1 · Why shouldn't you return 200 with an error body?

Short answer: Monitoring, caches, retries and client libraries all key off status codes; hiding failures in a 200 breaks them.

B1 · Name three backward-compatible API changes.

Short answer: Adding an optional request field, adding a response field, adding a new endpoint (with tolerant clients).

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Compare URI, header and media-type versioning.

Short answer: URI is visible and easy to route/cache but pollutes URLs; header keeps URLs clean but is invisible in logs/browsers; media type is HTTP-native but awkward for tooling. Pick one and be consistent.

B2 · How do you deprecate an API version properly?

Short answer: Announce it, send Deprecation/Sunset/Link headers, measure usage per client, nudge top callers with deadlines, optionally brown out, then return 410 Gone after the sunset date.

B2 · How do you design a bulk endpoint?

Short answer: Bounded batch size, per-item results with individual statuses and error codes, overall 200 when the request itself was valid, and idempotency where it creates things.

B2 · What headers communicate rate limiting?

Short answer: RateLimit-Limit/Remaining/Reset (draft standard) plus Retry-After with a 429 and a problem body with a stable code.

B2 · How do you keep documentation in sync with code?

Short answer: Generate the spec from the code, commit it, and fail CI if the generated output differs from the committed one; lint and diff it for breaking changes.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does Framework 7's API versioning work?

Short answer: A configured strategy resolves the version from a header, path segment, query parameter or media-type parameter; the version becomes a request-mapping condition (version = "1" or "1.2+"), with configurable supported/default versions and errors for unsupported ones.

B3 · How do you run two versions without duplicating business logic?

Short answer: Keep one domain/service layer; versions differ only in DTO mapping at the delegate/controller boundary. Shared tests assert the invariants, version-specific tests assert the representation.

B3 · How do you detect breaking changes automatically?

Short answer: Diff the generated OpenAPI spec against the base branch with a tool that classifies changes (oasdiff, Redocly), failing on breaking ones; complement with consumer-driven contract tests.

B3 · How do ETags and idempotency keys differ?

Short answer: ETags prevent lost updates (conditional writes on a known version); idempotency keys prevent duplicate effects from retries of a non-idempotent operation. Money-moving flows often need both.

B3 · How do you add a value to an enum used in responses without breaking clients?

Short answer: Only if clients are tolerant readers that map unknown values to a fallback; otherwise treat it as breaking. Document enums as open, test client behaviour with an unknown value, and roll out behind telemetry before relying on it.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · You must change the meaning of a field used by a million installed apps. How?

Short answer: Never mutate meaning in place. Add the new fields alongside, dual-populate, version the representation, migrate clients with telemetry-driven outreach, then retire the old field after the sunset window. Gateways can adapt for the longest tail.

B4 · How do you govern APIs across 26 services?

Short answer: A written standard, lint rules in CI, a shared platform library implementing the conventions (errors, pagination, headers), design review for new public APIs, spec diffing, SDK generation, and usage/version dashboards.

B4 · Contract-first or code-first?

Short answer: Code-first with generated, committed, linted specs works well when the same team owns both sides and CI enforces review of spec diffs. Contract-first pays off with external partners or when several teams must agree before implementation.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you treat APIs as products?

Short answer: Named owners, published standards and changelogs, versioning and deprecation policies with SLAs, usage analytics per consumer, support channels, and roadmaps — the same discipline as a customer-facing product, because integrators are customers.

B5 · When do you choose GraphQL or gRPC over REST?

Short answer: GraphQL for flexible client-driven aggregation across many resources (mobile screens with varying needs); gRPC for internal high-volume, low-latency RPC with schemas; REST for public, cacheable, widely consumable APIs. Chapter 32 covers both in Spring.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A field rename shipped and 12% of orders fail

deliveryFee was renamed delivery_charge in a sprint "cleanup". Older apps read deliveryFee, got null, and crashed on the checkout screen. Fixes: revert immediately, add the field back permanently, add a spec-diff gate that fails on removed/renamed properties, add contract tests with the mobile team, and document the rename as a v2 change.

Scenario · v1 can't be retired after two years

Nobody knew who was calling it. Fixes: add per-client, per-version telemetry (token client id + user agent), publish a usage dashboard, contact the top 10 callers with deadlines, run brownouts, and set an explicit sunset date with 410 afterwards. Institutionalize the policy so v2 doesn't repeat it.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Version the order response

GET /api/orders/{ref} currently returns {"orderRef","status","total","placedAt"}. Version 2 must return {"orderRef","status","subtotal","deliveryFee","total","placedAt","statusHistory"}. Implement both versions sharing one service, add deprecation headers to v1, document both in OpenAPI, and add tests proving each shape.

Solution OrderViews.java
public record OrderViewV1(String orderRef, String status, String total, Instant placedAt) {
    public static OrderViewV1 from(OrderDetail d) {
        return new OrderViewV1(d.orderRef(), d.status(), d.total().asString(), d.placedAt());
    }
}

public record OrderViewV2(String orderRef, String status, String subtotal, String deliveryFee,
                          String total, Instant placedAt, List<StatusChange> statusHistory) {
    public record StatusChange(String status, Instant at) {}

    public static OrderViewV2 from(OrderDetail d) {
        return new OrderViewV2(d.orderRef(), d.status(), d.subtotal().asString(), d.deliveryFee().asString(),
                d.total().asString(), d.placedAt(),
                d.history().stream().map(h -> new StatusChange(h.status(), h.at())).toList());
    }
}
OrderQueryController.java (Boot 3.5 path versioning)
@RestController
class OrderQueryController {

    private final OrderQueryDelegate delegate;
    private final DeprecationProperties deprecation;

    @GetMapping("/api/v1/orders/{ref}")
    @Operation(summary = "Get an order (deprecated)", deprecated = true)
    ResponseEntity<OrderViewV1> v1(@PathVariable String ref, @CurrentCustomer CustomerContext c) {
        OrderDetail detail = delegate.detail(c.customerId(), ref);
        return ResponseEntity.ok()
                .header("Deprecation", "@" + deprecation.v1DeprecatedAt().getEpochSecond())
                .header("Sunset", deprecation.v1SunsetHttpDate())
                .header("Link", "<https://docs.grocery.in/api/migrations/order-v2>; rel=\"deprecation\"")
                .body(OrderViewV1.from(detail));
    }

    @GetMapping("/api/v2/orders/{ref}")
    @Operation(summary = "Get an order")
    ResponseEntity<OrderViewV2> v2(@PathVariable String ref, @CurrentCustomer CustomerContext c) {
        return ResponseEntity.ok(OrderViewV2.from(delegate.detail(c.customerId(), ref)));
    }
}
OrderQueryControllerTest.java
