@GroceryWebTest(controllers = OrderQueryController.class)
class OrderQueryControllerTest {

    @Autowired MockMvcTester mvc;
    @MockitoBean OrderQueryDelegate delegate;

    @Test
    void v1ShapeAndDeprecationHeaders() {
        given(delegate.detail("C-1", "ORD-1")).willReturn(sampleDetail());
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/v1/orders/ORD-1").header("X-Customer-Id", "C-1"))
                .hasStatusOk()
                .hasHeader("Sunset", "Sun, 01 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT")
                .bodyJson()
                .satisfies(json -> {
                    assertThat(json).extractingPath("$.total").isEqualTo("578.00");
                    assertThat(json.getJson()).doesNotContain("deliveryFee");
                });
    }

    @Test
    void v2ShapeHasBreakdownAndHistory() {
        given(delegate.detail("C-1", "ORD-1")).willReturn(sampleDetail());
        assertThat(mvc.get().uri("/api/v2/orders/ORD-1").header("X-Customer-Id", "C-1"))
                .hasStatusOk()
                .bodyJson()
                .satisfies(json -> {
                    assertThat(json).extractingPath("$.deliveryFee").isEqualTo("35.00");
                    assertThat(json).extractingPath("$.statusHistory[0].status").isEqualTo("PLACED");
                });
    }
}

On Boot 4 the same result comes from one controller with version = "1" / version = "2" handlers and a header strategy; the DTOs and tests are unchanged.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Design for evolution: additive changes, tolerant readers, stable error codes.
  • One platform standard for URLs, payloads, errors, pagination, concurrency and idempotency.
  • Version only for breaking changes — path versions for the public API, Framework 7 versioning for finer control on Boot 4.
  • Deprecate with headers, telemetry and outreach, then 410 Gone after sunset.
  • Generate, commit, lint and diff the OpenAPI spec in CI; generate client SDKs from it.
  • Publish a generated error catalog so clients code against codes, not text.
  • Contract tests, not documentation, are the actual guarantee.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• RFC 9110 (HTTP semantics), RFC 9457 (problem details), RFC 8594 (Sunset), RFC 9745 (Deprecation), RFC 8288 (Link)
  • Spring Framework 7 Reference — Web MVC › API Versioning
  • springdoc-openapi documentation; OpenAPI Specification 3.1
  • Spectral, Redocly/oasdiff for linting and breaking-change detection

19 HTTP Clients · 21 Caching

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
On a normal evening the grocery catalog serves 12,000 product page views per minute. Prices depend on SKU and pincode (zone pricing, local taxes, hub-specific offers), so a naive implementation runs one pricing query per product per customer. During a Diwali sale that becomes 200,000 queries per minute against a database that comfortably handles 20,000.

Caching is how you serve the other 90% without buying nine more databases. Done well it is the highest-leverage performance work available. Done badly it produces the worst class of bug:

  • A price drops at 6 p.m.; some pods keep charging the old price for an hour because their local caches never heard about it.
  • A cached null for a SKU that existed five seconds later makes the product invisible until TTL expiry.
  • A popular key expires during peak traffic and 4,000 concurrent requests all miss and hit the database at once — a cache stampede that takes the database down.
  • Redis has a 200 ms hiccup; every request fails with RedisConnectionFailureException because the cache was allowed to break the request path.
  • Two customers see each other's cart because the cache key forgot the customer id.

This chapter covers Spring's cache abstraction properly: annotations and their internals, Caffeine for local caching, Redis for shared caching, TTLs with jitter, stampede protection, event-driven invalidation across pods, negative caching, fail-open error handling, metrics, and a two-level cache where it's genuinely worth the complexity. HTTP-level caching (ETags, Cache-Control) from Chapters 08 and 20 is the cheapest cache of all and comes first.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — @Cacheable, keys, TTL B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — Caffeine vs Redis, eviction, conditions, serialization B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — internals, stampede, invalidation across pods, metrics B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — cache architecture, failure modes, capacity B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — consistency trade-offs and when not to cache

docs.title: 2.1 What to cache
docs.text: Good candidates Why Reference data (categories, GST rate master, pincode → hub) Rarely changes, read constantly Computed prices per (sku, pincode) Expensive, high reuse Serviceability checks Called on every cart mutation Product detail projections Read-heavy, tolerant of seconds of staleness Idempotency/dedupe records Naturally key-value with TTL (Chapters 04, 18) Poor candidates Why Cart contents, stock counts Change constantly; staleness causes real errors Anything per-request unique No reuse Payment state Correctness over speed Data with legal accuracy requirements (invoices) Read from the source

docs.title: 2.2 Caching patterns
docs.text: Pattern How Notes Cache-aside (lazy) Read cache → miss → load → populate Spring's @Cacheable; the default Write-through Write cache and store together @CachePut; keeps cache warm, costs on every write Write-behind Write cache, flush to store later Risk of loss; rare in application code Refresh-ahead Refresh hot entries before expiry Caffeine refreshAfterWrite; hides latency Negative caching Cache "not found" briefly Stops repeated misses hammering the store

docs.title: 2.3 Spring's cache abstraction
docs.text:
Piece Role @EnableCaching Registers the caching AOP advisor CacheManager Provides named Cache instances Cache get, put, evict, clear, get(key, valueLoader) @Cacheable Return cached value if present, else invoke and store @CachePut Always invoke, then store the result @CacheEvict Remove entries (key, allEntries, beforeInvocation) @Caching Combine several of the above @CacheConfig Class-level defaults (cache names, key generator) KeyGenerator Builds keys when key isn't specified (SimpleKeyGenerator) CacheResolver Chooses caches dynamically CacheErrorHandler Decides what happens when the cache itself fails

It's AOP (Chapter 04): public methods, no self-invocation, proxies only.

docs.title: 2.4 Keys
docs.text:
The default SimpleKeyGenerator builds a SimpleKey from all method arguments. That's convenient and dangerous:

  • Adding a parameter silently changes the key space.
  • Arguments must have correct equals/hashCode — and for Redis, a sane toString(), since keys become strings.

Always specify keys explicitly for anything shared: @Cacheable(cacheNames = "price", key = "#sku + '|' + #pincode").

Forgetting the tenant/customer dimension

A key that omits the customer, seller or pincode dimension leaks data between users. Key design is a security decision, not just a performance one.

docs.title: 2.5 Local vs distributed
docs.text:
Caffeine (in-process) Redis (shared) Latency ~100 ns ~0.3–1 ms (network) Consistency across pods ❌ each pod has its own copy ✅ one copy Capacity Heap-bound Large, independent of pods Survives restarts ❌ ✅ Failure impact None (in-process) Needs fail-open handling Invalidation Hard (must broadcast) Easy (delete the key)

Rule of thumb: Redis for anything that must be consistent across pods or must survive a restart; Caffeine for tiny, hot, tolerant-of-staleness data — and only add a two-level cache when measurements justify it.

docs.title: 2.6 TTL, eviction and jitter
docs.text:
• TTL bounds staleness. Pick it from the business tolerance ("prices may lag by up to 60 s"), not from a vibe.
  • Size limits bound memory: Caffeine maximumSize or maximumWeight.
  • Jitter: identical TTLs make thousands of keys expire in the same second after a deploy or warm-up — add ±10–20% randomness.

docs.title: 2.7 Stampede (thundering herd)
docs.text:
When a hot key expires, every concurrent request misses. Defences:

Technique Where @Cacheable(sync = true) Per-key locking inside one JVM (Caffeine); Redis needs a locking cache writer Distributed lock One pod recomputes, others wait or serve stale Refresh-ahead Recompute before expiry (Caffeine refreshAfterWrite) Stale-while-revalidate Serve the old value, refresh asynchronously Jittered TTL Spreads expiries out

docs.title: 2.8 Invalidation across pods
docs.text: Local caches need a broadcast: Redis pub/sub or a Kafka topic that every pod consumes and uses to evict its local entries. Alternative: versioned key prefixes (price:v42:{sku}|{pincode}) — bumping the version invalidates everything at once without touching individual keys.

docs.title: 2.9 Cache failures must not break requests
docs.text: By default a CacheManager exception propagates and fails the request. For a cache, that is almost never right: configure a CacheErrorHandler that logs, meters and continues to the underlying method.

docs.title: 2.10 Layers of caching
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Browser / app<br/>Cache-Control, ETag] --> B[CDN / edge<br/>public catalog pages]
    B --> C[Gateway response cache<br/>rare]
    C --> D[Application cache<br/>Caffeine / Redis]
    D --> E[Database cache<br/>buffer pool, materialized views]

Always ask whether the layer to the left can handle it: an ETag that avoids the request entirely beats any server-side cache.

docs.title: 3.1 The caching interceptor
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant P as Proxy
    participant CI as CacheInterceptor
    participant KG as KeyGenerator / SpEL
    participant CM as CacheManager → Cache
    participant T as Target method

    C->>P: priceFor("MILK-1L", "560102")
    P->>CI: invoke
    CI->>KG: evaluate condition / unless / key
    CI->>CM: cache.get(key)
    alt hit
        CM-->>CI: ValueWrapper
        CI-->>C: cached value (target never called)
    else miss and sync=true
        CI->>CM: cache.get(key, valueLoader)
        Note over CM: one thread computes,<br/>others wait on the same key
        CM->>T: valueLoader → target method
    else miss
        CI->>T: proceed()
        T-->>CI: value
        CI->>CM: cache.put(key, value) unless `unless` matches
    end

Key classes: CacheInterceptor (extends CacheAspectSupport), AnnotationCacheOperationSource, SimpleKeyGenerator, CacheResolver, SimpleCacheErrorHandler.

@CacheEvict(beforeInvocation = true) evicts before the method runs — useful when the method may throw but the cached value is already known to be wrong.

docs.title: 3.2 Where Redis fits
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[RedisCacheManager] --> B[RedisCache per name]
    B --> C[RedisCacheConfiguration<br/>TTL, prefix, null values, serializers]
    C --> D[RedisCacheWriter<br/>plain or locking]
    D --> E[Lettuce connection pool → Redis]
    F[Key: prefix + cacheName + '::' + key] --> D
  • Serializers decide the on-wire format. The value serializer is where JSON polymorphism risks live (Chapter 11) — prefer a typed serializer per cache over a generic one with default typing.
  • The locking cache writer provides sync = true semantics across pods at the cost of extra round trips.

docs.title: 3.3 Caffeine
docs.text: Window TinyLFU eviction (better hit rates than pure LRU for skewed workloads), expireAfterWrite/expireAfterAccess, maximumSize/maximumWeight, refreshAfterWrite with a CacheLoader, and statistics when recordStats() is enabled (needed for Micrometer metrics).

docs.title: 4.1 Enable caching with Caffeine
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-cache")
implementation("com.github.ben-manes.caffeine:caffeine")
application.yml
spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine
    cache-names: categories, pincode-hubs
    caffeine:
      spec: maximumSize=5000,expireAfterWrite=10m,recordStats      # (1)!
  1. recordStats is required for cache metrics (Chapter 27).
in/grocery/catalog/config/CachingConfig.java
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
@EnableCaching                                                      // (1)!
class CachingConfig {}
  1. Without it, the annotations do nothing — silently.

docs.title: 4.2 A first cached method
4.3 Seeing it work
5.1 Level 2 — Redis cache with per-cache configuration
5.2 Level 2 — Keys, conditions and unless
5.3 Level 2 — Self-invocation strikes again
5.4 Level 3 — Stampede protection and jittered TTL
5.5 Level 3 — Fail open when the cache is down
5.6 Level 3 — Metrics
docs.text:
application.yml
management:
  metrics:
    enable:
      cache: true

With recordStats (Caffeine) or enable-statistics (Redis) and caches registered in the CacheManager at startup, Boot exposes:

Metric Meaning cache.gets{result=hit\|miss} Hit ratio — the headline number cache.puts, cache.evictions Write and eviction volume cache.size Entries (Caffeine) cache.lock.duration (Redis) Time spent in locking writers grocery.cache.errors (ours) Cache infrastructure failures

A cache below ~70% hit rate is usually mis-keyed, too small, or caching the wrong thing.

docs.title: 6.1 The pricing cache end to end
docs.text:
Requirements: 2-minute staleness budget, immediate invalidation when a seller changes a price, no stampede, works across 6 pods, survives Redis outages, measurable.

flowchart LR
    A[pricing-service pod] -->|"1. @Cacheable get"| R[("Redis cache<br/>price::sku|pincode")]
    R -- miss --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
    S[seller updates price] --> W[pricing write path]
    W -->|2. commit| DB
    W -->|3. after commit: outbox| K[(Kafka grocery.pricing.price-changed.v1)]
    K -->|4. consumed by all pods| A
    A -->|5. evict / CachePut| R
in/grocery/pricing/service/PriceUpdateService.java
package in.grocery.pricing.service;

import in.grocery.pricing.outbox.OutboxWriter;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class PriceUpdateService {

    private final PriceRepository prices;
    private final OutboxWriter outbox;

    public PriceUpdateService(PriceRepository prices, OutboxWriter outbox) {
        this.prices = prices;
        this.outbox = outbox;
    }

    @Transactional
    public void updatePrice(String sku, String zone, java.math.BigDecimal newPrice) {
        prices.update(sku, zone, newPrice);
        outbox.append("price", sku, "PriceChanged", new PriceChanged(sku, zone));        // (1)!
    }
}
  1. The invalidation event is written in the same transaction as the price (Chapter 16) — a price change can never be committed without its invalidation being published.
in/grocery/pricing/cache/PriceCacheInvalidator.java
package in.grocery.pricing.cache;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.cache.CacheManager;
import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class PriceCacheInvalidator {

    private final CacheManager caches;
    private final PincodeDirectory pincodes;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    public PriceCacheInvalidator(CacheManager caches, PincodeDirectory pincodes, MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.caches = caches;
        this.pincodes = pincodes;
        this.meters = meters;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.pricing.price-changed.v1", groupId = "${spring.application.name}-cache")  // (1)!
    public void onPriceChanged(PriceChanged event) {
        var cache = caches.getCache("price");
        if (cache == null) return;
        List<String> affected = pincodes.pincodesInZone(event.zone());                    // (2)!
        affected.forEach(pincode -> cache.evict(event.sku() + "|" + pincode));
        meters.counter("grocery.cache.invalidations", "cache", "price").increment(affected.size());
    }
}
  1. Every pod consumes (unique group per instance isn't needed for a shared Redis cache — one eviction suffices; for local caches each pod must consume independently, so the group id must be per-instance).
  2. The cache key includes the pincode, but prices change per zone — the invalidator expands zone → pincodes. A versioned key (price:v{zoneVersion}:{sku}|{pincode}) is the alternative when that expansion gets large.

Key-space design determines invalidation cost

If invalidating one logical change means deleting 4,000 keys, redesign the key: either cache per zone (price:{sku}|{zone}) with a cheap pincode→zone lookup, or embed a version in the prefix so one counter bump invalidates everything.

docs.title: 6.2 Two-level cache where it pays
docs.text:
Serviceability (pincode → serviceable) is queried on every cart mutation, changes weekly, and has ~19,000 keys — ideal for a local cache with a Redis backstop.

in/grocery/delivery/cache/TwoLevelServiceabilityCache.java
package in.grocery.delivery.cache;

import com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.Caffeine;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class TwoLevelServiceabilityCache {

    private final com.github.benmanes.caffeine.cache.Cache<String, Boolean> local = Caffeine.newBuilder()
            .maximumSize(25_000)
            .expireAfterWrite(10, TimeUnit.MINUTES)                                        // (1)!
            .recordStats()
            .build();

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final ServiceabilityLoader loader;

    public boolean isServiceable(String pincode) {
        Boolean cached = local.getIfPresent(pincode);
        if (cached != null) return cached;

        String fromRedis = redis.opsForValue().get("svc:" + pincode);                      // (2)!
        if (fromRedis != null) {
            boolean value = Boolean.parseBoolean(fromRedis);
            local.put(pincode, value);
            return value;
        }
        boolean value = loader.load(pincode);
        redis.opsForValue().set("svc:" + pincode, String.valueOf(value), Duration.ofHours(6));
        local.put(pincode, value);
        return value;
    }

    /** Invoked by the Kafka listener on every pod when serviceability changes. */
    public void invalidate(String pincode) {
        local.invalidate(pincode);                                                          // (3)!
        redis.delete("svc:" + pincode);
    }
}
  1. Local TTL is the maximum staleness if an invalidation message is missed — keep it short enough to be a safety net (10 min), long enough to be useful.
  2. L1 miss → L2 → source. Each layer populates the ones above it.
  3. Local invalidation must happen on every pod, so the Kafka consumer group id is per-instance (${spring.application.name}-${random.uuid}) — a broadcast, not a queue.

Two levels double the failure modes

Only add L1 when you've measured that L2 latency matters (e.g. 3 Redis round trips per request in a hot path). Most caches should be single-level.

docs.title: 6.3 Warm-up
6.4 Testing cache behaviour
6.5 Capacity and cost
docs.text:
Question How to answer How many keys? SKUs × pincodes (or zones) × variants — compute it before choosing Redis instance size How big is a value? Serialize a real object and measure; multiply What hit rate justifies it? (misses × source cost) vs (cache cost + complexity) What's the memory ceiling? Redis maxmemory + allkeys-lru policy so it degrades instead of OOMs What if the cache is empty? The database must survive a cold start — test it (that's what a deploy does)

The last row is the one that causes outages: a system that only works with a warm cache is a system that fails on every restart.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Inventory cache names, TTLs, serializers and key patterns.
  • Bump the key prefix for the upgrade window; plan the cleanup.
  • Re-verify serializer classes and that no cache uses polymorphic default typing.
  • Re-run cache tests (hit/miss counts, invalidation) after the upgrade.
  • Check metric names and dashboards still resolve.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Cache the expensive and reusable; measure before and after.
  2. Explicit keys with every dimension (sku, pincode, customer, tenant, version).
  3. TTL from the business staleness budget, with jitter.
  4. Stampede protection (sync, stale-while-revalidate, or a lock) on hot keys.
  5. Event-driven invalidation written in the same transaction as the change.
  6. Fail open with a CacheErrorHandler and alert on cache error counters.
  7. Typed serializers; never polymorphic default typing.
  8. Metrics on hit rate, size, evictions, errors; alert on hit-rate drops.
  9. Design for a cold cache — every deploy is one.
  10. Prefer HTTP caching (ETag, Cache-Control, CDN) where the data is public.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ @Cacheable without @EnableCaching — silently does nothing.

❌ Default keys on multi-argument methods — invisible key-space bugs and data leaks.

❌ Caching mutable objects and mutating them afterwards (Caffeine stores references!).

❌ @CacheEvict(allEntries = true) on a hot cache for a single-row change — self-inflicted stampede.

❌ Caching inside a transaction and evicting before commit.

❌ Local caches for data that must be consistent across pods.

❌ Infinite TTLs "because we invalidate properly" — you will miss an event.

❌ Making the cache mandatory (no fallback path) — an outage becomes total.

❌ Caching personal data in a shared cache without the customer in the key.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Cache has no effect @EnableCaching missing; self-invocation; non-public method Fix wiring/structure Hit rate near zero Key includes a unique value (timestamp, request id) Fix the key Stale prices after a change Missed/absent invalidation; local cache; evict before commit Event-driven eviction after commit; shorter TTL Latency spike every N minutes Synchronized TTL expiry Jitter; refresh-ahead Database spike after deploy Cold cache Warm-up; ensure DB survives cold start RedisConnectionFailureException in responses No CacheErrorHandler Fail open, meter, alert SerializationException after a deploy Changed DTO or serializer Versioned key prefix; tolerant DTOs Memory grows until OOM Unbounded Caffeine cache maximumSize/maximumWeight + TTL Customer sees another's data Key missing a dimension Add it; audit all keys Redis memory full No maxmemory policy allkeys-lru, size the instance, shorter TTLs

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every cache has a documented purpose, key format, TTL and invalidation path
  • Keys include all identity/tenant dimensions
  • Hot caches have stampede protection and jittered TTLs
  • CacheErrorHandler installed; error counter alerted on
  • Hit-rate dashboards per cache, with alerts
  • Typed serializers, no default typing
  • Cold-start behaviour tested (cache flush in staging under load)
  • Redis maxmemory + eviction policy set; capacity computed

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · How do you cache a method result in Spring?

Short answer: @EnableCaching plus @Cacheable(cacheNames = "...", key = "...") on a public method of a Spring bean.

B1 · @Cacheable vs @CachePut vs @CacheEvict?

Short answer: @Cacheable skips the method on a hit; @CachePut always runs and stores the result; @CacheEvict removes entries.

B1 · What is the default cache key?

Short answer: A SimpleKey built from all method arguments (no-args → SimpleKey.EMPTY). Specify keys explicitly for shared caches.

B1 · Why does my @Cacheable method still hit the database?

Short answer: Missing @EnableCaching, self-invocation, a non-public method, a condition/unless that excludes it, or a key that's different every call.

B1 · Caffeine vs Redis in one sentence?

Short answer: Caffeine is a fast in-process cache private to each pod; Redis is a shared network cache all pods see.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you set different TTLs per cache?

Short answer: With Redis, per-cache RedisCacheConfiguration via RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer; with Caffeine, per-cache specs or separate CaffeineCacheManager configurations.

B2 · What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?

Short answer: Many concurrent requests missing the same expired hot key and all hitting the source. Prevent with sync = true/locking, refresh-ahead, stale-while-revalidate and jittered TTLs.

B2 · How do you invalidate caches across multiple pods?

Short answer: Shared cache (Redis) — delete the key once. Local caches — broadcast an event (Kafka/Redis pub/sub) that every pod consumes, or use versioned key prefixes.

B2 · Should you cache nulls?

Short answer: Often yes, briefly, to stop repeated misses for non-existent keys — but with a short TTL and explicit invalidation when the entity is created.

B2 · How do you verify caching in tests?

Short answer: Spy on the underlying repository/client and assert the number of invocations across repeated calls, plus tests for key separation and invalidation.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does the caching interceptor work?

Short answer: CacheInterceptor (AOP) resolves cache operations per method, evaluates condition, computes the key (SpEL or KeyGenerator), consults the Cache, and on a miss invokes the target and stores the result unless unless matches. sync uses cache.get(key, valueLoader) for per-key locking.

B3 · What are the risks of the Redis value serializer?

Short answer: Generic serializers with default typing allow arbitrary class instantiation from cached payloads (deserialization attacks) and break on DTO changes. Use typed serializers per cache and version key prefixes across incompatible changes.

B3 · Where should eviction happen relative to the transaction?

Short answer: After commit. Evicting before commit lets another thread repopulate from pre-commit state; use transaction synchronization or an after-commit event.

B3 · When is a two-level cache worth it?

Short answer: When L2 (network) latency is significant in a hot path and the data tolerates the L1 staleness window. It doubles invalidation complexity, so measure first.

B3 · What happens when Redis is unavailable?

Short answer: By default cache operations throw and fail requests. With a CacheErrorHandler the request falls through to the source — as long as the source can carry the load, which must be capacity-tested.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the caching strategy for the catalog and pricing services.

Short answer: HTTP caching/CDN for public catalog pages; Redis cache for computed prices keyed by sku+zone with a 2-minute staleness budget, jittered TTL and stale-while-revalidate; invalidation events emitted transactionally on price changes; local cache only for tiny hot reference data with broadcast invalidation; fail-open handling, metrics and cold-start capacity planning.

B4 · How do you decide TTLs?

Short answer: From business tolerance (how wrong may this be, for how long?) combined with change frequency and invalidation reliability. Short TTLs where invalidation may be missed; longer TTLs where events are reliable and the data is stable.

B4 · Your database is at 90% CPU and someone proposes 'just add caching'. Response?

Short answer: Measure first: which queries, what reuse, what staleness is acceptable? Caching helps repeated reads, not unique or write-heavy load. Also fix the obvious (indexes, N+1, pagination). And verify the database can still survive a cold cache — otherwise you've added a new single point of failure.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What are the organizational risks of caching?

Short answer: Invisible coupling (services depend on another's cache semantics), staleness bugs that appear only in production, capacity hidden behind a cache until it's flushed, and "cache as a fix" replacing real performance work. Mitigate with documented cache contracts, ownership, dashboards and periodic cold-start tests.

B5 · When would you deliberately not cache?

Short answer: When correctness beats latency (payments, stock at reservation), when reuse is low, when invalidation can't be made reliable, or when the added failure mode outweighs the gain. Sometimes the right fix is a better query, a denormalized read model, or a CDN.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Customers charged yesterday's price after a nationwide price drop

Prices were cached locally in Caffeine on six pods with a 30-minute TTL and no invalidation. Fixes: move the price cache to Redis (single copy), emit PriceChanged transactionally, consume it to evict, cut the TTL to two minutes as a safety net, and add a test asserting invalidation.

Scenario · Every deploy causes a 90-second database CPU spike

Cold caches across all pods at once. Fixes: warm the top keys in an ApplicationRunner before readiness, stagger pod rollout (maxSurge/maxUnavailable), keep the shared Redis cache warm across deploys (it isn't restarted), and load-test the cold path so the database can survive it.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Serviceability cache

Cache isServiceable(pincode) in Redis with a 6-hour TTL, negative caching, sync behaviour for stampedes and invalidation via a ServiceabilityChanged event. Write tests for: hit/miss counts, key separation, invalidation, and Redis being down.

Solution ServiceabilityService.java
@Service
public class ServiceabilityService {

    private final ServiceabilityRepository repository;

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "serviceability", key = "#pincode", sync = true)
    public boolean isServiceable(String pincode) {
        return repository.findHubFor(pincode).isPresent();          // false is cached too
    }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "serviceability", key = "#pincode")
    public void evict(String pincode) {}
}
ServiceabilityCacheConfig.java
@Bean
RedisCacheManagerBuilderCustomizer serviceabilityCache() {
    return builder -> builder.withCacheConfiguration("serviceability",
            RedisCacheConfiguration.defaultCacheConfig()
                    .entryTtl(Duration.ofHours(6))
                    .serializeKeysWith(SerializationPair.fromSerializer(new StringRedisSerializer()))
                    .serializeValuesWith(SerializationPair.fromSerializer(
                            new Jackson2JsonRedisSerializer<>(objectMapper, Boolean.class))));
}
ServiceabilityChangedListener.java
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.delivery.serviceability-changed.v1",
               groupId = "${spring.application.name}-serviceability-cache")
public void onChanged(ServiceabilityChanged event) {
    serviceability.evict(event.pincode());
}
ServiceabilityCacheTest.java (assertions)
@Test void cachesPositiveAndNegativeResults() { /* 2 calls per pincode → 1 repository hit each */ }
@Test void distinctPincodesAreDistinctKeys() { /* 2 repository hits */ }
@Test void eventEvictsEntry() { /* after event → repository hit again */ }
@Test void redisDownStillAnswers() { /* stop container → no exception, repository called */ }

Note that sync = true here protects a single JVM. Because the underlying query is a cheap indexed lookup, that's enough; for an expensive computation, add a distributed lock or stale-while-revalidate (5.4).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Cache what is expensive and reused; measure before and after.
  • Keys carry every dimension — a missing dimension is a correctness and security bug.
  • TTL = staleness budget, with jitter; invalidate via events written in the same transaction as the change.
  • Stampede protection for hot keys: sync, refresh-ahead or stale-while-revalidate.
  • Fail open on cache errors, meter them, and make sure the source survives a cold cache.
  • Redis for cross-pod consistency, Caffeine for tiny hot data; two levels only with evidence.
  • Typed serializers, versioned key prefixes across upgrades — cached data is a contract.
  • HTTP caching first where the data is public and cacheable.

20 API Design & Versioning · 22 NoSQL & Search

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
PostgreSQL is the grocery platform's system of record, and Chapters 12–14 made it fast and safe. But three workloads don't fit a relational table well:

  • Ephemeral, high-churn key-value data — OTP codes, idempotency records, rate-limit counters, distributed locks, delivery-partner locations. Writing these to PostgreSQL means millions of short-lived rows, vacuum pressure and wasted IOPS. This is Redis territory.
  • Variable-shaped documents — seller catalog feeds where a shampoo has volumeMl and a rice bag has grainLength, plus raw partner payloads kept for audit. A table with 200 nullable columns (or an EAV model) is the wrong answer. This is MongoDB territory.
  • Search — a customer types "atta 5kg", misspells it as "aata", filters by brand and price, sorts by relevance, and expects results in 80 ms with facet counts. LIKE '%atta%' cannot do this at any scale. This is OpenSearch/Elasticsearch territory.

The danger is the opposite mistake: treating these stores as a general-purpose database. Redis is not durable in the way money needs; MongoDB transactions have constraints; a search index is a derived view that will occasionally lag or be rebuilt from scratch.

This chapter covers each store as used in the platform — Redis data structures and Lua scripts beyond caching, MongoDB documents and aggregations, and a production search service with Indian-language analyzers, synonyms, zero-downtime reindexing and a fallback path — plus a decision table for choosing.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — Redis templates, basic documents B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — data structures, MongoDB modelling, simple search B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — atomicity with Lua, aggregation, index design B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — search architecture, reindexing, failure modes B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — polyglot persistence strategy

docs.title: 2.1 Choosing a store
docs.text:
Need Store Why Transactions, constraints, joins, reporting PostgreSQL System of record (Chapters 12–14) Sub-millisecond key-value, TTL, counters, locks, queues Redis In-memory data structures Variable-schema documents, nested arrays, flexible queries MongoDB Document model Full-text relevance, facets, typo tolerance, autocomplete OpenSearch / Elasticsearch Inverted index + scoring Massive write-heavy time series (delivery pings, event logs) Cassandra / time-series DB Linear write scale Analytics over history Warehouse (BigQuery/Snowflake/ClickHouse) Columnar

Derived stores are not sources of truth

Search indexes and read models are rebuildable projections. If a store can't be rebuilt from PostgreSQL (or the event log) in a reasonable time, you've accidentally made it a system of record — with none of the guarantees.

docs.title: 2.2 Redis beyond caching
docs.text:
Structure Commands Grocery use String SET, GET, INCR, SET NX EX OTP, counters, rate limits, locks Hash HSET, HGETALL, HINCRBY Session/cart snapshots, per-field counters List LPUSH, BRPOP Simple work queues (small scale) Set SADD, SISMEMBER Serviceable pincodes, feature cohorts Sorted set ZADD, ZRANGEBYSCORE, ZINCRBY Top-selling SKUs, delayed jobs, sliding-window rate limits Stream XADD, XREADGROUP Lightweight event streams with consumer groups Geo GEOADD, GEOSEARCH Nearest hub, nearby delivery partners HyperLogLog PFADD, PFCOUNT Unique visitors per pincode (approximate, tiny) Pub/Sub PUBLISH, SUBSCRIBE Cache invalidation broadcast (Chapter 21)

Atomicity: single commands are atomic; multi-step logic needs MULTI/EXEC, WATCH (optimistic) or — usually best — a Lua script, which executes atomically on the server.

docs.title: 2.3 Redis durability expectations
docs.text:
Mode Guarantee No persistence Everything lost on restart RDB snapshots Lose up to the snapshot interval AOF (everysec) Lose up to ~1 second AOF (always) Slow; still not a relational database

Design so that a total Redis loss is degradation, not corruption: caches repopulate, rate limits reset, locks expire, idempotency records are backed by unique constraints in PostgreSQL where it matters.

docs.title: 2.4 Distributed locks — with eyes open
docs.text: SET key token NX PX 30000 + a Lua compare-and-delete release is a good efficiency lock ("only one pod should run this job"). It is not a correctness guarantee under GC pauses, clock issues or failover — for correctness use database constraints, conditional updates (Chapter 12) or fencing tokens.

docs.title: 2.5 MongoDB essentials
docs.text: Concept Notes Document BSON; _id primary key; nested objects and arrays Collection Like a table, but schema-flexible (with optional JSON-schema validation) Embed vs reference Embed what is read together and bounded; reference what is large, shared or unbounded Indexes Single, compound (order matters: equality → sort → range), text, TTL, partial Aggregation pipeline $match, $group, $lookup, $facet, $project Transactions Multi-document transactions require a replica set; keep them short and rare Write concern / read preference w:majority for durability; primary reads for read-your-writes

docs.title: 2.6 Search fundamentals
docs.text: Concept Meaning Index / mapping Schema: field types and analyzers Analyzer Tokenizer + filters (lowercase, stemming, synonyms) applied at index and query time Inverted index term → documents; the reason search is fast Relevance (BM25) Term frequency vs document frequency and length Filter vs query Filters are cached and don't score (price range, category); queries score (text match) Facets (aggregations) Counts per brand/price bucket for the UI Alias A pointer to a concrete index — enables zero-downtime reindexing search_after Cursor pagination; from/size degrades past a few thousand

docs.title: 2.7 Search architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    DB[(PostgreSQL<br/>source of truth)] -->|outbox / CDC| K[(Kafka<br/>catalog events)]
    K --> IDX[indexer service]
    IDX --> OS[(OpenSearch<br/>products_v7)]
    A[alias 'products'] -.-> OS
    API[search API] -->|query alias| A
    API -.->|cluster down| DB
    B[bulk reindex job] --> OS2[(products_v8)]
    OS2 -.->|alias swap| A

The index is always eventually consistent with the database (typically < 2 s). The UI must tolerate that: after adding a product, the seller sees it in "my products" (read from PostgreSQL) before it appears in search.

docs.title: 3.1 Spring Data Redis
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[RedisTemplate / StringRedisTemplate] --> B[RedisConnectionFactory<br/>Lettuce, shared native connection]
    B --> C[Serializers: key, value, hash key, hash value]
    A --> D[opsForValue / Hash / ZSet / Stream / Geo]
    A --> E["execute(RedisScript, keys, args) → EVALSHA"]
    F[StreamMessageListenerContainer] --> B
    G["@EnableRedisRepositories → keyspace 'people:id', @Indexed secondary index sets"] --> A
  • Lettuce is netty-based and thread-safe: one connection multiplexes commands; pooling is only needed for blocking commands or transactions.
  • Serializers matter: StringRedisTemplate uses strings everywhere (readable in redis-cli); a raw RedisTemplate defaults to JDK serialization — avoid it.
  • Lua scripts are sent once and executed by SHA (EVALSHA), falling back to EVAL if the script isn't cached.

docs.title: 3.2 A search query
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as search-service
    participant OS as OpenSearch coordinating node
    participant Sh as Shards

    C->>S: /api/search?q=aata 5kg&brand=Aashirvaad&maxPrice=400
    S->>S: build query: multi_match + filters + aggregations + sort
    S->>OS: POST /products/_search
    OS->>Sh: scatter to shards (query phase: top-k doc ids + scores)
    Sh-->>OS: partial results
    OS->>Sh: fetch phase (documents for the final top-k)
    OS-->>S: hits + aggregations + search_after cursor
    S-->>C: results, facet counts, next cursor

Analysis happens twice: documents are analyzed at index time, the query string at search time — with the same analyzer, otherwise "aata" never matches "atta" even with synonyms configured.

docs.title: 3.3 Zero-downtime reindex
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[products_v7 behind alias 'products'] --> B[create products_v8<br/>new mapping/analyzers]
    B --> C[bulk index from PostgreSQL<br/>+ catch-up from Kafka]
    C --> D[verify: doc count, sample queries, relevance checks]
    D --> E[atomic alias swap v7 → v8]
    E --> F[keep v7 for rollback, delete later]

Mappings are mostly immutable: changing an analyzer or field type requires a new index. Aliases make that invisible to callers.

docs.text:
A sliding-window rate limiter (better than the fixed window in Chapter 17) needs several commands executed atomically:

src/main/resources/redis/sliding-window-rate-limit.lua
-- KEYS[1] = bucket key, ARGV[1] = now(ms), ARGV[2] = window(ms), ARGV[3] = limit, ARGV[4] = member
redis.call('ZREMRANGEBYSCORE', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1] - ARGV[2])
local count = redis.call('ZCARD', KEYS[1])
if count >= tonumber(ARGV[3]) then
  return 0
end
redis.call('ZADD', KEYS[1], ARGV[1], ARGV[4])
redis.call('PEXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[2])
return 1
in/grocery/platform/ratelimit/SlidingWindowRateLimiter.java
package in.grocery.platform.ratelimit;

import java.time.Clock;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.UUID;
import org.springframework.core.io.ClassPathResource;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.script.DefaultRedisScript;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.script.RedisScript;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class SlidingWindowRateLimiter {

    private final RedisScript<Long> script = RedisScript.of(                      // (1)!
            new ClassPathResource("redis/sliding-window-rate-limit.lua"), Long.class);

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;
    private final Clock clock;

    public SlidingWindowRateLimiter(StringRedisTemplate redis, Clock clock) {
        this.redis = redis;
        this.clock = clock;
    }

    public boolean allow(String bucket, int limit, Duration window) {
        Long allowed = redis.execute(script, List.of("rl:" + bucket),             // (2)!
                String.valueOf(clock.millis()),
                String.valueOf(window.toMillis()),
                String.valueOf(limit),
                UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        return allowed != null && allowed == 1L;
    }
}
  1. Loaded once; executed with EVALSHA.
  2. Keys passed as KEYS (required for Redis Cluster slot routing) and values as ARGV. All four steps happen atomically on the server — no race between the count and the insert.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — A safe(ish) distributed lock
5.4 Level 3 — MongoDB modelling and aggregation
docs.text:
Seller catalog documents have variable attributes and a history of revisions:

in/grocery/seller/catalog/SellerProductDocument.java
package in.grocery.seller.catalog;

import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.time.Instant;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.Id;
import org.springframework.data.annotation.Version;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.index.CompoundIndex;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.mapping.Document;

@Document("seller_product")
@CompoundIndex(name = "seller_sku_idx", def = "{'sellerId': 1, 'sku': 1}", unique = true)   // (1)!
public record SellerProductDocument(
        @Id String id,
        String sellerId,
        String sku,
        String title,
        String category,
        BigDecimal mrp,
        BigDecimal sellingPrice,
        Map<String, Object> attributes,                                                     // (2)!
        List<String> images,
        Instant updatedAt,
        @Version Long version) {}
  1. Unique compound index — MongoDB's equivalent of a composite unique constraint.
  2. The flexible part: {"volumeMl": 500, "fragrance": "rose"} for shampoo, {"grainLength": "long"} for rice.
in/grocery/seller/catalog/SellerCatalogQueries.java
package in.grocery.seller.catalog;

import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.aggregation.Aggregation.group;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.aggregation.Aggregation.match;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.aggregation.Aggregation.newAggregation;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.aggregation.Aggregation.project;
import static org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.aggregation.Aggregation.sort;

import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.domain.Sort;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.MongoTemplate;
import org.springframework.data.mongodb.core.query.Criteria;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class SellerCatalogQueries {

    public record CategoryStats(String category, long products, double avgSellingPrice) {}

    private final MongoTemplate mongo;

    public SellerCatalogQueries(MongoTemplate mongo) {
        this.mongo = mongo;
    }

    public List<CategoryStats> statsFor(String sellerId) {
        var aggregation = newAggregation(
                match(Criteria.where("sellerId").is(sellerId)),                                 // (1)!
                group("category")
                        .count().as("products")
                        .avg("sellingPrice").as("avgSellingPrice"),
                project("products", "avgSellingPrice").and("_id").as("category"),
                sort(Sort.Direction.DESC, "products"));
        return mongo.aggregate(aggregation, "seller_product", CategoryStats.class).getMappedResults();
    }
}
  1. $match first, always — filtering before grouping lets the pipeline use indexes.

MongoDB is not a relational database

No foreign keys, no cross-collection joins worth relying on ($lookup is limited and slow at scale), and multi-document transactions need a replica set and hurt throughput. Model documents so a single document is the unit of consistency — the same aggregate thinking as Chapter 13.

6.4 Relevance as a product concern
docs.text:
Signal Implementation Text match BM25 over title/brand/tags with boosts Popularity popularity field refreshed nightly from sales data Availability Out-of-stock items demoted (not removed — customers search for them) Business rules Sponsored placements as a separate, labelled slot — never silently mixed into organic ranking Personalization Later: re-rank top 100 by purchase history

Measure: zero-result rate, click-through on the top 3, search → add-to-cart conversion, and a golden query set (200 queries with expected results) run in CI against a test index so a mapping change can't silently wreck relevance.

docs.title: 6.5 Testing search
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Spring Data Redis 3.x (Lettuce default) 4.x (verify) Redis serializers Jackson 2 variants Jackson 3 equivalents (verify) Spring Data MongoDB 4.x 5.x (verify) Spring Data Elasticsearch 5.x targeting the ES Java client Next major (verify); OpenSearch via spring-data-opensearch Test slices @DataRedisTest, @DataMongoTest Moved into technology test modules (verify) @ServiceConnection Redis, Mongo, Elasticsearch supported Same

Serialized data outlives your deploy

Redis values, MongoDB documents and index documents written by Boot 3.5 pods are read by Boot 4 pods during a rolling upgrade. Same rule as Chapter 21: version the key/index namespace for the upgrade, keep DTOs tolerant, and test cross-version reads.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Inventory Redis key patterns, Mongo collections and search indices with their serialization formats.
  • Re-verify serializer classes after the Jackson 3 move; test reading old values.
  • Check Spring Data module versions against your server versions (Mongo/OpenSearch server compatibility matrices).
  • Re-run search golden queries after upgrading client libraries.
  • Update test slice imports.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. PostgreSQL is the source of truth; Redis, Mongo and the search index are derived or ephemeral.
  2. Namespace Redis keys by concern and always set TTLs.
  3. Lua (or single commands) for atomicity; keys in KEYS for cluster compatibility.
  4. Locks for efficiency, constraints for correctness.
  5. Model Mongo documents as aggregates; index deliberately; create indexes via migrations.
  6. Search: aliases + versioned indices, reindex from the database, swap atomically with guard rails.
  7. Synonyms and fuzziness tuned for Indian shopping vocabulary; search-time synonyms.
  8. Degrade gracefully when a derived store is down.
  9. Measure lag (index lag, replication lag) and quality (zero-result rate, golden queries).
  10. Rebuild drills: prove you can rebuild each derived store from scratch, and know how long it takes.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Using Redis as a database of record for anything financial.

❌ Keys without TTL — memory grows until eviction starts silently dropping data you assumed was there.

❌ KEYS * in production (blocking) — use SCAN.

❌ JDK serialization in RedisTemplate — opaque, fragile, insecure.

❌ Multi-document Mongo transactions used routinely instead of modelling aggregates properly.

❌ Unbounded arrays in Mongo documents (16 MB limit; also slow).

❌ Searching with LIKE '%term%' in PostgreSQL at scale (no index, full scans).

❌ Writing directly to the search index from business code — the index must be rebuildable from the source.

❌ Reindexing in place (delete + recreate the live index) — a window with zero search results.

❌ Relevance changes without golden-query tests.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Redis memory climbing Missing TTLs, big keys Audit with --bigkeys/MEMORY USAGE, add TTLs, set maxmemory-policy Redis latency spikes Blocking commands, big values, KEYS Use SCAN, split large values, monitor SLOWLOG Lock held forever Process died before release; no TTL Always set TTL; compare-and-delete on release Mongo query slow Missing/wrong compound index order explain(), index equality→sort→range Mongo writes rejected Write concern/replica set issues Check topology, w:majority semantics Search returns nothing for a valid term Analyzer mismatch, wrong field type (keyword vs text) Use _analyze API to compare index/search analysis Search misses new products Indexer lag, consumer stuck, failed bulk items Lag metric, DLT for failed events, replay Slow deep pagination from/size beyond a few thousand search_after cursors Relevance regression after a deploy Mapping/analyzer change Golden queries in CI; alias rollback Cluster red/yellow Shard allocation, disk watermarks Capacity, replicas, disk alerts

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Each derived store documented with its source and rebuild procedure
  • Redis: key namespaces, TTLs, maxmemory policy, slowlog monitoring
  • Mongo: indexes in migrations, document size bounds, backup/restore tested
  • Search: alias-based deploys, reindex runbook, index lag alert, zero-result alert
  • Golden query suite in CI
  • Fallback path when search is unavailable, with a monitored fallback rate
  • Cross-version serialization tested before upgrades

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · When would you use Redis instead of PostgreSQL?

Short answer: For ephemeral, high-churn key-value data needing sub-millisecond access and TTLs — caches, rate limits, OTPs, locks, counters — not for durable business records.

B1 · What is StringRedisTemplate and why prefer it?

Short answer: A RedisTemplate with string serializers for keys and values — readable in redis-cli, no JDK-serialization surprises.

B1 · Why does MongoDB suit variable-schema data?

Short answer: Documents can differ in shape within a collection, so optional attributes don't require nullable columns or an EAV model.

B1 · Why can't you use LIKE '%atta%' for product search?

Short answer: It can't use an index (leading wildcard), doesn't rank results, and has no typo tolerance, synonyms or facets.

B1 · What is a search index alias?

Short answer: A name that points to a concrete index, letting you rebuild into a new index and switch atomically.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Which Redis structure for a leaderboard, a lock, a queue?

Short answer: Sorted set (ZSET) for leaderboards; SET NX PX string with a token for locks; list (LPUSH/BRPOP) or Redis Streams for queues — Streams when you need consumer groups and acknowledgement.

B2 · How do you make multi-step Redis logic atomic?

Short answer: A Lua script executed server-side (EVAL/EVALSHA), or MULTI/EXEC with WATCH. Pass keys via KEYS for cluster routing.

B2 · Embed or reference in MongoDB?

Short answer: Embed data that is read together, bounded in size and owned by the document; reference large, shared or unbounded data. Model the document as an aggregate.

B2 · Filter vs query in a search request?

Short answer: Filters are boolean, cacheable and don't affect score (price range, category, availability); queries compute relevance (text match). Put everything structured in filters.

B2 · How do you keep the search index up to date?

Short answer: Consume change events (outbox/CDC), load the projection from the source of truth, and bulk index — with lag metrics and a DLT for failures.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · What are the limits of a Redis distributed lock?

Short answer: It's an efficiency lock: GC pauses, clock skew and failover can allow two holders. TTL plus compare-and-delete limits damage; for correctness use database constraints/conditional updates or fencing tokens.

B3 · How do you perform a zero-downtime reindex?

Short answer: Create a new index with the new mapping, bulk load from the source while the indexer keeps both current (or replay events from a recorded offset), validate counts and golden queries, then swap the alias atomically and keep the old index for rollback.

B3 · Why do synonyms belong in the search analyzer?

Short answer: Search-time synonyms let you change the list without reindexing; index-time synonyms bake them into the inverted index (faster, but any change means a reindex).

B3 · How do you paginate millions of search results?

Short answer: search_after with a stable sort (score + a unique tiebreaker) rather than from/size, which gets expensive because every shard must collect and discard deep offsets.

B3 · How do you decide MongoDB compound index order?

Short answer: Equality fields first, then sort fields, then range fields; verify with explain() that the index covers the query and avoids in-memory sorts.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design search for a 2-million-SKU marketplace.

Short answer: PostgreSQL as source of truth; events → indexer → OpenSearch with alias-versioned indices; mapping with keyword filters, boosted text fields, search-time synonyms and fuzziness; availability denormalized per pincode; facets for the UI; search_after pagination; popularity boosting refreshed nightly; circuit breaker with database fallback; lag, zero-result and golden-query monitoring; documented reindex runbook.

B4 · What breaks when Redis goes down and how do you prepare?

Short answer: Caches (fail open), rate limits (fail open or closed by policy), locks (jobs may double-run — make them idempotent), OTP/idempotency (back critical uniqueness with database constraints). Test it: stop Redis in staging under load and confirm degradation, not failure.

B4 · How do you keep polyglot persistence from becoming an operational burden?

Short answer: Limit the number of stores, give each a documented purpose, source and rebuild procedure; standardize clients and observability in the platform library; ensure every derived store can be rebuilt; and run periodic rebuild drills.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you decide whether a new store is justified?

Short answer: Show that the workload genuinely doesn't fit existing stores (measured), that the operational cost (backups, upgrades, on-call knowledge, security review) is accepted, and that data can be rebuilt. Otherwise extend PostgreSQL — it does JSONB, full-text, and geo well enough for many cases.

B5 · Search relevance is a product problem. How do you organize it?

Short answer: Shared ownership with the business: metrics (zero-result, CTR, conversion), a golden query set maintained with category managers, experimentation (A/B on ranking), clearly separated sponsored placements, and release discipline (aliases, rollback) so relevance changes are as reversible as code.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · After a mapping change, search returns nothing for 'atta'

The new mapping changed title from text to keyword for "exact matching", so only the full string matches. Fix: revert the alias to the previous index (instant), correct the mapping, reindex, and add a golden-query CI job that indexes fixtures into a container and asserts the top results.

Scenario · Redis memory hits maxmemory and OTP logins start failing

Trending sorted sets were written without TTL, filling memory; allkeys-lru evicted OTP keys. Fixes: TTLs on every key, separate Redis databases/instances for cache vs critical short-lived data, volatile-lru on the cache instance, memory alerts, and OTP verification that falls back to a database-backed store.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · 'Recently viewed products'

Store the last 20 products viewed per customer in Redis (most recent first, no duplicates, 30-day expiry) and return them with product details from PostgreSQL. Implement it with one atomic operation per view and write tests.

Solution RecentlyViewedStore.java
package in.grocery.catalog.recent;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.redis.core.StringRedisTemplate;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class RecentlyViewedStore {

    private static final int MAX = 20;

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public RecentlyViewedStore(StringRedisTemplate redis) {
        this.redis = redis;
    }

    public void recordView(String customerId, String sku) {
        String key = key(customerId);
        var ops = redis.opsForList();
        ops.remove(key, 0, sku);          // (1)!
        ops.leftPush(key, sku);
        ops.trim(key, 0, MAX - 1);
        redis.expire(key, Duration.ofDays(30));
    }

    public List<String> recent(String customerId) {
        return redis.opsForList().range(key(customerId), 0, MAX - 1);
    }

    private static String key(String customerId) {
        return "recent:" + customerId;
    }
}
  1. Four commands, not atomic as a group. For this use case that's fine (worst case: a duplicate or a slightly long list for microseconds). If atomicity mattered, the same logic in Lua would be four lines:
Lua script
redis.call('LREM', KEYS[1], 0, ARGV[1])
redis.call('LPUSH', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
redis.call('LTRIM', KEYS[1], 0, tonumber(ARGV[2]) - 1)
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], tonumber(ARGV[3]))
RecentlyViewedStoreTest.java
@Test
void keepsMostRecentFirstWithoutDuplicates() {
    store.recordView("C-1", "MILK-1L");
    store.recordView("C-1", "ATTA-5KG");
    store.recordView("C-1", "MILK-1L");                       // moves to front

    assertThat(store.recent("C-1")).containsExactly("MILK-1L", "ATTA-5KG");
}

@Test
void capsAtTwenty() {
    for (int i = 0; i < 25; i++) store.recordView("C-2", "SKU-" + i);
    assertThat(store.recent("C-2")).hasSize(20).startsWith("SKU-24");
}

Product details are then fetched from PostgreSQL by SKU (Chapter 12's IN query) — Redis holds only the ordering, which is exactly the kind of ephemeral, per-user state it's good at.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Right store for the workload: PostgreSQL for truth, Redis for ephemeral key-value, Mongo for variable documents, OpenSearch for relevance.
  • Redis is data structures, not just a cache — sorted sets, geo, streams, Lua for atomicity — but plan for total loss.
  • Locks are efficiency, not correctness.
  • Model Mongo documents as aggregates; indexes belong in migrations.
  • Search is a derived, rebuildable projection: alias-versioned indices, reindex from the source, swap atomically, guard with golden queries.
  • Degrade gracefully when a derived store is unavailable, and measure lag and quality.
  • Every derived store needs a rehearsed rebuild procedure.
