21 Caching · 23 Messaging with Kafka

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Synchronous HTTP couples services in availability and latency: if inventory is slow, checkout is slow; if notification is down, orders fail. Kafka breaks that coupling. When an order is placed, order-service writes one event and returns; inventory reserves stock, notification sends an SMS, analytics updates dashboards, search reindexes and loyalty awards points — independently, at their own pace, and they can be down for ten minutes without losing a single event.

That power comes with a new set of failure modes, and every one of them has a name and a fix:

  • Lost events — the database committed but the publish failed (dual write). Fix: the outbox (Chapters 16, 36).
  • Duplicate processing — Kafka is at-least-once; a rebalance or retry re-delivers. Fix: idempotent consumers.
  • Out-of-order processing — OrderPaid handled before OrderPlaced. Fix: partition by aggregate key.
  • Poison pills — one unparseable message blocks a partition forever. Fix: error handlers, retry topics, DLT.
  • Silent lag — a consumer falls 4 million messages behind and nobody notices until customers complain.
  • Schema breakage — a producer adds a required field and every consumer fails.

This chapter covers Kafka with Spring properly: producing and consuming, partitioning and ordering, serialization and schema evolution, acknowledgement modes, error handling with retry topics and dead-letter topics, idempotent consumers with an inbox, transactions (and why the outbox still wins), batch consumption, consumer lag and observability, rebalancing during deploys, and testing with Testcontainers.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — topics, KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — keys, offsets, error handling, DLT, testing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — rebalancing, idempotency, batching, tuning B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — topic/schema governance, delivery guarantees, operations B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — event-driven architecture strategy

docs.title: 2.1 Kafka in five sentences
docs.text: A topic is an append-only log split into partitions. Each partition is ordered and assigned to exactly one consumer within a consumer group, which tracks its position with offsets. Producers choose a partition by key (same key → same partition → ordered). Messages are retained by time or size (or compacted by key), so consumers can replay. Brokers replicate partitions for durability.

docs.title: 2.2 Grocery topics
docs.text:
Topic Key Retention Purpose grocery.order.placed.v1 orderRef 7 days Order lifecycle fan-out grocery.order.status-changed.v1 orderRef 7 days Status transitions grocery.payment.captured.v1 orderRef 30 days Payment outcomes grocery.inventory.stock-changed.v1 sku 3 days Search/catalog updates grocery.catalog.product-changed.v1 sku compacted Latest state per product grocery.pricing.price-changed.v1 sku 1 day Cache invalidation (Chapter 21) grocery.*.dlt original 30 days Dead letters

Convention: grocery.<domain>.<event>.v<major> — the version in the name makes an incompatible schema change a new topic, which consumers adopt on their own schedule.

docs.title: 2.3 Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
Guarantee Reality At-most-once Commit offset before processing — lose messages on crash. Rarely acceptable. At-least-once Process, then commit — duplicates possible. The default and the right choice, combined with idempotent consumers. Exactly-once (EOS) Kafka transactions for read-process-write-to-Kafka flows. Does not extend to your database.

Since your side effects are usually database writes, "exactly once" in practice means at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing.

docs.title: 2.4 Producer essentials
docs.text: Setting Recommended Why acks all Wait for in-sync replicas enable.idempotence true (default in modern clients) No duplicates from producer retries max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5 with idempotence Keeps ordering compression.type lz4 or zstd Cheaper network and disk linger.ms 5–20 ms Batching; small latency cost delivery.timeout.ms 120s (default) Total time before failing the send Key aggregate id Ordering and co-location

docs.title: 2.5 Consumer essentials
docs.text: Setting Notes group.id Identifies the consumer group; one offset per group per partition auto.offset.reset earliest for new consumers that must not miss history; latest for pure live feeds enable.auto.commit false — Spring commits offsets after successful processing max.poll.records Batch size per poll (default 500) max.poll.interval.ms Processing budget per poll before the consumer is considered dead concurrency (Spring) Number of consumer threads — never more than partitions isolation.level read_committed when producers use transactions

docs.title: 2.6 Spring for Apache Kafka
docs.text: Piece Role KafkaTemplate Send messages (returns CompletableFuture<SendResult>) @KafkaListener Consume; one or many topics; batch or record ConcurrentKafkaListenerContainerFactory Builds listener containers (concurrency, error handler, ack mode) AckMode BATCH (default), RECORD, MANUAL, MANUAL_IMMEDIATE DefaultErrorHandler Retries in place with back-off, then recovers (e.g. publish to DLT) DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer Sends failed records to <topic>.DLT with failure headers @RetryableTopic Non-blocking retries via separate retry topics KafkaAdmin + NewTopic beans Topic creation (dev only in this platform)

docs.title: 2.7 Ordering
docs.text:
Order is guaranteed only within a partition. Therefore:

  • Key by the entity whose order matters (orderRef), so all events for one order land on one partition.
  • More partitions = more parallelism but no global order.
  • Adding partitions later changes key→partition mapping — plan partition counts up front (they can only grow, and growth reshuffles keys).

docs.title: 2.8 Error handling ladder
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Listener throws] --> B{Retryable?}
    B -- no e.g. deserialization,<br/>validation --> D[DLT immediately]
    B -- yes e.g. downstream 503 --> C[Blocking retry with back-off<br/>DefaultErrorHandler]
    C -- still failing --> E{Blocking acceptable?}
    E -- no --> F["Non-blocking retry topics<br/>(@RetryableTopic): retry-0s, retry-5s, retry-30s"]
    E -- yes --> D
    F -- exhausted --> D
    D --> G[Alert + manual/automated replay tooling]

Blocking retries stall the partition (ordering preserved, throughput lost). Non-blocking retry topics keep the main partition moving but lose ordering for retried records. Choose per topic.

docs.title: 2.9 Idempotent consumers
docs.text:
Because delivery is at-least-once, every consumer must tolerate repeats:

Technique Example Natural idempotency UPDATE order SET status='PAID' WHERE ref=? AND status='PLACED' Inbox table Insert (consumer, event_id) with a unique constraint; skip on duplicate Versioned state Ignore events with version <= current Upsert INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE

docs.title: 2.10 Schema evolution
docs.text:
Format Notes JSON (typed DTOs) Simple, human-readable; evolution enforced by discipline and tests JSON + Schema Registry Validation and compatibility checks Avro/Protobuf + Schema Registry Compact, enforced compatibility (BACKWARD by default)

Rules, whatever the format: add optional fields, never remove or repurpose; keep enums open; breaking changes mean a new topic version.

Spring's JSON type headers

JsonSerializer adds a __TypeId__ header and JsonDeserializer instantiates that class. Always configure spring.kafka.consumer.properties.spring.json.trusted.packages (never *) or, better, configure the deserializer with an explicit target type — otherwise a malicious or wrong producer can drive class instantiation on the consumer.

docs.title: 3.1 Producing
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Application
    participant KT as KafkaTemplate
    participant P as KafkaProducer
    participant Part as Partitioner
    participant Acc as RecordAccumulator (batches)
    participant B as Broker leader
    participant R as Replicas

    A->>KT: send("grocery.order.placed.v1", orderRef, event)
    KT->>P: serialize key/value, add headers (trace, type)
    P->>Part: partition = hash(key) % partitions
    P->>Acc: append to batch (linger.ms, batch.size)
    Acc->>B: produce request (compressed)
    B->>R: replicate
    R-->>B: in-sync acks
    B-->>P: ack (acks=all) → offset
    P-->>KT: complete future with RecordMetadata

With enable.idempotence, each producer has a producer id and sequence numbers, so broker-side retries don't create duplicates.

docs.title: 3.2 Consuming with Spring
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as KafkaMessageListenerContainer
    participant K as KafkaConsumer
    participant L as @KafkaListener method
    participant EH as DefaultErrorHandler
    participant DLT as DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer

    loop poll cycle
        C->>K: poll(timeout) → records
        loop each record (or batch)
            C->>L: invoke (converted payload, headers)
            alt success
                C->>C: track offset
            else exception
                C->>EH: handle(record, exception)
                EH->>EH: back-off, seek back, retry n times
                EH->>DLT: recover → publish to <topic>.DLT
            end
        end
        C->>K: commitSync offsets (AckMode BATCH)
    end

Key facts:

  • Offsets are committed after processing (at-least-once).
  • Processing must finish within max.poll.interval.ms, or the broker removes the consumer from the group → rebalance → reprocessing.
  • concurrency = n creates n consumers in the same group inside one application instance; total useful parallelism is bounded by partitions.

docs.title: 3.3 Rebalancing
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Pod starts / stops / max.poll.interval exceeded] --> B[Group coordinator triggers rebalance]
    B --> C{protocol}
    C -- eager --> D[all consumers stop, partitions reassigned<br/>stop-the-world]
    C -- cooperative sticky --> E[only moved partitions pause<br/>others keep processing]
    E --> F[offsets committed before revoke]
    F --> G[processing resumes]

Rolling deploys cause rebalances. Mitigations: cooperative sticky assignment (the modern default), static membership (group.instance.id + longer session.timeout.ms) so a restarting pod reclaims its partitions without a full reshuffle, and short, idempotent processing so reprocessing after a rebalance is harmless.

docs.title: 4.1 Configuration
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springframework.kafka:spring-kafka")
testImplementation("org.springframework.kafka:spring-kafka-test")
testImplementation("org.testcontainers:kafka")
application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka:9092
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 10
        compression.type: lz4
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
    consumer:
      group-id: ${spring.application.name}
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer   # (1)!
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
        spring.json.trusted.packages: in.grocery.*.events                                         # (2)!
    listener:
      ack-mode: batch
      concurrency: 3
      observation-enabled: true                                                                    # (3)!
    template:
      observation-enabled: true
  1. ErrorHandlingDeserializer wraps the real deserializer so a malformed message becomes a handled failure (→ DLT) instead of an infinite poison-pill loop.
  2. Never * — this controls which classes a payload can instantiate.
  3. Micrometer observations for producers and consumers (traces across services, Chapter 27).

docs.title: 4.2 An event and a producer
4.3 A consumer
4.4 A first test with Testcontainers
5.1 Level 2 — Error handling and the dead-letter topic
5.2 Level 2 — Non-blocking retries
docs.text:
Blocking retries stall the partition. When a downstream is slow but ordering per key isn't critical, use retry topics:

in/grocery/loyalty/LoyaltyPointsConsumer.java
@RetryableTopic(
        attempts = "4",
        backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 3.0, maxDelay = 60_000),                 // (1)!
        dltTopicSuffix = "-dlt",
        include = {DependencyException.class},                                                  // (2)!
        autoCreateTopics = "false")                                                             // (3)!
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.order.placed.v1", groupId = "loyalty-service")
public void award(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
    loyalty.awardPoints(event.customerId(), event.orderRef(), event.total());
}

@DltHandler
public void dlt(OrderPlacedEvent event, @Header(KafkaHeaders.ORIGINAL_TOPIC) String topic) {
    log.error("Loyalty permanently failed for {} from {}", event.orderRef(), topic);
    incidents.raise("loyalty-dlt", event.orderRef());
}
  1. Creates ...-retry-0, ...-retry-1, ...-retry-2 topics with increasing delays; the main partition keeps flowing.
  2. Only dependency failures are retried; everything else goes straight to the DLT.
  3. Topics are provisioned by the platform (6.4) — auto-creation in production hides mistakes.

Retry topics lose ordering

A retried event is processed later than events that followed it. Use them for commutative work (awarding points, sending notifications, indexing), not for state machines where order matters.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Idempotent consumption with an inbox
5.4 Level 3 — Batch consumption for throughput
5.5 Level 3 — The outbox relay (publishing side)
docs.text:
Chapter 16 wrote outbox rows in the business transaction. Here they reach Kafka:

in/grocery/platform/outbox/OutboxRelay.java
package in.grocery.platform.outbox;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.kafka.core.KafkaTemplate;
import org.springframework.scheduling.annotation.Scheduled;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafka;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)                                                                 // (1)!
    @Transactional
    public void relay() {
        List<OutboxRow> batch = outbox.claimBatch(200);                                          // (2)!
        for (OutboxRow row : batch) {
            try {
                kafka.send(row.topic(), row.aggregateId(), row.payload())
                     .get(Duration.ofSeconds(5).toMillis(), java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);  // (3)!
                outbox.markSent(row.id());
            } catch (Exception e) {
                outbox.markFailed(row.id(), e.getMessage());                                     // (4)!
                meters.counter("grocery.outbox.failures", "topic", row.topic()).increment();
                break;                                                                            // (5)!
            }
        }
        meters.gauge("grocery.outbox.pending", outbox.countPending());
    }
}
  1. Polling every 500 ms is simple and adequate; CDC (Debezium, Chapter 36) removes the poll entirely.
  2. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED (Chapter 12) so multiple pods relay different rows.
  3. Synchronous wait: the row is only marked sent after the broker acknowledges.
  4. Failures leave the row pending for the next cycle — at-least-once, which consumers already tolerate.
  5. Stop the batch on failure to preserve per-aggregate order and avoid hammering a broken broker.

Pending outbox size is a first-class alert: growing means events aren't reaching consumers even though the database looks healthy.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Kafka transactions (and their limits)
docs.text:
For read-process-write-to-Kafka pipelines (e.g. enriching a stream), exactly-once within Kafka is real:

application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      transaction-id-prefix: enricher-${HOSTNAME}-        # (1)!
    consumer:
      isolation-level: read_committed                     # (2)!
Kafka transactions (and their limits) (snippet)
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.order.placed.v1", groupId = "enricher")
@Transactional("kafkaTransactionManager")                                                       // (3)!
public void enrich(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
    kafka.send("grocery.order.enriched.v1", event.orderRef(), enricher.enrich(event));
}
  1. A unique, stable transactional id per instance.
  2. Consumers only see committed records.
  3. Offsets and produced records commit atomically.

This does not include your database

A Kafka transaction plus a JDBC transaction is still two transactions. Ordering them ("commit DB then Kafka") reduces but never eliminates the window. The outbox is the correct answer whenever a database write and an event must be atomic (Chapters 16, 36).

docs.title: 6.1 The order fan-out, end to end
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order-service
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant R as outbox relay
    participant K as Kafka (grocery.order.placed.v1)
    participant I as inventory-service
    participant N as notification-service
    participant S as search-indexer

    O->>DB: TX: order + lines + outbox row (COMMIT)
    R->>DB: claim batch (SKIP LOCKED)
    R->>K: produce (key = orderRef, acks=all)
    R->>DB: mark sent
    K->>I: consume (group inventory-service) → inbox + reserve stock
    K->>N: consume (group notification-service) → SMS
    K->>S: consume (group search-indexer) → reindex affected SKUs
    I->>DB: TX: inbox row + stock reservation
    I->>K: produce grocery.inventory.stock-changed.v1 (via its own outbox)

Every consumer: own group, own offsets, own failure handling, own DLT. A notification outage delays SMS but never blocks stock reservation.

docs.title: 6.2 Production listener configuration
6.3 Consumer lag and observability
6.4 Topic governance
docs.text:
platform/topics/topics.yaml (managed by the platform team)
topics:
  - name: grocery.order.placed.v1
    partitions: 12                                                                              # (1)!
    replication: 3
    config:
      retention.ms: 604800000        # 7 days
      min.insync.replicas: 2                                                                    # (2)!
      cleanup.policy: delete
  - name: grocery.catalog.product-changed.v1
    partitions: 6
    replication: 3
    config:
      cleanup.policy: compact                                                                   # (3)!
      min.cleanable.dirty.ratio: 0.1
  1. Partition count is the hardest thing to change later (it reshuffles keys) — size for peak throughput and future consumer parallelism, e.g. 12 partitions ≈ 12 concurrent consumers.
  2. With acks=all, min.insync.replicas=2 means a write survives one broker loss; if only one replica is in sync, writes fail loudly instead of silently risking data.
  3. Compacted topics keep the latest value per key forever — ideal for "current state of a product" that a new consumer can bootstrap from.
application.yml — production
spring:
  kafka:
    admin:
      auto-create: false                                                                        # (4)!
  1. Topics are infrastructure, created by the platform pipeline with reviewed settings. Auto-creation gives you one-partition, default-retention topics nobody planned.

docs.title: 6.5 Schema evolution rules
6.6 Replaying dead letters
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Spring for Apache Kafka 3.x 4.x (verify) Kafka clients 3.x/4.x 4.x — KRaft only, ZooKeeper removed @RetryableTopic ✅ ✅ (verify attribute changes) Observations observation-enabled on template/listener Same Virtual threads Listener containers can use them when spring.threads.virtual.enabled Same Share groups (queue semantics) Preview in Kafka 4 Evolving — verify support in Spring JSON serializers Jackson 2 Jackson 3 — payload format must stay compatible across the rollout

Rolling upgrades and serialization

During a Boot 3.5 → 4 rollout, 3.5 producers and 4.x consumers (and vice versa) coexist. Keep the JSON payload identical (field names, date formats), verify __TypeId__ header handling, and test cross-version produce/consume before upgrading. Schema-registry formats (Avro) are safer here by design.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Upgrade brokers to KRaft before Kafka 4 clients.
  • Verify serializer/deserializer classes and trusted packages after the Jackson move.
  • Cross-version produce/consume test (3.5 ↔ 4.x) for every topic.
  • Re-check KafkaProperties.build*Properties signatures in custom factories.
  • Re-run error-handling and DLT tests; header names must still match tooling.
  • Confirm consumer group ids and static membership settings survive the deploy.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Outbox for publishing; never publish inside the business transaction, never rely on "log the error".
  2. Idempotent consumers (inbox, conditional updates, upserts) — at-least-once is the contract.
  3. Key by aggregate id for ordering; size partitions for peak parallelism up front.
  4. acks=all, idempotent producer, min.insync.replicas=2.
  5. Error handling ladder: classify retryable vs not, back off, DLT, alert on every dead letter.
  6. Non-blocking retries only for commutative work.
  7. Own group per consuming service; concurrency ≤ partitions.
  8. Cooperative sticky + static membership for smooth deploys.
  9. Monitor lag, DLT, outbox pending, rebalances; alert on all four.
  10. Topics and schemas are governed infrastructure: reviewed settings, versioned names, contract tests.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ kafka.send(...) inside a database transaction (dual write) — the event may be published for work that rolls back, or lost.

❌ Ignoring the send future ("fire and forget") for events that matter.

❌ spring.json.trusted.packages=* — remote class instantiation from message headers.

❌ Auto-creating topics in production — one partition, wrong retention, no review.

❌ Consumers that aren't idempotent ("we'll just make sure it's delivered once").

❌ Long processing inside the listener beyond max.poll.interval.ms → endless rebalances.

❌ Concurrency greater than partitions (idle threads) or a single partition for a high-throughput topic (no parallelism).

❌ Using a DLT as a queue nobody reads.

❌ Changing an event's field meaning in place instead of publishing a new topic version.

❌ Blocking retries on a hot partition for a downstream that's down for an hour.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Consumer lag grows steadily Too few partitions/consumers, slow processing, downstream latency Scale partitions+consumers, batch, profile the handler Same message processed repeatedly Exception after side effect, rebalance before commit, no idempotency Inbox/conditional updates; shorten processing Partition stuck Poison pill retried forever ErrorHandlingDeserializer, non-retryable classification, DLT Frequent rebalances max.poll.interval.ms exceeded, unstable pods, eager assignor Reduce max.poll.records, cooperative sticky, static membership Events out of order Wrong key, retry topics, multiple producers per aggregate Key by aggregate; avoid retry topics for ordered flows SerializationException after a deploy Incompatible payload change Versioned topics, contract tests, tolerant readers Messages published but never consumed Wrong group/topic, auto-offset-reset=latest on a new consumer Check group, offsets, reset policy Duplicate side effects after an incident Replay without idempotency Make consumers idempotent before replaying Broker full / retention surprises Wrong retention/compaction settings Governed topic configs Producer blocks/times out buffer.memory full, broker unreachable Alert on producer errors; back-pressure upstream

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• All publishing goes through the outbox
  • Every consumer is idempotent (documented mechanism)
  • Error handler with classified exceptions, back-off and DLT on every listener
  • DLT monitoring + replay tooling, tested
  • Lag, DLT, outbox-pending and rebalance alerts configured
  • Topics provisioned with reviewed partitions/retention/replication; auto-create off
  • Trusted packages restricted; schemas versioned and contract-tested
  • Cooperative sticky + static membership; deploys verified not to cause reprocessing storms
  • Integration tests with a real broker (Testcontainers)

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is a Kafka topic, partition and consumer group?

Short answer: A topic is a named log split into partitions; each partition is ordered and consumed by one consumer per group; a group tracks offsets so different services (groups) each get all messages.

B1 · How do you send and receive messages in Spring Boot?

Short answer: KafkaTemplate.send(topic, key, payload) to produce; a @KafkaListener method to consume, with spring.kafka.* configuration.

B1 · What does the message key do?

Short answer: It determines the partition, so all messages with the same key are ordered and handled by the same consumer instance.

B1 · What delivery guarantee does Kafka give by default?

Short answer: At-least-once — messages can be redelivered, so consumers must be idempotent.

B1 · What is a dead-letter topic?

Short answer: A topic where messages that can't be processed after retries are published for inspection and replay.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How does Spring commit offsets?

Short answer: With enable.auto.commit=false, the listener container commits after successful processing (AckMode BATCH by default, or RECORD/MANUAL), giving at-least-once semantics.

B2 · How do you handle a poison pill?

Short answer: ErrorHandlingDeserializer turns deserialization errors into handled failures; classify them as non-retryable in DefaultErrorHandler so they go straight to the DLT instead of blocking the partition.

B2 · Blocking retries vs retry topics?

Short answer: Blocking retries pause the partition (ordering preserved, throughput lost); @RetryableTopic moves the record to delay topics so the main partition keeps flowing, at the cost of ordering.

B2 · How do you make a consumer idempotent?

Short answer: Natural idempotency (conditional updates/upserts) or an inbox table keyed by (consumer, eventId) written in the same transaction as the side effect.

B2 · How do you scale a consumer?

Short answer: Add instances or concurrency up to the partition count; beyond that, add partitions (planning for the key-reshuffle impact).

B2 · How do you test Kafka code?

Short answer: Testcontainers with a real broker (or @EmbeddedKafka), publishing and asserting with Awaitility; plus contract tests on event payloads.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Explain rebalancing and how to make deploys smooth.

Short answer: Group membership changes trigger partition reassignment. Cooperative sticky assignment only moves affected partitions; static membership (group.instance.id) lets a restarting pod reclaim its partitions without a reshuffle; keep processing short and idempotent so any reprocessing is harmless.

B3 · What exactly do Kafka transactions guarantee?

Short answer: Atomic produce of multiple records plus offset commits within Kafka (read_committed consumers see all-or-nothing). They do not make a database write atomic with a publish — that needs the outbox.

B3 · Why is the outbox preferred over publishing after commit?

Short answer: A crash between commit and publish loses the event silently. The outbox row commits with the business data, and a relay publishes with at-least-once semantics and retry.

B3 · How do you keep ordering guarantees?

Short answer: Key by aggregate id; one partition per key; single producer per aggregate; idempotent producer with bounded in-flight requests; avoid retry topics for ordered flows.

B3 · What happens when processing exceeds max.poll.interval.ms?

Short answer: The broker considers the consumer dead, removes it from the group and rebalances; the in-flight work's offsets aren't committed, so records are reprocessed. Reduce max.poll.records, speed up processing, or pause the container explicitly.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the event architecture for the order lifecycle.

Short answer: Versioned topics keyed by orderRef; outbox publishing from each service; per-service consumer groups with inbox idempotency; classified error handling with DLTs and replay tooling; governed topic configs (partitions, retention, replication); schema evolution rules with contract tests; lag/DLT/outbox dashboards and alerts.

B4 · How do you choose the partition count?

Short answer: From peak throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, plus headroom for future parallelism and ordering requirements (one key's events must fit one partition's throughput). Increasing later reshuffles keys, so start generous but not absurd (broker overhead per partition).

B4 · How do you migrate an event schema that must change incompatibly?

Short answer: Publish a new versioned topic; producers dual-publish; consumers migrate individually; monitor consumer groups on the old topic; retire it when empty. With a schema registry, enforce compatibility modes and use them to prevent accidental breaks.

B4 · Kafka or a database queue for a small workload?

Short answer: If you already run Kafka and need fan-out, replay or high throughput, use it. For a single consumer with modest volume, a PostgreSQL queue (SKIP LOCKED) is simpler to operate and transactional with your data — fewer moving parts is a real benefit.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · When does event-driven architecture hurt?

Short answer: When teams use events for request/response, when eventual consistency isn't reflected in the UX, when there's no schema governance (every change breaks someone), when debugging requires tracing across ten hops without correlation, or when operational maturity (lag monitoring, replay, DLT triage) is missing.

B5 · How do you govern events across many teams?

Short answer: An event catalog with owners and schemas, naming/versioning standards, compatibility enforcement in CI, platform libraries for outbox/idempotency/error handling, shared dashboards, and a review step for new topics — treating events as public APIs (Chapter 20).

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Stock reserved twice for some orders during a deploy

Pods restarted mid-batch; offsets weren't committed, so events were redelivered, and the consumer reserved stock again. Fixes: inbox table with (consumer, eventId) unique constraint committed in the same transaction as the reservation, plus conditional SQL (WHERE NOT EXISTS), cooperative sticky rebalancing and shorter batches.

Scenario · Notification consumer stuck for 6 hours, 2M messages behind

One malformed message (produced by an old service version) threw on deserialization; the default error handler retried forever, blocking the partition. Fixes: ErrorHandlingDeserializer + non-retryable classification → DLT, lag alerting (would have paged in minutes), DLT monitoring, and a contract test for the producing service.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Payment-captured consumer

Consume grocery.payment.captured.v1 (key orderRef) in order-service: mark the order paid (only if currently PLACED), write an outbox event OrderPaid, be idempotent, retry only dependency failures (max 3, exponential back-off), and send anything else to the DLT. Write tests for happy path, duplicate delivery and poison pill.

Solution PaymentCapturedConsumer.java
package in.grocery.order.consumer;

import in.grocery.order.outbox.OutboxWriter;
import org.springframework.dao.DuplicateKeyException;
import org.springframework.kafka.annotation.KafkaListener;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Component
public class PaymentCapturedConsumer {

    private static final String CONSUMER = "order.payment-captured";

    private final InboxRepository inbox;
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final OutboxWriter outbox;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.payment.captured.v1", groupId = "order-service")
    @Transactional
    public void onPaymentCaptured(PaymentCapturedEvent event) {
        try {
            inbox.markProcessed(CONSUMER, event.eventId());
        } catch (DuplicateKeyException duplicate) {
            return;                                                       // already handled
        }

        int updated = orders.markPaidIfPlaced(event.orderRef(), event.paymentId());   // (1)!
        if (updated == 0) {
            return;                                                       // (2)!
        }
        outbox.append("order", event.orderRef(), "OrderPaid",
                new OrderPaid(event.orderRef(), event.paymentId(), event.amount()));
    }
}
  1. Conditional update — a second mechanism of idempotency alongside the inbox.
  2. Order already paid or cancelled: nothing to do. Don't throw — that would send a perfectly valid duplicate to the DLT.
PaymentCapturedConsumerTest.java
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class PaymentCapturedConsumerTest {

    @Container @ServiceConnection static KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer("apache/kafka:3.9.0");
    @Container @ServiceConnection static PostgreSQLContainer<?> pg = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17-alpine");

    @Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, Object> template;
    @Autowired OrderRepository orders;
    @Autowired OutboxRepository outbox;

    @Test
    void marksOrderPaidAndWritesOutbox() {
        String ref = seedPlacedOrder();
        template.send("grocery.payment.captured.v1", ref, new PaymentCapturedEvent("evt-1", ref, "pay_1", "578.00"));

        await().atMost(TEN_SECONDS).untilAsserted(() -> {
            assertThat(orders.findByOrderRef(ref).orElseThrow().getStatus()).isEqualTo(OrderStatus.PAID);
            assertThat(outbox.findByAggregateId(ref)).extracting(OutboxRow::eventType).contains("OrderPaid");
        });
    }

    @Test
    void duplicateDeliveryIsIgnored() {
        String ref = seedPlacedOrder();
        var event = new PaymentCapturedEvent("evt-2", ref, "pay_2", "578.00");
        template.send("grocery.payment.captured.v1", ref, event);
        template.send("grocery.payment.captured.v1", ref, event);

        await().atMost(TEN_SECONDS).untilAsserted(() ->
                assertThat(outbox.findByAggregateId(ref)).hasSize(1));                 // exactly one OrderPaid
    }

    @Test
    void poisonPillGoesToDlt() {
        template.send("grocery.payment.captured.v1", "ORD-X", "{not json".getBytes());
        await().atMost(TEN_SECONDS).untilAsserted(() ->
                assertThat(dltConsumer.received()).isNotEmpty());
    }
}

The duplicate test is the one that matters: it proves the consumer survives Kafka's at-least-once reality.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Kafka decouples services in time and availability; the price is at-least-once delivery and eventual consistency.
  • Publish via the outbox, consume idempotently (inbox or conditional updates) — together these give effective exactly-once.
  • Key by aggregate id for ordering; plan partitions early.
  • Classify errors: retry transient ones with back-off, send the rest to a DLT — and treat DLT messages as incidents.
  • Non-blocking retry topics only for commutative work.
  • Cooperative sticky + static membership make deploys boring.
  • Monitor lag, DLT rate, outbox pending, rebalances.
  • Topics and schemas are governed contracts, versioned like APIs.

22 NoSQL & Search · 24 RabbitMQ, Pulsar, JMS & Cloud Stream

docs.title: 24 · RabbitMQ, Pulsar, JMS & Spring Cloud Stream
1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Kafka (Chapter 23) is a log: ordered, replayable, fan-out to many independent consumer groups. That makes it perfect for OrderPlaced — five services each want every event, at their own pace, with replay after an outage.

It is a poor fit for other jobs in the same platform:

  • Delivery dispatch. A packed order must go to exactly one available rider, express orders before standard ones, with a retry in 30 seconds if nobody accepts. That's a work queue with priorities and delays — RabbitMQ's home ground.
  • Legacy ERP integration. The finance ERP speaks JMS over ActiveMQ Artemis, because it was built in 2012 and isn't changing.
  • Multi-tenant streaming with tiered storage. Pulsar does queueing and streaming in one system, with per-tenant isolation.
  • Binder-agnostic pipelines. Some teams want to write the handler once and decide Kafka-or-Rabbit in configuration — Spring Cloud Stream's functional model.

This chapter covers those: the AMQP model and Spring AMQP with publisher confirms, manual acknowledgements, prefetch, dead-letter exchanges, delayed retries and quorum queues; Spring Pulsar; JMS with Artemis; and Spring Cloud Stream's functional programming model with its trade-offs. It closes with a decision guide so "which broker?" stops being an argument and becomes a lookup.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — AMQP concepts, send/receive B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — acks, prefetch, DLQ, retries, JMS basics B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — delivery guarantees, delayed retry, quorum queues B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 7, 8 — broker choice, operations, migration B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — messaging strategy across a platform

docs.title: 2.1 Log vs queue
docs.text:
Kafka (log) RabbitMQ (queue) Storage model Append-only log, retained by time/size Messages removed when acknowledged Replay ✅ re-read by offset ❌ (once consumed, it's gone) Routing By topic + partition key Exchanges, routing keys, headers — very flexible Fan-out to N services Consumer groups, independent offsets Bind N queues to one exchange Per-message features — TTL, priority, delay, per-message ack Ordering Per partition Per queue (with one consumer) Throughput Very high (millions/s) High (tens of thousands/s per queue) Typical use Event streams, audit, analytics, CDC Work dispatch, RPC, task queues, routing

Both are "messaging"; they solve different problems. Most mature platforms run both.

docs.title: 2.2 The AMQP model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    P[Producer] -->|routing key<br/>dispatch.express.BLR| X{{Exchange<br/>grocery.dispatch topic}}
    X -->|binding dispatch.express.#| Q1[(queue: dispatch.express)]
    X -->|binding dispatch.standard.#| Q2[(queue: dispatch.standard)]
    X -->|binding dispatch.#| Q3[(queue: dispatch.audit)]
    Q1 --> C1[rider-app consumer]
    Q2 --> C2[rider-app consumer]
    Q3 --> C3[audit consumer]
Concept Meaning Exchange Receives messages and routes them. Types: direct (exact key), topic (patterns with */#), fanout (all bound queues), headers Queue Stores messages until consumed and acknowledged Binding Rule linking exchange → queue (with a routing key pattern) Routing key The producer's label, e.g. dispatch.express.BLR Consumer Subscribes to a queue; competing consumers share the queue's messages

docs.title: 2.3 Delivery guarantees in RabbitMQ
docs.text:
Concern Mechanism Message survives a broker restart Durable queue + persistent message (Spring's default delivery mode) Producer knows it was stored Publisher confirms (publisher-confirm-type: correlated) Producer knows it was routable Publisher returns (mandatory: true) — otherwise an unroutable message is silently dropped Consumer doesn't lose work Acknowledge after processing (AUTO ack mode in Spring means "ack after the handler returns") Retries and poison messages Dead-letter exchange + retry with back-off High availability Quorum queues (Raft-replicated)

As with Kafka: at-least-once plus idempotent consumers (Chapter 23) is the practical contract.

docs.title: 2.4 Prefetch (QoS)
docs.text: prefetch is how many unacknowledged messages a consumer may hold. Too high: one consumer hoards the queue and others idle, and a crash re-delivers a big batch. Too low: round-trip latency per message limits throughput. Start at prefetch = 1 for slow, long tasks (fair dispatch) and 20–250 for fast ones.

docs.title: 2.5 Dead letters, delays and priorities
docs.text: Need RabbitMQ mechanism Failed message parking x-dead-letter-exchange on the queue; rejected/expired messages go there Retry after 30 s Message published to a delay queue with TTL and DLX pointing back at the work queue Scheduled/delayed publish rabbitmq_delayed_message_exchange plugin (or the TTL+DLX pattern) Priority x-max-priority queue argument + per-message priority Expiry Per-message TTL or per-queue x-message-ttl Length limits x-max-length, x-overflow (drop-head or reject-publish)

docs.title: 2.6 Spring AMQP
docs.text: Piece Role RabbitTemplate Send (and RPC-style convertSendAndReceive) @RabbitListener Consume; container-managed acks SimpleRabbitListenerContainerFactory Concurrency, prefetch, ack mode, error handler Queue, TopicExchange, Binding beans + RabbitAdmin Declare topology MessageConverter Jackson2JsonMessageConverter for JSON RepublishMessageRecoverer After retries, republish to a DLQ with failure headers

docs.title: 2.7 Spring Pulsar
docs.text: Apache Pulsar unifies queueing and streaming: topics with subscriptions whose type decides the semantics — Exclusive, Failover, Shared (queue-like, competing consumers), Key_Shared (ordered per key, parallel across keys). Built-in delayed delivery, retry letter topics and dead-letter policy, multi-tenancy and tiered storage. Spring Boot auto-configures PulsarTemplate and @PulsarListener.

docs.title: 2.8 JMS
docs.text: The Jakarta Messaging API (jakarta.jms), typically with ActiveMQ Artemis: JmsTemplate to send, @JmsListener to receive, queues (point-to-point) and topics (pub/sub, with durable subscriptions). Mostly relevant for integrating with existing enterprise systems.

docs.title: 2.9 Spring Cloud Stream
docs.text:
A binder abstraction: write Supplier/Function/Consumer beans, bind them to destinations in configuration, and swap Kafka for RabbitMQ without touching the handler.

Pros Cons Binder-agnostic code; consistent DLQ/retry config An abstraction layer over an abstraction layer Functional, testable handlers Broker-specific features need binder properties anyway Good for simple, uniform pipelines Harder to reason about than @KafkaListener/@RabbitListener

Platform stance: direct clients (spring-kafka, spring-amqp) for services with real broker-specific needs; Cloud Stream where pipelines are simple and portability genuinely matters.

docs.title: 3.1 Publishing with confirms and returns
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Application
    participant RT as RabbitTemplate
    participant Ch as Channel (confirm mode)
    participant B as Broker
    participant Q as Queue

    A->>RT: convertAndSend(exchange, routingKey, payload, correlationData)
    RT->>Ch: basic.publish (persistent, mandatory)
    Ch->>B: publish
    alt routable
        B->>Q: enqueue (fsync for persistent)
        B-->>Ch: basic.ack (confirm)
        Ch-->>RT: ConfirmCallback(ack = true)
    else unroutable
        B-->>Ch: basic.return (mandatory)
        Ch-->>RT: ReturnsCallback → message came back
        B-->>Ch: basic.ack
    end
    RT-->>A: (async callbacks)

Confirms are asynchronous: convertAndSend returning doesn't mean the broker stored the message. Either wait (waitForConfirms) for critical sends or, better, publish from an outbox (Chapter 23) and mark rows sent inside the confirm callback.

docs.title: 3.2 Consuming and acknowledging
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[SimpleMessageListenerContainer] --> B[Consumer holds up to `prefetch` unacked messages]
    B --> C["Invoke @RabbitListener method"]
    C --> D{outcome}
    D -- returns --> E[basic.ack]
    D -- throws, retries exhausted --> F{requeue?}
    F -- AmqpRejectAndDontRequeueException --> G[basic.reject requeue=false → DLX]
    F -- default --> H[basic.nack requeue=true → redelivered immediately]
    H -.->|poison loop| C

The default "requeue on exception" is the classic RabbitMQ poison-message loop: the same message is redelivered thousands of times per second. Always configure retries plus a recoverer that stops requeuing.

docs.title: 3.3 Delayed retry with TTL + DLX
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    W[(dispatch.work)] -->|reject: DLX| R[(dispatch.retry.30s<br/>x-message-ttl=30000<br/>DLX → work exchange)]
    R -->|TTL expires → dead-lettered back| W
    W -->|attempt header > 3| P[(dispatch.parked — DLQ)]

A message that fails is dead-lettered into a TTL queue with no consumers; when the TTL expires, RabbitMQ dead-letters it back to the work exchange. That's a delay without any scheduler.

6.1 Delivery dispatch, production shape
docs.text:
Requirements: express before standard, exactly one rider per task, retry with back-off for 5 minutes, park and alert after that, survive broker node loss, visible queue depth.

flowchart LR
    O[order-service<br/>outbox] -->|OrderPacked| P[dispatch-service]
    P -->|publish confirms| X{{grocery.dispatch<br/>topic exchange}}
    X --> E[(dispatch.express<br/>quorum, priority)]
    X --> S[(dispatch.standard<br/>quorum)]
    E & S --> C[rider assignment consumers<br/>prefetch 5, concurrency 4-8]
    C -->|transient failure| R[(dispatch.retry.30s<br/>TTL → back to exchange)]
    R --> X
    C -->|attempts exhausted / invalid| PK[(dispatch.parked)]
    PK --> H[ops alert + dispatch desk UI]
in/grocery/delivery/dispatch/RiderAssignmentService.java
package in.grocery.delivery.dispatch;

import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.transaction.annotation.Transactional;

@Service
public class RiderAssignmentService {

    private final AssignmentRepository assignments;
    private final RiderPool riders;

    @Transactional
    public void assign(DispatchTask task) {
        if (assignments.existsForOrder(task.orderRef())) {                                  // (1)!
            return;
        }
        String riderId = riders.claimNearest(task.hubCode(), task.express())                 // (2)!
                .orElseThrow(() -> new RiderPoolExhaustedException(task.hubCode()));
        int inserted = assignments.insertIfAbsent(task.orderRef(), riderId);                 // (3)!
        if (inserted == 0) {
            riders.release(riderId);
            return;
        }
        riders.notifyAssignment(riderId, task.orderRef());
    }
}
  1. Cheap idempotency check for the common redelivery case.
  2. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED over available riders (Chapter 12) — two consumers never claim the same rider.
  3. The unique constraint is the real guarantee; the check above is just an optimization. Release the rider if we lost the race.
application-prod.yml
spring:
  rabbitmq:
    listener:
      simple:
        prefetch: 5                       # (1)!
        concurrency: 4
        max-concurrency: 8
        default-requeue-rejected: false
        retry:
          enabled: true
          max-attempts: 2                 # (2)!
          initial-interval: 500ms
  1. Low prefetch for fair dispatch: assignment takes ~200 ms and involves a rider claim, so hoarding 250 messages in one consumer would starve the others.
  2. Only a token in-memory retry; real back-off uses the delay queue (5.2).

docs.title: 6.2 Operations and observability
6.3 Choosing a broker — the decision guide
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[New asynchronous flow] --> B{Many independent consumers<br/>need every message?}
    B -- yes --> K[Kafka: topic + consumer groups]
    B -- no --> C{Need replay / audit history?}
    C -- yes --> K
    C -- no --> D{Per-message routing, priority,<br/>delay or TTL?}
    D -- yes --> R[RabbitMQ]
    D -- no --> E{Very high throughput<br/>or ordering per key?}
    E -- yes --> K
    E -- no --> F{Integrating a system<br/>that speaks JMS/AMQP already?}
    F -- yes --> G[Use that protocol]
    F -- no --> H{Would a database queue do?<br/>single consumer, modest volume}
    H -- yes --> DB["PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED<br/>(Chapter 12) — fewest moving parts"]
    H -- no --> R

The last branch matters: not every asynchronous need requires a broker. A SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED queue in PostgreSQL is transactional with your data, needs no new infrastructure, and handles thousands of messages per minute comfortably.

Platform decision Broker Order/payment/inventory events, search indexing, analytics Kafka Rider dispatch, notification retries with delays, per-hub routing RabbitMQ ERP settlement exchange JMS (their broker) Nightly report generation queue PostgreSQL job table

docs.title: 6.4 Migrating a flow between brokers
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Producer publishes to old broker] --> B[Dual-publish to old + new]
    B --> C[New consumer on new broker<br/>idempotent, shadow mode]
    C --> D[Compare outcomes / metrics]
    D --> E[Cut consumers over]
    E --> F[Stop dual-publish, decommission]

Idempotent consumers (Chapter 23) make the overlap safe: during the cutover both may process the same logical message, and nothing breaks.

docs.title: 6.5 Testing the delayed-retry path
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Spring AMQP 3.x 4.x (verify) RabbitMQ server 3.13 / 4.x 4.x — classic mirrored queues removed, use quorum AMQP 1.0 Limited RabbitMQ 4 supports AMQP 1.0 natively; Spring AMQP client support — verify JMS Jakarta Messaging 3.1 (Artemis) Jakarta Messaging 3.1+ (verify) Spring Pulsar 1.x (Boot 3.2+) Next major (verify) Spring Cloud Stream 4.x release train Release train aligned with Boot 4 (verify) Message converters Jackson 2 Jackson 3 — payload compatibility across a rollout (Chapter 23)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace classic mirrored queues with quorum queues before RabbitMQ 4 (this is a queue re-declaration, i.e. a migration — plan drain/cutover).
  • Verify Jackson2JsonMessageConverter equivalents and trusted-package settings after the Jackson move.
  • Re-test confirm/return callbacks and retry configuration after upgrading Spring AMQP.
  • Check Spring Cloud Stream release-train compatibility before upgrading Boot.
  • Cross-version publish/consume test during the rollout window.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Pick the broker per flow using the decision guide; write the reason in an ADR.
  2. Durable queues, persistent messages, publisher confirms, mandatory — otherwise messages vanish silently.
  3. Never requeue blindly: default-requeue-rejected: false, retry with back-off, then park.
  4. Delayed retries via TTL+DLX (or the delay plugin) rather than in-memory sleeps.
  5. Quorum queues for anything that matters.
  6. Idempotent consumers — the same rule as Kafka.
  7. Tune prefetch to the work profile; low for slow tasks, higher for fast ones.
  8. Alert on parked queues, unroutable messages and consumer count = 0.
  9. Topology as infrastructure, reviewed and provisioned, not invented at startup.
  10. Prefer a database queue when a broker isn't justified.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Using RabbitMQ as an event log ("we'll replay from the queue") — consumed messages are gone.

❌ Using Kafka as a work queue with per-message delays and priorities — it has neither.

❌ Auto-acknowledging before processing (acknowledge-mode: none).

❌ Unbounded requeue on exception — a poison message spins the consumer at 100% CPU.

❌ Publishing without mandatory and without confirms, then wondering where messages went.

❌ Very high prefetch on slow handlers — one consumer hoards the queue.

❌ Declaring production topology from application code with different arguments per service.

❌ Cloud Stream chosen for "portability" that nobody will ever use, at the cost of clarity.

❌ Long processing while holding an unacked message beyond the consumer timeout.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Messages disappear Unroutable (no binding), no mandatory/returns Enable returns; alert; fix routing key Queue grows, consumers idle Prefetch exhausted by stuck messages; consumers crashed Check unacked count, consumer count, restart, lower prefetch Same message processed forever Requeue on exception default-requeue-rejected: false + DLX 100% CPU with no progress Poison loop Same as above; inspect x-death headers PRECONDITION_FAILED - inequivalent arg Queue declared with different arguments Align declarations; provision topology centrally Consumers rebalance/disconnect Heartbeat/network timeouts, long processing blocking the connection thread Tune heartbeat, move work off the listener thread High memory on broker Unbounded queues, no TTL/max-length x-max-length, TTLs, consumer scaling Duplicate side effects Redelivery without idempotency Inbox/unique constraints (Chapter 23) JMS messages stuck in ERP queue No durable subscription / wrong ack mode Check subscription and acknowledge mode

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Broker choice documented per flow
  • Durable + persistent + confirms + mandatory on all producers
  • Retry/park topology declared and provisioned centrally
  • Parked queue alerting to a human channel
  • Prefetch/concurrency tuned and load-tested
  • Quorum queues everywhere that matters
  • Consumers idempotent (documented mechanism)
  • Queue depth, unacked, consumer count dashboards
  • Delayed-retry path covered by an integration test

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What are exchanges, queues and bindings?

Short answer: Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key; bindings route matching messages into queues; consumers read from queues. Exchange types: direct, topic, fanout, headers.

B1 · How is RabbitMQ different from Kafka?

Short answer: RabbitMQ is a queue — messages are removed once acknowledged, with rich routing, priorities and TTLs. Kafka is a retained log — consumers track offsets and can replay, with fan-out to independent groups.

B1 · How do you consume messages in Spring?

Short answer: @RabbitListener(queues = "...") for AMQP, @JmsListener(destination = "...") for JMS; the container acknowledges after the handler returns successfully.

B1 · What is a dead-letter queue?

Short answer: A queue that receives messages rejected or expired elsewhere, so failures can be inspected and replayed instead of being lost or retried forever.

B1 · What does prefetch control?

Short answer: How many unacknowledged messages a consumer may hold at once — the trade-off between throughput and fair distribution.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you make sure a published message isn't lost?

Short answer: Durable queue, persistent message, publisher confirms (know it was stored) and mandatory + returns (know it was routable) — and publish from an outbox so the database write and the publish can't diverge.

B2 · How do you retry a failed message after 30 seconds without blocking the consumer?

Short answer: Publish it to a TTL queue with no consumers whose dead-letter exchange points back at the work exchange (or use the delayed-message plugin), carrying an attempt counter and parking after N attempts.

B2 · Why is default-requeue-rejected: false important?

Short answer: Otherwise a failing message is immediately requeued and redelivered in a tight loop, burning CPU and blocking the queue — the classic poison-message incident.

B2 · Quorum vs classic queues?

Short answer: Quorum queues replicate via Raft with predictable failover and are the supported HA option (classic mirrored queues are removed in RabbitMQ 4). They trade some memory/throughput for safety.

B2 · What does Spring Cloud Stream give you?

Short answer: Binder-agnostic messaging with functional handlers (Supplier/Function/Consumer) and consistent retry/DLQ configuration, at the cost of an extra abstraction over broker-specific features.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through delivery guarantees in RabbitMQ.

Short answer: Producer → broker: confirms (+ mandatory for routability). Broker durability: durable queue + persistent message (+ quorum replication). Broker → consumer: acknowledge after processing; rejected messages dead-letter. Net effect is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

B3 · How do you choose prefetch?

Short answer: Roughly, prefetch ≈ consumer throughput × round-trip latency, clamped by fairness needs: 1–5 for slow tasks so work spreads evenly, tens to hundreds for fast tasks. Watch unacked counts and per-consumer distribution.

B3 · When would you use Pulsar's Key_Shared subscription?

Short answer: When you need ordering per key with parallelism across keys without fixing a partition count up front — e.g. rider pings ordered per rider but processed in parallel across riders.

B3 · What's the risk of long processing inside a listener?

Short answer: Held unacked messages, heartbeat/timeout issues, redelivery storms after restarts and unfair distribution. Keep handlers short; offload long work to a task executor or a job table, and acknowledge deliberately.

B3 · How do you migrate a flow from RabbitMQ to Kafka?

Short answer: Dual-publish, run the new consumer in shadow mode with idempotent processing, compare outcomes and metrics, cut consumers over, then stop dual-publishing and decommission.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Kafka, RabbitMQ or a database queue — how do you decide?

Short answer: Fan-out/replay/high throughput/ordering by key → Kafka. Per-message routing, priority, delay, competing consumers → RabbitMQ. Single consumer, modest volume, needs transactional consistency with your data → a PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED queue. Document the choice; every broker is operational cost.

B4 · How do you operate RabbitMQ safely in production?

Short answer: Quorum queues, bounded queue lengths with overflow policies, TTLs, alerting on depth/unacked/consumer count/parked, provisioned topology, tested failover, and capacity planning for memory and disk watermarks.

B4 · Would you standardize on Spring Cloud Stream across all services?

Short answer: No. Use it where pipelines are simple and uniform; use direct clients where broker features (transactions, retry topics, priorities, manual acks) matter. Mandating either universally causes either leaky abstraction workarounds or duplicated plumbing.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you prevent broker sprawl?

Short answer: A documented decision guide, platform libraries for the sanctioned brokers, review for anything new (who operates it, backup/upgrade/on-call story), and a default answer of "use what we already run" unless the workload demonstrably doesn't fit.

B5 · What does 'exactly once' mean across brokers?

Short answer: Practically nothing without idempotent consumers. Every broker gives at-least-once with acknowledgements; the application makes effects idempotent (inbox, unique constraints, conditional updates). Design for duplicates rather than trying to eliminate them.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Riders stop receiving dispatch tasks at 8 p.m.

A deploy changed the routing key from dispatch.standard.BLR to dispatch.std.BLR; no binding matched, and because mandatory wasn't set, the broker discarded every message silently. Fixes: enable returns with an alert on unroutable messages, add a contract test asserting routing keys against bindings, and monitor publish→consume counts per flow.

Scenario · One consumer at 100% CPU, queue not draining

A malformed task threw on deserialization and was requeued immediately in a loop. Fixes: default-requeue-rejected: false, retries with back-off, DLX to dispatch.parked, an alert on parked depth, and a trusted-package setting so the payload can't instantiate arbitrary types.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Notification retry pipeline

Consume notification.requests (RabbitMQ). On a transient SMS-gateway failure, retry after 10 s, 60 s and 300 s, then park. Invalid requests park immediately. Implement the topology, consumer and attempt tracking, and write tests for the retry and park paths (use short TTLs in tests).

Solution NotificationTopology.java
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class NotificationTopology {

    static final String EXCHANGE = "grocery.notification";
    static final String WORK = "notification.requests";
    static final String PARKED = "notification.parked";
    static final int[] DELAYS_SECONDS = {10, 60, 300};

    @Bean TopicExchange exchange() { return new TopicExchange(EXCHANGE, true, false); }

    @Bean Queue work() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable(WORK).quorum().build();
    }

    @Bean Queue parked() { return QueueBuilder.durable(PARKED).quorum().build(); }

    @Bean Binding workBinding() {
        return BindingBuilder.bind(work()).to(exchange()).with("notification.request.#");
    }

    @Bean Binding parkedBinding() {
        return BindingBuilder.bind(parked()).to(exchange()).with("notification.parked");
    }

    @Bean
    Declarables retryQueues(@Value("${grocery.notification.retry-scale:1}") int scale) {   // (1)!
        var queues = java.util.Arrays.stream(DELAYS_SECONDS)
                .mapToObj(seconds -> QueueBuilder.durable("notification.retry." + seconds + "s")
                        .quorum()
                        .ttl(seconds * 1000 / scale)
                        .deadLetterExchange(EXCHANGE)
                        .deadLetterRoutingKey("notification.request.retry")
                        .build())
                .map(Declarable.class::cast)
                .toList();
        return new Declarables(queues);
    }
}
  1. retry-scale lets tests shrink 10 s → 100 ms without changing code.
NotificationConsumer.java
@Component
public class NotificationConsumer {

    private final NotificationSender sender;
    private final RabbitTemplate rabbit;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @RabbitListener(queues = NotificationTopology.WORK, concurrency = "2-6")
    public void onRequest(NotificationRequest request, Message message) {
        int attempt = (int) message.getMessageProperties().getHeaders().getOrDefault("x-attempt", 1);
        try {
            sender.send(request);
        } catch (InvalidNotificationException invalid) {
            park(request, "invalid: " + invalid.getMessage());                       // (1)!
        } catch (DependencyException transientFailure) {
            if (attempt > NotificationTopology.DELAYS_SECONDS.length) {
                park(request, "retries exhausted");
                return;
            }
            int delay = NotificationTopology.DELAYS_SECONDS[attempt - 1];
            rabbit.convertAndSend("", "notification.retry." + delay + "s", request, m -> {
                m.getMessageProperties().setHeader("x-attempt", attempt + 1);
                return m;
            });
            meters.counter("grocery.notification.retry", "attempt", String.valueOf(attempt)).increment();
        }
    }

    private void park(NotificationRequest request, String reason) {
        rabbit.convertAndSend(NotificationTopology.EXCHANGE, "notification.parked", request, m -> {
            m.getMessageProperties().setHeader("x-park-reason", reason);
            return m;
        });
        meters.counter("grocery.notification.parked").increment();
    }
}
  1. Non-retryable failures park immediately — no point waiting 370 seconds to discover the mobile number is malformed.
NotificationRetryTest.java (assertions)
@Test void transientFailureRetriesWithBackoff() { /* fail twice, succeed third → sender called 3 times */ }
@Test void exhaustedRetriesPark()               { /* always fail → parked depth == 1, sender called 4 times */ }
@Test void invalidRequestParksImmediately()     { /* parked depth == 1, sender called once */ }

Run with grocery.notification.retry-scale=100 in the test profile so the three delays become 100 ms, 600 ms and 3 s.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Log vs queue is the core distinction: Kafka for replayable event streams, RabbitMQ for routed work queues with priorities, delays and per-message acks.
  • RabbitMQ safety = durable + persistent + confirms + mandatory + quorum queues.
  • Never requeue blindly: retry with back-off via TTL+DLX, then park and alert.
  • Prefetch is the throughput/fairness dial; tune it to handler duration.
  • Pulsar offers queue and stream semantics (including Key_Shared) in one system.
  • JMS is for integrating with systems that already speak it.
  • Spring Cloud Stream buys portability at the cost of an abstraction — use it selectively.
  • Sometimes the right broker is no broker: a PostgreSQL SKIP LOCKED queue.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring AMQP Reference — templates, listener containers, publisher confirms, error handling, retries
  • RabbitMQ documentation — quorum queues, dead lettering, TTL, priorities, monitoring
  • Spring Pulsar Reference; Apache Pulsar documentation — subscription types, retry/dead-letter policies
  • Spring Cloud Stream Reference — functional binding model, binders, error handling
  • Spring Boot Reference — Messaging (AMQP, JMS, Pulsar)

23 Messaging with Kafka · 25 Async, Scheduling & Virtual Threads

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Not everything should happen inside the request. When a customer taps "Place order", the response must come back in 300 ms; sending the SMS, updating the loyalty balance, warming a cache and pushing an analytics event can all happen afterwards. And some work has no request at all: cancelling unpaid orders after 15 minutes, settling sellers nightly, refreshing the pricing cache every two minutes.

Spring gives you three tools for this — @Async, @Scheduled, and (since Java 21) virtual threads — and all three are easy to misuse:

  • @Async on a method of the same class: silently synchronous (Chapter 04).
  • Boot's default task executor has an unbounded queue: under load it accumulates millions of tasks and the pod dies of OutOfMemoryError instead of shedding work.
  • The default scheduler pool size is 1: one slow job delays every other scheduled job in the service.
  • A @Scheduled job on six pods runs six times — sending six SMS messages per late order.
  • Virtual threads remove the thread-count limit, so 5,000 concurrent requests all reach for a 20-connection database pool at once (Chapter 12).
  • Fire-and-forget work is lost on shutdown unless the executor drains (Chapter 03).

This chapter covers all of it: the executor model and how Boot configures it, @Async done safely with bounded queues and rejection policies, virtual threads (what changed in Java 21–25, where pinning still matters, and why they need bulkheads rather than pools), scheduling with cron and fixed delays, cluster-safe scheduling with ShedLock, Quartz for durable schedules, context propagation, graceful shutdown and testing.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — @Async, @Scheduled, basic executors B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — pool sizing, rejection, cron, ShedLock B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — virtual threads, pinning, bulkheads, propagation B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — platform executor strategy, scheduling architecture B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — concurrency strategy and its failure modes

docs.title: 2.1 Executors in Spring Boot
docs.text:
Bean Purpose Property prefix applicationTaskExecutor @Async, ApplicationRunner async work, some auto-configurations spring.task.execution.* taskScheduler @Scheduled spring.task.scheduling.* Your own executors Per-dependency bulkheads — application.yml
spring:
  task:
    execution:
      pool:
        core-size: 8
        max-size: 32
        queue-capacity: 100        # default is Integer.MAX_VALUE — effectively unbounded!
      thread-name-prefix: grocery-task-
      shutdown:
        await-termination: true
        await-termination-period: 20s
    scheduling:
      pool:
        size: 4                    # default is 1
      shutdown:
        await-termination: true
        await-termination-period: 20s

The two defaults that cause outages

Unbounded queue: ThreadPoolTaskExecutor only grows past core-size when the queue is full, so with an unbounded queue max-size is never reached — tasks pile up in memory until the pod dies. Scheduler pool size 1: one long job blocks all others. Set both explicitly in every service.

docs.title: 2.2 @Async
2.3 Virtual threads
docs.text:
Java 21 introduced virtual threads: JVM-scheduled threads that unmount from a carrier (platform) thread while blocked on I/O. Millions can exist; blocking is no longer expensive.

application.yml
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true

With this, Boot uses virtual threads for the web server's request handling, the task executor, the scheduler and several listener containers (Kafka, RabbitMQ).

Myth Reality "Virtual threads make code faster" They make blocking code scale; a CPU-bound task is no faster "Pool them for efficiency" Never pool — create one per task (newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor) "Unlimited concurrency is fine" Downstream resources (DB pool, API quotas) are still bounded — you need bulkheads "ThreadLocals are free" A million threads × a fat ThreadLocal = a lot of heap

Pinning: a virtual thread that can't unmount blocks its carrier thread. Historically synchronized blocks around I/O were the main cause; JDK 24 removed that limitation (JEP 491). Native frames (JNI) still pin. On Java 21–23, replace synchronized around I/O with ReentrantLock.

Verify for your JDK

Pinning behaviour differs between Java 21, 24 and 25. Confirm with your runtime (and -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads / JFR events on older JDKs) rather than assuming.

docs.title: 2.4 Structured concurrency and scoped values
docs.text:
• Structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope) ties the lifetime of concurrent subtasks to a scope: if one fails, siblings are cancelled; the scope doesn't return until all finish. It has been a preview feature through Java 21–25 with API changes along the way — good to know, not yet a platform default. Verify the API for your JDK before using it.
  • Scoped values (finalized in Java 25) are an immutable, inheritance-friendly alternative to ThreadLocal for per-request context — a better fit for virtual threads.

docs.title: 2.5 @Scheduled
docs.text:
Attribute Meaning fixedDelay Wait N after the previous run finished — never overlaps fixedRate Start every N regardless of duration — can overlap (unless the scheduler is busy) initialDelay Delay before the first run cron 6-field expression (second minute hour day month weekday) zone e.g. Asia/Kolkata — essential for business-day boundaries scheduler Named scheduler bean (Framework 6.1+)

Cron examples for the platform:

Example
0 */2 * * * *        every 2 minutes
0 0 2 * * *          02:00 every day (in `zone`)
0 30 23 * * SAT      23:30 every Saturday (weekly settlement)
0 0 0 1 * *          midnight on the 1st (monthly GST report)

docs.title: 2.6 Cluster-safe scheduling
docs.text:
Six pods = six executions. Options:

Approach Notes ShedLock A lock row in PostgreSQL/Redis; only one pod runs the job. Simple, recommended Quartz clustered Durable, database-backed schedules with failover and misfires Kubernetes CronJob Runs the app in "job mode" (Chapter 05); separate lifecycle, no in-app scheduler Leader election One pod is leader (Spring Integration / Kubernetes lease)

ShedLock takes a lock around the job; it doesn't make the job idempotent. lockAtMostFor must exceed the worst-case duration, or a second pod may start while the first is still running.

docs.title: 2.7 Sweepers vs timers
docs.text:
To cancel unpaid orders after 15 minutes you could schedule a per-order timer (Quartz job per order, or a delayed message). Much simpler and far more robust:

SQL
select id from customer_order
where status = 'PLACED' and placed_at < now() - interval '15 minutes'
order by placed_at limit 500 for update skip locked

A sweeper query every minute is idempotent, self-healing after downtime, needs no per-entity state, and scales with a single index. Prefer sweepers; use timers/delayed messages only when the delay must be precise to the second.

docs.title: 2.8 Context propagation
docs.text: Context Propagates to @Async? How to propagate Transaction ❌ (and shouldn't — a new thread needs its own) Start a transaction in the async method Security ❌ DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor (Chapter 17) MDC / tracing ❌ ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator (Chapter 07) Request-scoped beans ❌ Pass data explicitly

docs.title: 3.1 ThreadPoolTaskExecutor growth rules
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[submit task] --> B{active threads < core-size?}
    B -- yes --> C[create a thread]
    B -- no --> D{queue has space?}
    D -- yes --> E[enqueue]
    D -- no --> F{threads < max-size?}
    F -- yes --> G[create a thread]
    F -- no --> H[RejectedExecutionHandler]
    H --> I[AbortPolicy default → exception<br/>CallerRunsPolicy → backpressure<br/>DiscardPolicy → silent loss]

The counter-intuitive part: the queue fills before extra threads are created. With an unbounded queue, max-size is dead configuration and the queue is the only thing absorbing load — until memory runs out.

docs.title: 3.2 @Async invocation
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller (request thread)
    participant P as Proxy
    participant AI as AsyncExecutionInterceptor
    participant E as TaskExecutor
    participant T as Target method

    C->>P: notifyCustomer(order)
    P->>AI: invoke
    AI->>AI: resolve executor (annotation value / default)
    AI->>E: submit(Callable)
    AI-->>C: null / CompletableFuture (immediately)
    E->>T: run on a pool (or virtual) thread
    alt void method throws
        T-->>E: AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler
    else future
        T-->>E: complete / completeExceptionally
    end

docs.title: 3.3 Virtual thread mounting
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Virtual thread runs on a carrier] --> B{blocking call}
    B -->|JDBC, HTTP, sleep| C[unmount: carrier freed<br/>continuation parked on heap]
    C --> D[I/O completes]
    D --> E[remount on any carrier]
    B -->|native frame / JNI| F[PINNED: carrier blocked]
    F -.-> G[carrier pool starvation if widespread]

Carrier threads are a ForkJoinPool sized to the CPU count by default (jdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism). Pinning matters because it removes a carrier from that small pool.

docs.title: 3.4 Scheduling
docs.text: ThreadPoolTaskScheduler wraps a ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor. A fixedDelay task schedules its next run after completion; a cron task computes the next time from a CronTrigger. If the pool is busy, executions are delayed, not parallelized — the pool size is the ceiling on concurrent scheduled work.

docs.title: 4.1 Async done right
4.2 A first scheduled job
4.3 Enabling virtual threads
docs.text:
application.yml
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true          # Java 21+

Now request handling, @Async (unless a specific executor is injected), @Scheduled and Kafka/Rabbit listener containers run on virtual threads. Nothing else changes in your code — that's the point.

docs.title: 4.4 Testing async and scheduled code
5.1 Level 2 — Cluster-safe scheduling with ShedLock
5.2 Level 2 — Sweeper pattern done properly
5.3 Level 2 — Quartz when you need durable schedules
5.4 Level 3 — Virtual threads and bulkheads
docs.text:
Virtual threads remove the thread limit; they do not remove downstream limits. A product page needs price, stock and delivery ETA:

in/grocery/catalog/page/ProductPageAssembler.java
package in.grocery.catalog.page;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.concurrent.Callable;
import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService;
import java.util.concurrent.Executors;
import java.util.concurrent.Future;
import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class ProductPageAssembler implements AutoCloseable {

    private final ExecutorService executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor();   // (1)!
    private final Semaphore pricingBulkhead = new Semaphore(50);                            // (2)!

    private final PricingClient pricing;
    private final InventoryClient inventory;
    private final DeliveryClient delivery;

    public ProductPage assemble(String sku, String pincode) throws Exception {
        Future<String> price = executor.submit(bulkheaded(pricingBulkhead,
                () -> pricing.price(sku, pincode)));                                        // (3)!
        Future<Integer> stock = executor.submit(() -> inventory.stock(sku, pincode));
        Future<String> eta = executor.submit(() -> delivery.eta(pincode));

        return new ProductPage(sku, price.get(), stock.get(), eta.get());                   // (4)!
    }

    private static <T> Callable<T> bulkheaded(Semaphore semaphore, Callable<T> task) {
        return () -> {
            if (!semaphore.tryAcquire(200, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
                throw new BulkheadFullException("pricing");                                  // (5)!
            }
            try {
                return task.call();
            } finally {
                semaphore.release();
            }
        };
    }

    @Override
    public void close() {
        executor.close();
    }
}
  1. One virtual thread per task — never pool virtual threads; creation is nearly free.
  2. The bulkhead, not the thread count, limits concurrent calls to pricing. Without it, 5,000 concurrent requests × 1 pricing call = 5,000 concurrent HTTP calls to a service sized for 200.
  3. Only the constrained dependency is limited.
  4. Each client already has its own timeouts (Chapter 19); get() inherits them.
  5. Fail fast when saturated — that's a 503 with Retry-After, not a 30-second queue (Chapters 10, 26).

Structured concurrency, when it stabilizes

StructuredTaskScope expresses exactly this fan-out — cancel siblings when one fails, join with a deadline — more safely than futures. It has been in preview through Java 21–25 with API churn; verify before adopting, and keep the semaphore bulkhead either way.
