6.1 The platform executor policy
6.2 Async work that must not be lost
docs.text:
Fire-and-forget is fine for an SMS; it is not fine for a loyalty credit. The rule:

flowchart TD
    A[Work triggered by a request] --> B{Can we afford to lose it<br/>if the pod dies now?}
    B -- yes --> C["@Async on a bounded executor"]
    B -- no --> D{Must it be transactional<br/>with the write?}
    D -- yes --> E[Outbox row in the same transaction<br/>→ relay/consumer]
    D -- no --> F[Job table / sweeper]
in/grocery/order/service/OrderPlacementService.java (applying the rule)
@Transactional
public Order place(...) {
    Order saved = orders.save(order);
    outbox.append("order", saved.getOrderRef(), "OrderPlaced", payload);   // durable: loyalty, inventory, search
    return saved;
}

@TransactionalEventListener                                                 // after commit (Chapter 03)
@Async("notificationExecutor")                                              // best-effort: SMS
public void sendConfirmation(OrderPlaced event) { ... }

The SMS can be lost on a crash and a customer still has their order; a loyalty credit cannot, so it travels through the outbox (Chapter 23).

docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Enable in staging<br/>spring.threads.virtual.enabled] --> B[Load test:<br/>compare p99, CPU, DB pool waits]
    B --> C[Check pinning: JFR / tracePinnedThreads]
    C --> D[Verify bulkheads on every outbound dependency]
    D --> E[Check ThreadLocal-heavy libraries<br/>and thread-name assumptions]

Findings from a typical rollout:

Observation Action p99 improves under load; CPU similar Expected — blocking no longer costs threads Hikari pending rises sharply Add bulkheads / raise pool deliberately (Chapter 12) A library pins on synchronized (JDK < 24) Upgrade the library, upgrade the JDK, or exclude that path Thread dumps huge Use JFR and per-request tracing instead Metrics tagged by thread name become useless Tag by endpoint/dependency, not thread

docs.title: 6.6 Testing concurrency and scheduling
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Set queue-capacity and scheduler pool.size explicitly (defaults bite in both versions).
  • Audit synchronized around I/O before enabling virtual threads on Java < 24.
  • Re-check bulkheads and database pool sizing after enabling virtual threads.
  • Verify ShedLock/Quartz versions against Boot 4.
  • Re-test graceful shutdown timings end to end.
  • Consider scoped values instead of ThreadLocal for request context on Java 25.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Bounded queues and explicit rejection policies on every executor; CallerRunsPolicy for backpressure.
  2. Named executors per concern — notifications must not starve audits.
  3. Instrument executors; alert on queue depth and rejections.
  4. Async ≠ durable: use the outbox for work that must not be lost.
  5. fixedDelay over fixedRate unless overlap is genuinely wanted; add jitter across pods.
  6. ShedLock (or CronJob) for cluster-wide single execution; jobs still idempotent and resumable.
  7. Sweepers over per-entity timers.
  8. Virtual threads + bulkheads, never virtual-thread pools.
  9. Propagate context (MDC, tracing, security) explicitly to async work.
  10. Drain executors on shutdown within the pod's grace period.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ @Async with the default unbounded queue — an OOM waiting for the next traffic spike.

❌ @Async on a method called from the same class (does nothing).

❌ Scheduler pool of 1 with several jobs — one slow job delays everything.

❌ @Scheduled without cluster coordination — N pods, N executions.

❌ fixedRate on a job that sometimes runs longer than the interval — overlapping runs corrupting shared state.

❌ Cron expressions without a zone — jobs fire at the wrong local time.

❌ Pooling virtual threads or sizing "virtual thread pools".

❌ Assuming a new thread inherits the transaction, security context or MDC.

❌ Long, non-interruptible jobs that die mid-way on every deploy.

❌ Using async to hide slowness the user actually waits for.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Memory grows, tasks delayed by minutes Unbounded executor queue Bound it; CallerRunsPolicy; scale consumers RejectedExecutionException Queue + pool saturated Expected under overload — shed load, alert, then tune Async method runs synchronously Self-invocation, missing @EnableAsync Restructure; enable Async exceptions disappear void method without a handler AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler, or return a future Job runs N times No cluster lock ShedLock/CronJob/leader election Job never runs Scheduler pool exhausted; exception killed a fixedDelay task Size pool; catch exceptions inside the task Job fires at the wrong hour Missing zone / UTC pods Set zone = "Asia/Kolkata" Latency high with virtual threads, CPU low Downstream saturation (DB pool, API) Bulkheads, pool sizing, circuit breakers Carrier threads blocked Pinning (JDK < 24 synchronized, native frames) ReentrantLock, upgrade JDK, remove I/O from locks Work lost on deploy No drain / not durable await-termination, outbox for critical work

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every executor: bounded queue, named threads, rejection policy, metrics
  • Scheduler pool sized; all cron jobs carry a zone
  • Cluster-wide jobs protected by ShedLock/CronJob and idempotent
  • Critical async work durable (outbox/job table)
  • Bulkheads on every outbound dependency when virtual threads are on
  • Pinning checked on the target JDK
  • Context propagation configured (MDC, tracing, security)
  • Shutdown drains verified in a kill test
  • Tests for rejection policy, ShedLock single-execution, and the sweeper

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What does @Async do?

Short answer: Runs the method on another thread via an executor, returning immediately (void or a CompletableFuture). Requires @EnableAsync and goes through a proxy.

B1 · fixedDelay vs fixedRate?

Short answer: fixedDelay waits N after the previous run finished (no overlap); fixedRate starts every N regardless of duration.

B1 · Why doesn't my @Async method run asynchronously?

Short answer: Self-invocation (called from the same class), missing @EnableAsync, or a non-public method — the proxy isn't involved.

B1 · What is a virtual thread?

Short answer: A lightweight thread managed by the JVM that unmounts from a carrier thread while blocked, so blocking I/O scales to millions of concurrent tasks.

B1 · How do you run a job at 2 a.m. IST?

Short answer: @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * *", zone = "Asia/Kolkata").

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · What's wrong with the default task executor settings?

Short answer: The queue is effectively unbounded, so max-size is never reached and tasks accumulate until the JVM runs out of memory. Always set queue-capacity and a rejection policy.

B2 · How does ThreadPoolTaskExecutor decide to create threads?

Short answer: Below core-size it creates threads; then it queues; only when the queue is full does it grow to max-size; beyond that the rejection handler runs.

B2 · How do you stop a scheduled job from running on every pod?

Short answer: ShedLock (a lock row in the database/Redis around the job), a Kubernetes CronJob running the app in job mode, or leader election.

B2 · Does an @Async method join the caller's transaction?

Short answer: No. It runs on a different thread with no transaction, security context or MDC; it must start its own transaction if needed.

B2 · How do you test asynchronous behaviour?

Short answer: Awaitility for integration tests; a same-thread executor for deterministic unit tests. Never Thread.sleep.

B2 · What are the risks of fixedRate?

Short answer: Overlapping executions if a run exceeds the interval, leading to double processing and contention — use fixedDelay unless overlap is intended and safe.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · What actually changes when you enable virtual threads?

Short answer: Request handling, task execution/scheduling and some listener containers create a virtual thread per task instead of using a bounded pool. Blocking is cheap, so thread count stops being the limit — downstream resources (DB pool, HTTP pools, API quotas) become the constraint, which is why bulkheads are mandatory.

B3 · What is pinning and how do you detect it?

Short answer: A virtual thread that can't unmount blocks its carrier. On Java 21–23 synchronized around blocking I/O was the main cause (fixed in JDK 24); native frames still pin. Detect with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads or JFR VirtualThreadPinned events.

B3 · Why never pool virtual threads?

Short answer: Pooling exists to amortize expensive thread creation; virtual threads are cheap. Pooling reintroduces a concurrency limit in the wrong place and defeats the model. Limit concurrency with semaphores/bulkheads instead.

B3 · How do you propagate MDC and security to async tasks?

Short answer: A TaskDecorator (ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator for Micrometer context; DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor for security), applied to the executor.

B3 · Sweeper or per-entity timer for 'cancel after 15 minutes'?

Short answer: Sweeper: a chunked query with SKIP LOCKED every minute. It's idempotent, self-healing after downtime, has no per-entity state, and scales with one index. Timers only when second-level precision matters.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the executor strategy for a service.

Short answer: Separate, named, bounded executors per concern with rejection policies matching the work (backpressure for tolerant work, fail-fast for heavy work), metrics and alerts on queue depth/rejections, context propagation, drain on shutdown, and a rule that anything which must not be lost goes through the outbox rather than an executor.

B4 · How do you roll out virtual threads safely?

Short answer: Enable in staging, load test and compare p99/CPU/pool waits, check pinning on the target JDK, ensure every outbound dependency has a bulkhead and timeouts, review ThreadLocal-heavy libraries, then roll service by service with dashboards.

B4 · When is Quartz justified over @Scheduled + ShedLock?

Short answer: When schedules are dynamic and per-entity, must survive restarts, need misfire policies, or require a job history — e.g. campaign activations. For fixed code-defined schedules, Quartz is unnecessary infrastructure.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · Does reactive programming still have a place after virtual threads?

Short answer: Yes, but a narrower one: streaming with backpressure, very high fan-out, and event-driven pipelines. For request/response services, virtual threads deliver most of the scalability with far simpler code, debugging and libraries (Chapter 31).

B5 · How do you prevent asynchronous work from becoming invisible?

Short answer: Treat it as a first-class workload: metrics per executor and job, tracing that spans the async boundary, durable queues for anything important, dashboards showing backlog, and runbooks for "the backlog is growing" — otherwise failures surface only as customer complaints.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Pods OOM every evening at peak

Heap dumps showed millions of queued Runnables: @Async notifications used the default executor with an unbounded queue, and the SMS gateway had slowed from 50 ms to 2 s. Fixes: bounded queue with CallerRunsPolicy, a dedicated notification executor, metrics/alerts on queue depth, a circuit breaker on the gateway, and durable delivery for anything that mattered.

Scenario · Sellers received six settlement emails

@Scheduled on six pods with no coordination. Fixes: ShedLock with the database clock, lockAtMostFor above the worst-case duration, idempotent settlement (unique constraint per seller and period), and a test asserting exactly one execution across two concurrent runners.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Nightly seller payout job

Implement a job that runs at 01:00 IST, on exactly one pod, processes sellers in chunks of 100 with one short transaction per seller, is resumable after a crash, stops promptly on shutdown, and records metrics. Write tests for single execution and resumability.

Solution PayoutJob.java
@Component
public class PayoutJob {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(PayoutJob.class);

    private final PayoutService payouts;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 1 * * *", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "nightly-seller-payout", lockAtMostFor = "PT3H", lockAtLeastFor = "PT1M")
    public void run() {
        LockAssert.assertLocked();
        Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(meters);
        int processed = 0;
        try {
            List<String> sellers;
            while (!(sellers = payouts.claimPendingSellers(100)).isEmpty()) {          // (1)!
                for (String sellerId : sellers) {
                    if (Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {                      // (2)!
                        log.info("Shutdown requested after {} sellers", processed);
                        return;
                    }
                    payouts.payoutSeller(sellerId);                                    // (3)!
                    processed++;
                }
            }
        } finally {
            sample.stop(meters.timer("grocery.payout.job"));
            meters.counter("grocery.payout.sellers").increment(processed);
            log.info("Payout job processed {} sellers", processed);
        }
    }
}
  1. claimPendingSellers uses SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED on a payout_run table and marks rows IN_PROGRESS — the job resumes where it stopped because completed sellers are marked DONE.
  2. Cooperative shutdown.
  3. One short transaction per seller (Chapter 16), idempotent via a unique (seller_id, period) constraint on the payout record.
PayoutJobTest.java
@Test
void onlyOneInstanceRuns() { /* two threads invoke run(); assert payouts.claimPendingSellers called once */ }

@Test
void resumesAfterInterruption() {
    seedPendingSellers(250);
    runUntil(120, () -> job.run());                        // simulate interrupt after 120 sellers
    assertThat(payouts.countDone()).isEqualTo(120);

    job.run();                                             // next night (or restart)
    assertThat(payouts.countDone()).isEqualTo(250);        // (1)!
}
  1. Resumability proven, not assumed — which is what separates a job that survives deploys from one that quietly skips 130 sellers.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Bound every executor queue and choose a rejection policy — the default is an OOM waiting to happen.
  • @Async is best-effort; anything that must not be lost belongs in the outbox or a job table.
  • Scheduler pool size 1 is a trap; size it, and always set zone on cron jobs.
  • One job per cluster via ShedLock (or a CronJob) — and still idempotent and resumable.
  • Sweepers beat per-entity timers for "do X after N minutes".
  • Virtual threads make blocking cheap but make bulkheads essential; never pool them.
  • Pinning matters on JDK < 24; keep I/O out of locks regardless.
  • Propagate context and drain executors on shutdown.

24 RabbitMQ, Pulsar, JMS & Cloud Stream · 26 Resilience

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Every chapter so far added a dependency: PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, RabbitMQ, OpenSearch, Razorpay, an SMS gateway, five internal services. On a Diwali evening, one of them will be slow. The question resilience answers is: does that become "express delivery estimates are unavailable" or "the grocery app is down"?

The mechanics of the second outcome are always the same:

  1. A dependency's latency goes from 80 ms to 4 s.
  2. Callers have no timeout, or one longer than their own SLA.
  3. Request threads, connections and memory accumulate.
  4. Retries at three layers multiply the load 27×, keeping the dependency down.
  5. Services that don't even use that dependency start failing, because they share a thread pool or database pool.

Every step has a countermeasure: timeouts, bulkheads, circuit breakers, retries with budgets and jitter, rate limiting, load shedding and graceful degradation. This chapter builds them with Resilience4j and Spring Framework 7's built-in resilience annotations, composes them in the right order, and — most importantly — decides per dependency what "degraded" means: a cached price is fine; a guessed payment result is not.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — timeouts, retries, first circuit breaker B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — configuration, fallbacks, bulkheads, rate limiting B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — composition order, tuning, degradation design B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — platform policy, load shedding, chaos testing B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — availability strategy, error budgets

docs.title: 2.1 The failure modes
docs.text: Failure Symptom Countermeasure Slow dependency Threads/connections held Timeout + bulkhead Dead dependency Every call waits then fails Circuit breaker Transient blip Occasional 503/timeout Retry (idempotent only) Retry amplification Load multiplies during an incident Retry budget, one retry layer, jitter Noisy neighbour One endpoint starves others Bulkhead per dependency Overload Everything slows until it fails Load shedding, concurrency limits Abusive client One caller consumes the service Rate limiting Cascading failure Failure spreads upstream All of the above + degradation

docs.title: 2.2 Timeouts are the foundation
docs.text:
Nothing else works without them. Every wait needs a bound:

Wait Where HTTP connect / read Client config (Chapter 19) Connection pool lease Hikari connection-timeout, HTTP pool lease timeout SQL statement statement_timeout, @Transactional(timeout) (Chapters 12, 16) Cache Redis timeout (Chapter 21) Message processing max.poll.interval.ms (Chapter 23) Lock acquisition tryAcquire(timeout) Async task future.get(timeout) / @TimeLimiter

Rule: every downstream timeout must be smaller than the caller's remaining budget (Chapter 19's budget diagram).

docs.title: 2.3 Circuit breaker
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CLOSED
    CLOSED --> OPEN: failure rate ≥ threshold<br/>(over the sliding window)
    OPEN --> HALF_OPEN: after waitDurationInOpenState
    HALF_OPEN --> CLOSED: permitted trial calls succeed
    HALF_OPEN --> OPEN: a trial call fails
    CLOSED --> CLOSED: calls pass through
    OPEN --> OPEN: calls fail fast (CallNotPermittedException)

Purpose: stop hammering something that's already down, fail fast (milliseconds instead of seconds), and give the dependency room to recover.

Key settings:

Setting Meaning Typical slidingWindowType / Size COUNT (last N calls) or TIME (last N seconds) TIME_BASED, 60 minimumNumberOfCalls Don't judge on 2 calls 20 failureRateThreshold % failures to open 50% slowCallDurationThreshold / slowCallRateThreshold Treat slow as failed 2s / 60% waitDurationInOpenState How long before trying again 10–30 s permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState Trial calls 5 recordExceptions / ignoreExceptions What counts as failure count 5xx/timeouts; ignore 4xx

Business failures must not open the circuit

A declined payment or a validation error is the dependency working correctly. If PaymentDeclinedException counts as a failure, a spike of genuine declines opens the breaker and blocks everyone. Always configure ignoreExceptions for domain outcomes (Chapter 10's DomainException).

docs.title: 2.4 Retry — with discipline
docs.text: Rule Why Only idempotent operations Otherwise duplicates (Chapters 04, 19) Only transient failures Timeouts, 5xx, connect errors — never 400/422 Exponential backoff with jitter Prevents synchronized retry waves Small attempt count (2–3) The rest is the circuit breaker's job One retry layer Gateway or service or client, not all three Retry budget Cap retries as a fraction of traffic (e.g. ≤ 10%)

docs.title: 2.5 Bulkhead
docs.text:
Isolate resources so one dependency can't consume everything:

Type Mechanism Use Semaphore Limit concurrent calls Default, especially with virtual threads (Chapter 25) Thread pool Separate pool per dependency When you also need queueing/timeouts on platform threads Connection pools Per-dependency HTTP/DB pools Chapters 12, 19

docs.title: 2.6 Rate limiting
docs.text:
Two different things, often confused:

Direction Goal Where Outbound (client-side) Respect a partner's quota (Razorpay, maps API) Resilience4j RateLimiter Inbound (server-side) Protect us from abuse/overload Gateway or filter with a shared store (Chapters 17, 22)

Inbound limiting returns 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers (Chapter 20).

docs.title: 2.7 Load shedding
docs.text:
When the service is saturated, reject some work immediately rather than degrading everything:

  • Concurrency limit per endpoint class (checkout > browse > search).
  • Queue-depth-based rejection (Chapter 25's CallerRunsPolicy/AbortPolicy).
  • Priority: never shed payment callbacks or webhooks.
  • Return 503 with Retry-After so clients back off (Chapter 10).

Adaptive approaches (measuring latency to infer capacity, à la Little's law) exist; start with static limits derived from load tests.

docs.title: 2.8 Graceful degradation
docs.text:
Dependency down Degraded behaviour Acceptable? Pricing Serve last cached price; mark "price may vary" ✅ with a short staleness bound Search Category browse from PostgreSQL (Chapter 22) ✅ Recommendations Show best sellers ✅ Inventory Allow shelf-stable items, reserve later ⚠️ business decision Payment gateway — ❌ never guess; fail clearly Auth — ❌ never fail open

Degradation is a product decision with an owner, documented per dependency — not something a developer picks at 2 a.m.

docs.title: 2.9 Libraries
docs.text: Library Gives Notes Resilience4j Circuit breaker, retry, bulkhead, rate limiter, time limiter, metrics The standard choice; resilience4j-spring-boot3 starter Spring Framework 7 core resilience @Retryable, @ConcurrencyLimit via @EnableResilientMethods No extra dependency; no circuit breaker Spring Retry @Retryable, RetryTemplate Pre-Framework-7 standard Spring Cloud CircuitBreaker Abstraction over implementations Useful if you must stay implementation-agnostic Service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) Timeouts, retries, outlier detection at the network Complements, doesn't replace, app-level semantics

docs.title: 3.1 Decorator composition
docs.text:
Resilience4j decorates a call with nested functions; Spring applies them as AOP advisors (Chapter 04), so order matters:

flowchart LR
    A[Caller] --> R[Retry]
    R --> CB[CircuitBreaker]
    CB --> RL[RateLimiter]
    RL --> TL[TimeLimiter]
    TL --> BH[Bulkhead]
    BH --> T[Actual call]

Reading outside-in: a retry attempt goes through the circuit breaker (so a retry can be short-circuited), which checks the rate limiter, which enforces the time limit, which enters the bulkhead. This is Resilience4j's default aspect order (Retry outermost); it is configurable via ...AspectOrder properties.

Verify

Confirm the default aspect order and property names for your Resilience4j version — getting Retry and CircuitBreaker the wrong way round means retries never trip the breaker (or the breaker counts each attempt separately).

docs.title: 3.2 Circuit breaker internals
docs.text:
A ring-bit-buffer (count-based) or sliding time window records outcomes. On each call the breaker checks state:

  • CLOSED: record result; if minimumNumberOfCalls reached and failure/slow rate ≥ threshold → OPEN.
  • OPEN: throw CallNotPermittedException immediately (no call made); after waitDurationInOpenState → HALF_OPEN.
  • HALF_OPEN: allow permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState; all succeed → CLOSED, any fails → OPEN.

State transitions emit events — subscribe to them for logging, metrics and alerts.

docs.title: 3.3 Where timeouts actually fire
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[TimeLimiter] -->|"CompletableFuture.get(timeout)"| B[Wraps an async call]
    C[HTTP read timeout] --> D[Socket-level: abandons the response]
    E[Transaction timeout] --> F[Rolls back at the next checkpoint]
    G[Bulkhead wait] --> H[Rejects when full]

A TimeLimiter cancels the future, not necessarily the underlying socket — the HTTP client's own timeouts still matter. Prefer client-level timeouts; use @TimeLimiter to bound composite async work.

docs.title: 4.1 Setup
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts
implementation("io.github.resilience4j:resilience4j-spring-boot3:2.x")     // verify for Boot 4
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-aop")
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator")
application.yml
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    configs:
      default:                                            # (1)!
        slidingWindowType: TIME_BASED
        slidingWindowSize: 60
        minimumNumberOfCalls: 20
        failureRateThreshold: 50
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 2s
        slowCallRateThreshold: 60
        waitDurationInOpenState: 20s
        permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState: 5
        automaticTransitionFromOpenToHalfOpenEnabled: true
        registerHealthIndicator: true                     # (2)!
        ignoreExceptions:
          - in.grocery.platform.error.DomainException     # (3)!
    instances:
      pricing:
        baseConfig: default
      razorpay:
        baseConfig: default
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 3s
        waitDurationInOpenState: 30s
  1. Shared defaults, per-instance overrides — the same pattern as cache configuration (Chapter 21).
  2. Breaker state appears in /actuator/health details.
  3. Business failures never open the circuit.

docs.title: 4.2 A first circuit breaker with a fallback
4.3 Retry for a transient blip
docs.text:
in/grocery/inventory/InventoryGateway.java
@Retry(name = "inventory")                                                    // (1)!
@CircuitBreaker(name = "inventory")
public int stock(String sku, String pincode) {
    return api.stock(sku, pincode).available();
}
application.yml
resilience4j:
  retry:
    instances:
      inventory:
        maxAttempts: 3
        waitDuration: 100ms
        enableExponentialBackoff: true
        exponentialBackoffMultiplier: 2
        enableRandomizedWait: true          # (2)!
        randomizedWaitFactor: 0.5
        retryExceptions:
          - in.grocery.platform.error.DependencyException
          - java.io.IOException
        ignoreExceptions:
          - in.grocery.platform.error.DomainException   # (3)!
  1. @Retry outside @CircuitBreaker: retries pass through the breaker, so once it's open they fail fast instead of waiting.
  2. Jitter — without it, thousands of clients retry at exactly 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms in lockstep.
  3. Don't retry "SKU not found".

docs.title: 4.4 Seeing it work
5.1 Level 2 — Bulkheads
docs.text:
application.yml
resilience4j:
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      pricing:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 50          # (1)!
        maxWaitDuration: 50ms           # (2)!
      razorpay:
        maxConcurrentCalls: 20
        maxWaitDuration: 0              # (3)!
  1. At most 50 concurrent pricing calls from this pod, whatever the request concurrency (Chapter 25).
  2. A short wait absorbs micro-bursts; a long wait just converts rejection into latency.
  3. Payment calls fail fast when saturated — queuing money-moving operations is worse than rejecting them.
Bulkheads (snippet)
@Bulkhead(name = "razorpay")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "razorpay")
public String createOrder(String orderRef, BigDecimal amount) { ... }

Thread-pool bulkheads (type = THREADPOOL) also give you a queue and isolation from the caller's thread — useful on platform threads, largely unnecessary with virtual threads.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — Outbound rate limiting
docs.text:
The maps provider allows 100 requests/second across the platform:

application.yml
resilience4j:
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      maps:
        limitForPeriod: 8               # (1)!
        limitRefreshPeriod: 1s
        timeoutDuration: 200ms          # (2)!
  1. 100/s across ~12 pods ≈ 8 per pod per second. A shared Redis limiter (Chapter 22) is more accurate; a per-pod approximation is simpler and usually good enough with a safety margin.
  2. Wait briefly for a permit, then fail — the caller gets a dependency error, not a 30-second stall.
Outbound rate limiting (snippet)
@RateLimiter(name = "maps")
@CircuitBreaker(name = "maps", fallbackMethod = "straightLineDistance")
public int drivingDistanceMeters(String fromPincode, String toPincode) { ... }

private int straightLineDistance(String from, String to, Throwable cause) {
    return haversineMeters(centroid(from), centroid(to));                    // (1)!
}
  1. A worse but usable answer — exactly what degradation should look like.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Framework 7's built-in resilience
docs.text:
For simple cases you may not need Resilience4j at all:

Spring Boot 3.5 (Spring Retry)Spring Boot 4.x (Framework 7 core resilience) RetryConfig.java
@EnableRetry
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class RetryConfig {}

@Retryable(retryFor = DependencyException.class, maxAttempts = 3,
           backoff = @Backoff(delay = 100, multiplier = 2, random = true))
public StockView stock(String sku) { ... }

@Recover
public StockView fallback(DependencyException e, String sku) { ... }
ResilienceConfig.java
@EnableResilientMethods
@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
class ResilienceConfig {}

@Retryable(includes = DependencyException.class, maxRetries = 2, delay = 100, multiplier = 2)
@ConcurrencyLimit(20)                                                     // (1)!
public StockView stock(String sku) { ... }
  1. A built-in semaphore bulkhead. Verify annotation attributes in the Framework 7 reference.

Choose: Framework 7 annotations for retries and concurrency limits with no extra dependency; Resilience4j when you need circuit breakers, rate limiters, rich metrics and event streams — which most production services do.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Composing everything correctly
5.5 Level 3 — Retry budgets
docs.text:
Even well-behaved retries amplify load exactly when a dependency is struggling. Cap them globally:

in/grocery/platform/resilience/RetryBudget.java
package in.grocery.platform.resilience;

import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

/** Token bucket: retries may not exceed ~10% of primary calls. */
@Component
public class RetryBudget {

    private final AtomicLong tokens = new AtomicLong();
    private final long maxTokens = 500;

    public void recordPrimaryCall() {
        tokens.updateAndGet(t -> Math.min(maxTokens, t + 1));                 // (1)!
    }

    public boolean tryConsume() {
        return tokens.updateAndGet(t -> t >= 10 ? t - 10 : t) >= 0            // (2)!
                && tokens.get() >= 0;
    }
}
  1. Each successful primary call earns a token.
  2. A retry costs 10 tokens → retries are capped at ~10% of traffic. When the budget is exhausted, calls fail immediately instead of retrying — the system stops making the incident worse.

Wire it into a RetryConfig#retryOnResultPredicate/custom Retry decorator, or check it in the code path before retrying. Some service meshes and gRPC implement retry budgets natively.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Inbound rate limiting and load shedding
5.7 Level 3 — Circuit breaker events and alerts
6.1 The platform resilience policy
docs.text:
Every outbound dependency is registered with an explicit policy:

Dependency Timeout Retry Breaker Bulkhead Degradation pricing-service 600 ms 2 attempts (reads) 50% / 60 s window 50 Last known price (≤ 15 min), else fail inventory-service 500 ms 2 attempts (reads) 50% 50 Shelf-stable: assume available; perishable: fail search (OpenSearch) 800 ms none 50% 30 Category browse from PostgreSQL Razorpay 3 s none (writes) 50% / 30 s 20 None — fail with a clear message SMS gateway 2 s 3 attempts (async) 50% 10 Queue and retry later (Chapter 24) maps 1 s 1 attempt 50% 20 Straight-line distance Redis cache 200 ms none none — Fail open to the database (Chapter 21) in/grocery/platform/resilience/DependencyPolicy.java
/** Documented, code-visible policy — the table above, enforced. */
public record DependencyPolicy(
        String name,
        Duration timeout,
        int retryAttempts,
        int bulkheadConcurrency,
        Degradation degradation) {

    public enum Degradation { CACHED_VALUE, ALTERNATIVE_COMPUTATION, QUEUE_FOR_LATER, FAIL_FAST }
}

Keeping this in code (and asserting it in a test) stops the table drifting from reality.

docs.title: 6.2 Checkout under partial failure
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[POST /api/orders] --> B{pricing available?}
    B -- yes --> C[live price]
    B -- no, breaker open --> D{cached price ≤ 15 min?}
    D -- yes --> E["use cached price + flag 'price may vary'"]
    D -- no --> F[503 PRICING_UNAVAILABLE]
    C & E --> G{inventory available?}
    G -- yes --> H[reserve]
    G -- no --> I{perishable?}
    I -- yes --> F2[422 CANNOT_VERIFY_STOCK]
    I -- no --> J[accept, reserve asynchronously]
    H & J --> K{payment gateway available?}
    K -- yes --> L[create payment order → 201]
    K -- no --> M[503 PAYMENT_GATEWAY_UNAVAILABLE + Retry-After]

Each branch is a decision someone made deliberately, with a metric behind it:

in/grocery/order/delegate/OrderDelegate.java (degradation metrics)
private PriceView priceFor(String sku, String pincode) {
    try {
        return pricing.price(sku, pincode);
    } catch (DependencyException e) {
        meters.counter("grocery.degraded", "dependency", "pricing", "mode", "cached").increment();   // (1)!
        throw e;   // the gateway's fallback already handled cache lookup; this path means no cache either
    }
}
  1. Measure degradation, not just failure: "we served 4% of checkouts with cached prices for 20 minutes" is the number a post-incident review needs.

docs.title: 6.3 Health, readiness and resilience
docs.text:
application.yml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db, redis                 # (1)!
        liveness:
          include: livenessState                             # (2)!
  health:
    circuitbreakers:
      enabled: true                                          # (3)!
  1. Readiness includes dependencies the service cannot work without. If PostgreSQL is down, this pod can't serve — take it out of rotation.
  2. Liveness is internal only (Chapter 03): never restart pods because a dependency is down.
  3. Breaker states appear in health details for humans — but an open breaker must not make the service unready, because the whole point is that we're still serving degraded traffic.

docs.title: 6.4 Chaos testing
6.5 Anti-amplification checklist for incidents
docs.text: Question Where to check Is anyone retrying more than once? Gateway config, client config, mesh config Are retries jittered? Retry config Is there a retry budget? Platform policy Do breakers cover this dependency? Config + health details Are timeouts shorter than the caller's? Timeout budget doc (Chapter 19) Is degradation actually working? grocery.degraded counters Are we shedding low-priority traffic? grocery.load.shed counters

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Decide per service: keep Spring Retry, move to Framework 7 annotations, or standardize on Resilience4j.
  • Don't mix two retry implementations on one method.
  • Re-verify aspect ordering after changing annotations (retry must wrap the breaker).
  • Re-run chaos tests after the upgrade — configuration typos are invisible until a dependency fails.
  • Check metric names if dashboards depend on them.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Timeouts everywhere, always shorter than the caller's budget.
  2. A documented policy per dependency: timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead, degradation.
  3. Breakers ignore business exceptions and count slow calls as failures.
  4. Retry only idempotent operations, once, with jitter, within a budget, at one layer.
  5. Bulkheads on every outbound dependency (essential with virtual threads).
  6. Degrade deliberately — cached values, alternative computations, queue-for-later — and never for payments or auth.
  7. Shed low-priority load with 503 + Retry-After before the service collapses.
  8. Alert on breaker transitions and degradation counters, with runbooks.
  9. Chaos-test latency and outages, not just exceptions.
  10. Readiness ≠ dependency health: stay in rotation while degraded.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Circuit breaker without timeouts — the breaker opens after threads are already exhausted.

❌ Counting 4xx/business errors as breaker failures.

❌ Retrying at gateway, service and client simultaneously.

❌ Retrying non-idempotent writes (double charges).

❌ Fallbacks that invent data (a guessed price, an assumed payment success).

❌ Fallbacks that hide bugs — catching Exception and returning empty results makes outages invisible.

❌ One shared breaker for unrelated calls, or a breaker per instance of a client object (state resets constantly).

❌ Unbounded queues instead of load shedding (Chapter 25).

❌ Marking the pod unready when a dependency is down — you remove capacity exactly when you need it.

❌ Resilience config that has never been tested under real latency.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Breaker never opens Business exceptions excluded but real failures also ignored; minimumNumberOfCalls too high for low traffic Check recordExceptions, lower minimum, use TIME_BASED window Breaker opens constantly Threshold too low, slow-call threshold below normal p99 Tune from real latency data Retries make things worse No budget, multiple layers, no jitter One layer, budget, jitter Latency unchanged during dependency outage Timeouts too long / missing Fix timeouts first Fallback throws Fallback signature mismatch or fallback itself depends on the broken thing Test the fallback path explicitly CallNotPermittedException leaking to customers Not mapped Map to 503 + Retry-After (Chapter 10) Everything fails when Redis is slow Cache not failing open CacheErrorHandler (Chapter 21) Pods restart during a dependency outage Liveness includes dependencies Liveness internal only Resilience works in tests, not production Annotations on self-invoked methods Proxy rules (Chapter 04)

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every outbound call has a timeout and a bulkhead
  • Every dependency has a documented policy and degradation mode
  • Breakers configured with business exceptions ignored and slow calls counted
  • Retry budget and single retry layer verified
  • Inbound rate limiting and priority-aware load shedding in place
  • Breaker/degradation metrics with alerts and runbooks
  • Chaos tests for latency and outage per critical dependency
  • Game day run at least once before peak season

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What does a circuit breaker do?

Short answer: After enough failures it stops calling a failing dependency and fails fast (or falls back), then periodically tries again to see if it recovered.

B1 · Why are timeouts essential?

Short answer: Without them a slow dependency holds threads and connections indefinitely, so your service fails even for unrelated requests.

B1 · When is it safe to retry?

Short answer: For idempotent operations failing transiently (timeout, 5xx, connection error) — never for non-idempotent writes or business errors like validation failures.

B1 · What is a fallback?

Short answer: Alternative behaviour when a call fails — a cached value, a simpler computation, or a clear error. It must never fabricate data.

B1 · What is a bulkhead?

Short answer: A limit on concurrent calls to one dependency so it can't consume all the service's threads or connections.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you configure a circuit breaker sensibly?

Short answer: Time-based window (~60 s), minimum calls (~20), failure rate ~50%, slow-call threshold above normal p99, wait duration 10–30 s, a few half-open trial calls, and business exceptions ignored.

B2 · Why must the retry wrap the circuit breaker (and not the reverse)?

Short answer: With retry outermost, each attempt passes through the breaker, so once it's open retries fail fast. Reversed, the breaker sees one "call" per retried group and retries keep hammering a dead dependency.

B2 · Semaphore vs thread-pool bulkhead?

Short answer: Semaphore limits concurrency on the calling thread — simple and the right choice with virtual threads. Thread-pool bulkheads add isolation and queueing at the cost of context switching and propagation complexity.

B2 · How do you rate-limit calls to a partner API?

Short answer: A client-side rate limiter sized to your share of the quota (per pod, or shared via Redis), with a short wait then fail, plus a circuit breaker for when you're throttled anyway.

B2 · How should a 429 from a dependency be handled?

Short answer: Don't retry immediately; respect Retry-After, back off, and surface a degraded response or a 503 upstream. Count it separately from 5xx.

B2 · Why shouldn't business exceptions open the breaker?

Short answer: They mean the dependency is working. Opening on declines or validation errors takes down a healthy dependency during a legitimate spike.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Explain retry amplification and how to prevent it.

Short answer: Retries at several layers multiply (3×3×3 = 27 requests per user action) exactly when a dependency is struggling. Prevent with a single retry layer, small attempt counts, jitter, retry budgets (retries ≤ ~10% of traffic) and circuit breakers that stop retries at the source.

B3 · Where does load shedding belong and how do you choose limits?

Short answer: At the gateway for global/per-client limits and in the service for internal protection. Limits come from load tests (concurrency at which latency degrades), applied per priority class so checkout survives while browsing is shed.

B3 · How do you design degradation?

Short answer: Per dependency, with the business: what's the worst acceptable answer? Cached data with a staleness bound, an alternative computation, deferred processing, or honest failure. Never fabricate money, stock or auth outcomes. Measure how often degradation is used.

B3 · How do you test resilience properly?

Short answer: Inject latency and network faults (Toxiproxy/WireMock delays) rather than exceptions, assert bounded response times and breaker state transitions, verify fallback paths, and run game days in staging under load.

B3 · Should an open circuit breaker make the service unready?

Short answer: No. Readiness removes the pod from load balancing; if the dependency is down, every pod would drop out and the degraded path — the whole point of the breaker — would never serve traffic. Surface the state in health details and alerts instead.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Define the resilience policy for a platform.

Short answer: A per-dependency table (timeout, retry, breaker, bulkhead, degradation) implemented in a platform library, enforced by defaults, visible in metrics, tested with chaos tests, reviewed when SLAs change, and referenced in runbooks.

B4 · Application-level resilience or service mesh?

Short answer: Mesh gives uniform, language-agnostic timeouts, retries, outlier detection and mTLS; it can't know whether an operation is idempotent or what a good fallback is. Use the mesh for transport concerns, the app for semantics — and never let both retry.

B4 · How do you tune a circuit breaker for a low-traffic endpoint?

Short answer: Count-based windows and high minimums never trigger; use a time-based window with a low minimum call count, accept slower detection, or rely on timeouts plus upstream breakers. For very low traffic, a breaker may add little — measure before adding complexity.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How does resilience relate to SLOs and error budgets?

Short answer: Resilience converts dependency failures into degraded-but-successful responses, protecting the availability SLI. Degradation should be measured as its own metric so the organization knows the difference between "healthy", "degraded" and "down", and error-budget burn drives investment in the weakest dependency.

B5 · What's the organizational failure mode of resilience work?

Short answer: Configuration that exists but was never exercised — breakers that don't open, fallbacks that throw, timeouts longer than the caller's. Without chaos tests and game days, resilience is theatre. Ownership per dependency and post-incident review of degradation behaviour keep it real.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Search cluster degraded, entire catalog page fails

Search calls had no timeout and no fallback; the page waited 30 s and then 500'd. Fixes: 800 ms timeout, breaker, PostgreSQL category-browse fallback (Chapter 22), a grocery.degraded metric with an alert, and a chaos test asserting the page renders within 1.5 s with search dead.

Scenario · Payment provider incident, our pods OOM

Razorpay latency rose to 20 s. Calls had a 30 s timeout, no bulkhead, and @Async notification retries queued unboundedly (Chapter 25). Fixes: 3 s timeout, bulkhead of 20, breaker with 30 s open window, bounded executor with CallerRunsPolicy, 503 + Retry-After to clients, and a game day to verify.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Resilient delivery-ETA lookup

GET /api/delivery/eta?pincode=... calls the maps service. Requirements: 1 s timeout, at most 1 retry on timeout, breaker opening at 50% failures over 60 s, bulkhead of 20 concurrent calls, 8 requests/second outbound limit, and a fallback to a static per-zone ETA table. Write tests for: fallback used when maps is down, breaker opens, and response time stays under 2.5 s when maps is slow.

Solution application.yml
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      maps:
        baseConfig: default
        slowCallDurationThreshold: 1s
  retry:
    instances:
      maps:
        maxAttempts: 2
        waitDuration: 100ms
        enableRandomizedWait: true
        retryExceptions: [in.grocery.platform.error.DependencyException]
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      maps: { maxConcurrentCalls: 20, maxWaitDuration: 50ms }
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      maps: { limitForPeriod: 8, limitRefreshPeriod: 1s, timeoutDuration: 100ms }
EtaGateway.java
@Component
public class EtaGateway {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(EtaGateway.class);

    private final MapsApi maps;
    private final ZoneEtaTable zoneTable;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @Retry(name = "maps")
    @CircuitBreaker(name = "maps", fallbackMethod = "zoneEta")
    @RateLimiter(name = "maps")
    @Bulkhead(name = "maps")
    public EtaView eta(String pincode) {
        return maps.eta(pincode);                    // client timeout 1s (Chapter 19)
    }

    private EtaView zoneEta(String pincode, Throwable cause) {
        meters.counter("grocery.degraded", "dependency", "maps", "mode", "zone-table").increment();
        log.debug("Maps unavailable ({}), using zone ETA for {}", cause.toString(), pincode);
        return zoneTable.etaFor(pincode);            // (1)!
    }
}
  1. Always available, coarse but honest ("2–3 hours" instead of "47 minutes"). The response marks the estimate as approximate so the UI can say so.
EtaGatewayChaosTest.java
@Test
void usesZoneTableWhenMapsIsDown() {
    mapsProxy.disable();
    assertThat(gateway.eta("560102").approximate()).isTrue();
}

@Test
void breakerOpensAndFailsFast() {
    mapsProxy.disable();
    IntStream.range(0, 30).forEach(i -> gateway.eta("560102"));
    assertThat(registry.circuitBreaker("maps").getState()).isEqualTo(State.OPEN);

    long start = System.nanoTime();
    gateway.eta("560102");
    assertThat(Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - start)).isLessThan(Duration.ofMillis(50));   // (1)!
}

@Test
void slowMapsStillRespondsQuickly() throws Exception {
    mapsProxy.toxics().latency("slow", DOWNSTREAM, 5_000);
    long start = System.nanoTime();
    gateway.eta("560102");
    assertThat(Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - start)).isLessThan(Duration.ofMillis(2_500));  // (2)!
}
  1. Open breaker = no network call at all.
  2. 1 s timeout × 2 attempts + jitter < 2.5 s — the latency contract of this dependency, asserted.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Timeouts first — every other pattern depends on them.
  • Circuit breakers stop hammering a dead dependency and fail fast; they must ignore business exceptions and count slow calls.
  • Retries are dangerous: idempotent only, one layer, jittered, budgeted.
  • Bulkheads stop one dependency from consuming the service — mandatory with virtual threads.
  • Load shedding with priorities keeps checkout alive when the service is saturated.
  • Degradation is a product decision per dependency, measured with its own metric, never applied to payments or auth.
  • Chaos-test latency and outages; configuration you haven't exercised is a guess.
  • Readiness stays green while degraded — that's the whole point.

docs.text:

  • Spring Framework 7 Reference — Core › Resilience Features
  • Release It! (Michael Nygard) — stability patterns and anti-patterns

25 Async, Scheduling & Virtual Threads · 27 Observability

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
It's 9:15 p.m. during a sale. Support reports "checkout is slow for some customers". You have 26 services and 180 pods. Which of these can you answer in under two minutes?

  • Is it slow for everyone, or only in Mumbai, only on Android, only for UPI payments?
  • Which hop is slow: our order service, pricing, the database, or Razorpay?
  • Did it start at 21:03 with the deploy, or at 20:47 with the traffic spike?
  • How much of our monthly error budget has this burned?
  • Is the degradation path working — are we serving cached prices, or failing?

With logs alone: no. With dashboards nobody maintained: no. With metrics for aggregates, traces for causality, logs for detail and a shared correlation id: yes, in about ninety seconds.

Spring Boot gives you most of this out of the box — Actuator, Micrometer metrics, the Observation API, Micrometer Tracing with OpenTelemetry, and automatic instrumentation of HTTP, JDBC pools, caches, Kafka and more. What Boot cannot give you is the decisions: which SLIs matter, what tags to allow, what to alert on, and what a responder should do when the alert fires.

This chapter covers both: the mechanics (endpoints, meters, observations, tracing, exporters) and the judgement (cardinality budgets, SLOs and burn-rate alerts, business metrics, runbooks, cost control).

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — Actuator, built-in metrics, health B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — custom metrics, tags, health indicators, tracing setup B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — Observation API, cardinality, sampling, exemplars B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — SLOs, alerting, dashboards, cost B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — observability strategy and incident culture

docs.title: 2.1 The three signals (plus one)
docs.text:
Signal Answers Cost driver Retention Metrics How much, how often, how fast — in aggregate Cardinality (tag combinations) Long (months) Traces Where did the time go for this request, across services Sampling rate × span count Short (days) Logs What exactly happened in this case Volume × verbosity (Chapter 07) Medium, tiered Profiles (continuous profiling) Which code burned the CPU Sampling Short

Rule: alert on metrics, debug with traces, confirm with logs.

docs.title: 2.2 Actuator
docs.text:
Endpoint Use health (+ groups liveness, readiness) Kubernetes probes, dependency status info Build version, git commit (Chapter 01) metrics, prometheus Metric scraping loggers Change log levels at runtime (Chapter 07) startup Slow beans at startup (Chapter 03) env, configprops Effective configuration (sanitized, Chapter 06) conditions, beans, mappings Why is this bean/endpoint here (Chapter 05) threaddump, heapdump Incident forensics httpexchanges, scheduledtasks, caches, flyway, sbom Targeted diagnostics application.yml
management:
  server:
    port: 9090                      # separate port; not exposed publicly
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus,loggers,startup,metrics
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true
      show-details: when-authorized

docs.title: 2.3 Micrometer meter types
docs.text:
Type Use Example Counter Monotonic count grocery.orders.placed Timer Duration + count (+ histogram) http.server.requests Gauge Current value grocery.outbox.pending DistributionSummary Non-time distribution order value in ₹ LongTaskTimer In-flight long operations reindex job duration

Built-in instrumentation you get for free: http.server.requests, http.client.requests, jvm.*, process.*, system.*, hikaricp.*, cache.*, kafka.*, spring.data.repository.invocations, tomcat.*, logback.events, executor.*, resilience4j.*.

docs.title: 2.4 Cardinality — the one rule that matters
docs.text:
A metric's cost is the number of distinct tag combinations (time series). http.server.requests{uri, method, status, outcome, exception} with 40 URIs × 4 methods × 8 statuses ≈ 1,280 series — fine. Add customerId and you have millions, and your monitoring bill (and Prometheus) fall over.

Allowed as a tag Never a tag endpoint/URI template, method, status, outcome order id, customer id, SKU, mobile number service, environment, region, version free-text error messages dependency name, cache name, queue name timestamps, UUIDs, full URLs with ids bounded enums (payment method, channel) anything unbounded

High-cardinality data belongs in traces and logs, which are indexed for exactly that.

docs.title: 2.5 The Observation API
docs.text:
One instrumentation call produces metrics and a trace span (and optionally logs):

The Observation API (snippet)
Observation.createNotStarted("grocery.checkout", registry)
    .lowCardinalityKeyValue("channel", "mobile")     // → metric tag
    .highCardinalityKeyValue("orderRef", ref)        // → span attribute only
    .observe(() -> doCheckout());

ObservationHandlers turn observations into timers, spans and log events. @Observed does the same via AOP when management.observations.annotations.enabled=true.

docs.title: 2.6 Tracing
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Trace One request's journey, identified by traceId Span One operation (HTTP call, DB query, Kafka consume) with parent/child links Propagation W3C traceparent header (and tracestate), Kafka headers Sampling Head-based probability in the app, or tail-based in a collector Exemplars Links from a metric bucket to an example trace

Spring integrates via Micrometer Tracing with an OpenTelemetry (or Brave) bridge, exporting OTLP to a collector → Tempo/Jaeger/vendor.

docs.title: 2.7 Health indicators
docs.text:
Boot auto-configures indicators for DataSource, Redis, Kafka, Mongo, disk space, Elasticsearch, and more; you add domain ones. Aggregation: any DOWN makes the group DOWN.

The rule from Chapters 03 and 26: liveness = internal only; readiness = "can this pod serve?"; dependency status is visible but doesn't necessarily remove the pod from rotation.

docs.title: 2.8 SLIs, SLOs and error budgets
docs.text:
Term Grocery example SLI Fraction of checkout requests answered < 2 s without a 5xx SLO 99.5% over 30 days Error budget 0.5% ≈ 3.6 hours/month of "bad" Burn rate How fast the budget is being consumed

Alert on burn rate, not on every error: a multi-window, multi-burn-rate alert (e.g. 14.4× over 1 h and 6× over 6 h) pages when the budget is genuinely at risk and stays quiet for one-off blips.

docs.title: 3.1 From code to dashboards
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Instrumentation:<br/>auto + @Observed + custom"] --> B[ObservationRegistry]
    B --> C[MeterObservationHandler → Micrometer]
    B --> D[TracingObservationHandler → spans]
    C --> E[MeterRegistry + MeterFilters]
    E --> F["/actuator/prometheus scrape"]
    D --> G[OTLP exporter]
    F --> H[(Prometheus / Mimir)]
    G --> I[OpenTelemetry Collector]
    I --> J[(Tempo / Jaeger)]
    H & J --> K[Grafana dashboards + alerts]
    L[JSON logs with traceId<br/>Chapter 07] --> M[(Loki / Elasticsearch)]
    M --> K

The collector is where tail sampling, redaction and fan-out to multiple backends happen — keeping that logic out of 26 services.

docs.title: 3.2 An HTTP request, fully observed
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant F as Server filter (observation)
    participant H as Controller
    participant D as DB / client calls
    participant R as Registries

    C->>F: GET /api/orders/{ref} (traceparent?)
    F->>R: start server observation<br/>(extract or create trace context)
    F->>H: dispatch (MDC: traceId, spanId — Chapter 07)
    H->>D: JDBC / RestClient calls → child spans
    D-->>H: results
    H-->>F: response
    F->>R: stop observation<br/>timer http.server.requests{uri,method,status,outcome}<br/>span ended, exported

The uri tag uses the template (/api/orders/{ref}), not the actual path — that's what keeps cardinality bounded.

docs.title: 3.3 Meter filters
docs.text: MeterFilters run before a meter is registered: deny, rename, add common tags, cap tag values, or configure histograms/SLO buckets. This is your cardinality safety net — a filter that caps the number of values per tag stops one bad commit from creating a million series.

docs.title: 4.1 Actuator and Prometheus
docs.text:

implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-actuator")
implementation("io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus")

management:
  endpoints:
    web:

  endpoint:

  metrics:

Terminal
curl -s localhost:8080/actuator/prometheus | grep http_server_requests | head -5
Example
http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order-service",method="GET",outcome="SUCCESS",status="200",uri="/api/orders/{ref}"} 1423
http_server_requests_seconds_sum{...} 61.2

build.gradle.kts
implementation("io.micrometer:micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel")
implementation("io.opentelemetry:opentelemetry-exporter-otlp")
application.yml
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1                    # (1)!
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
  observations:
    annotations:
      enabled: true                       # (2)!
  metrics:
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true
spring:
  kafka:
    listener:
      observation-enabled: true           # (3)!
    template:
      observation-enabled: true
logging:
  pattern:
    correlation: "[${spring.application.name:},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}] "   # (4)!
  1. 10% head sampling. Errors and slow requests are usually kept by tail sampling in the collector (6.3) — configure that rather than raising this to 100%.
  2. Enables @Observed, @Timed, @Counted aspects.
  3. Trace context flows through Kafka headers (Chapter 23), so a trace spans producer → consumer.
  4. Logs carry traceId (Chapter 07) — the join key between all three signals.
