5.4 Level 3 — What to measure per layer
docs.text:
Layer Metric Alert on HTTP server http.server.requests (rate, errors, p99 by uri) SLO burn rate HTTP clients http.client.requests by dependency error rate, p99 Database hikaricp.connections.{active,pending,usage} pending > 0 sustained JPA/queries spring.data.repository.invocations p99 per repository method Cache cache.gets{result} hit ratio drop Kafka consumer lag, grocery.kafka.dlt lag growth, any DLT Outbox grocery.outbox.pending > 1,000 or rising Executors executor.queued, executor.rejected queue depth, any rejection Resilience breaker transitions, grocery.degraded any OPEN, degradation rate JVM heap, GC pause, threads GC pause p99, heap after GC Business orders/min, GMV, payment success %, checkout conversion deviation from baseline

Business metrics detect what technical metrics miss

A deploy that breaks the "Place order" button produces fewer errors and lower latency — everything looks great except grocery.orders.placed falling off a cliff. Alert on a sustained drop against the same hour last week.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Health groups that mean something
docs.text:
application.yml
management:
  endpoint:
    health:
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db, redis                       # (1)!
          show-details: always
        liveness:
          include: livenessState                                    # (2)!
      show-details: when-authorized
  health:
    redis:
      enabled: true
    defaults:
      enabled: true
  1. Without PostgreSQL or Redis this pod cannot serve → take it out of rotation. Note that if every pod loses the database, removing them all doesn't help — that's why the dependency list must be minimal and deliberate.
  2. Liveness never includes dependencies (Chapters 03, 26).
in/grocery/platform/observability/OutboxHealthIndicator.java
@Component("outbox")
class OutboxHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {

    @Override
    public Health health() {
        long pending = outbox.countPending();
        long oldestSeconds = outbox.oldestPendingAgeSeconds();
        return oldestSeconds < 120
                ? Health.up().withDetail("pending", pending).build()
                : Health.status("DEGRADED")                                       // (1)!
                        .withDetail("pending", pending)
                        .withDetail("oldestPendingSeconds", oldestSeconds)
                        .build();
    }
}
  1. Visible to humans and to a dashboard query; not in the readiness group, because a stuck relay shouldn't remove serving capacity.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Instrumenting a custom component
6.1 SLOs and burn-rate alerts
docs.text:
slo/order-service.yaml (documented SLOs)
service: order-service
slos:
  - name: checkout-availability
    sli: "successful (non-5xx) POST /api/v1/orders responses / total"
    objective: 99.5%
    window: 30d
  - name: checkout-latency
    sli: "POST /api/v1/orders responses faster than 2s / total"
    objective: 99%
    window: 30d
  - name: order-events-freshness
    sli: "outbox rows relayed within 60s / total"
    objective: 99.9%
    window: 7d
prometheus/rules/order-service.yaml
groups:
  - name: order-service-slo
    rules:
      - record: job:checkout_errors:ratio_rate5m                                      # (1)!
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order-service",uri="/api/v1/orders",status=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{application="order-service",uri="/api/v1/orders"}[5m]))

      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetBurningFast
        expr: |
          job:checkout_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.005)
          and
          job:checkout_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.005)                            # (2)!
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "Checkout burning error budget 14x (order-service)"
          runbook: "https://runbooks.grocery.in/order-service/checkout-errors"         # (3)!
          dashboard: "https://grafana.grocery.in/d/order-service"

      - alert: CheckoutErrorBudgetBurningSlow
        expr: |
          job:checkout_errors:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.005)
          and
          job:checkout_errors:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.005)
        for: 15m
        labels:
          severity: ticket                                                              # (4)!
  1. Recording rules keep alert expressions readable and cheap.
  2. Multi-window, multi-burn-rate: two windows must agree, which kills false pages from 30-second blips while still catching a real outage in minutes.
  3. Every alert links a runbook and a dashboard. An alert without a runbook is a 2 a.m. puzzle.
  4. Slow burn creates a ticket, not a page — the budget is at risk but nothing is on fire.

docs.title: 6.2 Dashboards that answer questions
docs.text:
A service dashboard, top to bottom:

Row Panels SLO Availability and latency SLI vs objective, error budget remaining, burn rate Traffic (RED) Requests/s by endpoint, error rate, latency p50/p95/p99 Dependencies http.client.requests per dependency (rate, errors, p99), breaker state, degradation counters Resources (USE) CPU, heap after GC, GC pause, Hikari active/pending, executor queues Async Kafka lag, DLT rate, outbox pending, scheduled job durations Business Orders/min vs last week, payment success %, checkout conversion Deploys Version annotations overlaid on every graph

The deploy annotation row is what turns "when did this start?" from an archaeology exercise into a glance.

docs.title: 6.3 Collector configuration: sampling and redaction
docs.text:
otel-collector.yaml (excerpt)
processors:
  tail_sampling:                                                                    # (1)!
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - name: errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] }
      - name: slow
        type: latency
        latency: { threshold_ms: 1000 }
      - name: baseline
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 5 }
  attributes/redact:                                                                # (2)!
    actions:
      - key: http.request.header.authorization
        action: delete
      - key: customer.mobile
        action: delete
  resource:
    attributes:
      - key: deployment.environment
        value: prod
        action: upsert
exporters:
  otlp/tempo: { endpoint: tempo:4317 }
  prometheusremotewrite: { endpoint: http://mimir/api/v1/push }
  1. Tail sampling: keep every error and slow trace, plus 5% of the rest. Head sampling alone forces a choice between cost and keeping the traces you actually need.
  2. Redaction in one place rather than in 26 services — and a second line of defence behind the application's own PII discipline (Chapter 07).

docs.title: 6.4 Tracing across the whole checkout
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["mobile app<br/>traceparent generated"] --> B[gateway span]
    B --> C[order-service: POST /api/v1/orders]
    C --> D[pricing-service HTTP span]
    C --> E[PostgreSQL spans]
    C --> F[Razorpay HTTP span]
    C --> G[Kafka produce span]
    G --> H[inventory-service consume span]
    H --> I[PostgreSQL spans]

What this gives a responder in one view: which hop consumed the 3.8 seconds, whether the Kafka consumer picked the event up, and the traceId to paste into the log search for the exact SQL and error.

Requirements for that picture to exist: clients built from Boot's builders (Chapter 19), observation-enabled on Kafka template and listeners (Chapter 23), context propagation to async work (Chapters 07, 25), and consistent traceparent propagation at the gateway.

docs.title: 6.5 Instrumenting an incident-ready service — checklist in code
6.6 Cost control
docs.text:
Lever Effect Cardinality guards and tag review The biggest single factor in metrics cost Drop unused meters (MeterFilter.deny) Fewer series scraped and stored Scrape interval (15 s → 30 s) Halves storage for slow-moving metrics Retention tiers (raw 15 d, downsampled 13 mo) Long-term trends without raw cost Tail sampling instead of 100% traces Keeps what matters, drops the rest Log level and retention tiers (Chapter 07) Usually the largest bill

Review the top 20 metrics by series count quarterly; a single forgotten tag is usually 80% of the growth.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Actuator Full endpoint set Same (module packages move — verify) Micrometer 1.14/1.15 1.15+ (verify) Observation API ✅ ✅ Tracing bridge micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel / -brave Same; OpenTelemetry starter available (verify name) OTLP export management.otlp.tracing.*, metrics OTLP registry Same (verify property names) Annotation aspects management.observations.annotations.enabled Same (verify) Prometheus micrometer-registry-prometheus Same; native histograms (verify support)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Verify metric names and tags are unchanged after the upgrade — dashboards and alerts break silently otherwise.
  • Re-check Actuator endpoint packages if you have custom endpoints or security matchers (EndpointRequest).
  • Confirm tracing bridge and exporter versions line up with the collector.
  • Re-run the observability contract test (6.5) in staging before rolling out.
  • Re-validate PII redaction rules after Jackson/serialization changes.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Alert on metrics, debug with traces, confirm with logs — one traceId joins all three.
  2. Common tags (application, env, region, version) on every metric; cardinality guards as a safety net.
  3. Low-cardinality keys for metrics, high-cardinality for spans (Observation API).
  4. SLOs with multi-window burn-rate alerts; every alert links a runbook and dashboard.
  5. Business metrics alongside technical ones — they catch failures that look healthy.
  6. Health groups: liveness internal, readiness minimal, degradation visible but non-fatal.
  7. Tail sampling and redaction in the collector, not in 26 services.
  8. Deploy annotations on dashboards.
  9. Test your observability: meter names, URI templates, health groups.
  10. Review cost and cardinality quarterly.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Unbounded tags (order id, customer id, SKU, raw URI) — the classic monitoring-bill explosion.

❌ Alerting on every 5xx instead of on budget burn — pager fatigue, then ignored pages.

❌ Alerts without runbooks or owners.

❌ Dashboards built once for a demo and never maintained; nobody trusts them during an incident.

❌ 100% trace sampling in production "to be safe" — cost with no added insight over tail sampling.

❌ Liveness probes that check dependencies — synchronized restarts during an outage.

❌ Logging what a metric should count (log.info("cache miss") at 50k/s).

❌ Exposing Actuator publicly, or show-details: always with secrets in env.

❌ Measuring only technical signals and missing "orders dropped 60%".

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Prometheus scrape times out / high memory Cardinality explosion Find top series by name; add cardinality guards; remove bad tags Gauge reports NaN The measured object was garbage collected Hold a strong reference uri tag shows raw ids Non-templated path or manual URI building Use path templates; assert in a test No traces across services Propagation broken (client not from Boot's builder, gateway strips headers) Use injected builders; allow traceparent Traces stop at Kafka Observations not enabled on template/listener observation-enabled: true traceId missing in logs No correlation pattern / no tracing on classpath Chapter 07 pattern, tracing bridge Metrics missing after upgrade Renamed meters/tags Contract test; check release notes Health always UP while broken No dependency indicators, or wrong group Add indicators; review groups Alert storm during deploys No deploy awareness, short windows Multi-window burn rate, deploy annotations, maintenance windows Monitoring bill doubled New tag, new service, retention change Quarterly cardinality review

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Actuator on a separate port, secured, probes enabled
  • Common tags + cardinality guards + SLO histograms configured
  • Tracing with OTLP to a collector doing tail sampling and redaction
  • Logs carry traceId (Chapter 07)
  • SLOs defined per critical journey with burn-rate alerts
  • Every alert: owner, runbook, dashboard link
  • Business metrics dashboarded and alerted
  • Observability contract test in CI
  • Cardinality and cost reviewed quarterly

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What does Spring Boot Actuator give you?

Short answer: Production endpoints — health (with liveness/readiness groups), info, metrics/Prometheus, loggers, startup, env, mappings, thread dump — for monitoring and diagnostics.

B1 · What is Micrometer?

Short answer: A vendor-neutral metrics facade: you record counters, timers and gauges, and a registry exports them to Prometheus, OTLP or a vendor backend.

B1 · Counter vs gauge vs timer?

Short answer: Counter only increases (events); gauge reports a current value (queue depth); timer records durations and counts.

B1 · Why shouldn't you tag a metric with a customer id?

Short answer: Each tag value creates a new time series; unbounded values explode storage and query cost. High-cardinality data belongs in traces and logs.

B1 · What is a trace?

Short answer: The record of one request's path across services, made of spans linked by a shared traceId, showing where time was spent.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do metrics, traces and logs work together?

Short answer: Metrics detect and alert (aggregates), traces localize the problem (which hop), logs explain the specific case. traceId in logs and exemplars on metrics join them.

B2 · How do you add a custom health indicator, and should it affect readiness?

Short answer: Implement HealthIndicator and register it as a bean. Include it in readiness only if the pod genuinely cannot serve without that dependency; otherwise expose it as detail/degraded status.

B2 · What does the Observation API add over plain Micrometer?

Short answer: One instrumentation point produces both a metric and a span (and log context), with an explicit split between low-cardinality keys (tags) and high-cardinality keys (span attributes).

B2 · How is trace context propagated?

Short answer: W3C traceparent/tracestate headers on HTTP (added automatically by Boot-built clients) and headers on Kafka/Rabbit messages when observations are enabled.

B2 · Why keep uri as a template in http.server.requests?

Short answer: Otherwise every id becomes a new time series. Templates keep cardinality bounded and make aggregates meaningful.

B2 · How do you change a log level without redeploying?

Short answer: POST to /actuator/loggers/<logger> with the desired level (secured, Chapter 07).

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · What are SLIs, SLOs and error budgets, and how do you alert on them?

Short answer: SLI = measured quality (e.g. fast, non-5xx checkout fraction); SLO = target over a window; error budget = allowed failure. Alert on burn rate with multiple windows (fast burn pages, slow burn tickets) instead of on individual errors.

B3 · Head vs tail sampling?

Short answer: Head sampling decides at the start (cheap, may discard the trace you need); tail sampling decides in the collector after seeing the whole trace, so you can keep all errors and slow traces plus a small baseline.

B3 · How do you control metric cardinality in practice?

Short answer: Tag allow-lists in review, MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags, denying unused meters, URI templates asserted by tests, and periodic reviews of top series by name.

B3 · What's the difference between a Timer and a LongTaskTimer?

Short answer: A Timer records completed durations; a LongTaskTimer reports currently running tasks and their elapsed time — useful for jobs that run for minutes and would otherwise be invisible until they finish.

B3 · Why can a gauge report NaN?

Short answer: Micrometer holds a weak reference to the measured object; if nothing else references it, it's garbage collected and the gauge has nothing to read. Keep a strong reference in a field.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design observability for a 26-service platform.

Short answer: Platform library with common tags, cardinality guards, SLO histograms, tracing bridges and health conventions; OTLP to a central collector doing tail sampling and redaction; per-service dashboards from a template with deploy annotations; SLOs per critical journey with burn-rate alerts and runbooks; contract tests for metric names; quarterly cost/cardinality review.

B4 · An incident is called. What's your first two minutes?

Short answer: SLO dashboard (what's failing, how fast the budget is burning), deploy annotations (did something change), dependency panels (which client calls are erroring/slow), breaker and degradation counters, then a representative trace, then logs by traceId.

B4 · How do you decide what to alert on?

Short answer: Only on symptoms users feel (SLO burn, business-metric drops) and on conditions that will become user-visible soon (queue lag, outbox backlog, saturation). Everything else is a dashboard. Every alert must have an owner, a runbook and a tested response.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How does observability change engineering culture?

Short answer: It moves debate from opinion to evidence: SLOs align product and engineering on acceptable failure; error budgets make reliability work fundable; post-incident reviews start from data; and teams instrument as part of "done" rather than after the second outage.

B5 · Build or buy?

Short answer: Instrument with open standards (Micrometer/OpenTelemetry) so the backend is replaceable. Buy managed backends unless scale makes them uneconomic and you have the operational maturity to run them. Never couple application code to a vendor SDK.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Everything is green but revenue dropped 40%

A deploy broke the Android checkout button; requests never arrived, so error rate fell and latency improved. Fixes: alert on grocery.orders.placed deviating from the same hour last week (and per channel), add funnel metrics (cart → checkout → payment), and include business panels on every service dashboard.

Scenario · Prometheus falls over after a release

A new endpoint built URIs with String.format so order ids leaked into the uri tag — millions of series. Fixes: cardinality guard (maximumAllowableTags), a contract test asserting URI templates, and a review rule that no metric tag may come from request data without an allow-list.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Instrument the payment flow

Add: a timer grocery.payment.attempt tagged by gateway, method and outcome (SUCCESS/DECLINED/UNAVAILABLE); a counter for declines by reason (bounded set); a gauge for pending settlements; an @Observed span around the capture flow with orderRef as a high-cardinality key. Write tests asserting the meter names/tags and that orderRef is not a metric tag.

Solution PaymentMetrics.java
package in.grocery.payment.metrics;

import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Gauge;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry;
import io.micrometer.core.instrument.Timer;
import java.util.Set;
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
public class PaymentMetrics {

    private static final Set<String> KNOWN_REASONS =
            Set.of("insufficient_funds", "card_declined", "payment_failed", "timeout");   // (1)!

    private final MeterRegistry meters;
    private final AtomicLong pendingSettlements = new AtomicLong();

    public PaymentMetrics(MeterRegistry meters, SettlementRepository settlements) {
        this.meters = meters;
        Gauge.builder("grocery.settlements.pending", pendingSettlements, AtomicLong::get)
             .register(meters);                                                            // (2)!
    }

    public <T> T recordAttempt(String gateway, String method, java.util.function.Supplier<T> call) {
        Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(meters);
        String outcome = "SUCCESS";
        try {
            return call.get();
        } catch (PaymentDeclinedException declined) {
            outcome = "DECLINED";
            meters.counter("grocery.payment.declines", "reason", normalize(declined.reason())).increment();
            throw declined;
        } catch (DependencyException unavailable) {
            outcome = "UNAVAILABLE";
            throw unavailable;
        } finally {
            sample.stop(Timer.builder("grocery.payment.attempt")
                    .tag("gateway", gateway).tag("method", method).tag("outcome", outcome)
                    .publishPercentileHistogram()
                    .register(meters));
        }
    }

    private static String normalize(String reason) {
        return KNOWN_REASONS.contains(reason) ? reason : "other";                          // (3)!
    }

    public void updatePendingSettlements(long count) { pendingSettlements.set(count); }
}
  1. Bounded reason set — gateways invent new codes, and each one would otherwise be a new time series.
  2. Strong reference kept in a field (otherwise NaN).
  3. Everything unknown collapses to other; the exact reason still appears in logs and spans.
PaymentCaptureService.java (observed)
@Observed(name = "grocery.payment.capture", contextualName = "capture-payment")
public PaymentResult capture(String orderRef, String paymentId) {
    return observationRegistry.getCurrentObservation() == null
            ? doCapture(orderRef, paymentId)
            : withOrderRef(orderRef, () -> doCapture(orderRef, paymentId));     // high-cardinality on the span
}
PaymentMetricsTest.java
@Test
void recordsOutcomeTags() {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> metrics.recordAttempt("RAZORPAY", "UPI", () -> {
        throw new PaymentDeclinedException("insufficient_funds");
    })).isInstanceOf(PaymentDeclinedException.class);

    assertThat(registry.get("grocery.payment.attempt")
            .tags("gateway", "RAZORPAY", "method", "UPI", "outcome", "DECLINED").timer().count()).isEqualTo(1);
    assertThat(registry.get("grocery.payment.declines").tag("reason", "insufficient_funds").counter().count())
            .isEqualTo(1.0);
}

@Test
void unknownDeclineReasonIsCollapsed() {
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> metrics.recordAttempt("RAZORPAY", "CARD", () -> {
        throw new PaymentDeclinedException("bank_gateway_error_42");
    })).isInstanceOf(PaymentDeclinedException.class);

    assertThat(registry.get("grocery.payment.declines").tag("reason", "other").counter().count()).isEqualTo(1.0);
}

@Test
void orderRefIsNeverAMetricTag() {
    metrics.recordAttempt("RAZORPAY", "UPI", () -> "ok");
    assertThat(registry.get("grocery.payment.attempt").timer().getId().getTags())
            .noneMatch(tag -> tag.getKey().equals("orderRef"));                             // (1)!
}
  1. The cardinality rule, enforced by a test — cheap insurance against an innocent-looking future commit.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Metrics alert, traces localize, logs explain — joined by traceId.
  • Cardinality is the budget: low-cardinality keys for metrics, high-cardinality for spans; guards as a safety net.
  • The Observation API gives metrics and traces from one instrumentation point.
  • SLOs with multi-window burn-rate alerts replace noisy per-error alerting.
  • Business metrics catch failures that look technically healthy.
  • Liveness internal, readiness minimal, degradation visible but non-fatal.
  • Tail sampling and redaction in the collector; deploy annotations on dashboards.
  • Test your observability, and review its cost.

26 Resilience · 28 Integration & Contract Testing

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 15 built the fast half of the suite: unit tests and slices, thousands of them, running in two minutes. They prove that each piece behaves — and they cannot catch the failures that actually take the grocery platform down:

  • A Flyway migration that works on an empty schema and locks customer_order for four minutes on production-sized data.
  • An @Query that passes against H2 and returns the wrong rows on PostgreSQL.
  • A Kafka consumer whose deserializer rejects the producer's new field — discovered in production, not in either team's test suite.
  • A cart-service release that renames deliveryFee while the Flutter app still reads it (Chapter 20).
  • A dependency that goes slow rather than down, and a circuit breaker that was never exercised (Chapter 26).
  • An architecture rule ("no remote calls inside transactions") that everyone agreed to and nobody enforces.

Integration and contract tests cover exactly this space: real infrastructure, real protocols, and agreements between teams. This chapter builds them: Testcontainers at suite scale, WireMock for HTTP dependencies including latency and faults, consumer-driven contracts with Pact and Spring Cloud Contract (for HTTP and Kafka events), ArchUnit as executable architecture, Spring Modulith verification, mutation testing where correctness matters most, and the CI orchestration that keeps all of it under ten minutes.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — what an integration test is, Testcontainers basics B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — WireMock, containers per technology, ArchUnit B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — contract testing, event contracts, suite performance B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — platform test architecture, CI gates, can-i-deploy B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — testing strategy across teams

docs.title: 2.1 What each test level proves
docs.text: Level Proves Doesn't prove Unit Business rules Wiring, SQL, serialization Slice One layer's wiring and contract Cross-layer behaviour, real infrastructure Integration The service works against real PostgreSQL/Kafka/Redis That other services agree with you Contract Two services agree on a message/API shape End-to-end business flow End-to-end A journey across services works Anything at scale or under failure Performance/chaos Behaviour under load and failure Correctness

docs.title: 2.2 Testcontainers
docs.text:
Real dependencies in Docker, started from the test JVM.

Feature Use @ServiceConnection Auto-wires spring.datasource.*, spring.kafka.*, etc. from the container @DynamicPropertySource Manual property wiring for anything not covered @TestConfiguration container beans Containers shared via the context cache (Chapter 15) withReuse(true) + testcontainers.reuse.enable Container survives between local runs SpringApplication.from(...).with(...) Run the app locally against containers (bootTestRun) spring-boot-docker-compose Boot starts a compose.yaml for development

Never substitute H2 for PostgreSQL in tests that exercise SQL: different types, different locking, different error codes (Chapter 12).

docs.title: 2.3 Stubbing HTTP dependencies
docs.text: Tool Use MockRestServiceServer (@RestClientTest) Fast unit-level client tests (Chapter 15) WireMock Real HTTP over a port: latency, faults, stateful scenarios, recording Toxiproxy Network-level latency/partition between app and a real dependency (Chapter 26) Pact stubs / SCC stub runner Stubs generated from contracts — cannot drift from the provider

docs.title: 2.4 Consumer-driven contract testing
docs.text:
The problem: order-service (consumer) and pricing-service (provider) each have green suites, and still break each other.

flowchart LR
    C[Consumer test<br/>order-service] -->|records expectations| P[(Pact file / contract)]
    P --> B[(Contract broker)]
    B --> V[Provider verification<br/>pricing-service replays the contract]
    V -->|results| B
    B --> G{can-i-deploy?}
    G -- yes --> D[deploy]
    G -- no --> X[block release]
Approach Who writes the contract Notes Pact (consumer-driven) The consumer, in its own test Broker + can-i-deploy gate; strong for many consumers Spring Cloud Contract (producer-driven) The provider, as Groovy/YAML Generates provider tests and consumer stubs

Both work for HTTP and for messages (Kafka/Rabbit). Pick one per organization — running both is confusing.

docs.title: 2.5 Event contracts
docs.text:
Events are APIs (Chapter 23). Three complementary guards:

  1. Golden-file tests on the serialized payload — catches accidental renames in the producer.
  2. Schema registry compatibility (Avro/JSON Schema) — blocks incompatible schema registration.
  3. Consumer contract tests — each consumer states what it needs; the producer verifies it still provides it.

docs.title: 2.6 Architecture tests
docs.text:
ArchUnit turns "we agreed to do it this way" into a failing build:

Rule (from earlier chapters) Chapter Controller → Delegate → Service → Repository layering 01, 08 No field injection 02 @Transactional only in services, only on public methods 16 No remote calls inside transactions 16 No entities in controllers / no new ObjectMapper() 11, 13 @Transactional + @TransactionalEventListener must be REQUIRES_NEW 03

FreezingArchRule records existing violations so a rule can be introduced on a legacy codebase and only new violations fail.

docs.title: 2.7 Mutation testing
docs.text: Line coverage says code ran; mutation testing (PIT) says the tests would notice if it were wrong. It mutates bytecode (flip a condition, change a return) and reports mutations that no test killed. Expensive — run it nightly on the packages where correctness costs money (pricing, tax, payments, stock).

docs.title: 2.8 The cost model
docs.text: Test kind Typical duration Where it runs Unit < 5 ms Every build Slice ~100 ms Every build Integration (containers) 1–10 s Every build (separate task) Contract (consumer) ~100 ms Every build Contract (provider verification) seconds Every build + on broker webhooks End-to-end minutes Pipeline stage / staging Performance, mutation minutes–hours Nightly

docs.title: 3.1 Testcontainers lifecycle and the context cache
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[First test class starts] --> B[Spring context created]
    B --> C["@TestConfiguration container beans instantiated"]
    C --> D[Docker: pull if needed, start, wait for readiness strategy]
    D --> E[ServiceConnection contributes properties]
    E --> F[Beans wired to the container]
    F --> G[Tests run]
    G --> H[Next test class: same context key?]
    H -- yes --> I[Context and container reused]
    H -- no --> B
    I --> J[Suite ends → Ryuk container removes leftovers]

Two consequences that decide suite speed (Chapter 15): containers declared as beans in a shared configuration are started once for the whole suite; containers declared as static @Container fields in each class are started per class unless the class is also sharing a context.

docs.title: 3.2 WireMock in a Spring test
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant T as Test
    participant W as WireMock server (random port)
    participant A as Application under test
    participant C as RestClient

    T->>W: stubFor(get("/api/prices/MILK-1L").willReturn(json))
    T->>A: call endpoint / service method
    A->>C: HTTP GET http://localhost:{wiremockPort}/api/prices/MILK-1L
    C->>W: real HTTP request
    W-->>C: stubbed response (optionally delayed / faulted)
    T->>W: verify(getRequestedFor(...))

Because it's real HTTP, this exercises the client's timeouts, connection pool, retries, error translation and observability — none of which MockRestServiceServer touches.

docs.title: 3.3 Contract verification (Pact)
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant CT as Consumer test
    participant M as Pact mock provider
    participant B as Pact broker
    participant PT as Provider verification test
    participant P as Provider app (real, with test state)

    CT->>M: given("price exists for MILK-1L") + expected request/response
    M-->>CT: stubbed response → consumer code asserted
    CT->>B: publish pact (tagged with consumer version/branch)
    PT->>B: fetch pacts for pricing-service
    PT->>P: set up provider state, replay request
    P-->>PT: actual response compared to the contract
    PT->>B: publish verification result
    B-->>PT: can-i-deploy: yes/no

The contract is generated from the consumer's real expectations, so it can't drift from what the consumer actually parses.

docs.title: 4.1 A first integration test
4.2 Shared containers
4.3 Stubbing a dependency with WireMock
5.1 Level 2 — WireMock for the failure paths
5.2 Level 2 — Architecture tests as a shared ruleset
5.3 Level 3 — Consumer-driven contracts with Pact
docs.text:
Consumer side (order-service consuming pricing):

src/test/java/in/grocery/order/contract/PricingConsumerPactTest.java
package in.grocery.order.contract;

import au.com.dius.pact.consumer.MockServer;
import au.com.dius.pact.consumer.dsl.PactDslWithProvider;
import au.com.dius.pact.consumer.junit5.PactConsumerTestExt;
import au.com.dius.pact.consumer.junit5.PactTestFor;
import au.com.dius.pact.core.model.RequestResponsePact;
import au.com.dius.pact.core.model.annotations.Pact;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.junit.jupiter.api.extension.ExtendWith;

@ExtendWith(PactConsumerTestExt.class)
@PactTestFor(providerName = "pricing-service")
class PricingConsumerPactTest {

    @Pact(consumer = "order-service")
    RequestResponsePact priceExists(PactDslWithProvider builder) {
        return builder
                .given("a price exists for MILK-1L in 560102")                          // (1)!
                .uponReceiving("a price lookup")
                .path("/api/prices/MILK-1L")
                .query("pincode=560102")
                .method("GET")
                .willRespondWith()
                .status(200)
                .headers(java.util.Map.of("Content-Type", "application/json"))
                .body(new au.com.dius.pact.consumer.dsl.PactDslJsonBody()
                        .stringType("sku", "MILK-1L")                                    // (2)!
                        .decimalType("price", 66.00)
                        .decimalType("mrp", 68.00))
                .toPact();
    }

    @Test
    @PactTestFor(pactMethod = "priceExists")
    void clientParsesPriceResponse(MockServer mockServer) {
        PricingApi api = pricingClient(mockServer.getUrl());                             // real client, real parsing
        var price = api.price("MILK-1L", "560102");

        assertThat(price.price()).isEqualByComparingTo("66.00");                         // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Provider state: a precondition the provider must set up before replaying this interaction.
  2. Type matchers, not exact values — the contract says "a string called sku", not "exactly MILK-1L", so the provider isn't pinned to test data.
  3. The assertion runs our real client code, so the contract captures what we actually parse.

Provider side (pricing-service verifying):

src/test/java/in/grocery/pricing/contract/PricingProviderPactTest.java
@Provider("pricing-service")
@PactBroker(url = "${PACT_BROKER_URL}", authentication = @PactBrokerAuth(token = "${PACT_BROKER_TOKEN}"))
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT)
@Import(ContainersConfig.class)
class PricingProviderPactTest {

    @LocalServerPort int port;
    @Autowired PriceRepository prices;

    @BeforeEach
    void target(PactVerificationContext context) {
        context.setTarget(new HttpTestTarget("localhost", port));
    }

    @TestTemplate
    @ExtendWith(PactVerificationInvocationContextProvider.class)
    void verifyContracts(PactVerificationContext context) {
        context.verifyInteraction();                                                     // (1)!
    }

    @State("a price exists for MILK-1L in 560102")
    void priceExists() {
        prices.upsert("MILK-1L", "BLR", new BigDecimal("66.00"), new BigDecimal("68.00"));  // (2)!
    }
}
  1. Replays every consumer's pact against the real running provider and publishes results to the broker.
  2. Provider states are small, explicit fixtures — the contract's only coupling to data.

The gate (Chapter 20's breaking-change protection, for services):

Terminal
pact-broker can-i-deploy \
  --pacticipant pricing-service --version "$GIT_SHA" \
  --to-environment production                                                             # (1)!
  1. Fails the pipeline if any consumer's contract would break — the release is blocked before deployment, not after an incident.

6.1 The platform testing architecture
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph "Every build (< 10 min)"
        A[unit + slice tests] --> B[architecture tests]
        B --> C[consumer contract tests<br/>publish pacts]
        C --> D[integration tests<br/>shared containers]
        D --> E[provider verification<br/>+ can-i-deploy]
    end
    subgraph Nightly
        F[mutation tests on critical packages]
        G[performance tests k6/Gatling]
        H[chaos tests Toxiproxy]
        I[flaky detection: suite × 5]
    end
    subgraph "Pre-release / staging"
        J[end-to-end journey tests]
        K[migration rehearsal on prod-sized snapshot]
    end

Shared building blocks live in a grocery-test-support library: ContainersConfig, WireMock stub factories per dependency, TestOrders/TestProducts builders (Chapter 15), UniqueIds, ArchUnit rules and Pact helpers. New services get the whole setup by adding one dependency.

docs.title: 6.2 Stub libraries: the dependency's own stubs
6.3 Keeping the suite fast
docs.text:
Technique Effect Shared containers via context cache (Chapter 15) Minutes → seconds per class withReuse(true) locally No container startup between runs Parallel test classes (junit.jupiter.execution.parallel.mode.classes.default=concurrent) 2–4× wall clock Unique test data instead of truncation Enables parallelism Separate test and integrationTest tasks run concurrently in CI Fast feedback first Docker layer caching + image pre-pull in CI Removes pull time Fail fast on the fast suite Don't spend 8 minutes to learn a unit test broke .github/workflows/ci.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  fast:
    steps:
      - run: ./gradlew test --configuration-cache            # (1)!
  integration:
    needs: fast
    services: {}
    steps:
      - run: docker pull postgres:17-alpine & docker pull apache/kafka:3.9.0 & wait   # (2)!
      - run: ./gradlew integrationTest
      - run: ./gradlew pactPublish
      - run: ./scripts/can-i-deploy.sh                       # (3)!
  1. Unit + slice + architecture + consumer contracts — under two minutes.
  2. Pre-pull images in parallel while the build starts.
  3. The deployment gate: contracts verified against what's currently in production.

docs.title: 6.4 Migration rehearsal
6.5 End-to-end journeys (few, high-value)
6.6 Flaky test management
docs.text:
.github/workflows/nightly.yml (flake detection)
      - name: Run suite five times
        run: |
          for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
            ./gradlew test integrationTest --rerun-tasks || true
            cp -r build/test-results "results-$i"
          done
      - run: ./scripts/flaky-report.sh results-*        # (1)!
  1. Any test with mixed outcomes is reported, tagged @Tag("flaky"), excluded from the gate, and ticketed with an owner and a due date (Chapter 15's policy). A flaky rate above 1% stops feature work.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Testcontainers support spring-boot-testcontainers, @ServiceConnection Same (module names — verify) Test slices boot.test.autoconfigure.* Technology test modules (verify packages) @MockBean Deprecated Removed → @MockitoBean (Chapter 15) Docker Compose support spring-boot-docker-compose Same (verify) Pact JVM 4.6.x Verify JUnit 5/6 compatibility Spring Cloud Contract 4.x train Train aligned with Boot 4 (verify) ArchUnit 1.x Same PIT 1.15+ Verify JUnit platform plugin version

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Update test slice imports and starters (the largest mechanical change).
  • Verify Pact/Spring Cloud Contract versions support your JUnit version before upgrading Boot.
  • Re-run contract verification against both old and new service versions during the rollout.
  • Re-check container images and @ServiceConnection coverage for your dependencies.
  • Re-baseline suite timings; context-cache behaviour can shift with module changes.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Real infrastructure in integration tests — Testcontainers, never H2 for SQL behaviour.
  2. Share containers and contexts; unique data instead of truncation so classes can run in parallel.
  3. WireMock for dependency behaviour, including latency, faults and stateful scenarios.
  4. Contract tests between every producer/consumer pair, with a can-i-deploy gate.
  5. Events are contracts too — golden files, schema compatibility, consumer contracts.
  6. ArchUnit for agreed rules, frozen where legacy code exists.
  7. Mutation testing nightly on money-critical packages.
  8. Few, owned end-to-end journeys, reused as synthetic monitors.
  9. Rehearse migrations on production-sized data with time and lock budgets.
  10. Track and fix flakiness as a first-class defect.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ H2 (or an in-memory broker) standing in for the real thing — green tests, red production.

❌ A container per test class — a ten-minute suite and a bored team.

❌ Truncating tables between tests — forces serial execution and hides ordering bugs.

❌ Hand-written stubs that drift from the provider's real responses.

❌ End-to-end tests as the main safety net — slow, flaky, and they fail without telling you why.

❌ Contract tests that pin exact values instead of types — every provider test-data change breaks the consumer's build.

❌ Chasing coverage percentages instead of testing the paths that cost money.

❌ Quarantining flaky tests and never fixing them.

❌ Running everything on every commit until developers start skipping CI.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Suite slow, many "Starting Application" lines Context/container per class Shared @TestConfiguration, consistent annotations (Chapter 15) Containers left running Ryuk disabled or JVM killed Re-enable Ryuk; docker ps cleanup in CI Tests pass locally, fail in CI Reuse hiding state, different images, timezone/locale Disable reuse in CI, pin image tags, set TZ/locale WireMock stub never matched URL/query/header mismatch server.findAllUnmatchedRequests(), near-miss diagnostics Pact verification fails on data Contract pinned exact values Use type matchers and provider states can-i-deploy blocks a safe release Missing verification results for the new version Publish pacts and results with the correct version/branch Flaky async assertions Thread.sleep, short timeouts Awaitility with generous max and fast polling ArchUnit rule unmaintainable on legacy All-or-nothing rule FreezingArchRule Mutation run takes hours Whole codebase targeted Target critical packages; nightly only

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Integration tests run against real PostgreSQL/Kafka/Redis
  • Shared container configuration; suite runs classes in parallel
  • WireMock coverage for each dependency's success, slow, fault and 4xx paths
  • Consumer contracts published; provider verification + can-i-deploy gate
  • Event payload golden files and schema compatibility checks
  • ArchUnit ruleset shared across services
  • Nightly mutation and performance runs on critical paths
  • Migration rehearsal on a production-sized snapshot before risky releases
  • Flaky detection job and quarantine policy with owners

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is an integration test in a Spring Boot service?

Short answer: A test that starts the application (or a large part of it) and exercises it against real infrastructure — database, broker, HTTP — instead of mocks.

B1 · Why use Testcontainers instead of H2?

Short answer: H2 differs from PostgreSQL in SQL dialect, types, locking and error codes, so tests can pass while production fails. Testcontainers runs the real database in Docker.

B1 · What does @ServiceConnection do?

Short answer: Wires Spring Boot's connection properties (datasource, Kafka, Redis) to a Testcontainers container automatically — no manual property plumbing.

B1 · What is WireMock for?

Short answer: Stubbing an HTTP dependency with a real server, so the client's timeouts, retries and error handling are exercised — including delays and network faults.

B1 · What is a contract test?

Short answer: A test that verifies two services agree on the shape of a request/response or message, so a change in one can't silently break the other.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you keep an integration suite fast?

Short answer: Share containers and Spring contexts, run test classes in parallel, use unique data instead of cleanup, split fast and slow suites, cache/pre-pull images, and enable container reuse locally.

B2 · How do you test that a client times out correctly?

Short answer: WireMock with a fixed delay (or Toxiproxy latency), then assert both the resulting error mapping and that the call returned within the expected budget.

B2 · Pact vs Spring Cloud Contract?

Short answer: Pact is consumer-driven with a broker and can-i-deploy gating, good for many/polyglot consumers. Spring Cloud Contract is producer-driven and generates provider tests plus consumer stubs. Choose one per organization.

B2 · How do you test Kafka integration?

Short answer: Testcontainers with a real broker, publish and assert with Awaitility, plus message contract tests and golden-file payload tests for the event shape.

B2 · What does ArchUnit add over code review?

Short answer: Agreed rules become executable and continuous — layering, injection style, transaction placement — so violations fail the build instead of depending on a reviewer noticing.

B2 · Why use type matchers in contracts?

Short answer: Pinning exact values couples the contract to the provider's test data; type matchers assert the shape (string, number, array of at least one) which is what the consumer actually depends on.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does consumer-driven contract testing prevent breaking changes?

Short answer: Consumers record their real expectations as pacts; the provider's build replays every consumer's pact against the running provider and publishes results; the can-i-deploy gate blocks a provider release that would break any consumer currently in production.

B3 · How do contract tests and schema registries complement each other for events?

Short answer: The registry enforces structural compatibility of the schema; contract tests capture what consumers actually read and how they behave. A change can be schema-compatible and still break a consumer's semantics.

B3 · How do you introduce architecture rules to a legacy codebase?

Short answer: FreezingArchRule snapshots existing violations so only new ones fail, then burn down the frozen list over time.

B3 · What does mutation testing tell you that coverage doesn't?

Short answer: Whether tests would detect a wrong implementation. High coverage with weak assertions leaves mutants alive — typically at boundaries (>= vs >) and in error branches.

B3 · Why rehearse migrations against production-sized data?

Short answer: Timing and locking behaviour depend on data volume; an ALTER that's instant on an empty table can hold ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for minutes on 40M rows (Chapter 14). The rehearsal converts a production surprise into a pipeline failure.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the test strategy for a 26-service platform.

Short answer: Fast unit/slice tests per service; integration tests on real infrastructure with shared containers; contract tests between every pair with broker gating; event golden files and schema checks; shared ArchUnit rules and test-support library; nightly mutation, performance, chaos and flake detection; a handful of owned end-to-end journeys reused as synthetic monitors; migration rehearsals before risky releases.

B4 · CI takes 40 minutes and people bypass it. What do you do?

Short answer: Measure per-task and per-class time; split fast/slow jobs running in parallel; fix context/container sharing; parallelize classes; cache dependencies and images; move mutation/performance to nightly; delete redundant end-to-end tests; set and defend a budget (fast < 2 min, full < 10 min).

B4 · How do you prevent contract testing from becoming bureaucracy?

Short answer: Contracts generated from real consumer code (not hand-written documents), automated publishing and verification in CI, one broker as the source of truth, can-i-deploy as the only manual-feeling step, and clear ownership so a failing verification has an obvious owner.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What's the right role for end-to-end tests?

Short answer: Small in number, for critical business journeys, owned centrally, and reused as production synthetic monitors. They validate integration of the whole system; contract and integration tests do the bulk of the work because they're faster, more precise and less flaky.

B5 · How do you know your test strategy is working?

Short answer: Escaped-defect rate and change-failure rate trending down, mean time to detect falling, flake rate < 1%, CI duration stable, and post-incident reviews rarely concluding "no test could have caught this".

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A pricing release broke checkout in three services

Pricing changed price from a JSON number to a string. Every service's own suite was green because all used hand-written stubs. Fixes: consumer-driven contracts with a broker, can-i-deploy gating, provider-published stub libraries, and the JSON golden-file tests from Chapter 11.

Scenario · Integration suite is green but production fails on every deploy night

Tests ran against an empty database; the release included a migration that locked a large table, and connection pools were sized differently in CI. Fixes: migration rehearsal on a production-sized snapshot with time and lock budgets, plus a staging load test using production-like configuration.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Contract-protect the inventory reservation flow

order-service calls POST /api/reservations on inventory-service and consumes StockChanged events from it. Write (1) a consumer Pact for the HTTP call including a 409 out-of-stock case, (2) a message pact for StockChanged, (3) the provider verification skeleton with provider states, and (4) an integration test using WireMock that proves the 409 maps to the platform error contract.

Solution InventoryConsumerPactTest.java (HTTP, both cases)
@Pact(consumer = "order-service")
RequestResponsePact reservationSucceeds(PactDslWithProvider builder) {
    return builder.given("stock is available for MILK-1L at BLR-HSR")
            .uponReceiving("a reservation request")
            .path("/api/reservations").method("POST")
            .body(new PactDslJsonBody()
                    .stringType("orderRef", "ORD-1")
                    .stringType("sku", "MILK-1L")
                    .integerType("quantity", 2)
                    .stringType("hub", "BLR-HSR"))
            .willRespondWith().status(201)
            .body(new PactDslJsonBody().stringType("reservationId", "RSV-1"))
            .toPact();
}

@Pact(consumer = "order-service")
RequestResponsePact reservationOutOfStock(PactDslWithProvider builder) {
    return builder.given("no stock for MILK-1L at BLR-HSR")
            .uponReceiving("a reservation request that cannot be fulfilled")
            .path("/api/reservations").method("POST")
            .body(new PactDslJsonBody().stringType("sku", "MILK-1L").integerType("quantity", 2))
            .willRespondWith().status(409)
            .headers(Map.of("Content-Type", "application/problem+json"))
            .body(new PactDslJsonBody()
                    .stringValue("code", "OUT_OF_STOCK")                       // (1)!
                    .integerType("availableQuantity", 0))
            .toPact();
}
  1. The error contract is part of the agreement (Chapter 10) — consumers switch on code, so it's pinned exactly while other fields use type matchers.
StockChangedConsumerPactTest.java (message)
@Pact(consumer = "order-service")
MessagePact stockChanged(MessagePactBuilder builder) {
    return builder.expectsToReceive("a StockChanged event")
            .withContent(new PactDslJsonBody()
                    .stringType("eventId")
                    .stringType("sku", "MILK-1L")
                    .stringType("hub", "BLR-HSR")
                    .integerType("available", 12))
            .toPact();
}
InventoryProviderPactTest.java (provider states)
@State("stock is available for MILK-1L at BLR-HSR")
void stockAvailable() { stock.upsert("BLR-HSR", "MILK-1L", 50); }

@State("no stock for MILK-1L at BLR-HSR")
void noStock() { stock.upsert("BLR-HSR", "MILK-1L", 0); }
OutOfStockIntegrationTest.java (WireMock)
@Test
void outOfStockFromInventoryBecomes409ForTheCustomer() {
    inventoryWireMock.stubFor(post(urlPathEqualTo("/api/reservations"))
            .willReturn(aResponse().withStatus(409)
                    .withHeader("Content-Type", "application/problem+json")
                    .withBody("""
                            {"type":"https://errors.grocery.in/out-of-stock","code":"OUT_OF_STOCK",
                             "status":409,"availableQuantity":0}
                            """)));

    var response = rest.postForEntity("/api/v1/orders", placeOrderRequest(), Map.class);

    assertThat(response.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CONFLICT);
    assertThat(response.getBody())
            .containsEntry("code", "OUT_OF_STOCK")                             // (1)!
            .containsKey("traceId");
}
  1. Proves the whole chain: inventory's error → our client's translation (Chapter 19) → our error contract (Chapter 10) → the customer's app.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Integration tests use real infrastructure; share containers and contexts or the suite becomes unusable.
  • WireMock tests the failure modes that matter — latency, faults, stateful retries — not just happy JSON.
  • Contract tests with a broker and can-i-deploy stop cross-service breakage before deployment.
  • Events are contracts: golden files + schema compatibility + consumer contracts.
  • ArchUnit makes agreed rules executable; freeze to adopt them on legacy code.
  • Mutation testing finds weak assertions where correctness costs money.
  • Rehearse migrations on production-sized data with time and lock budgets.
  • Few, owned end-to-end journeys, reused as synthetic monitors.
