docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
The code is written, tested and observable. Now it has to become an image that starts fast, is small enough to pull quickly, runs as a non-root user with a current JRE, carries a bill of materials, and can be rolled back by digest at 9 p.m. during a sale.

The decisions here have unglamorous but expensive consequences:

  • A naively built image copies the fat JAR as one layer: every deploy pushes and pulls 300 MB instead of 2 MB.
  • A 40-second startup times out the readiness probe during a scale-up, so autoscaling makes the incident worse.
  • A container without MaxRAMPercentage sizing sees the host's memory, sizes a 24 GB heap, and gets OOM-killed by Kubernetes at 2 GB.
  • An image built six months ago ships a JRE with three CVEs, and nobody knows which services are affected because there's no SBOM.
  • latest tags make "roll back to what was running yesterday" an archaeology exercise.

This chapter covers packaging and deployment mechanics: layered executable JARs, Dockerfiles that use them properly, Cloud Native Buildpacks, JVM tuning for containers, CDS and the JDK AOT cache for fast startup, Spring AOT and GraalVM native images (with an honest cost/benefit), SBOMs, scanning and signing, and the image-promotion pipeline that turns all of it into a safe release.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — executable JAR, first Dockerfile, buildpacks B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — layers, JVM container settings, image hygiene B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — CDS/AOT cache, startup profiling, native images B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — image pipeline, supply chain, base-image policy B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — platform strategy, native vs JVM economics

docs.title: 2.1 The artifacts
docs.text: Artifact What it is Executable JAR (bootJar) Your classes + dependencies + a launcher; java -jar app.jar Layered JAR The same JAR with a layers.idx grouping content by change frequency Container image OS + JRE + your application, addressable by tag and digest CDS archive / AOT cache Pre-parsed class data (and, with AOT, pre-linked classes) that speeds startup Native image An ahead-of-time compiled binary with no JVM startup at all SBOM The inventory of what's inside (Chapter 01)

docs.title: 2.2 Layers
docs.text:
Example
BOOT-INF/layers.idx
- "dependencies"            ← changes rarely (weeks)
- "spring-boot-loader"      ← changes on Boot upgrades
- "snapshot-dependencies"   ← changes often if you use snapshots
- "application"             ← changes every commit (your code, ~2 MB)

Extracting these into separate Docker layers means a code-only deploy pushes and pulls megabytes, not hundreds of them. Boot 3.3+ provides java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers (older versions used -Djarmode=layertools) — verify for your version.

docs.title: 2.3 Two ways to build an image
docs.text:
Dockerfile Cloud Native Buildpacks (bootBuildImage) Control Total Opinionated, configured by env vars Maintenance You patch base images rebase swaps the OS layer without rebuilding Extras You add them SBOM, memory calculator, CDS/AOT support, non-root by default Learning curve Familiar New vocabulary (builder, buildpack, rebase) Typical choice Platforms with strict base-image policy Teams wanting batteries included

Both are legitimate. What matters is that the result is small, layered, non-root, reproducible and scanned.

docs.title: 2.4 JVM settings that matter in containers
docs.text:
Setting Why -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 Heap sized from the container limit, leaving room for metaspace, threads, direct buffers -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError Die fast so Kubernetes restarts, instead of limping -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps Post-mortem evidence GC choice G1 default; SerialGC for tiny containers; Generational ZGC for large heaps/low pause -XX:ActiveProcessorCount Only if CPU limits confuse sizing; the JVM honours cgroup limits by default JFR (-XX:StartFlightRecording) Always-on low-overhead profiling for incidents

Non-heap memory (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, native) is why 75% is a starting point, not a rule — measure RSS.

docs.title: 2.5 Startup optimizations, in order of effort
docs.text: Technique Typical gain Cost Trim dependencies / auto-configurations 5–20% Free (and good hygiene) CDS archive 20–40% A training run at build time JDK AOT cache (Leyden, JDK 24+) More than CDS A training run; newer JDK Spring AOT on the JVM (spring.aot.enabled) 10–20% AOT-processed build Lazy initialization Varies Failures move to first request GraalVM native image ~10× (ms instead of seconds) Long builds, reflection config, no JIT peak, tooling limits

docs.title: 2.6 When native images pay
docs.text:
Native is attractive Native is a poor trade Serverless / scale-to-zero Long-running services with steady load Very high pod density (memory per pod matters) CPU-heavy workloads (JIT wins at peak) Short-lived CLI jobs Heavy reflection/dynamic proxies, agents Fast scale-up during spikes Teams without capacity for build/debug complexity

For the grocery platform: the gateway and a few stateless, spiky services are candidates; order/payment/inventory stay on the JVM with CDS.

docs.title: 2.7 Supply chain
docs.text: Step Tool SBOM generation CycloneDX Gradle plugin (Chapter 01); buildpacks also emit one Vulnerability scanning Trivy / Grype in CI and in the registry Signing & attestation cosign (keyless), SLSA provenance Base image policy One approved, regularly patched base; automated rebuild/rebase Immutable references Deploy by digest, not tag

docs.title: 3.1 Layered image build
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[bootJar with layers.idx] --> B["extract --layers"]
    B --> C[dependencies/]
    B --> D[spring-boot-loader/]
    B --> E[snapshot-dependencies/]
    B --> F[application/]
    C & D & E & F --> G[Docker COPY in that order]
    G --> H[Image: rarely-changing layers cached,<br/>only application/ layer rebuilt per commit]

Docker caches layers by content hash; ordering from least- to most-frequently-changing maximizes cache hits on build, push and pull.

docs.title: 3.2 Startup work and where CDS/AOT help
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[JVM start] --> B[Class loading & verification<br/>~10k classes]
    B --> C[Spring: scan, parse annotations,<br/>evaluate conditions, create beans]
    C --> D[Connection pools, Hibernate metamodel,<br/>Kafka clients]
    D --> E[Web server binds, runners, ready]
    B -. CDS/AOT cache .-> B2[pre-parsed / pre-linked classes]
    C -. Spring AOT .-> C2[generated bean definitions:<br/>no scanning or condition evaluation]

CDS and the AOT cache attack class loading; Spring AOT attacks context creation; native image eliminates both by doing everything at build time.

docs.title: 3.3 Native image: build-time closed world
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Spring AOT processing] --> B[Generated code + reachability hints]
    B --> C[GraalVM native-image analysis]
    C --> D{reachable?}
    D -- yes --> E[included in the binary]
    D -- no --> F[removed]
    C --> G[reflection / resources / proxies<br/>need explicit hints]
    E --> H[Native executable: no JIT, no class loading at runtime]

Anything discovered only at runtime (reflection on a class name from configuration, a dynamic proxy, a resource read by pattern) must be declared through reachability metadata or RuntimeHints — this is where native migrations spend their time.

docs.title: 4.1 The executable JAR
docs.text:
Terminal
./gradlew bootJar
ls -lh build/libs/order-service.jar        # one file, ~60 MB
java -jar build/libs/order-service.jar
build.gradle.kts (from Chapter 01's conventions)
tasks.named<BootJar>("bootJar") {
    archiveFileName = "${project.name}.jar"     // stable name for Dockerfiles
}
tasks.named<Jar>("jar") { enabled = false }     // no confusing -plain jar

docs.title: 4.2 A first Dockerfile — and why it's wrong
docs.text:
Dockerfile (naive)
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
COPY build/libs/order-service.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]

Problems: one 60 MB layer changes on every commit; runs as root; a full JDK-sized base; no memory settings; no health-friendly signal handling if you use the shell form.

docs.title: 4.3 A layered Dockerfile
docs.text:
Dockerfile
# ---- extract layers ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY build/libs/order-service.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers --destination extracted    # (1)!

# ---- runtime ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 grocery                                          # (2)!
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./                       # (3)!
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/application/ ./
USER 10001
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
    -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps"                      # (4)!
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]                                            # (5)!
  1. Boot 3.3+ jarmode=tools; older versions use -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract. Verify for your Boot version.
  2. Non-root with a fixed UID (matches Kubernetes runAsUser).
  3. Layer order = change frequency: dependencies first, your code last.
  4. JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS is picked up without changing the entrypoint — handy for per-environment overrides.
  5. Exec form so the JVM is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM directly (graceful shutdown, Chapter 03).
Terminal
docker build -t grocery/order-service:$(git rev-parse --short HEAD) .
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --memory=1g grocery/order-service:abc1234

Rebuild after a code change: only the application/ layer is rewritten — a few megabytes.

docs.title: 4.4 Buildpacks: no Dockerfile at all
5.1 Level 2 — Container-aware JVM settings
docs.text:
k8s/order-service-deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  containers:
    - name: order-service
      image: registry.grocery.in/grocery/order-service@sha256:9f2a...      # (1)!
      resources:
        requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "768Mi" }
        limits:   { memory: "1Gi" }                                        # (2)!
      env:
        - name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
          value: >-
            -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
            -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
            -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
            -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxsize=200M,maxage=1h,dumponexit=true,filename=/dumps/app.jfr
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 10001
        readOnlyRootFilesystem: true                                        # (3)!
        allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
        capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] }
      volumeMounts:
        - { name: dumps, mountPath: /dumps }
        - { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }                                    # (4)!
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40                                     # (5)!
  1. Digest, not tag — the deployed bits are unambiguous and rollback is exact.
  2. No CPU limit (only a request) is a common choice to avoid throttling; memory limit is required because the JVM sizes itself from it.
  3. Read-only root filesystem with explicit writable mounts — a cheap, large security win.
  4. The JVM writes to /tmp (JFR, temp files); mount an emptyDir.
  5. Longer than spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (Chapters 03, 25).

Sizing from the wrong number

Without a memory limit (or with -Xmx hardcoded from a laptop), the JVM sizes its heap from the node's memory and gets OOM-killed at the container limit. MaxRAMPercentage + a container limit is the correct pairing; leave ~25–30% for non-heap.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — Image hygiene
docs.text:
Dockerfile (hardened additions)
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre AS builder
# ... extraction as before ...

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/grocery/order-service" \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision="${GIT_SHA}" \
      org.opencontainers.image.version="${APP_VERSION}"                    # (1)!
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 grocery && mkdir /dumps && chown 10001 /dumps
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /build/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /build/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /build/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /build/extracted/application/ ./
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080 9090
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  1. OCI labels link the image back to its commit — the first thing you want during an incident.
.dockerignore
*
!build/libs/*.jar

Keeping the build context tiny makes builds faster and stops secrets (.env, .git) from leaking into layers.

Base image Trade-off eclipse-temurin:25-jre Familiar, glibc, good tooling -alpine Small, musl libc — verify library compatibility Distroless / -jre-ubi-minimal Minimal attack surface; no shell (harder debugging)

docs.title: 5.3 Level 3 — CDS: measurable startup gains
docs.text:
Dockerfile with CDS
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY build/libs/order-service.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --destination extracted           # (1)!

WORKDIR /build/extracted
RUN java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=/build/app.jsa \
         -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh \
         -jar app.jar                                                            # (2)!

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /build/extracted/ ./
COPY --from=builder /build/app.jsa /app/app.jsa
USER 10001
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa", "-jar", "app.jar"]     # (3)!
  1. The non-layered extraction (extract without --layers) produces the exploded application layout that CDS training needs.
  2. Training run: starts the context and exits at refresh (spring.context.exit=onRefresh), recording the classes loaded. It must run with the same classpath as production.
  3. Production uses the archive. Expect roughly 20–40% faster startup with no behaviour change.

Verify

CDS support in Spring Boot (the spring.context.exit property, jarmode=tools and the recommended layout) arrived in Boot 3.3 and has evolved; JDK 24+ adds the AOT cache (-XX:AOTMode=record/create, -XX:AOTCache=app.aot) which supersedes plain CDS with bigger gains. Check the Boot reference and your JDK's documentation, and measure rather than assuming.

Measuring
for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do
  docker run --rm grocery/order-service:cds 2>&1 | grep "Started OrderApplication"
done
# Started OrderApplication in 1.42 seconds (vs 2.31 without CDS)

Startup time is a budget (Chapter 05): track it per service in CI and fail the build if it regresses by more than, say, 30%.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Spring AOT on the JVM
docs.text:
Terminal
./gradlew bootJar -Pspring.aot.enabled=true      # or the processAot task, depending on setup

AOT processing generates bean definitions at build time, so the runtime skips classpath scanning and condition evaluation. It also freezes the context: profile-dependent bean graphs and runtime @Conditional decisions are resolved at build time, so an AOT-processed application must be built per profile combination if those differ. Confirm behaviour for your version before enabling it broadly.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — GraalVM native image
6.1 The image pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[CI: build + test] --> B[bootJar]
    B --> C[image build<br/>Dockerfile or buildpacks]
    C --> D[SBOM: CycloneDX]
    D --> E[Scan: Trivy/Grype<br/>fail on HIGH/CRITICAL fixable]
    E --> F[Sign: cosign keyless<br/>+ SLSA provenance]
    F --> G[Push to registry<br/>tag: git sha + semver]
    G --> H[Deploy to staging by digest]
    H --> I[Smoke + contract gate<br/>can-i-deploy]
    I --> J[Promote same digest to prod]
    J --> K[Record digest in release notes]

The essential property: the same digest flows from staging to production. Rebuilding for production means deploying something that was never tested.

.github/workflows/image.yml (excerpt)
      - name: Build image
        run: ./gradlew bootBuildImage --imageName=$REGISTRY/$SERVICE:$GIT_SHA

      - name: Generate SBOM
        run: ./gradlew cyclonedxBom

      - name: Scan
        run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 \
                 $REGISTRY/$SERVICE:$GIT_SHA                                   # (1)!

      - name: Sign
        run: cosign sign --yes $REGISTRY/$SERVICE@$DIGEST                      # (2)!

      - name: Attach SBOM attestation
        run: cosign attest --yes --predicate build/reports/bom.json --type cyclonedx \
                 $REGISTRY/$SERVICE@$DIGEST
  1. --ignore-unfixed keeps the gate actionable: fail only on vulnerabilities with a fix available; track the rest.
  2. Keyless signing binds the image to the workflow identity; the cluster's admission policy can require it.

docs.title: 6.2 Base image policy
docs.text:
Rule Detail One approved base per runtime eclipse-temurin:25-jre (plus a distroless variant for hardened workloads) Rebuild weekly Automated pipeline rebuilds all service images against the patched base Buildpack estate uses rebase Swaps the OS layer without a full rebuild — minutes for 26 services Fail builds on stale bases Reject images whose base is older than 30 days Track per-service Dashboard: base age, critical CVEs, image size, startup time Rebase with buildpacks
pack rebase registry.grocery.in/grocery/order-service:1.42.0 --publish      # (1)!
  1. Only the run-image layers change; application layers are untouched, so the app is byte-identical. This is buildpacks' strongest operational argument.

docs.title: 6.3 Startup and size budgets
6.4 Deployment mechanics
docs.text:
k8s/order-service-deployment.yaml (rollout)
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 2
      maxUnavailable: 0                                                      # (1)!
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt: "{{ .Values.configHash }}"        # (2)!
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 30                                           # (3)!
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }                      # (4)!
  1. Never fewer than the current replicas during a rollout — capacity is preserved during a sale.
  2. A hash of the ConfigMap/Secret forces a rollout when configuration changes (Chapter 06: config changes are deployments).
  3. Liveness must not fire during slow startup; alternatively use a startupProbe.
  4. A brief pause so the load balancer stops sending new requests before the container begins draining (Chapters 03, 30).

Rollback is then trivial and exact:

Terminal
kubectl set image deployment/order-service order-service=$REGISTRY/order-service@sha256:previous-digest

docs.title: 6.5 Native image in production — a bounded experiment
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Pick one stateless, spiky service] --> B["Add nativeTest to CI"]
    B --> C[Build both JVM and native images]
    C --> D[Deploy native to 20% of pods]
    D --> E[Compare: startup, RSS, p99, error rate, cost]
    E --> F{worth it?}
    F -- yes --> G["Expand; keep JVM build as fallback"]
    F -- no --> H[Stay on JVM + CDS/AOT cache]

Rules for the experiment: keep the JVM image building (so rollback is a deploy, not a rewrite), run nativeTest on every commit, and decide with numbers (pod density, scale-up latency, cost per request) rather than enthusiasm.

docs.title: 6.6 Deployment checklist per release
docs.text: Check Automated? Same digest promoted from staging ✅ pipeline Contracts verified (can-i-deploy) ✅ (Chapter 28) Migrations rehearsed and backward compatible ✅ (Chapter 14) Startup and size budgets respected ✅ nightly Image scanned and signed; SBOM attached ✅ Config changes reviewed via GitOps ✅ (Chapter 06) Rollout strategy preserves capacity ✅ manifest review Rollback digest recorded in release notes ✅ Dashboards annotated with the deploy ✅ (Chapter 27)

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Layer extraction jarmode=tools (3.3+); layertools deprecated jarmode=tools (verify) CDS support spring.context.exit=onRefresh, documented CDS workflow (3.3+) Same + JDK AOT cache integration (verify) Spring AOT processAot, spring.aot.enabled Same GraalVM support Mature (3.x) Mature; hint APIs stable (verify) Buildpacks bootBuildImage with Paketo Same; new env vars for AOT/CDS (verify) Java baseline 17 (25 recommended here) 17 (25 recommended) SBOM CycloneDX plugin; /actuator/sbom (3.3+) Same

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Replace layertools with jarmode=tools in Dockerfiles.
  • Re-measure startup and image size after the upgrade; adjust budgets.
  • Re-generate CDS archives/AOT caches (they are JDK- and classpath-specific — an upgrade invalidates them).
  • Re-run nativeTest for native services; hints may need updates for Jackson 3 and moved packages.
  • Verify buildpack builder version supports your JDK.
  • Re-scan images; a new base may introduce or fix CVEs.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Layered images with change-frequency ordering; small build context.
  2. Non-root, read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, fixed UID.
  3. Size the JVM from the container limit (MaxRAMPercentage), with OOM exit and heap dumps.
  4. Deploy by digest; promote the same artifact from staging to production.
  5. SBOM + scan + sign every image; enforce at admission.
  6. One approved base image, rebuilt/rebased weekly, with an age gate.
  7. CDS or the JDK AOT cache for startup; budget and track startup time.
  8. Native images only where the numbers justify them, with nativeTest in CI and a JVM fallback.
  9. Rollouts preserve capacity (maxUnavailable: 0) and honour graceful shutdown.
  10. Record the rollback digest with every release.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ One-layer images — slow pushes/pulls, no cache reuse.

❌ Running as root, or writable root filesystems.

❌ latest tags, or deploying by tag instead of digest.

❌ -Xmx copied from a laptop, or no memory limit at all.

❌ Building a separate image for production — you deploy untested bits.

❌ Shipping the JDK when a JRE suffices; shipping DevTools (Chapter 05).

❌ Secrets baked into image layers (they persist in history even if deleted later).

❌ Adopting native images for a JIT-friendly, long-running service because startup sounds nice.

❌ Ignoring startup time until autoscaling can't keep up.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Pod OOM-killed with a small heap Non-heap growth (metaspace, threads, direct buffers) Lower MaxRAMPercentage, cap threads, check native memory (NMT) Heap 24 GB in a 1 GB container No memory limit / old JVM Set limits; modern JVMs honour cgroups Deploys push 300 MB every time No layering / wrong COPY order Extract layers; order by change frequency Startup slower after an upgrade New auto-configurations, stale CDS archive /actuator/startup (Chapter 03), regenerate archive Native binary fails at runtime Missing reflection/resource hints nativeTest, tracing agent, explicit RuntimeHints Scan fails on unfixable CVEs No triage policy --ignore-unfixed + tracked exceptions with expiry Rollback deploys the wrong build Mutable tags Deploy and roll back by digest Requests fail during rollout No preStop/graceful shutdown; maxUnavailable > 0 Chapters 03, 30 settings Image works locally, fails in cluster Arch mismatch (arm64 vs amd64), missing env Multi-arch builds, verify base

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Layered, non-root, minimal-base images with OCI labels
  • JVM sized from container limits; JFR and heap dumps configured
  • SBOM generated, image scanned and signed; admission enforces signatures
  • Base image policy with weekly rebuild/rebase and an age gate
  • Startup and image-size budgets tracked per service
  • Digest-based promotion and rollback documented
  • nativeTest in CI for any natively built service
  • Rollout strategy and probes reviewed per service

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is a Spring Boot executable JAR?

Short answer: A JAR containing your classes, all dependencies in BOOT-INF/lib, and a launcher (JarLauncher) that sets up a nested-JAR classloader and calls your main.

B1 · Why layer a Docker image?

Short answer: Layers are cached by content; putting rarely-changing dependencies in earlier layers and your code last means a code change rebuilds and transfers only a few MB.

B1 · Why run containers as non-root?

Short answer: It limits the damage of a compromise and is required by most cluster security policies.

B1 · How do you tell the JVM how much memory it may use in a container?

Short answer: Set a container memory limit and use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage so the heap is derived from it, leaving room for non-heap memory.

B1 · What are buildpacks?

Short answer: A tool (./gradlew bootBuildImage) that builds an optimized, layered, non-root container image from your application without a Dockerfile.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Why deploy by digest instead of tag?

Short answer: Tags are mutable; a digest is the exact image content. Digest deployment makes promotion and rollback unambiguous and reproducible.

B2 · Dockerfile or buildpacks?

Short answer: Dockerfile for full control and strict base-image policies; buildpacks for batteries-included images with SBOMs, memory calculation and rebase for OS patching. Both must yield layered, non-root, scanned images.

B2 · What does jarmode=tools extract --layers do?

Short answer: Extracts the JAR into layer directories (dependencies, loader, snapshot dependencies, application) so a Dockerfile can copy them as separate layers.

B2 · How do you keep base images patched?

Short answer: One approved base, automated weekly rebuilds (or pack rebase for buildpack images), an age gate in CI, and a dashboard of base age and CVEs per service.

B2 · Why is -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError useful in Kubernetes?

Short answer: The process dies immediately on OOM so the pod restarts cleanly, instead of limping in a degraded state that health checks may not catch.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How does CDS improve startup, and what are its constraints?

Short answer: A training run records loaded classes into an archive of pre-parsed class data, which the JVM maps at startup instead of parsing again — typically 20–40% faster. The archive is tied to the JDK version and classpath, so it must be regenerated on any upgrade, and the training run must match production's classpath.

B3 · What does Spring AOT do on the JVM (not native)?

Short answer: Generates bean definitions and hints at build time, so startup skips classpath scanning and condition evaluation. It also fixes the context at build time, so profile/conditional differences must be considered.

B3 · When would you choose GraalVM native images?

Short answer: Scale-to-zero/serverless, very spiky scale-up, or high pod density where memory dominates. Not for steady, CPU-heavy, long-running services where JIT peak performance and build/debug simplicity matter more.

B3 · What breaks in native images and how do you find it?

Short answer: Reflection, dynamic proxies, resource loading by pattern, agents and dynamic class loading. Find them with nativeTest, the GraalVM tracing agent, and explicit RuntimeHints/@RegisterReflectionForBinding.

B3 · How do you diagnose a pod OOM-killed despite a small heap?

Short answer: Look at non-heap: metaspace, thread stacks (thread count × stack size), direct byte buffers, native libraries, JFR. Use Native Memory Tracking, reduce MaxRAMPercentage, cap pools, and measure RSS rather than heap.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the image pipeline for 26 services.

Short answer: Shared build conventions producing layered images; SBOM, scan (fail on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL), sign with provenance; push tagged by commit; deploy to staging by digest; gate on contracts and smoke tests; promote the same digest to production; weekly base rebuild/rebase; dashboards for base age, size, startup and CVEs.

B4 · How do you justify native images economically?

Short answer: Compare pod density and scale-up latency against build time, engineering effort and reduced peak throughput. Native wins when memory per instance and cold-start dominate cost (spiky, stateless); it loses for steady high-throughput services. Decide per service with measurements.

B4 · What's your policy for image vulnerabilities?

Short answer: Fail builds on fixable HIGH/CRITICAL; track unfixable ones with expiry dates and compensating controls; rebuild weekly so fixes land automatically; scan in the registry continuously (new CVEs appear after the build); use SBOMs to find affected services in minutes.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do packaging choices affect reliability?

Short answer: Startup time determines how fast you can scale during an incident; image size determines how fast a rollback reaches nodes; digest-based promotion determines whether you can trust what's running; base-image hygiene determines your exposure window. These are reliability decisions disguised as build configuration.

B5 · Would you standardize on one packaging approach platform-wide?

Short answer: Yes for the pipeline (SBOM, scan, sign, digest promotion, budgets) — that's where consistency pays. Allow a controlled exception for native builds where measurements justify them, with a JVM fallback maintained.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Autoscaling can't keep up during a flash sale

New pods took 40 s to become ready: a cold JVM start plus a cache warm-up in an ApplicationRunner (Chapter 03). Fixes: CDS/AOT cache to cut startup, warm only the top-N entries before readiness, pre-scale ahead of the sale, raise maxSurge, and track startup as a budget in CI.

Scenario · A critical CVE in the JRE; which services are affected?

Without SBOMs this is a week of archaeology. With them: query the SBOM attestations for the affected package, rebuild/rebase all matching images in one pipeline run, and redeploy by new digest — hours, not days.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Production image for catalog-service

Produce a Dockerfile that: extracts layers, creates a CDS archive during build, runs as UID 10001 on a read-only filesystem, sizes the JVM from the container limit, enables JFR to /dumps, and exposes 8080 (app) and 9090 (management). Then write the CI steps for SBOM, scan and signing, and a Kubernetes snippet deploying by digest with correct probes and graceful shutdown.

Solution Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre AS builder
WORKDIR /build
COPY build/libs/catalog-service.jar app.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --destination extracted
WORKDIR /build/extracted
RUN java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=/build/app.jsa -Dspring.context.exit=onRefresh \
         -Dspring.profiles.active=cds-training -jar app.jar || true            # (1)!

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.source="https://github.com/grocery/catalog-service"
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 grocery && mkdir /dumps && chown 10001 /dumps
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /build/extracted/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=10001:10001 /build/app.jsa /app/app.jsa
USER 10001
EXPOSE 8080 9090
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:SharedArchiveFile=/app/app.jsa \
    -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError \
    -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps \
    -XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxsize=200M,maxage=1h,dumponexit=true,filename=/dumps/app.jfr"
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  1. The training profile points at no real infrastructure and exits at refresh; || true tolerates a non-zero exit from the training run. Verify the exact flags for your Boot/JDK combination — and on JDK 24+ prefer the AOT cache workflow.
.github/workflows/image.yml (steps)
  - run: ./gradlew bootJar cyclonedxBom
  - run: docker build -t $REG/catalog-service:$GIT_SHA .
  - run: trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 $REG/catalog-service:$GIT_SHA
  - run: docker push $REG/catalog-service:$GIT_SHA
  - run: |
      DIGEST=$(docker inspect --format='{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' $REG/catalog-service:$GIT_SHA)
      cosign sign --yes "$DIGEST"
      cosign attest --yes --predicate build/reports/bom.json --type cyclonedx "$DIGEST"
      echo "IMAGE_DIGEST=$DIGEST" >> $GITHUB_ENV                                # (1)!
  1. The digest is the release artifact — it goes into the manifest, the release notes and the rollback instructions.
k8s/catalog-service.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 2, maxUnavailable: 0 } }
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      containers:
        - name: catalog-service
          image: registry.grocery.in/grocery/catalog-service@sha256:REPLACED_BY_PIPELINE
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }, { containerPort: 9090 }]
          resources: { requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 640Mi }, limits: { memory: 896Mi } }
          securityContext: { readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false,
                             capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"] } }
          startupProbe:   { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 },
                            failureThreshold: 20, periodSeconds: 3 }              # (1)!
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }, periodSeconds: 5 }
          livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }, periodSeconds: 10 }
          lifecycle: { preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] } } }
          volumeMounts: [{ name: dumps, mountPath: /dumps }, { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp }]
  1. A startupProbe gives slow starts room without making the liveness probe lenient forever — the cleanest way to handle variable startup time (Chapter 30 goes further).

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Layered images with change-frequency ordering make deploys and rollbacks fast.
  • Non-root, read-only, minimal base, dropped capabilities — cheap, large security wins.
  • Size the JVM from the container limit, exit on OOM, capture heap dumps and JFR.
  • Promote one digest from staging to production; roll back by digest.
  • SBOM + scan + sign on every image, with a weekly base-image rebuild or rebase.
  • CDS / the JDK AOT cache buy real startup gains cheaply; track startup as a budget.
  • Native images are a measured choice for spiky, stateless services — with nativeTest and a JVM fallback.
  • Packaging decisions are reliability decisions.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Boot Reference — Packaging Executable Archives, Container Images (layers, buildpacks, CDS, AOT), GraalVM Native Images
  • GraalVM Native Image documentation — reachability metadata, tracing agent
  • Cloud Native Buildpacks / Paketo documentation — builders, bindings, rebase
  • OpenJDK JEPs on Ahead-of-Time Class Loading & Linking (Project Leyden)

28 Integration & Contract Testing · 30 Kubernetes & Cloud-Native

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 29 produced an image. This chapter runs it: 26 services, six to sixty pods each, across three availability zones, with deploys during a Diwali sale and no maintenance window.

Kubernetes will happily run a badly configured Spring Boot service — and then surprise you:

  • A readiness probe that checks the database means every pod drops out when PostgreSQL blips, turning a degraded dependency into a total outage.
  • A liveness probe with a short initialDelaySeconds kills pods during a slow start, so the deployment never converges.
  • No PodDisruptionBudget, so a node drain evicts all six order-service pods at once.
  • An HPA scales from 6 to 40 pods, each with a 20-connection pool, and PostgreSQL rejects connections (Chapter 12).
  • terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 with a 45-second shutdown drain means SIGKILL mid-transaction (Chapter 03).
  • A ConfigMap change takes effect on new pods only, so half the fleet runs the old value for days.

None of these are Kubernetes bugs; they're contract mismatches between the platform and the application. This chapter covers that contract end to end: probes mapped to Boot's health groups, the exact shutdown sequence, resources and JVM memory, configuration and secrets, scaling (including on Kafka lag), disruption budgets and spread, deployment strategies with canary analysis on SLOs, GitOps, network policy, and the game days that prove it all works.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — probes, resources, a working manifest B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — config/secrets, rollouts, HPA basics B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — shutdown sequence, scaling signals, canary analysis B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — platform chart, capacity policy, disruption handling B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — platform strategy, mesh vs application, cost

docs.title: 2.1 The application ↔ platform contract
docs.text: Platform expects Spring Boot provides Chapter Fast, honest readiness signal /actuator/health/readiness 03, 27 Liveness that means "restart me" /actuator/health/liveness 03, 26 Graceful shutdown on SIGTERM server.shutdown=graceful + lifecycle timeouts 03, 25 Configuration from the environment Config data, config trees 06 Logs on stdout as JSON Structured logging 07 Metrics endpoint /actuator/prometheus 27 Bounded memory behaviour MaxRAMPercentage, OOM exit 29 Stateless pods No local state; sessions in Redis 17, 22

docs.title: 2.2 Probes
docs.text:
Probe Question Failure action Include dependencies? startup Has it finished booting? Keep waiting (then restart) No readiness Should traffic come here now? Remove from Service endpoints Only those without which the pod cannot serve liveness Is this process unrecoverable? Restart the container Never

The liveness trap

If liveness checks PostgreSQL and PostgreSQL has a 60-second blip, Kubernetes restarts every pod of every service simultaneously — turning a recoverable incident into a cold-start stampede against a database already under stress. Liveness is about this process: deadlock, corrupted internal state, unrecoverable error.

docs.title: 2.3 The shutdown sequence
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant K as kubelet / API server
    participant E as Endpoints controller
    participant LB as Service / ingress
    participant P as Pod (Spring Boot)

    K->>P: Pod marked Terminating
    K->>E: remove pod from Endpoints
    Note over E,LB: propagation is eventually consistent<br/>(ms to seconds)
    K->>P: preStop hook (sleep 5s)
    K->>P: SIGTERM
    P->>P: readiness → REFUSING_TRAFFIC
    P->>P: web server drains in-flight requests
    P->>P: SmartLifecycle stop by phase (consumers, schedulers)
    P->>P: executors drain, pools close
    P-->>K: exit 0
    Note over K,P: if still alive after terminationGracePeriodSeconds → SIGKILL

Two rules that avoid dropped requests:

  1. preStop sleep (≈5 s) covers the window where endpoints removal hasn't propagated yet but SIGTERM has arrived.
  2. terminationGracePeriodSeconds > preStop + spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase + margin (Chapters 03, 25).

docs.title: 2.4 Resources and QoS
docs.text:
Class How Behaviour Guaranteed requests == limits (CPU and memory) Last to be evicted; CPU throttling if the limit is hit Burstable requests < limits, or only requests Common for JVM services BestEffort nothing set Evicted first — never in production Setting Guidance Memory request ≈ limit The JVM sizes from the limit; wildly different values waste capacity or invite eviction Memory limit Required; pair with MaxRAMPercentage (Chapter 29) CPU request From observed usage (p95) + headroom CPU limit Often omitted for latency-sensitive JVM services to avoid CFS throttling; if set, be generous

CPU throttling looks like a slow application

A 500m CPU limit throttles the JVM in 100 ms slices; GC and JIT spikes hit the quota and p99 latency jumps with no obvious cause. Check container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total before blaming the code.

docs.title: 2.5 Configuration and secrets
docs.text:
Source Mechanism Chapter Non-secret env config ConfigMap mounted as a file, imported with spring.config.import 06 Secrets Secret mounted as files, read as a config tree 06, 18 Bootstrap only Env vars (SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT) 06 External secret stores External Secrets Operator / CSI driver syncing Vault → Secret 06

Config changes are deployments: annotate the pod template with a hash of the config so a change triggers a rollout (Chapter 06). Runtime reload (@RefreshScope, Spring Cloud Kubernetes reload) creates pods with divergent state and is rarely worth it.

docs.title: 2.6 Scaling
docs.text:
Signal Tool Good for CPU / memory HPA + metrics-server Simple CPU-bound services Requests per second, p99 latency HPA + Prometheus Adapter Web services Kafka consumer lag KEDA Consumers and indexers (Chapter 23) Queue depth (Rabbit/Redis) KEDA Workers (Chapter 24) Schedule (sale windows) KEDA cron / manual minReplicas Predictable peaks

Scaling multiplies your connection budget

Every new pod brings its own database pool, HTTP pools and Kafka consumers. maxReplicas × poolSize must fit the database's max_connections (Chapter 12) and the partition count (Chapter 23). Set maxReplicas from that budget, not from optimism.

docs.title: 2.7 Disruptions
docs.text: Control Purpose PodDisruptionBudget Limit voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades) topologySpreadConstraints Spread pods across zones/nodes Pod anti-affinity Avoid co-locating all replicas priorityClassName Critical services evict others, not vice versa Node pools / taints Isolate batch workloads from request-serving ones

docs.title: 2.8 Deployment strategies
docs.text:
Strategy Mechanism Cost Rolling (default) maxSurge/maxUnavailable Simple; both versions live briefly Blue-green Two deployments, switch the Service Double capacity; instant rollback Canary Small share of traffic, automated metric analysis (Argo Rollouts/Flagger) Best risk control; needs good SLIs (Chapter 27)

All of them require backward-compatible schema and APIs (Chapters 14, 20) — deployment mechanics can't rescue an incompatible change.

docs.title: 3.1 Readiness and traffic routing
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[kubelet probes /actuator/health/readiness] --> B{200?}
    B -- yes --> C[Pod Ready condition true]
    B -- no --> D[Ready false]
    C --> E[Endpoints/EndpointSlice includes pod IP]
    E --> F[kube-proxy / ingress / mesh route traffic]
    D --> G[Pod removed from EndpointSlice]
    G -.->|propagation delay| F

The propagation delay between "not ready" and "no traffic" is why the preStop sleep exists, and why readiness should flip before the server stops accepting connections (Boot does this automatically on shutdown).

docs.title: 3.2 Boot's availability state and probes
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Startup] --> B[LivenessState.CORRECT after context refresh]
    B --> C[Runners execute — cache warm-up etc.]
    C --> D[ApplicationReadyEvent]
    D --> E[ReadinessState.ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC]
    F[Application code] -->|AvailabilityChangeEvent| E
    G[SIGTERM] --> H[ReadinessState.REFUSING_TRAFFIC]
    H --> I[Graceful shutdown]

Warm-up in an ApplicationRunner therefore delays readiness automatically (Chapter 03) — no custom probe logic needed.

docs.title: 3.3 HPA control loop
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[metrics-server / Prometheus adapter / KEDA] --> B[HPA controller every ~15s]
    B --> C["desired = ceil(current × metric / target)"]
    C --> D{within stabilization window?}
    D -- scale up --> E[apply immediately]
    D -- scale down --> F[wait for stabilizationWindowSeconds]
    E & F --> G[Deployment replicas updated]

Scale-up is fast, scale-down is deliberately slow (default 5-minute stabilization) to avoid flapping. For JVM services with multi-second startup (Chapter 29), scale-up speed is bounded by startup time, which is why CDS/AOT matters operationally.

docs.title: 4.1 Application side
docs.text:
application-prod.yml
server:
  port: 8080
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s
management:
  server:
    port: 9090                                   # (1)!
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
  endpoint:
    health:
      probes:
        enabled: true                            # (2)!
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState, db
        liveness:
          include: livenessState
  1. Management on a separate port so probes and metrics are never exposed through the public ingress (Chapter 17).
  2. Creates /actuator/health/liveness and /actuator/health/readiness.

docs.title: 4.2 A correct Deployment
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 6
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 2, maxUnavailable: 0 }              # (1)!
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: order-service, version: "1.42.0" }
      annotations:
        prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
        prometheus.io/port: "9090"
        configHash: "{{ .Values.configHash }}"                     # (2)!
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45                            # (3)!
      securityContext: { runAsNonRoot: true, runAsUser: 10001, fsGroup: 10001 }
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: registry.grocery.in/grocery/order-service@sha256:9f2a...
          ports:
            - { name: http, containerPort: 8080 }
            - { name: management, containerPort: 9090 }
          env:
            - { name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, value: "prod" }
            - { name: SPRING_CONFIG_IMPORT,
                value: "optional:file:/etc/grocery/application.yml,optional:configtree:/var/run/secrets/grocery/" }
            - { name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError" }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "1Gi" }
            limits: { memory: "1Gi" }                              # (4)!
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: management }
            periodSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 20                                   # (5)!
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: management }
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 3
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: management }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 6                                    # (6)!
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }           # (7)!
          volumeMounts:
            - { name: config, mountPath: /etc/grocery, readOnly: true }
            - { name: secrets, mountPath: /var/run/secrets/grocery, readOnly: true }
      volumes:
        - { name: config, configMap: { name: order-service-config } }
        - { name: secrets, secret: { secretName: order-service-secrets } }
  1. Never lose capacity during a rollout.
  2. A hash of the ConfigMap/Secret content — changing config triggers a rollout (Chapter 06).

  3. preStop (5 s) + shutdown phase timeout (25 s) + margin.

  4. Memory request == limit gives predictable JVM sizing and better scheduling.
  5. Up to 60 s to start before the liveness probe takes over.
  6. Tolerant liveness — restarts only for genuine hangs.
  7. Covers the endpoint-propagation delay.

docs.title: 4.3 Service and PDB
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  selector: { app: order-service }
  ports:
    - { name: http, port: 80, targetPort: http }
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  minAvailable: 80%                                                # (1)!
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  1. A node drain can take at most 20% of the pods at a time — the difference between a rolling node upgrade and an outage.

docs.title: 4.4 Verifying the contract
docs.text:
Terminal
kubectl exec deploy/order-service -- curl -s localhost:9090/actuator/health/readiness
# {"status":"UP","components":{"db":{"status":"UP"},"readinessState":{"status":"UP"}}}

kubectl delete pod -l app=order-service --grace-period=45      # (1)!
# watch: no 5xx in the ingress logs, no dropped requests
  1. The simplest useful game day: delete pods under load and watch for errors (Level 4 formalizes this).

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Configuration and secrets
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/configmap.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: order-service-config
data:
  application.yml: |                                                  # (1)!
    grocery:
      order:
        auto-cancel-unpaid-after: 15m
        stock-reservation-ttl: 20m
    spring:
      datasource:
        url: jdbc:postgresql://orders-db-rw:5432/orders
        hikari:
          maximum-pool-size: 20
    logging:
      level:
        in.grocery: info
  1. One mounted YAML file rather than dozens of env vars: reviewable, supports maps and lists, no env-var name mangling (Chapter 06).
k8s/order-service/external-secret.yaml
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: order-service-secrets
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: { name: vault-backend, kind: ClusterSecretStore }
  target:
    name: order-service-secrets
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: grocery/payment/razorpay/key-secret                  # (1)!
      remoteRef: { key: grocery/prod/razorpay, property: key_secret }
    - secretKey: spring/datasource/password
      remoteRef: { key: grocery/prod/orders-db, property: password }
  1. The key layout matches the config tree: mounted at /var/run/secrets/grocery/, the file grocery/payment/razorpay/key-secret becomes the property grocery.payment.razorpay.key-secret (Chapter 06). Rotation in Vault propagates to the Secret; a rollout picks it up.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — Autoscaling a web service
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: order-service }
  minReplicas: 6                                                     # (1)!
  maxReplicas: 24                                                    # (2)!
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource: { name: cpu, target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 65 } }
    - type: Pods
      pods:
        metric: { name: http_server_requests_seconds_count_rate1m }  # (3)!
        target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "120" }
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 30 }]   # (4)!
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 20, periodSeconds: 60 }]    # (5)!
  1. A floor that covers baseline traffic plus zone loss.
  2. Derived from the connection budget: 24 × 20 = 480 connections; with three services sharing the cluster, that must fit max_connections (Chapter 12).
  3. Requests per second per pod via the Prometheus adapter — a better scaling signal than CPU for I/O-bound services.
  4. Double quickly when load rises.
  5. Shrink slowly to avoid flapping and cold-start churn.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Scaling consumers on Kafka lag
docs.text:
k8s/search-indexer/keda-scaledobject.yaml
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: search-indexer
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: search-indexer }
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 6                                                  # (1)!
  cooldownPeriod: 300
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: search-indexer
        topic: grocery.catalog.product-changed.v1
        lagThreshold: "5000"                                          # (2)!
        offsetResetPolicy: earliest
  1. Never more than the partition count (6) — extra consumers idle (Chapter 23).
  2. Scale out when lag exceeds 5,000 messages; lag is the signal that matters for consumers, not CPU.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Zone spread and disruption
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      priorityClassName: grocery-critical                             # (1)!
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway                           # (2)!
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
        - maxSkew: 1
          topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
          whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
          labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
  1. Checkout-critical services outrank batch jobs when the cluster is full.
  2. Prefer even spread across zones and nodes, but don't leave pods Pending if a zone is full — availability beats perfect balance during an incident.

Combined with the PDB from 4.3, a zone outage costs at most a third of capacity, and node upgrades never take more than 20% at a time.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Canary deployment with automated analysis
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/rollout.yaml (Argo Rollouts)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 10
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: order-service-canary
      stableService: order-service-stable
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService: { name: order-service, routes: [primary] }
      steps:
        - setWeight: 5                                                # (1)!
        - pause: { duration: 5m }
        - analysis:
            templates: [{ templateName: slo-check }]                  # (2)!
        - setWeight: 25
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - analysis:
            templates: [{ templateName: slo-check }]
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 100
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: slo-check
spec:
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 1m
      count: 5
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.005                             # (3)!
      failureLimit: 1
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{
              application="order-service",status=~"5..",version="{{args.canary-version}}"}[2m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{
              application="order-service",version="{{args.canary-version}}"}[2m]))
    - name: p99-latency
      successCondition: result[0] < 2.0
      provider:
        prometheus:
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket{
              application="order-service",version="{{args.canary-version}}"}[2m])) by (le))
  1. 5% of traffic first — enough to see errors, small enough that they don't matter.
  2. Automated analysis against the SLIs from Chapter 27. Failing the check rolls back automatically, without a human noticing at 2 a.m.
  3. The same error-budget threshold used for alerting — one definition of "good", used for both alerting and release gating.

This is where Chapter 27's version common tag pays off: without it, you cannot compare canary and stable.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Migrations, init containers and jobs
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/migrate-job.yaml (Helm pre-upgrade hook — Chapter 14)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: order-service-migrate-{{ .Release.Revision }}
  annotations:
    "helm.sh/hook": pre-upgrade,pre-install
    "helm.sh/hook-weight": "-5"                                       # (1)!
    "helm.sh/hook-delete-policy": before-hook-creation,hook-succeeded
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 900
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: registry.grocery.in/grocery/order-service@sha256:9f2a...    # (2)!
          args: ["--spring.profiles.active=prod,migrate"]
          envFrom: [{ secretRef: { name: order-service-migration-credentials } }]
  1. Runs before the deployment upgrade; failure blocks the release.
  2. The same image being deployed — migrations and code are always in sync.

Init container vs Job

An init container runs per pod (N migrations attempts, serialized by Flyway's lock); a Job runs once with privileged credentials. Use the Job for anything non-trivial, and keep the app's database user without DDL rights (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 5.7 Level 3 — Network policy
docs.text:
k8s/order-service/networkpolicy.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: api-gateway } }          # (1)!
        - namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { name: monitoring } }
          ports: [{ port: 9090 }]
      ports: [{ port: 8080 }]
  egress:
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: pricing-service } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 8080 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 5432 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: kafka } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 9092 }]
    - to: [{ namespaceSelector: {} , podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 53, protocol: UDP }]                            # (2)!
  1. Only the gateway may call this service's HTTP port; only the monitoring namespace may scrape the management port. Defence in depth behind token validation (Chapter 18).
  2. Always allow DNS in egress policies — the most common cause of "everything broke when we added NetworkPolicy".

docs.title: 6.1 A platform Helm library chart
docs.text:
Twenty-six services should not each maintain 300 lines of YAML.

charts/grocery-service/values.yaml (library chart defaults)
image:
  repository: registry.grocery.in/grocery
  digest: ""                                                          # (1)!
replicaCount: 3
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 300m, memory: 768Mi }
  limits: { memory: 768Mi }
java:
  options: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps"
probes:
  startupFailureThreshold: 20
  readinessPath: /actuator/health/readiness
  livenessPath: /actuator/health/liveness
shutdown:
  preStopSleepSeconds: 5
  terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45
pdb:
  minAvailable: 80%
spread:
  zones: true
networkPolicy:
  enabled: true
  allowedIngress: [api-gateway]
charts/order-service/values.yaml (service overrides only)
replicaCount: 6
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 500m, memory: 1Gi }
  limits: { memory: 1Gi }
networkPolicy:
  allowedEgress: [pricing-service, inventory-service, postgres, kafka, redis]
hpa:
  enabled: true
  minReplicas: 6
  maxReplicas: 24
  1. Filled by the pipeline with the promoted digest (Chapter 29).

The library chart encodes every lesson in this handbook — graceful shutdown timings, probe configuration, security context, PDB, spread, management port, scrape annotations — so a new service gets them by default rather than by remembering.

docs.title: 6.2 GitOps
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[CI builds image, promotes digest] --> B[Update env repo:<br/>values-prod.yaml digest]
    B --> C[Pull request + review]
    C --> D[Argo CD detects the change]
    D --> E[Sync: pre-upgrade migration Job]
    E --> F[Rollout: canary with analysis]
    F --> G[Health assessment]
    G -- degraded --> H[Auto-rollback to previous digest]

Properties that matter operationally:

Property Benefit Desired state in Git "What is running?" is a git log, not a kubectl archaeology session Review on config change Chapter 06's rule enforced by the tool Drift detection Manual kubectl edit is reverted and reported Rollback = revert commit Same path as any code change

docs.title: 6.3 Capacity and cost
docs.text:
Question Method Are requests right-sized? VPA in recommendation mode; compare with p95 usage over two weeks Do limits cause throttling? container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total per pod What does one service cost? Cost allocation by namespace/label (Kubecost or cloud billing tags) Can we use spot nodes? Yes for stateless, non-critical (indexers, batch) with PDBs and tolerations What's the sale-day plan? Pre-scale minReplicas, raise pool budgets, verify DB headroom, freeze risky deploys Pre-scaling for a sale (KEDA cron trigger)
  triggers:
    - type: cron
      metadata:
        timezone: Asia/Kolkata
        start: "0 17 * * *"                                            # (1)!
        end: "0 23 * * *"
        desiredReplicas: "16"
  1. Scale up at 5 p.m. IST, before the evening peak — pre-scaling beats reacting, especially with multi-second JVM startup.

docs.title: 6.4 Game days
docs.text:
Exercise What it proves Expected result kubectl delete pod under load Graceful shutdown, preStop timing Zero 5xx Drain a node PDB, spread, scheduling Capacity maintained Kill a zone (cordon + drain) Multi-AZ resilience Degraded capacity, no outage Stop PostgreSQL for 60 s Readiness/liveness correctness Pods stay alive, recover automatically Scale a dependency to zero Circuit breakers, degradation (Chapter 26) Degraded responses, no cascade Roll back by digest Rollback path and speed < 2 minutes Fill the disk / hit memory limit OOM behaviour, restart Clean restart with a heap dump Pod deletion test under load
k6 run --vus 200 --duration 5m scripts/checkout.js &
for i in $(seq 1 10); do
  kubectl delete pod -l app=order-service --field-selector 'status.phase=Running' \
    --grace-period=45 --wait=false | head -1
  sleep 20
done
wait
# assert in k6 output: http_req_failed rate == 0

If this test produces errors, the shutdown configuration is wrong — and you will otherwise discover that during a deploy at peak traffic.

docs.title: 6.5 Service mesh — what to delegate
docs.text:
Concern Mesh Application mTLS between services ✅ — Traffic splitting for canary ✅ — Connection-level timeouts, outlier ejection ✅ — Semantic retries (is this idempotent?) ❌ ✅ (Chapters 19, 26) Circuit-breaking with business-aware fallbacks ❌ ✅ Error translation, idempotency keys ❌ ✅ Distributed tracing Both (mesh adds hops; app adds context) ✅

Never enable retries in both. Pick one layer, document it, and verify with a chaos test (Chapter 26) that retry counts are what you expect.

docs.title: 6.6 The platform checklist per service
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[New service] --> B[Library chart applied]
    B --> C{Probes: readiness minimal, liveness internal?}
    C --> D{Shutdown: preStop + grace > drain timeouts?}
    D --> E{Resources: memory limit + MaxRAMPercentage?}
    E --> F{maxReplicas within connection budget?}
    F --> G{PDB + zone spread configured?}
    G --> H{Config via mounted file, secrets via config tree?}
    H --> I{NetworkPolicy with DNS allowed?}
    I --> J{Canary analysis wired to SLOs?}
    J --> K[Game day scheduled]

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Probes / availability states management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled, groups Same (module packages — verify) Graceful shutdown Default since 3.4 Default Config trees / spring.config.import ✅ ✅ Spring Cloud Kubernetes 3.x train Train aligned with Boot 4 (verify) Actuator on separate port management.server.port Same Startup time Baseline Similar; CDS/AOT cache options improve it (Chapter 29)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Re-verify health group configuration and endpoint paths after upgrading.
  • Re-measure startup time; adjust startupProbe.failureThreshold if it changed.
  • Confirm shutdown timings still fit terminationGracePeriodSeconds.
  • Re-run the pod-deletion game day in staging after the upgrade.
  • Check any Spring Cloud Kubernetes usage against the new release train.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Liveness internal, readiness minimal, startup probe for slow boots.
  2. preStop sleep + grace period > drain timeouts — verified by a pod-deletion test under load.
  3. Memory limit + MaxRAMPercentage; avoid CPU limits on latency-sensitive services or set them generously.
  4. maxUnavailable: 0 and a PDB; spread across zones and nodes.
  5. Config as mounted files, secrets as config trees, rollout on config hash.
  6. Scale on the right signal (RPS, lag), with maxReplicas from the connection budget.
  7. Canary with automated SLO analysis for risky services; rolling for the rest.
  8. GitOps: desired state in Git, rollback = revert, drift detected.
  9. NetworkPolicy with DNS allowed; least-privilege ingress/egress.
  10. Game days on a schedule, especially before peak season.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Liveness probes that check dependencies — synchronized restarts during an outage.

❌ Readiness probes that never fail (always 200) — traffic to broken pods.

❌ terminationGracePeriodSeconds shorter than the app's drain time — SIGKILL mid-work.

❌ No PDB — a node drain takes out the service.

❌ latest images or tag-based deploys (Chapter 29).

❌ Autoscaling without a connection budget — the database becomes the casualty.

❌ Runtime config reload creating divergent pods instead of a rollout.

❌ Retries in both the mesh and the application.

❌ kubectl edit in production (drift, lost on the next sync).

❌ Treating game days as optional.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix CrashLoopBackOff on startup Liveness fires before boot completes Add startupProbe, raise initialDelaySeconds 502/504 during deploys No preStop; grace period too short; maxUnavailable > 0 Fix shutdown contract; test with pod deletion All pods unready during a DB blip Dependency in readiness (or liveness) Minimal readiness; degrade instead (Chapter 26) OOMKilled Heap sized from node, or non-heap growth MaxRAMPercentage, memory limit, check RSS (Chapter 29) p99 spikes, CPU looks fine CFS throttling from CPU limits Inspect throttling metric; raise/remove limit Pods Pending Requests too large, no capacity, strict spread constraints Right-size requests; ScheduleAnyway Database connection errors after scaling maxReplicas × pool exceeds max_connections Lower maxReplicas/pool; PgBouncer (Chapter 12) Consumer lag grows though pods scaled More pods than partitions Scale partitions, not replicas (Chapter 23) Config change had no effect ConfigMap updated without rollout Config hash annotation Everything breaks after NetworkPolicy DNS egress blocked Allow kube-dns

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Probes configured per the contract; verified in staging
  • Shutdown timings consistent app ↔ pod; pod-deletion test green under load
  • Memory limits + JVM percentage; throttling monitored
  • PDB, spread constraints, priority class set
  • Config and secrets mounted; rollout on config change
  • HPA/KEDA signals and maxReplicas within resource budgets
  • Canary analysis wired to SLO queries for critical services
  • NetworkPolicies in place with DNS allowed
  • GitOps with drift detection and digest-based rollback
  • Game day calendar, including a pre-sale rehearsal

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What's the difference between readiness and liveness probes?

Short answer: Readiness decides whether the pod receives traffic; liveness decides whether the container is restarted. Readiness may consider essential dependencies; liveness should only reflect this process's own health.

B1 · Which Spring Boot endpoints back those probes?

Short answer: /actuator/health/readiness and /actuator/health/liveness, enabled with management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true.

B1 · Why set a memory limit on a JVM container?

Short answer: The JVM sizes its heap from the container limit (with MaxRAMPercentage); without a limit it may size from the node's memory and get OOM-killed.

B1 · What does terminationGracePeriodSeconds do?

Short answer: How long Kubernetes waits after SIGTERM before SIGKILL. It must exceed the application's graceful-shutdown time plus any preStop hook.

B1 · What is a PodDisruptionBudget?

Short answer: A limit on how many pods may be down due to voluntary disruptions (node drains, upgrades), protecting availability during maintenance.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Why is a preStop sleep recommended?

Short answer: Endpoint removal is eventually consistent; without a brief pause, SIGTERM can arrive while the load balancer is still sending traffic, producing errors during every rollout.

B2 · How do you deliver configuration and secrets to a Spring Boot pod?

Short answer: ConfigMap mounted as a YAML file imported via spring.config.import, secrets mounted as files read as a config tree, and env vars only for bootstrap settings like the active profile.

B2 · Why does a ConfigMap change not take effect?

Short answer: Mounted files update, but the application read them at startup. Trigger a rollout with a config-hash annotation; treat config changes as deployments.

B2 · How do you scale a Kafka consumer?

Short answer: KEDA on consumer lag, with maxReplicaCount capped at the partition count — extra pods idle.

B2 · What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control?

Short answer: How many extra pods may be created and how many existing pods may be unavailable during a rolling update. maxUnavailable: 0 preserves capacity.

B2 · Why avoid CPU limits for JVM services?

Short answer: CFS throttling within 100 ms windows causes latency spikes during GC/JIT bursts. Use requests for scheduling and omit (or generously set) limits for latency-sensitive services.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through what happens when a pod is deleted.

Short answer: Pod marked Terminating and removed from EndpointSlices (propagation is async) → preStop hook → SIGTERM → Boot flips readiness to refusing, drains in-flight requests, stops lifecycle components by phase, drains executors, closes pools → exit; SIGKILL if the grace period expires.

B3 · Why must autoscaling limits consider the database?

Short answer: Each pod carries connection pools; maxReplicas × poolSize × services must fit max_connections. Autoscaling without that budget can take the database down precisely under load.

B3 · How do you implement a canary with automated rollback?

Short answer: Progressive traffic shifting (Argo Rollouts/Flagger) with analysis templates querying SLI metrics for the canary version; failing thresholds abort and roll back. Requires a version tag on metrics and stable SLO definitions.

B3 · Init container or Job for migrations?

Short answer: Job (as a pre-upgrade hook) for anything non-trivial — one execution, privileged credentials, clear failure handling; init containers run per pod and serialize on Flyway's lock, delaying every pod's start.

B3 · How do mesh and application resilience overlap?

Short answer: The mesh handles transport concerns (mTLS, connection timeouts, outlier ejection, traffic splitting); the application handles semantics (idempotency-aware retries, fallbacks, error translation). Retries must be enabled in exactly one layer.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you standardize Kubernetes configuration for 26 services?

Short answer: A platform Helm library chart encoding probes, shutdown timings, security context, resources, PDB, spread, network policy and scrape annotations, with per-service value overrides; GitOps for delivery; conformance checks in CI; game days to validate.

B4 · Plan a Diwali sale from a platform perspective.

Short answer: Pre-scale minReplicas on a schedule, verify connection and partition budgets, raise database/cache capacity in advance, freeze risky deploys, rehearse rollback, run game days beforehand, watch SLO burn dashboards, and have degradation switches (Chapter 26) ready.

B4 · How do you reduce Kubernetes cost without hurting reliability?

Short answer: Right-size requests from observed p95 (VPA recommendations), remove over-provisioned limits, use spot nodes for stateless non-critical workloads with PDBs, improve bin packing, scale down aggressively off-peak, and reduce startup time so scale-down is safe.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What belongs to the platform team versus service teams?

Short answer: Platform owns the chart, base images, probes/shutdown contract, network policy templates, CI/CD, observability stack and cluster operations; service teams own their configuration values, SLOs, degradation behaviour and runbooks. The interface is the library chart plus documented contracts.

B5 · When is Kubernetes the wrong choice?

Short answer: Small estates where a managed PaaS covers the need, teams without operational capacity for cluster upgrades and incident response, or workloads better served by serverless. Kubernetes pays off with many services, heterogeneous scaling and a platform team to run it.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Every deploy produces a spike of 502s

No preStop hook and maxUnavailable: 25%: pods received traffic after SIGTERM and capacity dropped during the rollout. Fixes: preStop sleep 5 s, grace period above the drain timeout, maxUnavailable: 0, and a pod-deletion test under load in CI.

Scenario · PostgreSQL restarts and the whole platform goes down for 20 minutes

Readiness and liveness included the database, so all pods were restarted simultaneously; when the database returned, hundreds of cold JVMs opened connections at once and exhausted it. Fixes: liveness internal only, readiness minimal, degradation where possible (Chapter 26), staggered restarts, connection budget enforced, and a game day that repeats the scenario.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Production manifest for search-indexer

The indexer consumes Kafka (6 partitions), writes to OpenSearch, takes ~8 s to start and ~20 s to drain. Produce a Deployment with correct probes and shutdown settings, a KEDA ScaledObject on consumer lag (max 6), a PDB, zone spread, and a NetworkPolicy allowing only Kafka, OpenSearch, PostgreSQL and DNS.

Solution deployment.yaml
spec:
  replicas: 2
  strategy: { type: RollingUpdate, rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 } }
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40                       # preStop 5 + drain 25 + margin
      topologySpreadConstraints:
        - { maxSkew: 1, topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone,
            whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway, labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: search-indexer } } }
      containers:
        - name: search-indexer
          image: registry.grocery.in/grocery/search-indexer@sha256:...
          env:
            - { name: SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE, value: prod }
            - { name: JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS, value: "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError" }
          resources: { requests: { cpu: 400m, memory: 768Mi }, limits: { memory: 768Mi } }
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 15                              # (1)!
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 6
          lifecycle: { preStop: { exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] } } }
  1. 30 s of headroom for an 8 s start — generous, because a slow start must not be mistaken for a hang.
scaledobject.yaml
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { name: search-indexer }
  minReplicaCount: 2
  maxReplicaCount: 6                                          # (1)!
  cooldownPeriod: 300
  advanced:
    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
      behavior:
        scaleDown: { stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600 }        # (2)!
  triggers:
    - type: kafka
      metadata:
        bootstrapServers: kafka:9092
        consumerGroup: search-indexer
        topic: grocery.catalog.product-changed.v1
        lagThreshold: "5000"
  1. Partition count — the hard ceiling on useful parallelism.
  2. Slow scale-down: every scale event triggers a consumer-group rebalance (Chapter 23), so flapping is expensive.
pdb.yaml + networkpolicy.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
spec: { minAvailable: 1, selector: { matchLabels: { app: search-indexer } } }
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
spec:
  podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: search-indexer } }
  policyTypes: [Ingress, Egress]
  ingress:
    - from: [{ namespaceSelector: { matchLabels: { name: monitoring } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 9090 }]                                 # (1)!
  egress:
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: kafka } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 9092 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: opensearch } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 9200 }]
    - to: [{ podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 5432 }]
    - to: [{ namespaceSelector: {}, podSelector: { matchLabels: { k8s-app: kube-dns } } }]
      ports: [{ port: 53, protocol: UDP }]                    # (2)!
  1. No HTTP ingress at all — the indexer serves no traffic, only metrics scraping.
  2. DNS, always.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The platform/application contract is probes, shutdown, config, logs, metrics and bounded memory — Spring Boot provides all of it if configured deliberately.
  • Liveness internal, readiness minimal, startup probe for slow boots.
  • preStop + grace period > drain time, proven by a pod-deletion test under load.
  • Memory limits with MaxRAMPercentage; watch CPU throttling.
  • PDB + zone spread + maxUnavailable: 0 keep maintenance boring.
  • Scale on the right signal, with maxReplicas bounded by connection and partition budgets.
  • Canary with automated SLO analysis turns risky releases into cheap experiments.
  • GitOps makes "what's running?" and "roll it back" trivial; game days prove the rest.

docs.text:
