  • KEDA documentation — scalers (Kafka, Rabbit, cron); Argo Rollouts / Flagger — progressive delivery
  • Spring Cloud Kubernetes Reference (when you need in-cluster discovery/config beyond plain manifests)

29 Packaging & Deployment · 31 Reactive Spring

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Between 2018 and 2023, "reactive" was the answer to scalability in the Spring world: WebFlux, Reactor, R2DBC, non-blocking everything. Then Java 21 shipped virtual threads (Chapter 25), and blocking code became cheap to scale. So does reactive still matter?

Yes — but for narrower, sharper reasons than before:

  • Streaming with backpressure. The delivery-tracking feed pushes rider positions to 40,000 open browser connections. The producer is faster than some consumers; someone must slow down. Backpressure is a first-class Reactive Streams concept and has no equivalent in plain blocking code.
  • Very high connection counts with little work per connection. Server-sent events, WebSockets, long-polling: the cost is memory per connection, not threads.
  • Composition of concurrent calls with declarative timeouts, retries, and cancellation propagation — when one leg fails, the rest are cancelled automatically.
  • Reactive data stores that are reactive end to end (Redis, MongoDB, Kafka via Reactor Kafka).

Equally important is knowing when not to use it: for ordinary request/response services with JPA, Spring MVC on virtual threads gives you most of the scalability with none of the debugging difficulty.

This chapter covers Reactor and WebFlux properly — operators, schedulers, backpressure, error handling, context propagation, R2DBC, testing and debugging — and then gives an honest decision guide, plus the hybrid architecture the grocery platform actually uses.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — Mono/Flux, a first WebFlux endpoint B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — operators, error handling, WebClient, testing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — schedulers, backpressure, context, R2DBC B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — when to adopt, hybrid architecture, operations B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — strategy after virtual threads

docs.title: 2.1 Reactive Streams in one picture
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Subscriber
    participant P as Publisher
    S->>P: subscribe(subscriber)
    P-->>S: onSubscribe(subscription)
    S->>P: request(n)                      
    P-->>S: onNext(item) × up to n
    S->>P: request(n) — when ready for more
    P-->>S: onComplete() / onError(t)
    S->>P: cancel() — stop early

The request(n) call is backpressure: the consumer states how much it can handle, so a fast producer cannot overwhelm it. Everything else in Reactor is built on this four-method protocol.

docs.title: 2.2 Reactor types
docs.text:
Type Meaning Mono<T> 0 or 1 element, then complete or error Flux<T> 0..N elements, then complete or error

Nothing happens until you subscribe. A Mono returned but never subscribed is a no-op — the single most common beginner bug. In WebFlux, the framework subscribes for you when you return the publisher from a handler.

docs.title: 2.3 Operators you actually need
docs.text:
Operator Use map Synchronous transform flatMap Async transform, interleaved (concurrent) concatMap Async transform, ordered, one at a time flatMapSequential Concurrent execution, ordered results zip Combine results of parallel publishers then, thenReturn Sequence, discarding the previous value switchIfEmpty, defaultIfEmpty Handle "no result" filter, take, distinct Stream shaping timeout Bound the wait retryWhen Retry with backoff (Chapter 26 rules still apply) onErrorResume, onErrorReturn, onErrorMap Error handling / translation doOnNext, doOnError, tap Side effects: logging, metrics cache Share and replay a Mono's result

flatMap has a concurrency limit

flatMap(f) runs up to 256 inner publishers concurrently by default. That's an accidental bulkhead — sometimes too many for a fragile dependency, sometimes too few for throughput. Set it explicitly: flatMap(f, 20).

docs.title: 2.4 Schedulers
docs.text:
Scheduler Threads Use Schedulers.parallel() CPU-count, fixed CPU work Schedulers.boundedElastic() Elastic, capped Wrapping blocking calls Schedulers.single() One Serialized work Schedulers.immediate() Caller's Testing, no switch

subscribeOn decides where the subscription (and source) runs; publishOn switches the thread for downstream operators. In WebFlux you usually need neither: the event loop handles everything, and you only switch for blocking work.

Never block the event loop

WebFlux runs on a handful of Netty event-loop threads (typically CPU count). One blocking JDBC call there stalls all requests on that loop. If you must call blocking code, wrap it: Mono.fromCallable(this::jdbcCall).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()). Use BlockHound in tests to detect accidental blocking.

docs.title: 2.5 WebFlux
docs.text: Feature Notes Programming models Annotated controllers (same annotations as MVC) or functional RouterFunction Server Reactor Netty by default; Jetty/Undertow/Tomcat possible Return types Mono<T>, Flux<T>, Flux<ServerSentEvent<T>>, ResponseEntity<Mono<T>> Streaming text/event-stream (SSE) or application/x-ndjson Filters WebFilter instead of servlet Filter Errors @ControllerAdvice works; ProblemDetail supported (Chapter 10) Security SecurityWebFilterChain with @EnableWebFluxSecurity Test client WebTestClient

docs.title: 2.6 Backpressure strategies for streaming
docs.text: Strategy Behaviour Use for onBackpressureBuffer(n) Buffer up to n, then error/drop Bursty but bounded onBackpressureDrop() Discard when the consumer is slow Live positions — stale data is worthless onBackpressureLatest() Keep only the newest Dashboards, gauges limitRate(n) Prefetch in batches Database/stream reads sample(Duration) Emit at most one per interval Throttling high-frequency updates

docs.title: 2.7 R2DBC
docs.text: Reactive relational access: ReactiveCrudRepository, R2dbcEntityTemplate, DatabaseClient, a reactive transaction manager and a reactive connection pool. It is not JPA: no lazy loading, no dirty checking, no automatic joins across aggregates — closer to Spring Data JDBC (Chapter 12) in mapping power.

docs.title: 2.8 Reactive versus virtual threads
docs.text:
Dimension MVC + virtual threads WebFlux + Reactor Programming model Imperative, familiar Declarative pipelines Debugging Normal stack traces Assembly-time vs runtime traces, checkpoint() Blocking libraries (JDBC/JPA) Fine Must be isolated or replaced Streaming with backpressure Manual Built in Memory per connection Higher (stack per virtual thread) Lower Throughput (request/response) Comparable Comparable Ecosystem maturity Everything works Reactive variants needed Team cost Low Real, ongoing

Default to MVC + virtual threads; reach for WebFlux when streaming, backpressure or very high connection counts are intrinsic to the problem.

docs.title: 3.1 Assembly time vs subscription time
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A["Mono.fromCallable(...)"] --> B[".map(...)"]
    B --> C[".flatMap(...)"]
    C --> D[".timeout(2s)"]
    D --> E[Assembled operator chain — nothing has run]
    E --> F[subscribe]
    F --> G[Subscription propagates upstream]
    G --> H["request(n) flows up"]
    H --> I[onNext/onError/onComplete flow down]

This two-phase nature explains both the "nothing happened" bug and why stack traces are confusing: the assembly location (where the chain was built) differs from the execution location.

docs.title: 3.2 A WebFlux request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant N as Netty event loop
    participant D as DispatcherHandler
    participant H as Handler method
    participant R as Reactive repository / WebClient

    C->>N: HTTP request
    N->>D: handle(exchange)
    D->>H: invoke → returns Mono/Flux (nothing executed yet)
    D->>D: subscribe to the returned publisher
    H->>R: reactive call (non-blocking I/O registered)
    Note over N: event loop is free to serve other requests
    R-->>H: onNext when I/O completes (possibly another loop thread)
    H-->>D: result
    D-->>C: write response (with backpressure from the socket)

The key property: between issuing I/O and receiving the result, no thread is parked. That is what allows tens of thousands of concurrent connections with a handful of threads.

docs.title: 3.3 Backpressure to the socket
docs.text: For SSE and streaming responses, the TCP send buffer and the client's read speed propagate upstream as request(n) demand. A slow mobile client therefore slows the source — which is either exactly what you want (paged data) or a memory risk (live feeds), which is why an explicit strategy (2.6) is mandatory for infinite streams.

docs.title: 4.1 Setup
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webflux")
testImplementation("io.projectreactor:reactor-test")

Don't mix web starters

With both spring-boot-starter-web and -webflux on the classpath, Boot starts a servlet application and WebFlux endpoints don't behave as expected. Pick one per service (spring.main.web-application-type can force it, but separate services are cleaner).

6.1 The tracking service, end to end
docs.text:
The grocery platform's one genuinely reactive service: live delivery tracking for up to 40,000 concurrent customer connections.

flowchart LR
    R[Rider app] -->|position ping every 5s| I[tracking-ingest<br/>WebFlux]
    I --> RD[(Redis pub/sub + geo)]
    I --> DB[(PostgreSQL via R2DBC<br/>position history)]
    C[Customer app] -->|SSE| S[tracking-stream<br/>WebFlux]
    RD --> S
    S -->|drop + sample| C
    S --> M[Micrometer metrics<br/>open connections, dropped]
in/grocery/tracking/web/TrackingStreamController.java
package in.grocery.tracking.web;

import java.time.Duration;
import org.springframework.http.MediaType;
import org.springframework.http.codec.ServerSentEvent;
import org.springframework.security.core.annotation.AuthenticationPrincipal;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import reactor.core.publisher.Flux;

@RestController
class TrackingStreamController {

    private final DeliveryTrackingService tracking;
    private final io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry meters;
    private final java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger openStreams = new java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger();

    TrackingStreamController(DeliveryTrackingService tracking,
                             io.micrometer.core.instrument.MeterRegistry meters) {
        this.tracking = tracking;
        this.meters = meters;
        io.micrometer.core.instrument.Gauge
                .builder("grocery.tracking.streams.open", openStreams, java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger::get)
                .register(meters);                                                        // (1)!
    }

    @GetMapping(path = "/api/v1/deliveries/{orderRef}/stream",
                produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    Flux<ServerSentEvent<DeliveryView>> stream(@PathVariable String orderRef,
                                               @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
        return tracking.authorizedPositions(orderRef, jwt.getSubject())                    // (2)!
                .map(view -> ServerSentEvent.builder(view)
                        .id(String.valueOf(view.recordedAt().toEpochMilli()))
                        .event("position")
                        .retry(Duration.ofSeconds(5))                                      // (3)!
                        .build())
                .mergeWith(heartbeat())                                                    // (4)!
                .doOnSubscribe(s -> openStreams.incrementAndGet())
                .doFinally(signal -> {                                                     // (5)!
                    openStreams.decrementAndGet();
                    meters.counter("grocery.tracking.stream.ended", "signal", signal.name()).increment();
                });
    }

    private Flux<ServerSentEvent<DeliveryView>> heartbeat() {
        return Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(20))
                .map(i -> ServerSentEvent.<DeliveryView>builder().comment("keep-alive").build());
    }
}
  1. Open connection count is the key capacity metric for a streaming service — not requests per second.
  2. Ownership check inside the reactive chain (Chapter 17's rule, reactive form).
  3. Tells the browser how long to wait before reconnecting — SSE reconnects automatically.
  4. Heartbeats keep proxies and load balancers from closing idle connections (a very common cause of "the map freezes after 60 seconds").
  5. doFinally runs on completion, error and cancellation — the only reliable place to release per-connection resources.

docs.title: 6.2 Capacity for streaming services
docs.text:
Factor Consideration Memory per connection Netty buffers + per-subscription state; measure with a load test, budget ~10–50 KB File descriptors ulimit -n and container limits must exceed max connections Idle timeouts Ingress, load balancer and server.netty.idle-timeout must all exceed the heartbeat interval Event loop threads CPU count; one blocking call ruins everything (BlockHound) Backpressure strategy Explicit per stream (5.4) Scale-out Connections are sticky for their lifetime; a rollout disconnects clients — SSE auto-reconnect makes that acceptable, WebSockets need reconnect logic application.yml — tracking-stream
server:
  netty:
    idle-timeout: 5m                                                                  # (1)!
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 20s                                                   # (2)!
  1. Longer than the 20 s heartbeat, shorter than a forgotten tab's lifetime.
  2. On shutdown, open streams are closed; clients reconnect to another pod (Chapter 30's rollout settings apply).

docs.title: 6.3 Reactive in a mostly-imperative platform
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph "MVC + virtual threads (24 services)"
        A[order-service]
        B[catalog-service]
        C[payment-service]
    end
    subgraph "WebFlux (2 services)"
        D[tracking-stream]
        E[api-gateway]
    end
    A & B & C -->|Kafka events| D
    Client -->|SSE| D
    Client -->|REST| E
    E --> A & B & C

Rules the platform applies:

Rule Reason WebFlux only for streaming and the gateway The two cases where it clearly wins No JPA in reactive services R2DBC or no relational store at all Shared DTOs, platform error format, observability conventions A client can't tell which stack served it (Chapters 10, 27) BlockHound in every reactive service's tests Prevents the classic regression Blocking clients (RestClient) in MVC services, WebClient in reactive ones Don't mix models inside a service

WebClient in an MVC service is fine

Using WebClient from a blocking service (and calling .block()) is a common, supported pattern — but with virtual threads, RestClient (Chapter 19) is simpler and observably equivalent. Prefer it unless you need streaming responses.

docs.title: 6.4 Migration decision guide
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[New or existing service] --> B{Streaming to clients<br/>SSE/WebSocket, long-lived connections?}
    B -- yes --> W[WebFlux]
    B -- no --> C{Tens of thousands of concurrent<br/>connections with tiny work each?}
    C -- yes --> W
    C -- no --> D{Backpressure between<br/>producer and consumer required?}
    D -- yes --> W
    D -- no --> E{Data layer is JPA/JDBC?}
    E -- yes --> M["MVC + virtual threads (Chapter 25)"]
    E -- no --> F{Team experienced with Reactor?}
    F -- no --> M
    F -- yes --> G{Measured benefit in a spike?}
    G -- yes --> W
    G -- no --> M

The honest summary after virtual threads: most services should be MVC. Reactive earns its complexity in streaming and connection-dense workloads, and there it earns it decisively.

docs.title: 6.5 Testing reactive services
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x WebFlux ✅ ✅ Reactor 3.6/3.7 3.7+ (verify) R2DBC Spring Data R2DBC 3.x 4.x (verify) API versioning Convention Built-in for WebFlux too (Chapter 20, verify) Context propagation Micrometer context-propagation Same Test slice @WebFluxTest Moved to the WebFlux test module (verify) Jackson codecs Jackson 2 Jackson 3 (Chapter 11)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Verify Reactor and reactive driver versions align with Boot 4.
  • Re-run BlockHound-enabled tests after upgrading (new blocking paths can appear in libraries).
  • Check @WebFluxTest and security test configurer packages.
  • Re-test SSE behaviour end to end (codec changes can alter framing).
  • Confirm context propagation still bridges traceId into logs.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Choose deliberately: WebFlux for streaming, backpressure and connection-dense workloads; MVC + virtual threads otherwise.
  2. Never block the event loop; wrap unavoidable blocking in boundedElastic and prove it with BlockHound.
  3. Explicit backpressure strategy on every infinite stream — usually drop or latest.
  4. Timeouts, retries with jitter, and fallbacks as operators (Chapter 26 semantics unchanged).
  5. Bound flatMap concurrency explicitly.
  6. Reactor Context, not ThreadLocal; bridge to MDC with context propagation.
  7. Heartbeats and idle timeouts for SSE/WebSocket; measure open connections.
  8. doFinally for per-connection cleanup (cancellation included).
  9. Don't mix JPA and R2DBC in one service.
  10. Virtual time in tests; StepVerifier for signal-level assertions.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Adopting WebFlux for "performance" on a JPA-backed CRUD service — complexity without benefit.

❌ Blocking calls (JDBC, RestTemplate, Thread.sleep, .block()) inside a reactive chain.

❌ Forgetting to subscribe — the code silently does nothing.

❌ Unbounded onBackpressureBuffer on a live feed — a slow client becomes an OOM.

❌ Subscribing to the same Mono several times without cache() — duplicate database calls.

❌ Hooks.onOperatorDebug() in production (large overhead).

❌ ThreadLocal-based MDC/security assumptions carried over from MVC.

❌ Mixing spring-boot-starter-web and -webflux in one service.

❌ Streaming data that must not be lost without a persistent, replayable source.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Nothing happens No subscription Return the publisher, or subscribe explicitly All requests stall Blocking call on an event loop BlockHound; boundedElastic; remove blocking libraries Memory grows with connected clients Buffering backpressure strategy onBackpressureDrop/latest, sample Duplicate database calls Same Mono subscribed multiple times .cache() SSE stream freezes after ~60 s Proxy/LB idle timeout Heartbeat comments, align idle timeouts Stack traces are useless Assembly vs runtime checkpoint(), ReactorDebugAgent in dev traceId missing in logs Context not bridged Micrometer context propagation Transaction not applied Blocking transaction manager, or mixed JDBC/R2DBC Use ReactiveTransactionManager consistently Connections refused at scale File descriptor limits Raise ulimit -n, container limits Tests slow/flaky with delays Real time in sample/retryWhen StepVerifier.withVirtualTime

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Reactive used only where it's justified, documented per service
  • BlockHound enabled in tests
  • Backpressure strategy chosen per stream
  • Timeouts, bounded flatMap, retries with jitter
  • Heartbeats + aligned idle timeouts across ingress/LB/app
  • Open-connection gauge and dropped-message counters
  • Context propagation verified (traceId in logs)
  • doFinally cleanup on every long-lived stream
  • Load test at target connection count with memory measured

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What are Mono and Flux?

Short answer: Reactor publishers: Mono emits at most one element, Flux emits zero to many, each followed by a completion or error signal.

B1 · Why does my reactive code not run?

Short answer: Nothing happens until subscription. In WebFlux, return the publisher from the handler so the framework subscribes; elsewhere, subscribe explicitly.

B1 · map vs flatMap?

Short answer: map applies a synchronous function; flatMap applies a function returning a publisher and flattens the result — use it for asynchronous calls.

B1 · What is backpressure?

Short answer: The consumer telling the producer how many elements it can handle (request(n)), so a fast producer can't overwhelm a slow consumer.

B1 · When should a team use WebFlux instead of MVC?

Short answer: For streaming to clients, backpressure requirements, or very large numbers of concurrent connections. Otherwise MVC with virtual threads is simpler.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · What happens if you block inside a WebFlux handler?

Short answer: You block one of the few event-loop threads, stalling all requests on that loop. Wrap unavoidable blocking in Mono.fromCallable(...).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) and detect violations with BlockHound.

B2 · subscribeOn vs publishOn?

Short answer: subscribeOn affects where the subscription and source execute (one per chain, position-independent); publishOn switches the thread for operators downstream of it.

B2 · How do you handle errors in a reactive chain?

Short answer: onErrorResume (fallback publisher), onErrorReturn (fallback value), onErrorMap (translate), retryWhen (retry with backoff) — errors are signals, not thrown exceptions.

B2 · How do you test reactive code?

Short answer: StepVerifier for signal sequences, WebTestClient for endpoints, withVirtualTime for time-based operators, and BlockHound to catch blocking calls.

B2 · What is R2DBC and how does it differ from JPA?

Short answer: Reactive relational access with non-blocking drivers. No lazy loading, no dirty checking, no JPA ecosystem — closer to Spring Data JDBC with reactive types.

B2 · How do you stream data to a browser?

Short answer: Return Flux<ServerSentEvent<T>> with produces = text/event-stream (or NDJSON), add heartbeats, set a backpressure strategy and an idle timeout.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Explain assembly time vs subscription time.

Short answer: Building the operator chain (assembly) creates a blueprint; nothing executes until subscription, when the subscription and demand propagate upstream and signals flow downstream. This is why stack traces need checkpoint()/debug agents to be meaningful.

B3 · How do you choose a backpressure strategy?

Short answer: By data semantics. Live values (positions, prices): drop or keep latest. Bounded bursts: buffer with a limit. Paged/replayable data: limitRate and let demand drive the source. Never buffer unbounded on infinite streams.

B3 · How does context propagation work in Reactor?

Short answer: The Reactor Context is attached to the subscription and written with contextWrite, flowing upstream; Micrometer's context-propagation library bridges it to and from ThreadLocals (MDC, tracing, security) at scheduler boundaries.

B3 · Do virtual threads make WebFlux obsolete?

Short answer: No — they remove the scalability-only argument. WebFlux remains superior for streaming with backpressure, cancellation propagation and very high connection counts at low memory. For request/response services, MVC on virtual threads is simpler and comparable.

B3 · What are the pitfalls of mixing blocking and reactive?

Short answer: Blocking on event loops (fatal), transaction managers that don't match the data access model, ThreadLocal-based context lost across schedulers, and .block() inside a reactive chain causing deadlocks in constrained pools.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How would you decide whether to adopt WebFlux for a service?

Short answer: Requirements first (streaming, backpressure, connection density), data layer second (JPA rules it out effectively), team capability third, and a measured spike fourth. Without a clear requirement, choose MVC with virtual threads.

B4 · How do you operate a service with 40,000 open SSE connections?

Short answer: Measure memory per connection and file descriptors; align idle timeouts across ingress, load balancer and app; send heartbeats; apply drop-based backpressure and sampling; gauge open connections as the capacity metric; accept reconnects on rollout and verify client reconnect logic.

B4 · What's the cost of a mixed reactive/imperative estate?

Short answer: Two sets of libraries, idioms, debugging skills, security and test configurations. Contain it: reactive only where justified, shared contracts (error format, observability), and platform libraries that work for both.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What did the industry get wrong about reactive?

Short answer: Treating it as a general performance upgrade rather than a programming model for streams and backpressure. Many teams paid the complexity cost for services whose bottleneck was the database. Virtual threads corrected the default; reactive remains the right tool for a smaller, well-defined set of problems.

B5 · Would you rewrite an existing WebFlux service to MVC?

Short answer: Only with a concrete driver — maintenance pain, hiring, or a need for JPA. A working, well-understood reactive service is not a defect. Apply the decision guide to new services and to major rewrites, not as a blanket migration.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · The tracking service OOMs when riders go through a tunnel

Positions were pushed into onBackpressureBuffer() with no limit; mobile clients on poor networks stopped consuming, buffers grew per connection, and the pod died. Fix: onBackpressureDrop with a dropped counter, sample(2s), a per-connection idle timeout, and a load test at target connection count with memory measured.

Scenario · A new WebFlux service has worse latency than the MVC one it replaced

A JDBC-backed repository was called directly inside the reactive chain, blocking event-loop threads. Fix: BlockHound in tests (would have failed immediately), move to R2DBC or wrap in boundedElastic, and re-evaluate whether the service needed WebFlux at all.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Live price feed

Build GET /api/v1/prices/stream?skus=A,B,C as an SSE endpoint that emits price updates from Redis pub/sub, at most one update per SKU every 3 seconds, drops updates for slow clients (with a counter), sends heartbeats every 20 s, closes idle streams after 10 minutes, and authorizes the caller. Write tests using virtual time.

Solution PriceStreamController.java
@RestController
class PriceStreamController {

    private final PriceStreamService prices;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @GetMapping(path = "/api/v1/prices/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
    Flux<ServerSentEvent<PriceUpdate>> stream(@RequestParam List<String> skus,
                                              @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
        if (skus.size() > 50) {
            return Flux.error(new TooManySkusException(skus.size()));                 // (1)!
        }
        return prices.updatesFor(skus)
                .groupBy(PriceUpdate::sku)                                             // (2)!
                .flatMap(group -> group.sample(Duration.ofSeconds(3)), 50)             // (3)!
                .onBackpressureDrop(dropped ->
                        meters.counter("grocery.price.stream.dropped").increment())
                .map(update -> ServerSentEvent.builder(update).event("price")
                        .retry(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build())
                .mergeWith(Flux.interval(Duration.ofSeconds(20))
                        .map(i -> ServerSentEvent.<PriceUpdate>builder().comment("ping").build()))
                .timeout(Duration.ofMinutes(10))                                       // (4)!
                .onErrorResume(TimeoutException.class, e -> Flux.empty())              // (5)!
                .doFinally(signal -> meters.counter("grocery.price.stream.ended",
                        "signal", signal.name()).increment());
        }
}
  1. Bound the request — an unbounded SKU list is a resource attack (Chapter 20's rule, streaming edition).
  2. Group by SKU so sampling is per SKU, not global.
  3. Explicit concurrency bound on flatMap.
  4. Close abandoned streams.
  5. A timeout on an infinite stream is a normal completion, not an error the client should see.
PriceStreamControllerTest.java
@Test
void samplesPerSkuAndDropsForSlowClients() {
    given(prices.updatesFor(List.of("A", "B")))
            .willReturn(Flux.interval(Duration.ofMillis(500))
                    .map(i -> new PriceUpdate(i % 2 == 0 ? "A" : "B", "10.00", Instant.now())));

    StepVerifier.withVirtualTime(() -> controller.stream(List.of("A", "B"), jwt()))   // (1)!
            .thenAwait(Duration.ofSeconds(12))
            .expectNextCount(8)                                                        // (2)!
            .thenCancel()
            .verify();
}
  1. Twelve seconds of stream asserted instantly.
  2. Two SKUs × one update per 3 s over 12 s ≈ 8 events (plus heartbeats, depending on assembly) — adjust the assertion to the exact composition; the point is that sampling is verified deterministically.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Reactive Streams is about backpressure; Reactor is its implementation and WebFlux its web layer.
  • Nothing runs until subscription, and never block the event loop — BlockHound enforces it.
  • Choose a backpressure strategy explicitly for every infinite stream; drop or keep-latest for live data.
  • Timeouts, bounded flatMap, jittered retries and fallbacks are the same discipline as Chapter 26, expressed as operators.
  • Reactor Context replaces ThreadLocal; bridge it for logs, tracing and security.
  • R2DBC is a commitment — no JPA in that service.
  • After virtual threads, MVC is the default; reactive wins for streaming and connection-dense workloads.
  • Test with StepVerifier, WebTestClient and virtual time.

30 Kubernetes & Cloud-Native · 32 GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket & SSE

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
REST (Chapters 08, 20) carries most of the grocery platform's traffic, and should. But four problems fit it badly:

  • The mobile home screen needs banners, categories, a personalized "buy again" list, cart badge counts and delivery-slot availability. Over REST that's six round trips on a 3G connection in Coimbatore, each returning fields the screen ignores. One GraphQL query returns exactly what the screen needs, in one round trip — and the next app version can change its needs without a backend release.
  • Internal pricing calls run at 60,000 requests per second between services in the same cluster. JSON over HTTP/1.1 spends most of its cost on serialization and connection overhead. gRPC with protobuf over HTTP/2 cuts payload size and latency, and gives a typed contract with generated clients.
  • The rider app needs bidirectional communication: the server pushes assignments, the rider accepts or rejects, and both sides need to know the connection is alive. That's WebSocket, not request/response.
  • Order tracking for customers is server-push only, over mobile networks, through proxies. SSE (Chapter 31) is simpler than WebSocket and reconnects automatically.

This chapter covers all four in Spring: schema-first GraphQL with batch loading, depth and complexity limits, persisted queries and error handling; gRPC with deadlines, interceptors and proto evolution; WebSocket with STOMP, user destinations and a broker relay for scaling; and SSE for the cases where it beats WebSocket. It ends with a decision guide so each protocol is a choice, not a fashion.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — what each protocol is, a first GraphQL query B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — resolvers, batch loading, gRPC services, STOMP B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — N+1, limits, deadlines, scaling WebSocket B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — BFF architecture, protocol governance B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — API strategy across clients and services

docs.title: 2.1 Choosing a protocol
docs.text: Need Protocol Public, cacheable, widely consumable API REST (Chapters 08, 20) Many clients with different field needs; aggregation across resources GraphQL High-volume internal RPC with typed contracts gRPC Bidirectional, low-latency, stateful client sessions WebSocket Server → client push only SSE Fire-and-forget, decoupled in time Messaging (Chapters 23, 24)

docs.title: 2.2 GraphQL in five points
docs.text:
1. One endpoint (POST /graphql), one schema, queries describe the exact shape of the response.
  2. Schema-first in Spring: .graphqls files are the contract; @Controller methods bind to fields.
  3. Resolvers can nest, which creates N+1 by default — solved with @BatchMapping/DataLoader.
  4. HTTP caching doesn't apply (everything is a POST to one URL) — use persisted queries, CDN on GET variants, or server-side caching (Chapter 21).
  5. Every query is potentially expensive: depth, complexity and rate limits are mandatory, not optional.
Spring for GraphQL piece Role @QueryMapping / @MutationMapping Root fields @SchemaMapping A field on a type (Order.lines) @BatchMapping Batched resolution for a field across parents (kills N+1) @Argument, @ContextValue, @AuthenticationPrincipal Inputs and context @SubscriptionMapping Streaming fields over WebSocket/SSE DataFetcherExceptionResolver Error mapping GraphQlTester Testing

docs.title: 2.3 gRPC in five points
docs.text:
1. Protobuf IDL defines messages and services; code is generated for every language.
  2. HTTP/2: multiplexed streams, header compression, one long-lived connection.
  3. Four call types: unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidirectional.
  4. Deadlines, not timeouts: a deadline propagates across hops, so the whole call chain gives up together.
  5. Status codes (NOT_FOUND, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED, RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED) replace HTTP statuses; rich error details travel in trailers.

Verify

Spring's gRPC story has moved: community starters (net.devh:grpc-spring-boot-starter) were the norm for Boot 3, and the Spring gRPC project provides first-class support aligned with Boot 4. Confirm which is available for your version before choosing dependencies — the service code below is nearly identical either way.

docs.title: 2.4 Proto evolution rules
docs.text:
Change Safe? Add a field with a new number ✅ Rename a field (same number) ✅ on the wire, ❌ for generated code Change a field's type ❌ Reuse a deleted field's number ❌ — always reserved Add an enum value ✅ (consumers must tolerate unknown) Add an RPC ✅

Same discipline as Chapters 20 and 23: additive changes only; breaking changes mean a new service version.

docs.title: 2.5 WebSocket and STOMP
docs.text:
Raw WebSocket is a byte pipe. STOMP over WebSocket adds a messaging model: destinations, subscriptions, acknowledgements — so Spring can route messages like it routes HTTP requests.

Piece Role @MessageMapping Handle a message sent to a destination @SendTo / @SendToUser Route the return value to a topic/user SimpMessagingTemplate Push from anywhere in the application Simple broker In-memory; fine for one instance Broker relay (RabbitMQ/ActiveMQ STOMP) Required for multiple instances SockJS Fallback for environments blocking WebSocket

Scaling: WebSocket connections are stateful and sticky. Multiple instances need either sticky routing plus a shared broker relay, or the relay alone to fan messages out to whichever instance holds the connection.

docs.title: 2.6 SSE vs WebSocket
docs.text:
SSE WebSocket Direction Server → client Bidirectional Protocol Plain HTTP Upgrade handshake Reconnect Automatic (Last-Event-ID) You implement it Proxies/CDNs Usually fine (watch buffering) Sometimes blocked Binary No (text) Yes Per-connection cost Low Low

Rule: if the client only receives, use SSE.

docs.title: 3.1 A GraphQL request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Mobile app
    participant H as GraphQL HTTP handler
    participant E as graphql-java engine
    participant I as Instrumentation (depth, complexity, metrics)
    participant R as @SchemaMapping / @BatchMapping
    participant D as DataLoader registry

    C->>H: POST /graphql {query, variables}
    H->>E: parse → validate against schema
    E->>I: instrumentation hooks (reject if too deep/complex)
    E->>R: execute root field
    R->>D: nested fields register loads by key
    D->>D: dispatch one batched call per field
    D-->>R: results mapped back to parents
    E-->>H: data + errors (partial results possible)
    H-->>C: 200 with {"data": ..., "errors": [...]}

Two things surprise REST developers: a GraphQL response is 200 even on errors (errors live in the body), and a single response can be partially successful.

docs.title: 3.2 N+1 and batch loading
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A["query { orders(last:20) { lines { product { name } } } }"] --> B[20 orders]
    B --> C{naive resolvers}
    C --> D[20 line queries + 200 product queries = 221]
    B --> E{"@BatchMapping"}
    E --> F[1 query for lines by order ids<br/>1 query for products by sku set = 3 total]

Same root cause as Chapter 13's JPA N+1, same fix shape: collect keys, one query per level.

docs.title: 3.3 gRPC call with a deadline
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as order-service
    participant P as pricing-service
    participant I as inventory-service

    O->>P: PriceRequest (deadline = now + 600ms)
    Note over P: remaining budget travels in call context
    P->>I: StockRequest (deadline = remaining − margin)
    alt deadline expires anywhere
        I-->>P: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
        P-->>O: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED
    end
    I-->>P: StockResponse
    P-->>O: PriceResponse

The deadline is absolute and propagated — unlike HTTP timeouts, which each hop configures independently and which Chapter 19 had to reconcile manually with a budget.

docs.title: 3.4 WebSocket across instances
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R1[Rider app A] -->|WS| P1[pod 1]
    R2[Rider app B] -->|WS| P2[pod 2]
    P1 & P2 <-->|STOMP relay| B[(RabbitMQ STOMP broker)]
    S[dispatch-service] -->|send to /user/R-9/queue/assignments| B
    B --> P2 --> R2

Without the relay, a message published on pod 1 never reaches a rider connected to pod 2 — the single most common WebSocket scaling bug.

Persisted query support (sketch)
@Bean
PersistedQuerySupport persistedQuerySupport(PersistedQueryRegistry registry) {          // (1)!
    return new PersistedQuerySupport(registry);

Benefits: smaller requests, an allow-list of permitted queries (no arbitrary query execution), and the ability to serve them over GET so CDNs can cache. Verify the exact API and registry types for your Spring for GraphQL version.
Caching layer How it applies to GraphQL CDN/HTTP Only with persisted queries over GET DataLoader per-request cache Automatic within one request Server-side cache (Chapter 21) Cache the data sources, not the GraphQL response Client cache (Apollo/Relay) Normalized by entity id — expose stable id fields

6.1 The mobile BFF

The home-screen query (one round trip)
query HomeScreen($pincode: String!) {
  banners(pincode: $pincode) { id imageUrl deepLink }
  categories(limit: 12) { id name iconUrl }
  buyAgain(limit: 10) { sku name imageUrl price(pincode: $pincode) }

in/grocery/bff/graphql/HomeScreenController.java (concurrency)
@QueryMapping
CompletableFuture<List<BannerView>> banners(@Argument String pincode) {                 // (1)!
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> catalog.banners(pincode), bffExecutor);
}

@QueryMapping
CompletableFuture<List<ProductView>> buyAgain(@Argument int limit, @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    return CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orders.frequentlyBought(jwt.getSubject(), limit), bffExecutor);
}
  1. Root fields returning CompletableFuture execute concurrently; on virtual threads (Chapter 25) this is cheap, and a bulkhead-bounded executor keeps downstream pressure sane (Chapter 26).

BFF rules the platform applies:

Rule Reason The BFF owns no data and no business rules It aggregates; rules live in services (Chapter 37) Every downstream call has timeout + breaker + fallback Chapter 26; one slow dependency must not kill the home screen Partial results are allowed A failed banners returns an error entry, the screen still renders Persisted queries only in production No arbitrary queries from the internet Depth, complexity, and per-client rate limits Chapter 20's limits, GraphQL flavour One error vocabulary with REST Chapter 10's code in extensions

6.3 Rider WebSocket at scale
docs.text:
Concern Setting Connections 8,000 riders, one socket each, spread over 6 pods Sticky routing Ingress session affinity or rely on the relay + user registry broadcast Heartbeats STOMP heartbeat 10 s each way; detects dead sockets fast Message size limits setMessageSizeLimit — cap inbound frames Backpressure setSendBufferSizeLimit, setSendTimeLimit; close slow consumers Reconnect App retries with jitter; server tolerates duplicate accepts (idempotent, Chapter 23) Rollout Connections drop on every deploy; client must reconnect and re-subscribe Auth expiry Re-authenticate on reconnect; server closes sessions on token expiry Transport limits
@Override
public void configureWebSocketTransport(WebSocketTransportRegistration registration) {
    registration.setMessageSizeLimit(32 * 1024)
                .setSendBufferSizeLimit(512 * 1024)
                .setSendTimeLimit(10_000);                                                // (1)!
}
  1. A rider on a train in a tunnel stops reading; without these limits the server buffers until memory runs out — the WebSocket version of Chapter 31's backpressure lesson.

docs.title: 6.4 Protocol governance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[New interface] --> B{Who consumes it?}
    B -- Public/partners --> R[REST + OpenAPI]
    B -- Our mobile/web apps --> C{Aggregation across many services<br/>with varying field needs?}
    C -- yes --> G[GraphQL BFF]
    C -- no --> R
    B -- Internal services --> D{High volume or streaming?}
    D -- yes --> P[gRPC]
    D -- no --> R2[REST — fewer moving parts]
    B -- Long-lived client session --> E{Bidirectional?}
    E -- yes --> W[WebSocket + STOMP]
    E -- no --> S[SSE]

Platform decisions recorded in ADRs: REST for public APIs and most internal calls; one GraphQL BFF for mobile; gRPC for pricing/inventory hot paths; WebSocket for the rider app; SSE for customer tracking.

7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Decide the gRPC dependency strategy early; migrating starters touches annotations and configuration.
  • Re-verify GraphQL instrumentation and persisted-query APIs after upgrading.
  • Re-test STOMP message converters after the Jackson move.
  • Re-run protocol-level tests (GraphQlTester, in-process gRPC, real WebSocket) rather than trusting compilation.
  • Check that proto-generated code targets a compatible protobuf runtime.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Pick the protocol by need, record it in an ADR, and keep the list short.
  2. GraphQL: batch everything (@BatchMapping), with a test asserting call counts.
  3. GraphQL: depth, complexity, persisted queries, per-client rate limits — always.
  4. One error vocabulary across REST, GraphQL and gRPC (code in extensions, mapped status codes).
  5. gRPC: deadlines on every call, propagated; alert on DEADLINE_EXCEEDED.
  6. Proto and schema evolution is additive; reserve removed field numbers.
  7. WebSocket: broker relay, heartbeats, transport limits, authenticated CONNECT, idempotent message handling.
  8. SSE when push-only, with heartbeats and buffering disabled on proxies.
  9. Observability tagged by operation/method, never by query text.
  10. BFF owns no business rules and degrades partially.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Exposing GraphQL publicly without depth/complexity limits or persisted queries.

❌ Naive nested resolvers (N+1 across the network) — the default failure mode.

❌ Anonymous GraphQL operations, making metrics and rate limits useless.

❌ Putting business logic in the BFF, creating a second source of truth.

❌ gRPC without deadlines — the whole point of the model wasted.

❌ Reusing a proto field number, or changing a field's type.

❌ float/double for money in proto or GraphQL.

❌ WebSocket with the simple broker across multiple pods — messages vanish.

❌ Authenticating only the handshake and never re-checking; or ignoring token expiry on long-lived sockets.

❌ Using WebSocket where SSE would do (push-only) — twice the client complexity.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix GraphQL query slow, downstream flooded N+1 resolvers @BatchMapping, assert call counts in tests 200 with errors and null fields Partial failure Map exceptions deliberately; decide nullability in the schema GraphQL responses uncacheable POST to one endpoint Persisted queries + GET, or cache data sources Metrics cardinality explosion Tagging by query text Tag by operation name gRPC UNAVAILABLE under load Channel/connection limits, no load balancing Tune channels; use round-robin/xDS; check server concurrency gRPC DEADLINE_EXCEEDED everywhere Budget too small, or a slow hop Recheck the chain's budget (Chapter 19) Old clients crash after a proto change Non-additive change Additive only; reserve numbers; version the service WebSocket messages lost across pods Simple broker Broker relay + user destination broadcast Sockets die after 60 s Proxy idle timeout STOMP heartbeats; align ingress timeouts SSE events arrive in bursts Proxy buffering X-Accel-Buffering: no, disable ingress buffering

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Protocol choice recorded per interface
  • GraphQL: batch loaders, depth/complexity limits, persisted queries, named operations
  • GraphQL field-level authorization reviewed
  • gRPC: deadlines, interceptors for auth/tracing, status mapping, bounded batch sizes
  • Proto/schema evolution rules enforced in review
  • WebSocket: relay, heartbeats, transport limits, authenticated sessions, idempotent handlers
  • SSE: heartbeats, timeouts, proxy buffering disabled
  • Observability per operation/method; alerts on deadline/error rates
  • Protocol-level tests (GraphQlTester, in-process gRPC, real WebSocket client)

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What problem does GraphQL solve?

Short answer: Clients fetch exactly the fields they need in one request, instead of several REST calls returning over- or under-fetched data — useful when many clients have different needs.

B1 · What is gRPC?

Short answer: An RPC framework using protobuf for typed messages over HTTP/2, with generated clients and servers, supporting unary and streaming calls.

B1 · SSE or WebSocket for order tracking?

Short answer: SSE — the client only receives updates, and it reconnects automatically over plain HTTP.

B1 · How do you expose a GraphQL query in Spring?

Short answer: Define the field in a .graphqls schema and implement a @QueryMapping method in a @Controller, binding inputs with @Argument.

B1 · Why does GraphQL return 200 even for errors?

Short answer: Errors are part of the response body (errors array) because a query can be partially successful.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how do you fix it?

Short answer: Nested field resolvers run once per parent, producing many downstream calls. Fix with @BatchMapping/DataLoader so all keys at one level are fetched in a single batched call.

B2 · Why are depth and complexity limits necessary?

Short answer: A single crafted query can otherwise request deeply nested or enormous result sets and exhaust the server — GraphQL moves cost control from the API design to runtime limits.

B2 · What are gRPC deadlines and why prefer them to timeouts?

Short answer: A deadline is an absolute point in time propagated through the call chain, so every hop gives up together and no work continues after the caller has given up.

B2 · How do you scale WebSocket across multiple instances?

Short answer: Replace the simple broker with a STOMP broker relay (RabbitMQ/ActiveMQ) and configure user-destination and user-registry broadcasts so user-specific messages reach the right pod.

B2 · How do you evolve a protobuf message safely?

Short answer: Add fields with new numbers, never change types or reuse numbers, reserve removed numbers and names, and give enums an _UNSPECIFIED zero value.

B2 · How do you test GraphQL and gRPC?

Short answer: GraphQlTester/@GraphQlTest for queries and error mapping (plus batch-call-count assertions); in-process channels for gRPC including deadline and status-code behaviour.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How do you secure a GraphQL API?

Short answer: Authenticate as usual; enforce ownership in resolvers; apply method security on sensitive fields; limit depth/complexity; use persisted queries as an allow-list in production; rate-limit per client; disable introspection and GraphiQL publicly.

B3 · How does caching work with GraphQL?

Short answer: HTTP caching doesn't apply to POST-to-one-endpoint; use persisted queries over GET for CDN caching, per-request DataLoader caching, and server-side caching of the underlying data sources rather than of GraphQL responses.

B3 · When is gRPC worth it over REST internally?

Short answer: High call volume, strict latency budgets, streaming, or a desire for generated typed clients across languages. For modest internal traffic, REST is simpler to debug, observe and evolve.

B3 · What are the operational pitfalls of WebSocket?

Short answer: Sticky, stateful connections; message loss without a relay; proxy idle timeouts; unbounded send buffers for slow consumers; authentication that outlives token validity; and full reconnect storms on deploys.

B3 · How do you keep observability useful across these protocols?

Short answer: Tag by low-cardinality identifiers — GraphQL operation name, gRPC method, STOMP destination pattern — never by query text or user ids, and alert on protocol-specific signals (deadline exceeded, error types, dropped sockets).

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design a BFF for mobile.

Short answer: One GraphQL service owning no data, aggregating REST/gRPC calls concurrently with timeouts, breakers and partial-failure handling; batch loaders everywhere; persisted queries and limits; shared error codes with REST; separate deployment and scaling from core services; contract tests with the app teams.

B4 · How do you govern protocol choice across 26 services?

Short answer: A documented decision tree, ADRs per interface, platform libraries for each sanctioned protocol (error mapping, auth, observability), review for new protocol adoption, and a bias toward REST unless a specific need justifies more.

B4 · How would you migrate a hot internal REST call to gRPC?

Short answer: Define the proto from the existing contract, run both endpoints in parallel, move one consumer behind a flag, compare latency/error metrics and cost, then migrate the rest and retire the REST endpoint after telemetry shows zero use.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What are the hidden costs of GraphQL?

Short answer: Runtime cost control (limits, persisted queries), a new caching model, schema governance across teams, observability and rate limiting that don't come free from HTTP, and the risk of a BFF accumulating business logic. It pays off with several clients and heavy aggregation, not as a default REST replacement.

B5 · How do you avoid protocol sprawl?

Short answer: Make REST the default, require a documented reason (and an owner) for anything else, provide platform support for the sanctioned few, and periodically review whether each non-REST interface still earns its complexity.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · The GraphQL BFF takes down pricing every morning

A new app version requested price on every product in a 100-item list, and the resolver called pricing per item — 100 calls per request, thousands per second. Fixes: @BatchMapping with a bulk pricing call, a call-count test, complexity limits, per-client rate limits, and a circuit breaker with cached prices (Chapter 26).

Scenario · Riders stop receiving assignments after scaling to three pods

The simple in-memory broker was still configured: messages published on one pod never reached riders connected to another. Fixes: STOMP broker relay with user-destination broadcast, a test with two application instances, and an alert on assignment acknowledgement rate.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Add delivery slots to the BFF

Expose deliverySlots(pincode: String!, days: Int = 2): [DeliverySlot!]! in GraphQL. It calls delivery-service, must batch when requested for several pincodes in one query, must return an error entry (not a failure) when delivery-service is down, and must be limited to 7 days. Write tests for batching, the limit and the failure path.

Solution schema.graphqls
extend type Query {
  deliverySlots(pincode: String!, days: Int = 2): [DeliverySlot!]!
}
type DeliverySlot { start: String!, end: String!, available: Boolean!, feeRupees: String! }
DeliverySlotController.java
@Controller
class DeliverySlotController {

    private final DeliveryClient delivery;
    private final MeterRegistry meters;

    @QueryMapping
    List<DeliverySlotView> deliverySlots(@Argument String pincode, @Argument int days) {
        if (days < 1 || days > 7) {
            throw new InvalidRequestException("days must be between 1 and 7");        // (1)!
        }
        try {
            return delivery.slots(pincode, days);
        } catch (DependencyException e) {
            meters.counter("grocery.bff.degraded", "field", "deliverySlots").increment();
            throw new PartialFailureException("Delivery slots unavailable", e);        // (2)!
        }
    }

    @BatchMapping(typeName = "Product", field = "deliveryEstimate")                    // (3)!
    Map<ProductView, String> deliveryEstimate(List<ProductView> products,
                                              @ContextValue String pincode) {
        var estimates = delivery.estimatesFor(
                products.stream().map(ProductView::sku).distinct().toList(), pincode);
        return products.stream()
                .filter(p -> estimates.containsKey(p.sku()))
                .collect(Collectors.toMap(Function.identity(), p -> estimates.get(p.sku())));
    }
}
  1. Bound the request in the resolver; the schema default handles the common case.
  2. Resolved by the exception resolver (5.3) into an errors entry with a code, leaving the rest of the query's data intact.
  3. Batched across products so a 100-item list is one call.
DeliverySlotControllerTest.java
@Test
void rejectsTooManyDays() {
    tester.document("""query { deliverySlots(pincode:"560102", days: 30) { start } }""")
          .execute()
          .errors().satisfy(errors ->
                  assertThat(errors.get(0).getExtensions()).containsEntry("code", "INVALID_REQUEST"));
}

@Test
void batchesEstimatesAcrossProducts() {
    tester.document("""query { buyAgain(limit: 20) { sku deliveryEstimate } }""").execute();
    then(delivery).should(times(1)).estimatesFor(any(), any());                         // (1)!
}

@Test
void returnsPartialDataWhenDeliveryIsDown() {
    willThrow(DependencyException.unavailable("delivery", null)).given(delivery).slots(any(), anyInt());

    tester.document("""query { cartSummary { itemCount } deliverySlots(pincode:"560102") { start } }""")
          .execute()
          .errors().expect(e -> "DEPENDENCY_UNAVAILABLE".equals(e.getExtensions().get("code")))
          .verify()
          .path("cartSummary.itemCount").hasValue();                                    // (2)!
}
  1. One batched call regardless of list size.
  2. Partial success: the cart summary still renders while delivery slots report an error — the behaviour that makes a BFF resilient rather than a single point of failure.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Choose per need: REST by default, GraphQL for client-driven aggregation, gRPC for hot internal paths, WebSocket for bidirectional sessions, SSE for push-only.
  • GraphQL's defaults are dangerous: batch every nested field, cap depth and complexity, use persisted queries, name operations.
  • gRPC's superpower is deadlines — absolute and propagated; its discipline is additive proto evolution.
  • WebSocket needs a broker relay, heartbeats, transport limits and authenticated, idempotent message handling.
  • SSE is the simpler answer whenever the client only receives.
  • One error vocabulary and one observability convention across protocols.
  • A BFF aggregates and degrades; it never owns business rules.

31 Reactive Spring · 33 Spring Batch & Integration

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Not everything is a request. The grocery platform runs a second, quieter system behind the API:

  • Weekly seller settlement: 14,000 sellers, ~2.8 million order lines, commission and TDS calculations, a payout file for the bank, and a settlement report per seller. It must be restartable — failing at seller 9,000 cannot mean redoing 9,000.
  • Catalog feed ingestion: sellers drop CSV files on SFTP, up to 400,000 rows each, with malformed rows that must be rejected individually rather than failing the file.
  • Razorpay reconciliation: a daily settlement file matched against our payment records; mismatches become finance tickets.
  • Monthly GST reports: aggregate, format, archive, and never produce a partial file.

Writing these as a @Scheduled method with a for loop works until the day it doesn't: a network blip at row 380,000 leaves the job half-applied with no idea where to resume, no record of what was skipped, and no way to re-run just the failed portion.

Spring Batch exists for exactly this: chunk-oriented processing with transactional boundaries, a job repository that records every execution, restartability, skip and retry policies, and partitioning for parallelism. Spring Integration covers the adjacent problem — moving data between systems (SFTP, files, JMS, HTTP, Kafka) with the Enterprise Integration Patterns, including polling, filtering, routing, aggregating and idempotent receipt.

This chapter builds both: a production settlement job, a resilient file-ingestion flow, and the operational wiring — Kubernetes CronJobs, metrics, alerts and tests.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — jobs, steps, readers/writers B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — chunking, skip/retry, listeners, file flows B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — restartability, partitioning, idempotency B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — batch platform, operations, capacity B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — when batch, when streaming, when neither

docs.title: 2.1 Spring Batch domain model
docs.text:
Concept Meaning Job A named batch process composed of steps Step One phase: chunk-oriented (read/process/write) or a tasklet (do one thing) JobParameters Inputs that identify an execution (runDate, sellerBatch) JobInstance A job + its identifying parameters — one logical run JobExecution / StepExecution An attempt at that instance, with status and counts JobRepository Persistence for all of the above (your database) ExecutionContext Key-value state saved per execution — how restart knows where to resume JobLauncher / JobOperator Start, restart, stop, query

Restart works because of two facts: a JobInstance is identified by its parameters, and readers save their position in the ExecutionContext at every chunk commit.

docs.title: 2.2 Chunk-oriented processing
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[ItemReader.read] -->|until chunk size| B[ItemProcessor.process]
    B --> C[ItemWriter.write — one call per chunk]
    C --> D[Commit transaction + save reader position]
    D -->|next chunk| A

The chunk size is the transaction boundary: 500 items read and processed, written once, committed once. Small chunks mean more commits and slower throughput; large chunks mean more work lost on failure and longer locks (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 2.3 Readers, processors, writers
docs.text:
Reader Use JdbcPagingItemReader Preferred for SQL: restartable, safe with parallelism JdbcCursorItemReader Single-threaded streaming; holds a connection open JpaPagingItemReader When you need entities (beware of the persistence context) FlatFileItemReader CSV/fixed-width, with LineMapper and FieldSetMapper MultiResourceItemReader Many files as one stream KafkaItemReader Consume a topic range as a batch Writer Use JdbcBatchItemWriter Batched JDBC inserts/updates (Chapter 12) FlatFileItemWriter Output files (payout files, reports) CompositeItemWriter Write to several destinations ClassifierCompositeItemWriter Route items to different writers

Processors transform, enrich or filter (returning null drops the item).

docs.title: 2.4 Failure handling
docs.text:
Policy Meaning Skip Tolerate bad items up to a limit (skipLimit), record them Retry Retry transient failures within the step Fault tolerance faultTolerant() enables both, with rollback and re-processing of the chunk item by item Listeners SkipListener, ItemReadListener, StepExecutionListener for reporting Restart Re-launch the same JobInstance; completed steps are skipped, the failing step resumes

Skips are a business decision

"Skip up to 1,000 malformed rows" must be agreed with the business, and every skipped row must land in a rejects file with a reason. A silent skip is data loss.

docs.title: 2.5 Parallelism
docs.text: Technique Scope Multi-threaded step Several threads over one reader — reader must be thread-safe; breaks restartability unless handled carefully Parallel flow Independent steps run concurrently Partitioning Split the data into partitions (by seller, date, id range), each with its own StepExecution — restartable and the usual choice Remote partitioning / chunking Partitions or chunks processed by other JVMs via messaging

docs.title: 2.6 Spring Integration essentials
docs.text: Concept Meaning Message Payload + headers Channel Direct (synchronous), Queue (buffered), PublishSubscribe, Executor Endpoint Transformer, filter, router, splitter, aggregator, service activator Adapter Inbound/outbound connectors: file, SFTP, JDBC, JMS, Kafka, HTTP, mail Gateway @MessagingGateway — a plain Java interface hiding the flow Poller How often an inbound adapter checks for work IntegrationFlow The Java DSL that wires the above Idempotent receiver A MetadataStore-backed filter that drops duplicates

docs.title: 2.7 Batch or Integration or neither?
docs.text:
Need Tool Process a large dataset with restart, skip, reporting Spring Batch Move/transform data between systems and protocols Spring Integration React to events one at a time, continuously Kafka consumer (Chapter 23) Sweep a table every minute @Scheduled + SKIP LOCKED (Chapter 25) One-off script A CLI runner (Chapter 05)

The platform uses all five. The mistake is using Batch for a 200-row sweep, or a hand-rolled loop for a 3-million-row settlement.

docs.title: 3.1 Job execution and restart
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant L as JobLauncher
    participant R as JobRepository
    participant J as Job
    participant S as Step
    participant DB as Database

    L->>R: find JobInstance for (jobName, parameters)
    alt new instance
        R-->>L: create JobInstance + JobExecution
    else existing FAILED instance
        R-->>L: reuse instance, new JobExecution (restart)
    end
    L->>J: execute
    J->>R: is this step already COMPLETED?
    alt yes (restart)
        J->>J: skip the step
    else no
        J->>S: execute with saved ExecutionContext
        loop chunks
            S->>DB: read (from saved position) → process → write
            S->>R: commit chunk + save reader position
        end
    end
    J->>R: final status

The JobRepository is why all this works — and why it needs its own tables in your database (created by Flyway, Chapter 14).

docs.title: 3.2 Chunk transaction and fault tolerance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Begin transaction] --> B[Read N items]
    B --> C[Process each]
    C --> D[Write chunk]
    D --> E{success?}
    E -- yes --> F[Commit + save context]
    E -- no --> G[Rollback chunk]
    G --> H{faultTolerant?}
    H -- no --> I[Step FAILED]
    H -- yes --> J[Re-run the chunk item by item<br/>to find the culprit]
    J --> K{retryable?}
    K -- yes --> L[Retry that item]
    K -- no --> M{skippable and under limit?}
    M -- yes --> N[Skip + SkipListener]
    M -- no --> I

The item-by-item replay after a chunk failure is why processors and writers must be idempotent or side-effect-free: an item may be processed more than once.

docs.title: 3.3 An integration flow
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[SFTP inbound adapter<br/>poller every 5 min] --> B[Idempotent receiver<br/>MetadataStore by filename+hash]
    B --> C[Filter: *.csv, size limits]
    C --> D[Transformer: move to work dir]
    D --> E[Service activator: launch batch job]
    E --> F{outcome}
    F -- ok --> G[Archive channel]
    F -- error --> H[errorChannel → alert + quarantine]

Spring Integration gives polling, retry, routing and error channels for free; the heavy data processing is delegated to Spring Batch.
