6.1 The settlement job, production shape
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[CronJob Sat 23:30 IST] --> B[Job: sellerSettlementJob<br/>params: runDate, from, to]
    B --> C[Step 1: validate window<br/>tasklet]
    C --> D[Step 2: partitioned calculation<br/>8 partitions by seller]
    D --> E[Step 3: aggregate per seller<br/>+ TDS, adjustments]
    E --> F[Step 4: generate payout file<br/>FlatFileItemWriter]
    F --> G[Step 5: reconcile totals<br/>fail if mismatch]
    G --> H[Step 6: publish SettlementCompleted<br/>via outbox]
    H --> I[Archive + notify finance]
in/grocery/settlement/batch/ReconciliationStep.java
@Bean
Step reconcileStep(JobRepository jobRepository, PlatformTransactionManager txManager,
                   SettlementRepository settlements, JdbcClient jdbc) {
    return new StepBuilder("reconcileStep", jobRepository)
            .tasklet((contribution, chunkContext) -> {
                String runDate = runDateOf(chunkContext);
                BigDecimal lineSum = settlements.sumNetAmount(runDate);
                BigDecimal payoutSum = settlements.sumPayouts(runDate);
                if (lineSum.compareTo(payoutSum) != 0) {                                    // (1)!
                    throw new SettlementMismatchException(
                            "Lines total %s but payouts total %s for %s".formatted(lineSum, payoutSum, runDate));
                }
                contribution.getStepExecution().getExecutionContext()
                        .put("settlementTotal", lineSum.toPlainString());                   // (2)!
                return RepeatStatus.FINISHED;
            }, txManager)
            .build();
}
  1. Fail the job rather than pay out wrong numbers. Money jobs need an internal consistency check before producing an artifact anyone acts on.
  2. Recorded in the execution context so the summary and alerts can report it.
Publishing the result (never a direct call to other services)
@Bean
Step publishStep(JobRepository jobRepository, PlatformTransactionManager txManager, OutboxWriter outbox) {
    return new StepBuilder("publishStep", jobRepository)
            .tasklet((contribution, chunkContext) -> {
                String runDate = runDateOf(chunkContext);
                outbox.append("settlement", runDate, "SettlementCompleted",
                        new SettlementCompleted(runDate, totalOf(chunkContext)));            // (1)!
                return RepeatStatus.FINISHED;
            }, txManager)
            .build();
}
  1. The outbox (Chapter 23) — the job's database transaction and the event stay atomic, and downstream services get the news with at-least-once delivery.

docs.title: 6.2 Running batch jobs in Kubernetes
docs.text:
k8s/settlement-cronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: seller-settlement
spec:
  schedule: "30 23 * * 6"                                                                    # (1)!
  timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata"
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid                                                                  # (2)!
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 3600
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 7
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 14
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 0                                                                        # (3)!
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 14400
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: settlement
              image: registry.grocery.in/grocery/settlement-service@sha256:...               # (4)!
              args:
                - "--spring.profiles.active=prod,batch"
                - "--spring.batch.job.name=sellerSettlementJob"                              # (5)!
                - "--runDate=$(RUN_DATE)"
              env:
                - name: RUN_DATE
                  value: "{{ now | date \"2006-01-02\" }}"
              resources:
                requests: { cpu: "2", memory: "3Gi" }
                limits: { memory: "3Gi" }
  1. Saturday 23:30 IST — Kubernetes CronJobs support timeZone (1.27+); otherwise schedules run in UTC.
  2. Never two settlement runs at once.
  3. No automatic retry: a failed money job needs a human to look before restarting, and Spring Batch's restart is smarter than a fresh pod anyway.
  4. The same image as the service (Chapter 29) — code and job logic never diverge.
  5. Boot's JobLauncherApplicationRunner runs the named job and exits with a meaningful exit code.
Exit codes matter
@Bean
ExitCodeGenerator batchExitCodeGenerator(JobExplorer explorer) {
    return () -> explorer.getLastJobExecution(...) .getStatus() == BatchStatus.COMPLETED ? 0 : 1;   // (1)!
}
  1. A non-zero exit marks the Kubernetes Job failed, which is what alerting keys off. A job that logs an error and exits 0 is invisible.

docs.title: 6.3 Observability for batch
6.4 Batch platform conventions
docs.text: Convention Rationale One job per business outcome, named <domain><Purpose>Job Findable in the repository and dashboards Identifying parameters always include runDate Restartable, and re-running a day is explicit All writes idempotent (natural keys / on conflict) Chunk replay and restarts are safe Rejects always written to a file with reasons Data quality is a deliverable Money jobs end with a reconciliation step Never produce an unchecked artifact Results published via the outbox No direct calls from batch to services Batch runs in a separate pod with its own resources Long jobs must not disturb request serving Every job has a runbook: how to restart, how to skip, who to call 2 a.m. clarity

docs.title: 6.5 Choosing batch vs streaming
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Bulk work] --> B{Must results be a consistent snapshot<br/>at a point in time?}
    B -- yes --> BA[Batch]
    B -- no --> C{Continuous arrival, react per item?}
    C -- yes --> S[Streaming consumer — Chapter 23]
    C -- no --> D{Dataset small and bounded?}
    D -- yes --> SW["Scheduled sweeper — Chapter 25"]
    D -- no --> BA

Settlement is batch (a weekly snapshot with a reconciliation guarantee). Search indexing is streaming (Chapter 22). Auto-cancelling unpaid orders is a sweeper. Getting this right saves far more effort than optimizing the wrong choice.

docs.title: 6.6 Testing batch jobs
7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 / Batch 5 Boot 4.x / Batch 6 Builders JobBuilder/StepBuilder with repository + tx manager Same (verify signature changes) @EnableBatchProcessing Optional; Boot auto-configures Same — adding it can disable auto-configuration (verify) Job repository schema Provided DDL per database Verify schema changes between Batch 5 and 6 JobParameters types Typed parameters (Batch 5 changes) Verify converter behaviour Spring Integration 6.x 7.x (verify package/DSL changes) Observability spring.batch.* meters Same (verify names)

Batch schema upgrades are database migrations

A major Spring Batch upgrade may change the job repository schema. Plan it as a migration (Chapter 14), test restart of an in-flight job across versions, and prefer letting all jobs complete before upgrading.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Review Batch 6 release notes for repository schema and API changes; migrate the schema via Flyway.
  • Re-verify job parameter conversion (typed parameters changed in Batch 5).
  • Re-run restart tests after the upgrade — this is the behaviour most likely to break silently.
  • Check Spring Integration DSL compatibility and adapter package moves.
  • Re-validate metric names used by dashboards and alerts.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Chunk size tuned deliberately (hundreds to low thousands), balancing throughput against work lost on failure.
  2. Paging readers with a deterministic sort key; @StepScope for parameterized readers.
  3. Idempotent writes so chunk replay and restarts can't duplicate.
  4. Skips are bounded, recorded and reported back to the data's owner.
  5. Restartability tested, not assumed.
  6. Partition by a business key, sized against database capacity.
  7. Money jobs reconcile before producing artifacts, and publish via the outbox.
  8. Run as Kubernetes CronJobs with Forbid concurrency, meaningful exit codes and no blind retries.
  9. Alert on failure and absence; track business totals as a correctness signal.
  10. Spring Integration moves data; Spring Batch processes it — with an idempotent receiver and an error channel.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ A @Scheduled loop over three million rows — no restart, no skip handling, no visibility.

❌ Non-deterministic reader ordering with paging — silently skipped or duplicated rows.

❌ Unbounded skipLimit (or skips with no rejects file) — quiet data loss.

❌ Chunk size 1 (glacial) or 100,000 (long locks, huge rollbacks).

❌ Multi-threaded steps over a non-thread-safe reader, breaking restart.

❌ Calling other services directly from a job instead of publishing events.

❌ Jobs that exit 0 on failure — invisible to Kubernetes and alerting.

❌ Running heavy jobs in the request-serving pods.

❌ Auto-creating the batch schema in production.

❌ Using Spring Integration where a five-line Kafka consumer would do.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Restart reprocesses everything New JobInstance (parameters differed) Keep identifying parameters stable Duplicate rows after restart Non-idempotent writes Natural keys / on conflict do nothing Rows missing with paging reader No/duplicate sort key, or data changing mid-run Unique sort key; snapshot or filter by a fixed window Job hangs Long transaction, lock contention, external call in a chunk Smaller chunks; move remote calls out (Chapter 16) OutOfMemoryError Huge chunk, accumulating processor state, JPA persistence context growth Reduce chunk size; clear the context; use JDBC readers Partitions uneven, one runs for hours Range partitioning over skewed data Partition by business key with balanced groups Skips silently swallow bad data No SkipListener Rejects file + metrics + threshold alert Job didn't run at all CronJob misconfiguration, timezone, cluster maintenance Absence alerting (6.3) Two runs collided concurrencyPolicy: Allow Forbid + ShedLock for in-app schedules Integration flow stops processing Poller error with no error channel; stuck lock in the metadata store Error channel; inspect/clear metadata store entries

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Batch schema under Flyway; initialize-schema: never
  • Jobs launched explicitly (spring.batch.job.enabled: false), never on startup
  • Identifying parameters include a run date; restart tested
  • Idempotent writes verified by a restart test
  • Skips bounded with a rejects file and alerting
  • Reconciliation step for financial jobs
  • Results published via the outbox
  • CronJob with Forbid, resource limits, correct exit codes
  • Metrics, failure alerts and missed-run alerts
  • Runbook per job (restart, skip, escalation)

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What problem does Spring Batch solve?

Short answer: Processing large volumes reliably: chunked transactions, restart after failure, skip and retry policies, execution history and reporting — none of which a plain loop provides.

B1 · What is a chunk?

Short answer: A group of items read and processed, then written and committed together. The chunk size is the transaction boundary.

B1 · What are JobParameters for?

Short answer: They identify a job instance (e.g. runDate), which is how Spring Batch knows whether a launch is a new run or a restart.

B1 · What does returning null from an ItemProcessor do?

Short answer: Filters the item — it is not written and is not an error.

B1 · What is Spring Integration used for?

Short answer: Moving and transforming messages between systems using Enterprise Integration Patterns — polling files/SFTP, routing, filtering, aggregating, adapting protocols.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How does restart work?

Short answer: The same identifying parameters resolve to the same JobInstance; completed steps are skipped and the failing step resumes from the reader position saved in the ExecutionContext at the last chunk commit.

B2 · How do you choose a chunk size?

Short answer: Large enough to amortize commit cost (hundreds to low thousands), small enough to limit work lost on failure, lock duration and memory. Measure with a realistic dataset.

B2 · Cursor or paging reader?

Short answer: Paging for restartability and parallelism (with a deterministic unique sort key); cursor for single-threaded streaming where holding a connection open is acceptable.

B2 · How do you handle malformed rows in a file import?

Short answer: faultTolerant() with skip(...) and a skipLimit, plus a SkipListener writing every rejection with a reason to a rejects file, and metrics/alerts on skip counts.

B2 · How do you run a batch job in Kubernetes?

Short answer: As a CronJob running the same image in job mode (spring.batch.job.name), with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, resource limits, a proper exit code and alerting on failure and absence.

B2 · When would you use Spring Integration instead of plain code?

Short answer: For protocol adapters and EIP-shaped flows — SFTP polling, filtering, routing, aggregation, retry and error channels — where hand-written equivalents would be substantial and fragile.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · What makes a batch job safely restartable?

Short answer: Deterministic reader ordering, idempotent writes, no dependence on mutable global state, identifying parameters kept stable, and readers that persist their position. Prove it with a fail-mid-run-then-restart test asserting exact final counts.

B3 · Compare multi-threaded steps and partitioning.

Short answer: A multi-threaded step shares one reader across threads (fast, but the reader must be thread-safe and restartability suffers). Partitioning splits data into independent StepExecutions, each restartable — the safer default, and the basis for remote partitioning.

B3 · Why must processors and writers tolerate re-processing?

Short answer: On chunk failure in fault-tolerant mode, Spring Batch replays the chunk item by item to isolate the offender, so items can be processed more than once. Side effects must be idempotent.

B3 · How do you prevent a batch job from destabilizing the online system?

Short answer: Run it in separate pods with its own resources and connection pool, limit partition concurrency against database capacity, schedule off-peak, keep transactions short, and use read replicas for read-heavy phases (Chapter 12).

B3 · What is an idempotent receiver in Spring Integration?

Short answer: An interceptor backed by a MetadataStore that discards messages already seen (keyed by, say, filename plus timestamp) — the integration-flow equivalent of the inbox pattern (Chapter 23).

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design the weekly settlement job for 14,000 sellers.

Short answer: Partitioned by seller, idempotent writes keyed by (order_line_id, run_date), chunked at ~500, a reconciliation step that fails the job on mismatch, a payout file produced only after reconciliation, results published via the outbox, run as a CronJob with Forbid, with metrics on totals and alerts on failure, absence and deviation from last week.

B4 · Batch, streaming, or a sweeper — how do you decide?

Short answer: Batch when a consistent point-in-time snapshot and reporting/restart guarantees matter; streaming when items arrive continuously and can be handled independently; sweepers for small bounded datasets on a schedule. Most platforms need all three, chosen per use case.

B4 · How do you operate dozens of batch jobs?

Short answer: Shared conventions (naming, parameters, idempotency, rejects, outbox), a job catalog with owners and runbooks, uniform dashboards and alerts including missed runs, standard CronJob templates, and periodic reviews of duration trends against their windows.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · Is batch processing obsolete in an event-driven architecture?

Short answer: No. Reconciliation, regulatory reporting, settlements and bulk corrections need point-in-time consistency, restartability and auditable artifacts that stream processing doesn't naturally provide. Events and batch coexist: events keep things current, batch proves they're correct.

B5 · What's the biggest risk in financial batch jobs?

Short answer: Silent wrongness — a job that completes successfully with bad numbers. Mitigate with reconciliation steps, business-total monitoring against expectations, dual controls on payout files, immutable audit records and rehearsed restart procedures.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Settlement failed at 78% and the restart paid some sellers twice

Writes used plain inserts, so the replayed chunk and the restarted step duplicated rows. Fixes: unique key (order_line_id, run_date) with on conflict do nothing, a restart test asserting exact row counts, a reconciliation step comparing line totals against payouts, and a correction run for the affected sellers.

Scenario · A seller's 400,000-row feed fails after 40 minutes every night

One malformed row aborted the whole job because fault tolerance wasn't enabled, and the reader wasn't restartable (no unique sort key). Fixes: faultTolerant() with skips and a rejects file returned to the seller, a paging reader with a unique sort key, a throughput budget test with a 50,000-row file, and alerting on skip counts.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Razorpay reconciliation job

Daily, read the gateway settlement CSV, match each row against our payment table by payment_id, mark matched payments reconciled, and write mismatches (missing on either side, amount differences) to a report. Must be restartable, idempotent, skip malformed rows up to 100, and fail if more than 1% of rows are unmatched.

Solution ReconciliationJobConfig.java
@Bean
Job reconciliationJob(JobRepository jobRepository, Step matchStep, Step assessStep) {
    return new JobBuilder("razorpayReconciliationJob", jobRepository)
            .validator(parameters -> requireNonBlank(parameters, "settlementDate", "inputFile"))
            .start(matchStep)
            .next(assessStep)                                                     // (1)!
            .build();
}

@Bean
Step matchStep(JobRepository jobRepository, PlatformTransactionManager txManager,
               FlatFileItemReader<GatewayRow> reader, ReconciliationProcessor processor,
               ItemWriter<ReconciliationResult> writer, MismatchSkipListener skips) {
    return new StepBuilder("matchStep", jobRepository)
            .<GatewayRow, ReconciliationResult>chunk(500, txManager)
            .reader(reader).processor(processor).writer(writer)
            .faultTolerant()
            .skip(FlatFileParseException.class).skipLimit(100)
            .listener(skips)
            .build();
}
  1. Assessment is a separate step so the 1% rule is evaluated once over the whole run, not per chunk.
ReconciliationProcessor.java
@Component
class ReconciliationProcessor implements ItemProcessor<GatewayRow, ReconciliationResult> {

    private final PaymentRepository payments;

    @Override
    public ReconciliationResult process(GatewayRow row) {
        var payment = payments.findByGatewayPaymentId(row.paymentId());
        if (payment.isEmpty()) {
            return ReconciliationResult.missingLocally(row);                       // (1)!
        }
        if (payment.get().amountPaise() != row.amountPaise()) {
            return ReconciliationResult.amountMismatch(row, payment.get());
        }
        return ReconciliationResult.matched(row, payment.get());
    }
}
  1. Mismatches are results, not exceptions — they belong in the report, and the job continues.
ReconciliationWriter.java (idempotent)
@Bean
ItemWriter<ReconciliationResult> reconciliationWriter(JdbcClient jdbc, MismatchReportWriter report) {
    return results -> {
        for (var result : results) {
            jdbc.sql("""
                    insert into payment_reconciliation (payment_id, settlement_date, outcome, detail)
                    values (:paymentId, :date, :outcome, :detail)
                    on conflict (payment_id, settlement_date) do update
                      set outcome = excluded.outcome, detail = excluded.detail
                    """)                                                            // (1)!
                .params(result.asParams()).update();
            if (result.isMismatch()) {
                report.write(result);                                               // (2)!
            }
        }
    };
}
  1. Upsert keyed by (payment_id, settlement_date) — restart- and replay-safe.
  2. The mismatch report is regenerated from the table at the end of the run, so a restart doesn't produce a duplicated file.
AssessStep — the 1% rule
@Bean
Step assessStep(JobRepository jobRepository, PlatformTransactionManager txManager, JdbcClient jdbc) {
    return new StepBuilder("assessStep", jobRepository)
            .tasklet((contribution, chunkContext) -> {
                String date = dateOf(chunkContext);
                long total = jdbc.sql("select count(*) from payment_reconciliation where settlement_date = :d")
                        .param("d", date).query(Long.class).single();
                long mismatched = jdbc.sql("""
                        select count(*) from payment_reconciliation
                        where settlement_date = :d and outcome <> 'MATCHED'
                        """).param("d", date).query(Long.class).single();
                double ratio = total == 0 ? 0 : (double) mismatched / total;
                meters.gauge("grocery.reconciliation.mismatch.ratio", ratio);       // (1)!
                if (ratio > 0.01) {
                    throw new ReconciliationThresholdExceededException(mismatched, total);
                }
                return RepeatStatus.FINISHED;
            }, txManager)
            .build();
}
  1. The ratio is a business health metric even when the job passes; a slow upward drift is an early warning that something in the payment flow is diverging.
Tests
@Test void matchesPaymentsAndMarksReconciled() { }
@Test void mismatchesAreReportedButDoNotFailTheStep() { }
@Test void jobFailsWhenMismatchRatioExceedsOnePercent() { }
@Test void restartDoesNotDuplicateReconciliationRows() { }
@Test void malformedRowsAreSkippedUpToTheLimit() { }

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Spring Batch is for bulk work that must be restartable, auditable and tolerant of bad data — chunks, job repository, skip/retry, partitioning.
  • Restartability depends on three things: stable identifying parameters, deterministic reader ordering, idempotent writes. Test it.
  • Skips must be bounded and reported; a rejects file is a deliverable.
  • Partition by business key, sized against database capacity.
  • Financial jobs reconcile before producing artifacts and publish results via the outbox.
  • Spring Integration moves data (SFTP, files, protocols) with idempotent receipt and error channels; Batch processes it.
  • Run as CronJobs with Forbid, real exit codes, and alerts on failure and absence.
  • Choose deliberately between batch, streaming and sweepers.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Batch Reference — domain model, configuring steps, fault tolerance, scaling and partitioning, testing
  • Spring Boot Reference — Batch Applications (job launching, exit codes, schema)
  • Spring Integration Reference — Java DSL, channel adapters, idempotent receiver, error handling
  • Enterprise Integration Patterns (Hohpe & Woolf) — the vocabulary Spring Integration implements

32 GraphQL, gRPC, WebSocket & SSE · 34 Performance Engineering

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Two weeks before Diwali, someone asks: "can we handle 5× traffic?" The honest answer is a number, not a feeling — and producing that number is what performance engineering does.

Most performance work in the wild is guesswork: a developer suspects the JSON serializer, spends three days optimizing it, and ships a 2% improvement while the real cost was an N+1 query (Chapter 13) and a missing index (Chapter 12). The discipline that avoids this is boring and reliable:

  1. Define the target — a latency budget per endpoint and a throughput goal.
  2. Measure under realistic load — with an open-model load test, not a laptop benchmark.
  3. Find the bottleneck — profiler and flame graph, not intuition.
  4. Fix the top item, then re-measure. The bottleneck moves; the second-biggest problem is now the biggest.
  5. Guard the gain — a performance test in CI so it doesn't quietly regress.

This chapter covers that loop concretely: latency budgets and Little's law, load testing (including the coordinated-omission trap that makes most load tests lie), JFR and async-profiler with flame graphs, JVM memory and GC analysis, heap dumps and leak hunting, the Spring-specific bottlenecks that account for most real incidents, JMH for the rare micro-benchmark, capacity planning and sale-day readiness.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — percentiles, a first load test, obvious bottlenecks B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — profiling, GC basics, common Spring problems B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — flame graphs, allocation, leak analysis, tail latency B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — capacity planning, budgets, regression gates B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — performance as an organizational practice

docs.title: 2.1 Measure the right numbers
docs.text:
Metric Why p50 / p95 / p99 / p99.9 Averages hide everything; a 40 ms average with a 3 s p99 means thousands of angry customers Throughput (req/s) at a given latency "Fast" is meaningless without load Concurrency The link between the two (2.2) Error rate under load Degradation often appears as errors before latency Saturation (queue depth, pool waits) The leading indicator — it rises before latency does

RED for services (Rate, Errors, Duration), USE for resources (Utilization, Saturation, Errors) — the two checklists from Chapter 27, used here as a diagnostic order.

docs.title: 2.2 Little's law
docs.text:
L = λ × W: concurrency = throughput × latency.

  • 2,000 req/s at 50 ms → 100 requests in flight.
  • Those 100 requests each hold a database connection for 20 ms → 40 connections needed (Chapter 12).
  • If latency doubles to 100 ms at the same arrival rate, concurrency doubles to 200 — which is why latency growth causes resource exhaustion, not the other way round.

This one formula sizes thread pools, connection pools, bulkheads and partition counts.

docs.title: 2.3 Utilization and the latency cliff
docs.text:
Queueing theory, simplified: as utilization approaches 100%, queue length (and latency) grows non-linearly.

Utilization Relative queue wait 50% 1× 70% ~2.3× 80% ~4× 90% ~9× 95% ~19×

Which is why capacity plans target 60–70% at peak, not 95%. The last 30% is headroom for spikes, deploys and losing a zone.

docs.title: 2.4 Latency budgets
docs.text:
Example
Checkout p99 target: 2000 ms
  gateway + network            120 ms
  auth (token validation)       10 ms
  pricing (2 attempts × 600)  1200 ms worst case  ← the dominant risk
  inventory                    500 ms
  database transactions        200 ms
  serialization + overhead      50 ms

Budgets make trade-offs explicit: if pricing worst-case doesn't fit, either its timeout shrinks, its retry disappears, or it moves out of the synchronous path (Chapters 19, 26).

docs.title: 2.5 Load test types
docs.text:
Type Question Smoke Does it work at all under a trickle? Load Does it meet the target at expected peak? Stress Where does it break, and how? Spike Can it survive a sudden 10× (flash sale, push notification)? Soak Does it degrade over 8 hours (leaks, fragmentation, log growth)? Breakpoint What is the maximum throughput per pod, for capacity math?

Coordinated omission

A closed-model test (N virtual users, each sending the next request after the previous completes) stops sending requests when the system is slow, so it never measures the queueing that real users experience. Use an open model (constant or ramping arrival rate) so requests keep arriving regardless of response time. This one setting is the difference between a load test that predicts production and one that flatters it.

docs.title: 2.6 Profiling tools
docs.text:
Tool Use Overhead JFR (Java Flight Recorder) Always-on production profiling: CPU, allocation, locks, GC, I/O ~1–2% async-profiler CPU, allocation, lock and wall-clock flame graphs; no safepoint bias ~1–3% Heap dumps + MAT/JOL Leak analysis, retained sizes Pause to capture Micrometer metrics Continuous, aggregate (Chapter 27) Negligible EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) Where the database actually spends time — JMH Micro-benchmarks of small, hot code Offline only

Sampling profilers (JFR, async-profiler) show where time goes with low overhead; instrumenting profilers distort the very hot paths you're measuring.

docs.title: 2.7 Flame graphs
docs.text:
Example
width  = share of samples (time or allocations)
stacked = call depth

Read them top-down for "what is running" and look for wide plateaus: a single wide frame is the bottleneck. A flat, evenly-divided graph usually means the bottleneck is not CPU — it's I/O, locks or a downstream service (check wall-clock mode).

docs.title: 2.8 GC in one table
docs.text:
Collector Best for Trade-off G1 (default) General server workloads Balanced pauses (target MaxGCPauseMillis) Generational ZGC Large heaps, low pause requirements More CPU/memory overhead Parallel Batch throughput (Chapter 33) Long pauses Serial Tiny containers Single-threaded

Tune allocation before tuning GC. Most "GC problems" are allocation-rate problems: the fix is producing less garbage, not a new flag.

docs.title: 3.1 Where a request's time goes
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Network + TLS] --> B[Ingress / gateway]
    B --> C[Server accept + thread/virtual thread]
    C --> D[Filters: security, tracing, logging]
    D --> E[Controller + validation + mapping]
    E --> F[Service: business logic]
    F --> G[Database: pool wait + query + fetch]
    F --> H[HTTP clients: pool wait + network + parse]
    F --> I[Cache: network + serialization]
    E --> J[Serialization of the response]
    J --> K[Network write]

In practice, for a typical Spring service: G and H dominate, J matters for large payloads, and everything else is noise — which is why profiling before optimizing matters so much.

docs.title: 3.2 Latency under saturation
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Arrival rate rises] --> B{Service rate sufficient?}
    B -- yes --> C[Latency ≈ service time]
    B -- no --> D[Queues form: connection pool, thread pool, socket backlog]
    D --> E[Wait time grows non-linearly]
    E --> F[Concurrency grows — Little's law]
    F --> G[More memory, more context switches, more contention]
    G --> H[Service rate falls further]
    H --> E

That feedback loop is why an overloaded system doesn't degrade gracefully by itself — and why load shedding (Chapter 26) exists.

docs.title: 3.3 GC and allocation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Allocation in Eden] --> B{Eden full?}
    B -- yes --> C[Young GC: copy survivors]
    C --> D{Survived enough cycles<br/>or survivor space full?}
    D -- yes --> E[Promote to Old]
    E --> F{Old fills up?}
    F -- yes --> G[Concurrent cycle / mixed GC]
    G --> H{Can't keep up?}
    H -- yes --> I[Full GC — long pause]

Key signals: allocation rate (MB/s), promotion rate (how much survives — high means objects live too long, often a cache or a big request buffer), and pause time distribution. Rising heap-after-full-GC over hours is the leak signature.

docs.title: 4.1 A first load test (open model)
4.2 Reading the result
docs.text:
Example
     http_req_duration{endpoint:checkout}
       p(50)=142ms  p(95)=690ms  p(99)=2.41s   ← threshold breached
     http_req_failed................: 0.04%
     dropped_iterations.............: 0        ← the load generator kept up

The p99 breach is the question; the p50 is fine, which means something occasional is slow — GC, a pool wait, a cold cache or a slow dependency. That's a profiling job, not a guessing job.

docs.title: 4.3 Turning on JFR
docs.text:
Terminal
# Always-on in production (Chapter 29 sets this in JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS)
-XX:StartFlightRecording=disk=true,maxsize=200M,maxage=1h,dumponexit=true,filename=/dumps/app.jfr

# Ad hoc, on a running pod
kubectl exec order-service-abc -- jcmd 1 JFR.start name=triage settings=profile duration=120s \
    filename=/dumps/triage.jfr                                                   # (1)!
kubectl cp order-service-abc:/dumps/triage.jfr ./triage.jfr                      # (2)!
  1. settings=profile gives richer sampling than the default at slightly higher cost — fine for two minutes.
  2. Open in JDK Mission Control: hot methods, allocation by class, lock contention, GC pauses, and slow socket reads — all correlated in time.

docs.title: 4.4 The cheapest wins first
docs.text:
Before any tuning, check the list that explains most Spring performance incidents:

Check How N+1 queries Query-count test (Chapter 13); spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics Missing index EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) on the slow query (Chapter 12) No pagination Any endpoint returning an unbounded list Pool exhaustion hikaricp.connections.pending > 0 (Chapter 12) Chatty HTTP Calls per request to each dependency (Chapter 19) DEBUG logging in production logging.level (Chapter 07) Serializing huge payloads Response size histogram Remote calls inside transactions Chapter 16

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Profiling with async-profiler
docs.text:
Terminal
# CPU flame graph for 60 seconds
./profiler.sh -d 60 -e cpu -f /dumps/cpu.html $(pgrep -f order-service)          # (1)!

# Allocation profile (who creates the garbage)
./profiler.sh -d 60 -e alloc -f /dumps/alloc.html 1                              # (2)!

# Wall-clock: where wall time goes, including waiting
./profiler.sh -d 60 -e wall -t -f /dumps/wall.html 1                             # (3)!

# Lock contention
./profiler.sh -d 60 -e lock -f /dumps/lock.html 1
  1. CPU mode answers "what burns CPU".
  2. Allocation mode answers "what creates garbage" — usually more actionable than GC tuning.
  3. Wall-clock mode is the one people forget: when the service is slow but CPU is at 20%, the time is spent waiting, and only wall-clock profiling shows where.

A real finding from a checkout profile:

Example
[wall] 62% in JdbcTemplate.query → PgConnection.receiveResponse   ← waiting on the database
[cpu]  18% in ObjectMapper.writeValue                              ← serializing a 400 KB response
[alloc] 41% char[] from StringBuilder in a logging call            ← string concatenation at DEBUG

Three fixes, in order of value: index the query, paginate the response, and use parameterized logging (Chapter 07). None of them is a JVM flag.

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — Database-side measurement
docs.text:
Find the expensive statements
select calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, rows, query
from pg_stat_statements
order by total_exec_time desc
limit 20;                                                                          -- (1)
Understand one of them
explain (analyze, buffers, verbose)
select o.* from customer_order o
where o.customer_id = 'C-1' and o.status = 'DELIVERED'
order by o.placed_at desc limit 20;                                                -- (2)
  1. total_exec_time (not mean) finds what actually costs the system: a 3 ms query called 2 million times beats a 400 ms query called twice.
  2. Look for sequential scans on large tables, rows removed by filter, and Buffers: read (disk) versus hit (cache).

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Memory and GC analysis
docs.text:
Is it a leak?
kubectl exec order-service-abc -- jcmd 1 GC.heap_info                              # (1)!
# Repeat over an hour: heap used *after* full GC trending upward = leak
kubectl exec order-service-abc -- jcmd 1 GC.heap_dump /dumps/heap.hprof            # (2)!
  1. Cheap, repeatable. Transient spikes are normal; a rising floor is not.
  2. Heap dumps pause the JVM and are large — take one from a single pod, ideally one already removed from rotation.

In Eclipse MAT, the workflow is always: Leak Suspects report → dominator tree → path to GC roots. Typical culprits in Spring applications:

Leak Cause Unbounded ConcurrentHashMap cache No eviction (Chapter 21's maximumSize) ThreadLocal not cleared Pooled threads retain per-request objects Growing listener/observer lists Registration without deregistration Session data Large objects in HTTP sessions Large ExecutionContext/batch state Accumulating per-chunk state (Chapter 33) Classloader retention Hot reload/DevTools in the wrong environment (Chapter 05) The leak that hides in plain sight
private final Map<String, PriceView> priceCache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();        // ❌ (1)!
  1. It works beautifully for a week, then the pod OOMs. Use Caffeine with maximumSize and a TTL (Chapter 21), or Redis.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Allocation reduction where it matters
docs.text:
Before: 41% of allocations
log.debug("Pricing " + sku + " for pincode " + pincode + " with rules " + rules);    // (1)!
After
log.debug("Pricing {} for pincode {} with rules {}", sku, pincode, rules);           // (2)!
  1. String concatenation happens even when DEBUG is disabled — the arguments are evaluated and joined before the call.
  2. Parameterized logging defers formatting until the level check passes (Chapter 07).

Other high-yield patterns:

Pattern Fix Boxing in hot loops (Map<String, Integer> counters) Primitive maps, or accumulate then box once Rebuilding the same immutable objects per request Cache them as constants Copying large collections defensively in hot paths Return unmodifiable views Serializing fields nobody reads Trim DTOs (Chapter 11) Regex compiled per call static final Pattern

Don't micro-optimize the 2%

Allocation work pays off when the profiler shows a wide allocation frame. Rewriting a stream into a loop because "streams are slow" without a profile is how teams spend a sprint gaining nothing and adding bugs.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — GC tuning, carefully
docs.text:
Measure first
-Xlog:gc*:file=/dumps/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20M       # (1)!

Micrometer already exposes jvm.gc.pause, jvm.gc.memory.allocated and jvm.gc.memory.promoted (Chapter 27) — graph those before touching flags.

Symptom Likely cause Action Frequent young GCs, short pauses High allocation rate Reduce allocation (5.4) Rising promotion rate Objects surviving too long: caches, large per-request buffers Fix lifetimes, cap caches Long mixed/full GCs Heap too small, fragmentation, humongous objects More heap, reduce large arrays, consider ZGC p99 spikes matching GC pauses Pause-sensitive workload Generational ZGC; smaller heap per pod, more pods Heap grows until OOM Leak Heap dump, not flags If (and only if) the data supports it
-XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational        # large heap, pause-sensitive (verify flags for your JDK)
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100              # G1 target — a goal, not a guarantee
  1. GC logs remain the ground truth; keep them on disk with rotation, like JFR.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Tail latency
docs.text:
p99 is rarely "the code is slow". The usual contributors, in the order worth checking:

Cause Evidence Fix Connection pool waits hikaricp.connections.pending Size pools (Chapter 12), shorten transactions GC pauses jvm.gc.pause p99 aligned with request p99 Allocation, collector choice CPU throttling container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total Remove/raise CPU limits (Chapter 30) Cold caches after deploy Hit-rate dip after rollout Warm-up (Chapter 21) JIT warm-up First-minute latency CDS/AOT (Chapter 29), traffic ramping Retries Duplicate downstream calls One retry layer, budget (Chapter 26) Lock contention lock profile, LongTaskTimer Reduce critical sections Slow dependency p99 http.client.requests p99 Timeouts, bulkheads, degradation Noisy neighbours Node-level metrics Resource requests, anti-affinity Making tail latency visible per dependency
Timer.builder("grocery.dependency.call")
     .tag("dependency", "pricing")
     .publishPercentileHistogram()
     .serviceLevelObjectives(Duration.ofMillis(200), Duration.ofMillis(600))        // (1)!
     .register(meters);
  1. SLO buckets make "how often did pricing exceed its budget?" a cheap query rather than an estimate (Chapter 27).

docs.title: 5.7 Level 3 — JMH, for the rare case it's warranted
6.1 Sale-day readiness programme
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Forecast: 5× peak orders/min] --> B[Model per-service load<br/>from production ratios]
    B --> C[Breakpoint tests: max req/s per pod]
    C --> D[Capacity plan: pods, DB, cache, partitions]
    D --> E[Load test at 1.5× forecast<br/>full journey, open model]
    E --> F{Thresholds met?}
    F -- no --> G[Profile → fix top bottleneck → repeat]
    F -- yes --> H[Soak test 8h + spike test]
    H --> I[Game day: chaos + degradation<br/>Chapters 26, 30]
    I --> J[Pre-scale, freeze deploys, runbooks ready]
Capacity math, written down
Forecast peak: 3,000 orders/min = 50 orders/s
Checkout path per order: 1 cart write, 1 pricing call, 1 inventory call, 1 payment call, 3 DB tx

order-service:
  measured breakpoint: 180 req/s per pod at p99 < 800ms (2 vCPU, 1 GiB)
  target utilization 65% → 117 req/s per pod
  checkout req/s at peak ≈ 50 × 4 (cart, quote, order, poll) = 200 req/s
  pods = ceil(200 / 117) = 2 → minimum 6 for zone loss + headroom      ← replicas: 6

database:
  connections = pods × pool(20) = 120 (order) + 80 (catalog) + ...  = 340 < max_connections 500  ✅
  writes/s at peak ≈ 150 → within measured 1,200/s headroom          ✅

Kafka:
  order events 50/s × 5 consumers; partitions 12 ✅
Redis:
  price cache 2,000 gets/s, p99 0.6 ms at 3× load ✅

The value isn't the numbers — it's that each one is measured, written down, and rechecked when something changes.

docs.title: 6.2 Performance regression gate
docs.text:
.github/workflows/nightly-perf.yml (excerpt)
      - name: Deploy to perf environment
        run: ./scripts/deploy-perf.sh "$IMAGE_DIGEST"                                # (1)!

      - name: Run checkout scenario
        run: k6 run --out json=results.json perf/checkout.js

      - name: Compare against baseline
        run: |
          python scripts/compare_perf.py results.json baselines/checkout.json \
            --max-p95-regression 15 --max-p99-regression 20                          # (2)!
  1. Same digest as the release candidate (Chapter 29) against production-like data volumes.
  2. Fail on a relative regression: absolute thresholds drift with environment noise, while "15% slower than last week" is a real signal. Update baselines deliberately, with a comment explaining why.
What to guard Budget Checkout p95 / p99 800 ms / 2 s Product page p95 300 ms Search p95 400 ms Startup time (Chapter 29) 5 s Batch throughput (Chapter 33) 50k rows / 2 min Image size 250 MB

docs.title: 6.3 Incident-time performance triage
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Latency alert fires] --> B[SLO dashboard: which endpoint, since when?]
    B --> C{Deploy or config change at that time?}
    C -- yes --> D[Roll back by digest first, investigate after]
    C -- no --> E[Dependency panel: which client call is slow?]
    E -- a dependency --> F["Their dashboards; breaker state; degrade"]
    E -- none --> G[Resource panel: pool pending, GC pause, CPU throttling]
    G -- pool pending --> H[Long transactions? Slow query? Pool too small?]
    G -- GC --> I[Allocation spike? Leak? Heap after full GC?]
    G -- throttling --> J[CPU limits — Chapter 30]
    G -- clean --> K[JFR/async-profiler wall-clock for 60s on one pod]
    K --> L[Flame graph → the wide frame]

The first branch matters most: most latency regressions are changes, and rolling back is faster than diagnosing.

docs.title: 6.4 The fixes that actually moved the needle
docs.text:
A record from the platform's own tuning cycles, roughly in order of impact:

Problem Fix Result N+1 on order lines @EntityGraph + query-count test (Chapter 13) p99 2.4 s → 380 ms Missing composite index on (customer_id, placed_at) Index + EXPLAIN verification Order history 1.1 s → 40 ms Pricing called per cart line Bulk endpoint (Chapter 20) 22 calls → 1 per checkout Unbounded product list endpoint Pagination + size cap 400 KB → 18 KB responses Remote call inside a transaction Moved outside (Chapter 16) Pool pending → 0 DEBUG logging in production Level fixed; parameterized logging 15% CPU reclaimed Cold cache after every deploy Warm-up before readiness (Chapter 21) Post-deploy spike removed CPU limits causing throttling Limits removed on latency-sensitive services p99 −220 ms Synchronous notification in checkout Moved to outbox/async (Chapters 23, 25) −150 ms p50

Not one of them was a JVM flag. That's the pattern, not a coincidence.

docs.title: 6.5 Performance as a practice
docs.text: Practice Cadence Latency budget per critical endpoint Defined once, reviewed quarterly Nightly perf run with regression gate Every night Breakpoint test per service Quarterly and before peak season Soak test Before peak season, and after major runtime upgrades Capacity model refresh Quarterly, and on traffic-pattern changes Profiling during load tests Every load test, not only when it fails "Top 5 slow queries" review Monthly with the database owner Post-incident performance actions Tracked like any other defect

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Baseline throughput — Similar; gains come from the JDK and your code Virtual threads Java 21+ Same; bottleneck moves to dependencies (Chapter 25) Startup CDS supported CDS + JDK AOT cache (Chapter 29) Jackson 2 3 — re-measure serialization-heavy paths (Chapter 11) Micrometer histograms ✅ ✅ (verify metric names) GC defaults JDK-dependent Generational ZGC matured in recent JDKs

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Re-run the full load suite before and after the upgrade on the same data and hardware.
  • Compare allocation profiles (Jackson 3 and Framework changes shift them).
  • Re-measure startup and batch throughput budgets.
  • Re-check pool sizing if virtual threads are newly enabled.
  • Refresh performance baselines deliberately, with a note explaining the change.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Budget first: latency targets per endpoint, derived from user expectations, decomposed across dependencies.
  2. Open-model load tests with thresholds as pass/fail gates.
  3. Profile before optimizing; use wall-clock mode when CPU looks idle.
  4. Fix the top item, then re-measure — bottlenecks move.
  5. Reduce allocation before tuning GC; tune GC only with data.
  6. Watch saturation (pool pending, queue depth) as the leading indicator.
  7. Target 60–70% utilization at peak; the rest is headroom.
  8. Guard gains with a nightly regression gate on relative change.
  9. Capacity math written down and rechecked when anything changes.
  10. Triage starts with "what changed?", and rollback beats diagnosis during an incident.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Optimizing without a profile ("I think it's the serializer").

❌ Closed-model load tests that hide queueing (coordinated omission).

❌ Reporting averages; ignoring p99 and p99.9.

❌ Load testing against an empty database or a single pod, then extrapolating.

❌ GC flag tuning as a first response to latency problems.

❌ Micro-benchmarks of code that never appears in a profile.

❌ Adding caching to hide an unindexed query (now you have two problems, and a cold-start cliff).

❌ Running at 90% utilization "for efficiency".

❌ Performance work with no regression guard — the gain is gone in two sprints.

❌ Using production as the load-test environment without controls.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom First checks Typical cause p99 high, p50 fine GC pauses, pool pending, CPU throttling, retries Saturation or pauses, not code Throughput plateaus below target Pool sizes, downstream limits, CPU saturation A bounded resource (Little's law) Latency rises steadily over hours Heap after full GC, cache size, connection counts Leak or unbounded growth CPU low, latency high Wall-clock profile Waiting on I/O, locks or a dependency Slow only after deploy Cold caches, JIT warm-up, config change Warm-up, CDS/AOT Fast in staging, slow in production Data volume, network, noisy neighbours, config differences Test with production-sized data Database CPU pegged pg_stat_statements, missing indexes, N+1 Query problems, not app problems Memory OK but pods OOM-killed Non-heap (metaspace, threads, direct buffers) Chapter 29's sizing Load generator is the bottleneck dropped_iterations, generator CPU Scale the generator, distribute it

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Latency budget documented per critical endpoint
  • Load, stress, spike and soak scenarios exist and run on a schedule
  • Load tests use an open model with thresholds
  • JFR always on; async-profiler available for triage
  • GC logs and JVM metrics collected and graphed
  • Breakpoint numbers per service feed a written capacity model
  • Nightly performance regression gate with maintained baselines
  • Triage runbook linked from latency alerts
  • Pre-peak programme: capacity, soak, game day, pre-scale, deploy freeze

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Why look at p99 instead of the average?

Short answer: Averages hide the slow tail. With 2,000 requests/s, a 1% slow tail is 20 users per second having a bad experience — and the tail is what drives timeouts and retries.

B1 · What is a latency budget?

Short answer: A target for an endpoint, split across its dependencies and internal work, so every component knows how much time it may consume.

B1 · Name three common causes of slow Spring endpoints.

Short answer: N+1 queries, missing database indexes, and unpaginated responses. Chatty HTTP calls and long transactions are close behind.

B1 · What does a profiler tell you that metrics don't?

Short answer: Which code paths consume time or memory. Metrics say that something is slow; the profiler says where.

B1 · What is JFR?

Short answer: Java Flight Recorder — a low-overhead, built-in profiler that records CPU, allocation, locks, GC and I/O events, suitable for always-on production use.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · What is Little's law and how do you use it?

Short answer: Concurrency = throughput × latency. It sizes thread and connection pools, explains why rising latency exhausts resources, and converts a throughput target into a capacity number.

B2 · What is coordinated omission?

Short answer: A closed-model load test stops sending requests while waiting for slow responses, so it under-reports latency. Use an arrival-rate (open model) executor so load continues regardless of response time.

B2 · How do you find a memory leak?

Short answer: Track heap used after full GC over time; if the floor rises, take a heap dump and analyze the dominator tree and paths to GC roots. Common causes: unbounded caches, uncleaned ThreadLocals, growing listener lists.

B2 · How do you decide whether to tune GC?

Short answer: Only after looking at allocation rate, promotion rate and pause distribution. Most GC symptoms are allocation problems; reduce garbage first, and change collectors only with supporting data.

B2 · Why can adding a cache make things worse?

Short answer: It hides the real problem (an unindexed query), adds a cold-start cliff, invites staleness bugs and creates a new failure mode. Fix the query first; cache afterwards if reuse justifies it.

B2 · What's the difference between CPU and wall-clock profiling?

Short answer: CPU profiling shows where processing time goes; wall-clock shows where elapsed time goes, including blocking. When CPU is low and latency high, wall-clock is the mode you need.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through diagnosing a p99 regression.

Short answer: Check what changed (deploy/config) and roll back if so; otherwise look at dependency latency, then saturation signals (pool pending, queue depth, GC pause, CPU throttling); if those are clean, capture a 60-second wall-clock profile and read the flame graph for a wide frame.

B3 · Why does latency explode near 100% utilization?

Short answer: Queueing: wait time grows non-linearly with utilization, and rising latency increases concurrency (Little's law), which increases contention and reduces service rate — a feedback loop. Hence 60–70% targets and load shedding.

B3 · How do you read a flame graph?

Short answer: Width is share of samples; look for wide plateaus rather than deep stacks. An even, flat distribution usually means the bottleneck isn't CPU — switch to wall-clock or lock profiling.

B3 · When is JMH the right tool?

Short answer: For small, CPU-bound routines that a profiler has shown to be hot, comparing implementations — with warm-up, forks and Blackhole to avoid JIT artifacts. Never for I/O-bound code or code that never appears in a profile.

B3 · How do virtual threads change performance work?

Short answer: Thread count stops being the limit, so bottlenecks move to downstream resources — connection pools, dependency capacity, API quotas. Pool sizing and bulkheads become the tuning surface (Chapters 25, 26).

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you prepare a platform for 5× traffic?

Short answer: Forecast and decompose per service; measure per-pod breakpoints; build a written capacity model covering pods, connections, partitions and cache; load test the full journey at 1.5× forecast with thresholds; profile and fix iteratively; soak and spike test; run game days; pre-scale and freeze deploys.

B4 · How do you stop performance from regressing?

Short answer: Budgets per endpoint, a nightly load test with relative-regression thresholds, startup and batch budgets, profiling during load tests, and treating regressions as defects with owners rather than "we'll look at it later".

B4 · A team asks to double the connection pool to fix latency. Response?

Short answer: Check pending and query durations first. Pool waits usually mean slow queries or long transactions; doubling the pool moves contention into the database, where it's worse. Fix the query, shorten the transaction, then size the pool against database capacity (Chapter 12).

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How do you build performance into engineering culture?

Short answer: Budgets as part of design; load tests and profiles as normal deliverables; regression gates in CI; capacity models owned and reviewed; incident reviews that produce performance actions; and visible dashboards so the organization sees the cost of decisions rather than discovering it during a sale.

B5 · When is 'good enough' the right answer?

Short answer: When latency is within budget and headroom is adequate at forecast peak, further optimization has negative return compared with features or reliability work. Performance effort belongs where user-visible budgets are threatened or costs scale badly — not everywhere.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Checkout p99 is 2.4 s but CPU is 20%

A wall-clock profile showed 62% of time waiting on a single query missing a composite index, plus pool waits behind it. Fixes: add (customer_id, status, placed_at), verify with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), add a query-count test, re-run the load test — p99 fell to 380 ms and pool pending returned to zero.

Scenario · Pods OOM after eight hours, never in a load test

The load test ran for ten minutes; the soak test (added afterwards) reproduced it in three hours. A ConcurrentHashMap price cache had no eviction. Fixes: Caffeine with maximumSize and TTL, heap-after-GC monitoring, and an 8-hour soak test added to the pre-peak programme.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Diagnose and fix a slow endpoint

GET /api/v1/customers/{id}/orders?page=0&size=20 takes 1.8 s at p95 under load. Produce: a load test isolating it, the profiling commands you'd run, the database analysis, the likely fixes, and the regression guard you'd add.

Solution perf/order-history.js
export const options = {
  scenarios: { history: {
    executor: 'constant-arrival-rate', rate: 150, timeUnit: '1s',
    duration: '5m', preAllocatedVUs: 100, maxVUs: 800,
  }},
  thresholds: { 'http_req_duration': ['p(95)<300'], 'http_req_failed': ['rate<0.001'] },
};
export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.BASE}/api/v1/customers/${randomCustomer()}/orders?page=0&size=20`,   // (1)!
           { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.TOKEN}` } });
}
  1. Random customers, not one repeated id — otherwise the database and caches serve one hot row and the test proves nothing.
Profile during the run
./profiler.sh -d 60 -e wall -t -f wall.html 1          # where does elapsed time go?
./profiler.sh -d 60 -e alloc -f alloc.html 1           # garbage from serialization?
kubectl exec pod -- jcmd 1 JFR.start settings=profile duration=120s filename=/dumps/t.jfr
Database analysis
select calls, mean_exec_time, total_exec_time, query from pg_stat_statements
where query ilike '%customer_order%' order by total_exec_time desc limit 5;

explain (analyze, buffers)
select o.* from customer_order o where o.customer_id = $1
order by o.placed_at desc limit 20 offset 0;

Findings and fixes (the usual shape):

Finding Fix Seq scan on customer_order (8M rows) Index (customer_id, placed_at desc) Each order triggers a query for its lines (N+1) @EntityGraph / projection, plus a query-count test (Chapter 13) Response includes full line details nobody displays Slim the DTO; separate detail endpoint (Chapter 11) count(*) for total pages on every page Cursor pagination, or drop the exact total (Chapter 20) Pool pending > 0 during the test Falls to zero once the query is fast — no pool change needed Regression guard
@Test
void orderHistoryUsesBoundedQueries() {
    var count = QueryCountAssertions.measure(() -> service.history("C-1", PageRequest.of(0, 20)));
    assertThat(count.selects()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);                                   // (1)!
}
And in the nightly gate
  - run: k6 run perf/order-history.js        # thresholds: p95 < 300ms
  - run: python scripts/compare_perf.py results.json baselines/order-history.json --max-p95-regression 15
  1. The query-count test catches the N+1 returning long before the nightly load test would — fast feedback for a cheap assertion.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Budget, measure, profile, fix the top item, re-measure, guard — in that order.
  • Little's law connects throughput, latency and concurrency; it sizes everything.
  • Latency explodes above ~80% utilization — plan for 60–70% at peak.
  • Open-model load tests or your numbers are optimistic fiction.
  • Wall-clock profiling when CPU is idle but latency is high.
  • Reduce allocation before tuning GC; heap-after-full-GC trending up means a leak, not a flag.
  • The real fixes are usually indexes, N+1s, pagination, transaction scope and logging — not JVM tuning.
  • Guard every gain with a regression gate and a written capacity model.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Systems Performance (Brendan Gregg) — USE method, flame graphs, methodology
