docs.title: Part 3 · Enterprise
docs.text:
Chapters 35–44 · 8–15+ years. Microservices, distributed consistency, architecture styles, multi-tenancy, security architecture, Spring AI, platform starters, upgrades, leadership and the capstone — everything a platform needs to scale across teams and years.

Primary bands: B3–B5. Every chapter follows the same nine-part structure — introduction, core concepts, internals, Levels 1–4 of hands-on code, Boot 3 vs 4, production playbook, and interview questions — so you can read any chapter at the depth your band needs.

Chapter 35 · Microservices & Spring Cloud 36 · Distributed Data & Consistency 37 · DDD, Hexagonal Architecture & the Modular Monolith 38 · Multi-Tenancy 39 · Enterprise Security Architecture 40 · Spring AI 41 · Spring Internals & Custom Starters 42 · Migration & Upgrade Engineering 43 · Engineering Leadership for Senior Spring Engineers 44 · Capstone — The Grocery Marketplace

See Reading Paths for suggested routes through the handbook by experience level and goal.

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Part 2 made a single service production-grade. Part 3 asks the harder question: how do twenty-six of them work together without becoming a distributed monolith?

The grocery platform's services were not all created equal. Some were carved from a monolith along real business seams and can deploy independently. Others were split because "microservices" was the plan, and now a checkout change requires coordinated releases of four services, a shared library version bump and a schema migration nobody owns. The second group is the expensive one.

The difference is rarely technology. It is:

  • Boundaries drawn along business capabilities rather than database tables.
  • Data ownership — one service writes each piece of data; others get copies through events.
  • Independent deployability — a service can ship without a synchronized release train.
  • A gateway that centralizes cross-cutting edge concerns instead of duplicating them 26 times.
  • Operational maturity — every service has an owner, SLOs, runbooks and on-call.

This chapter covers the platform layer: decomposition principles and the strangler-fig migration that produced these services, Spring Cloud Gateway as the edge (routing, authentication, rate limiting, resilience), service discovery in and out of Kubernetes, configuration strategy, inter-service communication patterns, shared-library governance, local development across many services, and the anti-patterns that turn microservices into a slower monolith with network calls.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — what the pieces are, a gateway route B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — gateway filters, discovery, config, client calls B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — boundaries, data ownership, extraction B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — platform architecture, governance, migration B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — organizational design, when not to split

docs.title: 2.1 What actually justifies a separate service
docs.text:
Good reason Why Independent deployability of a business capability Different change rates and release risk Independent scaling Search scales with browsing; settlement with sellers Clear ownership by one team Conway's law works for you instead of against you Different technology or data needs Search needs OpenSearch, not PostgreSQL Failure isolation A broken recommender must not stop checkout Bad reason What happens "Microservices are best practice" Distributed monolith One service per database table ("entity services") Chatty chains, no real boundary Reuse of a shared library Coupling without independence A layer per service (controller-service / data-service) Network calls inside what should be one process

Start with a modular monolith

Chapter 37 covers modules with enforced boundaries inside one deployable. Most teams should start there and extract services when a module's deployment, scaling or ownership genuinely diverges. Extraction from a well-modularized monolith is a refactor; extraction from a tangled one is a rewrite.

docs.title: 2.2 Data ownership
docs.text:
Rule Consequence Each piece of data has exactly one writing service No two services can disagree about the truth Others hold copies, updated by events (Chapter 23) Reads are local and fast; consistency is eventual No shared database between services The schema is an implementation detail, not an API Cross-service queries are compositions, not joins BFF or API composition (Chapter 32) Cross-service writes are sagas, not transactions Chapter 36

A shared database is the single most reliable way to build a distributed monolith: every schema change becomes a multi-team, lockstep release.

docs.title: 2.3 The grocery platform's services
docs.text:
Domain Services Owns Customer-facing mobile-bff, api-gateway Nothing (composition only) Catalog catalog, search-indexer, pricing Products, prices, search index Purchase cart, order, payment Carts, orders, payments Fulfilment inventory, delivery, dispatch, tracking Stock, deliveries, assignments Seller seller, settlement, catalog-feed Sellers, payouts, feeds Platform identity, notification, config/ops tools Identity, message delivery

Twenty-six in total, including smaller supporting services. The count isn't a target; it's the result of applying 2.1.

docs.title: 2.4 The edge: an API gateway
docs.text:
Concern Why it belongs at the edge Routing to services Clients see one host TLS termination, request size limits Once, not 26 times Authentication (token validation) Cheap rejection before fan-out (Chapter 18) Rate limiting and quotas per client Global view of a caller (Chapter 26) CORS, compression, header hygiene Uniform policy Canary/traffic splitting Chapter 30 Observability at the boundary One place to see all traffic

What does not belong at the edge: business logic, response aggregation (use a BFF — Chapter 32), and per-service authorization (services re-validate tokens and enforce ownership themselves, Chapter 17).

docs.title: 2.5 Spring Cloud components, current status
docs.text:
Component Use in this platform Spring Cloud Gateway The edge (reactive, or the servlet "Gateway Server MVC" variant) Spring Cloud LoadBalancer Client-side load balancing where DNS isn't enough Spring Cloud Config Not used — ConfigMaps + GitOps (Chapters 06, 30) Spring Cloud Netflix Eureka Not used in Kubernetes; relevant for VM estates Spring Cloud OpenFeign Maintenance — replaced by HTTP interfaces (Chapter 19) Spring Cloud Stream Optional; direct clients preferred (Chapter 24) Spring Cloud Contract Alternative to Pact (Chapter 28) Spring Cloud Circuit Breaker Thin abstraction; Resilience4j used directly (Chapter 26) Spring Cloud Bus / Task / Function Situational

Hystrix, Ribbon and Zuul are retired; their replacements are Resilience4j, Spring Cloud LoadBalancer and Spring Cloud Gateway. Pin the release train to your Boot version — it is the most common upgrade blocker.

docs.title: 2.6 Service discovery
docs.text:
Environment Mechanism Kubernetes Service DNS (http://pricing-service:8080) — nothing else needed Kubernetes, client-side balancing needed Headless service + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, or a mesh VMs / hybrid Eureka (or Consul) with Spring Cloud Discovery Across clusters/regions Mesh, global load balancer, or explicit endpoints

In Kubernetes, adding Eureka duplicates what the platform already provides — and adds a component that can fail.

docs.title: 2.7 Communication patterns
docs.text:
Pattern When Synchronous request/response (REST/gRPC) The caller needs the answer now Events (Kafka) Notify others of a fact; decouple availability (Chapter 23) Commands (queue) Ask one service to do work later (Chapter 24) Data replication via events Local reads of another service's data (Chapter 36) Composition (BFF/gateway aggregation) Client needs several services' data at once (Chapter 32)

Rule of thumb: prefer events. Every synchronous hop adds latency, a failure mode and a coupling in availability.

docs.title: 2.8 The distributed monolith smell test
docs.text: Symptom Verdict Services must be deployed together in a specific order Distributed monolith One user action synchronously traverses 5+ services Chatty chain Services share a database schema Not separate services A shared library contains domain logic and must be upgraded everywhere at once Coupled A change to one service's API requires immediate changes in others Contracts not versioned (Chapter 20) Local development requires running 12 services Boundaries or tooling problem

docs.title: 3.1 A request through the platform
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Mobile app
    participant G as api-gateway
    participant B as mobile-bff
    participant O as order-service
    participant P as pricing-service
    participant K as Kafka

    C->>G: POST /api/v1/orders (Bearer token)
    G->>G: TLS, size limit, rate limit, token validation
    G->>B: route (+ traceparent, X-Request-Id)
    B->>O: create order (service token)
    O->>P: price check (deadline 600ms)
    P-->>O: prices
    O->>O: TX: order + outbox row
    O-->>B: 201 Created
    B-->>G: 201
    G-->>C: 201
    Note over O,K: outbox relay publishes OrderPlaced
    K-->>O: consumed by inventory, notification, search, loyalty

The synchronous path is deliberately short: gateway → BFF → order → pricing. Everything else happens through events after the response.

docs.title: 3.2 Gateway request pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Request] --> B[Global pre-filters:<br/>correlation id, metrics]
    B --> C[Route predicates:<br/>path, method, header, host]
    C --> D[Route filters:<br/>auth, rate limit, strip prefix, circuit breaker, retry]
    D --> E[Forward to the service]
    E --> F[Post-filters: headers, metrics, error mapping]
    F --> G[Response]

Predicates decide which route; filters decide what happens on the way in and out. Order matters: authenticate and rate-limit before forwarding, never after.

docs.title: 3.3 Extraction with the strangler fig
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A[Monolith owns pricing] --> B[New pricing-service<br/>reads the same data, read-only]
    B --> C[Gateway routes GET /prices to the new service<br/>monolith still writes]
    C --> D[Shadow traffic + compare results]
    D --> E[Move writes: new service owns the tables<br/>monolith calls it or consumes events]
    E --> F[Delete pricing code from the monolith]

Each arrow is independently deployable and reversible. The dangerous version — build everything, cut over once — is how extractions become six-month incidents.

docs.title: 4.1 A gateway with routes
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts (api-gateway)
implementation("org.springframework.cloud:spring-cloud-starter-gateway")          // (1)!
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server")
implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-data-redis-reactive")
  1. The reactive gateway (Chapter 31's stack). A servlet-based variant exists — verify the artifact name and capabilities for your Spring Cloud version.
application.yml
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: catalog
          uri: http://catalog-service:8080                       # (1)!
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/v1/products/**,/api/v1/categories/**
        - id: orders
          uri: http://order-service:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/v1/orders/**
          filters:
            - name: CircuitBreaker                                # (2)!
              args:
                name: orders
                fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/orders
        - id: bff
          uri: http://mobile-bff:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/graphql
      default-filters:
        - RemoveRequestHeader=Cookie                              # (3)!
        - AddResponseHeader=X-Content-Type-Options, nosniff
  1. Kubernetes service DNS — no discovery client required (2.6).
  2. Edge-level circuit breaking, complementing service-level resilience (Chapter 26).
  3. Strip headers clients shouldn't be sending to a token-based API.

docs.title: 4.2 Authentication at the edge
docs.text:
application.yml
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://id.grocery.in
          audiences: grocery-api
in/grocery/gateway/config/GatewaySecurityConfig.java
@Bean
SecurityWebFilterChain gatewaySecurity(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http
            .authorizeExchange(exchanges -> exchanges
                    .pathMatchers("/api/v1/public/**", "/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
                    .pathMatchers("/webhooks/**").permitAll()                       // (1)!
                    .anyExchange().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
            .csrf(ServerHttpSecurity.CsrfSpec::disable)
            .build();
}
  1. Webhooks authenticate by signature inside the service (Chapter 18), so the gateway lets them through — but still applies rate limits and size caps.

The gateway is not the only guard

Services must validate tokens and enforce ownership themselves (Chapter 17). A gateway-only model means anything that reaches a pod — a misconfigured NetworkPolicy, a compromised sidecar, an internal caller — is fully trusted.

docs.title: 4.3 Calling another service
5.1 Level 2 — Gateway rate limiting and quotas
5.2 Level 2 — Cross-cutting edge concerns
5.3 Level 3 — Drawing and enforcing boundaries
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Catalog["Catalog capability (team: Discovery)"]
        C1[catalog-service<br/>owns: product, category]
        C2[pricing-service<br/>owns: price, promotion]
        C3[search-indexer<br/>owns: index projection]
    end
    subgraph Purchase["Purchase capability (team: Checkout)"]
        P1[cart-service<br/>owns: cart]
        P2[order-service<br/>owns: order, order_line]
        P3[payment-service<br/>owns: payment, refund]
    end
    subgraph Fulfilment["Fulfilment capability (team: Ops)"]
        F1[inventory-service<br/>owns: stock, reservation]
        F2[delivery-service<br/>owns: delivery, slot]
    end
    C2 -. events: PriceChanged .-> P1
    P2 -. events: OrderPlaced .-> F1
    F1 -. events: StockChanged .-> C3

Boundary rules the platform enforces in review:

Rule Check One writer per table Database grants: only the owning service has write access No cross-service joins No service has credentials for another's schema Synchronous calls only within a request's critical path Architecture review; trace analysis Events for everything else Chapter 23 Contracts versioned and tested Chapter 28's broker gate Ownership enforced by the database, not by goodwill
grant select, insert, update, delete on order_line to order_service_app;
grant select on order_line to analytics_reader;                                     -- (1)
revoke all on order_line from inventory_service_app;                                -- (2)
  1. Read-only access for analytics is fine and explicit.
  2. The most effective boundary control available: another service cannot write your data even if someone writes the code.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — Replicating data instead of calling
docs.text:
The cart needs product names and prices for display. Calling catalog and pricing on every cart read is 2 extra hops per request.

in/grocery/cart/projection/ProductProjectionUpdater.java
@Component
class ProductProjectionUpdater {

    private final ProductProjectionRepository projections;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.catalog.product-changed.v1", groupId = "cart-service")
    @Transactional
    public void onProductChanged(ProductChanged event) {
        projections.upsert(new ProductProjection(                                    // (1)!
                event.sku(), event.name(), event.imageUrl(), event.brand(), event.updatedAt()));
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.pricing.price-changed.v1", groupId = "cart-service")
    @Transactional
    public void onPriceChanged(PriceChanged event) {
        projections.updatePrice(event.sku(), event.zone(), event.price(), event.updatedAt());   // (2)!
    }
}
  1. A local, read-only copy of the fields cart needs — not the whole product model.
  2. Prices are zone-scoped; the projection stores what cart displays, and checkout still calls pricing for the authoritative amount.
Aspect Consequence Latency Cart reads are local — no network hop Availability Cart works when catalog is down Consistency Eventually consistent (seconds); acceptable for display, not for charging Storage Duplicated data, owned by the consumer, rebuildable by replay Rule Display from the projection, decide from the owner

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Extracting a service from the monolith
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S0["Step 0: module inside the monolith<br/>(Chapter 37) — clean boundary, no DB sharing"]
    S0 --> S1[Step 1: new service, read-only,<br/>same database, read replica]
    S1 --> S2[Step 2: gateway routes reads<br/>shadow-compare old vs new]
    S2 --> S3[Step 3: move the tables<br/>new service owns writes]
    S3 --> S4[Step 4: monolith calls the service<br/>or consumes its events]
    S4 --> S5[Step 5: delete the old code and grants]
Step 2: shadow comparison
@Component
class PricingShadowComparator {

    @Async("shadowExecutor")                                                        // (1)!
    public void compare(String sku, String pincode, PriceView legacy) {
        try {
            PriceView candidate = newPricingClient.price(sku, pincode);
            if (!legacy.price().equals(candidate.price())) {
                meters.counter("grocery.shadow.mismatch", "endpoint", "price").increment();
                log.warn("Shadow mismatch for {}/{}: legacy={} new={}",                // (2)!
                        sku, pincode, legacy.price(), candidate.price());
            }
        } catch (Exception e) {
            meters.counter("grocery.shadow.error").increment();                       // (3)!
        }
    }
}
  1. Shadow calls run off the request path — they must never add latency or failure to production traffic.
  2. Mismatches are data, not alarms; investigate the pattern (rounding, timezone, stale cache) before cutting over.
  3. Shadow failures are logged and counted, never propagated.

Cut over when the mismatch rate is zero for a sustained period, and keep the route switch a configuration change so rollback is instant.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Shared libraries without coupling
docs.text:
Library Contents Coupling risk grocery-platform-web Error handling, problem format, correlation filter, common OpenAPI config Low — cross-cutting only grocery-platform-security Token validation, authorities converter, entry points Low grocery-platform-observability Common tags, meter filters, health conventions Low grocery-platform-test Containers config, builders, ArchUnit rules Low grocery-order-client HTTP interface + DTOs for order-service Medium — owned by the order team, versioned grocery-domain-model Shared entities/business rules Don't

Rules: platform libraries contain no business logic; client libraries are owned by the providing team and versioned semantically; nothing forces a lockstep upgrade — services run N and N-1 (Chapter 41 covers building starters).

docs.title: 6.1 The platform topology
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    Client[Mobile / Web] --> CDN[CDN + WAF]
    CDN --> GW[api-gateway<br/>authN, rate limit, routing, canary]
    GW --> BFF[mobile-bff · GraphQL]
    GW --> REST[REST services]
    BFF --> SVC
    REST --> SVC
    subgraph SVC[26 services, per-capability ownership]
        direction LR
        A[catalog / pricing / search]
        B[cart / order / payment]
        C[inventory / delivery / dispatch]
        D[seller / settlement / feeds]
        E[identity / notification]
    end
    SVC <--> K[(Kafka · events)]
    SVC <--> DB[(Per-service PostgreSQL)]
    SVC <--> R[(Redis)]
    SVC --> OBS[Prometheus / Tempo / Loki]
Decision Choice Rationale Discovery Kubernetes DNS One less component (2.6) Configuration ConfigMaps + GitOps Chapters 06, 30 Edge Spring Cloud Gateway Routing, authN, quotas, canary Aggregation mobile-bff (GraphQL) Chapter 32 Inter-service auth Client credentials Chapter 18 Sync calls RestClient + HTTP interfaces; gRPC for hot paths Chapters 19, 32 Async Kafka with outbox/inbox Chapters 23, 36 Resilience Resilience4j in services; mesh for transport Chapters 26, 30 Contracts Pact + broker gate Chapter 28

docs.title: 6.2 Service ownership records
docs.text:
platform/catalog/service.yaml (the service catalog entry)
name: order-service
team: checkout
slack: "#team-checkout"
oncall: checkout-primary
tier: 1                                                # (1)!
description: Owns orders and order lines; orchestrates checkout.
owns_data: [customer_order, order_line, order_outbox]
depends_on:
  sync: [pricing-service, inventory-service, payment-service]
  async: [grocery.payment.captured.v1]
publishes: [grocery.order.placed.v1, grocery.order.status-changed.v1]
slos:
  - name: checkout-availability
    objective: 99.5%
  - name: checkout-latency-p99
    objective: 2s
runbooks:
  - https://runbooks.grocery.in/order-service
  1. Tier drives on-call expectations, review requirements and capacity headroom. A machine-readable catalog powers dependency graphs, ownership lookups during incidents and automated compliance checks ("every tier-1 service has SLOs and a runbook").

docs.title: 6.3 Gateway in production
docs.text:
api-gateway/application-prod.yml (excerpt)
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      metrics:
        enabled: true                                   # (1)!
      default-filters:
        - RemoveRequestHeader=Cookie
        - RemoveRequestHeader=X-Customer-Id
        - name: Retry
          args:
            retries: 1
            methods: GET                                # (2)!
            statuses: BAD_GATEWAY,SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
            backoff:
              firstBackoff: 50ms
              maxBackoff: 200ms
              basedOnPreviousValue: false
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: http://order-service:8080
          predicates: [ "Path=/api/v1/orders/**" ]
          filters:
            - name: CircuitBreaker
              args: { name: orders, fallbackUri: "forward:/fallback/orders" }
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 50
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 100
                key-resolver: "#{@clientKeyResolver}"
  1. spring.cloud.gateway.requests metrics per route feed the edge dashboard (Chapter 27).
  2. Idempotent methods only, one retry — the gateway is one retry layer; services must not retry the same call again (Chapter 26).
Fallbacks that say something useful
@RestController
class FallbackController {

    @RequestMapping("/fallback/orders")
    ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> orders() {
        ProblemDetail problem = ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE);
        problem.setTitle("Orders temporarily unavailable");
        problem.setProperty("code", "ORDERS_UNAVAILABLE");                           // (1)!
        problem.setProperty("retryable", true);
        return ResponseEntity.status(503).header("Retry-After", "5").body(problem);
    }
}
  1. Same error contract as everywhere else (Chapter 10) — clients handle an edge failure with the code they already know.

docs.title: 6.4 Local development across 26 services
docs.text:
Approach Use Run one service + Testcontainers The default: real PostgreSQL/Kafka/Redis, stubs for peers (Chapter 28) Stub libraries from providers WireMock stubs published by each team (Chapter 28) bootTestRun with containers Local app against local infrastructure (Chapter 15) Shared development cluster + port-forward When you truly need a real peer Telepresence/Tilt-style tooling Occasional deep integration work Running 12 services locally ❌ a symptom to fix, not a workflow What a developer actually runs
./gradlew :order-service:bootTestRun          # app + PostgreSQL + Kafka + WireMock stubs

If a task genuinely requires four real services, that's a signal about coupling (2.8) worth raising in review.

docs.title: 6.5 Anti-patterns, with their cures
docs.text: Anti-pattern Cure Shared database Split schemas, grants per service, events for copies Synchronous chain of 5 services Move work to events; compose at the BFF; cache projections Lockstep releases Versioned contracts (Chapter 20), consumer-driven tests (Chapter 28) Shared domain library Platform libraries only; DTOs per client library Entity services (user-service, address-service) Merge into a capability Distributed transactions attempted Sagas and idempotency (Chapter 36) Nobody owns service X Service catalog with an owning team, or delete it "We'll fix boundaries later" Boundaries are the product; later never comes cheaply

docs.title: 6.6 When to merge services back
docs.text:
Splitting is reversible, and sometimes correct to reverse:

Signal Action Two services always change together Merge them A service has no independent scaling or deployment need Merge The network hop exists only for a layer boundary Merge One team owns six tiny services with identical lifecycles Consolidate into a modular monolith (Chapter 37)

Merging is unglamorous and frequently the highest-value architectural work available.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 / Spring Cloud 2024.x–2025.x Boot 4.x / matching train Release train alignment Pinned per Boot minor Must match — verify before upgrading Spring Cloud Gateway Reactive + Gateway Server MVC variant Same (verify artifact names) OpenFeign Maintenance Maintenance — migrate to HTTP interfaces (Chapter 19) Eureka / Config Server Available Available (verify) Spring Cloud LoadBalancer ✅ ✅ Spring Cloud Stream 4.x Aligned train (verify)

The release train is the upgrade gate

Spring Cloud lags Boot releases. Plan platform upgrades around the train's availability, upgrade the gateway and shared libraries first, and never mix trains across services that share a client library.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Confirm the Spring Cloud train supporting your target Boot version exists and is stable.
  • Upgrade the gateway in isolation first; re-test routes, filters, rate limiting and auth.
  • Migrate remaining Feign clients to HTTP interfaces before the upgrade, not during.
  • Re-run contract tests across services while versions are mixed.
  • Verify metric names used by edge dashboards.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Boundaries by business capability, one owning team per service.
  2. One writer per dataset, enforced by database grants; copies via events.
  3. Short synchronous paths; everything else asynchronous.
  4. Gateway owns edge concerns; services still authenticate and authorize.
  5. Service DNS in Kubernetes — skip discovery servers you don't need.
  6. Contracts versioned and tested, with a deployment gate (Chapters 20, 28).
  7. Platform libraries without business logic; client libraries owned by providers.
  8. A service catalog with owners, SLOs, dependencies and runbooks.
  9. Extract with the strangler fig, shadow-compare, switch by configuration.
  10. Merge services back when they don't earn their separation.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ A shared database between services.

❌ Long synchronous chains for a single user action.

❌ Coordinated, ordered deployments.

❌ Shared domain libraries that force lockstep upgrades.

❌ Entity services and layer services.

❌ Running Eureka/Config Server inside Kubernetes for no reason.

❌ Trusting gateway-injected identity headers inside services.

❌ Retrying at both the gateway and the service.

❌ Services without an owner, SLOs or a runbook.

❌ Splitting before the boundary is understood — start modular (Chapter 37).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix One service's deploy breaks others Unversioned contract changes Additive evolution, contract gate Latency grows with each release Longer synchronous chains Move to events, cache projections A schema change needs four teams Shared database Split ownership, grants, events Gateway becomes a bottleneck CPU limits, heavy filters, no scaling Profile filters, scale out, move aggregation to the BFF Duplicate retries during incidents Retry at gateway and service One layer only Trace stops at the gateway Propagation headers stripped Allow traceparent, keep instrumentation Nobody knows who owns a failing service No catalog Service catalog with on-call Local dev requires 12 services Coupling / missing stubs Stub libraries, Testcontainers, boundary review Data inconsistent between services Two writers, or missed events Enforce single writer; inbox/outbox (Chapters 23, 36)

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Every service has an owning team, SLOs, runbooks and a catalog entry
  • One writer per dataset; grants enforce it
  • Contracts versioned with consumer-driven tests and a deploy gate
  • Gateway: authN, rate limits, size limits, single retry layer, fallbacks with the platform error format
  • Services validate tokens and enforce ownership independently
  • Event-first communication; synchronous chains reviewed and bounded
  • Platform libraries free of business logic; client libraries versioned
  • Local development runs one service with stubs and containers
  • Extraction plan (or merge plan) recorded for services under change

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is an API gateway for?

Short answer: A single entry point handling routing, TLS, authentication, rate limiting, size limits and edge observability, so services don't each implement them.

B1 · How do services find each other in Kubernetes?

Short answer: Through Service DNS (http://pricing-service:8080); no separate discovery server is needed.

B1 · Why shouldn't microservices share a database?

Short answer: It couples their schemas and releases — a change requires coordinating every service that touches those tables, which defeats independent deployability.

B1 · What is a distributed monolith?

Short answer: Services that must be deployed together, share a database or call each other synchronously for every action — all the costs of distribution with none of the independence.

B1 · Name a good reason to split a service.

Short answer: A business capability that needs to deploy, scale or be owned independently — not "one service per table".

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Which Spring Cloud components are still current?

Short answer: Gateway, LoadBalancer, Config (where needed), Stream, Contract, Circuit Breaker, Eureka for non-Kubernetes estates. Hystrix, Ribbon and Zuul are retired; OpenFeign is in maintenance in favour of HTTP interfaces.

B2 · How do you rate-limit per client at the gateway?

Short answer: RequestRateLimiter with a Redis limiter and a KeyResolver that keys on the authenticated subject (falling back to IP), returning 429 with Retry-After and RateLimit-* headers.

B2 · Should the gateway aggregate responses?

Short answer: No — aggregation belongs in a BFF, which can own client-specific shaping, partial failure and batching. Keeping the gateway thin keeps it fast and operable.

B2 · How does one service get another's data for display?

Short answer: Preferably a local projection maintained from events; call the owner synchronously only when the value must be authoritative at that instant.

B2 · Why must services authenticate even behind a gateway?

Short answer: Defence in depth — network controls fail, internal callers exist, and trusting an injected header makes any pod-level access a full compromise.

B2 · How do you avoid lockstep releases?

Short answer: Additive, versioned contracts; consumer-driven contract tests with a can-i-deploy gate; tolerant readers; feature flags for behaviour changes.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How do you decide service boundaries?

Short answer: By business capability and bounded context (Chapter 37), aligned with team ownership and differing change/scaling profiles; validated by asking whether the service can deploy alone, owns its data, and doesn't need synchronous chatter with its neighbours.

B3 · Describe extracting a service from a monolith.

Short answer: Modularize inside the monolith first; stand up the new service read-only against the same data; route reads through the gateway with shadow comparison; move table ownership and writes; have the monolith call or consume events; delete the old code and revoke grants — each step deployable and reversible.

B3 · What are the costs of replicating data between services?

Short answer: Storage duplication, eventual consistency, projection-rebuild machinery and event-schema coupling. The benefits are local reads, availability isolation and no synchronous hop. Use it for display data; read from the owner for decisions.

B3 · Gateway resilience vs service resilience?

Short answer: The gateway provides coarse protection (rate limits, circuit breaking, one retry for idempotent calls); services provide semantic resilience (idempotency-aware retries, fallbacks, degradation). Retries must exist at exactly one layer.

B3 · How do you govern shared libraries?

Short answer: Platform libraries carry cross-cutting concerns only and are backward compatible; client libraries are owned by the providing team and versioned; no shared domain model; services must be able to run N-1 without breaking.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How would you assess whether a platform is truly microservices or a distributed monolith?

Short answer: Check deployment independence (can one service ship alone?), data ownership (shared schemas?), synchronous depth per user action, release coordination, shared-library coupling, and whether local development needs many services. Fix the worst offender first — usually the shared database.

B4 · Kubernetes DNS, Eureka, or a service mesh?

Short answer: DNS in Kubernetes by default; Eureka only for non-Kubernetes estates; a mesh when you need mTLS, uniform transport policy and traffic shifting across many languages — accepting its operational cost and being careful not to duplicate application-level retries.

B4 · How do you keep 26 services operationally consistent?

Short answer: Platform libraries (error format, security, observability, testing), a Helm library chart (Chapter 30), a service catalog with tiers and SLOs, CI conformance checks, shared runbook templates, and periodic architecture reviews with the dependency graph in hand.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · When would you advise against microservices?

Short answer: Small teams, unclear domains, modest scale, or organizations without the operational capability (CI/CD, observability, on-call). A well-modularized monolith delivers most benefits at far lower cost and preserves the option to split later.

B5 · How does organizational design shape service architecture?

Short answer: Conway's law: systems mirror communication structures. Aligning services with long-lived, capability-owning teams produces clean boundaries; splitting services across teams — or giving one team many unrelated services — produces coupling and unowned code regardless of technology choices.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Every checkout release requires deploying four services in order

Shared DTO library with business logic, a shared order schema read by inventory, and synchronous calls without versioning. Fixes: split schemas with per-service grants, replace the shared model with per-client DTO libraries, version APIs additively with consumer-driven contract tests and a deploy gate, and move notification/loyalty to events.

Scenario · Checkout latency grew from 400 ms to 1.4 s over a year

Each new feature added a synchronous call; the chain reached six services. Fixes: trace analysis to list synchronous hops, move non-critical work to events (loyalty, notifications, analytics), replace display lookups with local projections, set a latency budget per endpoint (Chapter 34), and add a review rule requiring justification for any new synchronous dependency.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Route and protect a new service

A new recommendation-service exposes GET /api/v1/recommendations. Add it to the gateway with: authentication required, 10 req/s per user with burst 20, a circuit breaker with a fallback returning best sellers, one retry for GET only, and edge metrics. Then show the client configuration in mobile-bff with timeout, breaker and degradation.

Solution api-gateway/application.yml
    - id: recommendations
      uri: http://recommendation-service:8080
      predicates:
        - Path=/api/v1/recommendations/**
        - Method=GET                                                # (1)!
      filters:
        - name: RequestRateLimiter
          args:
            redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 10
            redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 20
            key-resolver: "#{@clientKeyResolver}"
        - name: CircuitBreaker
          args:
            name: recommendations
            fallbackUri: forward:/fallback/recommendations
        - name: Retry
          args:
            retries: 1
            methods: GET
            statuses: BAD_GATEWAY,SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
  1. Constrain the route to what the service actually exposes — predicates are a security control as much as a routing one.
FallbackController (best sellers, not an error)
@RequestMapping("/fallback/recommendations")
ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> recommendations() {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header("X-Degraded", "true")                                          // (1)!
            .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
            .body(Map.of("items", bestSellersCache.top(10), "source", "fallback"));
}
  1. Degrade visibly: the client still renders a carousel, and the header plus a metric tell us how often it happens (Chapter 26).
mobile-bff client
@Bean
RecommendationApi recommendationApi(RestClient.Builder builder, RecommendationProperties props) {
    RestClient client = builder
            .baseUrl(props.baseUrl())
            .requestFactory(RequestFactories.pooled(Duration.ofMillis(500), Duration.ofMillis(400)))  // (1)!
            .defaultStatusHandler(new InternalServiceErrorHandler("recommendation-service"))
            .build();
    return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(client))
            .build().createClient(RecommendationApi.class);
}

@CircuitBreaker(name = "recommendations", fallbackMethod = "bestSellers")            // (2)!
@Bulkhead(name = "recommendations")
public List<ProductView> forCustomer(String customerId, String pincode) {
    return api.recommendations(customerId, pincode);
}

private List<ProductView> bestSellers(String customerId, String pincode, Throwable cause) {
    meters.counter("grocery.degraded", "dependency", "recommendations").increment();
    return bestSellersCache.top(10);                                                  // (3)!
}
  1. A 400 ms read timeout — recommendations are decoration; they may never delay the home screen.
  2. Breaker and bulkhead at the service level too (Chapter 26): the gateway protects the edge, the BFF protects the screen.
  3. The same degradation in both layers, measured in both — so "how often do customers see fallback recommendations?" has an answer.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Boundaries by capability, one owner, one writer per dataset — technology choices matter far less.
  • Prefer events; keep synchronous chains short and budgeted.
  • The gateway owns edge concerns; services still authenticate, authorize and degrade.
  • Kubernetes DNS beats a discovery server you don't need; ConfigMaps beat a config server.
  • Contracts versioned and gated are what make independent deployment real.
  • Platform libraries yes, shared domain libraries no.
  • Extract with the strangler fig, shadow-compare, switch by configuration — and merge back when a split doesn't pay.
  • A service catalog with owners, SLOs and runbooks is infrastructure, not paperwork.

docs.text:
• Spring Cloud Gateway Reference — routes, predicates, filters, rate limiting, circuit breaker
  • Spring Cloud documentation — release trains, LoadBalancer, Config, Discovery
  • Building Microservices (Sam Newman) — boundaries, extraction, organizational aspects
  • Monolith to Microservices (Sam Newman) — strangler fig and data decomposition patterns

34 Performance Engineering · 36 Distributed Data & Consistency

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 16 gave one service ACID transactions. Chapter 35 then split the platform into twenty-six services, each with its own database — and took those transactions away.

Placing an order now means: create the order (order-service), reserve stock (inventory-service), authorize payment (payment-service), award points (loyalty-service), notify the customer (notification-service). Five databases, five failure points, no BEGIN/COMMIT spanning them. The naïve implementations fail in specific, expensive ways:

  • Dual write: the order commits, the Kafka publish fails, inventory never reserves stock. The customer waits for groceries that were never picked.
  • Two-phase commit: technically possible, practically a coordinator that blocks everything when it fails, and few modern datastores support it well.
  • "We'll just retry": retries without idempotency produce double charges and double stock deductions.
  • Half-completed workflows: payment authorized, stock reservation failed, nobody compensates, money is held on a customer's card for a week.

The patterns that actually work are the subject of this chapter: the outbox (with polling and CDC), idempotent consumers, sagas with compensations (choreography and orchestration), CQRS read models, an honest look at event sourcing, handling eventual consistency in the user interface, migrating data during service extraction, and reconciliation — because in a distributed system, drift is not a possibility but a certainty you must detect.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — dual writes, outbox, idempotency B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — sagas, compensations, read models B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — CDC, orchestration, stuck sagas B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — consistency strategy, reconciliation, migrations B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — trade-offs and organizational consequences

docs.title: 2.1 What you give up, precisely
docs.text:
Within one service Across services ACID transaction Saga with compensations Foreign keys Eventual reference validity Joins Composition or local projections Unique constraints across entities Per-service constraints + reconciliation Read-your-writes Requires deliberate design (2.7) Rollback Compensating actions (semantically, not physically)

PACELC in one line: when the network partitions you choose availability or consistency; else (normal operation) you choose latency or consistency. Most e-commerce choices trade consistency for latency and availability — deliberately, per use case, not by accident.

docs.title: 2.2 The dual-write problem
2.3 The outbox
docs.text:
Write the event into the same database, same transaction as the business change; a separate process publishes it.

flowchart LR
    A[Business transaction] -->|one COMMIT| B[(order table + outbox table)]
    B --> C{publisher}
    C -->|polling relay| K[(Kafka)]
    C -->|CDC / Debezium| K
    K --> D[Consumers]
Property Result Atomicity Business data and event commit together Delivery At-least-once (consumers must be idempotent) Ordering Per aggregate, if relayed in order and keyed correctly Failure mode Event stays pending; nothing is lost

docs.title: 2.4 Polling relay vs CDC
docs.text:
Polling relay (Chapter 23) CDC (Debezium) Mechanism SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publish, mark sent Reads the write-ahead log, publishes changes Latency Poll interval (100–500 ms) Near-real-time Load Extra queries + updates on the hot database Log reading, minimal query load Operations Just your application Kafka Connect, replication slots, monitoring Failure risk Simple, well understood Replication slot growth if the connector stops — can fill the disk Good for Most services High-volume services, and capturing changes without code

Start with polling; move to CDC when volume or latency justifies the operational cost.

docs.title: 2.5 Idempotent consumers
docs.text:
At-least-once delivery means every consumer must tolerate repeats (Chapter 23):

Technique Example Inbox table insert into processed_event(consumer, event_id) with a unique key Conditional update update order set status='PAID' where ref=? and status='PLACED' Upsert insert ... on conflict do update Version check Ignore events with version <= current Natural key unique (order_ref, run_date) (Chapter 33)

docs.title: 2.6 Sagas
docs.text:
A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action for rollback.

Style How Good for Choreography Each service reacts to events and emits the next Short flows (2–3 steps), loose coupling Orchestration A coordinator issues commands and tracks state Longer flows, visibility, timeouts, complex compensation 
flowchart LR
    subgraph Choreography
        A1[OrderPlaced] --> B1[inventory reserves] --> C1[StockReserved] --> D1[payment authorizes] --> E1[PaymentAuthorized] --> F1[order confirms]
    end
    subgraph Orchestration
        A2[Saga coordinator] -->|ReserveStock| B2[inventory]
        B2 -->|StockReserved| A2
        A2 -->|AuthorizePayment| C2[payment]
        C2 -->|PaymentDeclined| A2
        A2 -->|ReleaseStock — compensation| B2
        A2 --> D2[Order CANCELLED]
    end

Compensation is semantic, not a rollback: you can't un-charge a card, you issue a refund; you can't un-send an SMS, you send a correction.

docs.title: 2.7 Eventual consistency and the user
docs.text:
Problem Fix "I placed an order but the list is empty" Return the created resource; the client renders from the response "My cart badge is stale" Read-your-writes: read from the writing service, or pass a version token "Stock said available, checkout failed" Reserve at checkout; display is advisory "Points didn't appear" Show a pending state with an expected time Seller edits a product, search doesn't show it Read the seller's own view from the owner; search is eventually consistent

The rule: display may be eventually consistent; decisions must read from the owner.

docs.title: 2.8 CQRS and event sourcing — proportionate use
docs.text:
Pattern Use when Cost Read models (projections from events) Read/write asymmetry, cross-service views Rebuild machinery, staleness CQRS (separate write and read models) Complex domain writes, very different read shapes Two models, sync logic Event sourcing (events are the source of truth) Audit is the product; temporal queries; complex invariants over history Large commitment: schema evolution, snapshots, replay, tooling, team skill

The platform uses read models widely, CQRS in one service, and event sourcing nowhere — the outbox gives integration-level event benefits without making events the system of record.

docs.title: 3.1 Outbox with CDC
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as order-service
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant W as WAL
    participant D as Debezium connector
    participant K as Kafka

    S->>DB: BEGIN, insert order, insert outbox, COMMIT
    DB->>W: write-ahead log records
    D->>W: stream changes from the replication slot
    D->>D: outbox event router SMT: topic from `aggregate_type`, key from `aggregate_id`
    D->>K: publish to grocery.order.placed.v1
    D->>DB: advance slot offset (confirm)
    Note over DB,D: if the connector stops, the slot retains WAL — disk grows!

Two operational facts: the connector's offset advance is what frees WAL, and the outbox table can be pruned once rows are captured (or written as insert-then-delete in the same transaction, if your connector supports it).

docs.title: 3.2 Saga state machine
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> STARTED
    STARTED --> STOCK_RESERVED: ReserveStock ok
    STARTED --> FAILED: ReserveStock failed
    STOCK_RESERVED --> PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED: AuthorizePayment ok
    STOCK_RESERVED --> COMPENSATING: payment failed/timeout
    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> COMPLETED: order confirmed
    PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED --> COMPENSATING: confirmation failed
    COMPENSATING --> COMPENSATED: stock released, payment voided
    COMPENSATING --> STUCK: compensation failed repeatedly
    STUCK --> [*]: manual intervention
    COMPLETED --> [*]
    COMPENSATED --> [*]
    FAILED --> [*]

Every state is persisted, every transition is idempotent, and STUCK exists because compensation can fail too — pretending otherwise produces silent money leaks.

docs.title: 3.3 Read-model projection
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[(order-service DB)] -->|outbox| K[(Kafka)]
    K --> P[Projector]
    P --> R[(read model: order_history)]
    R --> Q[Query API: fast, denormalized]
    K -.->|replay from offset 0| P

The read model is disposable: if it's wrong, truncate and replay. That property is what makes projections safe; if a projection can't be rebuilt, it has become a system of record by accident (Chapter 22's warning).

docs.title: 4.1 The outbox table and write
docs.text:
V90__outbox.sql
create table outbox (
    id             bigserial primary key,
    aggregate_type varchar(40)  not null,      -- (1)
    aggregate_id   varchar(64)  not null,
    event_type     varchar(60)  not null,
    payload        jsonb        not null,
    headers        jsonb        not null default '{}'::jsonb,
    created_at     timestamptz  not null default now(),
    sent_at        timestamptz,
    attempts       int          not null default 0,
    last_error     text
);
create index outbox_pending_idx on outbox (created_at) where sent_at is null;   -- (2)
  1. aggregate_type maps to a topic, aggregate_id becomes the Kafka key (ordering per order).
  2. A partial index on pending rows only — the relay's query stays fast even with millions of sent rows.
in/grocery/platform/outbox/OutboxWriter.java
@Component
public class OutboxWriter {

    private final JdbcClient jdbc;
    private final ObjectMapper mapper;

    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.MANDATORY)                          // (1)!
    public void append(String aggregateType, String aggregateId, String eventType, Object payload) {
        jdbc.sql("""
                insert into outbox (aggregate_type, aggregate_id, event_type, payload, headers)
                values (:type, :id, :eventType, :payload::jsonb, :headers::jsonb)
                """)
            .param("type", aggregateType)
            .param("id", aggregateId)
            .param("eventType", eventType)
            .param("payload", writeJson(payload))
            .param("headers", writeJson(Map.of(
                    "eventId", UUID.randomUUID().toString(),                      // (2)!
                    "traceparent", currentTraceParent(),
                    "occurredAt", Instant.now().toString())))
            .update();
    }
}
  1. MANDATORY — writing to the outbox outside a transaction is the bug this pattern exists to prevent, so fail loudly.
  2. A stable eventId is what consumers deduplicate on (Chapter 23).

docs.title: 4.2 Using it
4.3 The relay (recap from Chapter 23)
4.4 Proving it works
5.1 Level 2 — Choreographed saga
docs.text:
The simplest saga: services react to each other's events.

inventory-service: reacts to OrderPlaced
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.order.placed.v1", groupId = "inventory-service")
@Transactional
public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
    if (inbox.alreadyProcessed(CONSUMER, event.eventId())) return;                 // (1)!
    inbox.markProcessed(CONSUMER, event.eventId());

    try {
        reservations.reserve(event.orderRef(), event.lines(), event.pincode());
        outbox.append("inventory", event.orderRef(), "StockReserved",
                new StockReserved(event.orderRef()));                               // (2)!
    } catch (InsufficientStockException e) {
        outbox.append("inventory", event.orderRef(), "StockReservationFailed",
                new StockReservationFailed(event.orderRef(), e.getSku()));           // (3)!
    }
}
  1. Idempotency first (Chapter 23).
  2. Success continues the saga.
  3. Failure is an event, not an exception. Throwing here would retry forever; the saga needs to know the step failed so it can compensate.
order-service: reacts to the outcomes
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.inventory.stock-reservation-failed.v1", groupId = "order-service")
@Transactional
public void onReservationFailed(StockReservationFailed event) {
    orders.findByOrderRef(event.orderRef()).ifPresent(order -> {
        order.cancel("out-of-stock");                                               // (1)!
        outbox.append("order", order.getOrderRef(), "OrderCancelled",
                new OrderCancelled(order.getOrderRef(), "out-of-stock"));
    });
}
  1. Compensation for this flow is simply cancelling — nothing else has happened yet.
Choreography ✅ No coordinator; services stay decoupled; easy for 2–3 steps ❌ The flow exists nowhere explicitly; adding a step means touching several services; timeouts and stuck states are nobody's job; debugging means reading five services' logs

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — When choreography stops scaling
docs.text:
Checkout's real flow: reserve stock → authorize payment → confirm order → schedule delivery → award points, with timeouts and compensations at each step. In choreography that logic is scattered across five services and cannot be answered in one place:

"Where is order ORD-7F3A91C2 in the checkout flow, and why has it been 4 minutes?"

That question is what orchestration answers.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 3 — Saga orchestration
5.4 Level 3 — CDC with Debezium
docs.text:
Kafka Connect: outbox connector
{
  "name": "order-outbox-connector",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "database.hostname": "orders-db", "database.dbname": "orders",
    "plugin.name": "pgoutput",
    "slot.name": "order_outbox_slot",                                                             
    "publication.autocreate.mode": "filtered",
    "table.include.list": "public.outbox",
    "transforms": "outbox",
    "transforms.outbox.type": "io.debezium.transforms.outbox.EventRouter",
    "transforms.outbox.route.by.field": "aggregate_type",
    "transforms.outbox.route.topic.replacement": "grocery.${routedByValue}.events.v1",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.key": "aggregate_id",
    "transforms.outbox.table.field.event.payload": "payload",
    "heartbeat.interval.ms": "10000"
  }
}
Prerequisites
alter system set wal_level = logical;             -- restart required
alter table outbox replica identity full;         -- (1)
  1. Needed for the connector to see all column values on change events.

Replication slots retain WAL

If the connector stops (crash, misconfiguration, Kafka down), PostgreSQL keeps every WAL segment the slot hasn't confirmed. On a busy database that fills the disk in hours and takes the database down — a far worse outage than the one you were avoiding. Non-negotiable safeguards:

  • Alert on pg_replication_slots.confirmed_flush_lsn lag and on WAL directory size.
  • Configure max_slot_wal_keep_size so the database sacrifices the slot rather than itself.
  • Have a runbook: restart the connector, or drop the slot and re-snapshot.
  • Test connector downtime in staging.
Choose polling when Choose CDC when Volume is moderate (< a few thousand events/s) High volume, or latency below ~200 ms matters You want zero extra infrastructure You already run Kafka Connect The team is small You have operational capacity for slots and connectors

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Read models
5.6 Level 3 — Eventual consistency in the interface
6.1 The checkout saga, end to end
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Customer
    participant O as order-service (saga)
    participant I as inventory-service
    participant P as payment-service
    participant D as delivery-service

    C->>O: POST /orders
    O->>O: TX: order(PLACED) + saga(STARTED) + ReserveStockCommand (outbox)
    O-->>C: 201 Created (order PLACED)
    O->>I: ReserveStockCommand
    I->>I: TX: inbox + reservation + StockReserved (outbox)
    I->>O: StockReserved
    O->>O: TX: saga(STOCK_RESERVED) + AuthorizePaymentCommand
    O->>P: AuthorizePaymentCommand
    alt authorized
        P->>O: PaymentAuthorized
        O->>O: TX: saga(PAYMENT_AUTHORIZED) + order(PAID) + OrderConfirmed
        O->>D: OrderConfirmed → schedule delivery
    else declined or timeout
        P->>O: PaymentFailed
        O->>O: TX: saga(COMPENSATING) + ReleaseStockCommand + order(CANCELLED)
        O->>I: ReleaseStockCommand
        I->>I: release reservation (idempotent)
    end

Note what the customer sees: 201 Created immediately with status PLACED, then a push or poll to PAID. The alternative — holding the HTTP request open through five services — trades a 300 ms response for a 4-second one that fails whenever any service is slow.

docs.title: 6.2 Saga observability
docs.text:
Signal Meaning Alert grocery.saga.open Sagas in flight Sustained growth Saga duration histogram End-to-end checkout time p99 above budget grocery.saga.compensated{reason} Compensation rate by cause Spike in any reason grocery.saga.stuck Compensation failing Any — page immediately grocery.saga.out-of-order Guarded transitions Spike indicates a flow bug Per-state age Where sagas linger "STOCK_RESERVED > 5 min" The query the on-call engineer actually runs
select state, count(*), min(started_at), max(now() - started_at) as oldest
from order_saga
where state not in ('COMPLETED','COMPENSATED','FAILED')
group by state order by count(*) desc;                                                -- (1)
  1. One query answers "what's stuck and where?" — the whole point of orchestration over choreography.

docs.title: 6.3 Reconciliation: assume drift
docs.text:
Even with outbox, inbox and sagas, distributed state drifts: a missed event during a Kafka outage, a manual database fix, a bug in a compensation path. Detection is a scheduled job (Chapter 33), not hope.

in/grocery/reconciliation/OrderPaymentReconciler.java
@Component
class OrderPaymentReconciler {

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 15 * * * *", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")                              // (1)!
    @SchedulerLock(name = "order-payment-reconciliation")
    public void reconcileLastHour() {
        var window = Window.lastHour(clock);

        var paidOrdersWithoutPayment = jdbc.sql("""
                select o.order_ref from customer_order o
                left join payment_projection p on p.order_ref = o.order_ref
                where o.status = 'PAID' and o.updated_at between :from and :to
                  and (p.order_ref is null or p.status <> 'CAPTURED')
                """).params(window.asParams()).query(String.class).list();               // (2)!

        var paymentsWithoutPaidOrder = paymentClient.capturedBetween(window)
                .stream().filter(p -> !orders.isPaid(p.orderRef())).toList();            // (3)!

        meters.gauge("grocery.reconciliation.drift", 
                paidOrdersWithoutPayment.size() + paymentsWithoutPaidOrder.size());
        if (!paidOrdersWithoutPayment.isEmpty() || !paymentsWithoutPaidOrder.isEmpty()) {
            tickets.raise("order-payment-drift", report(paidOrdersWithoutPayment, paymentsWithoutPaidOrder));  // (4)!
        }
    }
}
  1. Hourly, over a window with a lag so in-flight sagas aren't flagged as drift.
  2. Orders marked paid with no captured payment — money we didn't collect.
  3. Payments captured with no paid order — money we took without fulfilling. Both directions matter.
  4. Tickets, not automatic repair: auto-fixing financial drift without understanding the cause turns one bug into two.
Reconciliation pair Frequency Orders ↔ payments Hourly Orders ↔ stock reservations Hourly Payments ↔ gateway settlement file Daily (Chapter 33) Settlements ↔ bank transfers Weekly Catalog ↔ search index Continuous (index lag, Chapter 22)

docs.title: 6.4 Moving data during service extraction
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Monolith owns pricing tables] --> B[New service reads the same tables<br/>read-only]
    B --> C[Dual write: monolith writes both<br/>compare + alert on mismatch]
    C --> D[Backfill history into the new schema<br/>verify counts and checksums]
    D --> E[Flip writes to the new service<br/>monolith calls it]
    E --> F["Revoke monolith grants; drop old tables"]
Dual-write verification during step C
@Transactional
public void updatePrice(String sku, String zone, BigDecimal price) {
    legacyPrices.update(sku, zone, price);                                                // (1)!
    try {
        newPricingClient.update(sku, zone, price);                                        // (2)!
    } catch (Exception e) {
        meters.counter("grocery.dualwrite.failure", "target", "pricing-service").increment();
        log.warn("Dual write to pricing-service failed for {}/{}", sku, zone, e);          // (3)!
    }
}
  1. The legacy write remains authoritative during the transition.
  2. The new system is written best-effort.
  3. Never fail the request because the shadow target failed; alert instead, and reconcile with a comparison job before flipping authority.

The flip itself should be a configuration change so rollback is instant (Chapter 35).

docs.title: 6.5 Testing distributed consistency
6.6 Choosing the pattern
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Cross-service change] --> B{Single service can own it?}
    B -- yes --> C[Local ACID transaction — best answer]
    B -- no --> D{Two steps, simple failure handling?}
    D -- yes --> E[Choreography with events + compensations]
    D -- no --> F{Need visibility, timeouts, complex compensation?}
    F -- yes --> G[Orchestrated saga with persisted state]
    F -- no --> E
    C & E & G --> H[Always: outbox + idempotent consumers + reconciliation]

The first branch is the one to fight for. Many "distributed transactions" exist only because the boundary was drawn in the wrong place (Chapters 35, 37) — moving the data into one service is cheaper than any saga.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Outbox / inbox Application patterns, unchanged Unchanged Transactional event listeners @TransactionalEventListener Same Spring Modulith event publication registry Available (Chapter 37) Available (verify) Debezium / Kafka Connect External, version-independent Same Saga frameworks (Temporal, Camunda) External clients Verify client compatibility JSON payload format Jackson 2 Jackson 3 — event payload compatibility during rollout (Chapter 23)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Verify stored outbox payloads remain readable across the Jackson change (test explicitly).
  • Drain in-flight sagas before upgrading services that share a saga flow, or ensure both versions handle the same events.
  • Re-test compensation and timeout paths after upgrade — they run rarely and break silently.
  • Re-check CDC connector compatibility with any database upgrade.
  • Re-run reconciliation immediately after the rollout to catch events lost in the window.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Never dual-write: business change and event commit in one transaction via the outbox.
  2. Every consumer idempotent — inbox, conditional updates or natural keys.
  3. Sagas persist state, guard transitions, and have deadlines; STUCK is a real state with an alert.
  4. Compensate only steps that happened, idempotently.
  5. Read models are disposable and rebuildable; verify rebuild time.
  6. Display from projections, decide from the owner.
  7. Design the UX for eventual consistency — return the write result, show pending states.
  8. Reconcile continuously in both directions; raise tickets rather than auto-repairing money.
  9. Prefer moving the boundary over adding a saga.
  10. Test compensation, duplicates, out-of-order events and timeouts — they are the whole risk.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Publishing inside (or right after) a transaction without the outbox.

❌ Consumers that assume exactly-once delivery.

❌ Sagas without persisted state — "the flow is in the events somewhere".

❌ Sagas without timeouts: orders stuck forever with reserved stock.

❌ Compensation that isn't idempotent (double refunds).

❌ Throwing exceptions for business failures in a saga step (infinite retry instead of compensation).

❌ Distributed locks used for correctness across services (Chapter 22).

❌ Two-phase commit across microservices.

❌ Event sourcing adopted for integration when the outbox would do.

❌ No reconciliation — drift accumulates silently until finance finds it.

❌ A read model nobody can rebuild.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Orders exist, downstream never reacts Dual write lost the event; relay stopped Outbox pending gauge, relay alerting Stock reserved but order cancelled Compensation missing/failed Saga state audit, compensation retries, reconciliation Double charges Non-idempotent consumer or retry Inbox + idempotency keys (Chapters 04, 23) Sagas accumulate in one state Missing event, consumer down, no timeout Per-state age dashboard, timeout sweeper PostgreSQL disk filling Stalled CDC replication slot Slot lag alerts, max_slot_wal_keep_size, connector runbook Read model wrong Projector bug or missed events Replay from the beginning; verify rebuild time "Order not in my list" complaints Reading an eventually-consistent projection after a write Return the write result; version tokens Drift found by finance No reconciliation Hourly two-directional jobs (6.3) Compensations spike Upstream failing (payments, stock) Check grocery.saga.compensated{reason} and the dependency

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Outbox in every service that publishes events; MANDATORY propagation enforced
  • Pending-outbox gauge and relay/connector alerts
  • CDC slot lag and WAL size alerts, with a documented runbook
  • Inbox or equivalent idempotency in every consumer
  • Saga state persisted with deadlines, guarded transitions and a STUCK alert
  • Compensation paths tested, including duplicates and out-of-order events
  • Read models rebuildable, rebuild time measured
  • Reconciliation jobs in both directions, with drift metrics and tickets
  • UX designed for eventual consistency on every write path

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is the dual-write problem?

Short answer: Writing to two systems (database and broker) without atomicity — one can succeed while the other fails, leaving them inconsistent with no way to detect it.

B1 · What is the outbox pattern?

Short answer: Write the event into a table in the same transaction as the business change; a separate relay or CDC connector publishes it. Atomic, at-least-once, nothing lost.

B1 · Why must consumers be idempotent?

Short answer: Delivery is at-least-once — retries, rebalances and replays redeliver messages. Without idempotency you get duplicate side effects.

B1 · What is a saga?

Short answer: A sequence of local transactions across services, each with a compensating action, used instead of a distributed transaction.

B1 · What does "eventually consistent" mean for a user?

Short answer: Different parts of the system briefly show different states — a placed order may not appear in search or history for a second or two.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Choreography or orchestration?

Short answer: Choreography for short flows where services simply react to events; orchestration when you need visibility, timeouts, ordering guarantees and complex compensation — checkout usually qualifies.

B2 · How do you compensate a payment?

Short answer: Semantically: void the authorization if not captured, refund if captured. You never undo it physically; you perform an offsetting business action, idempotently.

B2 · Polling relay or CDC for the outbox?

Short answer: Polling is simpler with no extra infrastructure and adequate for most services; CDC gives lower latency and less database load but adds Kafka Connect and replication-slot operations — including the risk of WAL growth when it stalls.

B2 · What makes a read model safe?

Short answer: It owns no truth and can be rebuilt by replaying events. If it can't be rebuilt, it has silently become a system of record.

B2 · How do you handle "I placed an order but don't see it"?

Short answer: Return the created resource so the client renders from the response; where a projection must be read, use version tokens or a pending state rather than showing stale data as current.

B2 · Why not use two-phase commit?

Short answer: It requires participant support, blocks resources during the protocol, and makes the coordinator a critical failure point — availability suffers badly. Sagas trade atomicity for availability, which is usually the right trade.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through an orchestrated saga's failure handling.

Short answer: State is persisted with an expected-state guard on each transition; step failures arrive as events and move the saga to COMPENSATING; compensations are emitted only for completed steps and are idempotent; a sweeper enforces deadlines; repeated compensation failure moves the saga to STUCK with an alert.

B3 · What are the operational risks of CDC?

Short answer: A stalled replication slot retains WAL and can fill the database disk; connector lag delays all events; schema changes can break the connector; snapshots on large tables are heavy. Mitigate with slot-lag alerts, max_slot_wal_keep_size, runbooks and staging tests of connector downtime.

B3 · How do you prevent duplicate compensation?

Short answer: Guarded state transitions plus idempotent compensating commands (release by reservation id, refund keyed by payment id), and consumers that deduplicate by event id.

B3 · When is event sourcing justified?

Short answer: When history is the product (audit, temporal queries, regulatory replay) or invariants genuinely require the full event history. It's a large commitment — schema evolution, snapshots, replay tooling, team skill. For integration alone, the outbox achieves the same without making events the source of truth.

B3 · How do you migrate data when extracting a service?

Short answer: Read-only phase, then dual write with mismatch alerting, backfill with verification (counts, checksums), flip authority via configuration, verify with reconciliation, then revoke old access and drop the tables.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design consistency for checkout across five services.

Short answer: Outbox in each service; inbox idempotency in each consumer; an orchestrated saga in order-service with persisted state, deadlines and compensations; immediate 201 with PLACED and asynchronous progression; read models for history; hourly two-directional reconciliation between orders, payments and reservations; dashboards for open/stuck sagas.

B4 · How do you decide between fixing the boundary and building a saga?

Short answer: If two services must change together for a single business invariant, the boundary is probably wrong — merging the data into one service gives a local transaction and removes an entire class of failure. Build a saga only when the steps genuinely belong to different capabilities with independent lifecycles.

B4 · What does a mature reconciliation strategy look like?

Short answer: Pairs of systems reconciled on a cadence matched to risk, checks in both directions, windows that exclude in-flight work, drift metrics with alerts, tickets rather than silent auto-repair for financial data, and periodic review of drift causes as defects.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What's the real cost of eventual consistency?

Short answer: It spreads beyond engineering: product must design pending states, support must explain delays, finance must accept reconciliation windows, and operations must monitor drift. The technical patterns are the easy part; the organizational agreement about acceptable inconsistency windows is the hard part.

B5 · How do you keep distributed-data complexity from compounding?

Short answer: Prefer boundaries that keep invariants local; standardize the few patterns (outbox, inbox, saga) in platform libraries; forbid ad-hoc variants; require reconciliation for every cross-service invariant; and review saga count and complexity as an architectural health metric.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · 300 orders paid, stock never reserved

A Kafka outage coincided with a deploy; the service published directly after commit, so events during the window were lost. Fixes: outbox with a pending gauge and relay alerting, a backfill job replaying affected orders through the saga, reconciliation between orders and reservations, and a test that kills the broker mid-flow.

Scenario · Customers charged for cancelled orders

Payment authorization succeeded after the saga had timed out and compensated; the late PaymentAuthorized event was applied unguarded and marked the order paid, while stock had been released. Fixes: guarded transitions (ignore events for terminal states), void/refund on late authorization, longer deadline than the payment provider's own timeout, and an out-of-order metric with alerting.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Refund saga

A customer requests a refund for a delivered order. Steps: validate eligibility (order-service), initiate gateway refund (payment-service), adjust seller settlement (settlement-service), notify the customer. Compensations: if settlement adjustment fails after a successful refund, the refund cannot be undone — record an adjustment task instead. Implement the saga with state, deadlines and idempotency, and list the tests.

Solution refund_saga
create table refund_saga (
    refund_ref    varchar(40) primary key,
    order_ref     varchar(40) not null,
    amount_paise  bigint      not null,
    state         varchar(30) not null,
    gateway_refund_id varchar(64),
    settlement_adjustment_id varchar(64),
    deadline_at   timestamptz not null,
    last_error    text,
    version       bigint not null default 0,
    unique (order_ref, amount_paise, requested_at)                                    -- (1)
);
  1. A natural key preventing accidental duplicate refund requests for the same order and amount.
RefundSaga.java (core)
@Transactional
public void start(String orderRef, long amountPaise, String reason) {
    Order order = orders.require(orderRef);
    if (!order.isRefundable(amountPaise)) {                                            // (1)!
        throw new RefundNotAllowedException(orderRef);
    }
    String refundRef = RefundRef.next();
    sagas.insert(refundRef, orderRef, amountPaise, State.STARTED,
            clock.instant().plus(Duration.ofHours(24)));                               // (2)!
    outbox.append("refund", refundRef, "InitiateRefundCommand",
            new InitiateRefundCommand(refundRef, orderRef, amountPaise, reason));
}

@Transactional
public void onRefundSucceeded(RefundSucceeded event) {
    transition(event.refundRef(), State.STARTED, State.REFUND_ISSUED, saga -> {
        saga.setGatewayRefundId(event.gatewayRefundId());
        outbox.append("refund", saga.refundRef(), "AdjustSettlementCommand",
                new AdjustSettlementCommand(saga.refundRef(), saga.orderRef(), saga.amountPaise()));
    });
}

@Transactional
public void onRefundFailed(RefundFailed event) {
    transition(event.refundRef(), State.STARTED, State.FAILED, saga -> {               // (3)!
        saga.setLastError(event.reason());
        outbox.append("refund", saga.refundRef(), "RefundRejected",
                new RefundRejected(saga.orderRef(), event.reason()));
    });
}

@Transactional
public void onSettlementAdjusted(SettlementAdjusted event) {
    transition(event.refundRef(), State.REFUND_ISSUED, State.COMPLETED, saga -> {
        saga.setSettlementAdjustmentId(event.adjustmentId());
        outbox.append("refund", saga.refundRef(), "RefundCompleted",
                new RefundCompleted(saga.orderRef(), saga.amountPaise()));
    });
}

@Transactional
public void onSettlementAdjustmentFailed(SettlementAdjustmentFailed event) {
    transition(event.refundRef(), State.REFUND_ISSUED, State.MANUAL_ADJUSTMENT_REQUIRED, saga -> {
        saga.setLastError(event.reason());
        financeTasks.create("settlement-adjustment", saga.orderRef(), saga.amountPaise());   // (4)!
        meters.counter("grocery.refund.manual-adjustment").increment();
        alerts.raise("refund-settlement-failed", saga.refundRef());
    });
}
  1. Eligibility is checked before any external step — the cheapest failure is the one that never starts.
  2. A 24-hour deadline: gateway refunds can legitimately take hours, so the timeout must reflect the real-world SLA, not a technical guess.
  3. Failure before money moved is clean: no compensation needed.
  4. The interesting case: the refund succeeded, the settlement adjustment failed, and the refund cannot be reversed. The compensation is a finance task, not a technical rollback — the saga records reality instead of pretending it can undo it.
Tests
@Test void happyPathCompletesAndNotifies() { }
@Test void ineligibleOrderIsRejectedBeforeAnyExternalCall() { }
@Test void gatewayFailureEndsSagaWithoutCompensation() { }
@Test void settlementFailureCreatesFinanceTaskAndAlerts() { }                          // (1)!
@Test void duplicateRefundSucceededEventsAdjustSettlementOnce() { }
@Test void lateEventsForCompletedSagaAreIgnored() { }
@Test void deadlinePassedWithoutGatewayResponseRaisesStuck() { }
  1. The test that protects real money: a refund issued without a settlement adjustment means the platform absorbs the cost silently unless someone is told.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The outbox eliminates dual writes; polling first, CDC when volume justifies the operational cost (and its WAL risk).
  • At-least-once + idempotent consumers = effectively once. There is no other exactly-once.
  • Sagas need persisted state, guarded transitions, deadlines and a STUCK alert — compensation can fail too.
  • Compensation is semantic, idempotent, and applied only to steps that happened.
  • Read models are disposable; display from projections, decide from the owner.
  • Design the interface for eventual consistency, don't hide it.
  • Reconcile in both directions on a schedule; drift is certain, silence is the danger.
  • Fixing the boundary beats building a saga whenever it's possible.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) — consistency, replication, distributed transactions
  • Chris Richardson, Microservices Patterns — saga, outbox, CQRS with worked examples
  • Debezium documentation — outbox event router, PostgreSQL connector, replication slot operations
  • Spring Modulith Reference — event publication registry (Chapter 37)

35 Microservices & Spring Cloud · 37 DDD, Hexagonal & Modular Monolith

docs.title: 37 · DDD, Hexagonal Architecture & the Modular Monolith
1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapter 35 said boundaries matter more than technology. This chapter is about how to find them, and how to structure code so they hold.
