Two failure modes bracket most enterprise Java:

  • The big ball of mud: a 400,000-line monolith where OrderService calls InventoryService calls PricingService calls back into OrderRepository, every class can reach every other, and a change to delivery fees breaks seller payouts. Nobody can extract anything because everything touches everything.
  • The distributed ball of mud: the same graph, now with HTTP between the nodes. Every previous problem, plus network failures, serialization, and deployment coordination.

The cure for both is the same and it isn't microservices. It's boundaries with meaning — drawn along the business's own divisions — and dependency direction that keeps the domain independent of frameworks and infrastructure.

This chapter covers: strategic DDD (bounded contexts, ubiquitous language, context mapping) as the method for finding boundaries; tactical DDD (aggregates, value objects, domain events) as the method for enforcing invariants; hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters) for dependency direction; and the modular monolith with Spring Modulith — a structure that gives you module boundaries, verified at build time, inside one deployable, so extraction later is a refactor rather than a rewrite.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — entities, value objects, package structure B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — aggregates, ports and adapters, domain events B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — aggregate design, module boundaries, Modulith B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — context mapping, extraction strategy, governance B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — architecture as an organizational instrument

docs.title: 2.1 Strategic DDD: finding boundaries
docs.text:
Concept Meaning in the grocery platform Ubiquitous language "Order" means the same thing in code, conversation and the database — within a context Bounded context The scope in which a model and its language are consistent Subdomain Core (what differentiates: pricing, delivery slotting), supporting (seller onboarding), generic (notifications, auth) Context map How contexts relate, and who depends on whom

The single most useful DDD insight: the same word means different things in different contexts.

"Product" in… Means Catalog Title, images, attributes, category, brand Pricing SKU, zone prices, GST rate, promotions Inventory SKU, hub, quantity, reservation state Search Indexed document with analyzers and boosts Settlement SKU, commission rate, seller

Forcing one Product class across all five is what produces the god object with 80 fields and five teams editing it. Five models, each small and complete for its context, is the correct answer — with events carrying what's shared (Chapter 36).

docs.title: 2.2 Context mapping patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Use Partnership Two teams succeed or fail together; coordinate closely Customer–Supplier Downstream needs influence upstream planning Conformist Downstream accepts the upstream model as-is (a legacy ERP) Anticorruption layer (ACL) Translate an external model into yours at the boundary Shared kernel A small shared model, jointly owned — expensive; use sparingly Published language A documented contract (our REST/event schemas — Chapters 20, 23) Open host service One upstream API serving many downstreams

The platform's ERP integration is a classic ACL: the ERP's PartnerAccount and LedgerEntry never appear in our domain; an adapter translates them into Seller and Settlement.

docs.title: 2.3 Tactical DDD
docs.text: Building block Rule Value object Immutable, no identity, equality by value (Money, Pincode, Gstin) Entity Identity that persists through change (Order, Seller) Aggregate A cluster with one root; the consistency and transaction boundary Aggregate root The only entry point; enforces invariants Domain event Something that happened, named in past tense (OrderPlaced) Repository Persistence per aggregate, not per table Domain service Logic that belongs to no single aggregate (CommissionCalculator) Application service Orchestrates use cases: transaction, repositories, events — no business rules

docs.title: 2.4 Aggregate design rules
docs.text:
1. Protect true invariants inside the aggregate ("an order's total equals the sum of its lines"; "a cart may not exceed 50 items").
  2. Keep aggregates small. A Seller aggregate containing all their orders is unusable.
  3. One aggregate per transaction. Changing two aggregates atomically is a design smell — use a domain event and eventual consistency (Chapter 36).
  4. Reference other aggregates by id, never by object reference (Chapter 13's rule, with a reason behind it).
  5. Eventual consistency between aggregates is normal and expected.
Example
Order (root)
 ├── OrderLine (part of the aggregate — no independent life)
 ├── customerId  → reference to another aggregate
 └── sellerId    → reference

docs.title: 2.5 Hexagonal architecture (ports and adapters)
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Adapters_In[Inbound adapters]
        W[REST controller]
        K[Kafka listener]
        S[Scheduled job]
    end
    subgraph Core[Application core]
        UC[Use cases / application services]
        D[Domain model: aggregates, value objects, events]
        P1[[Outbound ports — interfaces]]
    end
    subgraph Adapters_Out[Outbound adapters]
        R[JPA repository]
        H[HTTP client]
        Q[Kafka producer]
    end
    W & K & S --> UC
    UC --> D
    UC --> P1
    P1 -.implemented by.-> R & H & Q

The one rule: dependencies point inward. The domain knows nothing about HTTP, JPA, Kafka or Spring. Adapters depend on the core; the core defines interfaces (ports) that adapters implement.

Benefit Cost Domain testable without any framework Mapping between domain and persistence models Infrastructure swappable (JPA → JDBC, REST → gRPC) More types, more files Business rules readable without framework noise Team discipline to keep the direction

Proportionality: apply it fully to core subdomains (pricing, order lifecycle, settlement); for generic CRUD (a banner-management screen), the pragmatic layering from Chapter 08 is fine. Hexagonal everywhere is as wrong as hexagonal nowhere.

docs.title: 2.6 How this maps to the handbook's layering
docs.text:
Handbook layer (Chapters 01, 08) Hexagonal role Controller Inbound adapter Delegate Inbound port implementation / use-case entry Service Application service (+ domain services) Domain model The core Repository interface Outbound port Repository implementation (JPA) Outbound adapter HTTP client interface Outbound port RestClient implementation Outbound adapter

The familiar four-layer structure is hexagonal when the dependency direction is respected and the domain doesn't import jakarta.persistence or org.springframework.web.

docs.title: 2.7 The modular monolith
docs.text:
One deployable, several modules with enforced boundaries:

Property Monolith Modular monolith Microservices Deployment One One Many Boundaries None enforced Compile/test-time enforced Network-enforced Transactions Local ACID Local ACID Sagas Refactoring across boundaries Trivial Moderate Expensive Team autonomy Low Medium High Operational cost Low Low High Extraction later Rewrite Refactor —

For most teams, the modular monolith is the right starting point and often the right ending point.

docs.title: 2.8 Spring Modulith
docs.text:
Feature What it gives ApplicationModules.of(App.class).verify() Fails the build on boundary violations Package conventions Top-level package per module; nested packages are internal @ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = …) Explicit allowed dependencies Named interfaces Expose more than one public package deliberately @ApplicationModuleListener Async, transactional module-to-module events Event publication registry Persists publications, completes them, republishes incomplete ones on restart Documenter Generates module diagrams and a component canvas Scenario API Tests that publish an event and await its effects

The event publication registry is the detail that matters most: it makes in-process module events reliable, which is exactly the property you need if those modules might later become services (Chapter 36's outbox, at module scale).

docs.title: 3.1 Module detection and verification
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["ApplicationModules.of(GroceryApplication.class)"] --> B[Scan direct subpackages of the application package]
    B --> C[Each subpackage = a module]
    C --> D[Module API = types in the module's base package]
    D --> E[Nested packages = internal]
    E --> F[verify: does any module reference another's internals?]
    F -->|yes| G[Violation — build fails]
    F -->|no| H[Pass]
Example
in.grocery.seller                      ← the application package
├── catalog/                           ← module "catalog"
│   ├── CatalogService.java            ← module API (public)
│   └── internal/                      ← internal, unreachable from other modules
│       ├── ProductEntity.java
│       └── ProductRepository.java
├── settlement/                        ← module "settlement"
└── onboarding/                        ← module "onboarding"

docs.title: 3.2 Module events with the publication registry
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Module A (transaction)
    participant E as ApplicationEventPublisher
    participant R as event_publication table
    participant B as Module B listener

    A->>E: publishEvent(SettlementDue)
    E->>R: insert publication (same transaction)
    Note over A,R: COMMIT
    E->>B: @ApplicationModuleListener (async, new transaction)
    alt success
        B->>R: mark completed
    else failure / crash
        Note over R: publication stays incomplete
        Note over R: republished on restart (if enabled)
    end

This is the outbox pattern (Chapter 36) applied within a process — and the reason a Modulith module can be extracted into a service later without changing the sender's code.

docs.title: 3.3 Dependency direction in practice
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph web["adapter.web (Spring MVC)"]
        C[OrderController]
    end
    subgraph app["application"]
        UC[PlaceOrderUseCase]
        P1[[OrderRepository — port]]
        P2[[PaymentGateway — port]]
    end
    subgraph domain["domain (no framework imports)"]
        O[Order aggregate]
        M[Money, Pincode value objects]
        EV[OrderPlaced event]
    end
    subgraph persistence["adapter.persistence (JPA)"]
        RA[JpaOrderRepository implements OrderRepository]
    end
    subgraph payment["adapter.payment"]
        PA[RazorpayGateway implements PaymentGateway]
    end
    C --> UC
    UC --> O
    UC --> P1
    UC --> P2
    RA -.->|implements| P1
    PA -.->|implements| P2
    RA --> O

An ArchUnit rule (Chapter 28) makes the arrows real: domain may not depend on application, adapter.*, Spring or JPA.

docs.title: 4.1 Value objects
4.2 An aggregate
4.3 Testing the domain
5.1 Level 2 — Ports and adapters
5.2 Level 2 — Anticorruption layer
5.3 Level 3 — Aggregate boundaries in practice
docs.text:
The wrong aggregate (a very common mistake):

Seller.java
public class Seller {                                                             // ❌
    private List<Product> products;        // 40,000 products
    private List<Order> orders;            // 2.8 million orders
    private List<Settlement> settlements;
}

Loading a seller loads a gigabyte; every product edit locks the seller row; nothing scales.

The right decomposition:

Aggregate Contains Invariant it protects Seller Profile, status, commission rate "An inactive seller cannot receive new orders" Product SKU, attributes, seller id "Selling price ≤ MRP" Order Lines, status, totals "Total = subtotal + fee"; valid transitions Settlement Period, lines, payout "Payout = Σ lines − commission − TDS"

Cross-aggregate rules ("a seller's outstanding payout must not exceed X") are handled by a domain service plus eventual consistency, not by fusing aggregates.

One aggregate per transaction
@Transactional
public void confirmOrder(OrderRef ref, PaymentId paymentId) {
    Order order = orders.findByRef(ref).orElseThrow();
    order.markPaid(paymentId);                                                     // (1)!
    orders.save(order);
    events.publishAll(order.pullEvents());                                         // (2)!
}
  1. Exactly one aggregate changes.
  2. Effects on other aggregates (stock, loyalty, settlement) happen via events — eventually consistent by design (Chapter 36).

A practical test for aggregate boundaries

Ask: must these two things always be consistent at the same instant, or is "within a few seconds" acceptable? Only the first case justifies one aggregate. In practice, that's rarer than teams assume — and the assumption is what produces god aggregates.

docs.title: 5.4 Level 3 — The modular monolith with Spring Modulith
docs.text:
The seller portal is one deployable with four modules — a good fit because the modules share a database, change together, and are owned by one team.

build.gradle.kts
implementation(platform("org.springframework.modulith:spring-modulith-bom:1.x"))   // (1)!
implementation("org.springframework.modulith:spring-modulith-starter-core")
implementation("org.springframework.modulith:spring-modulith-starter-jpa")
testImplementation("org.springframework.modulith:spring-modulith-starter-test")
  1. Verify the version matching your Boot release.
Module structure
in.grocery.sellerportal
├── SellerPortalApplication.java
├── catalog/
│   ├── CatalogService.java              ← public API of the module
│   ├── ProductView.java                 ← published types
│   └── internal/                        ← everything else
├── onboarding/
│   ├── OnboardingService.java
│   └── internal/
├── settlement/
│   ├── SettlementService.java
│   └── internal/
└── shared/                              ← minimal: ids, Money (a small shared kernel)
src/test/java/in/grocery/sellerportal/ModularityTest.java
class ModularityTest {

    static final ApplicationModules modules = ApplicationModules.of(SellerPortalApplication.class);

    @Test
    void modulesRespectTheirBoundaries() {
        modules.verify();                                                          // (1)!
    }

    @Test
    void writeDocumentation() {
        new Documenter(modules)
                .writeModulesAsPlantUml()
                .writeIndividualModulesAsPlantUml()
                .writeModuleCanvases();                                            // (2)!
    }
}
  1. The build fails if settlement imports catalog.internal.ProductEntity. Boundaries stop being a convention and become a compile-time property.
  2. Generated diagrams and a canvas per module (its API, events published and consumed, dependencies) — documentation that cannot drift.
Explicit dependencies
@ApplicationModule(allowedDependencies = {"catalog", "shared"})                     // (1)!
package in.grocery.sellerportal.settlement;
  1. Declared in package-info.java: settlement may use catalog and shared, nothing else. Any other dependency fails verification — including one added accidentally by an IDE import.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — Module events
5.6 Level 3 — Enforcing architecture with ArchUnit
6.1 The platform's context map
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Core["Core subdomains — invest here"]
        P[Pricing & Promotions]
        D[Delivery slotting & routing]
        O[Order lifecycle]
    end
    subgraph Supporting["Supporting"]
        C[Catalog]
        S[Seller onboarding & settlement]
        I[Inventory]
    end
    subgraph Generic["Generic — buy or keep simple"]
        N[Notifications]
        A[Identity]
        R[Reporting]
    end
    O -->|published language: events| I
    O -->|customer–supplier| P
    C -->|open host service| Search[Search]
    S -->|ACL| ERP[(Legacy ERP)]
    A -->|conformist| IdP[(Corporate IdP)]
    N -->|generic| SMS[(SMS/Email providers)]
Classification Implication Core Rich domain model, hexagonal, best engineers, heavy test coverage Supporting Pragmatic layering, straightforward models Generic Buy, or keep deliberately simple; never gold-plate

Recognizing that notifications are generic — and refusing to build an elaborate domain model for them — is as much a DDD decision as modelling pricing carefully.

docs.title: 6.2 From modular monolith to services
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Modules with verified boundaries] --> B{Does a module need<br/>independent deploy/scale/ownership?}
    B -- no --> C[Keep it in the monolith — this is fine]
    B -- yes --> D[Module already: own package, own tables,<br/>API-only access, events for cross-module effects]
    D --> E[Replace in-process events with Kafka topics]
    E --> F[Replace module API calls with an HTTP/gRPC client]
    F --> G[Move tables and revoke grants]
    G --> H[Deploy separately]

Because Modulith already forbade internal access and encouraged events, each step is mechanical. The extraction cost is proportional to how well the boundary was maintained — which is the entire argument for starting modular.

What changes when a module becomes a service
// before (in-process)
@ApplicationModuleListener
void onSettlementClosed(SettlementClosed event) { ... }

// after (across services) — Chapter 23
@KafkaListener(topics = "grocery.settlement.closed.v1", groupId = "notification-service")
@Transactional
public void onSettlementClosed(SettlementClosed event) {
    if (inbox.alreadyProcessed(CONSUMER, event.eventId())) return;                  // (1)!
    inbox.markProcessed(CONSUMER, event.eventId());
    notifications.sendPayoutNotice(event.sellerId(), event.payout());
}
  1. The one genuinely new concern: at-least-once delivery now requires explicit idempotency (the publication registry provided equivalent guarantees in-process).

docs.title: 6.3 Where the platform applies which style
docs.text:
Component Style Why order-service Full hexagonal, rich domain Core: complex invariants, high change rate pricing-service Full hexagonal, rich domain Core: the platform's differentiator settlement-service Hexagonal with an ACL to the ERP Money and an external model catalog-service Pragmatic layering (Chapter 08) Mostly CRUD with validation notification-service Pragmatic layering Generic subdomain seller-portal Modular monolith (Modulith) Four cohesive modules, one team, shared database mobile-bff Thin composition layer No domain at all (Chapter 32)

Uniformity is not a goal. Match the structure to the subdomain, and write the reason in an ADR so the next team knows it was a decision.

docs.title: 6.4 Governance
6.5 When to relax the rules
docs.text:
Situation Pragmatic choice Generic CRUD subdomain Layered structure, entities as the model Short-lived service (campaign microsite) Simplest thing that works Read-only reporting service Query objects straight to DTOs (Chapter 12) Prototype/spike No architecture; delete it afterwards Core domain under active change Full discipline — this is where it pays

The failure mode of architecture enthusiasm is mapping layers for a table with four columns. The failure mode of pragmatism is a 3,000-line OrderService that nobody can change safely. Both are real; the judgement is which subdomain you're in.

docs.title: 6.6 Refactoring toward boundaries
docs.text:
A practical sequence for an existing tangled codebase:

flowchart TD
    A[Identify contexts with domain experts<br/>language, not tables] --> B[Move code into per-context packages<br/>no behaviour change]
    B --> C[Add FreezingArchRule boundaries<br/>Chapter 28 — new violations fail]
    C --> D["Introduce module APIs; make internals package-private"]
    D --> E[Replace cross-context calls with events]
    E --> F["Split shared tables; one writer each"]
    F --> G[Modulith verification passes]
    G --> H{Extraction needed?}
    H -- yes --> I[Chapter 35's strangler fig]
    H -- no --> J[Stop here — a good place to be]

Steps B and C deliver most of the value for a fraction of the cost, and — importantly — can be done incrementally without a rewrite.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Spring Modulith 1.2/1.3 Version aligned with Boot 4 (verify) Event publication registry JPA/JDBC/MongoDB stores Same (verify schema/property names) @ApplicationModuleListener ✅ ✅ Documenter output PlantUML/Mermaid, canvases Same (verify) ArchUnit 1.x Same Domain code Framework-free by design Unaffected by the upgrade

The clearest benefit of a framework-free domain

A Boot 3 → 4 upgrade touches adapters — web, persistence, messaging, configuration — and leaves the domain untouched. On a hexagonal core service, that's the difference between reviewing a few adapter classes and auditing the whole codebase.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Check Spring Modulith's version compatibility before upgrading Boot.
  • Verify the event publication registry schema (it is a database migration — Chapter 14).
  • Re-run ApplicationModules.verify() after package moves in the upgrade.
  • Re-generate module documentation.
  • Confirm ArchUnit rules still match new framework package names (Jackson 3, moved Boot packages).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Find boundaries in the language, with domain experts — not in the database schema.
  2. Let the same word mean different things in different contexts; connect them with events.
  3. Small aggregates, one per transaction, referenced by id; eventual consistency between them.
  4. Value objects for domain concepts (Money, Pincode) — validation once, at construction.
  5. Dependencies point inward; the domain imports no framework.
  6. Enforce boundaries mechanically with ArchUnit and ApplicationModules.verify().
  7. Start with a modular monolith; extract only when deployment, scaling or ownership diverge.
  8. Use module events with the publication registry, so extraction is mechanical later.
  9. Match structure to subdomain: rich models for core, simple layering for generic.
  10. Record decisions in ADRs and review the context map as the business changes.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ A god aggregate (Seller containing orders and products).

❌ One canonical model shared across all contexts.

❌ Anemic domain with all logic in services, for a core subdomain.

❌ Framework annotations in the domain model, then claiming it's hexagonal.

❌ Mapping layers for a CRUD table with four columns.

❌ Two aggregates modified in one transaction because "it's easier".

❌ Package structure by technical layer (controllers/, services/, entities/) in a large codebase — it hides feature boundaries.

❌ Boundaries documented in a wiki and enforced nowhere.

❌ Extracting services before the modules are clean.

❌ Applying maximum ceremony uniformly to every subdomain.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix A change ripples through many classes Boundaries don't match the business Re-derive contexts from the language; re-package Aggregate loads are slow Aggregate too large Split; reference by id; separate read models Deadlocks on a shared row God aggregate as a lock point Smaller aggregates; eventual consistency "Hexagonal" but the domain imports JPA No enforcement ArchUnit rule; separate entity and domain models Modulith verification fails after refactoring Package moved into another module's space Fix the package, or declare the dependency Module events lost on crash Publication registry not enabled Enable it; monitor incomplete publications Every feature touches every module Wrong module split Merge or re-split around real cohesion Extraction takes months Boundary was never real Modularize in place first (6.6) Team resists the structure Ceremony applied to generic subdomains Relax it there; keep discipline in core

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Contexts identified with domain experts; a glossary per context
  • Subdomains classified core/supporting/generic, with matching investment
  • Aggregates small, one per transaction, referenced by id
  • Value objects for money, identifiers and domain constraints
  • ArchUnit rules enforcing dependency direction in core services
  • ApplicationModules.verify() in modular applications
  • Module events use the publication registry; incomplete publications monitored
  • Module documentation generated in CI
  • ADRs recording style decisions per service
  • Context map reviewed quarterly

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is a value object?

Short answer: An immutable object with no identity, compared by value — Money, Pincode, Gstin. Validation happens at construction, so invalid instances can't exist.

B1 · What is an aggregate?

Short answer: A cluster of objects with one root that enforces the group's invariants and is the transaction boundary. External code interacts only through the root.

B1 · What is a bounded context?

Short answer: The scope in which a model and its terms mean one thing. "Product" in catalog and "product" in pricing are different models in different contexts.

B1 · What does hexagonal architecture mean?

Short answer: The domain sits in the middle with no framework dependencies; inbound adapters (web, messaging) call it, and it calls outbound ports implemented by adapters (database, HTTP). Dependencies point inward.

B1 · What is a modular monolith?

Short answer: One deployable application split into modules with enforced boundaries — the organizational benefits of separation without the operational cost of distribution.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Why reference other aggregates by id?

Short answer: It keeps aggregates small, prevents accidental loading of huge object graphs, and makes the transaction boundary explicit — you can't modify two aggregates in one transaction by accident.

B2 · Is an anemic domain model always wrong?

Short answer: No. For generic or CRUD subdomains it's perfectly reasonable. It's a problem in core subdomains, where scattering rules across services makes them inconsistent and hard to test.

B2 · What does Spring Modulith add over package conventions?

Short answer: Verification that fails the build on boundary violations, declared module dependencies, module-scoped tests, generated documentation, and reliable module events through the publication registry.

B2 · What is an anticorruption layer?

Short answer: An adapter that translates an external system's model into yours, so its concepts and quirks never leak into your domain — essential when integrating with legacy or third-party systems.

B2 · What's the cost of hexagonal architecture?

Short answer: Mapping between domain and persistence models, more types and files, and the discipline to maintain direction. Worth it for core domains, overhead for simple CRUD.

B2 · How do you enforce that the domain stays framework-free?

Short answer: An ArchUnit rule forbidding dependencies from ..domain.. on Spring, JPA, Jackson and outer packages, running in every build.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How do you decide aggregate boundaries?

Short answer: By invariants that must hold at the same instant. If eventual consistency (seconds) is acceptable, they're separate aggregates connected by domain events. Keep aggregates small enough to load and lock cheaply.

B3 · Why does the same concept get different models in different contexts?

Short answer: Because each context cares about different attributes and rules. One canonical model becomes a god object owned by everyone and no one; separate models stay small and are connected by published contracts.

B3 · How does the Modulith event publication registry work, and why does it matter?

Short answer: Publications are persisted in the same transaction as the business change and marked complete when the listener succeeds; incomplete ones can be republished after a restart. It's the outbox pattern in-process — which means module-to-module events have the same reliability they'd have as Kafka events after extraction.

B3 · How would you refactor a tangled monolith toward boundaries?

Short answer: Identify contexts from the language with domain experts; re-package by context without behaviour change; add frozen architecture rules so new violations fail; introduce module APIs and make internals package-private; replace cross-context calls with events; split shared tables. Extraction, if ever, comes last.

B3 · How does hexagonal architecture help with framework upgrades?

Short answer: Framework changes are confined to adapters. A Boot major upgrade touches web, persistence and messaging code; the domain model — where the business rules and the hardest tests live — compiles unchanged.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you classify subdomains and what follows from it?

Short answer: Core (differentiating — invest: rich models, hexagonal, best people), supporting (necessary but not differentiating — pragmatic), generic (buy or keep simple). It directs effort where it creates value and prevents gold-plating notifications while pricing rots.

B4 · Modular monolith or microservices for a new platform?

Short answer: Modular monolith unless there's a concrete need for independent deployment, scaling or ownership. It preserves local transactions and cheap refactoring while the domain is still being learned — and with verified boundaries, extraction later is a refactor rather than a rewrite.

B4 · How do you keep architecture from eroding across many teams?

Short answer: Mechanical enforcement (ArchUnit, Modulith verification) in a shared library, generated documentation, ADRs, boundaries owned by teams, and periodic context-map reviews. Anything enforced only by review erodes with the first deadline.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What does DDD actually buy an organization?

Short answer: A shared language between business and engineering, boundaries that match how the business changes, and therefore changes that stay local. The tactical patterns are secondary; the strategic work — contexts, language, ownership — is where the value is.

B5 · When is DDD the wrong investment?

Short answer: Simple CRUD systems, short-lived projects, generic subdomains, or organizations without access to domain experts. Applying tactical patterns without strategic understanding produces ceremony with no benefit — the common failure mode.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Every pricing change breaks the seller portal

A single shared Product entity served catalog, pricing and settlement, with logic spread across services that all mutated it. Fixes: split into per-context models with events carrying what's shared, define the catalog's published language, enforce boundaries with ArchUnit, and move settlement's view of a product behind an ACL-style projection.

Scenario · Extraction of the settlement module was estimated at two weeks and took five months

The module shared tables with the monolith, accessed internal classes freely, and had no event-based decoupling. Fixes (applied to the next extraction): modularize in place first with verified boundaries, split tables with one writer each, replace direct calls with module events, and only then extract — which took nine days.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Model the cart

Model Cart as an aggregate with: at most 50 distinct SKUs, quantity 1–20 per line, a total, the ability to add/update/remove lines, a version for optimistic locking, and domain events for ItemAdded and CartCleared. Then define the ports for persistence and pricing, and write domain tests with no Spring.

Solution Cart.java (domain — no framework imports)
public class Cart {

    private static final int MAX_LINES = 50;
    private static final int MAX_QUANTITY_PER_LINE = 20;

    private final CartId id;
    private final CustomerId customerId;
    private final Map<Sku, CartLine> lines = new LinkedHashMap<>();             // (1)!
    private long version;
    private final List<DomainEvent> events = new ArrayList<>();

    public void addItem(Sku sku, int quantity, Money unitPrice) {
        if (quantity < 1 || quantity > MAX_QUANTITY_PER_LINE) {
            throw new InvalidQuantityException(sku, quantity, MAX_QUANTITY_PER_LINE);
        }
        CartLine existing = lines.get(sku);
        int newQuantity = existing == null ? quantity : existing.quantity() + quantity;
        if (newQuantity > MAX_QUANTITY_PER_LINE) {
            throw new InvalidQuantityException(sku, newQuantity, MAX_QUANTITY_PER_LINE);   // (2)!
        }
        if (existing == null && lines.size() >= MAX_LINES) {
            throw new CartLineLimitExceededException(MAX_LINES);
        }
        lines.put(sku, new CartLine(sku, newQuantity, unitPrice));
        events.add(new ItemAdded(id, sku, newQuantity));
    }

    public void removeItem(Sku sku) {
        if (lines.remove(sku) == null) {
            throw new LineNotInCartException(id, sku);                            // (3)!
        }
        events.add(new ItemRemoved(id, sku));
    }

    public void clear() {
        if (lines.isEmpty()) return;                                              // (4)!
        lines.clear();
        events.add(new CartCleared(id));
    }

    public Money subtotal() {
        return lines.values().stream().map(CartLine::lineTotal)
                .reduce(Money.rupees("0.00"), Money::plus);
    }

    public List<CartLine> lines() {
        return List.copyOf(lines.values());
    }
}
  1. A map keyed by SKU makes "adding an existing SKU increases its quantity" natural and keeps insertion order for display.
  2. The limit applies to the resulting quantity, not the increment — the subtle rule an anemic service usually gets wrong.
  3. Removing a missing line is an error the domain names, not a silent no-op.
  4. Clearing an empty cart is idempotent and emits no event — events describe things that actually happened.
Ports
public interface CartRepository {
    Optional<Cart> findFor(CustomerId customerId);
    void save(Cart cart);                       // optimistic locking on version
}

public interface PricingPort {
    Money priceFor(Sku sku, Pincode pincode);   // in the core's language, not the HTTP client's
}
CartTest.java — no Spring, milliseconds
@Test void addingSameSkuIncreasesQuantity() { }
@Test void quantityAboveTwentyIsRejectedEvenWhenAddedIncrementally() { }          // (1)!
@Test void fiftyFirstDistinctSkuIsRejected() { }
@Test void updatingAnExistingSkuDoesNotCountAgainstTheLineLimit() { }
@Test void subtotalSumsLineTotals() { }
@Test void clearingAnEmptyCartEmitsNoEvent() { }
@Test void removingAMissingLineThrows() { }
  1. The test that catches the incremental-addition loophole — exactly the kind of rule that belongs in the aggregate rather than in a controller's validation.

The application service then becomes trivial: load, call a domain method, save, publish events. All the business complexity lives in one small, fast-testable class.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Boundaries come from the business language, not the database schema; the same word legitimately means different things in different contexts.
  • Aggregates are consistency boundaries: small, one per transaction, referenced by id.
  • Value objects move validation to construction, eliminating scattered defensive checks.
  • Hexagonal architecture is dependency direction — enforce it with ArchUnit or it erodes.
  • Match structure to subdomain: rich models for core, pragmatic layering for generic.
  • The modular monolith is a first-class destination, not just a waypoint; Spring Modulith makes its boundaries verifiable.
  • Module events with the publication registry make later extraction mechanical.
  • A framework-free domain survives framework upgrades untouched.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design; Vaughn Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design — strategic and tactical patterns
  • Vaughn Vernon, Effective Aggregate Design (three-part paper) — the clearest guidance on aggregate boundaries
  • Alistair Cockburn on Ports and Adapters; Tom Hombergs, Get Your Hands Dirty on Clean Architecture
  • Spring Modulith Reference — module verification, events, documentation, testing

36 Distributed Data & Consistency · 38 Multi-Tenancy

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
The grocery platform now has a second business model: white-label. Regional chains — a 40-store chain in Kerala, a premium organic brand in Pune, a cooperative in Punjab — run their own storefront on our platform. Each is a tenant with its own catalog, pricing, sellers, branding and customers. They share our code, our clusters and (mostly) our databases.

The engineering question is simple to state and expensive to get wrong: how do we guarantee that tenant A can never see tenant B's data?

Every multi-tenant incident has the same shape. A developer writes orderRepository.findAll() for an admin screen, or forgets the tenant in a cache key (Chapter 21), or a scheduled job runs without a tenant context and processes everything, or an async task loses the tenant and writes rows under the wrong id. None of these looks dangerous in review; all of them are a data breach, a contract violation and — under India's DPDP Act — a reportable incident.

This chapter covers the isolation models and how to choose between them, tenant resolution and context propagation (including the async and messaging paths where it usually breaks), Hibernate's multi-tenancy support, PostgreSQL row-level security as a defence in depth, migrations across tenants, per-tenant quotas and the noisy-neighbour problem, onboarding and offboarding with data export and deletion, cell-based isolation for large tenants, and — most importantly — the automated cross-tenant leak tests that turn "we're careful" into "the build proves it".

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — models, tenant context, filtering B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — Hibernate support, caching, migrations B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — RLS, propagation, leak testing B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — model selection, quotas, cells, lifecycle B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — economics and compliance of tenancy

docs.title: 2.1 Isolation models
docs.text:
Model Isolation Cost per tenant Migrations Best for Shared schema (tenant column) Logical only — code and RLS enforce it Lowest One run Many small tenants Schema per tenant Strong-ish (separate namespaces) Medium Loop over schemas Tens to low hundreds Database per tenant Strongest Highest Per database Few large or regulated tenants Cell / stack per tenant Physical, including compute Very high Per cell Enterprise tiers, blast-radius control

The platform runs a hybrid: shared schema for the long tail of small chains, database per tenant for the three largest (who pay for it and demand it contractually).

docs.title: 2.2 The three questions any model must answer
docs.text:
1. Resolution — which tenant is this request for?
  2. Propagation — does that tenant identity follow the work through async tasks, messages and scheduled jobs?
  3. Enforcement — what stops a query from crossing tenants, even when a developer forgets?

Most implementations answer 1 well, 2 partially, and 3 with "code review". Question 3 is the one that requires machinery.

docs.title: 2.3 Tenant resolution
docs.text:
Source Use Risk JWT claim (tenant_id) Authenticated API calls — the default None; it's signed (Chapter 18) Subdomain (kerala.grocery.in) Browser entry, branding Must be validated against the token Path prefix (/t/{tenantId}/...) Admin tooling Easy to forge — never alone Header (X-Tenant-Id) Internal service calls only Must be stripped at the gateway (Chapter 35)

Rule: the tenant comes from the token. Anything else is a hint to be cross-checked, never a source of authority.

docs.title: 2.4 Tenant context
docs.text:
Tenant context (snippet)
TenantContext.set(tenantId);   // per request/task/message
try { ... } finally { TenantContext.clear(); }   // always

The context must reach: repositories (filtering), caches (key prefix), outbound calls (header), messages (header), logs and metrics, scheduled jobs (explicit loop), and async tasks (decorator). Forgetting clear() on a pooled thread leaks the previous request's tenant into the next one — the worst bug in this chapter.

docs.title: 2.5 Enforcement layers
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A[1. Application: tenant-scoped repositories] --> B["2. ORM: Hibernate @TenantId / filters"]
    B --> C[3. Database: Row-Level Security policies]
    C --> D[4. Physical: separate schema or database]
    E[5. Tests: automated cross-tenant leak suite] -.verifies.-> A & B & C

Defence in depth matters because each layer fails differently: application filters are forgotten, ORM filters are bypassed by native queries, RLS is bypassed by a superuser connection. Layers 1–3 together plus layer 5 is the practical minimum for a shared schema.

docs.title: 2.6 Hibernate multi-tenancy
docs.text:
Strategy Configuration Notes DATABASE MultiTenantConnectionProvider returns a connection per tenant For database-per-tenant SCHEMA Provider sets the schema (SET search_path) For schema-per-tenant Discriminator @TenantId field + CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver For shared schema (Hibernate 6+)

With @TenantId, Hibernate adds the tenant predicate to queries and sets the value on insert automatically — removing the most common source of mistakes.

What Hibernate does not cover

Native queries, JDBC/JdbcClient access (Chapter 12), bulk operations and anything outside the persistence context. Those need RLS or explicit filtering — which is exactly why layer 3 exists.

docs.title: 2.7 Row-level security
2.8 Noisy neighbours
docs.text: Problem Control One tenant floods the API Per-tenant rate limits and quotas (Chapters 26, 35) One tenant's query saturates the database Statement timeouts, per-tenant connection budgets, read replicas One tenant's batch job blocks others Separate executors/queues, fair scheduling (Chapters 25, 33) One tenant's data dwarfs the rest Partitioning, or promote them to their own database/cell One tenant's incident affects all Cells — blast-radius isolation

docs.title: 2.9 Lifecycle obligations
docs.text:
Event Requirement Onboarding Provision schema/database, run migrations, seed defaults, configure branding, create the first admin Suspension Block access without deleting data; make the state visible Export Machine-readable data export across every service that holds their data Deletion Verified removal within the contractual/regulatory window, with evidence Audit Who accessed tenant data, when, from where (Chapter 39)

Under the DPDP Act, export and deletion aren't nice-to-haves; they are obligations with deadlines, and they must work across all 26 services.

docs.title: 3.1 A request's tenant journey
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (kerala.grocery.in)
    participant G as Gateway
    participant F as TenantFilter
    participant S as Service
    participant H as Hibernate
    participant DB as PostgreSQL (RLS)

    C->>G: request + Bearer token (tenant_id claim)
    G->>G: strip any client X-Tenant-Id header
    G->>F: forward
    F->>F: tenant = token claim, validate against subdomain
    F->>F: TenantContext.set(tenant), MDC, metrics tag
    F->>S: proceed
    S->>H: repository call
    H->>H: append tenant predicate (@TenantId)
    H->>DB: SET LOCAL app.tenant_id = ..., SELECT ...
    DB->>DB: RLS policy filters rows again
    DB-->>S: only this tenant's rows
    F->>F: finally: TenantContext.clear()

Two filters run on the same data — the ORM's and the database's. That redundancy is the design, not waste.

docs.title: 3.2 Where the context is lost
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Request thread: context set] --> B["@Async task"]
    A --> C[Kafka producer]
    A --> D[Outbound HTTP]
    A --> E[Scheduled job — no request at all]
    B -->|TaskDecorator| B2[context copied ✅]
    B -->|without decorator| B3[context missing ❌]
    C -->|tenant header| C2[consumer restores ✅]
    C -->|no header| C3[consumer guesses ❌]
    D -->|interceptor adds header| D2[✅]
    E -->|explicit loop over tenants| E2[✅]
    E -->|assumes a context| E3[NPE or silent cross-tenant write ❌]

Every ❌ branch has happened to someone. The fixes are mechanical (5.3) and must be part of the platform library, not each service's memory.

docs.title: 3.3 Shared schema vs database per tenant
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Shared["Shared schema (long tail)"]
        A1[One database] --> A2[tenant_id column on every table]
        A2 --> A3[RLS policies]
        A3 --> A4[One migration run]
    end
    subgraph Dedicated["Database per tenant (large tenants)"]
        B1[Database per tenant] --> B2[No tenant column needed]
        B2 --> B3[Connection provider routes by tenant]
        B3 --> B4[Migration pipeline per database]
    end

The same application code serves both when tenant routing is abstracted behind a connection provider and the tenant column is populated automatically.

docs.text:
in/grocery/platform/tenancy/TenantSettings.java
public record TenantSettings(
        String tenantId,
        String displayName,
        String primaryColour,
        String logoUrl,
        Locale defaultLocale,
        ZoneId timeZone,                                                                      // (1)!
        Money minimumOrderValue,
        Set<String> enabledFeatures,                                                          // (2)!
        TenantTier tier) {}
Feature checks
if (!settings.current().enabledFeatures().contains("express-delivery")) {
    throw new FeatureNotEnabledException("express-delivery");                                 // (3)!
}
  1. Tenants span time zones even within India's single zone once you consider reporting boundaries and cut-offs — store it, don't assume.
  2. Feature flags per tenant enable staged rollouts (a new checkout flow for one chain first).
  3. Explicit, testable, and visible in logs — better than a silently different code path.

Settings are cached (tenant-keyed, Chapter 21) with a short TTL and invalidated by a TenantSettingsChanged event.

docs.title: 6.1 The automated leak suite
docs.text:
This is the single highest-value artifact in a multi-tenant system.

src/integrationTest/java/in/grocery/tenancy/TenantLeakTest.java
@SpringBootTest
@Import(ContainersConfig.class)
class TenantLeakTest {

    private static final String A = "tenant-a";
    private static final String B = "tenant-b";

    @Autowired ApplicationContext context;

    @BeforeAll
    void seedBothTenants() {
        TenantContext.runAs(A, () -> seedFullDataset("A"));
        TenantContext.runAs(B, () -> seedFullDataset("B"));
    }

    @TestFactory
    Stream<DynamicTest> everyRepositoryFindMethodIsTenantScoped() {                            // (1)!
        return context.getBeansOfType(CrudRepository.class).entrySet().stream()
                .flatMap(entry -> Arrays.stream(entry.getValue().getClass().getMethods())
                        .filter(m -> m.getName().startsWith("find") && m.getParameterCount() == 0)
                        .map(m -> DynamicTest.dynamicTest(
                                entry.getKey() + "." + m.getName(),
                                () -> assertNoCrossTenantRows(entry.getValue(), m))));
    }

    private void assertNoCrossTenantRows(Object repository, Method method) throws Exception {
        Object result = TenantContext.runAs(B, () -> invoke(repository, method));
        assertThat(rowsOf(result))
                .as("%s returned rows belonging to another tenant", method.getName())
                .allMatch(row -> tenantOf(row).equals(B));                                     // (2)!
    }

    @Test
    void nativeQueriesAreProtectedByRls() {                                                    // (3)!
        TenantContext.runAs(B, () -> {
            var rows = jdbc.sql("select order_ref from customer_order").query(String.class).list();
            assertThat(rows).allMatch(ref -> ref.endsWith("-B"));
            return null;
        });
    }

    @Test
    void missingTenantYieldsNoRowsRatherThanAll() {                                            // (4)!
        TenantContext.clear();
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> orders.findAll()).isInstanceOf(MissingTenantException.class);
    }

    @Test
    void connectionReturnedToPoolDoesNotLeakTenantSetting() {                                  // (5)!
        TenantContext.runAs(A, () -> orders.findAll());
        TenantContext.runAs(B, () -> {
            assertThat(jdbc.sql("select current_setting('app.tenant_id', true)")
                    .query(String.class).single()).isEqualTo(B);
            return null;
        });
    }

    @Test
    void asyncWorkKeepsTheTenant() { /* submit via the platform executor, assert rows written under A */ }

    @Test
    void kafkaConsumersRestoreTheTenantFromHeaders() { /* publish as A, assert consumer wrote as A */ }
}
  1. Reflection over every repository bean: new repositories are covered automatically, which is what makes this durable rather than a snapshot of today's code.
  2. The core assertion, repeated across the entire data layer.
  3. RLS is what protects the paths Hibernate doesn't see.
  4. Fail-closed behaviour, asserted.
  5. The pooled-connection leak from 5.1, tested explicitly.

Run it on every build. A failure is a security incident in the making, not a flaky test.

docs.title: 6.2 Tenant onboarding
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Contract signed] --> B[Create tenant record: id, tier, isolation model]
    B --> C{isolation}
    C -- shared --> D["No provisioning; RLS handles it"]
    C -- dedicated --> E[Provision database, role, secrets, run migrations]
    D & E --> F[Seed defaults: categories, settings, branding]
    F --> G[Create first admin user in the IdP]
    G --> H[Configure DNS/subdomain + TLS]
    H --> I[Smoke test as the tenant: login, browse, place a test order]
    I --> J["Enable in the registry; quotas per tier"]
in/grocery/platform/tenancy/TenantProvisioningService.java
@Transactional
public TenantRecord onboard(OnboardTenantCommand command) {
    TenantRecord tenant = registry.create(command.tenantId(), command.tier(), command.isolation());

    if (tenant.isolation() == DEDICATED_DATABASE) {
        provisioner.createDatabase(tenant);                                                    // (1)!
        migrations.migrateTenant(tenant.id());
    }
    TenantContext.runAs(tenant.id(), () -> {
        seeder.seedDefaults(command.locale());                                                 // (2)!
        return null;
    });
    outbox.append("tenant", tenant.id(), "TenantOnboarded", new TenantOnboarded(tenant.id()));  // (3)!
    return tenant;
}
  1. Database creation and migration are not transactional with the registry insert — provisioning is a saga (Chapter 36) with its own retry and compensation.
  2. Seeding runs inside the tenant's context so every row is tagged correctly.
  3. Other services (search, notification, analytics) react and create their own tenant-scoped structures.

6.4 Cells for large tenants
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Cell1["Cell 1 — shared (long tail, 40 tenants)"]
        A1[Services] --> D1[(Shared DB, RLS)]
    end
    subgraph Cell2["Cell 2 — dedicated (Kerala chain)"]
        A2[Services] --> D2[(Their database)]

Benefit Cost Blast radius limited to one cell N× infrastructure and deploy surface Per-cell capacity and scaling Routing layer to build and operate Staged rollouts (deploy to cell 1 first) Config drift between cells Contractual isolation for enterprise tiers More monitoring, more runbooks

Move a tenant to its own cell when they justify the cost — by revenue, contract, regulation, or the volume at which they would otherwise destabilize the shared cell.

docs.title: 6.5 Observability with tenants
6.6 Choosing the model
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[New multi-tenant system] --> B{Regulatory or contractual<br/>requirement for physical separation?}
    B -- yes --> C[Database or cell per tenant]
    B -- no --> D{How many tenants?}
    D -- "hundreds or thousands" --> E[Shared schema + RLS]
    D -- "tens" --> F{Very different sizes?}
    F -- yes --> G[Hybrid: shared for small, dedicated for large]
    F -- no --> E
    E & G --> H[Always: context propagation, RLS, leak tests, per-tenant quotas]

Start shared unless a requirement forces otherwise: it's cheaper to promote a tenant to a dedicated database later than to consolidate hundreds of databases into one schema.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text: Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x Hibernate multi-tenancy Hibernate 6 (@TenantId, connection/schema providers) Hibernate 7 (verify API and property names) AbstractRoutingDataSource ✅ ✅ Flyway multi-schema/database ✅ ✅ Tenant context ThreadLocal + TaskDecorator ScopedValue on Java 25 (verify) Cache key generators ✅ ✅ Test slices ✅ Module moves (verify)

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Verify Hibernate multi-tenancy interfaces and property names after the upgrade (they have changed between major versions).
  • Re-run the full leak suite immediately after upgrading — this is the one suite that must be green before release.
  • Re-test pooled-connection tenant reset behaviour.
  • Re-check that async and messaging propagation still work (executor and listener changes can drop decorators).
  • If moving to ScopedValue, migrate one service first and keep ThreadLocal compatibility for libraries that need it.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. The tenant comes from the token; other sources are hints to validate.
  2. Fail closed: no tenant means an exception and zero rows, never "all tenants".
  3. Defence in depth: application scoping, ORM @TenantId, database RLS.
  4. Propagate everywhere — async, messaging, outbound HTTP, scheduled jobs — via platform-provided decorators.
  5. Tenant in every cache key, enforced by a default key generator.
  6. Always clear the context in a finally; reset connection state before returning to the pool.
  7. Per-tenant quotas and rate limits; promote noisy or large tenants to dedicated resources.
  8. Automated leak suite covering every repository, native queries, pooling, async and messaging.
  9. Onboarding and offboarding as engineered workflows, with export manifests and deletion reports.
  10. Tenant in logs and traces always; in metrics only when bounded.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Trusting a client-supplied X-Tenant-Id header.

❌ Defaulting to "all tenants" when the context is missing.

❌ Tenant filtering only in application code ("we always remember").

❌ Cache keys without the tenant.

❌ ThreadLocal without remove() on pooled threads.

❌ Session-level database settings not reset before pool return.

❌ Scheduled jobs that assume a tenant context exists.

❌ Database per tenant for hundreds of tenants (connection and migration explosion).

❌ Tenant id as an unbounded metric tag.

❌ Deletion that skips a service nobody remembered held tenant data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Tenant sees another tenant's data Missing filter, forgotten cache key, context leak Leak suite, RLS, key generator Empty results for a valid tenant Context not propagated (async/message/job) Decorators, headers, explicit runAs MissingTenantException in a job Job assumes a context Loop over tenants explicitly Intermittent wrong-tenant rows Pooled connection retains the setting Transaction-local settings or explicit reset Connection exhaustion Pool per dedicated tenant × pods Fewer dedicated tenants, shared pool, PgBouncer Migrations leave tenants on mixed versions Per-database failures Expand/contract, per-tenant status tracking, retries One tenant slows everyone No quotas Per-tenant limits; promote to a dedicated cell Prometheus cardinality explosion Tenant tag on every metric Bounded tagging (6.5) Deletion audit fails A service was missed Service catalog as the source of truth

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Isolation model documented per tenant, with the reason
  • Tenant resolved from the token; gateway strips client tenant headers
  • @TenantId (or equivalent) on every tenant-scoped entity
  • RLS enabled and forced on every tenant-scoped table
  • Context propagation in async, messaging, HTTP and jobs — platform-provided
  • Tenant-aware cache key generator as the default
  • Leak suite green in every build
  • Per-tenant quotas and rate limits by tier
  • Onboarding/offboarding runbooks with export and deletion evidence
  • Per-tenant dashboards for dedicated tenants; bounded metric tags elsewhere

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What are the main multi-tenancy isolation models?

Short answer: Shared schema with a tenant column, schema per tenant, database per tenant, and full cell/stack per tenant — increasing isolation and cost in that order.

B1 · Where should the tenant identifier come from?

Short answer: A signed token claim. Subdomains and headers can be hints, but a client-supplied header must never be authoritative.

B1 · Why must the tenant be part of cache keys?

Short answer: Otherwise one tenant's cached value is served to another — a data leak through the cache rather than the database.

B1 · What is row-level security?

Short answer: A PostgreSQL feature that applies a filter policy to every query on a table, so even hand-written SQL only sees the current tenant's rows.

B1 · Why clear the tenant context in a finally block?

Short answer: Threads are pooled; a leftover value is inherited by the next request, which then reads or writes the wrong tenant's data.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How does Hibernate support multi-tenancy?

Short answer: DATABASE and SCHEMA strategies via a MultiTenantConnectionProvider and CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver, and discriminator-based tenancy with @TenantId, which adds the predicate to queries and sets the value on insert.

B2 · What does Hibernate's tenant filtering not cover?

Short answer: Native queries, plain JDBC access, bulk operations and anything outside the persistence context — which is why database-level RLS is needed as a second layer.

B2 · How do you keep the tenant through async work and messaging?

Short answer: A TaskDecorator that captures the context on submission and restores/clears it on execution; a tenant header on messages that the consumer restores; an interceptor adding the header to internal HTTP calls.

B2 · How do scheduled jobs handle tenancy?

Short answer: Explicitly — enumerate active tenants and run the work inside each tenant's context. A job with no context must fail rather than operate across tenants.

B2 · Shared schema or database per tenant?

Short answer: Shared schema for many tenants (cheap, one migration, RLS for safety); dedicated databases for a few large or regulated tenants. Hybrids are common and supported by abstracting connection routing.

B2 · What's the noisy-neighbour problem?

Short answer: One tenant consuming shared capacity — API quota, database, queues — and degrading others. Controls: per-tenant rate limits, statement timeouts, separate executors, and promotion to dedicated resources.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How do you prove tenant isolation?

Short answer: An automated suite that seeds two tenants and, reflectively over every repository, asserts that queries executed as tenant B never return tenant A's rows — plus explicit tests for native queries, pooled-connection state, async propagation and message-driven paths. It runs on every build.

B3 · What are the pitfalls of RLS with connection pooling?

Short answer: Session-level settings survive connection reuse, so a returned connection can carry a previous tenant's identifier. Use transaction-local settings or reset explicitly on release, and test borrow-as-A-then-borrow-as-B.

B3 · How do migrations differ across tenancy models?

Short answer: Shared schema is a single migration; schema or database per tenant means N runs with partial-failure handling and mixed versions in flight, which makes backward-compatible expand/contract migrations mandatory rather than advisable.

B3 · How do you handle tenant deletion across many services?

Short answer: Drive it from the service catalog so no service is missed; each service exposes delete and export operations; record deleted and retained counts with legal bases; verify afterwards that no rows remain; keep the report as audit evidence.

B3 · When would you move a tenant to a dedicated database or cell?

Short answer: Contractual or regulatory separation, data volume that destabilizes the shared store, a need for independent maintenance windows, or blast-radius requirements — weighed against the per-tenant operational cost.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · Design multi-tenancy for a platform expecting 500 tenants with a long tail.

Short answer: Shared schema with @TenantId plus forced RLS; tenant from the token, propagated by platform decorators; tenant-aware cache keys by default; per-tier quotas; a leak suite in CI; hybrid promotion to dedicated databases for the few largest; cells for enterprise contracts; catalog-driven export/deletion; bounded metric tagging with full logs and traces.

B4 · What are the operational costs of database-per-tenant at scale?

Short answer: Connection multiplication across pods, N migration runs with partial failures and version skew, N backup/restore procedures, N monitoring targets, slower incident response and higher cloud spend. It's justified for a handful of tenants, not for hundreds.

B4 · How do you handle a suspected cross-tenant leak?

Short answer: Treat it as a security incident: preserve evidence, identify affected tenants and records from logs with tenant tags, contain (disable the path, revoke sessions), notify per contract and the DPDP Act timeline, fix with a test that reproduces the leak, then review every layer that should have caught it.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · How does tenancy affect business economics?

Short answer: Isolation is a pricing tier. Shared schema keeps marginal cost near zero for small tenants; dedicated databases and cells carry real cost and should be sold accordingly. Architecture and commercial model must agree, or engineering absorbs costs the contract never covered.

B5 · What's the hardest part of multi-tenancy?

Short answer: Not the first implementation — the ongoing discipline. Every new feature, query, cache, job and integration can leak. Sustaining it requires platform-level defaults, database-level enforcement and automated leak tests, so correctness doesn't depend on each developer remembering.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A tenant sees another chain's orders in an export

An admin export used a native query for performance, bypassing Hibernate's tenant filter, and RLS was enabled but not forced, so the application's owning role bypassed the policy. Fixes: force row level security, a leak test for native queries, review of every native query, incident notification, and a rule that exports go through tenant-scoped repositories.

Scenario · Nightly job wrote data under the wrong tenant

An @Async cleanup task submitted from a request inherited no context on the executing thread; a fallback defaulted to the first active tenant. Fixes: remove the fallback (fail closed), install the tenant-propagating TaskDecorator platform-wide, add async propagation tests, and repair the affected rows using audit logs.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Tenant-aware pricing cache and job

Implement: (1) a cache for prices that is safe across tenants without relying on developers writing keys, (2) a scheduled job that refreshes the top 100 SKUs for every active tenant, (3) tests proving no cross-tenant cache hits and that the job writes under the correct tenant.

Solution TenantAwareKeyGenerator (platform default)
@Component("tenantKeyGenerator")
public class TenantAwareKeyGenerator implements KeyGenerator {
    @Override
    public Object generate(Object target, Method method, Object... params) {
        return TenantContext.require() + "|"                                    // (1)!
                + target.getClass().getSimpleName() + "." + method.getName() + "|"
                + SimpleKeyGenerator.generateKey(params);
    }
}
  1. require() throws when there is no tenant, so a cacheable method can never silently share an entry.
PricingService
@Service
@CacheConfig(cacheNames = "price", keyGenerator = "tenantKeyGenerator")
public class PricingService {

    @Cacheable
    public PriceView priceFor(String sku, String pincode) {
        return prices.lookup(TenantContext.require(), sku, pincode);            // (1)!
    }

    @CachePut
    public PriceView refresh(String sku, String pincode) {
        return prices.lookup(TenantContext.require(), sku, pincode);
    }
}
  1. Belt and braces: the query is tenant-scoped even though RLS would also filter it.
PriceWarmupJob
@Component
public class PriceWarmupJob {

    @Scheduled(cron = "0 */10 * * * *")
    @SchedulerLock(name = "price-warmup", lockAtMostFor = "PT9M")                // (1)!
    public void warmAllTenants() {
        for (String tenantId : tenants.activeTenantIds()) {
            TenantContext.runAs(tenantId, () -> {
                var skus = analytics.topSkus(100);
                var pincodes = analytics.topPincodes(10);
                skus.forEach(sku -> pincodes.forEach(p -> pricing.refresh(sku, p)));
                meters.counter("grocery.price.warmed",
                        "tenant", tenants.isLargeTenant(tenantId) ? tenantId : "shared")   // (2)!
                      .increment(skus.size() * pincodes.size());
                return null;
            });
        }
    }
}
  1. One pod runs it (Chapter 25); the lock duration exceeds the worst case across all tenants.
  2. Bounded tenant tagging (6.5).
Tests
@Test
void cacheEntriesAreNotSharedAcrossTenants() {
    TenantContext.runAs("tenant-a", () -> pricing.priceFor("MILK-1L", "560102"));
    TenantContext.runAs("tenant-b", () -> pricing.priceFor("MILK-1L", "560102"));

    then(prices).should(times(2)).lookup(any(), eq("MILK-1L"), eq("560102"));    // (1)!
}

@Test
void cachingWithoutATenantFails() {
    TenantContext.clear();
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> pricing.priceFor("MILK-1L", "560102"))
            .isInstanceOf(MissingTenantException.class);                          // (2)!
}

@Test
void warmupCoversEveryActiveTenantUnderItsOwnContext() {
    given(tenants.activeTenantIds()).willReturn(List.of("tenant-a", "tenant-b"));
    job.warmAllTenants();

    assertThat(cacheKeys()).anyMatch(k -> k.startsWith("tenant-a|"))
                           .anyMatch(k -> k.startsWith("tenant-b|"));             // (3)!
}
  1. Two lookups, not one — proof that the cache did not serve tenant A's price to tenant B.
  2. Fail-closed behaviour verified.
  3. The job's per-tenant context verified through the resulting cache keys.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Choose isolation per tenant, hybrid is normal: shared schema for the long tail, dedicated databases or cells for the few who need (and pay for) them.
  • Tenant from the token; fail closed when it's absent.
  • Three enforcement layers: application scoping, ORM @TenantId, database RLS — because each fails differently.
  • Propagation is where it breaks: async, messaging, outbound calls and scheduled jobs need platform-provided plumbing.
  • Tenant in every cache key, by default rather than by memory.
  • Clear contexts and reset connection state; pooled resources carry state.
  • Per-tenant quotas control noisy neighbours; cells control blast radius.
  • The automated leak suite is the deliverable that keeps all of this true as the codebase grows.

37 DDD, Hexagonal & Modular Monolith · 39 Enterprise Security Architecture

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Chapters 17 and 18 secured a service: filter chains, tokens, ownership checks, webhook signatures. This chapter steps back to the platform: what an attacker could do, what data we hold, who may see it, how we would know, and what we are legally required to do about it.

The grocery platform holds, at any moment: 4 million customers' names, mobile numbers and delivery addresses; order histories that reveal household composition and habits; seller bank accounts and PAN/GSTIN; payment tokens; staff credentials with production access. The relevant threats are not hypothetical:

  • Credential stuffing against OTP login using leaked mobile numbers.
  • Seller account takeover to redirect payouts to a different bank account.
  • An insider exporting a customer table for a competitor.
  • A supply-chain compromise — a transitive dependency, a build plugin, a base image.
  • SSRF through a seller-supplied image URL reaching the cloud metadata endpoint.
  • A regulator's question: under India's DPDP Act, can you delete one customer's data across 26 services and prove it?

Security architecture is the set of decisions that make these bounded rather than existential: trust boundaries, data classification, encryption and key management, PCI scope reduction, secrets handling, least privilege, audit logging, supply-chain controls, security gates in CI, and an incident process that has been rehearsed.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — OWASP mapping, secrets, safe defaults B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — threat modelling, encryption, SSRF, uploads B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — key management, audit, PII handling B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — architecture, compliance, incident response B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — risk, governance, security culture

docs.title: 2.1 Threat modelling with STRIDE
docs.text:
Threat Grocery example Primary control Spoofing Fake webhook claiming payment succeeded Signature verification (Chapter 18) Tampering Modified price in a client request Server-side pricing; never trust client amounts Repudiation "I never changed that bank account" Immutable audit log with actor and source Information disclosure Customer data in logs or error bodies PII redaction (Chapter 07), problem details (Chapter 10) Denial of service OTP flooding to exhaust SMS budget Rate limits, quotas (Chapters 17, 26) Elevation of privilege Seller reaching admin endpoints Authorization + ownership (Chapter 17)

Model per flow, not per service: checkout, seller payout changes, customer login, catalog import, admin access. One page per flow, reviewed when the flow changes.

docs.title: 2.2 Trust boundaries
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I[Internet: customers, sellers, bots] -->|boundary 1| E[Edge: CDN, WAF, gateway]
    E -->|boundary 2| S[Service mesh: our services]
    S -->|boundary 3| D[(Data stores)]
    S -->|boundary 4| T[Third parties: Razorpay, SMS, maps]
    A[Staff: admin portal, kubectl, DB access] -->|boundary 5| S & D
    B[Build pipeline: CI, registry] -->|boundary 6| S

Every boundary needs: authentication, authorization, input validation, rate limiting, logging. Boundaries 5 and 6 are the ones organizations under-invest in — staff access and the build pipeline are how most serious breaches actually happen.

docs.title: 2.3 Data classification
docs.text:
Class Examples Controls Public Product catalog, prices None beyond integrity Internal Aggregate metrics, non-personal config Access control Confidential Order history, seller performance Access control + audit Sensitive personal Name, mobile, address, PAN, GSTIN, bank account Encryption, masking, audit, minimization Regulated Payment credentials Never stored — tokenize (2.6)

Classification drives everything else: what's encrypted, what's logged, what's exported, what's deleted, who may query it.

docs.title: 2.4 Encryption
docs.text:
Layer Control In transit, external TLS 1.3, HSTS, certificate management In transit, internal mTLS via the mesh (Chapter 30) At rest, storage Disk/volume encryption (cloud-managed keys) At rest, field-level Application encryption for bank accounts, PAN/GSTIN Backups Encrypted with separate key access Keys KMS with envelope encryption, rotation, audited use

Disk encryption protects against a stolen disk. It does not protect against a compromised application, a leaked database dump, or an over-privileged query — which is why sensitive fields get application-level encryption.

docs.title: 2.5 Envelope encryption
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[KMS master key — never leaves KMS] --> B[Generate data key]
    B --> C[Plaintext data key: encrypt the field]
    B --> D[Encrypted data key: stored beside the ciphertext]
    C -.->|discarded from memory| X[ ]
    D --> E[Decrypt: KMS unwraps the data key on demand]

Why not encrypt directly with the KMS key: payload size limits, a KMS call per operation, and no way to rotate without re-encrypting everything. Envelope encryption stores the wrapped data key with the record, so key rotation re-wraps keys rather than re-encrypting data.

docs.title: 2.6 PCI scope reduction
docs.text:
The cheapest way to secure card data is to never possess it.

Approach Scope Card fields on our page, posted to our server Full PCI DSS scope — avoid Gateway-hosted checkout / SDK collects the card Drastically reduced scope Network tokens / gateway tokens for repeat payments We store a token, never a PAN

India specifics: RBI's card-on-file tokenization rules mean merchants generally must not store actual card numbers; tokens issued by the network or gateway are used for repeat payments. The platform stores razorpay_token_id and the last four digits (Chapter 18's never-store rule for full numbers), and nothing else.

docs.title: 2.7 Secrets
docs.text: Rule Why Never in Git, images or environment dumps They persist in history and layers (Chapters 06, 29) Mounted as files, read as a config tree No accidental logging of the environment From a secret manager (Vault / cloud KMS) via an operator Central rotation and audit Rotated on a schedule, and immediately on suspicion Limits exposure windows Two values valid during rotation Zero-downtime rollover (Chapter 18) Access audited Who read which secret, when

docs.title: 2.8 Least privilege
docs.text: Principal Privilege Application DB user DML on its own tables only; no DDL, no access to other services' schemas (Chapters 14, 35) Migration user DDL, used only by the migration job Support/analytics Read-only on masked views, time-boxed, audited Service accounts Scoped tokens (Chapter 18), short-lived Staff SSO + MFA/passkeys, role-based, break-glass with approval CI Push to registry, deploy to staging; production deploys require a gated approval

docs.title: 2.9 Audit logging
docs.text:
Log Don't log Who (actor), what (action), which resource, when, from where, outcome Passwords, tokens, OTPs, card data Authorization denials and privilege changes Full request/response bodies with PII Bank account/payout changes, refunds, price overrides Anything you'd be embarrassed to see in a dump Data exports and bulk reads — Break-glass access —

Audit logs are append-only, retained per policy, stored separately from application logs, and access to them is itself audited.

docs.title: 2.10 Indian regulatory context
docs.text:
Requirement Practical impact DPDP Act 2023 Consent records, purpose limitation, data-principal rights (access, correction, erasure), breach notification, a grievance officer RBI payment data storage Payment data storage restrictions and tokenization for cards; data localization requirements for payment system data GST e-invoicing / records Retention of invoices and financial records (conflicts with deletion — record the legal basis, Chapter 38) Sectoral/state rules Vary; legal counsel decides, engineering implements

Verify with counsel

Regulation changes, and its interpretation is a legal question. This chapter describes engineering patterns for meeting such requirements — consent records, deletion workflows, audit trails, localization-aware deployment. Confirm the current obligations with your legal team; don't take a technical handbook's word for compliance.

docs.title: 3.1 Defence in depth for one request
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Request] --> B[CDN/WAF: bot rules, IP reputation, size limits]
    B --> C[Gateway: TLS, rate limit, token validation, header stripping]
    C --> D[Service: token re-validation, authorization, ownership]
    D --> E[Validation: constraints, canonicalization]
    E --> F[Business logic: server-side amounts, state machine guards]
    F --> G[Data: least-privilege user, RLS, field encryption]
    G --> H[Response: problem details, no internals, security headers]
    I[Audit + metrics + traces] -.-> C & D & F & G

Each layer assumes the ones before it may have failed. The service re-validates the token even though the gateway did; the database filters by tenant even though the ORM did (Chapter 38).

docs.title: 3.2 Envelope encryption in the write path
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as seller-service
    participant K as KMS
    participant DB as PostgreSQL

    S->>K: GenerateDataKey(keyId = seller-pii)
    K-->>S: plaintext key + encrypted key
    S->>S: AES-GCM encrypt(bankAccount, plaintextKey, nonce)
    S->>S: zero the plaintext key
    S->>DB: store {ciphertext, nonce, encryptedKey, keyVersion}
    Note over S,DB: reading reverses it: KMS Decrypt(encryptedKey) → unwrap → decrypt

keyVersion stored with the row is what makes rotation possible without downtime: new writes use the new key, old rows decrypt with their own.

docs.title: 3.3 The supply chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Developer commit] --> B[CI: SAST, dependency scan, secret scan, tests]
    B --> C[Build image + SBOM]
    C --> D[Image scan + signature + provenance]
    D --> E[Registry]
    E --> F[Admission control: signature + policy]
    F --> G[Cluster]
    H[Dependency updates: Renovate] --> A
    I[Base image rebuild weekly] --> C

Every arrow is an attack surface: a malicious dependency, a compromised plugin, a poisoned base image, a registry without signature verification. The controls are the boring ones in Chapter 29 — SBOM, scan, sign, verify at admission.
