}
  1. One BOM, five lines, and a new service starts with correct error handling, security defaults, observability conventions, outbox plumbing and test fixtures — about 900 lines of configuration nobody writes again.

docs.title: 6.2 Versioning and compatibility policy
6.3 A release checklist for platform libraries
6.4 Debugging auto-configuration in anger
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Bean missing / unexpected behaviour] --> B["/actuator/conditions or --debug"]
    B --> C{negative match?}
    C -- missing class --> D[Dependency absent or wrong scope]
    C -- property --> E[Check /actuator/env precedence — Chapter 06]
    C -- bean already defined --> F[Your bean won — usually intended]
    C -- positive but wrong bean --> G["/actuator/beans: which definition, from where"]
    G --> H{two auto-configurations conflict?}
    H -- yes --> I["Check before/after ordering; exclude one explicitly"]
    A --> J[Startup failure?]
    J --> K["FailureAnalyzer message first; then the root cause"]
Explicit exclusion, when needed
spring:
  autoconfigure:
    exclude:
      - in.grocery.platform.web.autoconfigure.GroceryWebAutoConfiguration                   # (1)!
  1. The blunt instrument. If a service needs this, the starter is missing a property toggle or a @ConditionalOnMissingBean — treat it as a bug report against the platform library.

docs.title: 6.5 Native-image support in a starter
6.6 When not to build a starter
docs.text:
Situation Better choice One service needs it A @Configuration class in that service The abstraction isn't settled Copy it twice; extract on the third It wraps a library thinly Use the library directly It would force lockstep upgrades Keep it a plain library with explicit wiring It encodes business rules A domain library or a service (Chapters 35, 37) Nobody will maintain it Don't create it — an unmaintained starter blocks Boot upgrades for everyone

The last row is the real constraint. A platform library is a product with users, a support burden, a release cadence and an owner. Two well-maintained starters beat eight abandoned ones.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
Topic Boot 3.5 Boot 4.x AutoConfiguration.imports ✅ ✅ (verify path stability) @AutoConfiguration with before/after ✅ ✅ Auto-configuration packaging Largely in spring-boot-autoconfigure Modularized into per-technology artifacts — imports may move (verify) spring.factories Only for non-auto-configuration hooks Same (verify supported keys) Configuration processor ✅ ✅ ApplicationContextRunner ✅ ✅ Runtime hints ✅ ✅

Boot 4's modularization affects starters

If your auto-configuration references Boot's auto-configuration classes in before/after attributes or @ConditionalOnBean, those class names and packages may move. Compile against the target Boot version early, run the full condition test suite, and publish a compatibility matrix before your services upgrade.

docs.title: Migration checklist
docs.text:
• Compile each autoconfigure module against the target Boot version first; fix moved imports.
  • Re-run all ApplicationContextRunner tests, including FilteredClassLoader cases.
  • Verify before/after references still resolve after modularization.
  • Re-generate and review configuration metadata.
  • Re-run nativeTest for native-supporting consumers.
  • Publish the compatibility matrix and changelog before services upgrade.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Two artifacts: autoconfigure (code) and starter (dependencies only).
  2. Every bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean, with a back-off test proving it.
  3. Typed, validated properties with generated metadata and sensible defaults.
  4. Conditions that explain themselves; custom conditions return readable outcomes.
  5. Failure analyzers for every configuration mistake your library can cause.
  6. Test with ApplicationContextRunner, including FilteredClassLoader for optional dependencies.
  7. Ship native hints so the library never breaks a native build.
  8. Semantic versioning with N-1 support; deprecate before removing; never force lockstep upgrades.
  9. Measure startup cost — it multiplies across services and pods.
  10. No business logic; platform concerns only.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Missing the AutoConfiguration.imports file (the starter silently does nothing).

❌ Plain @Configuration instead of @AutoConfiguration (ordering and back-off break).

❌ Beans without @ConditionalOnMissingBean (consumers must exclude everything to change one thing).

❌ Mandatory dependencies in the autoconfigure module (conditions can never be false).

❌ Business logic in a platform library (Chapter 35).

❌ Breaking changes in a minor version.

❌ No property metadata (no IDE support, no discoverability).

❌ Eager work at startup — connections, scans, warm-ups — inside a starter.

❌ A starter nobody owns, blocking every Boot upgrade.

❌ Relying on the consumer's @ComponentScan reaching your package.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix Starter does nothing Missing or misspelled imports file Check META-INF/spring/…AutoConfiguration.imports Bean missing Condition not met /actuator/conditions or --debug Two beans of the same type Missing @ConditionalOnMissingBean Add it; add a back-off test Consumer's bean ignored Auto-configuration ran first (wrong annotation) Use @AutoConfiguration NoSuchBeanDefinitionException at startup @ConditionalOnBean evaluated too early Fix after ordering; use ObjectProvider Works in tests, not in the app Test adds a dependency the app lacks FilteredClassLoader tests Native image fails at runtime Missing hints Ship RuntimeHintsRegistrar Startup slower after adding the starter Eager initialization /actuator/startup; make it lazy or conditional Every service breaks on upgrade Breaking change without N-1 support Versioning policy; deprecation cycle Property typo silently ignored No metadata, no validation Configuration processor + @Validated

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Autoconfigure/starter split with compileOnly dependencies
  • Imports file present and verified by a test
  • All beans overridable, with back-off tests
  • Properties typed, validated, documented, with generated metadata
  • Failure analyzers for common misconfigurations
  • FilteredClassLoader tests for every optional dependency
  • Native hints shipped; nativeTest green
  • Startup cost measured and budgeted
  • Versioning policy, changelog, compatibility matrix published
  • A named owning team for every platform library

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · How does Spring Boot know which auto-configurations to apply?

Short answer: It reads META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports from every jar, filters by conditions and exclusions, sorts by ordering hints, and registers the ones that match.

B1 · Why is @ConditionalOnMissingBean important?

Short answer: It lets the application override a starter's bean. User configuration is registered before auto-configuration, so if the user defined a bean, the starter backs off.

B1 · How do you find out why a bean wasn't created?

Short answer: Run with --debug or call /actuator/conditions — the condition evaluation report lists every match and non-match with the reason.

B1 · What's the difference between a starter and an autoconfigure module?

Short answer: The autoconfigure module contains the code and conditions; the starter contains only dependencies, so adding one line brings in everything needed.

B1 · What does the configuration processor do?

Short answer: Generates spring-configuration-metadata.json from @ConfigurationProperties, giving IDE autocompletion, documentation and deprecation warnings for your properties.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · Why must an autoconfigure module use compileOnly dependencies?

Short answer: So consumers aren't forced to pull libraries they don't use, and so @ConditionalOnClass can actually evaluate false. With mandatory dependencies, every condition is always true.

B2 · How do you test auto-configuration?

Short answer: ApplicationContextRunner (or its web/reactive variants): assert beans exist, honour properties, back off when the user defines their own, fail on invalid configuration, and — with FilteredClassLoader — behave correctly when an optional library is absent.

B2 · How do you control the order of auto-configurations?

Short answer: @AutoConfiguration(before = …, after = …) or @AutoConfigureOrder. It matters because @ConditionalOnBean and @ConditionalOnMissingBean are evaluated against the registry as it exists at that moment.

B2 · What's a failure analyzer for?

Short answer: Converting a startup exception into a clear description and concrete remediation steps, registered via spring.factories — turning a stack trace into an actionable message.

B2 · How do you make a starter's behaviour optional?

Short answer: @ConditionalOnProperty with matchIfMissing for opt-out defaults, @ConditionalOnClass for library-dependent features, and @ConditionalOnMissingBean so consumers can substitute their own implementations.

B2 · What shouldn't go in a platform starter?

Short answer: Business logic, domain models, anything forcing a lockstep upgrade, and beans that can't be overridden.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Why does user configuration take precedence over auto-configuration?

Short answer: Auto-configurations are imported by @EnableAutoConfiguration and processed after the application's own configuration classes, so by the time @ConditionalOnMissingBean is evaluated, user beans are already registered.

B3 · How do you design a starter for overridability?

Short answer: Every bean @ConditionalOnMissingBean; feature toggles via properties; small focused beans rather than one monolith; interfaces so users can decorate; nested configurations guarded by class presence; back-off tests for each.

B3 · What are the pitfalls of @ConditionalOnBean?

Short answer: It depends on registration order, so a bean defined later isn't seen. Use after ordering, prefer @ConditionalOnMissingBean or ObjectProvider for optional collaborators, and avoid @ConditionalOnBean in regular @Configuration classes, where ordering isn't guaranteed at all.

B3 · How do you support native images from a library?

Short answer: Ship a RuntimeHintsRegistrar via @ImportRuntimeHints declaring reflection, resource and serialization needs, and run nativeTest in the library's own CI so consumers never debug missing hints.

B3 · How would you evolve a starter without breaking 26 services?

Short answer: Semantic versioning with N-1 support, additive changes in minors, deprecation with @DeprecatedConfigurationProperty and a working fallback for at least one major, a published compatibility matrix, changelogs with migration notes, and a sample service upgraded before release.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you decide what becomes a platform library?

Short answer: Cross-cutting concerns needed by most services, stable enough to standardize, with no business logic and a team willing to own them. If it's needed once, or still changing shape, keep it in the service; extract when the third copy appears.

B4 · What's the governance model for platform libraries?

Short answer: A named owning team, a versioning and support policy, a public changelog and compatibility matrix, contribution guidelines, release checklists, and adoption metrics — the /actuator/platform endpoint reporting library versions across the fleet makes upgrades measurable.

B4 · How do platform libraries interact with Boot upgrades?

Short answer: They're the gate. Compile and test them against the new Boot version first, publish a compatible release with a matrix, then upgrade services. Libraries that lag block the entire platform, which is why unowned starters are a serious risk.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What's the cost of a platform abstraction?

Short answer: A support burden, a release cadence, an upgrade dependency and a learning curve for newcomers who must understand both Spring and your layer. Worth it when it removes real duplication and enforces correctness; harmful when it wraps a library thinly or encodes decisions teams should make themselves.

B5 · How do you avoid a platform library becoming a bottleneck?

Short answer: Keep it small and focused, make everything overridable, never force lockstep upgrades, support N-1, accept contributions from service teams, and periodically delete what nobody uses. A platform team that says "wait for our release" too often gets routed around.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · A new starter had no effect in any service

The AutoConfiguration.imports file was under src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/ in the starter module, which contained no resources on the consumer's classpath order, and the class name had a typo from a package rename. Fixes: put the file in the autoconfigure module, add a test asserting the file lists the class and that the class loads, and add a smoke-test service to the release checklist.

Scenario · A platform release broke twelve services at once

A minor version changed a bean type and removed a property with no fallback. Fixes: revert, republish as a major with deprecation shims, adopt the N-1 policy, add back-off and property-compatibility tests, and upgrade a sample service in CI before any release.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Build the tenancy starter

Create grocery-platform-tenancy-spring-boot-starter contributing: a tenant resolution filter, a task decorator for async propagation, a tenant-aware cache key generator, and an RLS-setting datasource wrapper. Requirements: all beans overridable, disabled by a property, works without Spring Cache or Spring Security present, has property metadata and a failure analyzer, and is fully tested with ApplicationContextRunner.

Solution GroceryTenancyAutoConfiguration.java
@AutoConfiguration(after = {DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class, CacheAutoConfiguration.class,
                            SecurityAutoConfiguration.class})                            // (1)!
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "grocery.tenancy", name = "enabled",
        havingValue = "true", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(GroceryTenancyProperties.class)
public class GroceryTenancyAutoConfiguration {

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    TenantResolver tenantResolver(GroceryTenancyProperties properties) {
        return new TokenClaimTenantResolver(properties.claimName(), properties.hostPattern());
    }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean
    @ConditionalOnWebApplication(type = SERVLET)
    FilterRegistrationBean<TenantFilter> tenantFilter(TenantResolver resolver) {
        var registration = new FilterRegistrationBean<>(new TenantFilter(resolver));
        registration.setOrder(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE + 20);                          // (2)!
        return registration;
    }

    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean(name = "tenantTaskDecorator")
    TaskDecorator tenantTaskDecorator() {
        return new TenantPropagatingTaskDecorator();                                     // (3)!
    }

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @ConditionalOnClass(CacheManager.class)                                              // (4)!
    static class CacheConfiguration {

        @Bean("tenantKeyGenerator")
        @ConditionalOnMissingBean(name = "tenantKeyGenerator")
        KeyGenerator tenantKeyGenerator() {
            return new TenantAwareKeyGenerator();
        }
    }

    @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)
    @ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)
    @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "grocery.tenancy", name = "row-level-security",
            havingValue = "true")                                                        // (5)!
    static class RlsConfiguration {

        @Bean
        static BeanPostProcessor tenantAwareDataSourcePostProcessor() {
            return new TenantAwareDataSourcePostProcessor();                             // (6)!
        }
    }
}
  1. After the infrastructure it decorates.
  2. Tenant resolution runs after security (the token must be parsed) but before anything touching data (Chapter 38).
  3. Async propagation available for any executor the service builds.
  4. Cache support only if Spring Cache is present — services without caching pull nothing extra.
  5. RLS is opt-in: it requires database policies, so enabling it by default would break services that haven't created them.
  6. A static BeanPostProcessor (so it isn't subject to premature initialization) wrapping the DataSource.
Failure analyzer
public class MissingTenantClaimFailureAnalyzer extends AbstractFailureAnalyzer<MissingTenantClaimException> {
    @Override
    protected FailureAnalysis analyze(Throwable rootFailure, MissingTenantClaimException cause) {
        return new FailureAnalysis(
                "Tenancy is enabled but tokens do not contain the claim '%s'.".formatted(cause.claim()),
                """
                Either:
                  * set grocery.tenancy.claim-name to the claim your tokens use, or
                  * set grocery.tenancy.enabled=false for single-tenant deployments.
                """, cause);                                                             // (1)!
    }
}
  1. A misconfiguration that would otherwise present as every request failing with a confusing error at runtime.
Tests
@Test void registersFilterAndResolverByDefault() { }
@Test void disabledByPropertyRegistersNothing() { }
@Test void backsOffWhenTheUserDefinesATenantResolver() { }                               // (1)!
@Test void cacheKeyGeneratorAbsentWithoutSpringCache() { /* FilteredClassLoader(CacheManager.class) */ }
@Test void rlsDataSourceOnlyWhenExplicitlyEnabled() { }
@Test void nonWebApplicationGetsNoFilter() { }                                           // (2)!
@Test void invalidClaimNameFailsFastWithAMessage() { }
@Test void importsFileListsTheAutoConfigurationClass() { }                               // (3)!
  1. The override test, once per bean.
  2. Batch services (Chapter 33) use the decorator and key generator but have no filter.
  3. Reads the imports file and asserts the class name resolves — catching the silent-typo failure from the first scenario.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Auto-configuration is a file of class names plus conditions, applied after user configuration — no magic.
  • @ConditionalOnMissingBean on every bean is what makes a starter usable rather than imposing.
  • Two artifacts: autoconfigure (code, compileOnly dependencies) and starter (dependencies only).
  • ApplicationContextRunner with FilteredClassLoader is how you test conditions honestly.
  • Property metadata and failure analyzers are the difference between a library and a good library.
  • Ship native hints and measure startup cost — both multiply across the fleet.
  • Version with N-1 support; never force lockstep upgrades.
  • A platform library is a product with an owner; unowned starters block everyone's Boot upgrade.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text:
• Spring Boot Reference — Creating Your Own Auto-configuration and Starters, Condition Annotations, Testing Auto-configurations
  • Spring Boot source — AutoConfigurationImportSelector, OnBeanCondition, ConditionEvaluationReport
  • Spring Boot Reference — Configuration Metadata, Failure Analyzer, Runtime Hints
  • The Boot codebase itself: reading WebMvcAutoConfiguration teaches more about conditions than any tutorial

40 Spring AI · 42 Migration & Upgrade Engineering

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Every chapter in this handbook ended with a "Boot 3 vs 4" section. This chapter is about doing it — across 26 services, eight platform libraries, three JDK versions in flight, and a team that also has features to ship.

Upgrades fail in predictable ways:

  • The big bang: one team spends a quarter on a branch that upgrades everything, merges it, and spends the next quarter fixing production incidents from twenty simultaneous changes.
  • The indefinite deferral: "we'll upgrade after Diwali" — repeated until the Boot minor is out of open-source support, a CVE lands, and the upgrade becomes an emergency spanning three major versions.
  • The silent behaviour change: the code compiles, the tests pass, and a changed default (trailing-slash matching, a Jackson date format, a transaction propagation nuance) breaks a client in production.
  • The mixed-version trap: during a rolling deploy, old and new pods read each other's cache entries, Kafka messages and sessions — and disagree about the format (Chapters 21, 23).

Upgrade engineering is the discipline that makes this routine: a cadence that keeps upgrades small, automation (OpenRewrite, the properties migrator) that removes the mechanical work, tests that catch behaviour change rather than just compilation, wave-based rollout with platform libraries first, explicit handling of cross-version data, and dashboards that show where the fleet stands.

This chapter covers Java, Spring Boot, framework-replacement and database migrations, with the Boot 2 → 3 and 3 → 4 migrations as worked examples.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2, 4 — what changes, running the tools B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 5 — OpenRewrite, fixing breakages, testing B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 3, 5, 6 — behaviour changes, mixed versions, libraries B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — fleet programmes, waves, risk B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — cadence, funding and upgrade culture

docs.title: 2.1 Why upgrade at all
docs.text:
Reason Cost of not doing it Security fixes Unsupported versions stop receiving CVE patches Support window Open-source support for a Boot minor is limited (roughly a year); commercial support costs money Ecosystem Libraries drop support for old versions, blocking unrelated upgrades Performance JDK and framework improvements (virtual threads, CDS/AOT, GC) Hiring and morale Engineers don't want to work on 2019's stack Compounding Each skipped version makes the next jump larger and riskier

Verify support windows

Spring's support policy defines open-source and commercial support periods per release line. Check the current dates on the Spring support page — they drive the upgrade calendar, not the other way round.

docs.title: 2.2 The cadence that keeps upgrades cheap
docs.text:
Policy Effect Stay within N-1 Boot minors Each upgrade is a small step Patch releases within 2 weeks Security fixes land quickly JDK: stay on an LTS, move to the next LTS within a year Predictable, well-supported runtime Dependency updates via Renovate weekly No drift, small PRs (Chapter 39) Platform libraries released first Services are never blocked by the platform Upgrade work budgeted every quarter Not competing with features for permission

Six-monthly minor upgrades take days. A four-year jump takes quarters. The engineering difference is entirely cadence.

docs.title: 2.3 What changes in a major upgrade
docs.text:
Category Examples (Boot 2 → 3) Examples (Boot 3 → 4) Baseline Java 17, Jakarta EE 9/10 Jakarta EE 11, Java 25 recommended Namespaces javax.* → jakarta.* Jackson 2 → 3 packages (Chapter 11) Removed APIs WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter, Sleuth Deprecated 3.x APIs, non-lambda Security DSL Changed defaults Trailing-slash matching off, observation-based tracing Varies — read the migration guide Library majors Hibernate 6, Security 6 Hibernate 7, Security 7, Framework 7 Structure spring.factories → imports file for auto-configuration Modularized auto-configuration artifacts New capabilities Observation API, native images API versioning, HTTP service clients, core resilience

Behaviour changes are the real risk

Compilation errors are loud and cheap. Changed defaults are silent and expensive. Every major upgrade must be tested for behaviour: API responses (contract and golden-file tests), serialization (Chapter 11), security rules (Chapter 17), transaction behaviour (Chapter 16), and performance (Chapter 34).

docs.title: 2.4 The toolbox
docs.text: Tool What it does Migration guides The authoritative list of changes per release OpenRewrite Automated, reviewable source transformations (recipes for Boot, Jakarta, JUnit, Jackson…) spring-boot-properties-migrator Reports renamed/removed properties at runtime, temporarily remaps them Deprecation warnings Fix them on the old version before upgrading BOM One place to change versions (Chapter 01) Contract/golden-file tests Detect behaviour change at API boundaries (Chapters 11, 20, 28) Performance baselines Detect regressions (Chapter 34) Fleet version dashboard Where every service stands

docs.title: 2.5 The upgrade sequence
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Fix deprecations on the current version] --> B[Upgrade to the latest patch/minor of the current line]
    B --> C[Upgrade platform libraries + BOM]
    C --> D[Pilot service: automated recipes + manual fixes]
    D --> E[Behaviour tests, performance baseline, canary]
    E --> F[Waves: low-risk services → core services]
    F --> G["Remove compatibility shims; raise the floor"]

The first two steps are the most skipped and the most valuable: every deprecation fixed on the old version is a breakage that never happens on the new one.

docs.title: 2.6 Mixed-version compatibility
docs.text:
During a rolling deploy, old and new versions coexist. Anything shared must work in both directions:

Shared state Risk Mitigation Cache entries (Redis) Serialization format change Versioned key prefixes (Chapter 21) Kafka/Rabbit messages JSON/type-header differences Golden-file tests, cross-version produce/consume tests (Chapter 23) HTTP sessions Serialized session objects Session namespace per version, or stateless Database schema Migrations incompatible with old code Expand/contract (Chapter 14) Outbox payloads Old rows read by new relay Tolerant readers (Chapter 36) Batch job repository Schema changes between Batch majors Drain jobs first (Chapter 33)

docs.title: 3.1 OpenRewrite
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Source + classpath] --> B[Parse into a lossless semantic tree<br/>types resolved]
    B --> C[Recipes: visitors matching patterns]
    C --> D[Transformations preserving formatting]
    D --> E[Diff]
    E --> F[dryRun: patch for review]
    E --> G[run: apply to sources]

Because recipes operate on type-resolved trees, not text, they can distinguish javax.persistence.Entity from a string that happens to contain it — which is why they're safe to run across a large codebase and why their output is reviewable.

docs.title: 3.2 The properties migrator
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[App starts with the migrator on the classpath] --> B[Scan property sources]
    B --> C{property renamed or removed?}
    C -- renamed --> D["Log warning with the replacement;<br/>temporarily remap the value"]
    C -- removed --> E[Log error with the reason]
    D & E --> F[Report at startup]

It's a diagnostic, not a permanent shim: fix the properties, then remove the dependency.

docs.title: 3.3 A fleet upgrade over time
docs.text:
gantt
    title Boot 3.5 → 4.0 across the platform (illustrative)
    dateFormat  YYYY-MM-DD
    section Preparation
    Fix deprecations on 3.5          :a1, 2026-01-05, 21d
    Platform libraries on 4.0        :a2, after a1, 14d
    section Pilot
    notification-service            :b1, after a2, 7d
    section Wave 1 (low risk)
    8 supporting services            :c1, after b1, 14d
    section Wave 2 (medium)
    10 services                      :c2, after c1, 21d
    section Wave 3 (core)
    order, payment, pricing, inventory :c3, after c2, 21d

    Remove shims, raise floor        :d1, after c3, 7d

docs.title: 4.1 Before upgrading: clean the current version
4.2 The properties migrator
docs.text:
build.gradle.kts (temporarily)
runtimeOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-properties-migrator")                  // (1)!
Example
The use of configuration keys that have been renamed was found in the environment:

Property source 'Config resource 'class path resource [application.yml]'':
    Key: spring.redis.host
        Line: 14
        Replacement: spring.data.redis.host                                              # (2)!
  1. Add for the upgrade, remove afterwards.
  2. Exact file, line and replacement — fix them all, including in Kubernetes ConfigMaps (Chapter 30), which the migrator only sees if they're loaded in the environment you run it in.

docs.title: 4.3 OpenRewrite
4.4 A minimal upgrade PR, done properly
docs.text:
Example
PR: Upgrade catalog-service to Spring Boot 3.5.x

1. rewriteRun (UpgradeSpringBoot_3_5)                     — automated, reviewed
2. Property renames from the migrator                     — application.yml + ConfigMap
3. Manual fixes: 2 deprecated APIs recipes didn't cover   — listed below
4. Tests: unit, slice, integration, contract — all green
5. Golden-file JSON tests unchanged                       — no serialization drift  (1)
6. Performance: p95 within 3% of baseline                 — nightly run attached
7. Removed properties-migrator
  1. The line reviewers should look for first: no behaviour change at the API boundary.

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — Boot 2 → 3 in practice
5.2 Level 2 — Boot 3 → 4 in practice
docs.text:
Change Chapter Main risk Modularized auto-configuration 05, 41 Moved imports in platform libraries and tests Jackson 3 11 Package names, defaults, cross-version payloads Security 7: lambda DSL only, matcher changes 17 Rules that silently change meaning Framework 7: API versioning, HTTP service clients, @Retryable 19, 20, 26 Adoption is optional — don't bundle it with the upgrade Hibernate 7 13 Query and mapping edge cases Test slice packages 15 Mechanical, noisy JSpecify nullness annotations — New compiler warnings in strict builds Removed deprecations all Fixed in advance (4.1)

Separate the upgrade from the modernization

Upgrade to Boot 4 without adopting API versioning, HTTP service clients or core @Retryable in the same change. Get to a green, behaviour-identical state first; adopt new features in later, independent PRs. Mixing them makes every regression ambiguous.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Tests that catch behaviour change
5.4 Level 3 — Cross-version compatibility testing
5.5 Level 3 — Upgrading platform libraries first
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Platform BOM 3.x on Boot 3.5] --> B[Platform BOM 4.0 on Boot 4.0<br/>all starters compiled + tested]
    B --> C[Compatibility: services on 3.x keep working with BOM 3.x]
    C --> D[Services move one by one to BOM 4.0]
    D --> E[BOM 3.x in maintenance until the last service moves]

Rules from Chapter 41 that make this work: N-1 support, no lockstep upgrades, a compatibility matrix published before services start. The platform team upgrades first so service teams are never blocked.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Replacing frameworks, not just versions
5.7 Level 3 — JDK upgrades
6.1 A fleet upgrade programme
docs.text:
Phase Owner Exit criterion 0. Readiness Platform Deprecations at zero on the current version; migration guide read; risks listed 1. Platform libraries Platform All starters on the new version, tests + native tests green, matrix published 2. Pilot Platform + one team One low-risk service in production for a week with no regressions 3. Waves Service teams Each wave in production, contracts green, performance within budget 4. Core services Service teams + platform Canary with SLO analysis (Chapter 30), extra review 5. Cleanup Platform Shims removed, old BOM retired, floor raised upgrade/boot-4.yaml — the programme as data
target: spring-boot-4.0
waves:
  - name: pilot
    services: [notification-service]
  - name: wave-1
    services: [seller-onboarding, catalog-feed, search-indexer, tracking-stream, reporting]
  - name: wave-2
    services: [catalog, delivery, dispatch, cart, loyalty, settlement]
  - name: wave-3-core
    services: [order, payment, pricing, inventory]
    requires: [canary-with-slo-analysis, cross-version-payload-tests, on-call-aware]
freeze_windows:
  - 2026-10-15..2026-11-10   # Diwali — no core upgrades                         # (1)
  1. The upgrade calendar respects the business calendar. Core services never upgrade during peak season.

docs.title: 6.2 Readiness scorecard per service
docs.text:
in/grocery/platform/upgrade/UpgradeReadinessCheck.java
public record UpgradeReadiness(
        String service,
        int deprecationWarnings,
        boolean onLatestCurrentMinor,
        boolean onPlatformBomLatest,
        boolean goldenFileTestsPresent,
        boolean contractTestsPresent,
        boolean accessMatrixPresent,
        boolean perfBaselinePresent,
        List<String> blockingDependencies) {                                              // (1)!

    public boolean ready() {
        return deprecationWarnings == 0 && onLatestCurrentMinor && onPlatformBomLatest
                && goldenFileTestsPresent && contractTestsPresent && blockingDependencies.isEmpty();
    }
}
  1. Third-party libraries without a compatible release — the items that turn a two-day upgrade into a two-month one. Identify them in phase 0.

The scorecard is computed in CI for every service and rendered on the fleet dashboard. A service without golden-file and contract tests isn't ready to upgrade — the scorecard makes the prerequisite visible instead of discovering it in production.

docs.title: 6.3 Fleet version dashboard
docs.text:
Reporting versions from every service (Chapter 41's platform endpoint)
@ReadOperation
public PlatformVersions versions() {
    return new PlatformVersions(
            SpringBootVersion.getVersion(),
            SpringVersion.getVersion(),
            Runtime.version().toString(),
            platformBomVersion(),
            hibernateVersion(),
            jacksonVersion());                                                             // (1)!
}
  1. Scraped into a dashboard: Boot version by service, JDK by service, platform BOM by service, days behind the latest patch. "Where are we?" becomes a glance, not a spreadsheet chase.
Dashboard panel Question Services by Boot minor How much of the fleet is on the target? Days since last patch per service Who is falling behind on security fixes? Services on unsupported versions Where is the risk today? Wave progress Is the programme on schedule? Regressions attributed to the upgrade Is the process working?

docs.title: 6.4 Rollback and safety
docs.text:
Mechanism Detail Deploy by digest (Chapter 29) Rollback is exact Expand/contract migrations (Chapter 14) Old code works against the new schema Versioned cache namespaces Old pods keep their own cache Tolerant readers on messages Both versions consume each other's events Canary with SLO analysis (Chapter 30) Automatic rollback on regression Feature flags for new behaviour New framework features adopted separately, toggled independently Upgrade runbook — order-service (core)
## Before
- [ ] Readiness scorecard green
- [ ] Cross-version payload tests green (Kafka, cache, outbox)
- [ ] Canary analysis template references the new version label
- [ ] On-call informed; no freeze window active

## During
- [ ] Canary 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% with SLO analysis between steps
- [ ] Watch: error rate, p99, DLT rate, outbox pending, cache hit ratio

## Rollback
- Revert to digest sha256:… (recorded in release notes)
- Cache namespace v3 still warm; no data migration to undo

## After
- [ ] Remove properties migrator and temporary shims
- [ ] Update the readiness dashboard

docs.title: 6.5 Database major upgrades
docs.text:
PostgreSQL major versions follow the same logic with higher stakes:

flowchart LR
    A[Current primary v16] -->|logical replication| B[New cluster v17]
    B --> C[Verify: row counts, checksums, query plans]
    C --> D[Application tests against v17 in staging]
    D --> E[Cutover: stop writes briefly, catch up, switch the DNS/connection string]
    E --> F[Keep v16 as a rollback target for a defined window]
Concern Practice Downtime Logical replication or managed blue/green reduces it to seconds Query plan changes Compare EXPLAIN for the top queries from pg_stat_statements (Chapter 34) Extensions Verify versions (pgvector, PostGIS) exist for the new major CDC connectors Replication slots don't survive the move — re-create and re-snapshot (Chapter 36) Rollback Reverse replication or a defined window with the old cluster intact

docs.title: 6.6 Modernizing a legacy application
docs.text:
A decade-old Spring MVC 4 / Java 8 application is a different problem from a version bump:

Step Goal 1. Characterize Golden-file and approval tests around current behaviour, before touching anything 2. Build Move to Gradle/Maven with a BOM; reproducible builds (Chapter 01) 3. Runtime Java 8 → 11 → 17 (each step deployed), then Boot 2.7 as a bridge 4. Boot 3 jakarta migration with OpenRewrite 5. Structure Modularize in place (Chapter 37); extract only where justified (Chapter 35) 6. Operations Containers, probes, observability (Chapters 27, 29, 30)

Step 1 is non-negotiable. Without characterization tests, you can't distinguish "the upgrade changed behaviour" from "it always did that".

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 & Migration
docs.text:
This whole chapter is the migration section. The consolidated checklist, drawn from every chapter:

Area Check Chapter Build BOM, toolchain, reproducibility 01 Configuration Properties migrator clean; ConfigMaps updated 06 Logging Structured logging and MDC propagation intact 07 Web Error format, validation, API versioning adoption deferred 08–10, 20 JSON Jackson 3 packages, golden files green 11 Data Hibernate 7 queries, transaction tests, migrations 12–16 Security Lambda DSL, matcher semantics, access matrix 17, 18, 39 Clients Request factory APIs, timeouts intact 19 Caching Versioned namespaces, serializer classes 21 Messaging Cross-version payloads, trusted packages 23, 24 Async Executors, virtual threads, pinning 25 Resilience Aspect ordering, one retry implementation 26 Observability Metric names unchanged, tracing propagation 27 Testing Slice packages, @MockitoBean 15, 28 Packaging jarmode=tools, CDS/AOT regenerated, native tests 29 Platform libraries Compiled and tested first, matrix published 41

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Cadence over heroics: stay within N-1 minors; patch within two weeks.
  2. Fix deprecations on the current version before upgrading.
  3. Automate the mechanical work (OpenRewrite, properties migrator) and review it like code.
  4. Test behaviour, not compilation: golden files, access matrix, contracts, performance.
  5. Platform libraries first, with N-1 compatibility.
  6. Pilot, then waves, core services last and outside freeze windows.
  7. Plan for mixed versions: cache namespaces, tolerant payloads, expand/contract schemas.
  8. Separate upgrading from modernizing; adopt new features in later PRs.
  9. Measure the fleet: versions, patch age and readiness on a dashboard.
  10. Budget upgrade work every quarter so it never competes for permission.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Big-bang upgrades of everything at once.

❌ Deferring until a version is unsupported and a CVE forces an emergency.

❌ Upgrading and adopting new features in the same change.

❌ Trusting a green build without behaviour tests.

❌ Leaving the properties migrator in permanently.

❌ Services upgrading before the platform libraries they depend on.

❌ Ignoring cross-version data during rolling deploys.

❌ Upgrading core services during peak season.

❌ Applying OpenRewrite output without reading it.

❌ No record of which service runs which version.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Cause Fix 404s for some clients after Boot 3 Trailing-slash matching disabled Gateway rewrite + telemetry, then remove JSON fields changed format Jackson defaults changed Golden files; explicit mapper configuration (Chapter 11) Security rule stopped protecting a path Matcher semantics changed Access matrix; review every rule Deserialization errors during rollout Cross-version payloads Tolerant readers; versioned namespaces Bean missing after upgrade Auto-configuration moved or condition changed /actuator/conditions (Chapter 41) Performance regression New defaults, GC ergonomics, query plans Nightly baseline, profile (Chapter 34) Upgrade blocked for months Third-party library without a compatible release Identify in readiness; fork, replace or isolate Tests pass, production differs Config in ConfigMaps not migrated Run the migrator against production-like config Native build fails Hints missing for new versions nativeTest in CI (Chapter 29)

docs.title: Production checklist
docs.text:
• Support calendar tracked; upgrade programme scheduled against it
  • Deprecations at zero on the current version
  • Platform libraries upgraded first; compatibility matrix published
  • Readiness scorecard green for each service before its wave
  • Golden-file, access-matrix, contract and performance tests in place
  • Cross-version payload and cache compatibility verified
  • Canary with SLO analysis for core services; freeze windows respected
  • Rollback by digest documented per service
  • Temporary shims and the properties migrator removed afterwards
  • Fleet version dashboard updated

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · Why keep Spring Boot up to date?

Short answer: Security fixes and support end for old versions, libraries drop compatibility, and each skipped version makes the next upgrade bigger and riskier.

B1 · What does the properties migrator do?

Short answer: At startup it reports renamed or removed configuration properties with their replacements and temporarily remaps renamed ones. You fix the properties and then remove it.

B1 · What is OpenRewrite?

Short answer: A tool that applies automated, type-aware source transformations (recipes) — for example javax to jakarta, dependency upgrades, API replacements — producing reviewable diffs.

B1 · What was the biggest mechanical change in Boot 3?

Short answer: The move from javax.* to jakarta.* packages with Jakarta EE 9/10, alongside the Java 17 baseline.

B1 · Why fix deprecation warnings before upgrading?

Short answer: Deprecated APIs are usually removed in the next major; fixing them on the current version turns future compile errors into small, independent changes.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you detect behaviour changes during an upgrade?

Short answer: Golden-file tests for JSON and events, access-matrix tests for security, contract tests at API boundaries, integration tests on real infrastructure, and performance baselines — compilation alone proves very little.

B2 · How do you use OpenRewrite safely?

Short answer: Dry-run first, read the patch, apply on a branch, review it like any code change, and run the full test suite. Recipes handle the mechanical 80%; the remaining 20% is manual and deliberate.

B2 · Why separate upgrading from adopting new features?

Short answer: So regressions have a single cause. Reach a green, behaviour-identical state on the new version first, then adopt new capabilities in independent changes.

B2 · What breaks during a rolling upgrade that tests don't catch?

Short answer: Shared state read by both versions — cache entries, messages, sessions, database schema. Plan with versioned cache namespaces, tolerant readers and expand/contract migrations.

B2 · How do you handle a third-party library without a compatible release?

Short answer: Identify it early in the readiness phase, then upgrade it, replace it, isolate it behind a port, or temporarily fork it — before it blocks the whole programme.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · Walk through upgrading a service to a new Boot major.

Short answer: Clear deprecations on the current line, move to the latest minor, wait for platform libraries, run the OpenRewrite recipe and the properties migrator, fix remaining issues manually, verify golden files, access matrix, contracts and performance, test cross-version payloads, canary with SLO analysis, then remove shims.

B3 · How do you test cross-version message compatibility?

Short answer: Check real captured payloads from the old version into the repository and deserialize them with the new stack, and serialize with the new stack and read with an old-configured mapper — both directions, for every topic.

B3 · How do you replace a framework (Feign, Hystrix) without a big bang?

Short answer: Put a port in front of it, implement the new adapter alongside the old, switch by configuration per environment, compare metrics under canary, then flip the default and delete the old adapter.

B3 · What changes when upgrading the JDK?

Short answer: Strong encapsulation affecting reflective libraries, GC and memory ergonomics, invalidated CDS/AOT caches, virtual-thread behaviour, and base images. Run the suite on the new JDK in a parallel CI job well before switching.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you run an upgrade across 26 services?

Short answer: A programme with phases: readiness (deprecations, blockers), platform libraries first with a compatibility matrix, a pilot, waves from low-risk to core, canary for core services outside freeze windows, a readiness scorecard and fleet dashboard, then cleanup. Service teams own their waves; the platform team unblocks them.

B4 · How do you fund upgrade work against feature pressure?

Short answer: Make it continuous rather than episodic — a fixed quarterly allocation, Renovate for small constant updates, and a dashboard showing support-window risk in business terms (unpatched CVEs, unsupported versions). Small, regular upgrades are cheap enough that they stop needing special approval.

B4 · How do you upgrade a database major version safely?

Short answer: Logical replication to a new cluster, verification of data and query plans for the top statements, application tests against the new version, a short write-freeze cutover, and the old cluster retained as a rollback target — with CDC slots re-created afterwards.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What does a healthy upgrade culture look like?

Short answer: Upgrades are boring: small, frequent, automated, measured and owned. Teams trust the tests enough to upgrade without fear, the platform team is always one step ahead, and nobody remembers the last emergency upgrade because there hasn't been one.

B5 · When would you let a system stay on an old version?

Short answer: When it's scheduled for retirement soon, isolated from untrusted input, and the cost of upgrading exceeds the residual risk — with that decision recorded, time-bound and revisited. Indefinite exceptions are how estates end up three majors behind.

B5 · How do you choose between an in-place upgrade and a rewrite of a legacy application?

Short answer: Default to incremental upgrade: characterization tests, then Java and Boot steps, then modularization. Rewrite only when the domain has changed enough that the old model is wrong, not merely old — and even then strangle it piece by piece rather than cutting over at once.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · After the Boot 3 upgrade, the mobile app's order history broke

The Android app called /api/orders/ with a trailing slash; Boot 3 disabled trailing-slash matching by default. Fixes: a gateway rewrite as immediate mitigation, a metric counting trailing-slash requests by client version, a fix in the app, a golden-path contract test with the real client paths, and removal of the rewrite once telemetry reached zero.

Scenario · Checkout errors spiked during a rolling upgrade, then disappeared

New pods wrote Jackson-3-formatted price entries to the shared Redis cache; old pods failed to deserialize them until the rollout finished. Fixes: a versioned cache key prefix per major, cross-version cache tests, and the rule that shared serialized state is part of every upgrade's risk assessment.

docs.title: Coding exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Plan and automate one service's Boot 3.5 → 4 upgrade

For catalog-service: list the readiness checks, the automated steps, the tests proving behaviour is unchanged, the cross-version risks, and the rollout and rollback plan. Write the Gradle and CI configuration for the automated parts.

Solution

Readiness Example

deprecations = 0 on 3.5.x              ./gradlew compileJava -Xlint:deprecation -Werror
platform BOM 4.0 available + matrix    in.grocery:grocery-platform-bom:4.0.0
third-party blockers                   springdoc 4.x compatible? opensearch client? → verified
tests present                          golden JSON, access matrix, contracts, perf baseline

Automation build.gradle.kts

plugins { id("org.openrewrite.rewrite") version "7.x" }
rewrite { activeRecipe("org.openrewrite.java.spring.boot4.UpgradeSpringBoot_4_0") }   // (1)!
dependencies {
    rewrite("org.openrewrite.recipe:rewrite-spring:latest.release")
    implementation(platform("in.grocery:grocery-platform-bom:4.0.0"))
    runtimeOnly("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-properties-migrator")           // removed after
}

  1. Verify the recipe name for your OpenRewrite version.
.github/workflows/upgrade-check.yml
jobs:
  upgrade:
    steps:
      - run: ./gradlew rewriteDryRun
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with: { name: rewrite-patch, path: build/reports/rewrite/rewrite.patch }       # (1)!
      - run: ./gradlew rewriteRun build integrationTest
      - run: ./gradlew test --tests '*Golden*' --tests '*AccessMatrix*' --tests '*Contract*'
      - run: ./scripts/perf-compare.sh --max-p95-regression 10
  1. The patch is an artifact reviewers read before approving.

Cross-version risks | Shared state | Mitigation | |---|---| | Redis price and product caches | key-prefix: grocery:v4: | | product-changed Kafka events | Captured 3.5 payloads deserialized by the 4.0 build; 4.0 payloads read by a 3.5-configured mapper | | Search index documents | Unchanged mapping; indexer tolerant of both | | Database | No schema changes in this PR |

Rollout: canary 5% → 25% → 100% with SLO analysis (error rate, p99, cache hit ratio, DLT rate). Rollback: previous digest recorded; v3 cache namespace still warm; no data migration to reverse. Cleanup: remove the migrator, update the dashboard, delete the v3 cache namespace after 48 hours.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Cadence makes upgrades cheap; deferral makes them emergencies.
  • Fix deprecations first, on the version you're leaving.
  • Automate the mechanical work with OpenRewrite and the properties migrator — and review the output.
  • Test behaviour, not compilation: golden files, access matrix, contracts, performance.
  • Platform libraries lead; services follow in waves; core services go last, outside peak season.
  • Mixed versions coexist during rollouts — design caches, messages and schemas for it.
  • Upgrade and modernize separately.
  • Measure the fleet, and budget upgrade work continuously.

  • OpenRewrite documentation — Spring, Jakarta, JUnit and Jackson recipes
