41 Spring Internals & Custom Starters · 43 Engineering Leadership

docs.title: 43 · Engineering Leadership for Senior Spring Engineers
1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
At some point in a career — usually between eight and fifteen years — the highest-leverage work stops being the code you write. It becomes the decisions you shape, the standards you set, the incidents you prevent, the engineers you grow and the organization's ability to change safely.

Everything in the previous forty-two chapters depends on this:

  • Platform libraries (Chapter 41) exist only if someone argues for them, funds them and keeps them owned.
  • SLOs (Chapter 27) mean something only if product and engineering agree on them.
  • Upgrade cadence (Chapter 42) survives only if it's budgeted before it's urgent.
  • Boundaries (Chapters 35, 37) hold only if review culture enforces them.
  • Security (Chapter 39) works only if engineers threat model without being told to.

None of these is a technical problem. Each is a technical decision that needs alignment, persistence and communication to happen.

This chapter covers the leadership toolkit for a senior, staff or principal engineer in a Spring-based organization: technical strategy, decision records and RFCs, architecture governance that doesn't become bureaucracy, technical debt as a managed portfolio, code review and mentoring, incident leadership and blameless reviews, measuring delivery with DORA metrics, hiring with this handbook's interview bank, cost awareness, and influencing without authority. In keeping with the handbook, it uses concrete artifacts — templates, scripts, checklists — rather than exhortation.

docs.title: Who should read which section
docs.text: Band Focus B1 · 0–2 yrs Parts 1, 2 — how decisions get made; how to grow B2 · 2–5 yrs Parts 2, 4, 5 — reviews, ADRs, writing well B3 · 5–8 yrs Parts 5, 6 — leading projects, incidents, mentoring B4 · 8–12 yrs Parts 6, 8 — strategy, governance, metrics B5 · 12–15+ yrs Parts 8, 9 — organizational leverage

docs.title: 2.1 Where senior leverage comes from
docs.text:
Activity Leverage Writing a feature 1× Reviewing well Raises the quality of many features A platform library or starter Every service, every future service A decision record that prevents a bad decision Avoided cost, rarely visible Growing an engineer to the next band Compounds for years Setting a standard with enforcement Durable across team changes Leading an incident well Faster recovery and lasting fixes

The shift is from doing the work to making the work go well. It feels less productive and is usually more valuable.

docs.title: 2.2 Technical strategy
docs.text:
A strategy answers three questions in a few pages:

  1. Where are we? Honest diagnosis — the fleet version dashboard (Chapter 42), incident themes, delivery metrics, cost.
  2. Where do we need to be, and why? Tied to business outcomes, not technology preferences.
  3. What will we do, and not do? A small number of bets with explicit trade-offs.

Example for the grocery platform:

Diagnosis Direction Bets Explicitly not doing Checkout p99 regressions every sale; 6 synchronous hops Short synchronous paths, events elsewhere Outbox everywhere; saga for checkout; latency budgets Rewriting services in another language Upgrades take a quarter Continuous upgrades Platform-first, Renovate, readiness scorecard Freezing on Boot 3 "for stability" Tenant leak near-miss Isolation proven by tests RLS + leak suite in every build Database-per-tenant for everyone

docs.title: 2.3 Decision-making instruments
docs.text:
Instrument Use Size ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Record a decision and its reasons 1 page RFC (Request for Comments) Propose a significant change and gather input 2–6 pages Design review Examine a design before building 30–60 min Spike Reduce uncertainty with code Time-boxed days Standards Encode decisions that apply broadly Enforced by tooling

Decisions reversible in a day don't need an RFC. Decisions that constrain 26 services for years do.

docs.title: 2.4 Technical debt as a portfolio
docs.text:
Type Example Response Deliberate, prudent "Ship with a polling relay, move to CDC at 10k events/s" Record in an ADR with a trigger Accidental A god aggregate discovered later Refactor when touching the area Environmental Unsupported Boot version Scheduled (Chapter 42) Reckless No tests on payment code Fix now; it's a risk, not debt

Debt is managed like a financial portfolio: named, sized, owned, and paid down according to interest rate — the debt slowing every change is paid before the debt nobody touches.

docs.title: 2.5 Measuring delivery: DORA
docs.text:
Metric Measures Good sign Deployment frequency How often you ship On demand, many per day across the fleet Lead time for changes Commit to production Hours to a day Change failure rate Deploys causing incidents or rollbacks Low, and falling Time to restore service Incident to recovery Under an hour

These measure the system, not individuals. Using them to rank engineers destroys their usefulness within a quarter.

docs.title: 2.6 Incidents and learning
docs.text: Principle Practice Restore first, understand second Rollback by digest (Chapter 29) before root-cause analysis Clear roles Incident commander, communications, operations — not everyone debugging Blameless review "What made this possible?" not "who did this?" Actions with owners and dates Tracked like features Themes over incidents Quarterly review of recurring causes

docs.title: 2.7 Influence without authority
docs.text:
Staff and principal engineers rarely manage the people whose decisions they shape. Influence comes from:

Source How Credibility Being right, visibly, over time — and admitting when you weren't Clarity Writing that makes the decision easy Data Dashboards, incident themes, cost reports Relationships Understanding what each team is trying to achieve Making the right thing easy Platform libraries, templates, tooling Patience Standards adopted gradually beat mandates resisted

The last two matter most. An engineer who builds the starter that makes the secure path the easy path (Chapter 41) has more influence than any architecture board.

docs.title: 3.1 How a decision flows
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Problem noticed:<br/>incident, metric, request] --> B{Reversible cheaply?}
    B -- yes --> C["Team decides; optional ADR"]
    B -- no --> D[RFC drafted]
    D --> E[Comment period: affected teams, security, platform]
    E --> F[Decision meeting — 30 min, decision-maker named]
    F --> G[ADR recorded]
    G --> H[Enforced: library, lint, ArchUnit, template]
    H --> I[Revisited when the context changes]

The step organizations skip is H: a decision without enforcement is a suggestion, and suggestions erode with the first deadline (Chapters 28, 37).

docs.title: 3.2 From incident to systemic fix
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Incident] --> B[Restore service]
    B --> C[Timeline from logs, traces, deploy annotations — Chapter 27]
    C --> D[Contributing factors, not a single root cause]
    D --> E[Actions: detection, prevention, mitigation]
    E --> F[Owners + dates, tracked]
    F --> G[Quarterly theme review]
    G --> H[Platform changes: library, test, alert, standard]

A single incident produces local fixes; a pattern of incidents produces platform changes. The quarterly theme review is where the second happens.

docs.title: 3.3 How engineers grow through the bands
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    B1["B1: delivers tasks<br/>with guidance"] --> B2["B2: owns features<br/>end to end"]
    B2 --> B3["B3: owns a service or area;<br/>designs, reviews, mentors"]
    B3 --> B4["B4: shapes multiple teams' systems;<br/>leads cross-cutting initiatives"]
    B4 --> B5["B5: sets direction for the organization;<br/>multiplies others"]

The handbook's band tables map to these expectations: each chapter's B1–B5 questions describe what an engineer at that level should be able to reason about.

docs.title: 4.1 An ADR template
docs.text:
docs/adr/0023-outbox-polling-before-cdc.md
# ADR-0023: Use a polling outbox relay before adopting CDC

- Status: Accepted
- Date: 2026-03-12
- Deciders: Platform team, order/payment tech leads
- Supersedes: —
- Related: Chapter 36, RFC-0011

## Context
Services publish events after committing, losing events during broker outages
(incident INC-2031). We need atomic publish with at-least-once delivery.

## Decision
Every publishing service writes to an `outbox` table in the business transaction.
A polling relay (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, 300 ms) publishes to Kafka.

## Alternatives considered
- Debezium CDC — lower latency, but adds Kafka Connect and replication-slot risk
  (WAL growth) that we are not yet staffed to operate.
- Publish after commit with retries — does not solve the dual write.

## Consequences
- + No lost events; simple to operate.
- − ~300 ms added latency; extra load on the primary.
- Revisit when any service exceeds 2,000 events/s or needs < 100 ms latency.   ← the trigger

The revisit trigger turns a decision into a deliberate, bounded piece of debt rather than an accident waiting to be rediscovered.

docs.title: 4.2 A code review checklist
docs.text: Area Question Correctness Does it do what the ticket says, including edge cases? Tests Would a test fail if the logic were wrong? Boundary cases? Boundaries Does it respect module/service ownership? (Chapters 35, 37) Transactions Remote calls inside transactions? Right propagation? (Chapter 16) Security Ownership checks, validation, no PII in logs? (Chapters 17, 39) Failure Timeouts, idempotency, what happens on retry? (Chapters 19, 26) Observability Would we know if this broke? (Chapter 27) Compatibility API/event/schema changes additive? (Chapters 14, 20, 23) Operability Config, flags, runbook impact? Simplicity Is there a simpler way that meets the need?

docs.title: 4.3 How to give review feedback
docs.text:
Label Meaning blocking: Must change before merge (correctness, security, data loss) suggestion: Better, but the author decides question: I don't understand — explain or clarify in code nit: Trivial; ignore if you disagree praise: Something done well — say it Example
blocking: this calls pricing-service inside @Transactional — a slow pricing call holds
a DB connection for its full duration (Chapter 16). Could we fetch prices before
opening the transaction?

suggestion: an @EntityGraph here would avoid the N+1 on lines (Chapter 13).

praise: the idempotency test for duplicate events is exactly right.

Labels remove ambiguity about what matters, and explicit praise makes the critical comments easier to receive.

docs.title: 5.1 Level 2 — An RFC that gets decided
docs.text:
docs/rfc/0014-tenant-isolation-with-rls.md
# RFC-0014: Enforce tenant isolation with PostgreSQL RLS

Author: … | Reviewers: platform, security, order, catalog | Decision by: 2026-05-20
Decision-maker: Head of Platform Engineering

## Summary (5 lines)
Add row-level security to all tenant-scoped tables as a second enforcement layer
behind Hibernate @TenantId, plus an automated leak suite in every build.

## Problem
Near-miss INC-2207: a native export query bypassed tenant filtering.
Application-level filtering alone depends on every developer remembering.

## Proposal
(what changes, for whom, in what order — Chapter 38)

## Cost
~2 engineer-weeks platform, ~1 day per service; ~1–3% query overhead (measured).

## Risks and mitigations
Pooled connections leaking tenant settings → transaction-local settings + test.

## Alternatives
Database per tenant — rejected for cost at 400+ tenants.

## Rollout
Platform starter → 2 pilot services → remaining services over 6 weeks.

## Open questions
1. …

What makes RFCs get decided rather than debated forever:

Practice Why A decision date and a named decision-maker Prevents indefinite discussion A five-line summary Most readers read only this Cost and alternatives stated honestly Reviewers trust a proposal that admits trade-offs Explicit open questions Focuses comments where they're useful Link to data Incidents, metrics, measurements

docs.title: 5.2 Level 2 — A technical debt register
docs.text:
platform/debt-register.yaml
- id: DEBT-031
  title: order-service uses RestTemplate with no read timeout for inventory
  area: order-service
  type: accidental
  interest: high          # slows every change + incident risk (Chapter 19)
  principal: 2 days
  owner: checkout-team
  trigger: next change to inventory integration, or by 2026-06-30
  links: [INC-2144]

- id: DEBT-044
  title: polling outbox relay (ADR-0023)
  type: deliberate
  interest: low
  principal: 3 weeks
  owner: platform
  trigger: any service > 2,000 events/s
Field Why it matters Interest How much it costs now — prioritize by this, not by size Principal Effort to fix — enables "small high-interest items first" Owner Unowned debt is permanent Trigger When it must be paid, decided in advance

Review the register monthly; 15–20% of each team's capacity on high-interest items is a sustainable rate that keeps the codebase changeable.

docs.title: 5.3 Level 2 — Measuring DORA from your pipeline
5.4 Level 3 — Leading an incident
docs.text:
runbooks/incident-roles.md
## Incident commander (IC)
- Declares severity, owns decisions, keeps the timeline
- Does NOT debug — coordinates those who do
- Asks every 15 min: what do we know, what are we trying, what's next?

## Communications lead
- Updates status page and stakeholders on a fixed cadence (every 30 min for SEV-1)
- Shields responders from questions

## Operations lead(s)
- Investigate and mitigate; report findings to the IC

## First actions (SEV-1)
1. Did anything change? (deploy annotations — Chapter 27) → roll back by digest
2. Degrade before fixing: circuit breakers, feature flags, load shedding (Chapter 26)
3. Contain business impact: freeze payouts, disable a feature (Chapter 39)

The instinct of a senior engineer is to debug. During a SEV-1, the more valuable contribution is often to stop debugging and coordinate: one IC who keeps the team from five parallel theories is worth more than a sixth debugger.

docs.title: 5.5 Level 3 — A blameless post-incident review
docs.text:
postmortems/INC-2207.md
# INC-2207: Tenant export returned rows from another tenant (near-miss)

Severity: SEV-2 (caught in staging) | Duration: n/a | Author: … | Reviewed: 2026-04-18

## Summary
A native SQL export bypassed Hibernate tenant filtering. Caught by a QA engineer
comparing row counts before release.

## Timeline (IST)
- 10:42 export feature merged
- 14:15 QA notices 2× expected rows
- 14:40 feature flag disabled; release held

## Contributing factors
1. Native query outside Hibernate's @TenantId filter (known limitation — Chapter 38).
2. RLS enabled on only 4 of 31 tables.
3. No automated test for native queries across tenants.
4. Review checklist did not mention tenant scoping for native SQL.

## What went well
QA's row-count sanity check. Feature flag allowed instant disable.

## Actions
| Action | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|
| RLS on all tenant-scoped tables (RFC-0014) | platform | 2026-06-01 |
| Leak suite incl. native queries in every build | platform | 2026-05-15 |
| Review checklist: tenant scoping item | architecture | 2026-04-25 |
| Audit all native queries | each team | 2026-05-01 |

Note what isn't there: no names attached to mistakes. The factors are systemic — a known limitation without a second layer, a missing test, a checklist gap. Fixing those prevents the next team from making the same mistake; blaming one engineer prevents only honest reporting.

docs.title: 5.6 Level 3 — Mentoring with structure
docs.text:
growth-plans/engineer-b2-to-b3.md
## Current: B2 (owns features end to end)
## Target: B3 (owns a service; designs; mentors) — 9–12 months

| Capability | Evidence today | Next step | Chapter |
|---|---|---|---|
| Design | Implements designs well | Write the design for the refund saga | 36 |
| Operations | Fixes bugs in own code | Be secondary on-call; lead one post-incident review | 27, 43 |
| Performance | — | Run and interpret a profile during the next load test | 34 |
| Review | Reviews peers' PRs | Review a cross-team RFC with written feedback | 43 |
| Mentoring | — | Pair weekly with the new B1 on the cart service | — |

Check-in: fortnightly, 30 min. Evidence collected in a shared doc.

The handbook's band tables and interview questions double as a growth curriculum: "can reason about the B3 questions in Chapters 16, 26 and 36" is a concrete, discussable target rather than a vague aspiration.

docs.title: 6.1 Lightweight architecture governance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Change] --> B{Affects only one team,<br/>reversible?}
    B -- yes --> C["Team decides; ADR optional"]
    B -- no --> D{Crosses service boundaries,<br/>new technology, security/data impact?}
    D -- yes --> E[RFC + review by affected teams<br/>decision within 2 weeks]
    D -- no --> F[Design review in the team,<br/>ADR recorded]
    E --> G[Enforced by platform tooling]
Principle Implementation Most decisions stay in teams Autonomy with clear boundaries Cross-cutting decisions are visible RFCs in a shared repository Decisions have deadlines No RFC open longer than two weeks without a decision Standards are enforced by tools, not meetings Platform starters, ArchUnit, CI gates (Chapters 28, 41) Exceptions are allowed, recorded and time-bound ADR with a revisit date

An architecture board that reviews every change becomes the bottleneck it was meant to prevent. The goal is paved roads — the easy path is the right path — plus a lightweight process for leaving the road deliberately.

docs.title: 6.2 Service scorecards
docs.text:
Generated from the service catalog (Chapter 35) + CI + dashboards
service: order-service
owner: checkout
tier: 1
scores:
  slos_defined: ✅
  runbook: ✅
  on_call: ✅
  boot_version: 3.5.6 (target 4.0 — wave 3)          # Chapter 42
  platform_bom: 3.4.0 ✅
  deprecations: 0 ✅
  contract_tests: ✅                                    # Chapter 28
  golden_file_tests: ✅
  leak_suite: ✅                                        # Chapter 38
  image_age_days: 6 ✅                                  # Chapter 29
  critical_cves: 0 ✅                                   # Chapter 39
  dora:
    deploys_per_week: 14
    lead_time_p50: 5h
    change_failure_rate: 4%
    time_to_restore_p50: 22m

Scorecards turn the handbook's standards into something visible and comparable. Teams improve what they can see; leaders find where to help. Used as a map for support, they work. Used as a stick, they get gamed.

docs.title: 6.3 Hiring with the interview bank
docs.text:
The B1–B5 questions throughout this handbook (and Appendix A) support structured interviews:

Stage Design Screening 3–4 B1/B2 questions from different chapters; pass/fail Technical depth One domain (data, messaging, security) to B3/B4 depth, following the candidate's answers System design A grocery-domain scenario (checkout under partial failure, tenant isolation, a Diwali sale) Code A small exercise from Appendix B, reviewed together Leadership (B4+) An RFC to critique; an incident to lead verbally; a disagreement to navigate Interview rubric — system design (B4)
| Dimension | 1 (weak) | 3 (meets) | 5 (strong) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Requirements | Jumps to technology | Clarifies scale, consistency, SLOs | Identifies the business trade-off first |
| Failure | Ignores it | Timeouts, retries, idempotency | Degradation per dependency, reconciliation |
| Data | One database for all | Ownership per service | Consistency model justified per flow |
| Trade-offs | States a choice | Compares two options | Explains when they'd change their mind |
| Communication | Monologue | Structured | Checks understanding, adapts |

Structured rubrics, calibrated across interviewers, reduce the variance that makes hiring feel random — and they're fairer to candidates.

docs.title: 6.4 Cost as an engineering concern
docs.text:
Lever Chapter Right-sized requests, fewer idle pods 30 Startup time and CDS/AOT enabling faster scale-down 29 Caching and query fixes before bigger databases 12, 21, 34 Log volume and retention tiers 07, 27 Metric cardinality 27 AI token budgets and model routing 40 Deleting unused services, topics and environments 35 A monthly cost review, one page
Top 5 cost drivers by service           (from cloud billing tags)
Change vs last month, with explanation   ("search +18%: reindex experiment, ends 15th")
Cost per order                           (the business-normalized number)
Top 3 opportunities with estimated saving and owner

Cost per order (or per active user) is the metric that makes cost discussable with the business: absolute spend rising during growth is fine; cost per order rising is a problem.

docs.title: 6.5 Leading a platform-wide change
docs.text:
Taking RFC-0014 (tenant RLS) from idea to done across 26 services:

Phase Leadership work Diagnose Collect the near-miss, the native-query count, the risk in business terms Propose RFC with cost, alternatives and a measured overhead Align One-to-one conversations with affected tech leads before the RFC review Make it easy Ship it in the tenancy starter (Chapter 41) with a migration guide Pilot Two services, publish results Scale Scorecard column; office hours; pairing on tricky services Enforce Leak suite required by CI for tier-1 services Close Retrospective; update standards; celebrate the teams

The pre-alignment step is the one most engineers skip. A formal review where stakeholders see the proposal for the first time invites defensive objections; the same review after individual conversations is usually a formality.

docs.title: 6.6 Writing as a leadership skill
docs.text:
Principle Example Lead with the conclusion "We should adopt RLS. Here's why." — not three pages of background first One idea per paragraph Reviewers can respond precisely Numbers over adjectives "p99 2.4 s → 380 ms" not "much faster" State trade-offs honestly Credibility comes from admitting costs Make the ask explicit "Decision needed by the 20th from X" Cut ruthlessly A one-page ADR gets read; a twelve-page one gets skimmed

Most senior engineering influence is exercised in writing — RFCs, ADRs, reviews, incident summaries, strategy docs. Improving writing is among the highest-return investments at B4 and B5.

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 — Leading the Upgrade
docs.text:
Chapter 42 covered the mechanics; leadership covers everything around them:

Concern Leadership action Why now? Frame in business terms: support window, CVE exposure, performance gains Who pays? Secure a quarterly allocation rather than a one-off project Who goes first? Platform team, then a volunteer pilot team with visible support What's the plan? Waves, freeze windows, scorecard — published and visible How do teams know what to do? Migration guide, office hours, a Slack channel, pairing How do we know it's working? Fleet dashboard, regression tracking When is it done? Old BOM retired, shims removed, retrospective held

A well-led upgrade programme feels boring to the teams doing it. That's the goal.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
1. Write decisions down — ADRs with alternatives, consequences and revisit triggers.
  2. Give RFCs a deadline and a decision-maker.
  3. Enforce standards with tools, not meetings.
  4. Manage debt as a portfolio: interest, principal, owner, trigger.
  5. Review with labels and praise; distinguish blocking from preference.
  6. Run incidents with roles; restore first; review blamelessly with tracked actions.
  7. Measure the system with DORA, never individuals.
  8. Grow engineers deliberately with evidence-based plans tied to the bands.
  9. Hire with structured rubrics and calibrated interviewers.
  10. Make the right thing easy — paved roads beat mandates.

docs.title: Anti-patterns
docs.text:
❌ Decisions made in meetings and never recorded.

❌ RFCs open for months.

❌ An architecture board that reviews everything.

❌ Standards nobody enforces.

❌ "Tech debt sprints" instead of continuous paydown.

❌ Blame in post-incident reviews.

❌ DORA metrics used to rank engineers.

❌ The senior engineer debugging during a SEV-1 while nobody coordinates.

❌ Mentoring by osmosis only.

❌ Unstructured interviews decided by gut feel.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Response Same incident class recurring Local fixes only Quarterly theme review → platform change Decisions relitigated repeatedly Not recorded ADRs with context and alternatives Teams bypass standards Standards are hard to follow Build the paved road (starter, template) Upgrades always slip No budget, no cadence Quarterly allocation; scorecard visibility Review is a bottleneck Few reviewers, no labels Spread review; label feedback; smaller PRs Senior engineers burn out Doing instead of multiplying Delegate, mentor, build tooling Metrics gamed Used for evaluation Use for learning; discuss trends, not targets Good people leave No growth path visible Growth plans tied to bands

docs.title: Leadership checklist
docs.text:
• Technical strategy written, current, and linked to business outcomes
  • ADR and RFC repositories with templates and deadlines
  • Standards enforced by platform libraries and CI
  • Debt register reviewed monthly with owners and triggers
  • Incident roles defined; blameless reviews with tracked actions
  • DORA metrics per service/team, discussed as trends
  • Service scorecards generated from the catalog
  • Growth plans for every engineer, reviewed regularly
  • Structured interview rubrics, calibrated
  • Monthly cost review with cost per order

docs.title: B1 · 0–2 years
docs.text:
B1 · What is an ADR and why write one?

Short answer: A short record of a decision, its context, the alternatives considered and the consequences. It prevents relitigating decisions and lets future engineers understand why, not just what.

B1 · How should you respond to critical review feedback?

Short answer: Assume good intent, ask questions where unclear, fix blocking issues, and discuss preferences openly. Review is about the code, not you.

B1 · What does "blameless" mean in a post-incident review?

Short answer: Focusing on the conditions that made the failure possible rather than on who made the mistake — so people report honestly and fixes address systems.

B1 · How do you grow from B1 to B2?

Short answer: Take ownership of features end to end — design notes, tests, deployment, monitoring and follow-up — and ask for feedback on the parts you haven't done before.

docs.title: B2 · 2–5 years
docs.text:
B2 · How do you give useful code review feedback?

Short answer: Prioritize correctness, security and failure handling; label comments as blocking, suggestion, question or nit; explain the reason; offer an alternative; and call out what's done well.

B2 · When should a decision get an RFC?

Short answer: When it's hard to reverse, affects multiple teams, introduces new technology, or has security or data implications. Reversible, team-local decisions don't need one.

B2 · What are the DORA metrics?

Short answer: Deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to restore service — measures of delivery performance for the system, not individuals.

B2 · How do you handle technical debt in a feature team?

Short answer: Record it with interest, principal, owner and trigger; pay down high-interest items continuously as part of normal work; and fix reckless debt (missing tests on critical paths) immediately rather than scheduling it.

B2 · How do you write a design document that gets useful feedback?

Short answer: Lead with the problem and the proposed decision in a few lines, state the alternatives and trade-offs honestly, list explicit open questions, name the reviewers and a deadline, and keep it short enough to be read in one sitting.

docs.title: B3 · 5–8 years
docs.text:
B3 · How do you lead a SEV-1 incident?

Short answer: Declare roles (IC, comms, ops), restore first — roll back or degrade — keep a timeline, give updates on a cadence, avoid parallel uncoordinated debugging, and schedule a blameless review with tracked actions afterwards.

B3 · How do you mentor an engineer effectively?

Short answer: Agree a target level and concrete capabilities, give stretch assignments with support, collect evidence, give specific feedback regularly, and create opportunities for visible work — not just answer questions when asked.

B3 · How do you get an RFC decided rather than debated?

Short answer: A short summary, honest costs and alternatives, data, explicit open questions, a named decision-maker, a deadline, and one-to-one conversations with key stakeholders before the formal review.

B3 · What makes a good post-incident action item?

Short answer: Specific, owned, dated, and aimed at detection, prevention or mitigation of the contributing factors — ideally changing a system (a test, an alert, a library default) rather than asking people to be more careful.

docs.title: B4 · 8–12 years
docs.text:
B4 · How do you set technical direction for several teams?

Short answer: Write a short strategy grounded in an honest diagnosis and business outcomes, make a few explicit bets and say what you won't do, align stakeholders individually, make the direction easy to follow through platform tooling, and measure progress visibly.

B4 · How do you govern architecture without becoming a bottleneck?

Short answer: Keep most decisions in teams; use RFCs only for cross-cutting or irreversible changes with deadlines; enforce standards through libraries and CI; allow recorded, time-boxed exceptions.

B4 · How do you use metrics without them being gamed?

Short answer: Measure systems, not individuals; discuss trends in retrospectives rather than setting targets; pair each metric with its counter-metric (deploy frequency with change failure rate); and use them to decide where to help.

B4 · How do you make a case for platform investment?

Short answer: Quantify the current cost — duplicated effort, incident themes, upgrade duration, security exposure — show the platform's expected reduction, propose a pilot with measurable results, and report back.

docs.title: B5 · 12–15+ years
docs.text:
B5 · What distinguishes a principal engineer's impact?

Short answer: Multiplying others: setting direction that many teams follow willingly, building leverage (platforms, standards, people), preventing expensive mistakes before they happen, and raising the organization's ability to change safely — impact measured across the organization over years, not in personal output.

B5 · How do you handle a strong disagreement with another senior leader?

Short answer: Understand their goals and constraints first, find shared outcomes, bring data, separate reversible from irreversible choices (and experiment on the reversible ones), escalate only with a clearly framed decision, and commit fully once it's made.

B5 · How do you know your engineering organization is healthy?

Short answer: Delivery metrics improving, incidents less frequent and shorter, upgrades routine, standards adopted willingly, engineers growing and staying, cost per unit of business value stable or falling, and people raising concerns early without fear.

docs.title: Scenario questions
docs.text:
Scenario · Every team has its own error format; the mobile team is frustrated

Diagnosis: no enforced standard, and building one per service was easier than finding a shared one. Response: write the ADR (Chapter 10's problem format), build it into the web starter (Chapter 41) so adopting it is one dependency, pilot with two teams, add a scorecard column and a contract test, then set a date for tier-1 services — making the standard the easy path rather than a mandate.

Scenario · The same kind of outage happened three times this year

Each post-incident review produced local fixes. Response: a theme review across the three, identifying the systemic factor (synchronous calls without timeouts), then a platform change — default timeouts in the client starter, a CI check for clients without them, and a resilience section in the review checklist — followed by verification in a game day.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Your first 90 days as staff engineer for the checkout domain

Plan the first 90 days: what you'll learn, what artifacts you'll produce, which relationships you'll build, and how you'll measure whether you're having impact.

Solution Days Focus Artifacts 1–30 Listen and learn Read ADRs, incidents from the last year, service scorecards; 1:1s with every tech lead and product manager; shadow on-call 31–60 Diagnose and propose A two-page diagnosis (checkout p99, synchronous depth, incident themes, upgrade status); one or two RFCs; the debt register for the domain 61–90 Deliver a visible win and set direction Ship one high-leverage improvement (e.g. saga state visibility, Chapter 36); a short domain strategy; growth plans with two engineers

Relationships: tech leads (trust), product (business priorities), SRE/on-call (pain points), security (risk), platform (leverage).

Measures of impact at day 90: - A decision that would otherwise have gone badly, improved or prevented (recorded in an ADR). - One measurable improvement (p99, change failure rate, incident count, upgrade progress). - Teams asking for your input on designs before, not after, building. - At least one engineer visibly growing with your support.

What to avoid: arriving with a rewrite proposal in week two, before understanding why the system is the way it is. The first month's job is to learn which problems are real — and to earn the credibility to fix them.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Senior leverage comes from decisions, standards, platforms and people, not personal output.
  • Write decisions down (ADRs), decide on deadlines (RFCs), and enforce with tools.
  • Debt is a portfolio managed by interest rate, with owners and triggers.
  • Incidents are led with roles, restored first, and reviewed blamelessly with systemic actions.
  • DORA metrics measure the system — use them to learn and to help, never to rank.
  • Grow engineers deliberately; the band tables in this handbook are a curriculum.
  • Make the right thing easy: paved roads beat mandates.
  • Writing is a core leadership skill — most influence happens in documents.

docs.title: 1. Introduction & Why It Matters
docs.text:
Forty-three chapters taught one concern at a time: configuration, transactions, Kafka, resilience, tenancy, security. Real systems don't arrive one concern at a time. A single tap on "Place order" in the grocery app touches authentication, validation, pricing, caching, a database transaction, an outbox, a saga, three services over HTTP and Kafka, a payment gateway, observability, and — on a bad evening — circuit breakers and degradation paths.

This capstone does two things:

  1. Assembles the platform. It walks one order from a customer's phone to a rider's doorstep and back to a seller's settlement, naming at every step which chapter's pattern is doing the work and why. If you understand this walkthrough, you understand how the handbook fits together.
  2. Gives you a project. A staged build of a scaled-down version of the platform — four services, then eight — with milestones and acceptance criteria for each band (B1–B5). Built honestly, it is the best preparation for senior interviews there is, because every design question has a concrete answer you've implemented and tested.

It closes with a production readiness review — the checklist a principal engineer walks through before a platform like this handles a Diwali sale — and a set of system-design interview questions answered from the architecture itself.

docs.text:
Scope: cart-service and pricing-service, HTTP interface between them, Redis cache, ETags.

Acceptance criterion Chapter Cart mutations require If-Match; stale versions get 412 08, 16 Pricing called through an HTTP interface with 600 ms timeout 19 Prices cached in Redis with tenant-free keys (tenancy comes in M6) and jittered TTL 21 Cache failures fail open; test with Redis stopped 21 Cart is an aggregate with invariants (max 50 lines, 1–20 per line), unit-tested without Spring 37 Query-count test on cart reads (no N+1) 13 @Idempotent on the add-to-cart endpoint 04

docs.title: M3 · Orders with outbox and Kafka
docs.text:
Scope: order-service writing orders + outbox; inventory-service consuming with an inbox.

The heart of M3
@Transactional
public Order place(PlaceOrderCommand command) {
    var lines = pricing.authoritativePrices(command.items(), command.pincode());   // outside? see criterion
    Order order = Order.place(OrderRef.next(), command.customerId(), command.pincode(), lines, fee);
    orders.save(order);
    outbox.append("order", order.ref().value(), "OrderPlaced", OrderPlacedEvent.from(order));
    return order;
}
Acceptance criterion Chapter Pricing is fetched before the transaction opens 16 Order and outbox row commit atomically; failure test leaves neither 36 Relay publishes with acks=all, keyed by order ref 23 Inventory consumer is idempotent (duplicate-delivery test) 23 Poison pill goes to DLT; DLT monitor increments a metric 23 Event payload golden file 23 Consumer lag and outbox-pending metrics exposed 27

docs.title: M4 · Checkout saga and payments
docs.text:
Scope: orchestrated saga in order-service; payment-service with a stubbed gateway (WireMock) and HMAC webhooks.

Acceptance criterion Chapter Saga state persisted with deadlines and guarded transitions 36 Payment failure compensates (releases stock, cancels order) 36 Duplicate and out-of-order events are ignored, with metrics 36 Timeout sweeper compensates; STUCK after repeated failures 36 Webhook verified over raw bytes, constant-time compare, deduped 18 No automatic retry on payment capture 19, 26 Chaos test: slow gateway → checkout returns 503 within 3 s 26, 28

Scope: identity-service (OTP + JWT), resource servers everywhere, SLOs and tracing.

docs.title: 6.4 Production readiness review
docs.text:
The checklist a principal engineer walks through before a sale. Each line links to the chapter that explains it.

Area Question ✓ Ownership Every service has an owner, on-call, SLOs and a runbook? (35, 43) Capacity Capacity model current for forecast × 1.5; DB connections and partitions within budget? (12, 23, 30, 34) Load Full-journey open-model load test passed; soak and spike run? (34) Resilience Every dependency has timeout, breaker, bulkhead and a documented degradation? (19, 26) Data Outbox everywhere; consumers idempotent; reconciliation running? (23, 36) Consistency Sagas have deadlines and STUCK alerts? (36) Security Access matrix and leak suite green; no PAN; PII encrypted; secrets rotated? (17, 38, 39) Observability Burn-rate alerts with runbooks; business metrics alerted; dashboards annotated? (27) Delivery Images signed and scanned; canary with SLO analysis; rollback digest recorded? (29, 30) Operations Pod-deletion and zone-drain game days passed; freeze window declared? (30) Scaling Pre-scaling scheduled; HPA limits within budgets? (30) Batch Settlement and reconciliation jobs have missed-run alerts? (33) AI features Flags tested off; token budgets and fallbacks verified? (40) Upgrades No service on an unsupported version; no pending critical CVEs? (39, 42) People Incident roles assigned for the sale window; comms plan ready? (43)

A "no" is not a failure — it's a decision to make explicitly: fix it, accept the risk in writing, or reduce scope (disable a feature for the sale).

docs.title: 7. Spring Boot 3 vs 4 — The Capstone Upgrade
docs.text:
Build the capstone on Boot 3.5 first, then upgrade it to Boot 4 as a final exercise using Chapter 42's programme:

Step Capstone task 1 Fix all deprecations on 3.5 2 Upgrade the platform starters and BOM (M8) first 3 Pilot on catalog-service with OpenRewrite + properties migrator 4 Verify golden files, access matrix, contract tests and performance 5 Upgrade cart and pricing; then order and payment with cross-version payload tests 6 Version cache namespaces for the rollout 7 Remove shims; record an ADR and a short retrospective

Appendix E consolidates the version differences across every chapter.

docs.title: 8. Production Playbook — What the Capstone Teaches
The ten ideas that recur in every chapter
docs.text:
1. Boundaries decide everything — services, modules, aggregates, tenants (35, 37, 38).
  2. Every wait has a timeout, and every timeout fits a budget (19, 26, 34).
  3. At-least-once plus idempotency is the only exactly-once (04, 23, 36).
  4. Never dual-write — the outbox (36).
  5. Display from projections, decide from the owner (35, 36).
  6. Degrade deliberately, never guess money or permissions (26, 40).
  7. Enforce with tools, not goodwill — ArchUnit, leak suites, contract gates, starters (28, 38, 41).
  8. Measure what users feel — SLOs, burn rates, business metrics (27).
  9. Ship small, reversibly — digests, canaries, expand/contract, cadence (14, 29, 30, 42).
  10. Write it down — ADRs, runbooks, post-incident reviews (43).

docs.title: Anti-patterns the capstone deliberately avoids
docs.text: ❌ A shared database between services. ❌ Publishing events without an outbox. ❌ Consumers that assume exactly-once delivery. ❌ Remote calls inside transactions. ❌ LLMs or clients deciding prices. ❌ Liveness probes checking dependencies. ❌ Unbounded queues, caches or result sets. ❌ Tenant filtering in application code only. ❌ Big-bang upgrades. ❌ Standards without enforcement.

docs.title: Capstone completion checklist
docs.text:
• M1–M2 complete with all acceptance criteria (B2 level)
  • M3–M5 complete; saga explained from memory (B3 level)
  • M6–M7 complete; game days run; load test passed (B4 level)
  • M8 complete; starters extracted; ADRs and a post-incident review written (B5 level)
  • Readiness review answered for your implementation
  • Boot 4 upgrade executed with the Chapter 42 process

docs.title: 9. Interview Questions & Answers — System Design from the Capstone
docs.text:
These questions are best answered by pointing at what you built.

B3 · Design checkout for an online grocery platform.

Short answer: Customer-facing request writes the order, saga state and outbox in one transaction and returns 201 PLACED; an orchestrated saga reserves stock and authorizes payment via events with deadlines, guarded transitions and compensations; consumers are idempotent; payment webhooks are HMAC-verified; the UI shows progress via polling or SSE; reconciliation catches drift. Pricing is authoritative and fetched before the transaction, with a cached-price degradation. (Chapters 16, 19, 23, 26, 36.)

B3 · How do you keep search in sync with the catalog?

Short answer: Catalog writes go through the outbox; an indexer consumes product and stock events, loads projections from the source of truth, bulk-indexes into an alias-backed index, tracks index lag, and supports zero-downtime reindex with guard rails; search degrades to category browse if the cluster fails. (Chapters 22, 23, 36.)

B4 · The platform must handle 5× traffic for Diwali. What's your plan?

Short answer: Forecast per service from production ratios; breakpoint tests per pod; a written capacity model for pods, connections, partitions and cache; full-journey open-model load tests at 1.5× forecast with profiling between runs; soak and spike tests; game days for dependency failures; pre-scaling; load shedding priorities; a deploy freeze; incident roles staffed. (Chapters 26, 30, 34, 43.)

B4 · How do you offer the platform to other grocery chains?

Short answer: Shared-schema multi-tenancy with the tenant from the token, @TenantId plus forced RLS, propagation through async and messaging, tenant-aware cache keys, a reflective leak suite in CI, per-tenant quotas, dedicated databases or cells for large tenants, and catalog-driven export and deletion. (Chapters 35, 38, 39.)

B4 · A seller's payout went to the wrong account. Walk through response and prevention.

Short answer: Freeze payouts, contain via re-authentication and revoked sessions, investigate with the audit log, notify per contract and regulation; prevent with re-authentication and OTP to the registered contact for bank changes, a 24-hour payout hold, notifications to old and new contacts, field-level encryption, and anomaly detection. (Chapters 33, 39, 43.)

B5 · You inherit a platform where every release needs four services deployed in order. What do you do?

Short answer: Diagnose the coupling (shared database, shared domain library, unversioned APIs, synchronous chains); write a short strategy; split schemas with grants; replace the shared model with platform starters plus per-client DTOs; version APIs additively with consumer-driven contracts and a deploy gate; move non-critical work to events; measure progress with DORA and a scorecard; lead it through RFCs, pilots and paved roads rather than mandates. (Chapters 20, 28, 35, 41, 43.)

B5 · Where would you — and wouldn't you — use AI in this platform?

Short answer: Use it to explain, summarize, draft and route: a support assistant with read-only, session-scoped tools and human handoff; catalog enrichment with validation and human review; review summaries cached by content version. Don't use it to decide prices, refunds, permissions, stock or fraud outcomes, or anywhere in the checkout critical path. (Chapter 40.)

docs.title: The final exercise
docs.text:
Exercise · Present your capstone

Prepare a 20-minute architecture presentation of your capstone for a panel: the business problem, the service map and ownership, three key decisions with their ADRs, the checkout flow including its failure modes, one game-day result and what you changed afterwards, your SLOs and how you'd know they were at risk, and what you'd do next with another quarter.

What a strong presentation includes
  • Starts with the business, not the technology: customers, sellers, the sale-day peak, the cost of a failed checkout.
  • One diagram per idea: service map, checkout sequence, saga states, degradation paths.
  • Decisions with trade-offs: "we chose polling over CDC because…, and we'll revisit when…".
  • Evidence: load-test numbers, a trace screenshot, the leak suite, the game-day timeline.
  • Honesty about gaps: "reconciliation is hourly; for payouts I'd make it continuous next".
  • A clear next step tied to risk or value, not to novelty.

The panel is evaluating judgement more than implementation. A candidate who can say why each piece exists, what fails when it's missing and how they'd know is demonstrating exactly what the B4/B5 bands describe.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A single "Place order" tap exercises nearly every chapter of this handbook — and each concern is solved once, in one place, with a test.
  • The platform bends predictably under failure: timeouts, breakers, degradation, outbox, sagas and reconciliation mean nothing is lost and nothing is guessed.
  • The capstone milestones map directly to the bands: M1–M2 (B2), M3–M5 (B3), M6–M7 (B4), M8 (B5).
  • The readiness review is the principal engineer's pre-sale checklist; a "no" is a decision to make explicitly.
  • The ten recurring ideas — boundaries, timeouts, idempotency, outbox, projections, deliberate degradation, enforcement, user-facing measurement, reversible delivery and written decisions — are the handbook in one list.
